units.name: Unit 6: Inventors and Inventions (opinion writing)
units.el: Show real objects or photos (wiper, bicycle, clothespin) while reading, and practice irregular past tense with a "today I ___ / yesterday I ___" chant.

passages.x: Lucia's grandmother, Abuela Rosa, loved to garden, but bending down hurt her back. One afternoon, Lucia watched her try to pick up a fallen lemon. Abuela groaned and gave up. // "I'll invent something to help you," Lucia announced. // First, Lucia drew a plan in her notebook. She wanted a long tool that could grab things from the ground. She taped two rulers together with a clothespin at the end. When she squeezed the top, the clothespin was supposed to close. But nothing happened. The rulers just wobbled. // Lucia frowned. She tried again with two paint stirrers and a piece of string. This time, the clothespin snapped shut! But it was too weak to hold a lemon. The lemon dropped and rolled under a bush. // "Maybe inventing is too hard," Lucia sighed. // Abuela Rosa patted her shoulder. "Every mistake teaches you something," she said. // Lucia thought about it. The clothespin was too small. What could hold something round? She found two plastic spoons and taped them to the ends of the stirrers, facing each other. She pulled the string, and the spoons cupped the lemon perfectly. // Abuela laughed and clapped. "Now I can garden all day!" // Lucia named her invention the Lemon Lifter. Then she turned to a new page in her notebook. Next time, she would invent something even bigger.

passages.t: Mary Anderson and the Windshield Wiper
passages.x: In the winter of 1902, Mary Anderson rode a streetcar through New York City. Snow and sleet kept piling up on the front window. The driver could hardly see. Again and again, he had to open the window or stop and wipe off the glass by hand. Cold air blew in on the passengers. // An Idea Takes Shape // Mary Anderson thought there must be a better way. She went home to Alabama and sketched an idea. Her design had a handle inside the vehicle. When the driver turned the handle, a swinging arm with a rubber blade wiped across the outside of the window. The driver could clear the glass without stopping. // A Patent // In 1903, Mary Anderson received a patent for her invention. A patent is a paper from the government that says an invention belongs to the inventor. At first, companies were not interested. Some people even worried that the moving blade would distract drivers. // An Idea That Lasted // Years later, as more people drove cars, wipers became common. Today, almost every car, bus and truck has windshield wipers. Mary Anderson saw a problem, and her idea still helps drivers stay safe.

Mr. Okoye's class was learning about inventions. On Friday, each student would vote for the invention they thought was the most important. // "The wheel," said Jada. "Without wheels, we wouldn't have cars, bikes or skateboards." // "No way," said Felipe. "The light bulb is the best. Without it, we would be reading in the dark!" // The two friends argued all through recess. Jada made a list of everything with wheels. Felipe made a list of everything that lights up. Both lists grew longer and longer. // On Thursday, Jada noticed something. Felipe's list had flashlights, lamps and traffic lights. "Traffic lights help cars stop and go," she said slowly. "And cars need my wheels." // Felipe looked at her list. "Bike lights help people ride at night," he said. "So your wheels need my light bulbs, too." // They grinned at each other. When Mr. Okoye asked for votes on Friday, Jada and Felipe raised their hands together. // "We have an idea," Jada said. "Inventions work best when they work together. We vote for both!" // Mr. Okoye laughed. "That," he said, "is the most important idea I've heard all week."

The bicycle you ride today took many years and many inventors to create. // No Pedals // More than 200 years ago, in 1817, a German inventor named Karl Drais built a wooden "running machine." It had two wheels and a seat, but no pedals. Riders pushed their feet against the ground to roll along. // Pedals and a Giant Wheel // In the 1860s, inventors in France added pedals to the front wheel. Later, some bicycles were built with a huge front wheel and a tiny back wheel. A bigger wheel could go farther with each push of the pedals, so these bikes were fast. But riders sat very high up, and falling off was dangerous. // The Safety Bicycle // In the 1880s, a new design called the safety bicycle was built. Its two wheels were the same size, and a chain connected the pedals to the back wheel. Riders sat lower, so it was much easier to get on and off. Soon after, air-filled rubber tires made rides less bumpy. // Today's bikes look a lot like the safety bicycle. Each new idea made riding safer, faster or more comfortable.

passages.t: How the Canyon Got Its Stripes
passages.x: Long ago, when the world was new, the land was flat and plain. There were no hills, no valleys and no colors in the rock. River was young then, and she loved to sing as she ran. // One day, River grew curious. "What is under the flat ground?" she wondered. She began to dig, just a little each day, with her cool, rushing water. // Wind laughed at her. "You will never get anywhere," Wind howled. "You move one grain of sand at a time!" // River did not stop. Day after day, year after year, she carried away sand and pebbles. Slowly, the ground on each side of her grew taller. The walls of a canyon rose up around her. // Deep in the walls, River found treasures. There was a stripe of red rock, a stripe of orange and a stripe of tan, stacked like the layers of a cake. Each stripe was a story from long ago. // Wind stopped laughing. He swirled down into the canyon and whistled at the colors. "How did you do all this?" he asked. // "One grain at a time," River sang. // That is why, people say, canyons have stripes, and why rivers never stop moving.

Earth's surface may look like it stays the same, but it is always changing. Some changes happen so slowly that people do not notice them. Other changes happen in just a few minutes. // Slow Changes // Erosion is when water, wind or ice carries away bits of rock and soil. Rivers carry sand and pebbles downstream. Ocean waves wear away cliffs along the coast. Over millions of years, the Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon, which is more than one mile deep. Wind can blow sand against rocks and slowly shape them into arches and towers. // Fast Changes // Some changes happen very quickly. During an earthquake, the ground shakes and can crack or shift in seconds. California has many earthquakes because it sits where huge moving pieces of Earth's crust meet. A volcano can erupt and pour out hot, melted rock called lava. When lava cools, it hardens into new rock. Heavy rain can cause a landslide, when soil and rocks suddenly slide down a hill. // People Can Help // People cannot stop earthquakes, but they can slow erosion. Planting grass and trees on hillsides helps, because roots hold soil in place.

Nico was drawing a volcano when the alarm beeped three times. "Earthquake drill!" said Ms. Tanaka. "Remember what we practiced." // Nico's stomach flipped. Last spring, a real earthquake had rattled his family's apartment. The dishes had clattered in the cupboard, and his little sister had cried. He did not like thinking about it. // But his body remembered what to do. First, he dropped to his hands and knees. Next, he crawled under his desk and covered his head and neck with one arm. Then he held on to a desk leg with his other hand. // Beside him, Zara was under her desk, too. Her eyes were squeezed shut. "I don't like this," she whispered. // Nico remembered how scared he had felt last spring. "It's just practice," he whispered back. "And now we know exactly what to do. That makes it less scary." // Zara opened her eyes and nodded. She held her desk leg tightly. // When the drill was over, Ms. Tanaka smiled. "Everyone did a great job," she said. // Back at his desk, Nico picked up his crayon. He added a small boy to his drawing, standing safely at the bottom of the volcano. He felt a little braver than before.

Most people think of beaches and deserts when they think of California. But the state also has volcanoes! One of them is Lassen Peak, in the northern part of the state. // A Volcano Wakes Up // Lassen Peak was quiet for a very long time. Then, in 1914, it began to rumble. Steam and ash puffed out of the top. In May 1915, the volcano erupted with a huge blast. A cloud of ash rose miles into the sky. Hot rock melted snow on the mountain, and rivers of mud rushed down its sides. The mud knocked down trees and carried away giant boulders. // The Land Today // Lassen Peak has been quiet since 1917, but the land around it is still changing. Today, it is part of Lassen Volcanic National Park. Visitors can see bubbling pools of mud, steaming vents and hot springs. These are signs that the ground below is still very hot. // Watching Volcanoes // Scientists keep watch on Lassen Peak and other volcanoes. They use tools to measure small earthquakes and changes in the ground. These clues can warn people if a volcano might wake up again.

lessons.name: Tales that explain nature

gives true facts about science and nature
tells about the author's own real life

A volcano is one of the fastest ways that Earth's surface can change.

units.name: Unit 8: Citizens Who Make a Difference (opinion writing)
units.el: Act out shades of meaning on a word line (whisper, talk, shout; nibble, eat, gobble) and give the frame "I think ___ because ___. Another reason is ___."

passages.x: Every morning, Benji and his little brother Omar crossed Cedar Street to get to school. Cars zoomed by so fast that Omar squeezed Benji's hand. There was no crosswalk and no crossing guard. // "Somebody should fix this," Benji told his mom. // "Maybe that somebody is you," she said. // Benji wasn't sure. He was only eight. But he got a notebook and started to watch. For one week, he counted the cars that passed while he waited. On Monday, he counted 41. On Friday, he counted 52. He drew a map of the corner and marked where kids crossed. // Then Benji wrote a letter to the city council. "Dear City Council," he wrote. "Many kids cross Cedar Street to get to Lincoln School. The cars go very fast. Please paint a crosswalk and put up a sign so we can be safe." He added his map and his car counts. // A month later, a woman from the city called. She invited Benji to speak at a meeting. His knees shook as he stood at the microphone, but he read his letter in a loud, clear voice. // In the spring, workers painted bright white stripes across Cedar Street. A yellow sign showed two children walking. // The first morning, Omar let go of Benji's hand and walked across by himself. "You did it," Omar said. // Benji smiled. "We did it," he said. "I just asked."

passages.t: Dolores Huerta: A Voice for Farm Workers
passages.x: Dolores Huerta was born in 1930 in New Mexico. When she was a young girl, her family moved to Stockton, California. Her mother ran a small hotel and often let farm worker families stay for little or no money. Dolores learned from her mother that helping others matters. // A Teacher Sees a Problem // When Dolores grew up, she became a teacher. Many of her students were children of farm workers. Some came to school hungry and without shoes. Their parents worked long hours in the fields but earned very little money. Dolores decided she could help more by working to change those unfair conditions. // Working Together // In 1962, Dolores Huerta and Cesar Chavez started a group to help farm workers. The group worked for better pay and safer conditions in the fields. Dolores spoke at meetings, talked with lawmakers and helped lead a boycott of grapes. During a boycott, people stop buying something until a problem is fixed. Many people across the country joined in. // A Life of Helping // Dolores Huerta has spent her life working for fairness. In 2012, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, one of the highest honors in the United States.

passages.t: What Should We Do with the Money?
passages.x: Room 12 had earned forty dollars at their lemonade stand. Now they had to decide how to spend it. // Ms. Nguyen wrote two ideas on the board. Idea one: buy new balls for recess. Idea two: buy food and blankets for the animal shelter on Elm Road. // Hands shot up all over the room. "We need new balls!" said Carlos. "Our old soccer ball is flat, and the jump ropes are broken." // Mina shook her head. "The shelter is full of dogs and cats," she said. "My cousin volunteers there. She says they need blankets for winter." // The class argued until the room got loud. Ms. Nguyen held up her hand. "In a community, people don't always agree," she said. "So we listen, we share our reasons and then we vote. Everyone's vote counts the same." // Each student wrote an idea on a slip of paper and dropped it into a box. Carlos and Mina counted the votes together. Twelve votes were for the shelter. Ten votes were for recess balls. // Carlos frowned for a moment. Then he had an idea. "What if we have another lemonade stand next month to buy the balls?" he asked. // Everyone cheered. In December, Room 12 delivered a box of blankets to the shelter. In January, they had a brand-new soccer ball.

A citizen is a member of a community, such as a town, a state or a country. Your classroom and your school are communities, too. Good citizens help make their communities safe, fair and pleasant places to live. // Following Rules and Laws // Communities have rules and laws to keep people safe. Stopping at a red light, wearing a helmet on a bike and taking turns on the slide are all ways of following rules. // Taking Part // Good citizens take part in their communities. Adults can vote to choose leaders and decide on laws. Kids can vote in class, join a club or share ideas at a school meeting. When people take part, their voices are heard. // Helping Others // Good citizens help when they see a need. They might pick up litter, collect food for a food bank or read with a younger student. Even small acts of kindness make a community stronger. // Respecting Others // Good citizens treat others with respect, even when they disagree. They listen, take turns speaking and remember that everyone deserves to be treated fairly. // You do not have to be a grown-up to be a good citizen. You can start today!

passages.x: High on a mountain, a snowman named Pip stood beside a ski trail. Every day, skiers zoomed past and talked about summer. "I can't wait for summer," one girl said. "We'll swim in the lake!" // Pip had never seen summer. He imagined it was the best thing in the world. "I want to go there," he told a crow sitting on his carrot nose. // The crow tilted her head. "Summer is warm," she warned. "You are made of snow." // But Pip did not listen. When a truck stopped to drop off supplies, he hopped into the back. Down the mountain they bumped, past pine trees and into the valley, where green grass was poking through the snow. // The sun felt wonderful on Pip's face. Then he felt something drip. His stick arms began to droop. His coal buttons slid down his belly. "Oh no," Pip cried. "I'm melting!" // Just then, the crow landed beside him. She pointed her beak at a sign that said "Ice Rink." Inside, the air was cold, and children skated in circles. Pip slid inside and sighed with relief. His snow grew firm again. // Now Pip lives in the corner of the ice rink. He can't swim in a summer lake, but he hears children laugh every single day. And that, he decides, is good enough.

passages.t: How to Make Fruit Ice Pops
passages.x: On a hot day, nothing tastes better than an ice pop. You can make your own and watch a liquid turn into a solid! // What You Need // 2 cups of fruit juice, a measuring cup, 6 small paper cups, 6 craft sticks, plastic wrap and a freezer // What to Do // 1. Wash your hands. // 2. Use the measuring cup to pour juice into each paper cup. Fill each cup only about three-fourths full, because water expands, or takes up more space, when it freezes. // 3. Cover each cup with plastic wrap. Poke a craft stick through the middle of the wrap. The wrap will hold the stick straight. // 4. Ask a grown-up to help you set the cups in the freezer. // 5. Wait about four to six hours, or overnight. // 6. Peel off the paper cup and enjoy! // What Happened? // Juice is a liquid. It flows and takes the shape of its container. In the cold freezer, the juice lost heat and froze into a solid. A solid keeps its own shape. If you leave your ice pop in the sun, it will melt and turn back into a liquid. // Tip: For a striped pop, freeze one color of juice for an hour, then add a second color on top.

After the rainstorm, a big puddle sat in the middle of the playground. "It looks like a lake," said Kiri. // "It will be gone by tomorrow," said her friend Theo. // Kiri didn't believe him. "Where would it go?" she asked. // Theo pulled a piece of chalk from his pocket. He drew a line all the way around the edge of the puddle. "Let's find out," he said. // At lunch, Kiri raced outside. The puddle was still there, but it had shrunk. There was a gap of dry blacktop between the water and the chalk line. Theo drew a second line around the smaller puddle. // At the end of the day, the sun was shining brightly. The puddle had shrunk again. Now it was only as big as a pizza. Theo drew a third line. // The next morning, Kiri and Theo ran to the spot. The puddle was gone! Only three chalk circles remained, one inside the other, like the rings of a tree. // "Somebody stole our puddle," Kiri joked. // Their teacher, Mr. Abara, laughed. "The sun did it," he said. "The heat turned the water into a gas called water vapor, and it floated into the air. That's called evaporation." // Kiri looked up at the sky. "So our puddle is up there somewhere?" // "Maybe it will come back as rain," said Theo.

Everything around you is made of matter. Matter is anything that takes up space and has weight. Your desk, the milk in your lunch and the air you breathe are all matter. Matter can be a solid, a liquid or a gas. // Solids // A solid keeps its own shape. A rock, a pencil and an ice cube are solids. If you put a block in a bowl, it stays a block. // Liquids // A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container. Water, juice and honey are liquids. If you pour milk from a carton into a glass, the milk takes the shape of the glass. // Gases // A gas spreads out to fill all the space it is in. Most gases are invisible, which means you cannot see them. The air around you is a mix of gases. When you blow up a balloon, the air spreads out to fill it. // Changing States // Heating and cooling can change matter from one state to another. When ice is heated, it melts into liquid water. When water is heated, it can evaporate into a gas called water vapor. When water vapor cools, it can turn back into tiny drops of liquid. That is how clouds form! // Water is special because you can easily find it as a solid, a liquid and a gas.

passages.x: Version 1: A Village Long Ago // Long ago, a tired traveler came to a village in a hard winter. Every family had a little food, but each one kept it hidden. The traveler filled a big iron pot with water and dropped in a smooth river stone. "I am making stone soup," she said loudly. "Of course, it would taste even better with one carrot." A boy ran home and brought a carrot. Then a farmer brought beans, a woman brought an onion and an old man brought salt. That night, the whole village shared a delicious soup. "Imagine," they said, "soup from a stone!" // Version 2: An Apartment Today // Mei's family had just moved into a big apartment building in the city. Mei did not know anyone. One Saturday, she set a pot of water on a camp stove in the courtyard and dropped in a smooth stone from her old home. "What are you making?" asked a boy from the third floor. "Stone soup," said Mei. "It would be even better with some noodles." The boy brought noodles. Soon, Mrs. Ortiz brought corn, Mr. Ahmed brought tomatoes and the twins brought green onions. Everyone sat on the steps and ate together. By the end of the day, Mei knew everyone's name.

About 150 years ago, many children in the United States went to a one-room schoolhouse. Students of all ages, from about six to fourteen, learned together in a single room with one teacher. // A Day at School // Most children walked to school, sometimes for miles. In winter, an older student might arrive early to start a fire in the wood stove that heated the room. Students sat on long benches or at wooden desks. The teacher called up one grade at a time to read or recite lessons, while the others worked quietly. Older students often helped younger ones. // Tools for Learning // Paper cost a lot, so children wrote on small slates, which are flat pieces of dark stone. They wrote with a slate pencil and wiped the slate clean to use it again. Many students shared books, and some learned their lessons by repeating them out loud. // Then and Now // Today, most schools have many classrooms, and students are grouped by grade. Instead of slates, students use paper, whiteboards and computers. But some things have not changed. Children still learn to read, write and do math, and they still play games at recess.

Every Sunday, Mina visited her grandpa. On his shelf sat a big glass jar full of folded slips of paper. "Pick one," Grandpa always said. Each slip had a word on it, and each word was the start of a story. // This Sunday, Mina pulled out a slip that said "milk." // Grandpa laughed. "When I was your age, we lived on a farm in Korea," he said. "Every morning before school, I had to milk our goat. She was a stubborn goat named Pepper. One morning she kicked over the whole bucket! I walked to school with milk all over my shoes." // Mina giggled. "Did you get in trouble?" // "My teacher just handed me a rag," Grandpa said. "Then she made me write a poem about goats." // Mina thought about her own mornings. She poured milk from a carton in the fridge. She rode to school in Mom's car. "Things were so different," she said. // "Some things," Grandpa said. "But I still had a best friend, homework and a teacher who made me laugh. Just like you." // Before she left, Grandpa handed Mina an empty jar. "Now you start one," he said. "Someday, your grandchildren will want to hear your stories, too." // That night, Mina wrote her first slip of paper. It said "car."

Long before video games, children found plenty of ways to have fun. Many of the games they played are still played today. // Hoop Rolling // In the 1800s, children in many places rolled wooden or metal hoops down the street. They used a stick to push the hoop and keep it rolling. Children raced to see whose hoop could go the farthest without falling over. // Marbles // Marbles are small balls made of clay, stone or glass. Players drew a circle in the dirt and took turns flicking their marbles to knock other marbles out of the ring. // Jacks // To play jacks, a child tossed a small ball into the air, picked up small metal pieces called jacks and caught the ball after one bounce. Each round, the player had to pick up more jacks at once. // Hopscotch // Hopscotch has been played for hundreds of years. Children drew squares on the ground, tossed a small stone onto a square and hopped through the squares without stepping on any lines. // Many of these games needed only simple things, such as a stick, a stone or a piece of chalk. Ask a grown-up in your family what games they played as a child!

ela|3.about: Third grade marks the shift from learning to read to reading to learn. Students decode multisyllable words with prefixes and suffixes, recount stories and explain how key details convey the central message, describe characters and how their actions shape events, find main ideas and connections in informational texts, and write opinion, informative and narrative pieces in paragraphs. Ten knowledge units (about three weeks each) pair a science or social studies topic with a reading focus and a writing focus, plus grammar, conventions and vocabulary.
std: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills, including common prefixes and suffixes, Latin suffixes and multisyllable words.
Recount stories, including fables, folktales and myths from diverse cultures; determine the central message, lesson or moral and explain how it is conveyed through key details.
Describe characters in a story (their traits, motivations or feelings) and explain how their actions contribute to the sequence of events.
Determine the main idea of a text; recount the key details and explain how they support the main idea.
Describe the relationship between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or steps, using language about time, sequence and cause and effect.
Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons, linking words and a concluding statement.
Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly, with facts, definitions and details.
Demonstrate command of grade 3 grammar and usage, including abstract nouns, verb tenses, subject-verb agreement, comparatives and superlatives, conjunctions and compound and complex sentences.

units.name: Unit 1: Community Connections (personal narrative)
units.el: Pre-teach community words (volunteer, neighborhood, library card, donate) with photos, and give the frame "At first ___ felt ___, but after ___, she/he ___."

passages.x: When Marisol's family moved to Fresno, she did not know a single street. Everything felt too big and too loud. For the first week, she stayed inside and read the same comic books over and over. // On Saturday, her grandmother handed her a list. "I need tortillas from Garcia's Market," Abuela said. "It is only three blocks away." // Marisol's stomach tightened. "What if I get lost?" // "Then you will find your way back," Abuela said, and she gave Marisol a pencil and a notebook. "Draw what you see. A map remembers for you." // Marisol walked slowly, stopping at every corner. She drew the mailbox painted like a sunflower, the laundromat with the purring cat in the window and the mural of a farmer holding peaches. At the market, Mr. Garcia noticed her notebook. "Are you an artist?" he asked. Marisol shrugged, but she showed him the drawings. He laughed when he saw the cat. "That is Chispa. She lives here, too." // Every weekend after that, Marisol added something new: the library with the blue doors, the park with the creaky swings, the bakery that smelled like cinnamon. Her map grew until it covered four pages. // In October, a new boy joined her class. He sat alone at lunch, staring at his tray. Marisol recognized that look. She carefully tore the map out of her notebook and set it beside him. // "This is our neighborhood," she said. "I can show you the cat."

A public library is one of the busiest places in many communities, and it is free for everyone. With a library card, a person can borrow books, movies and music at no cost. But libraries offer much more than things to borrow. // A Place to Learn // Many libraries hold free classes for people of all ages. Children can join story times and summer reading programs. Teens can get homework help. Adults can learn how to use computers or practice speaking a new language. // A Place to Connect // Not every family has a computer or internet at home. Libraries give people a place to use computers to look for jobs, do schoolwork or video chat with relatives far away. Librarians are trained to help people find information, too. If you have a question, a librarian can show you how to search for the answer. // Surprising Things to Borrow // Some libraries lend items you might not expect. Depending on the library, people may be able to check out board games, musical instruments, garden seeds or even cake pans! These collections help people try new things without having to buy them. // A Community Space // Libraries also have meeting rooms, quiet study areas and spaces for art shows. Because everyone is welcome, the library is a place where neighbors of all backgrounds can meet. // The next time you visit, look around. Your library might surprise you.

I had never been to a food bank before. When my aunt Fatima asked me to volunteer with her on Saturday, I almost said no. I wanted to sleep late and watch cartoons. But Aunt Fatima said, "Hamza, you might be surprised," so I went. // The food bank was in a huge warehouse that smelled like cardboard. Rows of shelves stretched almost to the ceiling. A woman named Ms. Pham gave me a green apron and a job: sorting cans. Beans went in one box, soup in another and vegetables in a third. At first, I thought it was the most boring job in the world. // Then Ms. Pham told me something. "Every box you pack will feed a family this week." Suddenly the cans felt different. I started racing myself to see how fast I could sort them. I checked every date to make sure nothing was too old. By lunchtime, I had filled eleven boxes. // In the afternoon, families came to pick up food. A little girl about my sister's age peeked into one of my boxes and cheered, "Peaches!" Her mom smiled at me and said thank you. My face got warm, and I could not stop grinning. // On the drive home, I was tired, but it was a good kind of tired. "So?" Aunt Fatima asked. "Were you surprised?" // I looked out the window and nodded. "Can we go back next month?"

On many weekend mornings, parking lots and town squares across California fill with tents and tables. Farmers arrive before sunrise with trucks full of strawberries, lettuce, oranges and almonds. This is a farmers market, a place where farmers sell food directly to the people who will eat it. // Fresh from the Farm // At a grocery store, fruits and vegetables may travel a long way before they reach the shelf. At a farmers market, much of the food was picked just a day or two earlier, often on farms nearby. Because it is picked when it is ripe, it is often very fresh. // Helping Local Farmers // When farmers sell at a market, they keep more of the money they earn instead of sharing it with stores and trucking companies. This helps small family farms stay in business. Shoppers can also ask farmers questions, such as how a crop was grown or how to cook a vegetable they have never tried. // Bringing People Together // Farmers markets are also community events. Many have musicians, cooking demonstrations and activities for children. Neighbors run into each other and stop to talk. Some markets accept CalFresh benefits, which help families buy healthy food. // California grows more fruits and vegetables than any other state, so it is no surprise that the state has hundreds of farmers markets. Visiting one is a delicious way to learn where your food comes from.

test.ans: Last spring, my class cleaned up the park near our school. At first, I did not want to go, because it was hot and I thought picking up trash would be gross. units.name: Unit 2: Animal Life Cycles (informative writing)
units.el: Use a cycle diagram with pictures and labels (egg, larva, pupa, adult; egg, tadpole, froglet, frog) and a verb-tense chart with yesterday, today and tomorrow columns.

passages.x: Under a milkweed leaf, a small striped caterpillar named Zia munched and munched. Above her, monarch butterflies drifted through the warm air like orange paper. // "I want to fly now," Zia said to her neighbor, an old toad. // The toad blinked. "You are not ready. You are only a caterpillar." // Zia frowned. She climbed to the tip of the tallest leaf, closed her eyes and leaped. She did not fly. She tumbled into the grass and landed on her back, her little legs waving. // A grasshopper laughed. "Caterpillars can't fly!" // Zia felt her face grow hot. She crawled back up the stem, slowly, one leg at a time. "Then what can I do?" she asked the toad. // "Eat," said the toad. "Grow. Rest when it is time. Every part of your life is getting you ready for the next part." // So Zia ate. She grew so big that she split her skin and wriggled out of it again and again. One day she felt very still and sleepy. She hung upside down from a stem and wrapped herself in a green case that shone with tiny gold dots. Inside, for many days, she changed. // At last the case cracked open. Zia pulled herself out and waited while her damp, crumpled wings dried and spread. Then she rose, wobbling at first, into the sky. // From below, the old toad croaked, "Now you are ready." // Zia circled once over the milkweed. She had learned that the waiting was part of the flying.

A sea turtle's life begins on a sandy beach, but most of it is spent in the ocean. // Laying Eggs // On a warm summer night, a female sea turtle crawls out of the waves. She drags her heavy body up the beach and digs a deep hole with her back flippers. She lays about one hundred eggs, each about the size of a ping-pong ball. Then she covers the nest with sand and returns to the sea. She does not stay to care for her young. // Hatching // For about two months, the eggs stay buried in the warm sand. The temperature of the sand affects the babies. Warmer nests produce more females, and cooler nests produce more males. When the hatchlings are ready, they break out of their shells and dig their way up, usually at night. // The Race to the Sea // Hatchlings crawl toward the brightest light they can see. On a natural beach, that is the moon and stars shining over the water. As a result, bright lights from buildings and streets can confuse them and lead them the wrong way. Crabs and birds hunt the tiny turtles, so only a small number survive. // Growing Up // The young turtles that reach the ocean swim for many years. It can take twenty years or more for a sea turtle to become an adult. Then many females return to the same beach where they hatched to lay eggs of their own, and the cycle begins again.

In early spring, the pond is still, // the water cold and clear, // but under every lily pad // a jelly cloud is here. // A thousand tiny dark-dot eggs // are floating, soft and round. // They wait beneath the morning sun // without a single sound. // Then wiggle, wiggle, out they come, // small tadpoles, black as ink, // with tails that swish like little fans. // They dart and dive and blink. // They nibble on the soft green slime // that grows on every stone. // They hide beneath the reeds and roots // and never swim alone. // As summer warms the shallow pond, // two back legs start to grow. // Then two front legs come poking out, // and tails shrink, slow, slow, slow. // Their lungs grow strong for breathing air. // They paddle to the top. // One morning, from a mossy log, // I hear a little plop. // A froglet sits upon the log // and gulps the summer breeze. // It sings a small and croaky song // beneath the willow trees. // Someday, beneath the lily pads, // new eggs will float in rows, // and that is how the pond begins // the circle as it goes.

Many baby animals look almost the same as adults. A baby elephant looks like a small grown-up elephant. But some insects change so much as they grow that they look like completely different animals. This big change is called metamorphosis. // Complete Metamorphosis // Butterflies, beetles, bees and ladybugs go through four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult. A butterfly larva is called a caterpillar. Its main job is to eat and grow. When it is big enough, it forms a pupa. A butterfly's pupa is called a chrysalis. Inside, the caterpillar's body breaks down and rebuilds itself into a butterfly with wings. // Incomplete Metamorphosis // Grasshoppers, crickets and dragonflies change in a different way. They go through only three stages: egg, nymph and adult. A nymph looks like a small adult without full-size wings. As it grows, it molts, or sheds its hard outer skin, several times. After its last molt, it has full wings and is an adult. There is no pupa stage. // Why Change? // Metamorphosis can help young and adult insects survive. In many kinds of insects, the young and the adults eat different foods or live in different places, so they do not compete with each other. A caterpillar munches leaves, while an adult butterfly sips nectar from flowers. // Whether they change completely or only partly, these insects show how amazing growing up can be.

test.q: Write an informative paragraph that explains how complete and incomplete metamorphosis are alike and different. Introduce the topic, use facts and examples from "Two Ways to Change," use linking words such as also, however and both, and end with a concluding sentence.
test.ans: Some insects go through big changes called metamorphosis, but not all of them change in the same way. In complete metamorphosis, insects such as butterflies, bees and ladybugs have four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult. These two ways of changing help insects grow and survive.

units.name: Unit 3: Weather and Climate (informative writing)
units.el: Pair each weather word with a picture and a gesture (evaporate: hands rising; condense: hands coming together) and give the frame "Weather is ___, but climate is ___."

passages.x: I think rain is the worst weather there is. It cancels soccer games. It makes my socks soggy. It turns our backyard into a mud pit, and our dog, Biscuit, tracks paw prints all over the kitchen. // So when the weather report said a storm was coming to our town in the Central Valley, I groaned. But Grandma Nell clapped her hands. "Finally!" she said. // Grandma grows almonds and tomatoes on the land behind our house. For two years, there had hardly been any rain. The ground cracked like an old plate. Grandma had to pay for extra water to keep her trees alive, and she worried every day. // That night, rain drummed on the roof. I lay in bed feeling grumpy about Saturday's game. Then I heard a strange sound outside: laughing. I looked out the window. Grandma was standing in the yard in her raincoat, arms spread wide, spinning in slow circles. // In the morning, the game was canceled, just as I expected. I stomped into the kitchen. Grandma was humming as she made pancakes. "The reservoir is filling," she said. "The trees will drink for weeks." // I still don't like soggy socks. I still think rain is the worst weather for soccer. But when I looked out at the dark, wet soil around Grandma's trees, I had to admit something. Maybe rain is not the worst weather for everyone.

Look outside right now. Is it sunny, rainy, windy or foggy? That is the weather. Weather is what the air is like at a certain place and time. It can change from hour to hour. // What Is Climate? // Climate is different. Climate is the usual weather pattern in a place over a long time, usually thirty years or more. One rainy day in the desert does not change the desert's climate. The desert still has a dry climate because it is dry most of the time, year after year. // A State of Many Climates // California has many different climates. Along much of the coast, summers are cool and often foggy, and winters are mild. In the Central Valley, summers are hot and dry, which is good for growing crops like tomatoes and almonds when farmers can water them. High in the Sierra Nevada mountains, winters bring deep snow. In the southeast, deserts such as Death Valley are some of the hottest and driest places on Earth. // Wet Winters, Dry Summers // Much of California gets most of its rain and snow in winter and very little in summer. Mountain snow is important, because when it melts in spring, it fills rivers and reservoirs that people use all year. // A Map Can Help // A climate map uses colors to show places with similar climates. On a map of California, the coast, the valley, the mountains and the desert would each be shown in a different color. // Weather tells you whether to bring an umbrella today. Climate tells you what kind of clothes to pack if you move somewhere new.

passages.t: How Fog Came to the Bay
passages.x: Long ago, the Sun and the Ocean were the best of friends. Every day, the Sun shone warmly on the waves, and the Ocean sparkled back. Along the shore, people fished, played and dried their nets on the hot sand. // But one summer, the Sun grew proud. "Without me, nothing would grow," it bragged. "I will shine harder than ever, so everyone sees how strong I am." // The Sun blazed. The sand grew too hot to walk on. The hills turned brown and dry. The fish swam down deep to escape the heat, and the people's nets came up empty. // The Ocean worried about the people. It called to its cousin, the Cool Wind. "Help me make a blanket," the Ocean said. // So the Cool Wind blew across the cold waves, and the Ocean breathed up a soft gray mist. Together, they rolled the mist over the shore like a fluffy quilt. Under the gray blanket, the sand cooled. Drops of water settled on the dry hills. The fish rose again, and the nets came up full. // The Sun was angry at first. It pushed and burned at the edges of the mist. But by afternoon, it saw the people smiling in the shade and the hills turning green. The Sun felt ashamed. // "You were right to help them," the Sun said. "I will share the sky." // And so, people say, on summer mornings the fog rolls in from the Bay to keep the coast cool, and by afternoon the Sun is allowed to shine through.

The water you drink today may once have been part of a cloud, a glacier or even an ocean wave far away. That is because Earth's water moves in a never-ending loop called the water cycle. // Evaporation // The sun heats water in oceans, lakes and rivers. Some of the water turns into an invisible gas called water vapor and rises into the air. This change is called evaporation. Plants also give off water vapor through their leaves. // Condensation // As water vapor rises, the air around it gets cooler. Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapor, so some of the vapor turns back into tiny drops of liquid water. This is called condensation. Billions of these tiny drops gather together to form clouds. Fog is simply a cloud that forms near the ground. // Precipitation // Inside a cloud, tiny drops bump into each other and join to make bigger drops. When the drops become too heavy to float, they fall to the ground as precipitation. Precipitation can be rain, snow, sleet or hail, depending on how cold the air is. // Collection // The water that falls collects in oceans, lakes and rivers, or soaks into the ground. Snow may stay frozen on mountains until spring. Then the sun heats the water again, and the cycle continues. // Because of the water cycle, Earth keeps using the same water again and again.

test.ans: Earth's water moves in a loop called the water cycle. First, the sun heats water in oceans, lakes and rivers, and some of it evaporates into an invisible gas called water vapor. Then, as the vapor rises, the air gets cooler, so the vapor condenses into tiny drops that form clouds. units.el: Retell each folktale with a three-part story map (problem, attempts, solution) and practice antonym pairs with picture cards (strong/weak, loud/quiet, generous/selfish).

passages.x: Long ago, in a village at the foot of the mountains, there lived a weaver named Amaru. Her cloth was so fine that people walked for days to trade for it. // One windy morning, Amaru spread her newest cloth on a rock to dry. Before she could stop it, a gust of wind snatched it away and carried it up the mountain. // Amaru did not waste time complaining. She tied on her sandals and climbed after it. // Halfway up, she met a llama with a thorn in its foot. Though she was in a hurry, Amaru knelt and gently pulled the thorn out. The llama nuzzled her hand and followed her. // Higher up, she found a hummingbird tangled in a spider's web. Amaru carefully freed the tiny bird, and it zipped away into the clouds. // At the very top of the mountain, Amaru saw her cloth caught in the branches of a tall tree, far out of reach. She sat down, tired and discouraged. "I will never get it back," she sighed. // Just then, the hummingbird returned, followed by a dozen of its friends. Together they grabbed the edges of the cloth with their beaks and tugged it free. It floated down, and the llama caught it on its back. // When Amaru unfolded the cloth, she gasped. The wind had painted it with the colors of the mountain: rose pink from the dawn, gold from the sun and deep blue from the sky. // Amaru carried it home on the llama's back. From then on, she wove her cloth in mountain colors, and people said her kindness had been woven into every thread.

In parts of West Africa, including Mali, Senegal and The Gambia, some families have a very important job. For hundreds of years, members of these families have been griots. A griot is a storyteller, a historian and a musician all in one. // Living Libraries // Long ago, most people in the region did not write their history down. Instead, griots memorized it. They learned the names of kings and queens, the stories of great battles and the family histories of whole villages. Some griots could recite family histories going back many generations. Because they held so much knowledge, griots were sometimes called living libraries. // Music and Words // Griots usually tell their stories with music. Many play the kora, an instrument with a long neck, a round body made from a large gourd and about twenty-one strings. The music helps listeners pay attention and helps the griot remember the words. // Passing It On // A griot's knowledge is usually passed from parent to child. Young griots spend years listening, practicing and memorizing before they perform on their own. // Griots Today // Griots still perform today at weddings, naming ceremonies and festivals. Some have become famous musicians who travel the world. Even with books and computers, many people believe that hearing a story told aloud by a griot helps keep their history alive.

In a village beside a wide river, a great drum sat in the center of the square. Every evening at sunset, someone would beat it, and the deep BOOM, BOOM told everyone that the day's work was done. // One evening, the drum would not play. When the strongest man struck it, it gave only a dull thud. // "It is cracked," said the strongest man. "We must burn it and build a new one." // "No," said the oldest elder. "It is cursed. We must bury it." // The chief did not know whom to believe. He announced, "Whoever can make the drum sing again will be honored at the harvest feast." // Many people tried. A drummer from the next village pounded it until his hands ached. A boy danced around it, chanting. Nothing worked. // Then Nia, a quiet girl who carried water for her grandmother, asked if she could try. Some people laughed. "You are too small to play such a big drum," they said. // Nia did not hit the drum. Instead, she pressed her ear against its side and listened for a long time. She heard a tiny cheep, cheep from inside. // Carefully, Nia reached through a hole at the bottom of the drum and lifted out a nest with three baby birds. The mother bird fluttered down beside her. Nia set the nest gently in a tree. // Then she struck the drum once. BOOM! The sound rolled over the river. // At the harvest feast, the chief said, "Strength and wisdom are good, but tonight we honor someone who knew how to listen."

Drums may be the oldest musical instruments in the world. People in almost every culture have made them, and they use drums to celebrate, to dance, to tell stories and even to send messages. // Talking Drums // In West Africa, some drummers play talking drums. A talking drum is shaped like an hourglass and has strings running along its sides. When the drummer squeezes the strings under one arm, the pitch of the drum rises or falls. Because some West African languages use rising and falling tones, skilled drummers can copy the sound of words and phrases. // Taiko // In Japan, taiko drummers play huge drums at festivals. Some taiko drums are taller than an adult. Drummers move their whole bodies as they play, so a taiko performance looks almost like a dance. // Steel Pan // On the Caribbean island nation of Trinidad and Tobago, musicians found a new way to make a drum. In the 1900s, they began hammering the ends of empty steel oil barrels into bowls with many dents. Each dent plays a different note, so a steel pan can play whole melodies. // Drums Bring People Together // Whether they are made from wood, animal skin or recycled metal, drums often bring people together. A drumbeat can make a crowd clap, dance or listen as one.

test.q: Retell "The Silent Drum" from Nia's point of view, using "I." Include Nia's thoughts and feelings, some dialogue, the events in order and an ending that shows what Nia learned or felt.
test.ans: Every evening, I loved hearing the great drum boom across the river. One night it only thudded. The strongest man said it was cracked, and the elder said it was cursed, but I was not so sure. I watched everyone pound and chant, and nothing worked. When I asked to try, people laughed. "You are too small," they said. My cheeks burned, but I walked to the drum anyway. I pressed my ear against it and waited. Then I heard it: cheep, cheep! I reached inside and found three baby birds in a nest. I set them in a tree next to their mother. When I struck the drum, BOOM! At the feast, the chief honored me for listening. I learned that being quiet can be a kind of strength.

units.name: Unit 5: Inventions That Changed Our Lives (opinion writing)
units.el: Read the play aloud in parts with gestures for stage directions, and build a prefix chart (re-, un-, dis-, mis-, pre-) with a picture example for each.

passages.x: A Play in Two Scenes. Characters: ROSA, a third grader; DEV, her friend; MR. KIM, their teacher // Scene 1 // (A classroom. ROSA tugs at a backpack stuffed so full that the zipper will not close.) // ROSA: Ugh! Every day it's the same. My backpack is too heavy, and my shoulders hurt. // DEV: (peeking in) That's because you carry your whole desk in there. // ROSA: (laughing) Maybe. But lots of kids have this problem. Somebody should invent something. // MR. KIM: (walking over) Inventors start just like that, by noticing a problem. What could you design? // ROSA: (thinking hard) What if a backpack had wheels, like a suitcase? // DEV: Our school has stairs. Wheels won't help on stairs. // ROSA: (frowning) Good point. Back to the drawing board. // Scene 2 // (The next week. ROSA and DEV stand beside a table with a backpack covered in labels.) // ROSA: (proudly) Presenting the Stair-Climber Pack! It has wheels for the hallway and padded straps for the stairs. // DEV: And we added a list on the front flap, so you only pack what you need each day. // MR. KIM: (lifting it) It's lighter already! How did you get the idea for the list? // DEV: (grinning) We tested it on Rosa. She was carrying four library books she had already read. // ROSA: (rolling her eyes, but smiling) Okay, okay. The list was Dev's idea. // MR. KIM: That's what inventors do. They test, they listen and they make their ideas better.

Garrett Morgan was born in Kentucky in 1877. As a teenager, he moved to Ohio to look for work. He had gone to school only until about sixth grade, but he was curious and loved to figure out how machines worked. He taught himself to repair sewing machines, and later he opened his own repair shop. // The Safety Hood // Morgan cared about keeping people safe. He invented a safety hood, a kind of breathing device that helped protect people from smoke and dangerous gases. In 1916, there was an explosion in a tunnel under Lake Erie, and workers were trapped inside. Morgan and his brother put on safety hoods, went into the tunnel and helped carry men out. After that, many fire departments became interested in his invention. // A Better Traffic Signal // As more cars filled city streets, Morgan noticed that crashes happened often at busy corners. Early signals switched straight from "stop" to "go," which gave drivers no warning. Morgan designed a signal with a third position that stopped traffic in all directions for a moment before the signal changed. This gave drivers time to clear the intersection. He received a patent for it in 1923. // A Lasting Idea // Today's traffic lights work differently, but they still use the idea of a warning before the light changes. The yellow light is a reminder of Morgan's goal: to help people get where they are going safely.

Kenji had spent three weeks building his Automatic Plant Waterer for the school invention fair. It was made of a plastic bottle, a long straw, some tape and a cardboard stand. The idea was simple: water would drip slowly from the bottle through the straw into a flowerpot, so plants could be watered even when nobody was home. // On the morning of the fair, Kenji set it up on his table. He filled the bottle, stepped back and waited for the first drip. // Nothing happened. // He tapped the straw. He squeezed the bottle. Suddenly, water gushed out all at once, flooding the flowerpot and spilling across the table. Kenji grabbed paper towels while other students giggled. His cheeks turned red. // "It worked at home," he mumbled to his mom. // When the judges came by, Kenji wanted to hide under the table. Instead, he took a deep breath and told the truth. "My invention didn't work today," he said. "I think the straw got clogged, and when it came loose, too much water rushed out. Next time, I would use a smaller hole and a clip to control the flow." // One judge, Dr. Alvarez, wrote something on her clipboard. "Most inventions fail many times before they work," she said. "What matters is that you understand why." // Kenji didn't win first prize. But at the end of the day, he got a ribbon he hadn't expected. It said "Best Problem Solver." On the bus ride home, he was already sketching his next design.

Have you ever used an eraser to fix a mistake? Erasers seem simple, but they have an interesting history. // Before Rubber // The "lead" in a pencil is not really lead at all. It is a soft, dark mineral called graphite, mixed with clay. People have written with graphite pencils for hundreds of years. But for a long time, fixing a pencil mistake was messy. Many people rubbed out pencil marks with balls of soft, stale bread! // A Lucky Discovery // In 1770, people in England noticed that a piece of rubber could rub away pencil marks much better than bread. Rubber comes from the milky sap of certain trees. Because it "rubbed out" mistakes, people in England began calling it "rubber." Rubber erasers did not spoil like bread, so they quickly became popular. // Putting It All Together // For many years, pencils and erasers were sold separately. Then, in 1858, an American named Hymen Lipman received a patent for a pencil with an eraser attached to one end. Now writers could fix a mistake without searching for a separate eraser. // Erasers Today // Today, many erasers are made of vinyl or other materials instead of natural rubber. Artists use special kneaded erasers that can be shaped like clay. Still, the idea is the same: an eraser gives you the chance to try again. // Some people say the eraser is one of the most important inventions for students, because it reminds us that mistakes are a normal part of learning.

passages.x: Story 1: Lena Speaks Up // Lena wanted to be class representative, but the idea of giving a speech made her knees wobble. Her friend Marcus was running too, and everyone said he was the funniest kid in third grade. // On election day, Marcus told jokes, and the class laughed. Then it was Lena's turn. Her voice shook, but she held up a list. "I asked every person in our class what they wanted," she said. "Eleven of you want more books in our class library. Nine of you want a quieter lunchroom. If I win, I will bring your ideas to the student council." // The class voted. Lena won by three votes. Marcus shook her hand. "You listened," he said. "That's better than jokes." // Story 2: Lena and the Long Line // A month later, Lena noticed a problem. The lunch line was so long that some kids had only five minutes to eat. At the student council meeting, she raised her hand. "What if classes took turns going first?" she asked. // The principal liked the idea but said, "Let's try it for two weeks and see what happens." // Some kids grumbled at first, especially the fifth graders, who had always gone first. But by the end of two weeks, everyone had time to eat. The council voted to keep the new plan. // That afternoon, a first grader tugged Lena's sleeve. "Thanks for the extra lunch time," he whispered. Lena smiled. Being a leader, she decided, meant listening first and then speaking up.

Have you ever wondered who decides where a new park will go or how often the streets get swept? In most California cities, those decisions are made by local government. // The Mayor and City Council // Many cities have a mayor and a city council. Council members are elected by the people who live in the city. Together, they make local laws, called ordinances, and decide how to spend the city's money. For example, they might vote to fix a road, build a library or add a crosswalk near a school. // City Departments // The city council cannot do every job alone, so cities have departments. The fire department fights fires and responds to emergencies. The parks department takes care of playgrounds and sports fields. The public works department repairs streets and keeps water flowing to homes. Each department follows the plans that the council approves. // Counties and the State // Cities are part of larger areas called counties. California has 58 counties, and each one is led by a board of supervisors. Above the counties is the state government in Sacramento, led by the governor and a lawmaking group called the legislature. // How Citizens Help // Local government works best when people take part. Adults vote in elections. Anyone, including kids, can go to a city council meeting and share ideas during public comment. Some students have even convinced their city leaders to add bike lanes or ban plastic straws. // When you see a new stop sign or a freshly painted playground, remember: someone in your community helped make that decision.

Dear Members of the Riverside Heights City Council, // My name is Amaya Torres, and I am in third grade at Vista Elementary School. I am writing to ask you to build a dog park in Oakwood Park. // First, our town has many dogs but nowhere for them to run safely. On my street alone, nine families have dogs. Right now, people walk their dogs on the soccer field, and sometimes dogs run onto the field during games. A fenced dog park would keep dogs and players safe. // Second, a dog park would help neighbors meet each other. When my grandma walks our dog, Luna, she always stops to talk with other dog owners. A dog park would give people a regular place to gather and make friends. // Third, there is already empty land in the northeast corner of Oakwood Park. I measured it with my dad, and it is about as big as two basketball courts. The city would not need to buy new land. // Some people might say a dog park would be too noisy. However, the empty corner is next to the train tracks, not near any houses, so barking would not bother anyone. // My class collected 112 signatures from people who support a dog park. I have attached the list to this letter. Please vote yes on a dog park at your next meeting. // Thank you for reading my letter and for working to make our town a better place. // Sincerely, // Amaya Torres

How does an idea become a rule for a whole city? In many California cities, it follows several steps. // Step 1: An Idea // An idea for a new local law can come from a council member, a city worker or a resident. For example, a parent might notice that cars speed near a school and ask the city to lower the speed limit there. // Step 2: Research // City staff study the idea. They might count cars, measure speeds or look at how other cities solved the same problem. Then they write a report for the council. // Step 3: Public Meeting // The council discusses the idea at a public meeting. Residents can attend and share their opinions during public comment. Some people may support the idea, while others may worry about the cost or have a different plan. // Step 4: The Vote // After listening, council members vote. If a majority, or more than half, votes yes, the idea becomes an ordinance, which is a city law. Sometimes the council asks for changes and votes again at a later meeting. // Step 5: Putting It into Action // Once an ordinance passes, city departments carry it out. In the school example, the public works department would put up new speed limit signs, and police officers would make sure drivers follow the law. // Every step gives people a chance to be heard. That is one reason local government is sometimes called the government closest to the people.

passages.x: Rain drummed on the window, so Aiyana and her grandmother pulled the old family album off the shelf. // The first page showed a black-and-white photo of a girl with two long braids and a wide smile. "Is that you, Grandma?" Aiyana asked. // "That's me at eight years old," Grandma said. "Look closely. Do you see anything familiar?" // Aiyana leaned in. The girl had a dimple in her left cheek, just like Aiyana's. "We have the same dimple!" she said. // "You got that dimple from me, through your mother," Grandma said. "Some things are passed down in families, like dimples and the shape of your eyes. They are called inherited traits." // They turned the page. There was Aiyana's mother as a baby, with thick, curly black hair. Next was Uncle Ray, tall and skinny, holding a basketball. // "Is Uncle Ray good at basketball because he's tall?" Aiyana asked. // Grandma laughed. "Being tall came from his father. But being good at basketball came from practicing every single day. Skills like that are learned, not inherited." // Aiyana thought about that. She had learned to speak two languages, English and Navajo, by listening to her family. She had learned to make frybread by watching Grandma. Those things were not in her body from birth. She had practiced them. // At the end of the album, there was an empty page. Grandma handed Aiyana a photo from her last birthday, her dimple showing as she blew out the candles. "This page is for you," she said. // Aiyana pressed the photo onto the page. She was part inherited and part learned, she decided, and all of it was hers.

Along the rocky coast of central California, sea otters float on their backs among forests of tall, swaying kelp. These playful animals spend almost their whole lives in cold ocean water. To survive there, they have some amazing adaptations. An adaptation is a body part or behavior that helps a living thing survive in its environment. // The Warmest Coat // Most marine mammals, such as seals and whales, stay warm with a thick layer of fat called blubber. Sea otters do not have blubber. Instead, they have the thickest fur of any animal, with up to about one million hairs in a patch the size of a postage stamp. The fur traps a layer of air next to the otter's skin, which keeps it warm and dry. Sea otters spend hours each day grooming, or cleaning, their fur to keep it working well. // Big Appetites // Staying warm takes a lot of energy. A sea otter eats about one-fourth of its body weight in food every day. It dives to the sea floor to collect sea urchins, crabs, clams and snails. // Using Tools // Sea otters are one of the few mammals that use tools. An otter floats on its back, places a rock on its chest and bangs a hard shell against it until the shell cracks open. Some otters keep a favorite rock tucked in a loose pocket of skin under their arms. // Staying Put // When sea otters sleep, they often wrap themselves in strands of kelp so they do not drift away. Groups may also float together, sometimes holding paws. // Together, these adaptations help sea otters thrive in a cold, rough ocean.

When winter winds come howling // across the frozen plain, // the arctic fox wears snowy white // from nose to tail again. // She curls her bushy tail around // her small and furry face, // a blanket wrapped from head to toe // in her cold and windy place. // Her ears are short and rounded, // her legs are short and stout, // so heat stays snug inside her // and does not wander out. // She listens for the lemmings // that tunnel under snow, // then leaps and pounces, nose first, // to catch the prey below. // But when the summer sunshine // melts the snowy ground, // she sheds her coat of winter white // for one of gray and brown. // Among the rocks and tundra, // she's hard for eyes to see. // Two coats, one fox, all year long, // as clever as can be. // So if you walk the tundra // in winter or in May, // look closely at the rocks and snow. // A fox may watch you play!

passages.t: Arctic Foxes: Built for the Cold
passages.x: The arctic fox lives in the Arctic, the area around the North Pole. Winter temperatures there can drop below minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Few animals could survive such cold, but the arctic fox has many adaptations. // A Thick Coat // An arctic fox has one of the warmest coats of any mammal. Its fur is thick and has many layers. Even the bottoms of its paws are covered with fur, which helps it walk on ice and snow without getting cold feet. // A Body That Saves Heat // Compared with foxes that live in warmer places, the arctic fox has short ears, a short muzzle and short legs. Less of its body sticks out into the cold air, so it loses less heat. When it sleeps, it wraps its long, bushy tail around its body like a scarf. // Changing Colors // Most arctic foxes change color with the seasons. In winter, their fur is white, which blends in with the snow. In summer, they shed their white coat and grow a thinner brown or gray coat that matches the rocks and plants of the tundra. This camouflage helps them hide from predators and sneak up on prey. // Finding Food // Arctic foxes eat lemmings, birds, eggs and fish. In winter, when food is hard to find, a fox may follow a polar bear and eat the scraps it leaves behind. Arctic foxes can also hear small animals moving under the snow. They leap high and dive into the snow to catch them. // Each of these adaptations helps the arctic fox survive in one of the harshest places on Earth.

passages.t: The Fireflies Who Lit the Sky
passages.x: Long ago, before there were stars, the night sky was completely black. When the Sun went to sleep, the animals could not see. Owls bumped into branches. Rabbits lost their way home. Even the river grew quiet, afraid of the dark. // The animals held a meeting at the edge of the forest. "We need light at night," said Bear. "Who will bring it?" // Eagle spread his wings. "I am the strongest flier. I will carry a piece of the Sun into the sky." But when Eagle flew close to the Sun, the heat singed his feathers, and he tumbled back down. // Deer offered to carry a burning branch up the tallest mountain. But the wind blew out the flame before she reached the top. // Then a tiny voice spoke. "We will try," said Firefly. Behind her glowed hundreds of her sisters and brothers. // The other animals laughed. "You are too small!" they said. // But the fireflies did not argue. Night after night, they flew higher and higher, each one carrying its own little light. They flew until they were so high that they could not come back down. There they stayed, scattered across the sky, glowing softly. // The animals gazed up in wonder. Now the owls could see the branches, and the rabbits could find their way home. Bear bowed his great head. "We were wrong to laugh," he said. "Many small lights, working together, can light the whole night." // And that, the old stories say, is why the sky is full of stars.

On a clear night, the Moon is often the brightest object in the sky. But the Moon does not make its own light. It reflects light from the Sun, the way a mirror reflects a flashlight beam. // Why the Moon Seems to Change // The Moon travels around Earth in a path called an orbit. As it moves, we see different amounts of its sunlit side. When the side facing us is fully lit, we see a full moon. When the sunlit side faces away from us, we can barely see the Moon at all. This is called a new moon. In between, we see shapes called crescents and quarter moons. These shapes are the phases of the Moon, and the whole cycle takes about 29 and a half days. // A Rocky, Dusty World // The Moon has no air, no liquid water and no weather. Its surface is covered with gray dust and rocks. It also has thousands of craters, or bowl-shaped holes, made when space rocks crashed into it long ago. Because there is no wind or rain on the Moon, the craters, and even astronauts' footprints, can last for millions of years. // Visitors from Earth // On July 20, 1969, astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first people to walk on the Moon. Between 1969 and 1972, twelve astronauts walked on its surface. They collected rocks so scientists on Earth could study them. // Today, space agencies are planning new trips to the Moon. Someday, people may even live and work there.

Every year, the astronomy club held a star party in the desert, far from city lights. This year, Priya's dad finally said she could go. // When they arrived, the sun was sinking behind the mountains. People were setting up telescopes of every size, from small ones on tripods to one as tall as a refrigerator. A woman with a red flashlight waved them over. "I'm Dr. Okafor," she said. "We use red lights so our eyes can stay used to the dark." // As the sky darkened, more and more stars appeared, until Priya could hardly believe her eyes. At home in the city, she could see maybe ten stars. Here, there were thousands. A pale, cloudy stripe stretched across the whole sky. // "That's the Milky Way," Dr. Okafor said. "It's our galaxy. The stars you see tonight are all part of it." // Priya waited in line at the giant telescope. When it was her turn, she climbed a small ladder and pressed her eye to the eyepiece. There, floating in the darkness, was a tiny golden ball with a ring around it. // "Saturn!" Priya gasped. "It looks like a sticker!" // Dr. Okafor laughed. "Saturn is so far away that its light takes over an hour to reach us. You're seeing what Saturn looked like more than an hour ago." // On the drive home, Priya pressed her forehead to the car window and watched the stars fade as the city lights grew brighter. "Dad," she said, "can we come back next year?" // Her dad smiled. "I already signed us up."

When you look at the night sky, the stars look like tiny points of light. But the Sun is a star, too. It is the closest star to Earth, which is why it looks so much bigger and brighter than the others. // A Giant Ball of Gas // The Sun is a huge, glowing ball of hot gases. It is so big that about one million Earths could fit inside it. The surface of the Sun is about 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit, much hotter than any oven. // Far, Far Away // The Sun is about 93 million miles from Earth. Even light, the fastest thing in the universe, takes about 8 minutes to travel from the Sun to us. Other stars are much, much farther away. That is why they look so small. // Why the Sun Seems to Move // Each day, the Sun seems to rise in the east, cross the sky and set in the west. But the Sun is not really moving across our sky. Earth is spinning. It turns all the way around once about every 24 hours. As your part of Earth turns toward the Sun, you have day. As it turns away, you have night. // Why We Need the Sun // Without the Sun, Earth would be a frozen, dark place. The Sun's light helps plants grow, and plants provide food for animals and people. The Sun's heat warms our land, air and oceans. // Safety Tip // Never look directly at the Sun, even with sunglasses. Its light is so strong that it can damage your eyes.

lessons.name: Myths that explain the natural world

practice.q: What is a myth?
ch: a traditional story that often explains something in nature
a true science report about the stars
a set of directions for playing a game
a list of facts about the planets
practice.h: Myths were told long ago to answer "why" questions.

practice.q: Read: "Long ago, Moon was jealous of Sun's bright light, so each month she hid behind the clouds until only a thin sliver showed." What might this myth try to explain?

passages.x: Mateo's stomach was full of butterflies. It was the day of the field day relay, and his team was counting on him to run the last leg. // "You're as fast as a cheetah," his best friend Ji-woo said, giving him a thumbs-up. "Just keep your eyes on the prize." // Mateo wasn't so sure. Last year, he had tripped over his own feet and come in dead last. He still remembered how his face had burned like a stove. // The whistle blew. The first runner, Aisha, shot off the line like a rocket. She passed the baton to Ji-woo, who flew down the track. Then it was Carlos's turn. Halfway around, Carlos's shoelace came untied. He slowed down, and the other teams pulled ahead. // By the time Carlos reached him, Mateo's team was in third place. Mateo grabbed the baton and ran. The wind roared in his ears. His legs pumped like pistons. One runner, then another, fell behind him. The finish line was so close he could almost taste it. // With one last burst, Mateo leaned forward and broke through the ribbon. First place! // His teammates piled on him in a happy heap. "You ran like the wind!" Aisha shouted. // Mateo laughed, still trying to catch his breath. "I didn't run like the wind," he said. "I ran like a kid who finally stopped worrying." // That night, his legs felt like jelly, but his smile stayed glued to his face.

passages.t: Pushes, Pulls and the Forces Around Us
passages.x: Every time something starts moving, stops moving or changes direction, a force is at work. A force is a push or a pull. When you kick a soccer ball, your foot pushes it. When you open a drawer, your hand pulls it. // Balanced and Unbalanced Forces // Forces can work against each other. In a game of tug-of-war, both teams pull on the rope. If both teams pull with the same strength, the forces are balanced, and the rope does not move. If one team pulls harder, the forces are unbalanced, and the rope moves toward the stronger team. // Gravity // Some forces act without touching anything. Gravity is a force that pulls objects toward Earth. Gravity is why a ball comes back down after you throw it up and why you land after you jump. // Friction // Friction is a force that slows down moving things when two surfaces rub together. Rough surfaces, like carpet or a gravel path, make more friction than smooth surfaces, like ice. That is why a hockey puck slides a long way on ice but would stop quickly on a sidewalk. Friction is not always bad. Without friction, your shoes would slip with every step! // Bigger Forces, Bigger Changes // The stronger the force, the bigger the change in motion. A gentle tap moves a ball a short distance. A hard kick sends it flying across the field. // Scientists study forces to design everything from safer cars to faster bicycles. The next time you play, notice all the pushes and pulls around you.

For weeks, Zainab and her grandfather worked in the garage on her soapbox car. It had no engine and no pedals. It would roll down Hillcrest Avenue powered by nothing but gravity. // "A heavier car rolls better," Grandpa said, bolting on the last wheel. "But not too heavy. The rules have a limit." // On race day, the street was lined with cheering families. Zainab's car, painted bright purple with a lightning bolt on the side, sat at the top of the hill like a racehorse waiting at the gate. Her heart was pounding like a drum. // The starter dropped the flag. Zainab let go of the brake, and the car crept forward, then rolled faster and faster down the slope. The wind whistled past her helmet. Trees blurred into a green smear. // Halfway down, the car began to wobble. One wheel was rubbing against the side of the car. Zainab could feel it dragging, slowing her down. A blue car zipped past her. // "Keep it straight," she whispered, gripping the steering wheel. She steered gently, and the wobbling eased. The car picked up speed again. // She crossed the finish line in second place, just a nose behind the blue car. // Grandpa jogged up, out of breath. "That wheel!" he said. "Friction must have been fighting you all the way down." // Zainab grinned and pulled off her helmet. "Then next year," she said, "we'll fix the wheel and win by a mile."

Have you ever stuck a drawing to the refrigerator with a magnet? Magnets can push and pull certain objects without even touching them. This invisible push or pull is called magnetic force. // What Magnets Attract // Magnets attract, or pull on, objects that contain iron, such as paper clips, nails and safety pins. They do not attract most other materials. A magnet will not pick up a plastic toy, a wooden block or an aluminum can. // Two Poles // Every magnet has two ends called poles: a north pole and a south pole. When you hold two magnets near each other, something surprising happens. Opposite poles, north and south, attract each other and snap together. Like poles, north and north or south and south, repel, or push each other away. // Stronger Up Close // A magnet's force is strongest close to the magnet. As you move an object farther away, the pull gets weaker. If you slowly slide a paper clip toward a magnet, it will suddenly jump the last little distance. // Earth Is a Magnet // Earth itself acts like a giant magnet. That is why a compass works. A compass needle is a tiny magnet. It lines up with Earth's magnetic force and points north, helping travelers find their way. // Magnets at Work // Magnets are used in many machines. They help speakers make sound, keep cabinet doors closed and even lift heavy scrap metal at junkyards. Some trains in other countries use powerful magnets to float above their tracks and travel at very high speeds.
