passages.x: Saturday comes on tiptoe, // soft as a cat on the stair. // It slips through the crack in my curtains // and tangles itself in my hair. // Downstairs, the kitchen is singing: // the sizzle of eggs in the pan, // the radio humming a love song, // the clink of Dad's spoon on a can. // My sister is still in her blankets, // a lump like a loaf in the bed. // I tickle her toes till she giggles // and hides with a pillow instead. // We race to the table, still yawning, // pajamas a mismatched parade. // Mom flips the pancakes like magic. // The syrup's a sticky cascade. // No alarm clocks, no buses, no homework, // no hurry to get out the door, // just sunshine and pancakes and laughter. // Who could ever ask for more? // So when Monday comes stomping and grumbling // with backpacks and bells and a frown, // I'll think of my slow Saturday morning // and pancakes, all golden and brown.

passages.t: Langston Hughes: A Poet of the People
passages.x: Langston Hughes was born in 1901 in Joplin, Missouri. When he was young, his parents separated, and he spent much of his childhood living with his grandmother in Lawrence, Kansas. She told him stories about people who had worked bravely for freedom and fairness. Those stories stayed with him for the rest of his life. // A Young Writer // Langston loved books. In school, his classmates chose him to be their class poet, even though he had never written a poem before. He began writing, and he never stopped. In 1921, when he was only nineteen, one of his poems was published in a magazine. // The Harlem Renaissance // In the 1920s, Hughes moved to Harlem, a neighborhood in New York City. Harlem was full of Black writers, artists and musicians who were creating exciting new work. This time became known as the Harlem Renaissance. "Renaissance" means a rebirth, or a time of new ideas. // Poems with Rhythm // Hughes listened closely to jazz and blues music, and he used their rhythms in his poems. He wrote about everyday people: workers, families and children. He wrote about their hopes and their struggles, and he believed their lives were worth writing about. // A Lasting Voice // Over his life, Hughes wrote poems, stories, plays and books for children. He died in 1967, but his work is still read in classrooms around the world. Many readers say his words help them feel seen and heard.

For our class project, Ms. Begay asked us to interview an older family member and record a story from their life. I chose my abuelo, because he tells the best stories at every birthday party. // On Sunday, I set my tablet on the kitchen table and pressed the red button. "Abuelo," I said in my most serious reporter voice, "tell me about the day you came to California." // Abuelo leaned back in his chair and smiled. "I was nineteen years old," he said. "I had one suitcase, two shirts and a photo of my mother. I did not speak much English, and I did not know anyone in Los Angeles." // "Were you scared?" I asked. // "Terrified," he said, laughing. "On my first day, I got lost looking for my cousin's apartment. A woman selling oranges on the corner saw me looking confused. She did not speak Spanish, and I did not speak English, but she drew me a map on a paper bag. She even gave me an orange for the walk." // "Did you find the apartment?" // "I did," he said. "And I kept that paper bag for twenty years." // When the interview was over, Abuelo went to his room and came back with a faded, folded paper bag. The map was still on it, drawn in blue ink, with a tiny orange in the corner. // I held it carefully, as if it might crumble. In class the next week, I played the recording and showed the map. Ms. Begay said it was a perfect example of how one small kindness can stay with someone for a lifetime. // I think so too.

Every person carries stories inside them: memories of growing up, of jobs they did and of places they lived. When those stories are recorded and saved, they become oral history. Oral history is history told out loud by the people who lived it. // Why Oral History Matters // History books often tell about presidents, wars and famous events. But oral history can tell us what everyday life was really like. A grandmother might remember what her school looked like in 1965. A farmworker might describe picking grapes in the Central Valley. These first-hand stories help us understand the past in a personal way. // How to Do an Interview // First, choose someone to interview and ask their permission. Next, write your questions ahead of time. Good questions are open-ended, which means they cannot be answered with just "yes" or "no." For example, "What games did you play as a child?" is better than "Did you play games?" During the interview, listen carefully and ask follow-up questions, such as "How did that make you feel?" // Saving the Story // Record the interview with a phone, tablet or tape recorder, or take careful notes. Write down the date and the speaker's name. Many libraries and museums collect oral histories so that people in the future can listen to them. Some national projects have recorded hundreds of thousands of interviews with ordinary people. // Your Turn // You do not have to be a historian to save a story. All you need are good questions and a willingness to listen.

test.ans: Every summer, my grandma tells me about the night the lights went out in her village in the Philippines. "We had no electricity for three days," she told me last July, while we folded laundry. "So we sat outside and told stories by candlelight." She said her father played the guitar, and the neighbors brought rice cakes to share. I asked, "Weren't you scared of the dark?" She laughed and said, "No, because everyone was together." Then she showed me an old photo of her family on their front steps, all smiling. Now, whenever our power goes out, we light candles and tell stories, too. Her memory reminds me that being with family can make even a dark night feel bright.

ela|4.about: Fourth grade readers refer to details and examples when explaining what a text says and what it suggests, determine themes and main ideas, describe characters in depth, explain how authors use reasons and evidence, and compare firsthand and secondhand accounts. units.name: Unit 1: Citizens Who Make a Difference (opinion writing)
units.el: Pre-teach "citizen", "council", "evidence" and "opinion" with pictures of a city council meeting; give the frame "I think ___ because ___. The text says ___."

passages.x: Every morning, Mr. Okafor sat on the green bench outside the Alder Street library and fed bread crumbs to the sparrows. Every morning, Lucia Herrera waved to him on her way to school. So on the first Monday in October, when Lucia saw a sign taped to the empty bench, she stopped. // "BENCH TO BE REMOVED OCTOBER 20," the sign said. "Damaged. City Parks Department." // Lucia looked closer. One of the wooden slats was cracked, and a bolt had rusted through. Mr. Okafor was nowhere in sight. // At dinner she told her older brother, Mateo. "Where will Mr. Okafor sit? He walks with a cane, and the next bench is three blocks away." // Mateo shrugged. "It's the city's bench. You can't change what the city decides." // Lucia was not so sure. That night she wrote a letter to the Parks Department. She explained that the bench was the only place to rest between the bus stop and the senior apartments. She counted the people she saw using it on her walk home: eleven in one afternoon. She asked whether the bench could be repaired instead of removed. Then she made copies of the letter and asked her neighbors to sign them. // By Friday she had forty-two signatures. Her hand ached, and her shoes were dusty from climbing apartment stairs. Mr. Okafor signed twice by accident and laughed at himself. // Two weeks later, a city truck parked on Alder Street. Lucia held her breath. Two workers unloaded new boards, a can of green paint and a toolbox. By the afternoon, the bench looked better than ever. // The next morning, a small metal plate shone on the back of the bench. It read, "Repaired at the request of the neighbors of Alder Street." Mr. Okafor tapped it with his cane and grinned at Lucia. "The neighbors," he said, "had a very good letter writer."

The lunch line at Riverside Elementary wrapped around the cafeteria like a long, hungry snake. By the time the fourth graders got their trays, they had only eight minutes left to eat. // Darnell timed the line with his watch for a whole week. Monday: eight minutes to eat. Tuesday: seven. Wednesday: nine. On Thursday, his friend Amira dropped half her sandwich in the trash because the bell rang. // "Somebody should do something," Amira said. // "Somebody is going to," said Darnell. // He knew that the student council met on Fridays in Room 12. He had never been inside. He had never spoken to more than five people at once, and his stomach flipped at the thought. Still, he wrote his numbers on an index card, along with an idea: open a second line with grab-and-go lunches already packed in bags. // On Friday, Darnell stood at the front of Room 12. His voice wobbled on the first sentence. Then he looked at his card and read his numbers one by one. When he finished, the council president, a fifth grader named Rosa, asked, "How do you know a second line would help?" // Darnell had not expected that question. He took a breath and thought about it. "Because the grab-and-go bags are already made," he said. "Students would just pick one up. Nobody would wait for a server to fill a tray." // Rosa nodded slowly and wrote something down. // Three weeks later, a second table appeared by the cafeteria door with a sign that said GRAB AND GO. Amira finished her whole sandwich that day. She held up the empty bag like a trophy. // "Somebody did something," she said, and Darnell laughed.

Many people think only adults can make a difference in their city. In fact, young people can play an important part in local government. // Most California cities are run by a city council, a group of people elected by the voters. The council decides things like where to build parks, how to fix roads and when the library will be open. Council meetings are public, which means anyone may attend. A California law called the Brown Act requires these meetings to be open and gives members of the public a chance to speak. // This time to speak is called public comment. A speaker usually fills out a card, waits for their name to be called and then talks for a short time, often two or three minutes. Because the time is short, good speakers plan ahead. They state their request clearly, give one or two strong reasons and support each reason with facts. // Facts matter because council members must make choices for the whole city. Saying "Our park is dangerous" may not be enough. Saying "Three swings at Oak Park have been broken for six months" gives the council a clear picture of the problem. // Young people can also share ideas in other ways. They can write letters or emails to council members, join a youth commission if their city has one, or collect signatures from neighbors who agree with them. // Local government works best when people take part. A student who shows up, speaks clearly and brings evidence is practicing one of the most important jobs in a democracy: being an active citizen.

passages.t: Every School Should Have a Student Council
passages.x: Who knows the most about what happens at school? The students do. That is why every elementary school should have a student council, a group of students chosen by their classmates to share ideas with the principal and teachers. // First, a student council gives students a voice. Adults make many decisions about school, from the lunch menu to the recess schedule. When students have a group that speaks for them, adults can hear what is working and what is not. At Lakeview Elementary, for example, the council asked for more shade on the playground. The principal had not noticed that students crowded under one small tree on hot days. Today the playground has two shade sails. // Second, a student council teaches skills that students will need as adults. Council members learn to run meetings, listen to people who disagree and solve problems as a team. These are the same skills that city council members and other leaders use. // Third, a council helps students take care of their school. When students plan a recycling drive or a reading challenge themselves, more students join in. People tend to care about projects they helped create. // Some people worry that council meetings take time away from learning. However, most councils meet only once or twice a month, often at lunch. The lessons members learn about leadership are part of their education, too. // A school belongs to the whole community, and students are the biggest part of that community. Giving them a student council lets them help make their school a better place.

passages.t: The Little Library on Pepper Street
passages.x: When the Pepper Street branch library closed for repairs, Nadia thought the summer would be the longest of her life. The nearest open branch was across the freeway, and her mother worked until six every evening. // "No books for three months?" Nadia groaned, dropping onto the porch steps. // Her grandmother, Sitti, was watering the tomato plants. "No library," Sitti said, "is not the same as no books." She pointed her dripping hose at the garage. "There are four boxes of books in there, and nobody has opened them since your uncle moved away." // That afternoon Nadia and Sitti dragged the boxes onto the driveway. There were adventure stories with cracked spines, cookbooks, a bird guide and a stack of comic books. Nadia had an idea. She found an old wooden crate, painted it bright yellow and, with Sitti's help, nailed it to a post by the sidewalk. On the front she wrote: TAKE A BOOK. LEAVE A BOOK. // For three days nothing happened. Nadia checked the crate every hour. Every hour, the books sat exactly where she had left them. // "Maybe nobody reads anymore," she said. // "Patience," said Sitti. "Seeds don't sprout the morning you plant them." // On the fourth morning, the bird guide was gone. In its place was a picture book about a whale. By the end of the week, Nadia counted nine new books, and someone had tucked a note inside the crate: "Thank you, yellow box. My son reads every night now." // When the Pepper Street branch reopened in September, Nadia was first in line. But the yellow crate stayed by the sidewalk. Sitti said it had become a little like her tomato plants: something that kept growing because people took care of it.

Today, almost every town in the United States has a public library where anyone can borrow books for free. It was not always this way. // In the early 1700s, books were expensive, and few people owned more than a handful. In 1731, Benjamin Franklin and a group of friends in Philadelphia started the Library Company of Philadelphia. Members paid a fee, and the money was used to buy books that all the members could share. This kind of library was a step forward, but it was not free, so many people still could not use it. // In the 1800s, more towns began to pay for libraries with public money so that every resident could borrow books. Then, starting in the 1880s, a wealthy businessman named Andrew Carnegie gave money to build library buildings. Carnegie had grown up poor and believed that libraries gave people a chance to educate themselves. His gifts paid for more than 1,600 library buildings in the United States. Many of them are still used today, including some in California. // Libraries have kept changing. Modern libraries lend e-books, laptops and even tools. They offer homework help, story times and classes for adults who are learning English. // Some people have found ways to share books outside library walls. In 2009, a man named Todd Bol built a small wooden box shaped like a schoolhouse, filled it with books and placed it in his front yard in Wisconsin in honor of his mother, a teacher who loved reading. Neighbors loved it. His idea grew into the Little Free Library organization, and now there are many thousands of these little book-sharing boxes around the world. // From Franklin's book club to a box on a front lawn, the idea is the same: when people share books, the whole community grows.

units.name: Unit 2: California's Regions and First Peoples (informative writing)
units.el: Show a California map with the four regions colored; pre-teach landform and water words (coast, valley, mountain range, desert, reservoir, canal) with photos and gestures.

passages.x: Tomas pressed his forehead against the car window. Outside, the desert stretched flat and brown in every direction, dotted with gray bushes and a few spiny plants that looked like bundles of dead sticks. // "There's nothing here, Abuela," he said. // His grandmother smiled and kept driving. "Wait," she said. // Abuela had lived in Borrego Springs for forty years. She said the desert was like a person who doesn't talk much: you have to pay attention to hear what it is saying. Tomas thought the desert wasn't saying anything at all. He had only agreed to visit because his cousins had gone to the beach without him. // That night it rained. Tomas woke to the sound of drops drumming on the tin roof of the porch and the sharp, clean smell of wet creosote bushes drifting through the window. // A few days later, Abuela shook him awake before sunrise. "Come," she whispered. // They walked out into the cool gray light. Tomas stopped. The dead sticks were not dead after all. The tall, spiny stems of the ocotillo had sprouted tiny green leaves along every branch, and their tips glowed with flame-red flowers. At his feet, patches of yellow and purple flowers had opened where there had been only sand. A hummingbird zipped past his ear toward the red blossoms. // "Where did all this come from?" Tomas asked. // "It was here the whole time," Abuela said. "The seeds wait in the ground, sometimes for years, until there is enough rain. The desert is patient." // Tomas knelt and touched a tiny yellow petal. He thought about his cousins at the beach, splashing in the waves. For the first time all week, he did not wish he were with them. // "Abuela," he said, "can we come out again tomorrow?"

Jasmine had been counting down the days to the camping trip for a month. She had pictured sunshine pouring through giant trees, blue sky, maybe a view of the ocean from the trail. Instead, she woke up inside a cloud. // Fog filled the forest so thickly that she could barely see the picnic table ten steps away. The tops of the redwoods disappeared into gray nothing. Everything dripped. // "This is the worst," Jasmine said, pulling her hood over her head. "We drove six hours to see the trees, and we can't even see the trees." // Her dad handed her a mug of cocoa. "Come walk with me anyway." // The trail was soft with fallen needles, and their footsteps made no sound. Water collected on the tips of the redwood needles high above and fell in fat, cold drops. Jasmine flinched when one hit her nose. // A park ranger was standing near a trail sign, and Dad asked her about the fog. The ranger smiled as if she had been waiting for the question. // "This fog is a gift," she said. "In summer, it hardly rains here. The redwoods catch water from the fog on their needles, and it drips down and soaks into the soil. Some of the water even goes straight into the needles. Without the fog, these forests could not grow so tall." // Jasmine looked up into the gray. A drop landed on her cheek, and this time she didn't flinch. She imagined the giant trees above her, drinking from the clouds. // That night, writing in her journal by lantern light, Jasmine wrote: Today we couldn't see the redwoods. But I found out what keeps them alive.

California is a big state with many kinds of land. Geographers often divide it into four regions: the coast, the mountains, the Central Valley and the desert. Each region has its own landforms and climate, and each has shaped the way people live there. // The coast region stretches more than 800 miles along the Pacific Ocean. Because the ocean changes temperature slowly, coastal towns tend to have mild weather, cool in summer and rarely freezing in winter. Ports such as Los Angeles, Long Beach and Oakland ship goods around the world. // The mountain region includes the Sierra Nevada, a long range along the state's eastern side. Mount Whitney, the tallest peak in the lower 48 states, rises more than 14,000 feet in the Sierra Nevada. In winter, heavy snow piles up in these mountains. When it melts in spring and summer, it flows into rivers and reservoirs that supply water to cities and farms far away. // The Central Valley lies between the coastal mountains and the Sierra Nevada. It is about 450 miles long and very flat, with deep, rich soil. Water from the mountains and a long, sunny growing season make it one of the most productive farming areas in the world. Farmers there grow almonds, grapes, tomatoes, rice and hundreds of other crops. // The desert region covers much of southeastern California. Deserts get very little rain, and summer days can be extremely hot. Death Valley holds the lowest point in North America, about 282 feet below sea level. Even so, plants and animals have adapted to survive there, and people visit the desert parks to hike and see the stars. // From foggy beaches to snowy peaks, California's regions are connected. Snow in the mountains waters the valley, and the valley's crops feed people on the coast and far beyond.

passages.t: The Tomol: A Boat Built for the Channel
passages.x: For thousands of years, the Chumash people have lived along the coast of what is now Santa Barbara and Ventura counties and on the nearby Channel Islands. To travel between the mainland and the islands, the Chumash built a remarkable boat called a tomol. // A tomol is a plank canoe. Instead of carving a boat from one log, builders split wood into long, flat planks. They often used redwood logs that had floated down the coast and washed up on the beach. They smoothed the planks with tools of stone and shell, then fit them together edge to edge. // Builders drilled small holes along the edges of the planks and sewed the planks together with strong cord made from plants. Then they sealed every seam with a sticky mixture of natural tar and pine pitch. Natural tar seeps out of the ground in this part of California and washes up on the beaches, so the builders had a supply close at hand. The sealant kept water out, so the tomol could cross open ocean. // A tomol could carry several paddlers and a load of goods. People traveled across the channel to fish, to visit family and to trade. Island villages traded goods such as shell beads, which were used like money, while mainland villages traded foods such as acorns and seeds. Because tomols connected the islands and the mainland, they helped the Chumash build a large trading network. // Building a tomol took great skill, and the builders were highly respected. In the 1800s, after Spanish missions and later settlers changed Chumash life, the tomol nearly disappeared. Today Chumash communities have brought the tradition back. In 2001, Chumash paddlers crossed the channel to Santa Cruz Island in a newly built tomol, and crossings have continued since then.

Every winter morning, Grandpa Lee checked the snow report before he checked the weather. Mei thought this was strange. Their family's peach orchard was in the Central Valley, near Fresno, where it almost never snowed. // "Why do you care about snow?" she asked one February morning, as he frowned at the screen. "We don't have any." // "Not here," Grandpa said. "But our trees drink it all summer." // Mei laughed. She pictured peach trees sipping snow cones. // On Saturday, Grandpa drove her east, up the winding highway into the Sierra Nevada. The flat green fields gave way to oak-covered hills, then to dark pine forests. Mei's ears popped. Then, around a curve, the world turned white. Snow lay heaped along the roadside higher than the car. Branches drooped under its weight. // They parked at a turnout, and Mei jumped into a snowbank up to her knees. It was colder than anything she had ever felt, and she shrieked with surprise. // Grandpa scooped up a handful and let it melt in his glove. A thin stream of water trickled between his fingers. // "In June, when it's a hundred degrees at the orchard, this snow will be melting," he said. "It runs into the creeks, then the river, then the reservoir. Then it comes through the canals to our trees. A good snow year means good peaches." // Mei looked at the mountains around her, white and silent. She thought of the hot, dusty rows of peach trees at home, waiting. Suddenly the snow didn't look like something far away. It looked like a promise. // That night, back in the valley, Mei sat beside Grandpa as he checked the snow report. "How much did we get?" she asked. // He smiled. "Enough," he said. "This year, enough."

Where does California's water come from? For many Californians, the answer is a surprise: snow. // Most of California's rain and snow falls in winter, and much of it falls in the north and in the mountains. But most people live farther south, and farms need the most water in the hot, dry summer. The state's water system has to move water from where it falls to where it is needed, and from winter into summer. // Snow helps solve the timing problem. The thick layer of snow that builds up in the Sierra Nevada each winter is called the snowpack. The snowpack works like a frozen reservoir. Instead of running off all at once, it melts slowly in spring and early summer. On average, the snowpack supplies about a third of the water Californians use. // Because the snowpack matters so much, scientists measure it carefully. Every winter, snow surveyors travel to measuring sites, sometimes on skis or snowshoes. They push a long metal tube down through the snow, pull out a core of snow and weigh it. The weight tells them how much water the snow holds. This information helps water managers plan how much water cities and farms will have. // As the snow melts, the water flows into rivers. Dams hold the water in reservoirs. Then aqueducts and canals carry it to cities and farms. The California Aqueduct alone is more than 400 miles long. // The snowpack changes a lot from year to year. In a wet year, the snow may be deep enough to bury a house. In a dry year, much less snow falls, and water must be saved carefully. That is why many Californians, like farmers, watch the snow report closely each winter.

passages.x: Isabel had promised her little brother, Rafi, that they would make s'mores without a campfire. Now, standing in the backyard with an empty pizza box, a roll of foil and a library book, she was starting to worry. // "Step one," she read aloud. "Cut a flap in the lid." She cut three sides of a square with Mom's scissors and folded it back. They glued foil to the inside of the flap, shiny side out. They taped plastic wrap tightly over the hole in the lid, making a little window. Then they set a graham cracker, a square of chocolate and a marshmallow inside, closed the lid and waited. // Twenty minutes later, Rafi peeked. The marshmallow looked exactly the same. // "It's broken," Rafi said. "Your oven doesn't work." // Isabel's face felt hot, and not from the sun. She wanted to stuff the box in the recycling bin. Instead, she sat down on the patio and opened the book again. She read the instructions slowly, the way her teacher said to read a hard math problem. // "We skipped two things," she said at last. "We were supposed to put black paper on the bottom, because black soaks up heat. And the flap has to point the sunlight into the box. Ours is pointing at the fence." // They found black construction paper in the craft drawer. Rafi held the flap while Isabel propped it up with a ruler until a bright patch of light fell right across the marshmallow. They waited again. // This time, when Rafi peeked, the chocolate had turned glossy and soft, and the marshmallow had puffed up like a tiny pillow. Rafi squashed his s'more together and grinned with chocolate on his chin. // "Your oven works," he said. // "Our oven," said Isabel. "And it only works because the first one didn't."

passages.t: The Storm Wind and the Small Breeze
passages.x: Long ago, two winds lived above a village of farmers. The Storm Wind was enormous and proud. When he roared down the valley, trees bent to the ground and roofs rattled. The Small Breeze was quiet and gentle. She drifted over the fields, rippling the wheat and cooling the farmers' faces. // "You are hardly a wind at all," the Storm Wind boasted. "Nobody even notices you. When I blow, the whole world pays attention." // The Small Breeze said nothing, but she wondered if he was right. // At the edge of the village stood a windmill with four long sails. The miller used it to grind wheat into flour. One autumn, after the harvest, sacks of wheat were piled high beside the mill, and the whole village was waiting for flour to bake its winter bread. // "Watch this," said the Storm Wind. "I will grind all that wheat in a single afternoon." // He hurled himself at the windmill. The sails spun so wildly that the wooden gears shrieked. Then, with a loud crack, one sail snapped and crashed to the ground. The miller ran out and quickly tied the other sails still before the storm could tear them apart too. The Storm Wind blew on for a while, then grew bored and rushed away over the mountains. // For a week, the miller worked to repair the broken sail. When he finished, the Small Breeze drifted past, as she did every day. The sails began to turn: slowly, steadily, hour after hour. By the end of the month, every sack of wheat had become flour. // That winter, the smell of fresh bread filled the village. The Small Breeze floated over the rooftops and no longer wondered whether she was a real wind.

Energy is the ability to make things move or change. You cannot hold energy in your hand, but you can see what it does. Energy also has a remarkable habit: it moves from place to place and changes from one form to another. // Think about a game of marbles. When you flick a marble, your finger gives it energy of motion. The faster the marble rolls, the more energy it has. If it crashes into a second marble, some of its energy moves into that marble, which starts rolling. Some of the energy also turns into sound, which is why you hear a click. A tiny bit becomes heat, warming the marbles just slightly. // Energy can travel in other ways, too. Light carries energy from the sun across millions of miles of space to Earth. Heat moves from warmer objects to cooler ones, so a spoon in a cup of hot cocoa soon feels warm. Sound carries energy through the air as vibrations. If you stand near a big drum, you can sometimes feel the sound in your chest. // Electricity is another way energy moves. An electric current carries energy through wires from a power plant to your home. When you switch on a lamp, the electric energy changes into light and heat. When you plug in a fan, it changes into motion. // Scientists say that energy is never used up; it only changes form or moves somewhere else. When a car brakes to a stop, its energy of motion does not disappear. Much of it turns into heat in the brakes. // Next time you turn on a light or kick a ball, look for the energy. Where does it come from, and where does it go?

People have used the wind's energy for thousands of years. Sailboats caught the wind to cross oceans, and windmills used it to grind grain and pump water. Today, giant machines called wind turbines use the wind to make electricity. // HOW A TURBINE WORKS // A wind turbine looks like a tall, thin tower with a propeller on top. The propeller usually has three long blades, and on large turbines each blade can be longer than 100 feet. When wind pushes against the blades, they spin. The spinning blades turn a shaft inside the box at the top of the tower. The shaft is connected to a generator, a machine that changes energy of motion into electric energy. Wires carry the electricity down the tower and out to homes and businesses. // WIND FARMS IN CALIFORNIA // Because one turbine can only make so much electricity, companies often build many turbines together in a windy place. This is called a wind farm. California has several large wind farms in mountain passes, where wind squeezes through gaps between mountains and blows hard. Drivers heading to Palm Springs pass hundreds of turbines in the San Gorgonio Pass, and others turn in the Tehachapi Mountains and at Altamont Pass. // BENEFITS AND CHALLENGES // Wind is a renewable resource, which means it will not run out. Turbines also make electricity without burning fuel, so they do not pollute the air while they run. However, wind power has challenges. The wind does not blow all the time, so turbines cannot make electricity on calm days. Turbines can be noisy, and their spinning blades can harm birds and bats. Engineers are working on solutions, such as storing extra electricity in giant batteries and changing how turbines run when birds are migrating. // Wind power will not solve every energy problem, but it is an important part of how California keeps its lights on.

passages.t: The Night the Lights Went Out
passages.x: The power went out on Maple Court at 7:14 p.m., right in the middle of Kofi's video game. The screen blinked to black. The refrigerator stopped humming. Even the little green numbers on the microwave clock disappeared. // "Mom!" Kofi yelled into the darkness. "Everything's broken!" // "Nothing's broken," his mother called back. "A transformer down the street was damaged in the wind. The power company says it will take a few hours to fix." // A few hours! Kofi slumped against the couch. No games, no movies, no lamp to read by. He felt as if the whole house had stopped breathing. // His mother found a flashlight and a box of candles in the hall closet. His little sister, Ama, wanted to know why the heater wasn't blowing anymore. Kofi realized he didn't know. He had never thought about how many things in the house needed electricity until every one of them stopped. // Then someone knocked on the door. It was Mrs. Delgado from next door, holding a camping lantern and a thermos. "My stove is gas," she said, "so the burners still light with a match. I made hot chocolate. Want to come over?" // Soon half of Maple Court was crowded into Mrs. Delgado's kitchen. The Nguyen twins brought a deck of cards. Mr. Patel told a story about the year the power went out for three days in the town where he grew up. Ama fell asleep on a pile of coats. Kofi laughed so hard at Mr. Patel's story that he nearly spilled his hot chocolate. // At 10:52, the lights flickered on. Everyone cheered, then went home. // Back in his room, Kofi looked at the dark screen of his video game. He didn't turn it on. He was thinking about how strange it was that the lights had to go out for him to really meet his neighbors.

passages.t: Where Does Our Electricity Come From?
passages.x: When you flip a light switch, electricity flows instantly. But that electricity began its journey far away, at a power plant. // Most power plants work in a similar way. They use a source of energy to spin a machine called a turbine. The spinning turbine turns a generator, which produces electricity. The difference between power plants is what makes the turbine spin. // Some plants burn fuels such as natural gas or coal. The heat boils water into steam, and the steam pushes the turbine's blades. Burning these fuels releases gases that pollute the air and add to climate change. Also, these fuels formed underground over millions of years, so once they are used up, they cannot be replaced. // Other plants use renewable sources, which nature keeps supplying. At a hydroelectric dam, falling water spins the turbine. At a wind farm, the wind turns the blades directly. Solar power works differently: most solar panels change sunlight straight into electricity without any turbine at all. Over the past twenty years, California has built a great many solar farms, and on sunny afternoons solar panels now supply a large share of the state's electricity. // Once the electricity is made, it travels along high-voltage power lines that stretch for many miles. Near your neighborhood, a transformer lowers the voltage so the electricity is safe to use in homes. That is why, when a transformer is damaged, a whole street can go dark at once. // Each source of energy has benefits and drawbacks. Fuels like natural gas can make electricity at any hour, while the sun and wind come and go. Engineers are working to build better batteries to store renewable energy for nights and calm days. The goal is electricity that is reliable, affordable and clean.

units.name: Unit 4: Myths and Tales from Many Cultures (narrative writing)
units.el: Use a picture story map for each myth; pre-teach "myth", "goddess", "pride" and "punishment"; invite students to share nature or sky stories told in their families.

passages.x: In ancient Greece, there lived a young woman named Arachne who could weave more beautifully than anyone in the land. Her cloth was so fine that people traveled from distant villages just to watch her work. Her thread seemed to flow like water through her fingers, and the pictures she wove looked almost alive. // "Surely," said the visitors, "the goddess Athena herself must have taught you." // Arachne tossed her head. "No one taught me," she said. "My skill is my own. I am a better weaver than Athena, and I would prove it if she dared to compete with me." // Athena, the goddess of wisdom and of weaving, heard these words. She disguised herself as an old woman and came to Arachne's door. "Child," she said, "be proud of your gift, but do not compare yourself to the gods. Ask Athena's forgiveness, and she may be kind." // Arachne only laughed. "Let Athena come herself, if she is not afraid." // At once the old woman threw off her disguise and stood tall and shining before her. The visitors fell to their knees, but Arachne, though her face went pale, did not back down. The contest began. // Athena wove a tapestry showing the gods in all their glory, and in its corners she wove small scenes of people who had been punished for their pride, as a warning. Arachne wove scenes making fun of the gods' mistakes. Her work was flawless; even Athena could find no error in it. But its message was disrespectful, and the goddess's anger flared. // Athena touched Arachne with her weaving shuttle. Arachne began to shrink. Her arms and legs grew thin and long, and she became the first spider. // "Weave, then," said Athena, "you and all your children, forever." // And that is why, the ancient Greeks said, spiders are always spinning their beautiful webs. Even today, scientists call spiders and their relatives "arachnids," a word that comes from her name.

passages.t: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom
passages.x: This is a retelling of a folktale from the Ashanti people of Ghana, in West Africa. // Long ago, Anansi the spider was given all the wisdom in the world. It came to him in a clay pot, and he was told to share it with everyone. // Anansi peeked into the pot. Inside, he saw how to plant yams, how to build houses, how to cure a fever and how to settle an argument. He saw songs, stories and the secrets of the stars. // "Why should I share this?" Anansi thought. "If I keep all the wisdom for myself, everyone will have to come to me for advice. I will be the most important creature in the world." // So Anansi decided to hide the pot at the top of the tallest tree in the forest, where no one could ever reach it. He tied the pot to his belly with a vine and began to climb. // But the pot was big and round, and it bumped against the trunk with every step. Anansi slipped. He tried again and slipped again. Again and again he tried, huffing and grumbling, and he got no higher than a few feet off the ground. // His young son, Ntikuma, had been watching from below. "Father," he called, "why don't you tie the pot on your back? Then you could hold on to the tree." // Anansi stopped. His son was right. Ntikuma was only a child, and he had never looked inside the pot, yet he had found the answer Anansi could not. // Anansi felt foolish, then angry, then foolish again. "I carry all the wisdom in the world," he cried, "and a little boy still knows something I do not!" // In his frustration, he let go of the pot. It fell, struck a rock and cracked open. A wind blew through the forest and scattered the wisdom in every direction. // And that is why, the storytellers say, no one has all the wisdom in the world. Everyone has a little piece, and people must share what they know.

Thousands of years ago, the people of ancient Greece and Rome told stories about gods, goddesses and heroes. These stories, called myths, tried to explain things people wondered about, such as why the seasons change or where thunder comes from. The ancient Greek and Roman worlds are long gone, but their myths live on in a surprising place: the words we use every day. // Have you ever heard someone call a hard job a "Herculean task"? In Greek myths, the hero Heracles, whom the Romans called Hercules, was famous for his great strength. As a punishment, he had to complete twelve nearly impossible labors, such as capturing a fierce lion and cleaning enormous stables in a single day. Today, a Herculean task is any job that takes enormous effort. // Another hero, Achilles, was said to be impossible to hurt, except in one spot. When he was a baby, his mother dipped him in a magic river to protect him, but she held him by the heel, so the water never touched that spot. Today, a person's "Achilles' heel" is their one weakness. // Some words come from myths about nature. The nymph Echo was cursed so that she could only repeat the last words other people said. Now an echo is a sound that bounces back to us. The god Pan, who watched over shepherds and wild places, was said to fill travelers with sudden fear. From his name we get the word "panic." // Even breakfast has a myth inside it. Ceres was the Roman goddess of grain and harvests, and her name gave us the word "cereal." // When you meet one of these words, you are hearing an echo, so to speak, of stories told long ago. Knowing the myth behind a word can help you understand what it means.

On a clear night far from city lights, you can see thousands of stars. Long before telescopes, people all over the world looked up at the same stars and connected them into pictures. They told stories about these pictures, and the stories helped them remember the patterns, mark the seasons and find their way. // Take the seven bright stars that many Americans call the Big Dipper. To people in ancient Greece, these stars were part of a much larger pattern, the Great Bear. In England, the same seven stars are often called the Plough, because they look like an old farm tool. In India, they have long been known as the Saptarishi, or the Seven Sages, wise men from ancient stories. Among the Mi'kmaq and several other Native nations of northeastern North America, the four stars of the bowl are a bear, and the stars of the handle are hunters chasing it. As the bear circles through the sky during the year, the story changes with it, so the sky becomes a kind of calendar. // Another group of stars, a small, misty cluster, has been named again and again. The ancient Greeks called it the Seven Sisters and told a myth about sisters who were placed in the sky. In Japan, the cluster is called Subaru, a name now used by a car company whose logo shows the stars. Many farming peoples watched for this cluster to know when to plant. // Why did so many cultures tell sky stories? One reason is that the stars move in a regular way through the year. A story made the patterns easier to remember, and remembering them helped people track time and find their way. // Today, scientists divide the sky into 88 official constellations, many with Greek and Roman names. But the older stories have not disappeared. Each one shows how a group of people looked at the same sky and found meaning in it.

In ancient Greece, people told this story to explain why the earth turns cold and bare each year. // Demeter was the goddess of the harvest. Wherever she walked, wheat ripened, fruit swelled on the branches and flowers opened. She loved nothing in the world more than her daughter, Persephone, who spent her days gathering flowers in the sunny meadows. // One day, Hades, the god of the underworld, saw Persephone in the meadow. He drove his black chariot up through a crack in the earth, swept her away and carried her down to his dark kingdom to be his queen. // When Demeter discovered her daughter was gone, her grief was terrible. She wandered the earth searching for Persephone, and she stopped caring for the crops. Without her, the fields turned brown. Leaves fell from the trees. Frost covered the ground, and nothing would grow. People grew hungry, and they begged the gods for help. // At last Zeus, the king of the gods, ordered Hades to return Persephone to her mother. But there was a problem. In the underworld, Persephone had eaten six seeds from a pomegranate, and anyone who ate the food of the underworld was bound to it. // So the gods made an agreement. Persephone would spend six months of every year with her mother on the earth, and six months, one for each seed, in the underworld with Hades. // And so it has been ever since, the Greeks said. When Persephone returns each spring, Demeter rejoices. Flowers bloom, crops grow and the world is warm and green. But when Persephone goes back to the underworld, Demeter grieves, and the earth turns cold until her daughter returns.

Long ago, people told myths to explain why the weather changes through the year. Today, scientists can explain the seasons another way, using what we know about Earth and the sun. // Earth travels around the sun in a path called an orbit. One full trip takes about 365 days, or one year. At the same time, Earth spins like a top around an imaginary line called its axis. Here is the key fact: Earth's axis is not straight up and down. It is tilted, or tipped, at an angle of about 23 degrees. // Because of this tilt, different parts of Earth lean toward the sun at different times of the year. From about June through August, the northern half of Earth, where California is, leans toward the sun. Sunlight hits it more directly, like a flashlight shining straight down, and the days are long. That is summer. Six months later, Earth is on the other side of its orbit. Now the northern half leans away from the sun. Sunlight hits it at a low slant, spreading out over a wider area, and the days are short. That is winter. // Many people think summer happens because Earth is closer to the sun. Surprisingly, that is not true. Earth is actually a little closer to the sun in early January, during winter in the north! The tilt matters much more than the distance. // The tilt also explains why seasons are opposite in the two halves of the world. When it is summer in California, it is winter in Argentina and Australia, which are in the southern half of Earth. Children there may celebrate the new year in the middle of a hot summer. // The ancient Greeks did not know about Earth's tilt, but they noticed the same pattern we do: the world grows cold, then warm, then cold again, year after year. Their myth and our science both try to answer the same question.

test.q: Narrative writing: Write your own myth that explains something in nature, such as why the moon changes shape or why the wind blows. Like "Persephone and the Seasons," include characters with strong feelings, a problem, events that build to a solution, and an ending that explains the natural event. test.ans: Sample opening and key points: "Long ago, the Moon was a proud girl who wore a silver gown that glowed every night..." units.name: Unit 5: Earth's Changing Surface (informative writing)
units.el: Use photos and simple diagrams of a fault, a volcano and a canyon; act out "drop, cover and hold on"; give the cause-and-effect frame "Because ___, ___."

passages.x: The first thing Leilani noticed was the fish tank. The water in it began to slosh from side to side, as if an invisible hand were stirring it. Then the windows rattled, and a low rumble, like a truck passing too close, filled Room 9. // "Earthquake!" someone shouted. // For one frozen second, Leilani could not move. Pencils rolled off desks. The map on the wall swung on its hook. Then Ms. Ortiz's calm voice cut through the noise: "Drop, cover and hold on!" // Leilani's body remembered what to do before her brain did. She dropped to her knees, crawled under her desk and grabbed one of its metal legs with both hands. The desk shook against her palms. Across the aisle, Dylan, the new boy who had just moved from Ohio, was standing in the middle of the room with his mouth open. // "Dylan!" Leilani called. "Get under your desk! Hold the leg!" // Dylan blinked, then dove under his desk. // The shaking lasted only about ten seconds, but it felt like ten minutes. Then, as suddenly as it had started, it stopped. The fish tank sloshed a few more times and went still. Somewhere down the hall, a little kid was crying. // Ms. Ortiz counted heads. Everyone was fine. A few books had fallen, and the class's tomato plant had tipped over, spilling dirt across the windowsill. // On the way outside to the field, Dylan walked next to Leilani. His face was pale. "We never had one in my town in Ohio," he said. "I didn't know what to do." // "Nobody knows the first time," Leilani said. She didn't tell him that her own hands were still shaking. "That's why we practice. Next time, you'll know." // Dylan nodded. Then he almost smiled. "Thanks for yelling at me." // "Anytime," said Leilani.

Keoni stood at the edge of the black rock field and frowned. "This is it?" he asked. "It looks like a giant parking lot that nobody finished." // His grandmother laughed. She was leaning on her walking stick, the wind from the ocean tugging at her flowered shirt. "Look closer," she said. // Keoni crouched down. Up close, the rock was not flat at all. It was wrinkled and twisted into ropes and folds, like frosting someone had smeared with a knife and left to harden. In a crack between two ropes, a tiny fern had pushed up its bright green leaves. // "When I was a girl," Tutu said, "there was a road here. And a store that sold shave ice, and a beach with black sand where your great-uncle and I used to swim." // Keoni looked up. "What happened to it?" // "The volcano happened." She pointed her stick toward the long, gentle slope of the mountain rising behind them, its top hidden in clouds. "One spring, the lava came down slowly, slowly, for months. You could feel the heat on your face from far away. It covered the road. It covered the store. It went all the way into the ocean, hissing and steaming, and when it cooled, the shore was farther out than before." // "You lost your beach," Keoni said quietly. // "I did," said Tutu. "I cried about it for a long time." She tapped the rock with her stick. "But look at this. Our island is still being born. Every new flow makes new land. And already the plants are moving in." // Keoni touched the tiny fern with one finger. He thought about the store and the beach buried beneath his feet, and about the new shore stretching out into the waves. // "It's sad and amazing at the same time," he said. // His grandmother put her arm around his shoulders. "That," she said, "is exactly what it is."

Some changes to Earth's surface happen in seconds, like an earthquake. Others happen so slowly that you would never notice them in a lifetime. Yet these slow changes, called weathering and erosion, have carved some of the most famous landforms on the planet. // Weathering is the breaking down of rock into smaller pieces. One cause of weathering is ice. When rain trickles into a crack in a rock and then freezes, the water expands, pushing the crack a little wider. After the ice melts and refreezes again and again, the rock can split apart. Plant roots cause weathering, too. A tree root growing into a crack can slowly pry a boulder open. // Erosion is what happens next. Erosion is the moving of broken rock and soil from one place to another. Moving water is the most powerful cause of erosion. Rivers carry sand and pebbles downstream, and as the pebbles tumble along, they scrape the riverbed deeper. Wind blows sand across deserts, and ocean waves wear away cliffs along the shore. // Glaciers, huge slow-moving rivers of ice, cause erosion as well. As a glacier creeps downhill, it picks up rocks and drags them along, grinding the land beneath it. Long ago, glaciers helped shape California's Yosemite Valley, scraping it into a wide U shape with steep granite walls. // Given enough time, weathering and erosion can create enormous landforms. The Grand Canyon in Arizona was carved mainly by the Colorado River over millions of years. Layer by layer, the river cut down through the rock until the canyon was more than a mile deep. // The rock you stand on today may seem permanent. But water, ice, wind and plants are always at work on it, slowly changing the shape of the land.

Most people think of volcanoes as faraway mountains in places like Hawaii or Iceland. But California has volcanoes, too, and one of them erupted a little more than a hundred years ago. // A volcano forms where melted rock from deep inside Earth reaches the surface. Underground, this melted rock is called magma. Because magma is hotter and lighter than the solid rock around it, it slowly rises through cracks. Magma also holds gases, like the bubbles in a bottle of soda. When pressure builds up, the gases can burst out with great force, causing an eruption. Once magma flows out onto the surface, it is called lava. As layers of lava and ash pile up eruption after eruption, a volcano grows into a mountain. // In May 1915, Lassen Peak in Northern California exploded. A tall column of ash and gas rose miles into the sky, and ash drifted down on towns many miles to the east. Hot rock melted snow on the mountain, sending a mudflow rushing down the valleys and knocking down trees. Few people lived nearby, and no one was killed, but the eruptions changed the land. The next year, the area became Lassen Volcanic National Park so that people could study and enjoy it. // Lassen is not California's only volcano. Mount Shasta, a huge snowy peak, is also a volcano, and scientists consider both mountains active, even though they are quiet now. Scientists watch them with instruments that measure small earthquakes and changes in the ground. These signals can warn that magma is moving. // Volcanoes are dangerous, but they also help the land. Over time, volcanic ash and rock break down into rich soil, and some of the world's best farmland lies near old volcanoes. California's sleeping giants are a reminder that our planet is still changing beneath our feet.

Every October, on the morning of the statewide earthquake drill, Grandpa Hiro pulled the green plastic tub out from under the stairs and set it on the kitchen table. And every October, Emi rolled her eyes. // "We check it every year," she said. "Nothing ever changes." // "Something always changes," said Grandpa. He snapped open the lid. Inside were water bottles, cans of beans and peaches, a can opener, a flashlight, a first-aid kit, a radio with a crank on the side and a whistle on a string. // He handed Emi the flashlight. She clicked it. Nothing. // "Dead batteries," Grandpa said. "You see? Something always changes." // Emi sighed and found new batteries in the junk drawer. Grandpa checked the dates on the water bottles and set aside the cans that were too old. Then he pulled out a plastic bag with a small photo inside. It showed a much younger Grandpa standing in front of a building with a cracked wall and a broken chimney. // "Where is this?" Emi asked. // "San Francisco, 1989," he said. "I was at work when the Loma Prieta earthquake hit. The power was out for days. People who had water and flashlights shared with their neighbors. People who didn't had to wait in long lines." He tapped the photo. "I keep this in here to remind me why we check." // Emi was quiet for a moment. Then she picked up the crank radio and turned the handle. A crackle of static, then a voice reading the weather, filled the kitchen. // "It works," she said. // "Good," said Grandpa. "Now, what's missing?" // Emi looked into the tub. She thought about her cat, Mochi, curled up on the windowsill. "Cat food," she said. "And Mochi's medicine." // Grandpa smiled and wrote it on the list. "You see?" he said. "Something always changes."

California has thousands of earthquakes every year. Most are so small that no one feels them, but every so often a large one shakes the ground hard enough to knock down buildings. Why does California have so many earthquakes? The answer lies deep beneath our feet. // Earth's outer layer is broken into giant pieces called plates. These plates fit together like the pieces of a cracked eggshell, and they move very slowly, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Where two plates meet, their edges grind against each other. // California sits right on the boundary between two of these plates: the Pacific Plate and the North American Plate. The two plates slide past each other along a crack in Earth's crust called the San Andreas Fault, which runs for more than 700 miles through the state. The plates do not slide smoothly. Their rough edges catch and lock together while the rest of each plate keeps moving. Pressure builds up for years, or even hundreds of years. When the rocks finally slip, the stored energy is released all at once as an earthquake. // Some of California's earthquakes have become famous. The 1906 earthquake on the San Andreas Fault and the fires that followed destroyed much of San Francisco. In 1989, the Loma Prieta earthquake struck the San Francisco Bay Area just before a World Series baseball game, damaging bridges and freeways. // Scientists cannot predict exactly when an earthquake will happen. But they have built a warning system that uses sensors to detect an earthquake as it begins. Because these signals travel faster than the strongest shaking, the system can send an alert to phones a few seconds before the shaking arrives, enough time to drop, cover and hold on. // Earthquakes are part of life in California. Understanding why they happen helps Californians prepare for the next one.

test.q: Informative writing: Explain why earthquakes happen in California and how people can prepare for them. Write at least three paragraphs with an introduction, body paragraphs with facts and examples from both passages, transition words and a conclusion.
test.ans: Sample key points: The introduction says California has thousands of earthquakes a year. Body 1: Earth's outer layer is made of moving plates; the Pacific and North American plates slide past each other along the San Andreas Fault, lock together, build pressure and then slip, releasing energy as an earthquake. Body 2: the 1906 earthquake and the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake show the damage quakes can cause, including days without power. Body 3: people prepare by keeping a kit with water, food, a flashlight, a crank radio and first aid, checking it every year as Grandpa Hiro does, practicing drop, cover and hold on, and using phone alerts from the warning system. The conclusion says that understanding earthquakes helps Californians stay safe.
rub: Clear focus and strong organization; ideas fully developed with relevant details or text evidence; precise language; few errors in conventions.
Clear focus and organization; ideas adequately developed with some details or evidence; some errors that do not affect meaning.
Focus or organization is inconsistent; limited development or evidence; errors sometimes interfere with meaning.
Little focus or organization; minimal development; frequent errors.

units.name: Unit 6: Animal Survival and Adaptations (opinion writing)
units.el: Show photos or short videos of each animal; pre-teach "adaptation", "predator", "prey" and "survive"; use homophone picture cards (their, there, they're; to, too, two).

passages.x: The gophers were winning. Every morning, Marisol's father walked the rows of the family's vineyard near Lodi and found new mounds of fresh dirt and another young grapevine wilting where its roots had been chewed away. // "Poison would be quicker," said Mr. Alvarez from the farm next door, leaning on the fence. // Papa shook his head. "Poison can hurt the hawks and owls that eat the gophers, and the neighbors' cats too. I want a helper, not a poison." // That weekend, Papa and Marisol built the helper's house: a wooden box about the size of a suitcase, with a round hole in the front. They bolted it to the top of a tall pole at the edge of the vineyard. // "Who's going to live there?" Marisol asked. // "Barn owls, if we're lucky," Papa said. "A family of barn owls can eat hundreds of gophers and mice in a year." // For weeks, the box stayed empty. Marisol checked it every afternoon after school. Mr. Alvarez chuckled every time he saw her looking up. "Still waiting for your tenants?" he called. // Then, one evening in March, Marisol was carrying the trash out when a pale shape drifted over her head without a sound. It was white underneath, with a heart-shaped face that glowed in the dusk. It swooped low over the vines, dropped into the grass and rose again with something small and wriggling in its talons. Then it flew straight into the box. // Marisol ran inside so fast she forgot to close the door. "Papa! An owl! It moved in!" // By summer, there were five fuzzy owlets peering out of the box, hissing like tiny teakettles whenever their parents brought food. The new gopher mounds grew fewer and fewer. // One evening, Mr. Alvarez stood at the fence watching the owls hunt. He was quiet for a long time. Then he turned to Marisol. // "So," he said, rubbing his chin, "how big did you say that box was?"

Every year, the weekend after Thanksgiving, Ava and her grandmother drove to a grove of tall trees near the beach in Pismo to count monarch butterflies. // The first year Ava came, when she was six, the branches had been so crowded with monarchs that they looked like they were covered in dull brown leaves. Then the sun came out, and the "leaves" opened their wings all at once, flashing orange. Ava had gasped so loudly that a stranger laughed. // This year, Ava was ten, and she had brought a clipboard. Grandma Ruth showed her how to count: find a cluster, count the butterflies in a small part of it, then estimate how many parts the cluster had. // They counted for an hour. When they finished, Ava stared at the number on her clipboard. It was much smaller than she remembered. // "Where did they go?" she asked. // Grandma Ruth sighed. "Monarchs have had a hard time. Their caterpillars can only eat milkweed, and a lot of milkweed has been plowed under or sprayed. The butterflies need flowers for nectar on their long trip, too. When there's not enough food along the way, fewer of them make it here." // Ava looked up at the thin clusters hanging in the branches. She thought about a butterfly flying hundreds of miles and finding nothing to eat. Her throat felt tight. // "Can we do anything?" she asked. // "We can," said Grandma. "Scientists say planting native milkweed and flowers helps. Every garden is like a rest stop on the highway." // All winter, Ava saved her allowance. In March, she and Grandma planted twelve native milkweed plants along the back fence, plus purple sage and yellow goldenrod for nectar. // In June, Ava found a small striped caterpillar munching on a milkweed leaf. She crouched beside it for so long that her legs fell asleep. // "Welcome," she whispered. "Maybe your great-grandchildren will see me in Pismo."

passages.t: The Kangaroo Rat: A Desert Survivor
passages.x: In the deserts of Southern California, summer days can be blistering hot, and months may pass without rain. Most animals would not last long there without water. Yet one small rodent, the kangaroo rat, thrives in these harsh places. It has several adaptations, or special features and behaviors, that help it survive. // First, the kangaroo rat can live its whole life without drinking water. It eats dry seeds, and its body makes water as it breaks the seeds down for energy. This may sound impossible, but it works because the kangaroo rat is also very good at saving water. Its kidneys are so efficient that very little water leaves its body. // Second, the kangaroo rat avoids the heat. During the day, it stays in a cool burrow underground, often plugging the entrance with soil to keep out the hot, dry air. It comes out to look for seeds at night, when the desert is cooler. Inside the burrow, it stores seeds it has gathered, so it can stay hidden for long periods. // Third, the kangaroo rat's body helps it escape from predators such as owls, snakes and coyotes. It has huge back legs and a long tail with a tuft at the end. Like a kangaroo, it hops on its back legs, and it can leap several feet in a single bound, changing direction in midair. Its tail helps it balance. Its large eyes and sharp hearing help it notice danger in the dark. // Each of these adaptations helps the kangaroo rat survive where water is scarce and danger is everywhere. Scientists study kangaroo rats to learn how animals save water, a lesson that matters more and more as California faces dry years. This tiny desert hopper proves that you do not have to be big to be tough.

When a squirrel sits up and begs at a picnic table, it is hard to resist tossing it a cracker. When ducks paddle toward you at the pond, bread seems like a friendly gift. But feeding wild animals, even when it feels kind, does far more harm than good. People should never feed wildlife. // The first reason is that human food is unhealthy for wild animals. Their bodies are adapted to eat the foods found in nature, such as seeds, insects, plants and fish. Bread fills up ducks without giving them the nutrients they need, and salty or sugary snacks can make animals sick. An animal that fills up on chips may not eat the foods it actually needs. // The second reason is that fed animals lose their natural fear of people, and that makes them dangerous. A squirrel or raccoon that expects food may bite a hand that does not offer any. Larger animals are an even bigger problem. In Yosemite National Park, black bears that learned to get human food began breaking into cars and cabins. Bears that become too bold sometimes have to be killed to protect people. Park rangers have a saying: "A fed bear is a dead bear." // The third reason is that feeding animals changes how they live. When animals crowd together where people feed them, diseases can spread more easily among them, and the animals can become dependent on handouts instead of finding food on their own. // Some people argue that feeding animals helps them survive hard winters. But wild animals have survived for thousands of years without our help. The best way to help them is to protect the places where they find their natural food. // Next time a squirrel begs, admire it, take a picture and keep your snack to yourself. Keeping wildlife wild is the kindest choice.

The pup was found alone on a beach near Santa Cruz during a February storm, crying in a high, thin voice like a seagull. Volunteers named her by her number: Pup 719. // Jada's mom was one of the volunteers. She worked at an aquarium that cared for stranded sea otter pups, and on Saturdays Jada was allowed to watch from behind the glass. // "Why can't you just keep her?" Jada asked the first time she saw the pup, a ball of brown fluff floating on her back in a small pool. "She's so cute." // "That's exactly the problem," Mom said. "If people raise her, she'll learn to trust people instead of learning to be an otter. She'll never survive in the wild." // So the aquarium had a plan. Pup 719 would be raised by Juno, an adult female otter who lived at the aquarium and could not be released. Juno would teach the pup everything: how to groom her thick fur so it stayed waterproof, how to dive, how to crack open a crab with a rock. // To keep the pup from getting used to humans, the staff who fed her wore dark ponchos, welding masks and gloves. Jada thought they looked like strange robots. // Weeks went by. Pup 719 grew sleek and quick. Jada watched her twirl in the water, scrubbing her fur with her paws just as Juno did. Once, Jada saw her bang a clam against a rock on her chest until it cracked. Jada cheered so loudly that the otter looked up, and Mom gave her a look. // In August, Jada stood with Mom on a dock in Elkhorn Slough. A crate opened, and Pup 719 slid into the water. She floated for a moment, looking around. Then she dove and disappeared. // Jada felt a pang. "She didn't even say goodbye." // Mom squeezed her hand. "That's how you know she's ready," she said.

passages.t: Sea Otters: Small Animals with a Big Job
passages.x: Floating on its back in a bed of seaweed, a sea otter looks like it has nothing to do but nap. In fact, this furry animal has one of the most important jobs on the California coast. // Unlike whales and seals, sea otters have no thick layer of fat to keep them warm in cold ocean water. Instead, they have the densest fur of any animal, with up to a million hairs in a single square inch. To stay warm, otters must keep their fur clean and fluffy, so they spend hours each day grooming. They also need a lot of energy. A sea otter eats about one quarter of its body weight in food every day, diving for crabs, clams, snails and sea urchins. // Those sea urchins are the key to the otters' big job. Sea urchins are spiny animals that eat kelp, the giant seaweed that forms underwater forests along the coast. Kelp forests are home to hundreds of kinds of fish and other sea life. When there are no otters, sea urchins can multiply and chew through the kelp until a forest becomes a bare, rocky "urchin barren." By eating urchins, otters help keep kelp forests healthy. Scientists call an animal with such a large effect on its ecosystem a keystone species. // Sea otters were nearly wiped out in the 1700s and 1800s, when hunters killed them by the thousands for their valuable fur. By the early 1900s, many people thought California's otters were gone. Then, in 1938, a small group was spotted near Big Sur. Laws now protect them, and today about 3,000 southern sea otters live along the central California coast. // That is still far fewer than once lived here. Oil spills, disease and shark bites threaten them. Scientists and aquariums are working to help the population grow, because when otters thrive, the whole kelp forest thrives with them.

test.ans: Sample: People should spend time and money protecting sea otters. First, otters keep the ocean healthy. The article explains that otters eat sea urchins, which would otherwise chew through kelp forests that are home to hundreds of kinds of sea life, so otters are a keystone species. Second, the otter population is still small. Hunters nearly wiped them out, and today only about 3,000 southern sea otters live along the coast, threatened by oil spills and disease. Programs like the one in "Pup 719," where an adult otter teaches a stranded pup to groom, dive and crack shells before it is released, give each otter a chance to survive. Some people might say the money should be spent on people instead, but healthy kelp forests also support the fish that people catch and eat. For these reasons, protecting sea otters is worth it.
