passages.x: When the sun slips down behind the hills / and the parking lot turns blue, / my father strings the paper lamps / and the market wakes up new. // The grills begin their hissing song, / the smoke curls up like thread, / and Auntie Lin is folding dumplings / as soft as pillows on a bed. // I stack the cups and count the change, / I wipe the counter clean; / my little brother hands out napkins, / the proudest worker ever seen. // The crowd moves in, a river of people, / it rushes and it bends, / with grandmas pushing shopping carts / and teenagers with friends. // A drummer taps on plastic buckets, / a baby laughs nearby, / the mango slices glow like sunsets / stacked up three feet high. // The air is thick with garlic, ginger, / with sugar, salt and lime; / I'd know this smell with my eyes shut / in any place or time. // "Two skewers, please!" "Extra spicy!" / "Do you have any more?" / My father's hands are quick as sparrows; / he's done this all before. // By midnight all the lamps are dimming, / the grills are cooling down, / the river of people trickles home / across the sleepy town. // My feet are sore, my apron's sticky, / my eyes are full of sand, / but my father squeezes my shoulder / with his warm and smoky hand. // "Good work," he says. Two words. That's all. / But I carry them like gold / the whole way home, beneath the stars, / through the night so clear and cold.

Read these two poems. Each one is spoken by a different person on the same rainy morning. // THE FARMER SPEAKS OF RAIN // Come down, come down, you silver rain, / I've waited months for you. / My fields are cracked like an old man's hands, / my sky a hard, hot blue. // Come soak the roots of my almond trees, / come fill my empty pond, / come drum upon my dusty roof / and the thirsty hills beyond. // I'll stand outside in my muddy boots / and lift my face up high, / and let you run like a cool, clean river / from my hat brim past my eye. // Come down, come down, you silver rain, / stay all night and all day. / A farmer never says to you, / "Rain, rain, go away." // SATURDAY RAIN // Not today, rain! Not today! / The soccer game's at ten. / I've had my cleats on since six o'clock, / and now you're here again. // You tap the window, tap tap tap, / as if you've come to play. / You turn the field to chocolate pudding / and wash my game away. // Mom says the garden needs a drink, / Dad says the hills turn green, / but all I see is a puddle where / my goal should have been. // So go and visit the farmer's fields; / I hear he's begging you to stay. / Just let me have my Saturday, / then rain all Sunday, okay?

passages.t: Juan Felipe Herrera: A Poet from the Fields
passages.x: Juan Felipe Herrera was born in 1948 in Fowler, California, a small farm town in the Central Valley. His parents were farmworkers who had come from Mexico, and the family moved often, following the crops from harvest to harvest. Sometimes they lived in a trailer; sometimes they lived in a tent by the side of the road. // Moving so much was hard. Juan Felipe changed schools many times. When he started school, he spoke mostly Spanish, and he felt shy and unsure of his English. But his mother loved words. She sang songs, recited poems and told stories about her childhood in Mexico. From her, Juan Felipe learned that language could be beautiful and full of feeling. // A turning point came in third grade. His teacher asked him to sing a song in front of the class. Nervously, he sang. When he finished, his teacher told him he had a beautiful voice. Herrera later said those few kind words gave him the courage to believe in himself. // As he grew up, Herrera wrote poems about the people and places he knew: farmworkers, families, city streets and the colorful mix of cultures in California. He often wrote in both English and Spanish. He went to college, became a teacher and wrote many books for adults and children, including picture books about his own childhood in the fields. // In 2012, Herrera was named California's Poet Laureate, an honored poet chosen to share poetry with the people of the state. Then, in 2015, he became the Poet Laureate of the United States, the first Latino poet to hold that honor. He used the role to invite people of all ages to write poems together. // Herrera's life shows that a voice that begins quietly can grow strong enough to be heard across a whole nation.

Some poems fill pages. A haiku fits in a single breath. // Haiku is a form of poetry that began in Japan hundreds of years ago. One of the most famous haiku poets, Matsuo Basho, lived in the 1600s. He traveled across Japan on foot, writing short poems about what he saw: a frog jumping into an old pond, the moon over a field, a crow on a bare branch. // In Japanese, a traditional haiku has seventeen sound units arranged in three parts. When people write haiku in English, they often use three lines with five syllables, then seven, then five. Here is an example: // Gray fog on the bay / a pelican folds its wings / and drops like a stone // Count the syllables, and you will find 5, 7 and 5. // But a good haiku is more than counting. Most haiku focus on nature and capture one small moment, like a photograph made of words. Many include a word that hints at the season, such as "snow," "cherry blossoms" or "crickets." Haiku also often place two images side by side and let the reader feel the connection between them. In the example above, the quiet fog and the sudden dive of the pelican surprise us when they appear together. // Because haiku are so short, every word matters. Poets cut out extra words, such as "the" and "very," and choose precise nouns and verbs. Instead of writing "a bird goes down fast," a poet writes "a pelican drops like a stone." // Haiku are popular in classrooms because anyone can try writing one. All you need is to slow down and notice something: a spider web full of dew, a shadow on the sidewalk, the first warm day of spring. Then shape what you noticed into three short lines. You may be surprised how much a tiny poem can hold.

I knew the wind was too strong the moment we got to the park. The trees were bending like they were bowing to someone important, and my little sister Bea's hair was whipping across her face. But Bea had begged all week to fly the new dragon kite I got for my birthday, and I had promised. // "Just hold the string tight," I told her. "Really tight." // The kite shot up so fast that the string burned through my fingers. Up and up it climbed, its long red tail flicking like a real dragon's. Bea squealed and grabbed the string from me. "My turn!" // For about ten seconds, she was the happiest person in the world. Then a gust slammed into the kite, and the string slipped right out of her hands. // We both watched it go. It sailed over the baseball field, over the parking lot and right into the top of the tallest eucalyptus tree in the whole park. // I didn't say anything. I couldn't. My birthday kite, the one I'd saved my own money to add a tail to, was hanging forty feet up in a tree, and it was never coming down. // Bea's chin started to wobble. "I'm sorry, Nico," she whispered. "I'm so, so sorry." // Part of me wanted to yell, "I told you to hold it tight!" But then I looked at her face. She looked the way I felt the time I broke Dad's favorite mug, like the whole world had ended and it was all my fault. // So I took a breath. "It's okay," I said, even though it wasn't, exactly. "At least the dragon gets to live in a tree now. Dragons like high places." // Bea laughed a soggy laugh and wiped her nose on her sleeve. We walked home holding hands, and I didn't look back at the tree. Not even once.

Bea had been waiting all week. Every day after school, she had asked Nico, "Is it windy enough yet?" and every day he had said, "Not yet." On Saturday, the trees in the park were swaying and the flags at the baseball field were snapping, and Bea was sure that today was the day. // Nico didn't look so sure. He frowned up at the sky. He told her three times to hold the string tight. Bea nodded every time, but she was barely listening. She was watching the dragon kite climb, its red tail twisting against the clouds. It was the most beautiful thing she had ever seen. // When Nico finally let her hold it, the string tugged at her hands like a puppy pulling on a leash. Bea laughed out loud. She felt as if she were flying too. // Then the wind gave a hard yank, and the string was gone. // Bea stared at her empty hands. She could not believe how fast it had happened. By the time she looked up, the kite was tangled in the very top of a giant eucalyptus tree, and her brother was standing perfectly still, staring at it. // He did not say a word, and that was worse than yelling. Bea knew that he had saved his own money for that tail. She felt her eyes burning. "I'm sorry," she whispered. // Nico was quiet for a long moment. Then he said the dragon would like living in a tree, because dragons like high places. Bea knew he was only saying it to make her feel better. That was what made her laugh, even though she was crying. // On the way home, she held his hand the whole time. She decided right then that she would save her allowance until she could buy him a new kite, one with an even longer tail.

units.name: Unit 8: The California Gold Rush (opinion writing)
units.el: Show a map of routes to California (around South America, across Panama, overland) and photos of a pan, rocker and hydraulic mining scars; give the frame "One reason ___ is ___. For example, ___."

passages.x: In the spring of 1850, Clara Mendes and her mother arrived in the mining camp at Coloma with two trunks, a small iron stove and one sack of dried apples. Clara's father had come to California a year earlier to dig for gold. In his letters he had written that he would soon be rich. Instead, his last letter said he had found only enough gold to buy beans. // Clara looked around at the tents flapping in the wind, the muddy street and the men in torn shirts hurrying toward the river with picks and pans. "Where's all the gold?" she asked. // "In the river, mostly," said her father. "And in the pockets of anyone smart enough to sell the miners what they need." // Mama was already rolling up her sleeves. That night she baked six apple pies in the little stove. In the morning, Clara carried them through camp on a wooden board, calling, "Fresh pies! Apple pies!" // The miners stared as if they had seen a ghost. Most of them had not tasted pie since they left home. One man with a gray beard bought a whole pie and ate it standing in the street, his eyes closed. Another paid her with a pinch of gold dust from a leather pouch. By noon, all six pies were gone. // Every day after that, Mama baked more pies, and Clara sold them. Flour was expensive, and eggs sometimes cost a dollar each, but the miners paid gladly. By the end of the summer, the Mendes family had saved more gold from pies than Papa had found in a whole year at the river. // One evening, Papa sat on an overturned bucket and laughed until he wiped his eyes. "I came all this way to dig for gold," he said, "and it was in your mother's kitchen the whole time." // Clara grinned. She was thinking that the real treasure might be something else: the three of them, together, at the end of a long day.

This is a work of historical fiction written as a letter. // Weaverville, California, October 1852 // Dear Mother, // I hope this letter finds you and Grandfather well. I am sending it with Uncle Fong's cousin, who is sailing home next week, along with forty dollars in gold for the family. Please buy rice and pay what we owe for the roof. // You asked what Gold Mountain is like. It is not a mountain made of gold, as the men in our village said. It is a land of steep hills, cold rivers and dark pine forests. In the morning, the river fog is so thick I cannot see my own feet. // Our company of twelve works a claim on the creek that other miners left behind. They said it was played out, which means they thought no gold was left. But we are patient. We dig deeper and wash the gravel more carefully than they did, and each day we find a little gold. Not a lot. A little. // The work is hard. I stand in the icy water from sunrise until dark, rocking the wooden cradle that washes the gravel. My hands are cracked, and my back aches like an old man's. Every month we must also pay a tax that only foreign miners pay. Some men here are unkind to us because we look and speak differently. I keep my head down and work. // But there are good things, too. In the evenings, we cook together, and Lee Sam plays his flute, and for a little while the songs carry me home. I have learned many English words. A storekeeper named Mr. Harlan treats us fairly, and he says my English is better than his handwriting. // Do not worry about me, Mother. I eat well enough, and I remember everything you taught me. One more year, perhaps two, and I will come home. // Your son, // Wing

ACCOUNT 1: THE DISCOVERER REMEMBERS // In January 1848, James Marshall was building a sawmill for John Sutter on the American River at Coloma. Years later, he described the moment he found gold. This is adapted from his own account, published in 1857: // "One morning in January, it was a clear, cold morning, I shall never forget that morning, as I was taking my usual walk along the race after shutting off the water, my eye was caught with the glimpse of something shining in the bottom of the ditch. There was about a foot of water running then. I reached my hand down and picked it up; it made my heart thump, for I was certain it was gold. The piece was about half the size and of the shape of a pea." // ACCOUNT 2: A HISTORY OF THE DISCOVERY // On January 24, 1848, a carpenter named James Marshall noticed shiny flakes in the channel of water, called a tailrace, below the sawmill he was building at Coloma. Marshall and the workers tested the flakes. They bit them, hammered them flat and boiled one in lye soap. The metal did not break or darken, so they believed it was gold. // Sutter wanted to keep the discovery a secret so his workers would not leave to dig for gold. But news spread. In May 1848, a San Francisco merchant named Sam Brannan walked through the streets holding up a bottle of gold dust and shouting about gold on the American River. Soon thousands of people were heading for the hills. By 1849, people from around the world were rushing to California. They became known as the forty-niners. Neither Marshall nor Sutter became rich from the gold rush.

In 1848, San Francisco was a small town of about a thousand people, with sandy hills, a few wooden buildings and a quiet harbor. Two years later, it was one of the busiest cities on the Pacific Coast. The Gold Rush turned it into a boomtown almost overnight. // Most gold seekers who came by sea arrived in San Francisco first. The trip around South America could take five months or more. When the ships finally dropped anchor, many crews abandoned them and joined the passengers heading to the gold fields. Hundreds of empty ships crowded the harbor. Some were dragged onto the mud flats and turned into stores, a hotel and even a jail. // The city grew so fast that builders could not keep up. People lived in tents and shacks made of canvas and scrap wood. The streets turned to deep mud in winter. Prices soared because goods were scarce and many people had gold to spend. A loaf of bread or a pair of boots could cost many times what it cost back East. // Merchants who sold supplies often did better than the miners. One of them was a young immigrant from Germany named Levi Strauss. He arrived in 1853 and opened a business selling cloth and supplies to stores. Years later, he and a tailor named Jacob Davis began making sturdy work pants strengthened with metal rivets, the ancestors of today's blue jeans. // The rapid growth caused problems, too. Fires swept through the crowded wooden city several times in its first years and destroyed large areas. Each time, the people rebuilt. // By 1850, San Francisco had more than 20,000 residents, and that same year California became the 31st state. The little town on the bay had become the gateway to the West.

The California Gold Rush was one of the most important events in the state's history. In just a few years, it transformed California from a quiet frontier into a booming state that drew people from around the world. // First, the Gold Rush brought an enormous number of new people. In 1848, California had only about 14,000 residents who were not Native American. By 1852, that number had grown to roughly 200,000. People arrived from the eastern United States, Mexico, Chile, China, Europe, Hawaii and many other places. This mix of cultures still shapes California today. // Second, the Gold Rush helped California become a state very quickly. Usually, a territory had to wait many years before joining the United States as a state. But so many people had arrived by 1849 that Californians wrote a state constitution that year, and California became the 31st state in 1850. // Third, gold built the economy. Towns sprang up along rivers, and cities like San Francisco and Sacramento grew rapidly. Merchants, farmers, bankers and builders found work supplying the miners. Farmers discovered that California's soil and climate could grow wheat and fruit in huge amounts, and agriculture became one of the state's most important industries. New roads, a telegraph line and, in 1869, the first transcontinental railroad connected California to the rest of the nation. // The Gold Rush did bring hardships, and few miners struck it rich. Still, the energy and growth it sparked laid the foundation for the California we know: a state of big dreams, many cultures and new ideas.

Stories about the Gold Rush often focus on lucky miners and growing cities. But the rush for gold came with a heavy cost, and many people paid it. // The greatest cost was paid by California's Native peoples. Before the Gold Rush, about 150,000 Native people lived in California. Miners poured onto their lands, cut down trees, dammed rivers and drove away the fish and game that Native families depended on. Diseases spread. Violence against Native people was widespread, and the state government did little to stop it and sometimes even paid for it. Within about twenty years, the Native population had fallen to roughly 30,000. // Immigrant miners also faced unfair treatment. In 1850, California passed a Foreign Miners' Tax that charged miners from other countries twenty dollars a month, a huge sum at the time. The tax drove many Mexican and Chilean miners out of the gold fields. A later version targeted Chinese miners, who were often forced to work claims that others had abandoned. // The land itself was damaged, too. As easy-to-find gold ran out, miners began using hydraulic mining, blasting entire hillsides with powerful jets of water to wash out the gold. Tons of mud and gravel poured into rivers, causing floods and burying farms downstream. The damage was so serious that a court stopped most hydraulic mining in 1884. Scars from that mining can still be seen in the Sierra Nevada foothills today. // Finally, most miners never got rich. Many spent all their savings to reach California, worked in cold rivers for months and went home with little to show for it. // The Gold Rush changed California forever. But when we tell its story, we must remember the people and places that paid the price.

test.ans: California's Native peoples paid the highest price: miners took their land and drove away fish and game, and disease and violence cut their population from about 150,000 to about 30,000. test.q: Opinion writing: Did the Gold Rush do more good or more harm for California? Write an opinion essay of at least four paragraphs. State your opinion, give at least two reasons supported by evidence from both "A Golden Beginning" and "The Cost of Gold," use linking words such as "for example" and "however," respond to the other side, and end with a conclusion.
test.ans: Sample: The Gold Rush did more harm than good for California. First, it was devastating for Native Californians. According to "The Cost of Gold," miners took over their lands and drove away the fish and game they depended on, and their population fell from about 150,000 to roughly 30,000 in about twenty years. Second, it was unfair to many immigrants; for example, the Foreign Miners' Tax charged them twenty dollars a month and drove many Mexican and Chilean miners away. It also damaged the land, since hydraulic mining buried farms in mud. However, "A Golden Beginning" points out that the Gold Rush helped California become a state in 1850 and brought people from many cultures. Those benefits are real, but they came at too high a cost for the people who already lived here. In conclusion, the Gold Rush did more harm than good. (An essay arguing "more good" earns full credit if it uses evidence from both passages and responds to the other side.)
rub: Clear focus and strong organization; ideas fully developed with relevant details or text evidence; precise language; few errors in conventions.

Focus or organization is inconsistent; limited development or evidence; errors sometimes interfere with meaning.
Little focus or organization; minimal development; frequent errors.

units.name: Unit 9: Inventors and Problem Solvers (informative writing)
units.el: Have small groups act out each drama scene; highlight stage directions and dialogue in two colors; keep a roots chart (tele, aud, spect, scrib, graph) with picture examples.

passages.x: A play in one scene. // CAST: ROSA, a fourth grader; DEV, her teammate; MR. KIM, their teacher // SETTING: A classroom on the day of the bridge-building challenge. Two desks are pushed together. On them sits a bridge made of craft sticks and glue. // (MR. KIM places a small bucket on a table at the front of the room.) // MR. KIM: Each team's bridge must hold this bucket while I add pennies, one cup at a time. The bridge that holds the most wins. Rosa and Dev, you're first. // DEV: (whispering) Our bridge is going to be amazing. I can feel it. // ROSA: (nervously) I hope the glue dried. // (MR. KIM hangs the bucket from the middle of their bridge and pours in one cup of pennies. The bridge creaks. He pours in a second cup. With a loud CRACK, the bridge snaps in half. Pennies spill across the floor.) // DEV: (groaning and covering his face) Noooo! Two weeks of work! // ROSA: (kneeling to look at the broken pieces) Wait. Look where it broke, Dev. Right in the middle. // DEV: So? It broke. That's all that matters. // ROSA: No, it matters where. The middle is the weakest part. It had nothing underneath to hold it up. // MR. KIM: (smiling) That's exactly what engineers do, Rosa. They study failures to find out why something didn't work. // DEV: (slowly lowering his hands) So... if we added triangles under the middle, like on that bridge we saw in the book... // ROSA: (excited, grabbing a pencil) Triangles! They don't bend out of shape. We could build a truss! // MR. KIM: Teams who want to rebuild have until Friday. // DEV: (picking up a craft stick and grinning) Friday? We'll be ready by Thursday. // ROSA: (laughing) Let's let the glue dry overnight this time. // (They bend over the desks together, sketching. Lights fade.)

passages.t: The Boy Who Plowed a Picture
passages.x: This scene is based on a story the inventor Philo Farnsworth told about his teenage years. // CAST: PHILO FARNSWORTH, age 15; MR. TOLMAN, his chemistry teacher // SETTING: An empty classroom in Rigby, Idaho, in 1922, after school. A chalkboard covers one wall. // (PHILO bursts in, out of breath, holding a notebook full of drawings.) // PHILO: Mr. Tolman! Do you have a minute? I've been thinking about something all summer. // MR. TOLMAN: (putting down his papers) I always have a minute for an idea. What is it? // PHILO: Pictures. Moving pictures, sent through the air the way radio sends sound. // MR. TOLMAN: (raising his eyebrows) Many grown scientists are working on that, Philo. Most of them use spinning wheels with holes in them. // PHILO: (shaking his head) Spinning parts are too slow and clumsy. I want to do it with electricity alone. (He picks up chalk and begins drawing on the board.) This summer I was plowing the potato field, back and forth, row after row. And I thought, what if a picture could be broken into lines, just like a field? An electric beam could sweep across the picture one line at a time, faster than your eye can see. Then a tube on the other end could paint the lines back in the same order. // (MR. TOLMAN stands and walks slowly to the board. He studies the drawing for a long time.) // MR. TOLMAN: (quietly) Row by row. Like plowing. // PHILO: Exactly! Is it crazy? // MR. TOLMAN: (tapping the board) Some of it I don't understand yet. But it isn't crazy. (He tears a page from his notebook.) Draw it for me again, here, so I can keep it. And Philo, keep working. Don't let anyone tell you that you're too young. // (PHILO grins and begins drawing. Lights fade.) // NARRATOR: In 1927, in a laboratory in San Francisco, Philo Farnsworth sent his first electronic television image: a single straight line.

An engineer is a person who uses science and math to design solutions to problems. Engineers build bridges, design phones, invent medical tools and much more. Although their projects are very different, most engineers follow a similar set of steps called the engineering design process. // Step 1: Define the problem. Engineers start by asking questions. What exactly is the problem? Who has it? What would a good solution need to do? They also list the limits, called constraints, such as how much money they can spend, what materials they can use and how much time they have. // Step 2: Brainstorm and research. Next, engineers gather information and come up with as many ideas as possible. At this stage, no idea is too wild. Often a strange idea leads to a great one. // Step 3: Plan and build a prototype. A prototype is an early model used to test an idea. It does not have to be pretty. Many prototypes are made of cardboard, tape or clay. // Step 4: Test it. Engineers test the prototype to see whether it solves the problem. They measure results and look carefully at what goes wrong. A failure is not the end. It is information. // Step 5: Improve and repeat. Using what they learned, engineers change the design and test again. Most successful inventions go through this cycle many times. That is why the process is often drawn as a circle instead of a straight line. // Think of a team designing a better lunchbox. They might find that the problem is soggy sandwiches. They might try a box with a separate cold section, build one from a shoe box, test it with a real sandwich and discover that the ice pack leaks. Then they would fix the leak and test again. Step by step, the design gets better.

Lonnie Johnson grew up in Mobile, Alabama, in the 1950s and 1960s, taking apart his brothers' and sisters' toys to see how they worked. Sometimes he even put them back together. As a teenager, he built a robot out of scrap metal and parts from an old jukebox. He named it Linex. In 1968, Linex won first place at a science fair at the University of Alabama. At the time, Johnson was one of very few Black students in the contest. // Johnson went on to study engineering in college. He worked for the U.S. Air Force and for NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California, where he helped design power systems for spacecraft, including the Galileo mission to Jupiter. // One night in 1982, Johnson was at home experimenting with a new kind of cooling system that used water instead of harmful chemicals. He attached a nozzle to his bathroom sink and shot a powerful stream of water across the room. Instead of thinking only about his cooling system, he thought, "This would make a great water gun!" // Johnson built a prototype from plastic pipe, a soda bottle and other parts. His daughter tested it, and it soaked everything in sight. But turning the idea into a toy took years. Many toy companies were not interested. Johnson kept improving his design and contacting companies. Finally, in 1990, a toy company began selling his water gun. Renamed the Super Soaker, it became one of the best-selling toys in the world. // Johnson used money from the Super Soaker to start his own research company. He has earned more than 100 patents and continues to work on new ways to produce clean energy. His story shows that a great invention can begin with a surprise, but only hard work turns it into a success.

This scene is based on the true story of an inventor from Alabama. // CAST: MARY ANDERSON, a visitor to New York City; JOE, a streetcar driver; MRS. BELL, a passenger // SETTING: Inside a streetcar in New York City on a snowy day in the winter of 1902. Snow is falling hard outside the front window. // (The streetcar jerks to a stop. JOE pulls open the front window. Cold wind and snow blow in. The passengers shiver.) // MRS. BELL: (pulling her coat tight) Not again! That's the fourth time since Fifth Avenue! // JOE: (leaning out the window and wiping the glass with his sleeve) Sorry, ma'am. I can't see a thing through this snow. If I can't see, I can't drive. // (JOE closes the window and starts the streetcar again. MARY watches the snow pile up on the glass. She takes a small notebook and pencil from her bag.) // MARY: (to herself) Why must he reach outside? Why can't the glass be cleaned from inside? // MRS. BELL: (noticing her) Are you drawing the snow, miss? // MARY: (excitedly) No. I'm drawing an arm. A rubber blade on the outside of the window, connected to a handle on the inside. The driver turns the handle, the blade swings across the glass and pushes the snow away. He never has to open the window. // MRS. BELL: (laughing) A broom for a window! Whoever heard of such a thing? // MARY: (still sketching) No one, yet. // (The streetcar stops again. JOE groans and reaches for the window.) // MARY: (holding up her drawing) Sir, someday you won't have to do that. // JOE: (shaking snow off his sleeve) Miss, if you can make that work, I'll be the first in line to buy one. // NARRATOR: Mary Anderson went home to Alabama and had a working model of her design built. In 1903, she received a patent for her "window cleaning device." Today, windshield wipers are found on almost every car in the world.

When an inventor creates something new, how can the inventor keep others from copying it? In the United States, the answer is a patent. // A patent is a legal document from the government that gives an inventor the right to stop others from making, using or selling the invention for a certain number of years. To get a patent, an inventor sends an application to the United States Patent and Trademark Office. The application must explain exactly how the invention works, usually with detailed drawings. Experts then check whether the invention is truly new and useful, and not just an obvious change to something that already exists. // Patents are important because inventing takes time and money. An inventor might spend years building prototypes that fail before one finally works. A patent gives the inventor a chance to earn money from the idea, either by making the product or by selling or renting the rights to a company. The U.S. Constitution itself gives Congress the power to protect inventions in this way. // However, a patent does not last forever. Today most patents last about 20 years. In the early 1900s, they lasted 17 years. After a patent ends, anyone may use the idea. // Mary Anderson's story shows both sides. She received a patent for her windshield wiper in 1903. She tried to sell the rights to a company in Canada, but it told her the device had no commercial value. Few people owned cars at the time, so companies did not see the need. Her patent ended in 1920. Soon after, as more people drove cars, windshield wipers became standard equipment, and car companies made them without paying her anything. // A patent can protect an idea, but the timing of an invention matters, too. Sometimes an inventor is simply ahead of the world.

units.name: Unit 10: Water in California: Making Choices (opinion writing)
units.el: Show photos of a reservoir in a wet year and a dry year; have students sort phrases into "formal" and "informal" columns; illustrate each proverb on a card with its everyday meaning.

passages.t: Two Tales of Drops and Pebbles
passages.x: TALE 1: THE CROW AND THE PITCHER (a fable from ancient Greece, retold) // On a hot summer day, a crow was so thirsty that her wings drooped. At last she spotted a tall clay pitcher in a farmyard. She flew down and peered inside. There was water at the bottom, but the pitcher was narrow and deep, and her beak could not reach it. // The crow tried to tip the pitcher over, but it was too heavy. She pecked at its side, but the clay was too hard. Many birds would have given up and flown away. Instead, the crow looked around and thought. // Then she picked up a pebble and dropped it into the pitcher. Plop. She dropped in another, and another. With each pebble, the water rose a tiny bit. The crow worked all afternoon, one pebble at a time, until at last the water rose high enough for her to drink. // Little by little does the trick. // TALE 2: THE HUMMINGBIRD (a story told in South America, retold) // One day, a fire broke out in a great forest. The animals fled to the edge of the trees and watched in horror as the flames spread. The jaguar, the bear and the tapir stood frozen. "It is hopeless," they said. "The fire is too big." // But a tiny hummingbird flew to the river, scooped up a single drop of water in her beak and flew back to drop it on the flames. Then she did it again, and again. // The bigger animals laughed at her. "What do you think you are doing? You are too small. Your drops will never stop this fire!" // Without stopping, the hummingbird answered, "I am doing the best I can." // The Kenyan environmental leader Wangari Maathai, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004, often told this story. She said it reminded her that everyone can do something to help, no matter how small.

The summer the reservoir dropped so low that the old boat ramp stood high and dry in the sun, the city announced new rules. Lawns and gardens could be watered only twice a week, and only before eight in the morning. // Itzel's grandfather looked at his vegetable garden and sighed. His tomatoes, chiles and squash had grown in the same backyard for twenty years. "Twice a week will not be enough for them in this heat," he said. // Itzel didn't like seeing her grandfather worried. That night she searched the library's website for ideas and found a guide called "Saving Water at Home." One idea jumped out: rain barrels. When it rains, water rushes off roofs and down the gutters into the street. A barrel under a downspout can catch that water and save it for later. // "But it hardly ever rains in summer," her grandfather pointed out. // "Then we save the rain in winter," Itzel said. "And in the meantime, we can save other water." She made a list: a bucket in the shower to catch cold water while it warmed up, the water left after rinsing vegetables, the ice cubes left in glasses. All of it could go to the garden. // For the rest of the summer, they carried buckets. It wasn't glamorous. Itzel's arms ached, and her little cousin Mateo complained that the house was "full of buckets." But the tomatoes survived. // In November, Itzel and her grandfather set up two blue barrels under the gutters. When the first winter storm came, Itzel stood at the window and watched the barrels fill, the rain drumming on their lids. // By spring, three neighbors had barrels of their own. Mrs. Okoye from across the street called them "the Itzel barrels," which made Itzel's cheeks turn pink. // Her grandfather patted the side of a full barrel. "Every drop has a job," he said. "We just had to give it one."

California has some of the richest farmland and biggest cities in the country. It also has a water puzzle that is hard to solve. // The first piece of the puzzle is that California's rain and snow are unpredictable. Some winters bring huge storms that flood rivers. Others bring so little rain that the state falls into drought, a long period of dry weather. From 2012 to 2016, California suffered one of the worst droughts in its history. In April 2015, the Sierra Nevada snowpack measured only about 5 percent of its usual amount. That year, for the first time, the governor ordered cities and towns across the state to cut their water use by 25 percent. // The second piece is groundwater, the water stored underground in layers of soil and rock. During droughts, farmers and towns pump more groundwater to make up for the missing rain. But when too much water is pumped out, the ground above can actually sink. In parts of the San Joaquin Valley, the land has sunk by many feet over the past century, damaging roads, bridges and canals. In 2014, California passed a law requiring local areas to manage their groundwater so that it is not used up. // The third piece is the large number of people. Almost 40 million people live in California, and all of them need water for drinking, cooking and washing. Farms, businesses and wildlife need water, too. // People are working on many solutions. Some cities clean and reuse wastewater. Some capture storm water so it soaks back into the ground. Farmers are switching to drip irrigation, which delivers water straight to plant roots. And families are replacing thirsty lawns with native plants that need little water. // No single answer will solve California's water puzzle. But each piece of the solution helps the pieces fit together.

passages.t: Trade Your Lawn for a Garden
passages.x: Picture a typical California front yard: a rectangle of bright green grass, sprinklers ticking away in the early morning. It looks nice, but it comes at a high price. Californians should replace most of their lawns with native plants. // The most important reason is water. In many California homes, about half of all the water used goes to outdoor watering, and lawns are some of the thirstiest plants around. Grass from wetter parts of the world needs frequent watering to stay green through our long, dry summers. Native plants such as California poppies, sages and manzanitas, on the other hand, evolved here. Once their roots are established, many need little water beyond the winter rain. // A second reason is wildlife. A lawn offers almost nothing to bees, butterflies or birds. Native plants, however, provide nectar, seeds and shelter for the creatures that evolved alongside them. A yard full of native flowers can become a busy stop for hummingbirds and native bees. // A third reason is money. Watering and mowing a lawn costs time and money every month. Many water agencies in California even offer rebates, which are payments back to customers, for replacing grass with plants that need less water. // Some people say children need a lawn to play on. That is a fair point, and families can keep a small patch of grass for games while replacing the rest. Others worry that native gardens look messy. In fact, many native gardens are colorful all year, and they can be designed to look neat. // Our state's water is too precious to pour onto grass that does not belong here. By trading lawns for native gardens, Californians can save water, help wildlife and save money, all while making their neighborhoods more beautiful.

California has more than 800 miles of coastline and an entire ocean beside it. So why not simply drink the ocean? The problem is salt. Seawater is far too salty for people to drink or for farmers to use on crops. But a process called desalination can remove the salt. // Most modern desalination plants use a method called reverse osmosis. Powerful pumps push seawater through special membranes, thin sheets with holes so tiny that water can pass through but most salt cannot. What comes out on the other side is fresh water. What is left behind is a very salty liquid called brine. // The largest desalination plant in the Western Hemisphere opened in 2015 in Carlsbad, in San Diego County. It can produce about 50 million gallons of fresh water a day, enough for roughly 400,000 people, or about one tenth of the water used in the county. // Desalination has a big advantage: the ocean does not dry up during a drought. A desalination plant can keep producing water even in the driest years. // However, desalination also has drawbacks. It takes a lot of electricity to push water through the membranes, which makes desalinated water more expensive than water from rivers and reservoirs. Building a plant costs a great deal of money, too. The brine must be returned to the ocean carefully, because water that is too salty can harm sea life. Pumping seawater into a plant can also trap fish eggs and other tiny creatures. // Because of these costs and concerns, communities think carefully before building desalination plants. For some coastal cities, desalination is an important backup supply. For others, saving water and recycling it may make more sense.

When people imagine solving California's water problems, they often picture something huge: a giant new dam or a factory that turns seawater into drinking water. But the cheapest and fastest source of "new" water is the water we are already wasting. California should make conservation its first choice. // First, conservation works quickly. During the drought of 2015, Californians in cities and towns were asked to cut their water use by 25 percent. Within months, they came close to meeting that goal by taking shorter showers, fixing leaks and watering lawns less. A new desalination plant, by contrast, can take many years to plan and build. // Second, saving water usually costs much less than producing new water. Fixing a leaky toilet or installing a low-flow showerhead costs a few dollars, and these fixes save water every day for years. A desalination plant costs hundreds of millions of dollars or more to build and uses large amounts of electricity to run. // Third, conservation protects nature. Every gallon we save is a gallon that can stay in rivers for salmon or in the ground for future droughts. Conservation does not create salty brine or trap tiny sea creatures. // Some people argue that conservation alone cannot meet the needs of a growing state. That is true in some places. Coastal cities with few other choices may need desalination as a backup. But even those cities should save every drop they can first, so that expensive new water is used wisely. // Before we spend billions on new sources, let's stop pouring away the water we already have. Saving water is something every Californian can do, starting today.

test.ans: Sample: California should focus mainly on saving water. First, conservation is faster. "Save Water First" explains that in 2015 Californians came close to cutting water use by 25 percent within months, while a desalination plant takes years to build. Second, saving water costs less.
