passages.x: Every summer since I was eight, I had climbed exactly three rungs of the high-dive ladder at the Mariposa Street pool and then climbed back down. Three rungs was my record. I told everyone I was "warming up." Nobody believed me, but my friends were kind enough to pretend. // This summer was supposed to be different. I was twelve now, taller than my mom, and I had promised myself on the first day of June that I would jump before school started. It was now the last Saturday in August. // My little sister, Rosa, sat on the edge of the pool with her feet in the water. She was six and afraid of almost nothing, which I found deeply unfair. "Are you going to do it today, Teo?" she asked, loud enough for the lifeguard to hear. // "Maybe," I said. My stomach answered for me by twisting into a knot. // I climbed. One rung, two, three. My hands were slippery, and the metal was hot from the sun. On the fourth rung, I made the mistake of looking down. The pool looked like a blue postage stamp. I froze, and for a long moment the only sound I heard was my own breathing. // Then I heard Rosa. She was not shouting or teasing. She was counting, slowly and calmly, the way our grandmother counts when she braids our hair. "Four... five... six..." // I realized she was counting the rungs I had left. I did not decide to keep climbing so much as my feet decided for me, one number at a time. When Rosa said "ten," I was standing on the board. // The board bounced a little under my feet. I walked to the end, closed my eyes and stepped off before my brain could argue. The fall lasted about one second and also about a year. Then the water closed over me, cool and loud, and I came up laughing. // Rosa was clapping. The lifeguard gave me a thumbs-up. I swam to the edge, breathing hard, and Rosa leaned over. // "Can I count for you again?" she asked. // I climbed the ladder four more times that afternoon. I never looked down once, but I listened for her voice every time.

Imagine you are walking on a trail and see a long, curved shape in the path. Before you have time to think "snake," your heart is pounding and you have jumped backward. A moment later, you look again and see that it is only a stick. You may feel silly, but your brain did exactly what it was built to do. // Fear is one of the body's oldest alarm systems. Deep inside the brain is a small, almond-shaped area called the amygdala. Scientists have found that the amygdala plays a key role in noticing possible danger. When it senses a threat, it helps send signals that prepare the body to act. // Those signals set off what is often called the "fight-or-flight" response. The adrenal glands release a hormone called adrenaline. Your heart beats faster to send more blood to your muscles. Your breathing speeds up to bring in more oxygen. Your senses may feel sharper. All of these changes happen in seconds, and they prepare you either to face a danger or to get away from it. // This system is fast because speed can save lives. A person who jumps back from a stick loses nothing. A person who waits too long to react to a real snake could be hurt. In other words, the brain would rather make a harmless mistake than a dangerous one. // However, the same alarm can go off when there is no real danger at all. Many people feel their hearts race before giving a speech, taking a test or trying out for a team. These situations are not life-threatening, but the brain may react as if they were. // The good news is that people can teach their alarm systems to calm down. Psychologists have found that facing a feared situation in small, manageable steps often makes the fear weaker over time. Someone afraid of speaking in front of a class might first practice alone, then in front of one friend, then in front of a small group. Each success shows the brain that the situation is safe. // Fear, then, is not a weakness. It is a tool. Understanding how it works can help people use it wisely, listening to it when danger is real and gently retraining it when it is not.

When a building collapses after an earthquake, rescuers face a race against time. People may be trapped under concrete and twisted metal, and no one knows exactly where. In these moments, one of the most valuable members of a rescue team has four legs and a powerful nose. // Search-and-rescue dogs are trained to find people by scent. Every person constantly sheds tiny skin cells and gives off odors that a dog can detect. A dog's nose contains far more scent receptors than a human nose, so it can notice smells that people cannot. By following the strongest scent, a trained dog can lead rescuers to the spot where someone is buried. // Training a rescue dog takes patience. Most teams begin with a game. A trainer hides just out of sight, and the puppy is rewarded with a toy or praise when it finds the trainer. Little by little, the hiding places become harder: behind boxes, under piles of wood, inside dark spaces. Eventually the dog learns to search large areas and to bark when it finds a person. Many dogs train for a year or more before they are ready for a real disaster. // The dogs are not the only ones who must be brave. Their handlers travel into unstable buildings, flooded streets and smoky ruins. They learn first aid, map reading and safety rules. Most important, they learn to read their dogs. A slight change in a dog's tail or ears might be the first sign that it has caught a scent. // The work requires trust in both directions. The dog must trust that its handler will keep it safe on shifting ground. The handler must trust the dog's nose, even when nothing seems to be there. Handlers often describe moments when a dog stopped at a pile of rubble that looked empty, and a person was found underneath. They learn to believe their partners. // Not every search ends with a rescue. But when a dog's bark leads to a survivor, the team's long months of practice suddenly make sense. Courage, these teams show, is not just a feeling in a dangerous moment. It is built slowly, one practice search at a time.

When the lights went out, Hana was halfway through her math homework. The refrigerator hummed and then went silent. Outside, the whole block of apartment buildings had gone black, as if someone had pulled a blanket over the city. // Hana did not like the dark. She was eleven and knew it was silly, but she still slept with the hall light on. Now she sat perfectly still at the kitchen table, waiting for her eyes to adjust. Her mother was working the night shift at the hospital, and her older brother, Kenji, was at basketball practice across town. // Then she remembered Mrs. Okafor. // Mrs. Okafor lived alone on the fifth floor, two floors above Hana. She was eighty-one and walked with a cane, and last week she had told Hana that her flashlight batteries were dead. "I keep meaning to buy more," she had laughed. "At my age, everything is 'meaning to.'" // Hana found the emergency box under the sink. Inside were two flashlights, a pack of batteries and a candle her mother had told her never to light alone. She clicked on one flashlight. Its beam looked very small. // The stairwell was worse than she had imagined. The beam caught only a few steps at a time, and the rest of the space was a deep, waiting blackness. Somewhere below, a door banged. Hana's heart jumped into her throat. She thought about going back to the kitchen, locking the door and waiting for morning. // But she also thought about Mrs. Okafor sitting alone in the dark, maybe trying to find her way down the hall with her cane. // Hana took a breath and climbed. She counted the landings out loud, partly to keep track and partly because her own voice made the stairwell feel less empty. "Four. Five." // She knocked. "Mrs. Okafor? It's Hana from the third floor. I brought you a flashlight." // The door opened, and the flashlight beam fell across Mrs. Okafor's surprised face. "Child," she said, "you came up those stairs in the dark? For me?" // Hana nodded. She did not mention that her knees were still shaking. // Mrs. Okafor insisted that Hana stay. They sat by the window with both flashlights pointed at the ceiling, making a soft pool of light, while Mrs. Okafor told stories about growing up in Lagos, where, she said, the power went out so often that children learned to play games by moonlight. // When the lights finally flickered back on, Hana was almost disappointed. The dark, it turned out, was easier to sit in when you were not sitting in it alone.

lessons.name: Narrator's point of view and how characters respond

practice.q: Read: "I gripped the rail and told myself the bridge was perfectly safe." Which point of view is used?
practice.h: Look at the pronoun the narrator uses to talk about himself or herself.

practice.q: Read: "Jamal smiled at the crowd, but inside he was sure he would forget every line. Across the stage, Mei wondered why he looked so calm." What point of view is used?
practice.h: Whose thoughts does the narrator share? Is it more than one character?

practice.q: Read: "When the dog growled, Ana stepped in front of her little brother, even though her knees were shaking." What does Ana's response reveal about her?
ch: She protects others even when she is scared.
She is not afraid of dogs at all.
She wants her brother to be scared.
She does not notice the dog.
practice.h: Think about the difference between what Ana feels and what Ana does.

practice.q: A narrator says, "Everyone said the old Fenwick house was haunted, and I believed every word." How might this point of view affect the story?
ch: Readers see the house through the narrator's fears, which may not be accurate.
Readers learn every character's true thoughts.
Readers get only proven facts about the house.
The story cannot include any suspense.
practice.h: Can a narrator's beliefs shape how events are described?

practice.q: Read: "I told Grandpa I wasn't scared of the storm. Then the lights went out, and I was holding his hand before I knew it." Compare what the narrator says with what the narrator does. What does the difference show?
practice.ans: The narrator says he or she is not scared but grabs Grandpa's hand when the lights go out. The difference shows the narrator is more afraid than he or she admits.
practice.h: Compare the narrator's words with the narrator's actions.

quiz.q: From which point of view is "The Last Rung" told?
ch: third person, by an outside narrator
second person, speaking to the reader

quiz.q: What does Teo's claim that he was "warming up" reveal about him?
ch: He was embarrassed to admit he was afraid.
He believed he needed exercise before diving.
He wanted his friends to leave the pool.
He was proud of his three-rung record.

quiz.q: Why does Teo call it "deeply unfair" that Rosa is afraid of almost nothing?
ch: He wishes he were as brave as his younger sister.
He thinks Rosa is breaking the pool rules.
He is angry that Rosa jumped first.
He believes Rosa is only pretending to be brave.

quiz.q: How does Rosa's counting help Teo respond to his fear?
ch: It breaks the climb into small steps and calms him.
It embarrasses him into climbing faster.
It reminds him that the pool is closing soon.
It warns the lifeguard that he is about to jump.

quiz.q: Which detail shows the narrator's fear most clearly?
ch: "The pool looked like a blue postage stamp."
"I was twelve now, taller than my mom"
"I climbed the ladder four more times that afternoon."

quiz.q: Which statement best describes how Teo changes over the story?
ch: He moves from avoiding his fear to facing it with support.
He moves from trusting his sister to doubting her.
He moves from loving swimming to disliking it.
He moves from confidence to fear.

quiz.q: Because "The Last Rung" is told by Teo, readers learn some things and not others. Explain one thing the first-person point of view lets readers know and one thing it does not, using details from the story.
quiz.ans: Readers know Teo's private thoughts and feelings, such as his stomach "twisting into a knot" and the fall lasting "about a year." Readers do not know what Rosa is thinking or why she decided to count, so they only see her actions through Teo's eyes.

lessons.name: Central idea and how it is developed

practice.q: The central idea of an informational text is
ch: the most important point the whole text develops
the first fact in the text
the detail the author likes best
practice.h: Think about the point that most of the paragraphs support.

practice.q: Read: "Firefighters train for hundreds of hours. They practice in smoke-filled rooms, climb ladders in heavy gear and rehearse rescues until the steps feel automatic." What central idea do these details develop?
ch: Firefighters prepare carefully so they can act in emergencies.
practice.h: What do all three examples have in common?

practice.q: Which sentence would NOT belong in an objective summary of an article about mountain rescue teams?
ch: I think rescue workers are the coolest people alive.
Rescue teams search for lost or injured hikers.
Teams use dogs, helicopters and radios.
Volunteers train for months before joining a team.
practice.h: An objective summary leaves out personal opinions.

practice.q: An article about a swimmer who crossed a dangerous channel begins with her standing on a cold beach at dawn. What is the most likely purpose of this opening?
ch: to draw readers in and introduce the person the article is about
practice.h: How does a scene at the beginning affect a reader?

practice.q: Read: "Some people think courage means having no fear. In fact, many people who perform brave acts report feeling terrified. Courage is acting in spite of fear." What is the central idea, and which detail supports it?
practice.ans: Central idea: courage means acting even when you are afraid. Support: many people who perform brave acts report feeling terrified.
practice.h: Look for the sentence that sums up the point, then find the evidence behind it.

quiz.q: Which sentence best states the central idea of "Your Brain on Fear"?
ch: Fear is a fast alarm system that protects us, and people can learn to calm it when there is no real danger.
The amygdala is a small, almond-shaped part of the brain.
Snakes are the most common cause of fear on hiking trails.
People should avoid all situations that make them nervous.

quiz.q: According to the article, what happens to breathing during the fight-or-flight response?
ch: It speeds up to bring in more oxygen.
It slows down to save energy.

quiz.q: Why does the author begin with the example of the stick on the trail?
ch: to introduce how quickly the brain reacts to possible danger
to warn readers that snakes live on trails
to show that hikers are often careless
to prove that fear is always a mistake

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of the fourth paragraph, which begins "This system is fast"?
ch: to explain why a quick reaction is helpful even when it is wrong
to describe the parts of the brain
to give steps for overcoming fear
to argue that people should not hike

quiz.q: How does the author illustrate the idea of facing fear "in small, manageable steps"?
ch: with the example of practicing a speech alone, then with a friend, then with a group
with a list of studies that psychologists have done on fear
with a second story about a snake on a trail
with a definition of the amygdala and its job

quiz.q: Which statement would the author most likely agree with?
ch: A racing heart before a test is a normal reaction, not a sign of weakness.
People who feel fear are less brave than other people.
The amygdala should be trained to stop working.
Fear is useful only for wild animals.

quiz.q: Write an objective summary of "Your Brain on Fear" in two or three sentences.
quiz.ans: The article explains that fear is an alarm system, involving the amygdala, that triggers the fight-or-flight response to prepare the body for danger. The response is fast because reacting quickly can save lives, but it can also go off in safe situations. People can weaken unhelpful fears by facing them in small steps.

lessons.name: Prefixes, suffixes and context clues

practice.q: The prefix "un-" in "unafraid" means
practice.h: Try putting "not" in place of the prefix and read the word again.

practice.q: What does "preview" mean?
practice.h: The prefix "pre-" tells when something happens.

practice.q: Read: "The trail was so treacherous that the guides roped every hiker together." What does "treacherous" most likely mean?
practice.h: Why would guides need to rope hikers together?

practice.q: Which word means "able to be reached"?
practice.h: Which suffix means "able to be"?

practice.q: The word "fearless" has a base word and a suffix. Name the suffix, tell what it means and explain the meaning of the whole word.
practice.ans: The suffix is "-less," which means "without." Fearless means "without fear."
practice.h: Split the word into two parts first.

quiz.q: The prefix "re-" in "reconsider" means
Read: "After hours of rain, the stream became a torrent that swept branches downhill." Which meaning of "torrent" fits the context?
ch: a strong, fast rush of water

quiz.q: Which word means "not able to be believed"?
The prefix "mis-" means "wrongly." What does "misinterpret" mean?
Read: "Kiri was hesitant to join the team; she stood by the door for ten minutes before walking in." Which clue best shows what "hesitant" means?
ch: she stood by the door for ten minutes

quiz.q: A dictionary lists three meanings of "brave": (1) adjective, showing courage; (2) verb, to face something difficult; (3) adjective, splendid or fine (an old use). Which meaning is used in "The sailors braved the storm"?
Which word means "the state of not being able"?

Use the prefix and base word to explain the meaning of "previewing" in this sentence: "Previewing the questions before you read can help you focus." Then explain how you can check that your meaning fits.
quiz.ans: Pre- means "before" and view means "look at," so previewing means looking at something ahead of time. In the sentence it means looking at the questions before reading; I can check by putting my meaning in place of the word and seeing if the sentence still makes sense, or by looking it up.

lessons.name: Writing a narrative: setting, dialogue, pacing and resolution

practice.q: Which is the best opening for a narrative about a first day at a new school?
ch: My backpack felt like it was full of bricks as I stood outside Room 14, listening to laughter I was not part of.
This story is about my first day at a new school.
Schools are places where students learn.
I will now tell you what happened.
practice.h: Which opening puts the reader inside a moment?

practice.q: Which sentence punctuates dialogue correctly?
ch: "Wait for me," Lena called. "I'm almost there!"
"Wait for me" Lena called. "I'm almost there!"
Wait for me, Lena called, "I'm almost there!"
"Wait for me." Lena called "I'm almost there!"
practice.h: Check where the quotation marks and commas go around the speaker tag.

practice.q: A writer wants to slow down the most exciting moment of a story. Which strategy works best?
ch: adding sensory details and the character's thoughts during that moment
skipping ahead to the next day
summarizing the moment in one sentence
practice.h: Pacing slows down when a writer spends more words on a moment.

practice.q: Which transition best signals a shift in time?
practice.h: Which phrase tells the reader when the next event happens?

practice.q: Revise this sentence to show, not tell, that the character is nervous: "Marco was nervous before his piano recital."
practice.ans: Marco wiped his damp palms on his pants for the third time and counted the keys again, his heart thumping. (Any revision that uses actions, body language or thoughts to show nervousness.)
practice.h: What would nervousness look like or feel like in his body?

quiz.q: In a narrative, the resolution is
ch: how the conflict is settled at the end
the time and place of the story

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the most precise, sensory language?
ch: The cold lake water bit my ankles, and the pebbles shifted under my toes.
The lake was nice and stuff.
The water was very, very cold.

quiz.q: Which sentence would best establish the setting at the start of a story?
ch: Fog rolled off the bay and swallowed the tops of the shipping cranes along the dock.
I had a feeling something would happen.

quiz.q: A draft uses "and then" to begin almost every sentence. Which revision strategy is best?
ch: Vary the transitions, using phrases such as "moments later," "after that" and "by noon."
Use "and then" in every sentence for consistency.
Remove all transitions from the story.

quiz.q: Which ending best reflects on the narrator's experience?
ch: As the bus pulled away, I realized the scariest part had only been the waiting.
Then I went home and ate dinner.

quiz.q: Which pair of events shows cause and effect in a narrative?
ch: The power went out, so we lit candles and told stories.
We ate lunch, and it was Tuesday.
Ming has a cat, and a bus went by.
It was sunny, and I like blue.

quiz.q: Write two or three lines of dialogue between two characters that show one character is afraid to try something new. Punctuate the dialogue correctly.
quiz.ans: "You could sign up for the talent show," Priya said. "Me? On a stage?" Jonah stared at his shoes. "I would probably forget how to breathe." (Dialogue reveals the fear and uses correct quotation marks, commas and new speaker tags.)

test.q: The suffix "-ful" in "hopeful" means
What does "unpredictable" mean?
Read: "The climbers were exhausted, so weary that they could barely lift their packs." Which word is a context clue for "exhausted"?
Which word has a prefix meaning "before"?
Which line from a story is punctuated correctly?
Which transition best shows a sudden change in a narrative?
Which kind of narrator can share the thoughts and feelings of every character?
ch: a first-person narrator who is a minor character

test.q: According to "Partners in the Rubble," how do search-and-rescue dogs find people?
ch: by seeing movement in the dark
by reading maps with their handlers

test.q: Why does the author explain that a dog's nose has far more scent receptors than a human nose?
ch: to show why dogs can detect smells people cannot
to argue that people should train their noses
to compare dogs to other animals

test.q: How does the author develop the idea that training a rescue dog "takes patience"?
ch: by describing hiding places that get harder little by little over a year or more
by listing different breeds of dogs

test.q: What is the main idea of the fourth paragraph?
ch: Handlers also need courage, skills and the ability to read their dogs.
Dogs are braver than their handlers.
First aid is the most important skill in life.

test.q: What does "unstable" mean in "Their handlers travel into unstable buildings"?
Which sentence best expresses the central idea of the whole passage?
ch: Through long training, rescue dogs and handlers build the trust and courage needed to save lives.
Earthquakes destroy many buildings every year.
Dogs enjoy playing hide-and-seek with trainers.
Not every search ends with a rescue.

test.q: The author says the work "requires trust in both directions." Explain what this means using two details from the passage.
test.ans: The dog must trust its handler to keep it safe on shifting ground, and the handler must trust the dog's nose even when a pile of rubble looks empty. Each partner depends on the other.

test.q: From which point of view is "The Fifth Floor" told?
ch: third person omniscient, sharing every character's thoughts

test.q: What is Hana's main internal conflict?
ch: She is afraid of the dark but wants to help Mrs. Okafor.
She wants to finish her math but cannot see the page.
She is angry that her brother left her alone.
She does not want to listen to Mrs. Okafor's stories.

test.q: What causes Hana to go up to the fifth floor?
ch: She remembers that Mrs. Okafor's flashlight batteries are dead.
Her mother calls and tells her to go.
She hears Mrs. Okafor calling for help.
Kenji asks her to check on the building.

test.q: Why does Hana count the landings out loud?
ch: to keep track and to make the stairwell feel less empty
to practice for her math homework

test.q: What does Hana's choice not to mention her shaking knees reveal about her?
ch: She wants to seem calm and is not looking for praise.
She is no longer afraid at all.
She is upset with Mrs. Okafor.
She does not trust Mrs. Okafor.

test.q: Which theme is best supported by the story's last sentence?
ch: Fear becomes easier to face when we are connected to others.
Older people tell the best stories.
Power outages happen often in cities.

test.q: Explain how the author builds tension in the stairwell scene. Use two details from the story.
test.ans: The beam lights only a few steps and the rest is "a deep, waiting blackness," and a door bangs below so "Hana's heart jumped into her throat." She even thinks about going back, which makes readers wonder whether she will keep going.

test.q: Write a narrative that retells the blackout from Mrs. Okafor's point of view, beginning when the lights go out and ending when they come back on. Use first person, dialogue, sensory details and her thoughts and feelings, and stay consistent with the events in "The Fifth Floor."
test.ans: Key points: first-person narration as Mrs. Okafor; establishes the dark apartment and her situation (dead batteries, cane, living alone); describes the knock and her surprise that Hana climbed the stairs in the dark; dialogue consistent with the story; her thoughts and feelings (worry, gratitude, memories of Lagos); sensory details and clear transitions; ends with the lights returning and a reflection on what Hana's courage meant to her.
rub: Clear focus and strong organization; ideas fully developed with relevant details or text evidence; precise language; few errors in conventions.
Clear focus and organization; ideas adequately developed with some details or evidence; some errors that do not affect meaning.
Focus or organization is inconsistent; limited development or evidence; errors sometimes interfere with meaning.
Little focus or organization; minimal development; frequent errors.

units.name: Collection 2: Wild Partners (informative)
units.el: Preview animal words with photos or quick sketches (pollen, burrow, pup, nectar) and give a text-structure chart with signal words: because/so (cause and effect), both/however (compare), problem/solution, first/next (sequence).

passages.x: Lucia first noticed the crow in September, the week her family moved into the yellow house on Alder Street. It sat on the back fence every morning at seven, tilting its head at her as she waited for the school bus. // "It's watching you," said her neighbor, Mr. Haddad, who was trimming his roses. "Crows remember faces, you know. Be kind to it, and it may be kind to you." // Lucia was not sure what a crow could do to be kind, but she liked the idea of a friend in a new place. The next morning, she left three peanuts on the fence post. The crow did not move until she had walked all the way to the corner. When she looked back, the peanuts were gone. // She left peanuts every day after that. At first the crow waited until she was far away. By October, it waited only until she reached the gate. By November, it hopped down onto the post while she was still standing on the porch, close enough that she could see the purple shine on its feathers. She named it Pepper. // Then, one rainy morning, Lucia found something on the fence post: a small blue button. The next week there was a bottle cap, then a piece of green glass worn smooth, like a jewel. Lucia lined the gifts up on her windowsill. // "Do you think Pepper is paying me back?" she asked Mr. Haddad. // He shrugged and smiled. "Who can say what a crow thinks? But you did not grab at it or chase it. You let it decide how close to come. Trust works that way, with crows and with people." // In December, Lucia's class held a "get to know you" day, and her teacher asked her to share something about herself. Lucia had been dreading it for weeks. She still did not know many people. But that morning she brought the windowsill gifts in a shoebox and told the story of Pepper. // When she finished, a boy named Andre raised his hand. "There's a crow at my house too," he said. "Can you show me how you did it?" // "You have to be patient," Lucia said. "You let it come to you." // After school, they walked home together, and Lucia realized she was talking about more than birds.

Calling someone a "bird brain" is supposed to be an insult. The phrase suggests that birds are not very smart. But scientists who study crows and their relatives, such as ravens and jays, have found that the insult may not fit at all. // One well-known set of experiments took place at the University of Washington in Seattle. Researchers wore a rubber mask while they caught a few wild crows, put bands on their legs and then let them go unharmed. Later, when a person wore the same mask on campus, crows scolded and swooped at the wearer, even years afterward. The crows did not react the same way to people wearing a different mask. Even more surprising, crows that had never been caught joined in the scolding. The birds seemed to have learned from one another which face meant trouble. // Crows are also skilled toolmakers. On the Pacific island of New Caledonia, crows shape twigs and leaves into hooks and probes. They use these tools to pull insects out of holes in dead wood. Young crows spend a long time watching adults and practicing before they become skilled. In laboratory tests, some of these crows have solved puzzles that require using one tool to get another. // Why are crows so clever? Part of the answer may be their brains. A crow's brain is large compared with the size of its body. Bird brains are also packed with many tightly arranged nerve cells, so even a small brain can do a great deal of work. // Crows' intelligence helps them survive in many places, including cities. They learn which trash cans are easy to open, which parks have picnic scraps and which people are friendly. In other words, the same skills that help them in the wild help them live alongside humans. // The next time you see a crow watching you from a power line, remember that it may be paying close attention. It might even remember you.

Daniela had been waiting all spring to see the harbor seal pups. Her aunt Rocio was a volunteer at Point Larkin, a windy beach where harbor seals came ashore to rest and have their pups, and this year Daniela was finally old enough to help with the weekly count. // "Rule number one," Tia Rocio said as they walked up the sandy trail. "We stay on the path, and we stay far back from the seals. No exceptions." // Daniela nodded, but she was hardly listening. She had brought her new camera, and she imagined the photo she would take: a close-up of a pup's enormous dark eyes, so sharp that you could count its whiskers. She would enter it in the county fair. She would win. // From the overlook, the beach looked as if it were covered in smooth, spotted stones. Then one of the stones lifted its head and yawned, and Daniela laughed out loud. The stones were seals, dozens of them, lying in the sun. // They counted for an hour. Tia Rocio wrote numbers in a notebook while Daniela called them out: adults, pups, a few more adults sliding into the water. Near the end of the path, Daniela spotted a pup alone on the sand, just a short scramble down from the trail. No other seals were near it. // "It's lost," Daniela whispered. "Its mother left it. We should help." She raised her camera and stepped toward the edge of the path. // Tia Rocio's hand closed gently on her shoulder. "Look again," she said quietly. "Look at the water." // Daniela looked. Just beyond the waves, a round gray head was bobbing, turned toward the beach. It was watching the pup. It was also watching them. // "Mothers often leave their pups on the beach while they swim and feed nearby," Tia Rocio said. "If people crowd the pup, the mother may be too frightened to come back. Then that pup really would be alone." // Daniela lowered the camera. Her cheeks felt hot. She had been so busy imagining her perfect photo that she had almost caused the very thing she wanted to prevent. // They backed away slowly and waited. After a long while, the mother rode a wave onto the sand and hitched her way up the beach to the pup. From the trail, Daniela took one picture: small and a little blurry, the mother and pup together in the frame, with plenty of sand between them and her. // It did not win anything at the county fair. She hung it over her desk anyway.

Bite into an apple, a strawberry or a handful of almonds, and you can thank an animal you may never have noticed. Many of the foods people eat depend on pollinators, the bees, butterflies, birds, bats and other animals that carry pollen from flower to flower. // Pollination is how many flowering plants make seeds and fruit. Pollen is a powdery substance made by flowers. For most fruits to form, pollen must move from one flower part to another, often on a different plant. Some plants rely on wind to carry their pollen. Many others rely on animals. When a bee visits a flower to drink nectar, pollen sticks to its fuzzy body. When the bee visits the next flower, some of that pollen rubs off, and the plant can begin to form seeds. // California offers a striking example of how important pollinators are. Almond trees produce almonds only when their blossoms are pollinated, and the state grows most of the world's almonds. Each February, when the orchards bloom, beekeepers truck in more than a million honeybee hives to pollinate the trees. Without the bees, the almond harvest would shrink to a tiny fraction of its size. // Honeybees get most of the attention, but they are not the only workers. North America is home to thousands of species of native bees, from tiny sweat bees to large, fuzzy bumblebees. Hummingbirds pollinate many red and orange tube-shaped flowers. In the deserts of the Southwest, certain bats visit cactus and agave blossoms at night. // Unfortunately, many pollinators are in trouble. Some populations have declined because of habitat loss, disease and the misuse of pesticides, chemicals that kill insects. When fields, lawns and parking lots replace wildflowers, pollinators lose both food and nesting places. // The good news is that ordinary people can help. Planting native flowers gives pollinators food. Leaving a patch of bare ground or a few dead stems can give native bees places to nest. Using fewer pesticides, or none at all, protects the insects that visit gardens. Even a few pots of flowers on a balcony can become a rest stop for a passing bee. // The next time you see a bee drifting from blossom to blossom, remember that it is not just gathering food for itself. It is also helping to grow food for you.

lessons.name: Theme and how a plot unfolds

practice.q: A theme is
ch: a message about life that a story suggests
the place where a story happens
a list of the story's events
practice.h: A theme is bigger than one character; it applies to life in general.

practice.q: In a story, a boy ignores his grandmother's advice to bring water on a hike and becomes dizzy. Later he always packs extra water. Which theme fits?
ch: Learning from mistakes helps us make wiser choices.
practice.h: What does the boy learn, and how could that apply to anyone?

practice.q: Which event is most likely part of the rising action?
ch: A girl finds an injured fox and secretly tries to care for it in the barn.
The fox is released and runs into the woods.
The girl lives on a farm with her uncle.
Years later, the girl remembers the fox.
practice.h: Rising action builds the conflict toward the climax.

practice.q: Read: "Every time the stray dog came near, Omar shouted to scare it away. Then one night, the dog barked until Omar woke to find smoke in the kitchen." How is Omar most likely to respond next?
ch: He changes his attitude toward the dog.
He shouts at the dog again.
He moves to a new house.
practice.h: Think about how a turning point changes a character.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a story's topic and its theme. Use an animal story as your example.
practice.ans: A topic is a word or phrase, such as "friendship with a horse." A theme is a complete message, such as "Caring for others can change us as much as it changes them."
practice.h: A theme is written as a complete sentence.

quiz.q: What problem does Lucia face at the start of the story?
ch: She is new in town and does not know many people.
She keeps missing the school bus.
Her neighbor does not like her.

quiz.q: What is the first gift Lucia finds on the fence post?
How does the crow's behavior change from September to November?
ch: It comes closer to Lucia as it learns to trust her.
It becomes more afraid of Lucia.
It begins following Lucia to school.

quiz.q: How does Mr. Haddad's advice connect to the end of the story?
ch: Lucia uses the same patient approach with people, which helps her make a friend.
Lucia decides to stop feeding the crow.
Lucia gives Mr. Haddad the gifts.
Lucia realizes Mr. Haddad was wrong about crows.

quiz.q: Why does the author include the scene at school?
ch: to show that Lucia's experience with Pepper helps her connect with a classmate
to describe Lucia's teacher in detail
to explain how crows choose their gifts
to show that Lucia dislikes school

quiz.q: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
ch: Trust grows slowly when we are patient and let others come to us.
Moving to a new place is always easy.
Gifts are the best way to make friends.

quiz.q: What does the last sentence mean when it says Lucia "was talking about more than birds"? Use details from the story to explain.
quiz.ans: Lucia's advice to Andre, "You let it come to you," also describes how she is making friends in her new town. Just as Pepper trusted her slowly, she is letting a friendship with Andre grow at its own pace.

lessons.name: Text structure and central idea in informational texts

practice.q: A text that explains why something happened and what resulted uses which structure?
practice.h: Look for words like because, so and as a result.

practice.q: Read: "Both dolphins and bats use echolocation. However, dolphins send sounds through water, while bats send them through air." Which structure is used?
practice.h: Signal words like both, however and while point to a structure.

practice.q: Read: "Honeybee colonies have been shrinking in many areas. In response, farmers are planting wildflower strips, and scientists are studying ways to keep hives healthy." Which structure is used?
practice.h: Is something going wrong, and are people trying to fix it?

practice.q: In an article about sea otters, a section is headed "Why Otters Need Kelp." What will this section most likely explain?
ch: how kelp forests help otters survive
the history of the fur trade
practice.h: Headings preview the content of a section.

quiz.q: Which sentence best states the central idea of "The Bird Brain Myth"?

People should never wear masks near crows.
"Bird brain" is a kind thing to call someone.

quiz.q: How is the second paragraph mainly organized?

It states a problem and offers several solutions.
It lists definitions of scientific words.

quiz.q: What did the University of Washington experiment suggest?
ch: Crows can remember human faces and learn from other crows which faces mean danger.
Crows prefer people who wear masks.
Crows cannot tell one human from another.
Crows forget dangers within a few days.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the fourth paragraph, which begins with a question?

to argue that crows are dangerous
to describe how crows build nests

quiz.q: What does "probes" most likely mean in "crows shape twigs and leaves into hooks and probes"?

to show that the author dislikes crows
to give instructions for training crows

quiz.q: Cite two pieces of evidence from "The Bird Brain Myth" that support the idea that crows learn from one another.
quiz.ans: Crows that had never been caught joined in scolding the mask wearer, so they learned from other crows; young New Caledonian crows watch adults and practice before they become skilled toolmakers.

lessons.name: Pronoun case and intensive pronouns

practice.q: Which pronoun is in the subjective case?

quiz.ans: Topic sentence: Desert tortoises have several ways to survive extreme heat. Details: They dig burrows to escape the sun. They can store water in their bodies for long periods.

This essay will be about some owls and things.

test.q: Besides honeybees, name two other pollinators from the passage and tell what each one visits or pollinates.

test.q: Write an informative essay that explains why pollinators are important and what people can do to protect them. State a clear thesis, organize your ideas into paragraphs and include at least three facts or examples from "Small Animals, Big Jobs," quoted or paraphrased with credit to the article.
test.ans: Key points: a thesis that pollinators are essential for many foods and need protection; explains pollination (pollen carried from flower to flower so plants form seeds and fruit); the California almond example with more than a million hives; the variety of pollinators (native bees, hummingbirds, bats); threats (habitat loss, disease, misuse of pesticides); actions people can take (native flowers, nesting spots, fewer pesticides, flowers on a balcony); formal style, transitions and a conclusion; evidence quoted or paraphrased with credit.
rub: Clear focus and strong organization; ideas fully developed with relevant details or text evidence; precise language; few errors in conventions.
Clear focus and organization; ideas adequately developed with some details or evidence; some errors that do not affect meaning.
Focus or organization is inconsistent; limited development or evidence; errors sometimes interfere with meaning.
Little focus or organization; minimal development; frequent errors.

units.name: Collection 3: Beyond the Sky (argument)
units.el: Post a roots wall (astro, tele, vis, graph, terra, port) with a picture for each, and give argument frames: "I claim that ___ because ___. One piece of evidence is ___. Some people think ___; however, ___."

passages.x: Twelve-year-old Pilar Navarro had lived at Tranquility Station for three hundred and twelve days, and she had counted every one. The station sat at the edge of a crater on the Moon, a cluster of white domes connected by tunnels. It had everything a person needed: air, water, food, a schoolroom with six students, even a small gym. What it did not have was weather. // On Earth, in Salinas, Pilar's grandmother used to say that the fields could smell rain before it came. Pilar had laughed at that. Now she would have given anything to smell it herself. Inside the domes, the air was always seventy-one degrees and always smelled faintly of metal and recycled breath. Outside, beyond the thick windows, the gray ground stretched away under a black sky, as still as a photograph. // "You're doing it again," said her friend Tobias, finding her at the observation window. "Staring at nothing." // "It's not nothing," Pilar said. She pointed at the blue-and-white marble hanging above the horizon. "It's home." // Tobias had been born on the station. He had never stood in a rainstorm. He tilted his head at the Earth as though it were a puzzle he could not quite solve. // That week, Pilar volunteered for a job no one wanted: tending the station greenhouse during the night shift. The greenhouse was warm and damp, and the lettuce and tomato plants grew in long trays under purple lights. At two in the morning, a timer clicked and the misting system came on. A fine spray drifted down over the leaves, and the air filled with a smell Pilar had not breathed in almost a year: wet soil, green and alive. // She closed her eyes. For one moment she was standing at the edge of her grandmother's field, the sky heavy and gray, the first drops tapping her face. // The next night, she brought Tobias. She did not explain anything. She just waited with him until the timer clicked. // When the mist began to fall, Tobias held out his palm and watched the tiny drops gather. "Is this what it's like?" he whispered. // "Almost," Pilar said, and for the first time in three hundred and fourteen days, she did not feel quite so far from home.

People have dreamed of walking on Mars for more than a century. It is an exciting dream, but for now, it is the wrong plan. Space agencies should spend the next several decades sending robots, not people, to explore Mars. // First, robots can do the job more safely. A trip to Mars takes many months each way. During that time, astronauts would be exposed to harmful radiation from space, far from any hospital. Robots do not need air, food or water, and if something goes wrong, no one's life is lost. // Second, robots have already proven that they work. The rover Opportunity was designed to last about ninety days on Mars, but it kept exploring for more than fourteen years. Newer rovers, such as Curiosity and Perseverance, have drilled into rocks, studied the Martian air and even collected samples that could someday be returned to Earth. Perseverance carried a small helicopter, Ingenuity, that made the first powered flight on another planet. // Third, robots cost less. A human mission would need to carry everything people need to stay alive for years, plus a way to bring them home. A robot only needs a one-way ticket. The money saved could pay for many robotic missions to Mars and to other worlds, such as the icy moons of Jupiter and Saturn. // Some people argue that humans can do things robots cannot, such as making quick decisions and noticing surprising details. That is true. A geologist on Mars might spot an interesting rock in seconds, while a rover might take days to reach it. However, robots are getting smarter every year, and the risks to human life are simply too great right now. // Finally, everyone knows that robots are more exciting than astronauts anyway. // Mars will still be there in fifty years. By letting robots go first, we can learn which places are safest and most interesting to visit, test new technology and protect human lives. When people finally do set foot on Mars, they will walk in the tracks of the machines that made the journey possible.

"How many?" Kofi asked for the fourth time. // "Patience," his father said. "Give the sky a chance." // They were lying on a blanket in the desert outside town, far from any streetlights. It was the middle of August, the week of the Perseid meteor shower, and Kofi's father had promised it would be "the best show on Earth." So far the show had been forty-five minutes of absolutely nothing. Kofi's back ached from the rocky ground. A cricket was chirping somewhere, the same note over and over, like a broken alarm. // Kofi reached for his phone, then remembered that his father had made him leave it in the car. "So that your eyes can adjust," his father had said. Kofi had rolled those same eyes. // "I don't think there are any meteors," he said. "I think it's just a story grown-ups tell." // His father laughed softly but said nothing. That was the strange thing about his father out here. At home he was always busy, always on a call, always answering emails at the kitchen table. Out here he just lay with his hands folded on his chest, looking up as if he had all the time in the world. // Kofi sighed and looked up too. Slowly, the sky began to change. Stars he had never seen appeared between the stars he knew, and then more between those, until the dark was crowded with light. A pale, cloudy band stretched from one side of the sky to the other. // "Is that a cloud?" he whispered. // "That's the Milky Way," his father said. "Our own galaxy. You're looking at it from the inside." // Kofi was still trying to understand that when a streak of white light flashed across the sky and vanished. // "Dad! Did you see it?" // "I saw it." // Another one came, then two together. Kofi stopped counting. // After a while his father spoke again. "When I was your age in Kumasi, my father took me up to the roof of our house to watch the sky. He never said much. I thought he was the quietest man in Ghana." He paused. "Now I think he just knew that some things are better without talking." // Kofi did not answer. He moved a little closer to his father on the blanket, and they watched the sky together until the cricket stopped singing.

Two hundred years ago, anyone who stepped outside on a clear night could see thousands of stars and the glowing band of the Milky Way. Today, scientists estimate that most people in North America can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. The reason is light pollution, the glow from streetlights, signs and buildings that washes out the night sky. Our town should take simple steps to reduce light pollution. // First, too much light at night harms wildlife. Many birds migrate at night and use the stars to help find their way. Bright city lights can confuse them, causing some to circle buildings until they are exhausted. On beaches, newly hatched sea turtles naturally crawl toward the brighter horizon over the ocean. Lights from nearby buildings can lead them in the wrong direction, away from the water. // Second, much of the light we use at night is wasted. Many outdoor lights shine sideways and upward, into the sky, where no one needs them. Lighting an empty sky costs money and uses energy. Lights that point downward put the light where people actually need it, on streets and sidewalks. // Third, a dark sky is a natural treasure that belongs to everyone. People have used the stars for thousands of years to tell stories, mark the seasons and navigate the oceans. Children who grow up never seeing the Milky Way miss out on a connection to that long human history. // Some residents worry that less light will make streets less safe. This concern deserves attention, and no one is suggesting that we turn off every light. However, safety depends on good lighting, not just more lighting. A light that glares in a driver's eyes can make it harder to see. Shielded lights that point down can light a sidewalk clearly without lighting up the sky. // Our town can start with three changes: replace old streetlights with shielded fixtures, ask businesses to turn off signs after closing and encourage residents to use motion-sensor lights outside their homes. These steps cost little, save energy and protect wildlife. // Someday, a child in our town might look up and see the Milky Way for the first time. Let's give that child a sky worth seeing.

lessons.name: Word choice, tone and mood in literature

practice.q: In literature, tone is
ch: the author's attitude toward a subject, shown through word choice
the time and place of a story
practice.h: Think about how the words make the writing "sound."

practice.q: Read: "The rocket roared upward, a pillar of fire splitting the sky." Which word best describes the tone?
practice.h: How does the writer seem to feel about the launch?

practice.q: Read: "The capsule drifted silently through the endless dark." What feeling does "endless dark" create?
practice.h: Picture something with no end. How would it feel to be inside it?

practice.q: Which word has the most positive connotation for describing an astronaut?
practice.h: Which word suggests a good quality rather than a bad one?

practice.q: Read: "The Moon hung over the desert like a cold coin." Explain what the comparison suggests about the Moon.
practice.ans: It suggests the Moon looks round, pale and shiny like a coin, and the word "cold" makes it seem distant and unwelcoming.
practice.h: What do a coin and the Moon have in common? What does "cold" add?

quiz.q: What does the phrase "as still as a photograph" suggest about the land outside the station?
Which detail best shows that Pilar misses Earth?
ch: "a cluster of white domes connected by tunnels"

quiz.q: The author calls Earth "the blue-and-white marble hanging above the horizon." What is the effect of this description?
ch: It makes Earth seem small, distant and precious.
It shows that Earth is made of stone.
It suggests that Earth is only a toy.
It shows that Earth is very close to the Moon.

quiz.q: The air in the domes "smelled faintly of metal and recycled breath." What connotation does this description have?
ch: negative, suggesting the air feels stale and artificial
positive, suggesting the air is fresh and clean
positive, suggesting the station is brand new

quiz.q: How does the smell in the greenhouse affect Pilar?
ch: It brings back a vivid memory of rain on her grandmother's field.
It reminds her of the station's metal walls.
It makes her want to quit the job.

quiz.q: Why does Pilar bring Tobias to the greenhouse without explaining anything?
ch: She wants him to experience something like rain for himself.
She needs help finishing her work.
She is planning to trick him.
She is not allowed to talk during the night shift.

quiz.q: Explain how the author's word choice in the greenhouse scene creates a different mood from the description of the station at the beginning. Cite at least two words or phrases from each part.
quiz.ans: At the beginning, phrases like "always seventy-one degrees," "metal and recycled breath" and "as still as a photograph" create a flat, lifeless mood. In the greenhouse, "warm and damp," "wet soil, green and alive" and "the first drops tapping her face" create a warm, living, hopeful mood.

lessons.name: Tracing and evaluating an argument

practice.q: In an argument, a claim is
ch: the position the writer wants readers to accept
a fact that no one can argue with
practice.h: The claim is what the writer is trying to prove.

practice.q: Read: "Our school should start a rocketry club. Students who build model rockets practice measuring, graphing and testing ideas." Which sentence gives a reason?
ch: Students who build model rockets practice measuring, graphing and testing ideas.
Our school should start a rocketry club.
practice.h: A reason explains why the claim should be accepted.

practice.q: Which statement is a claim that is NOT supported?
ch: Space camp is the best summer activity in the world.
A survey of campers found that most said space camp taught them teamwork.
Campers at space camp build and launch model rockets.
Each space camp session lasts one week.
practice.h: Which statement is a strong opinion with no evidence?

practice.q: An author writes, "Some say space exploration costs too much. However, it has produced inventions we use every day." What is the author doing?
ch: stating a fact with no purpose
practice.h: What does "Some say" introduce, and what does "However" signal?

practice.q: Read: "Telescopes in space take clearer pictures than telescopes on the ground." Describe evidence that would best support this claim.
practice.ans: Side-by-side images of the same object taken by a space telescope and a ground telescope, or an explanation from astronomers that Earth's air blurs and dims starlight.
practice.h: What kind of proof would convince someone who doubts the claim?

quiz.q: What is the author's main claim in "Let the Robots Go First"?
ch: For now, space agencies should send robots, not people, to explore Mars.
People should never travel to Mars.
Mars is the most interesting planet.
Robots are more intelligent than humans.

quiz.q: Which evidence supports the reason that robots "have already proven that they work"?
ch: Opportunity was designed for about ninety days but explored for more than fourteen years.
A trip to Mars takes many months each way.
Robots do not need air, food or water.
Mars will still be there in fifty years.

quiz.q: Which claim in the passage is NOT supported by reasons or evidence?
ch: "everyone knows that robots are more exciting than astronauts anyway"
"robots can do the job more safely"
"robots have already proven that they work"

quiz.q: How does the author respond to the counterclaim that humans can do things robots cannot?
ch: The author admits it is true but argues that robots are improving and the risks are too great.
The author agrees completely and changes the main claim.
The author says geologists are not needed.

quiz.q: What does the author mean by saying a robot "only needs a one-way ticket"?
ch: A robot does not need to be brought back to Earth.
A robot can only make one trip in its life.
Tickets for robots are very cheap.
Robots travel faster in one direction.

quiz.q: Which piece of evidence, if added, would most strengthen the reason that robots cost less?
ch: a comparison of the cost of a recent rover mission with estimates for a human mission
a photo of a rover on Mars
a quote from someone who loves robots
a summary of a science fiction movie

quiz.q: Evaluate the argument in "Let the Robots Go First." Identify the strongest reason and the weakest claim, and explain your choices.
quiz.ans: Strongest: robots have already proven they work, because it is supported by specific facts about Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance and Ingenuity. Weakest: "everyone knows that robots are more exciting," because it is an opinion with no evidence and does not support the main claim.

practice.q: The Greek root "astro" means
practice.h: Think of "astronaut" and "astronomy."

practice.q: The Greek root "tele" means
practice.h: A telescope helps you see things that are...?

a tool for seeing things far away

lessons.name: Writing an argument: claim, reasons, evidence and counterclaim

practice.q: Which is a clear claim for an argument?
ch: Our city should build a public observatory.
Some people like to look at stars.

practice.q: Which evidence best supports the claim "Our school should add a space science elective"?
ch: Teachers at a nearby school reported that students in a space elective improved their science grades.

practice.q: Which sentence introduces a counterclaim?

practice.q: Which is the best rebuttal to "Space exploration costs too much"?
ch: Space research has led to useful tools, such as weather satellites that help forecasters warn people about storms.

practice.q: Write a claim and one reason for this question: Should our school hold a stargazing night once a month?

quiz.q: In an argument, evidence is

quiz.q: Which transition best introduces a rebuttal?

ch: Investing in space science would benefit students and the economy.
Space stuff is awesome, so let's do it.
You'd be crazy not to like space.

quiz.q: Which concluding sentence best restates the claim?

quiz.q: Write a counterclaim and a rebuttal for the claim "Every middle school should own a telescope."
