test.q: The Greek root "chron" means
The root "port" means "carry." Which word means "able to be carried"?
Which word has the most negative connotation for describing a quiet person?
"Astro" means "star" and "naut" means "sailor." What is the literal meaning of "astronaut"?
Which sentence best introduces a counterclaim in an argument?
ch: Critics argue that new streetlights would cost too much.
In conclusion, we need darker skies.
For example, owls hunt at night.

test.q: In "The telescope revealed a faint, distant galaxy," which word contains a Greek root meaning "far"?
Which phrase gives the most positive impression of a costly space program?
How does Kofi feel at the beginning of "The Long Wait"?
What does the simile "like a broken alarm" suggest about the cricket's chirping?
ch: Kofi finds it repetitive and annoying.
The cricket is about to stop.

test.q: Why did Kofi's father make him leave his phone in the car?
ch: so his eyes could adjust to the dark
so it would not get broken
so he would not call his friends

test.q: How is Kofi's father different in the desert than at home?
ch: He is relaxed and unhurried instead of busy.
He is louder and more talkative.
He is strict instead of kind.
He is tired instead of energetic.

test.q: What does the phrase "the dark was crowded with light" mean?
ch: So many stars appeared that the sky seemed full.
The Moon rose and lit the desert.

test.q: What does the father's story about his own father help Kofi understand?
ch: Sharing quiet moments can be a way of showing love.
People in Ghana do not talk much.
Rooftops are the best place to see stars.
His grandfather did not like children.

test.q: At first Kofi says meteors are "just a story grown-ups tell," but later he "stopped counting." Explain how and why his attitude changes.
test.ans: At first he is bored and doubtful because nothing seems to happen. As his eyes adjust, he sees the Milky Way and many meteors, so he becomes amazed and too absorbed to count, and he moves closer to his father.

test.q: What is the author's main claim in "Let the Stars Shine"?
ch: Our town should take simple steps to reduce light pollution.
Light pollution has existed for two hundred years.
Every light should be turned off at night.
Sea turtles nest on every beach.

test.q: Which evidence supports the reason that too much light harms wildlife?
ch: Lights can lead newly hatched sea turtles away from the water.
Lighting an empty sky costs money.
People used the stars to navigate the oceans.
Businesses can turn off signs after closing.

test.q: How does the author respond to the concern that less light will make streets less safe?
ch: by agreeing that it deserves attention, then explaining that shielded lights can light streets safely
by suggesting that people stay inside at night

test.q: What is the purpose of the paragraph that begins "Our town can start with three changes"?
ch: to propose specific actions the town can take
to describe the history of streetlights
to give evidence about sea turtles

test.q: Which statement from the passage is an opinion rather than a fact?
ch: "a dark sky is a natural treasure that belongs to everyone"
"Many outdoor lights shine sideways and upward"
"newly hatched sea turtles naturally crawl toward the brighter horizon"

test.q: Which evidence, if added, would best strengthen the reason that much outdoor light is wasted?
ch: data showing how much money a town saved after switching to shielded streetlights
a poem about the night sky
a photo of a sea turtle

test.q: Trace the argument in "Let the Stars Shine": state the claim and list the three reasons the author gives.
test.ans: Claim: the town should take steps to reduce light pollution. Reasons: (1) too much light harms wildlife such as birds and sea turtles; (2) much outdoor light is wasted, costing money and energy; (3) a dark sky is a natural treasure that connects people to human history.

test.q: Write an argument essay for or against this question: Should your town or city adopt rules to reduce light pollution? State a claim, support it with at least two reasons and evidence from "Let the Stars Shine" or your own knowledge, address a counterclaim and end with a conclusion.
test.ans: Key points: a clear claim for or against; at least two reasons with relevant evidence (harm to birds and sea turtles, wasted energy and money, the value of a dark sky; or safety concerns and the cost of new fixtures if arguing against); evidence quoted or paraphrased accurately; a counterclaim acknowledged and answered with a rebuttal; formal style, transitions (first, however, as a result) and a conclusion that restates the claim.
rub: Clear focus and strong organization; ideas fully developed with relevant details or text evidence; precise language; few errors in conventions.
Clear focus and organization; ideas adequately developed with some details or evidence; some errors that do not affect meaning.
Focus or organization is inconsistent; limited development or evidence; errors sometimes interfere with meaning.
Little focus or organization; minimal development; frequent errors.

units.name: Collection 4: Getting Through Hard Times (literary analysis)
units.el: Use a two-column chart (Evidence / What it shows) for every reading, and teach figurative language with picture cards that show the literal image beside the intended meaning (for example, "tighten our belts").

passages.x: In July of 1936, the Pruitt family's truck coughed its way over the mountains and down into the San Joaquin Valley. Eleven-year-old June sat in the back among the pots, mattresses and crates of everything they owned, watching the green fields roll by. In Oklahoma, the wind had carried their farm away one dust storm at a time. Here the orchards stood in neat rows, heavy with fruit. // "Peaches," her father said, pointing. "Work picking peaches, and maybe a cabin for the season." He said it the way some people say a prayer. // The cabin turned out to be one room with a tin roof and a single window. June's mother swept it twice, then hung their faded blue curtain over the window as if it were a fine hotel. "There," she said. "Now it's ours." // Every morning before dawn, June and her parents walked to the orchard with the other pickers. The ladders were tall and the fuzz from the peaches made June's arms itch, but she learned to twist each peach gently so it came free without bruising. At the end of each day, the foreman paid by the bucket. Some days it was enough for beans and bread. Some days it was not. // One evening June found her mother sitting on the cabin step, staring at the few coins in her palm. June sat beside her and said nothing. After a while her mother closed her hand and smiled a tired smile. // "Do you know what my mother told me when times were hard?" she asked. "She said, 'You can't always choose your weather, but you can choose to keep the lamp lit.'" // June did not fully understand. But that night, when the family next door came back with nothing because their child had been sick and they could not pick, June watched her mother wrap half their bread in a cloth and carry it across the yard. // "We barely have enough," June whispered when she returned. // "That's exactly when it matters," her mother said. // At the end of the season, the Pruitts loaded the truck again. June looked back at the cabin with its blue curtain. They had less money than they had hoped for. But in the back of the truck, wrapped in newspaper, were six peaches from the family next door, a gift for the road.

On the afternoon of April 14, 1935, people across the southern Great Plains watched a dark wall rise on the horizon. It was not a rainstorm. It was a cloud of dust, thousands of feet high, rolling toward them at terrifying speed. When it hit, day turned to night. People could not see their own hands in front of their faces. The day became known as "Black Sunday," and it was one of the worst storms of a disaster called the Dust Bowl. // The Dust Bowl did not happen overnight. In the early 1900s, farmers plowed up millions of acres of prairie grass to plant wheat. The deep roots of those grasses had held the soil in place for thousands of years. For a while, rains were good and crops were plentiful. Then, in the early 1930s, a long drought began. Without grass roots or rain, the dry soil turned to powder, and the strong winds of the plains lifted it into the sky. // The storms were more than frightening. Dust covered fences, buried farm equipment and sifted through cracks around doors and windows. Crops failed year after year. Many people developed breathing problems from the dust. At the same time, the whole country was suffering through the Great Depression, so jobs were hard to find everywhere. // Many families gave up. Hundreds of thousands of people left the Plains during the 1930s, and many headed west to California, hoping to find work on its farms. Some found it, but many faced low pay, crowded camps and unfriendly treatment from people who saw them as outsiders. // The disaster also taught the nation hard lessons. In 1935, the United States government created the Soil Conservation Service to help farmers protect their land. Farmers were paid to try new methods, such as plowing along the curves of hills instead of in straight lines and planting rows of trees to break the wind. When the rains finally returned near the end of the decade, these practices helped keep the soil in place. // Today, scientists still study the Dust Bowl. It remains a powerful example of how human choices and nature can combine to create a disaster, and of how people can work together to recover.

In 1917, during World War I, Americans were asked to do something unusual to help their country: plant vegetables. Much of the nation's food was being shipped to soldiers and to allies in Europe, where many farms had been damaged by fighting. To make sure there was enough to eat at home, the government encouraged people to grow their own food in "war gardens." // Families dug up backyards, schoolyards and empty lots. Children joined a program that called them "soldiers of the soil." Posters showed smiling gardeners and slogans that made growing beans and carrots feel like an act of patriotism. // The idea returned on an even larger scale during World War II. By then the gardens were called "victory gardens." Foods such as sugar, meat and canned goods were rationed, which meant each family could buy only a limited amount. Growing vegetables at home helped families stretch their ration stamps. Millions of victory gardens sprang up in cities, suburbs and small towns, and together they produced a large share of the fresh vegetables Americans ate during the war years. // Victory gardens did more than feed people. They gave ordinary citizens a way to contribute during a frightening time. Neighbors shared seeds, tools and advice. Experienced gardeners taught beginners. In many places, a garden plot became a gathering spot where people could talk, trade vegetables and support one another. // When the war ended, most victory gardens disappeared. But the idea behind them never completely faded. During later hard times, such as periods of high food prices, interest in home and community gardens has often grown again. Today, many cities have community gardens where residents rent small plots, grow food for their families and donate extra produce to food banks. // Some people argue that small gardens cannot solve large problems like hunger. That is true; a backyard tomato plant will not feed a city. Still, history suggests that gardens offer something besides food. They give people a sense of control when much of life feels uncertain, and they bring neighbors together. // In hard times, it seems, planting a seed can be an act of hope.

The fishing had been poor all spring. Day after day, Grandpa Ike's small boat came back to the harbor with only a few fish in its hold, and day after day the price of fuel went up. Ellis, who was twelve, heard his parents talking late at night in low voices, using words like "loan" and "maybe sell." He pretended to be asleep, but the words followed him into his dreams. // On Saturday, Grandpa Ike handed him a wooden needle wound with green twine. Spread across the dock was a fishing net with a hole in it as big as a kitchen table. // "A sea lion went right through it," Grandpa said. "Ripped it like paper. We'll fix it." // Ellis stared at the hole. "It would be faster to buy a new one." // "Faster," Grandpa agreed. "Not cheaper." He sat down on an overturned bucket, his knees creaking like an old door, and began to work. // He showed Ellis how to tie each knot, looping the twine around the needle and pulling it tight, one small square at a time. Ellis's first knots slipped loose. His fingers cramped. The sun climbed, and the hole did not look any smaller. // "This is hopeless," Ellis muttered. // Grandpa did not look up. "Do you know how many times this net has been torn? I stopped counting when your father was your age. Storms, rocks, a shark once. Every time, someone sat here and fixed it, one knot at a time." He tugged a finished knot. "A net isn't strong because it never breaks. It's strong because someone keeps mending it." // Ellis bent over the twine again. He stopped looking at the hole and looked only at the knot in front of him. Loop, pull, tighten. Loop, pull, tighten. Gulls cried overhead. The tide turned. // By late afternoon, Grandpa stood and stretched. Ellis looked down and blinked. The hole was gone. In its place was a patch of bright new twine, darker than the faded net around it, but tight and even. // "Those are your knots," Grandpa said. "Every one of them will hold." // That night, Ellis heard his parents talking again. This time he did not pretend to sleep. He got up, went into the kitchen and sat down at the table with them. // "What can I do to help?" he asked. // His mother looked surprised. Then she pulled out a chair, and they began, together, to work out a plan.

lessons.name: How structure and key scenes develop a theme

practice.q: The climax of a story is
ch: the turning point, when the conflict reaches its highest point
the ending after the conflict is solved
the time and place of the story
practice.h: Think of the moment of greatest tension.

practice.q: A story opens with a memory of a character's happy childhood before describing her family losing their home. Why might the author begin this way?
ch: to show what the character has lost, making the hardship feel stronger
to confuse the reader about the order of events
to explain how the story will end
practice.h: How does knowing what came before change how you feel about the hard times?

practice.q: Read: "Through the long winter, Abuelo's garden lay brown and frozen. But each night he studied his seed catalogs by lamplight." What does this detail suggest about Abuelo?
ch: He stays hopeful about the future.
He is planning to move away.
practice.h: Why would someone study seed catalogs when nothing can grow?

practice.q: Which statement is a theme, not a topic?
ch: Hardship can reveal a person's true strength.
practice.h: A theme is a complete idea about life.

practice.q: Explain how one scene can contribute to the theme of a whole story. Use this example: in a story about a struggling family, a boy gives his only coat to his younger sister during a snowstorm.
practice.ans: The scene shows the boy putting his sister's needs ahead of his own, which develops a theme such as "Love means sacrifice, especially in hard times."
practice.h: What does the boy's choice show about what matters in the story?

quiz.q: How does the first paragraph help the reader understand the rest of "Peaches in July"?
ch: It explains why the family has left Oklahoma and come to California.
It describes the end of the peach season.
It introduces the family next door.
It explains how to pick peaches without bruising them.

quiz.q: What does it suggest that June's father says "Peaches" "the way some people say a prayer"?
ch: The family is deeply hoping the work will save them.
The father is tired of talking.
The family already has plenty of money.

quiz.q: Why does June's mother hang the faded blue curtain?
ch: to make the bare cabin feel like a home
to block out the dust storms
to sell it to the neighbors

quiz.q: What does the grandmother's saying, "you can choose to keep the lamp lit," most likely mean?
ch: You can choose to stay hopeful and kind even in hard times.
You should always buy lamp oil before food.
You should work only at night.
You can control the weather if you try hard enough.

quiz.q: How does the scene in which June's mother shares bread develop the theme?
ch: It shows that generosity matters most when people have little.
It shows that June's family has extra food.
It shows that the neighbors are lazy.
It shows that June will always disagree with her mother.

quiz.q: Why is the gift of six peaches at the end important to the story's structure?
ch: It shows the kindness June's mother gave coming back to the family.
It explains why the family earned less money than expected.
It introduces a new conflict for the next season.
It shows that the neighbors had extra money to spend.

quiz.q: State a theme of "Peaches in July" and explain how two scenes from different parts of the story work together to develop it.
quiz.ans: Theme: Kindness and hope can carry people through hard times. When the mother shares half their bread with the neighbors even though "We barely have enough," she shows generosity at the hardest moment; the neighbors' gift of six peaches at the end shows that kindness is returned and builds community.

lessons.name: How informational texts introduce and develop key events and people

practice.q: In an informational text, an anecdote is
ch: a short account of a real event used to illustrate an idea
practice.h: Think of a brief true story.

practice.q: An article about a hospital during a hurricane begins by describing one nurse carrying a baby down nine flights of stairs. What does this anecdote mainly do?
ch: It introduces the topic in a personal, memorable way.
It proves that all nurses are strong.
practice.h: Why might an author start with one person's experience?

practice.q: Two accounts describe the same flood. One is a newspaper report with water levels and dates. The other is a farmer's diary entry. What would the diary most likely include that the report does not?
ch: personal feelings and details from one person's experience
official data from many river gauges
a list of every town affected
practice.h: What would a person write in a private journal?

practice.q: Which detail best elaborates on the idea "Many families struggled during the Great Depression"?
ch: Some families lost their homes and moved in with relatives to save money.
Cars were invented before the Depression.
practice.h: Which detail gives an example of struggle?

practice.q: Explain why an author might include both statistics and a personal story in an article about hard times.
practice.ans: Statistics show how large the problem was, while a personal story helps readers connect emotionally and understand what it felt like for real people.
practice.h: What does each kind of evidence do for the reader?

quiz.q: According to "When the Sky Turned Black," what was "Black Sunday"?
ch: a huge dust storm that turned day into night
the day the Great Depression began
the first day of a long rainstorm
the day the Soil Conservation Service was created

quiz.q: How does the author introduce the topic of the Dust Bowl?
ch: with a vivid description of one terrible storm
with a story about a modern scientist

quiz.q: According to the second paragraph, which two causes combined to create the Dust Bowl?
ch: plowing up prairie grass and a long drought
the Great Depression and new cars

quiz.q: What does "plentiful" mean in "crops were plentiful"?
Which detail shows that families who moved to California still faced hardship?
ch: many faced low pay, crowded camps and unfriendly treatment
some found work on its farms
hundreds of thousands left the Plains

quiz.q: How does the author develop the idea that people "can work together to recover"?
ch: by describing new farming methods that the government and farmers used to protect the soil
by describing the darkness of Black Sunday
by explaining how prairie grass roots held the soil
by listing the problems migrants faced in California

quiz.q: Explain how the author shows that the Dust Bowl was caused by both human choices and nature. Use details from the passage.
quiz.ans: Human choices: farmers plowed up millions of acres of prairie grass whose roots had held the soil. Nature: a long drought dried the soil into powder, and strong winds lifted it. Together these caused the dust storms.

lessons.name: Figurative language and word relationships

practice.q: Personification gives
ch: human qualities to something that is not human
a comparison using like or as
a word that imitates a sound
practice.h: Look for a non-human thing acting like a person.

practice.q: Which sentence contains personification?
ch: The hungry wind clawed at the windows.
The wind was cold and strong.
The wind blew at forty miles per hour.
The windows were covered in dust.
practice.h: Can wind really be hungry or have claws?

practice.q: Read: "Her hope was a candle in a storm." What does this metaphor suggest?
ch: Her hope was small and fragile but still alive.
practice.h: Think about what happens to a candle in a storm.

practice.q: Which sentence is hyperbole?
ch: I've told you a million times to close the gate.
I told you twice to close the gate.
practice.h: Hyperbole is an exaggeration that is not meant literally.

practice.q: Write a sentence that uses personification to describe a drought. Explain what your personification suggests.
practice.ans: "The sun stared down at the cracked fields without blinking." It suggests the sun is harsh and relentless, giving the land no relief.
practice.h: Make the sun, the land or the dust act like a person.

quiz.q: A simile compares two things using
Which sentence contains a simile?
ch: The dust fell like gray snow on the fields.
The fields were dusty and dry.

quiz.q: Read: "The old truck groaned up the hill." What does "groaned" suggest?
ch: The truck struggled and made straining sounds.

quiz.q: In "Grief sat beside her at the table every night," what kind of figurative language is used?
What does the idiom "tighten our belts" mean in "During hard times, we all had to tighten our belts"?
Which word pair shows a cause-and-effect relationship?
Read: "The town was a ghost of its former self." What does this metaphor suggest?
ch: The town was empty and lifeless compared with the past.
People in the town saw real ghosts.
The town had grown much larger.
The town was holding a celebration.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between a simile and a metaphor. Write one example of each about hard times.
quiz.ans: A simile compares using "like" or "as": "Money slipped away like water through our fingers." A metaphor says one thing is another: "Each paycheck was a thin bridge over a deep river."

lessons.name: Writing a literary analysis: thesis, evidence and commentary

practice.q: A literary analysis essay mainly
ch: makes a claim about a text and supports it with evidence from the text
tells whether the writer found the story boring
practice.h: Analysis explains how or why, not just what happens.

practice.q: Which is the strongest thesis for a literary analysis?
ch: The author uses the changing seasons to show how the main character's grief slowly turns into hope.
The story is about a girl and her grandmother.
The story has a beginning, a middle and an end.
practice.h: A strong thesis makes a claim about how the author develops an idea.

practice.q: Which sentence introduces a quotation correctly?
ch: When the storm ends, the narrator says, "The world felt washed clean."
"The world felt washed clean." This is when the storm ends.
The narrator says the world felt washed clean."
When the storm ends "the world felt washed clean" says the narrator.
practice.h: Introduce the quotation with your own words and put quotation marks around the exact words.

practice.q: After a quotation, commentary should
ch: explain how the evidence supports the claim
practice.h: Ask yourself, "So what? How does this prove my point?"

practice.q: Read this evidence: the main character saves half of his small lunch for his little brother every day. Write a sentence of commentary that connects this evidence to the theme "Love means sacrifice."
practice.ans: By giving up part of his own small lunch every day, the character shows that he puts his brother's needs before his own, which reveals that love sometimes means sacrifice.
practice.h: Explain what the action shows and link it to the theme.

quiz.q: In a literary analysis, textual evidence is
ch: quotations or specific details from the text

quiz.q: Which sentence is the best commentary?
ch: This detail reveals that even in poverty, the family values generosity over comfort.
This quote is from the story.

quiz.q: Which transition best introduces a second piece of evidence?
Which sentence should be removed from a literary analysis paragraph about a character's courage?
ch: My aunt is also a very brave person.
The character steps forward when no one else will.
This choice shows that courage can be quiet.
Her trembling hands reveal that she is afraid but acts anyway.

quiz.q: Which verb tense is usually used to discuss a story's events in a literary analysis?
What should the conclusion of a literary analysis do?
ch: restate the thesis and explain why the theme matters
introduce a new piece of evidence

quiz.q: Write a thesis statement for a literary analysis of a story in which a girl who loses her home in a fire learns to rely on her neighbors.
quiz.ans: Through the girl's growing trust in her neighbors after the fire, the author shows that a community can rebuild what a disaster destroys.

test.q: Which sentence contains a metaphor?
ch: The classroom was a beehive of activity.
The classroom was busy like a beehive.
The classroom had a beehive outside.

test.q: Which sentence gives human qualities to an object?
ch: The empty house waited patiently for its family to return.
The house was empty for a year.

test.q: What does the idiom "make ends meet" mean?
ch: to have just enough money for what you need

test.q: Read: "After the factory closed, the town fell silent as a held breath." What feeling does the simile create?
Which word pair shows the same relationship as "drought : thirst"?
In a literary analysis, which sentence introduces evidence most effectively?
ch: When the storm destroys the barn, the narrator admits, "I felt like the ground had disappeared."
"I felt like the ground had disappeared."
The quote is "I felt like the ground had disappeared" and it shows stuff.
I felt like the ground had disappeared, the narrator.

test.q: Which is the strongest thesis for a literary analysis of a story about a family that loses its farm?
ch: Through the family's choice to stay together after losing the farm, the author shows that home is defined by people, not places.
This story is sad and made me cry.
The story takes place on a farm in the 1930s.

test.q: According to "Gardens for Hard Times," why did the government encourage war gardens in 1917?
ch: Much of the nation's food was being shipped to soldiers and allies, so people needed to grow more at home.
Schools wanted children to spend more time outside.

test.q: What does "rationed" mean in the third paragraph?
ch: limited to a certain amount for each family

test.q: How is the passage mainly organized?
ch: in chronological order, from World War I to today
as a comparison of two kinds of vegetables
as a list of gardening steps
from the least to the most important idea

test.q: Which detail supports the idea that victory gardens "did more than feed people"?
ch: Neighbors shared seeds, tools and advice.
Foods such as sugar, meat and canned goods were rationed.
Most victory gardens disappeared after the war.
Much of the nation's food was shipped to Europe.

test.q: How does the author respond to the argument that small gardens cannot solve hunger?
ch: The author agrees but explains that gardens offer other benefits, such as hope and community.
The author insists that gardens can feed whole cities.
The author says hunger is no longer a problem.

test.q: What is the author's point of view about gardens in hard times?
ch: They are valuable because they provide food, community and hope.
They are a waste of time during emergencies.
They should be required by law.
They were useful only during wars.

test.q: Write an objective summary of "Gardens for Hard Times" in two or three sentences.
test.ans: During both world wars, the U.S. government encouraged people to grow war or victory gardens so there would be enough food at home. The gardens helped families cope with rationing and brought neighbors together. The idea continues today in community gardens, which provide food as well as hope and connection.

test.q: What is the main problem facing Ellis's family in "The Mended Net"?
ch: Poor fishing and rising costs have put the family in financial trouble.
A sea lion is living under the dock.

test.q: What does the simile "his knees creaking like an old door" suggest about Grandpa Ike?
ch: He is old, but he still takes on hard work.
He is about to fall off the bucket.
He needs to repair the dock.

test.q: Why does Grandpa choose to repair the net instead of buying a new one?
ch: The family cannot afford to spend extra money.
He enjoys spending time on the dock.
New nets are not sold nearby.
He wants to prove he is faster than Ellis.

test.q: How does Ellis's approach to the work change in the middle of the story?
ch: He focuses on one knot at a time instead of on the size of the hole.
He gives up and goes home.
He asks his father to take over.
He starts working faster and more carelessly.

test.q: What does Grandpa mean when he says a net is "strong because someone keeps mending it"?
ch: Strength comes from repairing what breaks, not from never breaking.
The net is made of unusually strong twine.
Nets should never be used in storms.
Only Grandpa can make a net strong.

test.q: How does the final scene connect to the net-mending scene?
ch: Ellis applies the lesson of the net to his family's problems by offering to help.
Ellis decides to become a fisherman like Grandpa.
Ellis tells his parents about the sea lion.
Ellis learns that the family will sell the boat.

test.q: Explain how the author uses the net as a symbol. What does it represent?
test.ans: The torn net represents the family in hard times. Just as the net is repaired one knot at a time, the family can recover through patient, shared effort; after mending it, Ellis joins his parents to make a plan.

test.q: Write a literary analysis essay that explains how the author of "The Mended Net" develops a theme about facing hard times. State the theme in a clear thesis, analyze at least two key scenes or details, such as Grandpa's words and Ellis's actions, and support your ideas with quotations and commentary.
test.ans: Key points: a thesis that states a theme (for example, hard times are overcome through patience and working together, one step at a time); analysis of the torn net and Grandpa's statement "A net isn't strong because it never breaks. It's strong because someone keeps mending it"; Ellis's change from "This is hopeless" to focusing on one knot at a time; the ending, when Ellis asks "What can I do to help?", connected to the theme; quotations introduced smoothly and followed by commentary; present tense, formal style and a conclusion.
rub: Clear focus and strong organization; ideas fully developed with relevant details or text evidence; precise language; few errors in conventions.
Clear focus and organization; ideas adequately developed with some details or evidence; some errors that do not affect meaning.
Focus or organization is inconsistent; limited development or evidence; errors sometimes interfere with meaning.
Little focus or organization; minimal development; frequent errors.

units.name: Collection 5: Raising Your Voice (research)
units.el: Model the research steps with a visual organizer (question, source, note in my own words, citation). Practice fixing vague pronouns orally first by asking "Who is 'she'?" before revising in writing.

passages.x: The sign-up sheet said each speaker would get three minutes. Diego had timed his speech eleven times in his bedroom. It took two minutes and forty seconds when he talked fast and three minutes and ten seconds when he remembered to breathe. // Now he sat in the third row of the school board meeting, his paper folded into a damp square in his fist. The room smelled like coffee and floor polish. At the long table in front, five board members sat behind name cards, looking tired. // The issue was Route 9, the bus that carried students from the apartments on Grove Street to Hillcrest Middle School. The district wanted to cut it to save money. Without it, kids like Diego and his neighbors would have to walk almost two miles, across a highway overpass with no sidewalk. // I'm only twelve, Diego thought. Why would they listen to me? // Before him, a man in a suit spoke about the budget. He used words like "efficiencies" and "projected savings." The board members nodded politely. Then a woman spoke about traffic. More polite nods. Diego felt his heart sink. They had heard everything already. What could he add? // "Diego Fuentes," the secretary called. // He walked to the microphone. His knees felt as if they belonged to someone else. He unfolded his paper and looked at the first line, and suddenly the words seemed stiff and borrowed, like a jacket that didn't fit. // He folded the paper back up. // "I walked the route," he said. "Last Saturday. From my building to school. It took me forty-one minutes. There's a part on the overpass where the trucks go by so close that the wind pushes you. My sister is in sixth grade. She's small. I kept thinking about her walking there in the dark in winter." // The room was quiet. One board member, a gray-haired woman, had stopped writing and was looking right at him. // "The man before me said 'projected savings,'" Diego went on. "I don't know how to project anything. I just know that overpass." // When the timer beeped, he had talked for two minutes and fifty seconds. He walked back to his seat on legs that were still shaking. // Two weeks later, the district found the money to keep Route 9. Diego never knew for sure whether his three minutes had made the difference. But the gray-haired board member had found him after the meeting. "Thank you," she had said. "Numbers are easy to forget. That overpass isn't."

It is easy to think that only adults can change the rules. History tells a different story. Again and again, young people in the United States have spoken up about problems that affected them, and sometimes the nation listened. // In the summer of 1899, thousands of "newsies," the young people who sold newspapers on the streets of New York City, went on strike. Two powerful newspapers had raised the price the newsies paid for each bundle of papers. Since the newsies earned only pennies per paper, the change cut into money that many of their families depended on. The newsies refused to sell those papers and urged the public not to buy them. After about two weeks, the publishers agreed to a compromise: they would buy back the papers the newsies could not sell. // Four years later, in 1903, a labor organizer known as Mother Jones led a group of child mill workers on a march from Philadelphia toward New York. Many of the children worked long hours in textile mills, and some had been injured by machines. The march drew newspaper attention to the problem of child labor. Real change came slowly, but over the following decades, states and the federal government passed laws limiting child labor. // Young people have also spoken up in their schools. In 1965, thirteen-year-old Mary Beth Tinker and several other students in Des Moines, Iowa, wore black armbands to school to protest the Vietnam War. The school suspended them. Their families took the case to court, and in 1969 the United States Supreme Court ruled in the students' favor. The Court declared that students do not lose their right to freedom of expression "at the schoolhouse gate," as long as their actions do not seriously disrupt school. // These stories have something in common. In each case, young people noticed a problem that directly affected their lives, joined with others and found a way to make adults pay attention. Not every effort succeeded right away. But each one showed that age does not decide whether a voice matters. // Today, students continue to speak at school board meetings, write letters to newspapers and organize projects in their communities. They are part of a long tradition.

The sign was rolled up in the back of Lola's closet, behind the winter coats, tied with a faded red ribbon. I found it while looking for a shoebox for my science project. When I unrolled it, the cardboard cracked along old folds. Painted in big, uneven letters was one word: HUELGA. // "What does this mean?" I asked, carrying it into the kitchen. // My grandmother set down her knife. For a moment she just looked at the sign, as if it were a person she had not seen in a long time. "It means strike," she said. "It's Spanish. I carried it, and I'm not even Spanish-speaking." She laughed. "Sit down, Nadia." // I sat. Lola told me that when she was seventeen, she had worked in the grape fields near Delano with her father. The pay was low and the hours were long. Some growers did not provide clean drinking water or toilets in the fields. In 1965, Filipino farmworkers, her father among them, walked out of the fields and refused to work until conditions improved. Soon Mexican American workers joined them. // "Weren't you scared?" I asked. // "Every day." She turned her teacup slowly in her hands. "People shouted at us. Some workers lost their jobs. My father worried about how we would pay rent. But he said, 'If we stay quiet, nothing changes for anyone who comes after us.'" // The next spring, Lola had marched with hundreds of others from Delano all the way to Sacramento, the state capital. It took weeks. Her shoes wore through, and she wrapped her feet in strips of cloth. // "Did it work?" I asked. // "Not all at once," she said. "It took years. But yes. Things got better. Not perfect, but better." // I looked at the sign again. I had always thought of Lola as someone who baked bread and grew tomatoes and fell asleep during movies. I had never imagined her young, with blistered feet, shouting a word in a language that wasn't even hers. // "Why did you keep it?" I asked. // She rolled the sign up carefully and retied the ribbon. "So that one day someone would ask me what it means." // That night I didn't work on my science project. I started a new one, with a title in big, uneven letters at the top of the page.

Many people believe that only voters can influence their local government. But in most cities, anyone, including students, can take part. Here are some of the most common ways young people make their voices heard. // Public comment. City councils and school boards usually hold public meetings, and most set aside time for public comment. During this time, any member of the public can speak about an issue, often for two or three minutes. Speakers typically sign up at the start of the meeting or in advance. Because time is short, effective speakers plan carefully. They state who they are, explain the problem clearly and describe what they want the officials to do. // Letters and emails. Officials also read written messages from the public. A strong letter is brief and polite. It focuses on one issue and includes specific facts or personal experiences. For example, a student concerned about a dangerous intersection might describe near misses she has seen and include the number of students who cross there each morning. // Youth councils. Some cities and counties have youth councils or commissions, groups of teenagers who advise local leaders on issues that affect young people. Members might study topics such as parks, transportation or mental health and then present recommendations. Joining one can be a powerful way to learn how government works from the inside. // Petitions. A petition is a written request signed by many people. Petitions show officials how many people care about an issue. However, a petition is most effective when it makes a clear, specific request and when organizers follow up by speaking at meetings or meeting with officials. // Research first. Whatever method young people choose, research makes their message stronger. Before speaking up, it helps to learn the facts: How serious is the problem? Who has the power to fix it? Have other communities solved it? Officials are more likely to listen to someone who has done their homework. // Speaking up does not always bring quick results. Decisions can take months, and the answer is sometimes no. But every comment, letter and signature becomes part of the public record. Over time, steady and well-informed voices can shape the decisions that shape a community.

lessons.name: A speaker's or narrator's point of view

practice.q: The speaker of a poem is
ch: the voice that talks in the poem
practice.h: The poet creates a voice; it may or may not be the poet.

practice.q: Read these lines: "They say I'm too young to matter, / too small to be heard, / but a river begins as a single drop / and a song with a single word." What is the speaker's point of view?
ch: Young people's voices matter even if they start small.
Rivers are more important than songs.
The speaker is angry at rivers.
practice.h: What does the speaker compare young voices to?

practice.q: A poem says, "They say I'm too young to matter, / too small to be heard, / but a river begins as a single drop / and a song with a single word." What does "a river begins as a single drop" suggest?
ch: Big changes can grow from small beginnings.
The speaker lives near a river.
practice.h: Think about how a river grows from its source.

practice.q: A story is told by a narrator who believes her town's mayor is a villain. Later she learns the mayor was secretly helping. How does the narrator's point of view affect the reader?
ch: Readers share her mistaken belief until the truth is revealed.
Readers know the truth from the beginning.
The point of view makes the story completely factual.
practice.h: Can readers know more than the narrator knows?

practice.q: Explain why an author might tell a story about speaking up from the point of view of a shy character instead of a confident one.
practice.ans: A shy character's thoughts show how hard it is to speak up, so readers feel the character's fear and understand the courage it takes, which makes the character's growth more meaningful.
practice.h: Whose experience of speaking up would be more surprising or meaningful?

quiz.q: From which point of view is "Three Minutes" told?
ch: third person limited, focusing on Diego
first person, by the board member
third person omniscient, sharing the thoughts of everyone in the room

quiz.q: How does Diego feel while he listens to the speakers before him?
ch: discouraged, because he thinks he has nothing new to add
bored, because the meeting is long
angry at the man in the suit

quiz.q: What does the simile "like a jacket that didn't fit" suggest about Diego's written speech?
ch: It no longer feels like his own words.
It is too long to finish.
It is written on old paper.

quiz.q: Why is Diego's spoken speech effective?
ch: He uses his own experience of walking the route to show the danger.
He uses more budget numbers than the other speakers.
He speaks for longer than three minutes.
He reads every word from his paper.

quiz.q: How does Diego's point of view about Route 9 differ from that of the man in the suit?
ch: Diego sees the issue in terms of safety, while the man sees it in terms of money.
Diego wants to cut the route, while the man wants to keep it.
Diego cares about traffic, while the man cares about schools.
They have exactly the same point of view.

quiz.q: What does the board member's comment, "Numbers are easy to forget. That overpass isn't," suggest?
ch: Personal stories can make an issue more memorable than statistics.
Numbers are never important in decisions.
The board member did not understand the budget.
Diego should become a bus driver.

quiz.q: Explain how the author develops Diego's point of view through his thoughts and actions. Use at least two details from the story.
quiz.ans: His thought "I'm only twelve... Why would they listen to me?" shows self-doubt. His choice to fold up the paper and describe walking the overpass shows he decides to trust his own experience. Together these details show him moving from doubt to confidence in his own voice.

lessons.name: Author's purpose, point of view and information in different formats

practice.q: An author's purpose for writing an article that explains a city's new recycling law is most likely to
practice.h: What do articles about laws usually do?

practice.q: Which phrase reveals that an author has a positive view of a youth protest?

practice.q: Explain the difference between an author's purpose and an author's point of view.
practice.ans: Purpose is why the author writes (to inform, persuade or entertain). Point of view is the author's attitude or opinion about the topic, shown through word choice and the details the author includes.
practice.h: One answers "Why write?" The other answers "How does the author feel about it?"

quiz.q: What is the author's main purpose in "Young Voices in History"?
ch: to inform readers about times young people spoke up and created change
to persuade readers to sell newspapers
to entertain readers with a made-up story
to explain every step of how the Supreme Court works

quiz.q: Why did the newsies go on strike in 1899?
ch: Two newspapers raised the price the newsies paid for bundles of papers.
They wanted to stop going to school.

ch: The publishers agreed to buy back papers the newsies could not sell.

from the most to the least important example

as a comparison of two newspapers

quiz.ans: In each, young people faced a problem affecting their lives and acted together: the newsies went on strike over the price increase, child mill workers marched to draw attention to child labor, and students wore armbands and took their case to court. Each effort made adults pay attention.

lessons.name: Clear pronouns and punctuating extra information

practice.q: A vague pronoun is one that
ch: does not clearly refer to a specific noun
practice.h: Ask yourself: who or what does the pronoun mean?

practice.q: Which sentence has a vague pronoun?

Maria seemed upset when she talked to Kim.
Maria and Kim talked about the vote.
Kim listened while Maria explained the vote.

practice.q: Which sentence has an inappropriate shift in pronoun person?

When students speak at meetings, they should prepare notes.
When you speak at meetings, you should prepare notes.
When I speak at meetings, I prepare notes.

Ms. Ortiz, our class adviser helped us write the petition.

practice.q: Rewrite this sentence to fix the vague pronoun: "The students told the teachers that they needed more time."
practice.ans: The students told the teachers, "We need more time." (Or: The students said the teachers needed more time. Any revision that makes clear who needed time.)

People they say the vote will happen Friday.

The petition signed by 300 students (was delivered on Monday.

If people wants to speak, you must sign up first.

Our mayor, who grew up in this neighborhood listened carefully.
Our, mayor who grew up in this neighborhood listened carefully.

The council's decision to delay the vote made people angry.

ch: Jada asked Rosa, "May I present first?"
Jada asked Rosa if she could present first, please.
Jada, asked Rosa, if she could present first.
She asked Rosa if she could present first.

quiz.q: Write a sentence about a community project that includes a nonrestrictive element set off by commas. Then explain why the commas are needed.
quiz.ans: "The garden, which students planted in May, now feeds twenty families." The commas are needed because "which students planted in May" adds extra information that is not necessary to identify the garden.

lessons.name: Research: questions, sources, notes and citations

practice.q: A good research question for a short project is
ch: focused enough to answer with research but open enough to explore
so broad that whole books cover it
practice.h: Think about a question you could answer in a short report.

practice.q: Which research question is best for a short report?
ch: How did the 1899 newsboys' strike change the newsies' working conditions?
practice.h: Look for a focused question that requires research to answer.

practice.q: Which source is most likely to be credible for a report on a city's bike lanes?
practice.h: Who has expert knowledge and no reason to sell something?

copy whole paragraphs without noting the source
write down only the website's colors
skip noting where the facts came from

practice.q: Explain the difference between quoting and paraphrasing. When might you choose each?
practice.ans: Quoting uses the author's exact words in quotation marks; paraphrasing restates the idea in your own words. Quote when the exact wording is powerful or important; paraphrase to explain information more simply. Both need credit.
practice.h: Think about exact words versus your own words.

quiz.q: Plagiarism is

ch: The march (which lasted almost a month) ended at the state capitol.
The march which (lasted almost a month ended) at the state capitol.
The (march which lasted) almost a month ended at the state capitol.
The march which lasted almost a month ended (at the state capitol.

ch: an advertisement for a law firm

test.q: Which is the best paraphrase of "Officials are more likely to listen to someone who has done their homework"?
ch: Leaders pay more attention to people who have researched the issue.
Officials are more likely to listen to someone who has done their homework.

test.q: Who narrates "Lola's Sign"?
ch: an outside narrator who knows every character's thoughts

test.q: What does the simile "as if it were a person she had not seen in a long time" suggest about Lola's reaction to the sign?
ch: It brings back strong memories and feelings.
She does not recognize the sign.
She is angry that Nadia found it.
She thinks the sign belongs to someone else.

test.q: According to Lola, why did the farmworkers refuse to work?
ch: to demand better pay and working conditions
because the grape season had ended
to protest the closing of a school
because they wanted to move to Sacramento

test.q: What does Lola's father's statement "If we stay quiet, nothing changes for anyone who comes after us" reveal about him?
ch: He believed speaking up mattered for future workers.
He wanted his family to stay silent.

He planned to leave farm work forever.

test.ans: She kept it "so that one day someone would ask me what it means." This shows that passing on stories of speaking up helps the next generation remember and continue the work, a theme about voices carrying forward through families.

test.q: According to "Your Voice at City Hall," what is public comment?
ch: time at a public meeting when any member of the public can speak
a vote taken by council members
a letter printed in the newspaper

test.q: How does the author organize most of the passage?
ch: by describing different ways to take part, each in its own section
as a story about one student
as a comparison of two cities

test.q: According to the passage, what makes a petition most effective?
ch: a clear, specific request plus follow-up such as speaking at meetings
a very long list of complaints

test.q: What is the purpose of the example about the dangerous intersection?
ch: to show how specific facts and experiences strengthen a letter
to argue that every intersection is dangerous
to explain how to sign up for public comment
to describe what a youth council does

test.q: What does "recommendations" most likely mean in "present recommendations"?
ch: suggestions about what should be done

test.q: Which statement best reflects the author's point of view?
ch: Young people can influence local government, especially when they are well informed and persistent.
Only voters can influence local government.
Petitions are the only method that works.
Officials rarely read letters from students.

test.q: Why does the author say research makes a message stronger? Use details from the passage.
test.ans: Research helps speakers learn how serious the problem is, who has the power to fix it and how other communities solved it, and officials are "more likely to listen to someone who has done their homework."

test.q: Write a short research report that explains how young people can make their voices heard in local government. Use at least three facts or ideas from "Your Voice at City Hall," paraphrased or quoted with credit, and end with two focused research questions you would investigate next and the kinds of sources you would use to answer them.
test.ans: Key points: an introduction with a clear focus; at least three methods explained accurately (public comment, letters and emails, youth councils, petitions); why research and persistence matter; information paraphrased in the student's own words or quoted with credit to the article; logical organization with headings or transitions; formal style; two focused research questions (for example, "Does our city have a youth commission, and how do students join?") and credible sources such as the city website, meeting minutes or interviews with officials.
rub: Clear focus and strong organization; ideas fully developed with relevant details or text evidence; precise language; few errors in conventions.
Clear focus and organization; ideas adequately developed with some details or evidence; some errors that do not affect meaning.
Focus or organization is inconsistent; limited development or evidence; errors sometimes interfere with meaning.
Little focus or organization; minimal development; frequent errors.

passages.t: The Keeper of the Last Ember
passages.x: Long ago, when the world was younger and the winters were longer, a village in the northern mountains kept a single fire burning in the center of its square. The elders said that as long as the fire lived, the village would live too. // One winter, a wind came down from the peaks so fierce that it blew out every flame in a single night. In the morning, the people found only gray ash and a single glowing ember, no bigger than a fingernail, buried at the bottom of the pit. // "There is a fire on the far side of the mountain," said the eldest woman, "kept by the people of the valley. Someone must carry this ember there, feed it from their flame and bring the fire home before the ember dies." // The strongest hunters stepped forward, but the eldest shook her head. "Strength will not keep an ember alive. Patience will." She looked at Nima, a quiet girl who tended the goats and had once spent a whole night keeping a sick young goat warm. "You," she said. // Nima set out with the ember in a clay pot packed with dry moss. On the first day, she crossed a frozen river, testing every step. On the second day, a snowstorm caught her, and she curled her body around the pot like a shell, breathing on the ember to keep it glowing. On the third day, she met a traveler who offered to trade her a warm coat for the pot. She was shivering, and the coat was thick. But she shook her head and walked on. // When she reached the valley, the people there welcomed her, fed her and let her light a torch from their great fire. "Why didn't you just ask us to come to you?" a child asked. // Nima thought about it. "Because then I would not have learned how far I could go." // She carried the torch home through the melting snow. When she lit the village fire again, the people cheered, but the eldest only smiled and handed her a small clay pot. // "Now," she said, "you are the keeper. Teach the next one."

passages.t: Two Views of the Endurance Rescue
passages.x: Account 1: The Boss's Gamble. In 1914, explorer Ernest Shackleton sailed for Antarctica with a crew of twenty-seven men, hoping to be the first to cross the continent on foot. He never got the chance. In early 1915, his ship, the Endurance, became trapped in the frozen Weddell Sea. Months later, the ice crushed the ship, and it sank. // Shackleton, whom his men called "the Boss," led his crew across the ice and finally into three small lifeboats, which carried them to Elephant Island, a rocky, uninhabited place. No ship would ever look for them there. So Shackleton made a bold decision. He and five men would sail one lifeboat, the James Caird, about 800 miles across some of the roughest ocean on Earth to the island of South Georgia, where there was a whaling station. // For more than two weeks, the tiny boat battled freezing waves. Then the men had to cross South Georgia's unmapped, icy mountains on foot. At last they stumbled into the whaling station. Shackleton immediately began organizing a rescue. Historians often point to this journey as one of the greatest examples of leadership in the history of exploration. // Account 2: The Men Who Waited. When the James Caird sailed away from Elephant Island in April 1916, twenty-two men stayed behind. Their story is told less often, but their survival required its own kind of courage. // Led by Frank Wild, Shackleton's second-in-command, the men turned the two remaining lifeboats upside down on low stone walls to make a hut. They lived in this cramped, smoky shelter for more than four months, eating mostly penguins and seals. Wild kept a strict routine. Each morning, he reportedly told the men to pack their things because "the Boss may come today." Whether or not they believed it, the routine gave them hope and a reason to keep going. // Rescue attempts failed three times because of sea ice. Finally, on August 30, 1916, a Chilean ship reached the island. Every man on Elephant Island was alive. // Both accounts end with the same remarkable fact: all twenty-eight members of the expedition survived.

For centuries, the peak that people in Nepal call Sagarmatha and people in Tibet call Chomolungma stood unclimbed. Known in English as Mount Everest, it rises about 29,000 feet above sea level, higher than any other mountain on Earth. Near its top, each breath holds only about a third as much oxygen as at sea level, winds can be strong enough to knock a person over, and temperatures fall far below zero. Many climbers had tried to reach the summit. All had failed, and some had died trying. // In the spring of 1953, a large British-led expedition set out to try again. Its leader, John Hunt, knew that no single climber could succeed alone. Hundreds of porters carried supplies, and teams of climbers set up a chain of camps higher and higher up the mountain. Each team's work made the next team's climb possible. // Two climbers were chosen for the final push: Edmund Hillary, a beekeeper from New Zealand, and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa mountaineer who had already joined several earlier attempts on Everest. On the morning of May 29, carrying heavy oxygen tanks, they climbed along a narrow, snowy ridge with steep drops on both sides. Near the top, they faced a nearly vertical wall of rock and ice. Hillary wedged himself into a crack and inched upward, with Tenzing holding the rope below. Then Tenzing followed. // At about 11:30 in the morning, the two men stood on the highest point on Earth. They stayed only about fifteen minutes. Hillary took photographs. Tenzing left small offerings in the snow. Then they began the dangerous trip down. // When the news reached the world, reporters wanted to know who had stepped onto the summit first. Both men refused to say, explaining that they had reached the top as a team. A few years later, Tenzing wrote that Hillary had stepped onto the summit first, but he insisted that it did not matter. // Today, thousands of people have climbed Everest. But the 1953 climb is still remembered not just for who reached the top, but for how they did it: together, with the help of hundreds of others whose names are rarely mentioned.

In the high country, where the river runs fast and cold through a deep canyon, there was once a village whose only path to the market towns was a bridge woven of grass. Every year, when the dry season came, the old bridge was cut down and a new one was woven, for grass rope grows weak with time. // Amaru was the finest young weaver in the village. His fingers were quick, his knots were tight, and he knew it. "When I am grown," he often said, "I will weave the bridge myself, and people will sing about me." // That year, a storm tore the old bridge from its posts before the dry season arrived. The village was cut off. The elders called a meeting to plan the weaving, but Amaru did not go. He had decided that this was his chance. That night, alone in his family's storehouse, he began to braid a great rope from the grass he had gathered. // He worked for three days and three nights. His hands blistered. His eyes burned. On the fourth morning, he dragged his rope to the edge of the canyon and threw one end across to show everyone what he had done. // It fell short. It dangled over the river, swinging, a full stone's throw from the other side. And where he had braided too fast, the strands had already begun to fray. // Amaru sat down on the rocks, ashamed. After a while, his grandmother sat beside him. She picked up the frayed end of his rope and turned it in her fingers. // "These are good knots," she said. "But a bridge is not one rope. It is many cords twisted into one. That is why it holds." // The next day, every family in the village came to the canyon, each carrying a cord braided at home: thin ones from children, thick ones from the strongest men and women, uneven ones from the very old. Amaru's task was to twist them together. He worked slowly now, listening to the elders and testing each twist. // When the new bridge stretched across the canyon, the people did sing, as Amaru had once dreamed. But they did not sing his name. They sang the names of every family whose cord was in the bridge. // Amaru found that he did not mind. When he crossed the swaying bridge for the first time, he could feel each cord beneath his feet, holding.

lessons.name: Quest stories and the hero's journey

practice.q: In a traditional quest story, the hero usually
ch: leaves home to reach a goal and faces challenges along the way
is always a king or queen
practice.h: Think about what the word "quest" means.

practice.q: A myth and a modern graphic novel both tell about a hero who defeats a monster. What is most likely different?
ch: the way the story is told, such as pictures and speech bubbles instead of narration
the idea that the hero faces a challenge
that there is a main character
practice.h: Think about the form of each text, not the basic story elements.

practice.q: Which is an example of a "trial" in a hero's journey?
ch: crossing a dangerous desert to reach a hidden spring
practice.h: A trial tests the hero.

practice.q: A poem and a story both describe a lost traveler finding home. How might the poem's form affect the reader's experience?
ch: Its line breaks, rhythm and images can create strong feeling in fewer words.
It is always divided into chapters.
practice.h: What tools does a poet use that a storyteller might not?

practice.q: Explain how a mentor character helps a hero in a quest story. Give an example from a story, movie or myth you know.
practice.ans: A mentor gives the hero advice, training or a gift that helps on the journey, such as a wise teacher who trains a young hero before a battle.
practice.h: Think of an older or wiser character who guides the hero.

quiz.q: What problem begins Nima's quest?
ch: The village fire has gone out except for one tiny ember.
Nima has lost her goats in the snow.
The valley people have stolen the fire.
The eldest woman has become sick.

quiz.q: Why does the eldest choose Nima instead of the strongest hunters?
ch: She believes the quest requires patience, which Nima has shown.
Nima is the fastest runner in the village.
Nima already knows the valley people.

quiz.q: Which detail best shows Nima's patience and care during the journey?
ch: She curls around the pot and breathes on the ember during the storm.
She lights a torch from the great fire.

quiz.q: Why does Nima refuse to trade the pot for the warm coat?
ch: Her duty to the village matters more than her own comfort.
The coat is too small for her.
She already has a warmer coat.

quiz.q: How is this tale similar to many traditional hero stories?
ch: A hero leaves home, faces trials and returns with something the community needs.
It takes place in a modern city.
The hero fails and never returns.
It is told through a series of letters.

quiz.q: What does the ending, when the eldest hands Nima a clay pot and says "Teach the next one," suggest?
ch: Knowledge and responsibility are passed from one generation to the next.
Nima must make the journey again the next day.
The eldest is disappointed in Nima.
The fire will soon go out again.

quiz.q: State a theme of "The Keeper of the Last Ember" and support it with two details from the tale.
quiz.ans: Theme: Patience and responsibility can be more powerful than strength. Details: the eldest says, "Strength will not keep an ember alive. Patience will"; Nima breathes on the ember through the storm and refuses the coat to protect it.

lessons.name: Comparing two authors' accounts of the same events

practice.q: When two authors write about the same event, they may
ch: emphasize different people, details or ideas
always use exactly the same facts and words
practice.h: Think about what each author chooses to focus on.

practice.q: A historian writes a biography of a mountain climber. The climber writes a memoir about the same climb. What might the memoir include that the biography does not?
ch: the climber's private thoughts and feelings during the climb
a list of the climber's awards
practice.h: A memoir is written from the writer's own experience.

practice.q: Two articles describe the Wright brothers' first airplane flights. One emphasizes their years of failed tests. The other emphasizes how slowly newspapers reported the news. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: Each author shapes the story by choosing what to emphasize.
One of the articles must be false.
practice.h: A different focus does not mean one account is false.

practice.q: Which question best helps you compare two accounts of the same event?
ch: What details does each author include or leave out, and why?
Which author has the longer name?
Which account was printed in color?
practice.h: Focus on the authors' choices.

practice.q: Explain why reading two accounts of the same historical event can help you understand it better.
practice.ans: Each author may focus on different people or details, so reading both gives a more complete picture, and comparing them helps you notice each author's point of view or gaps in the information.
practice.h: What might one author leave out?

quiz.q: Why did the Endurance sink?
ch: It was crushed by sea ice.
It hit a rock near South Georgia.
It was caught in a hurricane.
Its crew abandoned it in port.

quiz.q: What is the main focus of Account 1?
ch: Shackleton's leadership during the dangerous boat journey and rescue
daily life for the men on Elephant Island

quiz.q: What is the main focus of Account 2?
ch: the courage and routine of the men who waited on Elephant Island
the crossing of South Georgia's mountains

quiz.q: Why did Shackleton decide to sail the James Caird to South Georgia?
ch: No ship would look for them on Elephant Island, but South Georgia had a whaling station.
He wanted to cross Antarctica by boat.
The other men asked him to leave them behind.
South Georgia was the closest island to the ship.

quiz.q: According to Account 2, how did Frank Wild's routine help the men?
ch: It gave them hope and a reason to keep going.
It helped them build a new ship.
It let them catch more fish.
It made the rescue ship arrive sooner.

quiz.q: How do the two accounts together give a fuller picture of the rescue?
ch: One shows the bold journey to get help, and the other shows the endurance of those who waited.
They disagree about whether the men survived.
Both describe only the sinking of the ship.
One is fiction and the other is fact.

quiz.q: Compare how the two authors present the idea of courage. Use one detail from each account.
quiz.ans: Account 1 presents courage as bold action, such as sailing about 800 miles in a tiny boat through rough seas. Account 2 presents courage as patient endurance, such as living under overturned boats for more than four months and packing each morning because "the Boss may come today."

lessons.name: Varying sentences, keeping a consistent style and using reference materials

practice.q: A writer who wants to vary sentence patterns should
ch: combine some short sentences and begin sentences in different ways
make every sentence the same length
practice.h: Variety keeps readers interested.

practice.q: Which revision best combines these sentences: "The hero climbed the cliff. The cliff was icy. She did not slip."?
ch: The hero climbed the icy cliff without slipping.
The hero climbed. The cliff. It was icy.
The hero climbed the cliff, the cliff was icy, she did not slip.
Climbing, icy, the hero did not slip cliff.
practice.h: Combine the details into one smooth sentence.

practice.q: Which sentence would NOT fit the formal, serious tone of a report on ancient legends?
ch: Honestly, those old legends are kind of goofy.
Many cultures tell legends about great floods.
Legends often explain events in nature.
Some legends were passed down orally for centuries.
practice.h: Which sentence sounds casual?

practice.q: In a book about myths, a glossary is used to
ch: find the meanings of key words used in that book
find the page where a chapter begins
see a map of ancient Greece
practice.h: Glossaries are usually at the back of informational books.

practice.q: Rewrite this choppy passage using varied sentences: "The storm came. The ship rocked. The sailors were afraid. The captain stayed calm."
practice.ans: As the storm came and the ship rocked, the sailors grew afraid, but the captain stayed calm.
practice.h: Try starting with "As" or "When" and use a conjunction.

quiz.q: A thesaurus is most useful for finding
ch: how to pronounce a place name

quiz.q: Which sentence begins with a prepositional phrase to add variety?
ch: Across the frozen lake, the travelers walked in silence.
The travelers walked in silence across the frozen lake.
Silence was kept by the travelers.

quiz.q: A dictionary entry reads: "quest (kwest) noun 1. a long search for something important 2. (old use) an official inquiry." Which meaning fits "Her quest to find her brother took years"?
Which sentence best keeps a consistent formal style?
ch: The legend explains how the river was formed.
The legend is, like, about a river.

quiz.q: What does the label "verb" in a dictionary entry tell you about a word?
Which revision best fixes the repetitive pattern in "She ran. She jumped. She caught the rope."?
ch: She ran, jumped and caught the rope.
She ran. She jumped. She caught.
The rope caught her running jumping.

quiz.q: A student reads "The hero's resolve never wavered" and guesses that "resolve" means "determination." What is the best way to verify this guess?
ch: check the word in a dictionary and see whether that meaning fits the sentence
ask a friend to guess too

quiz.q: Explain why a writer might place a short sentence after several long ones. Give an example.
quiz.ans: A short sentence after long ones creates emphasis or a sudden pause. Example: "The travelers climbed for hours, through drifting snow and over slick rocks, until their legs burned. Then they stopped."

lessons.name: Writing a literary analysis that compares texts

practice.q: In a compare-and-contrast essay, point-by-point organization
ch: discusses one point at a time, comparing both texts on each point
discusses only one of the texts
practice.h: Each body paragraph covers one point for both texts.

practice.q: Which thesis best compares two texts?
ch: Although a myth and a modern story tell of very different heroes, both show that true courage means putting others first.
I liked the myth better than the story.
The myth is old, and the story is new.
practice.h: A strong comparison thesis names a meaningful similarity or difference.

practice.q: Which transition shows contrast?
practice.h: Contrast means difference.

practice.q: Which revision step is most helpful after finishing a draft?
ch: rereading to check that each paragraph supports the thesis with evidence
adding a new topic at the end
practice.h: Revision focuses on ideas and organization, not only small changes.

practice.q: Write a topic sentence for a body paragraph that compares how two heroes respond to a challenge.
practice.ans: While the first hero faces the storm with quiet patience, the second charges at danger with strength, showing two different kinds of courage.
practice.h: Name both heroes and the point you are comparing.

quiz.q: In a compare-and-contrast essay, the thesis should
ch: state the main similarity or difference the essay will analyze
list every detail from both texts
ask a question with no answer

quiz.q: Which transition shows similarity?
Which sentence gives the strongest evidence for a comparison of two quest stories?
ch: In both stories, the hero refuses a tempting offer: one turns down a warm coat, and the other turns down a bag of gold.
One story is longer than the other.

quiz.q: While revising, a writer notices that two body paragraphs both discuss setting. What should the writer do?
ch: combine them or refocus one paragraph on a different point
keep both exactly as they are
add a third paragraph about setting

quiz.q: Which conclusion is strongest for an essay comparing two hero tales?
ch: Though separated by centuries, both tales remind readers that the hardest journeys are often the ones we take for others.
That is the end of my essay.
I hope you liked my comparison.

quiz.q: When writing about two texts, why should you name each text's title?
ch: so readers know which text each piece of evidence comes from
because titles must appear twice in every paragraph
because the teacher likes capital letters

quiz.q: List one similarity and one difference between a myth and a modern realistic story about a journey.
quiz.ans: Similarity: both have a hero who faces challenges on a journey and changes. Difference: a myth may include gods or magic, while a realistic story includes only events that could really happen.

test.q: Which reference tool shows how to pronounce a word and gives its part of speech?
Which sentence varies the pattern by beginning with a dependent clause?
ch: When the bridge was finished, the village celebrated.
The bridge was finished and the village celebrated.

test.q: Which revision best combines "The climbers were tired. They kept going. The summit was close."?
ch: Although the climbers were tired, they kept going because the summit was close.
The climbers were tired, they kept going, the summit was close.
Tired climbers. Kept going. Summit close.
The climbers were tired and they kept going and the summit was close and.

test.q: Which word would a thesaurus most likely list as a synonym for "persevere"?
Which sentence does NOT match a formal style?
ch: The expedition was, like, totally epic.
The team set up several camps.

test.q: A glossary entry reads "summit: the highest point of a mountain." Where would you most likely find this entry?
ch: at the back of an informational book

test.q: Which transition best introduces a contrast in an essay comparing a legend and an article?
According to "Together at the Top," what made climbing Everest so dangerous?
ch: thin air, powerful winds and extreme cold

test.q: What does the second paragraph mainly explain?
ch: how the expedition depended on the teamwork of many people

test.q: How does the author describe the route near the summit?
ch: a narrow, snowy ridge with steep drops and a nearly vertical wall of rock and ice

test.q: Why did Hillary and Tenzing at first refuse to say who reached the summit first?
ch: They believed they had reached the top as a team.
They were not allowed to speak to reporters.
They had argued and stopped speaking.

test.q: What does "expedition" mean in "a large British-led expedition"?
ch: an organized journey with a specific goal

test.q: What is the author's main point in the final paragraph?
ch: The climb is remembered for its teamwork, including people whose names are rarely mentioned.
Hillary deserves more credit than Tenzing.
Most people who try to climb Everest fail.

test.q: Explain how the author develops the idea that reaching the summit was a team achievement. Use two details.
test.ans: Hundreds of porters carried supplies and teams set up camps that made the final climb possible; Hillary climbed the rock wall while Tenzing held the rope; and both men refused to say who stepped first because they reached the top as a team.

test.q: What does Amaru want at the beginning of "The Bridge of Grass"?
ch: to weave the bridge himself and be famous for it

test.q: Why does Amaru skip the elders' meeting?
ch: He wants to build the bridge alone and take the credit.
He is afraid of the canyon.

test.q: What happens when Amaru throws his rope across the canyon?
ch: It falls short and has already begun to fray.
It reaches the other side perfectly.

test.q: What does the grandmother mean when she says "a bridge is not one rope"?
ch: Strong things are made when many people contribute together.
Amaru used the wrong kind of grass.
Bridges should be built of wood.

test.q: How does Amaru's way of working change after he talks with his grandmother?
ch: He works slowly, listens to the elders and tests each twist.
He refuses to help at all.
He asks someone else to do his job.

test.q: Why is it significant that the people sing every family's name instead of Amaru's?
ch: It shows that the bridge belongs to the whole community and that Amaru has learned humility.
It shows that the people forgot Amaru had helped.
It shows that the elders are angry at Amaru.
It shows that singing is a village rule.

test.q: Explain how Amaru changes from the beginning to the end of the story. Use two details.
test.ans: At first he is proud and wants glory, saying people "will sing about me" and working alone in secret. By the end, he works slowly with the whole village and does not mind that they sing every family's name instead of his, showing humility.

test.q: Write a literary analysis essay that compares how "The Bridge of Grass" (a legend-style tale) and "Together at the Top" (an informational text) present the idea that great achievements require teamwork. Explain one similarity and one difference in how the two texts develop this idea, and support each point with evidence from both texts.
