test.ans: Key points: a thesis that names the shared idea and how the two genres present it differently; similarity: both show that success depends on many contributors (each family's cord; hundreds of porters and teams setting up camps; Tenzing holding the rope for Hillary); difference: the tale teaches through a fictional character's change from pride to humility and a symbol (a bridge of many cords), while the article informs with real people, dates and events; evidence from both texts with titles named; comparison transitions such as similarly and in contrast; formal style and a conclusion.
rub: Clear focus and strong organization; ideas fully developed with relevant details or text evidence; precise language; few errors in conventions.
Clear focus and organization; ideas adequately developed with some details or evidence; some errors that do not affect meaning.
Focus or organization is inconsistent; limited development or evidence; errors sometimes interfere with meaning.
Little focus or organization; minimal development; frequent errors.

ela|7.about: Seventh graders read literature and informational texts side by side in six themed collections. They cite several pieces of evidence, analyze how story elements interact, compare characters' points of view, analyze the structure of poems and dramas, compare fictional and historical accounts, trace and evaluate arguments for sound reasoning and sufficient evidence, use phrases, clauses and sentence types for effect, and write narratives, informative essays, arguments, literary analyses and research reports.
std: Cite several pieces of textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
Determine a theme or central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text; provide an objective summary of the text.
Analyze how particular elements of a story or drama interact (e.g., how setting shapes the characters or plot).
Determine two or more central ideas in a text and analyze their development over the course of the text; provide an objective summary of the text.
Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient to support the claims.
Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage, including the function of phrases and clauses and simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences.
Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas, concepts and information through the selection, organization and analysis of relevant content.

units.name: Collection 1: Turning Points (narrative)
units.el: Use a story-elements map (setting, characters, conflict, turning point, resolution) with arrows showing "this caused that," and give clause starters on cards (when, because, although, after, if).

passages.x: Every Saturday night from April to October, the parking lot behind the library turned into a night market. White tents went up in rows, strings of bulbs glowed overhead, and the air filled with smoke from the grills and the sound of six languages at once. For as long as Tuan could remember, his family's noodle stand had stood in the third row, between a woman who sold phone cases and a man who sold grilled corn. // Tuan was thirteen, which meant he was old enough to take orders, count change and carry steaming bowls without spilling. It also meant, according to his father, that he was old enough to understand that the stand paid for everything: rent, his sister's braces, even the trumpet Tuan practiced every afternoon. // The problem was the jazz band. The community youth band rehearsed on Saturday nights, and the director, Ms. Abernathy, had heard him play at a school concert. "We need a second trumpet," she had said. "Think about it." // Tuan thought about it every Saturday as he ladled broth. He did not ask his father. He already knew the answer. Saturday was the busiest night. Without Tuan, his mother would have to work the register and the stove at once. // Then, in late June, the man who sold grilled corn did not come back. In his place, a group of teenagers set up a small stage with a sign: OPEN MIC, ALL WELCOME. // For three weeks, Tuan listened to singers and a boy with a violin. On the fourth Saturday, during a slow hour, his mother nudged him. "Your horn is in the car," she said quietly. "Go." // "Dad will..." // "Your father is in the back. Go." // Tuan played one song, an old ballad his grandfather used to hum. He was halfway through when he saw his father standing at the edge of the crowd, still in his apron, arms folded. Tuan's heart stopped, but his fingers kept moving. // When he finished, people clapped. His father walked back to the stand without a word. // That night, as they packed up the tents, his father finally spoke. "That band," he said, wiping down the counter. "What time does it end?" // "Nine," Tuan said. // His father nodded slowly. "After nine, I still need you to help pack up." He paused. "Your mother says your cousin Linh wants to earn money. Maybe she can take your Saturday shift." // Tuan could not speak, so he picked up a stack of chairs instead. His father was not a man of many words. But Tuan understood that this was a turning point, for both of them.

In September 1928, a Scottish scientist named Alexander Fleming returned to his London laboratory after a summer vacation. Before he left, he had stacked dishes of bacteria on a bench. Now, sorting through them, he noticed something odd. In one dish, a fuzzy patch of mold had grown. Around the mold was a clear ring where the bacteria had died. // Many scientists might have thrown the dish away. Fleming did not. He was curious about why the bacteria near the mold had disappeared. He grew more of the mold, a type called Penicillium, and found that it released a substance that killed many kinds of harmful bacteria. He named the substance penicillin. // Fleming's discovery was a turning point, but it did not change medicine right away. Penicillin was difficult to produce and purify, and Fleming could not make enough of it to treat patients. For about ten years, his discovery attracted little attention. // The next turning point came at the University of Oxford. Around 1939, a team led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain began studying penicillin again. Working with other scientists, including Norman Heatley, who designed clever equipment to extract the drug, they found a way to purify it. In 1940, they showed that penicillin protected mice from deadly infections. Soon they tested it on human patients, with remarkable results. // World War II added urgency. Wounded soldiers often died from infected injuries, and penicillin could save them. British and American scientists and companies worked together to mass-produce the drug. By the end of the war, penicillin was being made in large quantities. // In 1945, Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Penicillin became the first widely used antibiotic and has since saved millions of lives. // The story of penicillin is often told as a lucky accident. Luck mattered. But the discovery became a turning point only because of a chain of people: one curious scientist who noticed something strange, a team that refused to give up on a difficult problem, and a world that urgently needed what they made.

On April 15, 1947, a twenty-eight-year-old first baseman trotted onto Ebbets Field in Brooklyn, New York. His name was Jackie Robinson, and by playing that day for the Brooklyn Dodgers, he became the first Black player in modern Major League Baseball. For decades, an unwritten rule had kept Black athletes out of the major leagues, forcing them to play in separate leagues. Robinson's first game marked a turning point not only for baseball but for the nation. // The turning point was carefully planned. Branch Rickey, the Dodgers' president, had wanted to integrate the team for years. He searched for a player who was not only talented but also able to stay calm under enormous pressure. Robinson, who had been a star athlete at UCLA and had served in the Army, seemed like the right choice. According to accounts of their first meeting, Rickey warned Robinson that he would face insults and threats and asked him to promise not to fight back, at least at first. Rickey wanted a player with the courage not to respond. // Robinson kept that promise, but it came at a cost. Some opposing players shouted cruel insults. Pitchers threw at him. He received hate mail and threats. Even a few of his own teammates at first signed a petition saying they did not want to play with him. Through it all, Robinson answered with his performance. He hit, ran and stole bases with a daring style that thrilled fans. At the end of the 1947 season, he was named the first winner of the league's Rookie of the Year award. // His success changed minds. Teammates who had doubted him came to defend him. Other teams began signing Black players. Within a few years, several of the game's biggest stars were players who would have been shut out entirely just a decade earlier. // Robinson's influence extended far beyond the ballpark. After retiring, he spoke out for civil rights and worked in business to create opportunities for Black Americans. In 1997, fifty years after his first game, Major League Baseball retired his uniform number, 42, for every team. Today, on April 15 each year, every major league player wears number 42 to honor him. // Robinson's gravestone carries his belief that a life is not important except in the impact it has on other lives. By that measure, his was one of the most important lives in American sports.

For two years, Priya had sat in the first chair of the Washington Middle School orchestra's violin section. First chair meant playing the solos. It meant tuning the orchestra before every concert, standing alone while everyone waited for her single, perfect A. It meant, Priya thought, that she was the best. // Then, in October, a new girl named Ximena arrived from Guadalajara. She was still learning English, and on her first day she sat in the very last chair, holding her violin case on her lap as if it might be taken away. At the November seating audition, she played a piece by Bach so beautifully that Mr. Okonkwo, the orchestra director, set down his pencil and simply listened. // The next day, the new seating chart was posted. Ximena: first chair. Priya: second. // Priya told herself she did not care. She told her mother she did not care. But at rehearsals she played a little too loudly, and when Ximena glanced over for help with a word in the music, like "ritardando" or "staccato," Priya pretended not to notice. // The winter concert came. The auditorium was full, and the stage lights were hot and bright. Mr. Okonkwo nodded to Ximena to stand and tune the orchestra. Ximena stood. She raised her bow. And nothing happened. // Priya saw Ximena's hand shaking. She saw her eyes move across the enormous crowd, her face pale. Someone in the audience coughed. The silence stretched: one second, two, three. // Priya knew that feeling. She remembered her own first concert, when her knees had shaken so badly that she had been sure the whole audience could see. She remembered the eighth grader who had leaned over and whispered, "Just look at your strings." // Before she could think about it, Priya leaned toward Ximena. "Mira las cuerdas," she whispered, using the little Spanish she had learned from her best friend. "Look at your strings." // Ximena looked down. She took a breath. Then she drew her bow across the string, and a clear, steady A filled the hall. // After the concert, Ximena found Priya backstage. "Gracias," she said, and then, carefully, in English: "Thank you. You helped me." // "You helped me too," Priya said, and she was surprised to find that she meant it. She was not sure exactly what Ximena had helped her with. But the second chair, she realized, felt a lot lighter than it had that morning.

lessons.name: How setting, character and plot interact

practice.q: Read: "In the drought-stricken town, water was rationed to one bucket a day, so when Rafael spilled his family's share, he could not bring himself to go home." How does the setting affect the plot?
ch: The water shortage turns a small accident into a serious conflict.
The setting has no effect on the events.
The setting explains what Rafael looks like.
practice.h: Would spilling water matter as much in a place with plenty of it?

practice.q: Read: "Because her family had just moved to a city where she knew no one, Aiko joined the first club that invited her, even though it was the chess club and she did not know how to play." What shapes Aiko's decision?
ch: her new setting and her loneliness
practice.h: Look at the clause that begins with "Because."

practice.q: How can a character's choice change the plot of a story?
ch: It can cause new events and conflicts.
practice.h: Think about cause and effect.

practice.q: Read: "The blizzard closed the only road out of town, trapping the two rival teams in the same small lodge." What is the most likely effect of this setting on the characters?
ch: It forces the rivals to interact and possibly settle their conflict.
It allows the teams to avoid each other.
It makes the teams forget the competition.
It has no effect on the characters.
practice.h: What happens when rivals cannot get away from each other?

practice.q: Choose a story, movie or show you know. Explain how one event changed a character or how a character's trait shaped an event.
practice.ans: Any accurate example with a clear cause-and-effect link, such as: "Maya's stubbornness leads her to hike alone, which causes her to get lost; being lost teaches her to ask for help."
practice.h: Use "because" or "so" to connect the character and the event.

quiz.q: How does the setting of the night market create Tuan's conflict?
ch: Saturday night is the stand's busiest time, and it is also when the band rehearses.
The market is too loud for Tuan to practice.
The market closes before band practice begins.
The market is too far from the band's rehearsal room.

quiz.q: Why does Tuan not ask his father about joining the band?
ch: He believes his father will say no because the family needs him at the stand.
He does not really want to join the band.
His father has already said yes.
He is afraid of Ms. Abernathy.

quiz.q: How does a change in the setting lead to the turning point?
ch: An open-mic stage replaces the corn stand, giving Tuan a chance to play where his father can see.
The market moves to a new parking lot.
The noodle stand closes for the summer.
The band starts rehearsing at the market.

quiz.q: What role does Tuan's mother play in the plot?
ch: She encourages him to play, setting the key event in motion.
She tells his father to fire him.
She quits working at the stand.

quiz.q: What does his father's question, "What time does it end?", reveal?
ch: He is beginning to accept Tuan joining the band.
He is annoyed by the noise.
He wants to close the stand early.
He plans to join the band himself.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes how Tuan and his father influence each other?
ch: Tuan's performance changes his father's view, and his father's solution lets Tuan keep both responsibilities.
Tuan's father forces him to give up music.

quiz.q: Explain how the setting, the characters and the plot interact in "Saturday Nights." Use at least two details.
quiz.ans: The busy Saturday market creates the conflict because the stand needs Tuan when the band rehearses. When the setting changes and an open-mic stage replaces the corn stand, Tuan's mother encourages him to play and his father sees him. His father's response, asking cousin Linh to cover Saturdays, resolves the conflict. The setting shapes the problem, and the characters' choices create the turning point.

lessons.name: Central ideas and how people and events interact

practice.q: The central idea of an informational text is best supported by
ch: key details found throughout the text
practice.h: Look for an idea that many details develop.

practice.q: Read: "After the levee broke, neighbors organized boat rescues. Their efforts inspired the city to create a volunteer emergency corps." How do the event and the individuals interact?
ch: The disaster led people to act, and their actions changed the city's plans.
The individuals caused the levee to break.
The event had no effect on people.
practice.h: Trace what caused what.

practice.q: Which detail best develops the idea that "one invention can change daily life"?
ch: After refrigerators became common, many families could store food for days instead of shopping daily.
practice.h: Which detail shows a change in daily life?

practice.q: Which is the best objective summary statement for an article about a scientist who found a new species after years of failure?
ch: After years of unsuccessful searches, a scientist discovered a new species.
This amazing scientist is my hero.
Scientists are boring until they find something.
I would never search that long.
practice.h: Objective summaries leave out personal opinions.

practice.q: Read: "When the town's factory closed, many workers lost their jobs. A former worker, Rosa Delgado, opened a training center that taught new skills. Within five years, a new business had moved into the old factory." Explain how the event and the individual influenced each other.
practice.ans: The factory closing (event) led Rosa Delgado to open a training center (her response); the center helped workers gain skills and helped attract a new business, so her actions shaped later events.
practice.h: Show the chain: event, response, result.

quiz.q: Which sentence best states the central idea of "A Moldy Turning Point"?
ch: Penicillin became a life-saving medicine through a chain of people and events, not luck alone.
Alexander Fleming took a summer vacation in 1928.
World War II was fought in many countries.

quiz.q: What did Fleming notice in the dish?
ch: a clear ring around a mold where bacteria had died
bacteria growing faster near the mold

quiz.q: How did Fleming's curiosity influence the events that followed?
ch: It led him to study the mold and identify penicillin.
It made him throw the dish away.
It caused the war to begin.
It stopped other scientists from studying mold.

quiz.q: Why did penicillin not change medicine right away?
ch: It was difficult to produce and purify in large amounts.
Doctors refused to use any new medicine.
It did not actually kill bacteria.

quiz.q: How did World War II affect the development of penicillin?
ch: The need to treat wounded soldiers pushed scientists and companies to mass-produce it.
The war stopped all research on penicillin.
The war caused Fleming to lose his notes.

quiz.q: Why does the author mention Norman Heatley?
ch: to show that people beyond the famous names contributed to the breakthrough
to argue that Heatley alone deserved the Nobel Prize

quiz.q: Explain how one individual and one event interacted to move the story of penicillin forward. Use details from the passage.
quiz.ans: Fleming's curiosity about the contaminated dish led to the discovery of penicillin; later, World War II created an urgent need to treat infected wounds, which pushed scientists and companies to mass-produce the drug that Florey and Chain's team had learned to purify.

lessons.name: Phrases and clauses

practice.q: A clause
ch: contains a subject and a verb
practice.h: Look for someone or something doing an action.

practice.q: Which group of words is an independent clause?
practice.h: An independent clause can stand alone as a sentence.

practice.q: In "Before the sun rose, Malik packed his bag," what is "Before the sun rose"?
practice.h: It has a subject and a verb, but can it stand alone?

practice.q: Which group of words is a prepositional phrase?
practice.h: A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and has no verb.

practice.q: Write a sentence that contains one dependent clause and one independent clause. Label each.
practice.ans: "When the bell rang (dependent clause), the students rushed outside (independent clause)."
practice.h: Start with a word like when, because, although or if.

quiz.q: A dependent clause
ch: has a subject and a verb but cannot stand alone

quiz.q: Which word often begins a dependent clause?
In "The girl with the red backpack won the race," what is the job of "with the red backpack"?
ch: It is a phrase that describes the girl.

quiz.q: Which sentence contains a dependent clause?
ch: Tuan practiced every day because he wanted to join the band.

quiz.q: In "The book that I borrowed was fascinating," what is "that I borrowed"?
In "We left early so that we could catch the bus," which words form an adverb clause?
ch: so that we could catch the bus

quiz.q: How does adding the clause "although she was terrified" change the meaning of "Lena stepped onto the stage"?
ch: It shows that Lena acted bravely despite her fear.
It shows that Lena was not afraid.
It shows that Lena did not step onto the stage.
It does not change the meaning.

quiz.q: Combine these sentences using a dependent clause: "The power went out. We told stories by candlelight."
quiz.ans: When the power went out, we told stories by candlelight.

lessons.name: Writing a narrative: point of view, pacing and reflection

practice.q: Which narrative technique shows what characters say to each other?
practice.h: Think of quotation marks.

practice.q: A writer wants readers to know only one character's thoughts. Which point of view should the writer use?
ch: first person or third person limited
practice.h: Which points of view stay inside one character's mind?

practice.q: Which sentence best uses a flashback?
ch: As I stared at the empty field, I remembered the day Dad first threw me a baseball, his laugh echoing across the grass.
practice.h: A flashback interrupts the present to show an earlier event.

practice.q: Which sentence uses the most precise verbs?
ch: The dog lunged, snapped and skidded across the tile.
The dog went fast and did things.
practice.h: Look for verbs that create a clear picture.

practice.q: Write a reflective final sentence for a narrative about a turning point when a character finally apologizes to a friend.
practice.ans: "Walking home, I realized that saying 'I'm sorry' had cost me nothing but pride, and it had given me back my best friend."
practice.h: Reflection shows what the narrator learned.

quiz.q: In a narrative, the conclusion should
ch: resolve the conflict and reflect on the experience

quiz.q: Which revision best slows the pacing at a story's climax?
ch: The ball hung in the air. I saw the stitches spinning, heard the crowd suck in its breath and felt my glove open almost by itself.
The ball came and I caught it and we won.

quiz.q: Which transition best signals a flashback?
Which detail best develops a character through action?
ch: Grandma tucked an extra twenty-dollar bill into my coat pocket when she thought I wasn't looking.

quiz.q: Which opening sentence best establishes a narrator's voice?
ch: I had exactly two goals for seventh grade: survive and stay invisible.
Seventh grade is a grade in middle school.
There are many students in seventh grade.

quiz.q: A story jumps from morning to night with no signal. What should the writer add?
ch: a transition that shows the time shift

quiz.q: Write two sentences that show a turning point in a character's attitude through dialogue and action.
quiz.ans: "Fine," Marisol muttered, grabbing the other end of the box. For the first time all week, she didn't roll her eyes when her stepbrother said thanks.

test.q: Which group of words is a dependent clause?
ch: because the concert was sold out

test.q: In "The violinist who sat in first chair tuned the orchestra," what is "who sat in first chair"?
Which sentence contains a prepositional phrase that tells where?
ch: The orchestra played on the stage.
The orchestra played because it was ready.

test.q: Which revision uses a dependent clause to combine "Robinson faced insults. He kept playing well."?
ch: Although Robinson faced insults, he kept playing well.
Robinson faced insults, he kept playing well.
Robinson faced insults and. He kept playing well.
Robinson faced, insults he kept playing well.

test.q: Which transition best signals a shift in time in a narrative?
Which sentence reveals a character through action rather than direct description?
ch: Priya pretended not to notice when Ximena looked over for help.

test.q: Which narrator would let readers know what both Priya and Ximena are thinking?
ch: a first-person narrator who is Priya
a first-person narrator who is Ximena
a third-person limited narrator who follows Priya

test.q: Why is April 15, 1947, an important date in "Number 42"?
ch: Jackie Robinson became the first Black player in modern Major League Baseball.
The Brooklyn Dodgers won the World Series.

test.q: Why did Branch Rickey choose Robinson?
ch: Robinson was talented and able to stay calm under enormous pressure.
Robinson was the oldest player available.
Robinson had never played sports before.
Robinson asked Rickey for the job first.

test.q: How did Rickey's request influence Robinson's actions?
ch: Robinson promised not to fight back and answered insults with his performance.
Robinson left baseball after one season.

test.q: Which detail best shows that Robinson's success changed people's attitudes?
ch: Teammates who had doubted him came to defend him.
He had served in the Army.

test.q: What does "integrate" mean in "had wanted to integrate the team"?
ch: to open the team to players of all races
to move the team to a new city
to reduce the number of players

test.q: How does the author develop the idea that Robinson's impact went "far beyond the ballpark"?
ch: by describing his civil rights work and the league-wide honors that continue today
by explaining the rules of baseball

test.q: Explain how the individuals (Rickey and Robinson) and the event (Robinson's first season) influenced each other.
test.ans: Rickey's plan and his request not to fight back shaped how Robinson responded to abuse. Robinson's calm courage and outstanding play during the 1947 season then changed teammates' and fans' attitudes and led other teams to sign Black players.

test.q: Why does first chair matter so much to Priya at the beginning of "Second Chair"?
ch: She sees it as proof that she is the best.
It lets her sit near her friends.
It means she does not have to practice.
It lets her choose the music.

test.q: What does the detail that Ximena held her violin case "as if it might be taken away" suggest?
ch: She feels nervous and out of place in her new school.
She does not like her violin.
She is angry at Mr. Okonkwo.

test.q: How does Priya respond to losing first chair?
ch: She hides her hurt but plays too loudly and ignores Ximena.
She congratulates Ximena warmly right away.

test.q: What is the turning point of the story?
ch: Priya whispers advice to Ximena when Ximena freezes on stage.
Ximena plays Bach at the audition.

test.q: Why is Priya able to help Ximena at the concert?
ch: She remembers feeling the same fear at her own first concert.
Mr. Okonkwo tells her to help.

test.q: What does the last sentence suggest about how Priya has changed?
ch: Letting go of her jealousy has made her feel freer and happier.
She is relieved to have less work.
She plans to win back first chair.

test.q: How does the flashback to Priya's first concert affect the story?
test.ans: It explains why Priya understands Ximena's fear and motivates her to help, turning jealousy into empathy. It also introduces the advice "Just look at your strings," which Priya passes on to Ximena.

test.q: Write a narrative that retells the winter concert from Ximena's point of view, from the moment she is asked to stand until she finds Priya backstage. Use first person, sensory details, her thoughts and feelings, and dialogue, and stay consistent with the events in "Second Chair."
test.ans: Key points: first-person narration as Ximena; vivid sensory details of the hot lights, the crowd and the silence; her inner thoughts (fear, homesickness, awareness of Priya's coldness); the turning point when Priya whispers "Mira las cuerdas"; her reaction and the steady A; dialogue consistent with the story; pacing that slows at the climax; a reflective ending about what the moment meant to her.
rub: Clear focus and strong organization; ideas fully developed with relevant details or text evidence; precise language; few errors in conventions.
Clear focus and organization; ideas adequately developed with some details or evidence; some errors that do not affect meaning.
Focus or organization is inconsistent; limited development or evidence; errors sometimes interfere with meaning.
Little focus or organization; minimal development; frequent errors.

units.name: Collection 2: Nature's Fury (informative)
units.el: Build a picture glossary of disaster words (fault, plate, wash, debris, contained) and color-code clauses (independent in one color, dependent in another) to show simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences.

passages.x: All August the hills held their breath, / brown as paper bags, / dry grass whispering secrets / to the wind that would not stop. / My grandfather watched the ridge each evening / the way some men watch the sea, / reading the sky for trouble. // Then came the night of the hot wind, / the wind that roars down canyons / like a freight train with no tracks. / By morning the ridge wore a crown of smoke, / orange at the edges, / and the sun rose red as a warning, / a coin dropped in ashes. // We packed what mattered: / photographs, the dog, / Grandma's recipe box with the broken lid, / the quilt my mother sewed / the winter I was born. / Funny how a whole life / fits in the back of a truck / when you have twenty minutes. // On the radio a calm voice / read the names of roads like a roll call: / Canyon Drive, Oak Hollow, Mission Lane, / each one a door closing. / My grandfather drove with both hands on the wheel / and did not look back, / so I looked back for him, / and watched the orange glow / grow small in the mirror / until it was only a rumor in the dark. // Crackle and hiss, / snap and pop, / the fire talked in a language / older than any of us. / Firefighters in yellow / stood shoulder to shoulder / at the edge of our road, / a wall of people / against a wall of flame. // For three days we waited / in the high school gym / on cots in crooked rows, / strangers passing coffee, / children trading crayons, / everyone checking phones / for the one word that mattered: / contained. // Our house still stands. / The Garcias' does not. / Now the hills are black, / and the air smells like a campfire / that will not end. / But last week, after the first rain, / my grandfather knelt / and pointed to the ash: / one green shoot, / small as a promise, / pushing up through the dark.

At 5:12 on the morning of April 18, 1906, most people in San Francisco were asleep. Then the ground began to roll. For less than a minute, the earth shook so violently that buildings collapsed, streets cracked open and church bells rang on their own. Scientists today estimate that the earthquake had a magnitude of about 7.9. // Why does California shake? The answer lies deep beneath the surface. Earth's outer layer is broken into enormous pieces called tectonic plates, which move very slowly, about as fast as fingernails grow. In California, two of these plates meet along the San Andreas Fault. The Pacific Plate is sliding northwest past the North American Plate. Usually the plates are stuck together by friction, and stress builds up over years or even centuries. When the rocks finally slip, the stored energy is released in waves that shake the ground. That is an earthquake. // In 1906, the shaking was only the beginning of the disaster. Broken gas lines and overturned stoves started fires across the city. Water pipes had also broken, so firefighters had little water to fight the flames. The fires burned for several days and destroyed far more of the city than the shaking itself. By the time they were out, thousands of buildings were gone, and roughly half of the city's residents had lost their homes. Historians now estimate that around 3,000 people died. // The disaster forced Californians to rethink how they built. Over the following decades, engineers and lawmakers developed building codes, rules that require structures to withstand strong shaking. Modern buildings in earthquake country may use steel frames that bend without breaking, or special bases that let a building sway as the ground moves beneath it. // Scientists still cannot predict exactly when the next large earthquake will strike. But people can prepare. Families can secure heavy furniture, store water and plan where to meet. Millions of Californians practice "Drop, Cover and Hold On" during yearly drills: drop to the ground, take cover under a sturdy table and hold on until the shaking stops. // The ground beneath California will keep moving, as it has for millions of years. The lesson of 1906 is not that earthquakes can be stopped, but that their damage can be greatly reduced by understanding, planning and preparation.

The wash behind Tio Ruben's house had been dry for as long as Mateo had been visiting, a wide sandy channel that curved through the desert like a pale, empty road. In the summers, Mateo and his cousin Alma used it as their own private highway, racing their bikes along the hard-packed sand, past mesquite trees and boulders as big as cars. // On the third afternoon of his visit, the sky over the mountains to the east turned the color of a bruise. Thunder muttered far away. Above the house, though, the sky was blue and the sun blazed. // "Let's ride to the big rock," Alma said. "We'll be back before the storm even gets here." // Mateo glanced at the mountains. They were miles away. He shrugged. "Okay." // They had ridden about half a mile when Mateo noticed something strange. The air smelled like wet dust, though not a drop of rain had fallen. Then he heard it: a low rumble that did not stop, like a truck on a highway that was not there. // Alma braked hard. "Do you hear that?" // Around the bend, something brown and churning appeared, moving toward them faster than seemed possible. It was not a wave exactly. It was a wall of muddy water, carrying branches, tumbleweeds and a whole fence post that rolled end over end. // "Up!" Alma shouted. "Get up the bank!" // They dropped their bikes and scrambled up the steep side of the wash, grabbing roots and rocks, sliding back, climbing again. Mateo reached the top just as the water roared past below, swallowing the path where they had been standing. His bike disappeared under the brown current as if it had never existed. // They sat on the bank, shaking, as the wash filled from side to side. Twenty minutes earlier it had been a road. Now it was a river. // When they finally walked home along the high ground, Tio Ruben was standing at the edge of the yard, his face gray. He did not yell. He just pulled them both into a hug so tight that Mateo could hardly breathe. // "The rain doesn't have to fall on you," he said quietly, "for the water to find you." // That night, Mateo lay awake listening to the wash, still rushing in the dark. He had always thought of the desert as empty and still. Now he understood that it had only been waiting.

Many visitors to the deserts of the American Southwest expect heat and drought. Few expect floods. Yet flash floods, which rise within minutes or a few hours of heavy rain, are among the most dangerous weather events in the United States, and deserts are especially at risk. // Several features of desert landscapes make flash floods likely. Desert soil is often hard and dry, so it cannot soak up water quickly. Instead of sinking into the ground, rainwater runs off the surface. Few plants grow there to slow it down. The water collects in low channels called washes, arroyos or canyons, where it gathers speed and force. // A flash flood can also strike where no rain is falling at all. A thunderstorm over mountains miles away can send water rushing downhill into dry channels. Hikers in a narrow slot canyon may see blue sky overhead while a wall of water races toward them from a storm they cannot see. // Moving water is far more powerful than it looks. According to the National Weather Service, just six inches of fast-moving water can knock an adult off his or her feet. About one foot of moving water can float many cars, and two feet of rushing water can carry away most vehicles, including large SUVs. Floodwater also carries rocks, branches and other debris that can injure anyone caught in it. // Because of these dangers, the National Weather Service promotes a simple slogan: "Turn Around, Don't Drown." Its advice is never to walk, swim or drive through flooded roads or washes. The water may be deeper than it looks, and the road underneath may have washed away. // Experts recommend several other safety steps. Before hiking or camping, check the weather forecast for the whole area, not just the spot where you will be. Avoid washes and narrow canyons when storms are possible. Watch for warning signs such as distant thunder, a sudden rise in water level, muddy water or a roar upstream. If you notice any of these, climb to higher ground immediately. // Flash floods cannot be stopped, but with knowledge and caution, they can be survived.

lessons.name: Poetry: form, structure and sound

practice.q: In a poem, a stanza is
practice.h: Stanzas are like paragraphs in poetry.

practice.q: Which line contains alliteration?
ch: The wild wind whipped the willows.
The wind blew hard all night.
practice.h: Look for repeated beginning consonant sounds.

practice.q: Read: "Thunder grumbled over the hills." What does "grumbled" suggest?
ch: The thunder sounded low, rumbling and threatening.
practice.h: What does a person sound like when he or she grumbles?

practice.q: A poet repeats the line "And still the river rose" at the end of each stanza. What is the most likely effect?
ch: It builds tension and emphasizes the growing danger.
It shows the poet ran out of ideas.
practice.h: Think about how a repeated line affects mood.

practice.q: Explain how a poem's form, such as very short lines or a sonnet's structure, can affect its meaning. Give an example.
practice.ans: Form shapes how readers experience a poem. Very short lines slow the reader and create emphasis or suspense, and a sonnet's final couplet can deliver a turn or conclusion.
practice.h: Think about how line length or a rhyme pattern changes the way you read.

quiz.q: In "The Ridge Fire," what does the simile "like a freight train with no tracks" suggest about the wind?
ch: It is loud, powerful and impossible to stop.

quiz.q: Which lines from "The Ridge Fire" use onomatopoeia?
How does the third stanza, which lists what the family packed, contribute to the poem's meaning?
ch: It shows what the family values most when they must flee.
It describes how the fire started.
It describes the land growing back after rain.

quiz.q: The speaker writes, "a wall of people / against a wall of flame." What is the effect of repeating the word "wall"?
ch: It emphasizes the firefighters standing firm against the fire.
It shows the house has thick walls.
It suggests the people are made of brick.

quiz.q: Why does the speaker include the short lines "Our house still stands. / The Garcias' does not."?
ch: to show the uneven loss and the speaker's mixed feelings of relief and sorrow
to brag about the family's house
to give directions to the neighborhood
to describe the weather after the fire

quiz.q: How does the poem's structure, moving from a dry summer to the fire to the first rain, develop its theme?
ch: It moves from threat to loss to renewal, suggesting that hope can follow disaster.
It moves from happiness to boredom.
It shows that fires happen only in August.
It has no effect on the theme.

quiz.q: In "The Ridge Fire," explain the meaning of the image "one green shoot, / small as a promise" and how it connects to the poem's theme.
quiz.ans: The green shoot growing through the ash is the first sign of new life after the fire, and "small as a promise" suggests hope that the land and the community will recover. It contrasts with the black hills and smoky air, showing that renewal can follow destruction.

lessons.name: Text structure and central ideas in informational texts

practice.q: Which text structure explains a series of events in the order they happened?
practice.h: Think about time.

practice.q: Read: "Hurricanes form over warm ocean water. As warm, moist air rises, it cools and forms clouds, releasing heat that powers the storm." Which structure is used?
practice.h: Look for how one thing leads to another.

practice.q: Which signal words most often show a problem-and-solution structure?
ch: one way to solve, to address this
practice.h: Which words point to fixing something?

practice.q: An article about tornadoes has the sections "How Tornadoes Form," "Where They Strike" and "Staying Safe." How do these sections work together?
ch: They move from causes to locations to safety, building a full understanding of the topic.
They argue that tornadoes are not dangerous.
practice.h: What does each heading add?

practice.q: Explain why an author writing about a flood might use both chronological order and cause and effect.
practice.ans: Chronological order shows how the flood unfolded over time, while cause and effect explains why it happened and what damage resulted; together they give a complete picture.
practice.h: Think about "when" and "why."

quiz.q: In "The Restless Ground," how is the second paragraph mainly organized?
ch: It explains the causes of earthquakes, ending with how stored stress is released.
It tells the events of 1906 in time order.
It lists several solutions to a problem.

quiz.q: According to "The Restless Ground," what causes an earthquake?
ch: Plates that are stuck together suddenly slip, releasing stored energy in waves.
Buildings collapse and shake the ground.

quiz.q: According to "The Restless Ground," why were the fires after the 1906 earthquake so destructive?
ch: Broken water pipes left firefighters with little water.
The fires started on ships in the bay.
Firefighters were away from the city.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the paragraph about building codes in "The Restless Ground"?
ch: to describe a solution that developed in response to the disaster
to describe the location of the fault
to explain how to drop, cover and hold on
to tell what time the earthquake struck

quiz.q: What does "withstand" mean in "rules that require structures to withstand strong shaking"?
Which choice names two central ideas developed in "The Restless Ground"?
ch: Earthquakes are caused by moving plates, and preparation can reduce their damage.
Earthquakes happen only in the morning, and fires are always caused by stoves.
Scientists can predict earthquakes, and buildings never fall.
San Francisco was abandoned, and people moved away.

quiz.q: Write an objective summary of "The Restless Ground" in three sentences.
quiz.ans: A powerful earthquake struck San Francisco in 1906, and fires from broken gas lines destroyed much of the city. Earthquakes happen when tectonic plates along faults such as the San Andreas slip and release stored energy. Since then, building codes and preparation such as "Drop, Cover and Hold On" have helped reduce earthquake damage.

lessons.name: Simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences

practice.q: A compound sentence has
practice.h: Look for clauses joined by and, but or so.

practice.q: Which sentence is complex?
ch: When the wind shifted, the fire moved toward the town.
The wind shifted, and the fire moved.
The wind and the fire moved.
practice.h: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

practice.q: Which sentence is compound-complex?
ch: Because the river rose, the town flooded, and families moved to higher ground.
The river rose, and the town flooded.
Because the river rose, the town flooded.
practice.h: Count the independent and the dependent clauses.

practice.q: Which sentence is simple?
ch: Although it was late, thunder rolled, and we woke.
practice.h: A simple sentence has one independent clause.

practice.q: Combine these sentences into one complex sentence: "The tsunami warning sounded. Residents moved inland."
practice.ans: When the tsunami warning sounded, residents moved inland. (Because or after also works.)
practice.h: Use a word such as when, because or after.

quiz.q: Which conjunction can join two independent clauses in a compound sentence?
Which sentence is compound?
ch: The earthquake ended, but the fires continued.
After the earthquake ended, fires started.

quiz.q: What type of sentence is "Although the storm weakened, the waves stayed high, so the beach remained closed"?
What type of sentence is "After the ash settled, the scientists collected samples"?
Which compound sentence is punctuated correctly?
ch: The volcano erupted, and ash covered the village.
The volcano erupted and, ash covered the village.
The volcano erupted, ash covered the village.
The volcano, erupted and ash covered the village.

quiz.q: Why might a writer place a short, simple sentence after several complex ones?
ch: to create emphasis or a sudden effect

quiz.q: Which revision turns "The levee broke. Water poured into the streets. People climbed onto roofs." into one compound-complex sentence?
ch: When the levee broke, water poured into the streets, and people climbed onto roofs.
The levee broke and water poured.
Water poured into the streets when the levee broke.

quiz.q: Write one complex sentence and one compound sentence about a natural disaster. Label each.
quiz.ans: Complex: "Because the hurricane was approaching, the city opened shelters." Compound: "The wind howled, and the windows rattled."

lessons.name: Writing an informative essay: thesis, definitions and organization

practice.q: In an informative essay, the writer's purpose is to
ch: explain a topic using facts, definitions and examples
persuade readers to agree with an opinion
practice.h: Informative writing informs.

practice.q: Which is the strongest thesis for an informative essay about wildfires?
ch: Wildfires are shaped by fuel, weather and terrain, and understanding these factors helps communities prepare.
practice.h: A strong thesis previews the main points.

practice.q: Which is the best way to define a technical term for readers?
ch: A fault is a crack in Earth's crust where blocks of rock move past each other.
Faults are things in the ground.
A fault is when you make a mistake.
practice.h: Give a clear, accurate definition in context.

practice.q: Which text feature would best help readers follow the steps of "Drop, Cover and Hold On"?
practice.h: Steps happen in order.

practice.q: Write a topic sentence and one supporting fact for a body paragraph explaining how tsunamis form.
practice.ans: Topic sentence: Most tsunamis begin with a sudden movement of the sea floor. Fact: When an undersea earthquake lifts or drops the sea floor, it pushes a huge amount of water and creates waves that spread outward.
practice.h: The fact should explain the topic sentence.

quiz.q: Which transition best introduces an effect?
Which sentence keeps a formal, objective style?
ch: Hurricanes can produce storm surges that flood coastal areas.
Hurricanes are the worst thing ever.

quiz.q: Which detail would best develop a paragraph about how volcanoes can affect climate?
ch: Large eruptions can send ash and gases high into the atmosphere, which can block sunlight and briefly cool the planet.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest conclusion for an informative essay about earthquakes?
ch: While no one can stop an earthquake, understanding faults and preparing ahead of time can save lives.
Next I will write about volcanoes.

quiz.q: A student quotes a source in an informative essay. What else must the student include?
Which graphic would best show how many earthquakes of different sizes occurred in one year?
Explain how headings can help organize an informative essay about severe weather.
quiz.ans: Headings divide the essay into clear sections, such as "Causes," "Effects" and "Safety," so readers can see the organization and find information easily.

test.q: What type of sentence is "The sky darkened, and thunder echoed through the canyon"?
What type of sentence is "When the water rose, Mateo climbed the bank"?
Which of these sentences contains two independent clauses and one dependent clause?
ch: Although the wash looked dry, the water arrived quickly, and the bikes were swept away.
The water arrived, and the bikes vanished.
When the water arrived, the bikes vanished.

test.q: Which line from a poem contains alliteration?
Which compound sentence uses a comma correctly?
ch: The storm passed, but the river kept rising.
The storm passed but, the river kept rising.
The storm, passed but the river kept rising.
The storm passed but the river, kept rising.

test.q: Which transition best introduces an example in an informative essay?
A writer wants a sudden, dramatic moment after a long, complex sentence. Which sentence would work best?
ch: Then, because the water had been rising for many hours, the levee, which was old, broke.
The levee was old, and the water rose.

test.q: How does the author describe the wash at the beginning of "The Dry Wash"?
ch: as a dry, sandy channel the cousins used like a private road

test.q: Why do the cousins decide to ride even though storm clouds are visible?
ch: The storm seems far away over the mountains, so they believe they are safe.
Tio Ruben told them to go.
They want to watch the flood.
They do not notice the clouds at all.

test.q: Which detail best foreshadows the danger?
ch: "The air smelled like wet dust, though not a drop of rain had fallen."
"They had ridden about half a mile"
"On the third afternoon of his visit"

test.q: What does the simile "like a truck on a highway that was not there" suggest about the sound?
ch: It is a loud, steady rumble with no visible source.
It is music from a radio.
It comes from a real truck on the road.

test.q: What does Tio Ruben mean by "The rain doesn't have to fall on you for the water to find you"?
ch: Rain far away can cause a flood where you are.
Rain always falls everywhere at once.
You should always carry an umbrella.

test.q: How does Mateo's view of the desert change by the end of the story?
ch: He realizes the calm desert can hold sudden, powerful danger.
He decides the desert is boring.
He learns to love riding bikes.
He believes floods never happen in deserts.

test.q: Explain how the author uses the setting to build suspense in "The Dry Wash." Use two details.
test.ans: The dry, sunny wash seems safe while a storm gathers far away over the mountains. The smell of wet dust with no rain and the low rumble with no visible source build tension before the wall of water appears around the bend.

test.q: According to "When Deserts Flood," what is a flash flood?
ch: a flood that rises within minutes or a few hours of heavy rain
a flood that lasts for several months
a flood caused only by melting snow
a small puddle left after rain

test.q: According to "When Deserts Flood," why does desert soil make flash floods more likely?
ch: It is hard and dry, so water runs off instead of soaking in.
It is soft and absorbs too much water.
It is covered with thick forests.

test.q: How is the second paragraph of "When Deserts Flood" mainly organized?
Which evidence from "When Deserts Flood" supports the idea that moving water is "far more powerful than it looks"?
ch: Six inches of fast-moving water can knock an adult off his or her feet.
Desert soil is often hard and dry.
Few plants grow in the desert.

test.q: What does "debris" mean in "Floodwater also carries rocks, branches and other debris"?
ch: scattered pieces of material carried along

test.q: Why does the author of "When Deserts Flood" explain that a flood can strike where no rain is falling?
ch: to warn readers that a sunny sky does not guarantee safety
to argue that forecasts are useless
to show that mountains cause all floods
to entertain readers with a surprise

test.q: According to "When Deserts Flood," what are two warning signs of a flash flood, and what should a person do after noticing one?
test.ans: Warning signs include distant thunder, a sudden rise in water level, muddy water or a roar upstream. A person who notices one should climb to higher ground immediately.

test.q: Write an informative essay that explains what flash floods are, why they are dangerous and how people can stay safe. State a clear thesis, organize your essay into paragraphs with transitions, define key terms and include at least three facts from "When Deserts Flood," paraphrased or quoted with credit.
test.ans: Key points: a thesis previewing causes, dangers and safety; definitions of flash flood and of washes or arroyos; causes (hard dry soil, few plants, storms miles away); dangers supported by National Weather Service facts (six inches can knock down an adult, one foot can float many cars, two feet can carry away most vehicles, debris); safety steps ("Turn Around, Don't Drown," checking forecasts for the whole area, avoiding washes, watching for warning signs, climbing to high ground); formal style, varied sentence types, transitions and a conclusion.
rub: Clear focus and strong organization; ideas fully developed with relevant details or text evidence; precise language; few errors in conventions.
Clear focus and organization; ideas adequately developed with some details or evidence; some errors that do not affect meaning.
Focus or organization is inconsistent; limited development or evidence; errors sometimes interfere with meaning.
Little focus or organization; minimal development; frequent errors.

units.name: Collection 3: Taking Risks (argument)
units.el: Sort word cards on a connotation line (negative, neutral, positive) such as reckless, bold, adventurous, and give argument frames: "Although some people believe ___, the evidence shows ___ because ___."

passages.x: Nadia had been training for the Cove Swim for four months: two miles in the open ocean, from the pier to the lighthouse and back, with safety kayaks paddling alongside. She swam laps at the community pool before school, and on Saturdays she practiced in the bay with her coach, getting used to the cold, the salt and the way the swells lifted her up and set her down. She was ready. She knew she was ready. // Her father did not see it that way. // "The pool is one thing," he said at dinner, not looking up from his plate. "The ocean is another. The ocean does not care how many laps you swam." // "There are lifeguards, Dad. There are kayaks every hundred yards. Coach Ramirez says I'm one of the strongest swimmers on the team." // "Coach Ramirez is not your father." // Nadia pushed her rice around her plate. To her, the race was a chance to prove something, mostly to herself. She had been the quiet kid, the careful kid, for as long as she could remember. In the water, she felt bold. Why couldn't he see that? // Across the table, her father was seeing something else entirely. He was seeing a beach in Batangas, forty years ago, and a ten-year-old boy who had swum out too far chasing a lost ball. He was remembering how the current had pulled him sideways, how the shore had shrunk, how his arms had turned to lead. A fisherman had pulled him into a boat. He had never told Nadia the whole story. He had never told anyone. // That night, Nadia found him on the back porch. She sat down beside him without speaking. After a long while, he told her. All of it. // "I'm not saying you're not strong," he finished. "I was strong too. I'm saying the ocean is stronger." // Nadia was quiet. Then she said, "So come with me. To practice. Watch me. If you see something you don't like, I'll listen." // He looked at her for a long time. // The next Saturday, her father stood on the beach in his windbreaker, arms crossed, while Nadia swam the course with her coach. He watched her sight the lighthouse, breathe on both sides and angle against the current instead of fighting it. He watched the kayaks. He asked the lifeguards questions until they began to look tired. // When Nadia came out of the water, he handed her a towel. // "You swim like you're listening to it," he said. "The water. That's good." // On race day, he was at the finish line. He did not cheer. But he was the first person she saw.

Walk onto many American playgrounds today and you will see low platforms, short slides and rubber mats spread beneath everything. These playgrounds are designed to prevent injuries, and that goal makes sense. But in trying to remove every risk, we may be taking away something children need. Schools and cities should make room for more challenging, "risky" play. // First, risky play helps children learn to judge danger for themselves. When children climb a little higher than last time or balance on a log, they practice deciding what they can handle. Psychologists who study play, such as Ellen Sandseter in Norway, have argued that this kind of play helps children face their fears gradually, in a setting where the stakes are small. A child who has never been allowed to climb may not know how to fall safely or how to tell when a branch is too thin. // Second, challenging play builds confidence and problem-solving skills. At the Adventure Playground in Berkeley, California, children use hammers, nails and scrap wood to build their own forts under the eye of trained staff. Instead of following a single path down a slide, they must plan, test and fix their creations. Children who work through challenges like these learn that they can solve problems on their own. // Third, children need exercise, and exciting play keeps them moving. Equipment that is too easy quickly becomes boring, and bored children often leave the playground for screens. // Finally, my cousin climbed trees every day when he was little and never got hurt, which proves that tree climbing is completely safe for all children. // Critics worry that more challenging equipment will lead to more injuries. This concern is understandable. However, supporters of risky play are not calling for dangerous play. They distinguish between risks, which a child can see and choose to take, and hazards, such as broken equipment or sharp edges, which a child cannot see. Hazards should always be fixed. Risks, in reasonable amounts, are part of growing up. // Children will face uncertainty all their lives. Giving them safe places to practice taking small risks today may help them handle bigger ones tomorrow.

When my grandmother announced at Sunday dinner that she was going to jump out of an airplane, my uncle choked on his iced tea. // "You're seventy-five," he said, once he could breathe. // "Seventy-six in May," Abuela Ines corrected him. "That's why I'm doing it in April." // Everyone started talking at once. My mom listed the risks: her heart, her knees, the medicine she takes for her blood pressure. My uncle said it was "frankly ridiculous." My little cousin asked if she could watch. I didn't say anything. I was too busy picturing my tiny grandmother, who still wouldn't drive on the freeway, falling through the sky. // To me it seemed like a terrible idea. Abuela was the person who made us wear jackets when it was sixty degrees. She was the person who called if we were five minutes late. Now she wanted to leap out of a plane? It didn't make sense. // After dinner, I found her in the kitchen, wrapping leftover tamales in foil. "Why?" I asked. "Seriously. Why?" // She kept wrapping. "When I was nineteen," she said, "I wanted to learn to fly airplanes. My father said no. Girls didn't do that, he said. Then I got married, and then your mother came, and then your uncle, and then there was always a reason to wait." She folded the foil tight. "I have waited fifty-seven years, mijo. I'm done waiting." // "But it's dangerous." // "So is getting old without ever doing what you dreamed about." She finally looked at me. "Don't worry. I asked my doctor, and he said my heart is fine for it. I'll be strapped to an instructor who has jumped thousands of times. I'm brave, not foolish." // I still thought she was a little bit foolish. But I noticed something I hadn't seen before. When she talked about the plane, she looked younger. Her eyes were bright, like a kid's on the first day of summer. // In April, I stood in a field with my family, staring up at a speck of an airplane. Then two tiny figures dropped out of it, and a parachute bloomed open, red and white against the blue. // When Abuela landed, she was laughing so hard she could barely stand. My uncle, who had called the whole thing ridiculous, was crying. // "Well?" she said to me, still breathless. // I didn't know what to say. So I just hugged her, and I didn't let go for a long time.

passages.t: Every Student Should Learn to Swim
passages.x: California has hundreds of miles of coastline, thousands of lakes and rivers, and more backyard pools than almost any other state. Yet many students here have never had a single swimming lesson. That is a dangerous gap. Every public school district in California should make sure that students learn basic water safety and swimming skills before they finish middle school. // The most important reason is safety. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, drowning is the leading cause of death for children ages 1 to 4 in the United States, and it is one of the leading causes of accidental death for older children as well. Many drownings happen quickly and silently, often when a child falls into water unexpectedly. A child who knows how to float, tread water and get to the edge has a far better chance of surviving. // Second, swimming lessons are not equally available to everyone. Private lessons can be expensive, and not every neighborhood has a public pool. Surveys have found that children from low-income families are less likely to have had swim lessons. When schools teach swimming, every child gets the same chance to learn a life-saving skill, not just the children whose families can pay. // Third, swimming opens doors. Students who can swim can join swim teams, water polo, surf clubs and junior lifeguard programs. They can take jobs as lifeguards or camp counselors. Fear of the water keeps many people away from these experiences for their whole lives. // Some people argue that schools cannot afford swim programs and that teaching swimming is a family's job, not a school's. These are fair points. Not every school has a pool, and budgets are tight. But programs do not have to be expensive. Districts can partner with city pools, YMCAs and community colleges, and lessons can be offered as part of physical education for a few weeks each year. Schools already teach other safety skills, such as fire drills and earthquake drills, because those skills save lives. Water safety belongs on that list. // A skill that can save a life should not depend on luck or a family's income. California's schools should make sure every student can swim.

lessons.name: Contrasting characters' points of view

practice.q: Dramatic irony occurs when
ch: the reader knows something a character does not
a story is told in first person
practice.h: Think about who knows more.

practice.q: Read: "Leo thought the abandoned mill was a perfect adventure. His sister, Rosa, saw only rotten boards and a 'No Trespassing' sign." How do their points of view differ?
ch: Leo sees excitement, while Rosa sees danger.
Rosa sees adventure, while Leo sees danger.
practice.h: Compare what each character "sees."

practice.q: Read: "Coach believed the team was ready for the tournament. The players, who had lost three practice games, were not so sure." What effect does the difference in points of view create?
ch: tension about whether the team will succeed
practice.h: How do readers feel when characters disagree?

practice.q: How can an author show a character's point of view?
ch: through the character's thoughts, words and actions
practice.h: Think about all the ways readers get to know a character.

practice.q: Write two sentences showing how two characters might view the same risk differently, such as trying out for a play.
practice.ans: Marcus pictured himself bowing to a cheering crowd. His best friend, Dev, pictured himself forgetting every line in front of the whole school.
practice.h: Give each character a different thought about the same event.

quiz.q: In "Open Water," how does Nadia view the Cove Swim at the beginning?
ch: as a chance to prove her strength and boldness
as a way to please her father

quiz.q: In "Open Water," why does Nadia's father oppose the race?
ch: Nearly drowning as a boy taught him that the ocean can overpower even strong swimmers.
He thinks swimming is a waste of time.
He wants Nadia to play another sport.

quiz.q: What does the reader of "Open Water" learn before Nadia does?
ch: her father's memory of nearly drowning at a beach in Batangas
that the race has been canceled

quiz.q: In "Open Water," how does Nadia's offer, "So come with me," change the conflict?
ch: It invites her father to judge her skill and the safety plan for himself, opening a path to compromise.
It forces her coach to quit.

quiz.q: In "Open Water," what does the father's comment "You swim like you're listening to it" show?
ch: He now respects her skill and her awareness of the ocean's power.
He thinks she swims too slowly.
He is still completely against the race.
He wants her to wear earplugs.

quiz.q: Why does the author of "Open Water" let readers into the father's memories while Nadia remains unaware of them?
ch: to help readers understand both points of view and see that the conflict is not simply right against wrong
to make the father seem foolish
to show that Nadia is selfish
to confuse readers about who is speaking

quiz.q: Contrast Nadia's and her father's points of view about the risk in "Open Water," and explain how the author resolves the difference. Use details.
quiz.ans: Nadia sees the race as a chance to be bold and trusts her training and the safety kayaks; her father, shaped by nearly drowning, believes "the ocean is stronger." The difference is resolved through an honest conversation and his watching her practice: he sees that she swims "like you're listening to it" and comes to the finish line.

lessons.name: Evaluating an argument: sound reasoning and sufficient evidence

practice.q: Evidence is sufficient when
ch: there is enough of it to convince a reasonable reader
it is only one personal story
it agrees with what the reader already thinks
practice.h: Think about both the amount and the strength of the evidence.

practice.q: Which evidence is most relevant to the claim "Bike helmets reduce head injuries"?
ch: hospital data showing fewer serious head injuries among riders who wore helmets
a survey showing most kids like blue helmets
a story about a bike race
practice.h: Relevant evidence connects directly to the claim.

practice.q: Read: "Every kid who skateboards ends up in the hospital." What is wrong with this claim?
ch: It is an overgeneralization that is not supported by evidence.
practice.h: Watch for words like "every" and "always."

practice.q: An author arguing for later school start times cites a study by a sleep scientist. How does this strengthen the argument?
practice.h: Who is the source, and what kind of evidence is it?

practice.q: Explain the difference between sound reasoning and faulty reasoning. Give an example of faulty reasoning.
practice.ans: Sound reasoning logically connects evidence to a claim. Faulty reasoning makes leaps the evidence does not support, such as "My friend failed one test after staying up late, so everyone who stays up late fails tests."
practice.h: Does the evidence really lead to the conclusion?

quiz.q: What is the author's claim in "Let Them Climb"?
ch: Schools and cities should make room for more challenging, risky play.
Playgrounds should be removed from cities.
All playground injuries are the fault of children.

quiz.q: In "Let Them Climb," which evidence supports the reason that risky play builds confidence and problem-solving skills?
ch: At the Adventure Playground in Berkeley, children build their own forts with tools under trained staff.

quiz.q: Which reason in "Let Them Climb" uses faulty reasoning?
ch: My cousin climbed trees every day and never got hurt, which proves tree climbing is completely safe for all children.
Risky play helps children learn to judge danger.

quiz.q: In "Let Them Climb," why is the reason about the author's cousin weak?
ch: One person's experience is not sufficient evidence for a claim about all children.

quiz.q: In "Let Them Climb," how does the author respond to critics who worry about injuries?
ch: by distinguishing between risks children can choose and hazards that should always be fixed
by agreeing that all risk should be removed

quiz.q: Which statement best evaluates the reason in "Let Them Climb" that bored children "often leave the playground for screens"?
ch: It is relevant but weakly supported, because the author gives no evidence for it.
It is the strongest reason because it cites expert research.
It has nothing to do with the claim.

quiz.q: Evaluate whether the evidence in "Let Them Climb" is relevant and sufficient. Identify one well-supported reason and one poorly supported reason, and explain your choices.
quiz.ans: Well supported: risky play builds confidence and problem-solving, backed by a specific example (the Berkeley Adventure Playground) and expert ideas (Ellen Sandseter). Poorly supported: the cousin example is a single anecdote that cannot prove safety for all children, and the claim about screens has no evidence at all.

lessons.name: Connotation, denotation and precise, concise language

practice.q: A word's denotation is
practice.h: Think "D" for dictionary.

practice.q: Which word has the most negative connotation?
practice.h: Which word suggests foolishness?

practice.q: Which verb makes this sentence most precise? "The firefighter ___ into the burning building."
practice.h: Which verb paints the clearest picture?

practice.q: Which revision removes the wordiness from "Due to the fact that it was raining, we decided to make the decision to stay home"?
ch: Because it was raining, we decided to stay home.
Due to the fact that it was raining, we stayed home.
It was raining, so we made the decision to decide.
Because of rain, we made a decision to make.
practice.h: Cut repeated or unnecessary words.

practice.q: Explain how the connotations of "confident" and "arrogant" differ. Use each word in a sentence.
practice.ans: Both describe believing in yourself, but "confident" is positive and "arrogant" is negative, suggesting too much pride. "The confident speaker smiled at the crowd." "The arrogant speaker ignored everyone's questions."
practice.h: The words share a meaning, but how do they feel different?

quiz.q: Which word has the most positive connotation?
One article describes a mountain climber as "fearless," and another describes her as "foolhardy." What does this word choice reveal?
ch: The writers have different attitudes toward the climber.
Both writers admire the climber equally.
The two words mean exactly the same thing.
One writer made a spelling error.

quiz.q: Which sentence is most concise?
ch: The climbers reached the summit at dawn.
The climbers, who were climbing, reached the summit at the time of dawn.
At dawn, the climbers reached the top summit at dawn.
The climbers reached the summit, which was the top, at dawn in the morning.

quiz.q: Which verb is the most precise replacement for "said" in "'Watch out!' she said"?
Which pair of words has a similar denotation but different connotations?
Which revision best removes the redundancy in "The team worked together cooperatively to reach a final conclusion"?
ch: The team cooperated to reach a conclusion.
The team worked together cooperatively to conclude.
The team cooperatively worked together finally.
The team reached a final conclusion together cooperatively.

quiz.q: An advertisement calls a new roller coaster "heart-pounding" instead of "scary." Why?
ch: "Heart-pounding" has a more exciting, positive connotation that attracts riders.
The two words create exactly the same effect.

quiz.q: Rewrite this sentence, replacing vague words with precise ones: "The guy did a really good thing at the place."
quiz.ans: Example: "The lifeguard pulled a struggling swimmer from the riptide at Ocean Beach."

lessons.name: Writing an argument: claims, counterclaims and logical reasoning

practice.q: In an argument, a counterclaim is
ch: an opposing view that the writer acknowledges
practice.h: "Counter" means against.

practice.q: Which claim is arguable?
ch: Middle schools should offer a rock-climbing elective.
practice.h: An arguable claim is one that reasonable people could disagree with.

practice.q: Which sentence acknowledges a counterclaim and responds to it?
ch: Although some parents worry about injuries, trained instructors and safety gear greatly reduce the risk.
practice.h: Look for both sides in one sentence.

practice.q: Which phrase best introduces evidence that supports a reason?
practice.h: Evidence often follows a phrase that introduces an example.

practice.q: Write a claim and two reasons for or against this question: Should middle schools offer tackle football?
practice.ans: Example: Claim: Middle schools should offer flag football instead of tackle football. Reasons: Flag football teaches the same teamwork and skills, and it reduces the risk of head injuries for growing players.
practice.h: Your reasons should explain why your claim is correct.

quiz.q: Which part of an argument essay restates the claim and leaves the reader with a final thought?
Which source is most credible for an argument about youth sports injuries?
ch: a report from a national organization of children's doctors
a blog post by an anonymous fan

quiz.q: Which sentence contains a logical flaw?
ch: If we allow one risky activity, soon students will be jumping off roofs.
Students must have a signed permission form.

quiz.q: Which sentence best maintains a formal style in an argument?
ch: Allowing supervised challenges can help students build resilience.
Only babies are scared of risks.
Come on, just let us try!

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a rebuttal?
ch: to explain why the counterclaim is weaker than the writer's claim
to agree completely with the other side

quiz.q: Which revision best strengthens the reason "Rock climbing builds focus"?
ch: Rock climbing builds focus because climbers must plan each move and concentrate to keep their balance.
Rock climbing builds focus, trust me.
Rock climbing builds focus a lot.

quiz.q: Write a counterclaim and a rebuttal for the claim "Students should be allowed to choose an outdoor adventure class."
quiz.ans: Counterclaim: Some argue that outdoor adventure classes are too dangerous. Rebuttal: However, trained instructors, safety equipment and clear rules make the risks manageable, and students gain confidence and teamwork skills.

test.q: Which word would a writer choose to criticize a risky choice most strongly?
Which word gives the most positive impression of a person who takes risks?
Which sentence expresses the idea without any wasted words?
ch: Abuela jumped from the plane at noon.
At noon, Abuela jumped from the plane at twelve o'clock.
Abuela, who was jumping, jumped from the plane at noon.
Abuela made a jump that was a jump from the plane at noon.

test.q: Which verb is most precise in "The parachute ___ open against the blue sky"?
Which statement is an overgeneralization?
ch: Everyone who goes skydiving gets hurt.

test.q: Which source is most credible for an argument about preventing drowning?
ch: the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

test.q: Which sentence best acknowledges and rebuts a counterclaim?
ch: Although swim programs cost money, partnerships with city pools can keep costs low.
Swimming is fun, so everyone should swim.

test.q: Who narrates "Abuela Takes the Leap"?
ch: an outside narrator who knows every character's thoughts

test.q: In "Abuela Takes the Leap," how does the narrator view his grandmother's plan at first?
ch: as a terrible idea that does not fit the careful person he knows
as an exciting adventure he wants to join
as a joke she does not mean
as a smart way to save money

test.q: In "Abuela Takes the Leap," what is Abuela's main reason for skydiving?
ch: She has waited most of her life to pursue a dream of flying.
She wants to prove her son wrong.
Her doctor told her to exercise more.
She lost a bet with her family.

test.q: In "Abuela Takes the Leap," what does Abuela mean when she says, "I'm brave, not foolish"?
ch: She has taken sensible precautions while still choosing to take a risk.
She is not afraid of anything at all.
She does not care about safety.
She plans to jump without a parachute.

test.q: Which detail from "Abuela Takes the Leap" shows that the narrator's view is beginning to change?
ch: He notices that she looks younger and her eyes are bright when she talks about the plane.
His uncle chokes on his iced tea.

test.q: How does the contrast between the narrator's and Abuela's points of view develop a theme in "Abuela Takes the Leap"?
ch: It suggests that taking a meaningful risk can matter more than always playing it safe.
It suggests that older people should never take risks.
It shows that families always agree.
It shows that skydiving is easy.

test.q: In "Abuela Takes the Leap," contrast the uncle's reaction at the beginning with his reaction at the end. What does the change suggest?
test.ans: At first he calls the plan "frankly ridiculous"; at the end he is crying after she lands safely. The change suggests that seeing her joy and courage moved him and changed his view of her choice.

test.q: What is the claim in "Every Student Should Learn to Swim"?
ch: Every California school district should make sure students learn to swim before finishing middle school.
Swimming should be banned at the beach.
Only athletes need to learn to swim.

test.q: In "Every Student Should Learn to Swim," which evidence supports the safety reason?
ch: CDC data showing that drowning is the leading cause of death for children ages 1 to 4
Students who swim can join water polo teams.

test.q: In "Every Student Should Learn to Swim," how does the author develop the reason about fairness?
ch: by explaining that lessons cost money and that children from low-income families are less likely to have had them
by describing a drowning in detail
by listing every pool in California
