passages.x: CHARACTERS: CAMILLE, 18, about to leave for college. DANIEL, 13, her brother. MOM, heard offstage. SETTING: A cluttered bedroom on a late August morning. Half-packed boxes cover the floor. A small, old-fashioned radio sits on the windowsill. // (CAMILLE is taping a box shut. DANIEL leans in the doorway, arms crossed.) // CAMILLE: Are you going to help, or are you just going to stand there looking tragic? // DANIEL: I'm not looking tragic. This is my normal face. // CAMILLE: (laughing) Then your normal face is tragic. Hand me the marker. // (DANIEL tosses her a marker without moving from the doorway. She writes BOOKS on the box.) // DANIEL: You're taking all your books? // CAMILLE: Most of them. // DANIEL: What about the mystery ones? We were going to finish the series. // CAMILLE: (pausing) You can finish it. You read faster than I do anyway. // DANIEL: That's not the point. (He kicks at a box.) The point was doing it together. // (Silence. CAMILLE sits down on the bed.) // CAMILLE: Danny, come here. // (He hesitates, then sits on the far end of the bed.) // CAMILLE: Remember when I started high school, and you were, what, eight? You cried because I wasn't going to walk you to school anymore. // DANIEL: I didn't cry. // CAMILLE: You cried so hard Mom thought you broke your arm. // DANIEL: (a small smile) Maybe a little. // CAMILLE: And then what happened? // DANIEL: (shrugging) I started walking with Marcus and Jun. // CAMILLE: And you liked it. You liked it better, actually. You stopped waiting for me after the first week. // (DANIEL doesn't answer. CAMILLE gets up, takes the radio from the windowsill and holds it out to him.) // CAMILLE: Here. // DANIEL: Your radio? You love that thing. Grandpa gave it to you. // CAMILLE: And now I'm giving it to you. Every Sunday night at nine, there's that mystery show we listen to. I'll listen at school. You listen here. Then you call me and tell me who you think did it. // (DANIEL takes the radio slowly, turning it over in his hands.) // DANIEL: You'll actually answer? // CAMILLE: Every Sunday. Even if I'm busy. Even if you're wrong. // MOM: (offstage) Camille! The car's here! // (CAMILLE picks up the last box. At the door she stops, looks back at DANIEL and nods. She exits. DANIEL sits alone, holding the radio. After a moment, he clicks it on. Static, then faint music. He turns the dial carefully, listening. Lights fade.)

Every weekday morning, millions of teenagers drag themselves out of bed while it is still dark. Many adults see this as a lesson in discipline. I see it as a problem that science has already explained, and California was right to address it. // In 2019, California became the first state to pass a law limiting how early public middle and high schools may start. Under the law, which took full effect in 2022, most high schools may not begin regular classes before 8:30 a.m., and most middle schools may not begin before 8:00 a.m. // The reasoning behind the law comes from sleep research. During puberty, the body begins releasing melatonin, a hormone that makes people feel sleepy, later at night than it did in childhood. As a result, many teenagers simply cannot fall asleep as early as younger children can, no matter how hard they try. Yet sleep experts recommend that teenagers get eight to ten hours of sleep each night. A student who cannot fall asleep until 11:00 p.m. and must wake at 6:00 a.m. will fall short every single day. In 2014, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. for exactly this reason. // Critics raised real concerns. Some parents worried about getting to work after dropping off their children. Some coaches worried that later dismissal would cut into practice time. Bus companies had to rearrange their routes. I do not dismiss these problems; changing schedules is hard. But I believe the evidence about student health outweighs the inconvenience. Families and schools have adjusted to schedule changes before, and they can do so again. // Others argue that teenagers would simply stay up later if school started later. Some might. But studies of schools that shifted to later start times have generally found that students got more sleep overall, not the same amount at a later hour. // Growing up involves learning to manage your own time, and that includes going to bed at a reasonable hour. Teenagers should do their part by putting phones away at night. But we should not ask them to fight their own biology every morning. A later start is not a reward for laziness. It is a schedule built for the way growing bodies actually work.

For a long time, people explained teenage behavior with a shrug: teens were moody, impulsive and fond of risks simply because they were teens. In recent decades, brain scientists have offered a more detailed explanation, and a more hopeful one. // Using brain-imaging technology, researchers have found that the brain continues to develop well beyond childhood. One of the last regions to mature is the prefrontal cortex, the area just behind the forehead. This region helps with planning, weighing consequences and controlling impulses. Scientists believe it continues developing into a person's mid-twenties. // Meanwhile, parts of the brain involved in emotion and reward become especially active during adolescence. Rewards, such as excitement, praise or a friend's approval, can feel unusually strong. Some researchers compare the teenage brain to a car with a powerful accelerator and brakes that are still being installed. // Friends play a surprising role. In one well-known study, psychologist Laurence Steinberg and a colleague at Temple University asked people to play a simulated driving game. Teenagers took far more risks, such as running yellow lights, when they knew friends were watching than when they played alone. Adults' choices changed much less in front of friends. // It would be easy to read these findings as bad news. But many scientists, including Steinberg, argue the opposite. Because the adolescent brain is changing so quickly, it is also especially able to learn. The same openness that can lead to risky choices also helps teenagers pick up new skills, explore new ideas and adapt to new situations. Some researchers call adolescence a second window of opportunity, comparable to early childhood. // This view changes what adults might do. Instead of simply warning teens to avoid all risks, parents and schools can offer positive risks: trying out for a play, starting a small business, learning a difficult instrument or leading a team. These challenges give the brain's reward system the excitement it craves, in settings where mistakes help people grow. // The teenage brain is not broken. It is under construction. And like any construction site, it is full of noise, energy and possibility.

Laila had ridden the Route 22 bus a hundred times, but always with her mother, who held the bus pass, watched for their stop and pulled the cord at exactly the right moment. Today, for the first time, Laila was riding alone, to her violin lesson across the city. // Her mother had made a list. It was in Laila's pocket, folded into a square: Get on at Fourth and Main. Sit near the driver. Get off at Lincoln Park, the stop after the library. Text me when you arrive. Don't talk to strangers. Don't fall asleep. Don't lose the list. // "Mom," Laila had said that morning, "I'm twelve, not five." // Her mother had smiled, but her eyes stayed worried. "I know. That's what scares me." // For the first fifteen minutes, everything went perfectly. Laila sat near the driver. She watched the city slide past the window: the taco trucks, the laundromat with the painted mural, the old movie theater with half its letters missing. She felt grown-up and a little bit proud. // Then the bus turned left where it had always gone straight. // Laila sat up. The library was supposed to be on the right. Instead there were warehouses and a gas station she had never seen. Her heart began to pound. She pulled the list from her pocket, but the list did not say what to do if the bus went the wrong way. // For a moment, she wanted to call her mother. Her thumb hovered over the phone. Then she took a breath and looked around. A sign above the driver's seat flashed: DETOUR, ROAD WORK ON MAIN. // Laila stood, holding the pole, and walked to the front. "Excuse me," she said, her voice smaller than she wanted. "I need Lincoln Park. Is this bus still going there?" // The driver glanced at her in the mirror. "Detour's just for six blocks. We'll get back on the regular route in a minute. I'll call out Lincoln Park for you." // "Thank you," Laila said, and this time her voice sounded more like her own. // When she stepped off at Lincoln Park, she texted her mother: Here. There was a detour but I figured it out. // Her phone buzzed almost immediately. Of course you did. // Laila smiled, refolded the list and put it back in her pocket. She did not need it anymore, but she thought she might keep it anyway.

passages.x: On the first Tuesday of every month, every pair of LensLink glasses in Harbor City shut down for one hour to install updates. The city called it Update Day. Most people called it the Dark Hour, even though the sun was shining. // Zara Okoye had worn her LensLinks since she was eight. They told her when the bus was coming, translated her grandmother's Igbo into English in tiny glowing letters, reminded her of homework and showed her friends' messages floating in the corner of her vision. She could not remember the last time she had been bored. She could not remember the last time she had wondered about anything for more than a second, either, because the answer always appeared before the question finished forming. // At 3:00 p.m., her glasses blinked, displayed a cheerful spinning circle and went dark. // Zara sat on the front steps of her building, blinking at a world that suddenly seemed too plain. The street was just a street. No labels. No arrows. No messages. // Her grandmother came out with two cups of tea and sat down beside her. Grandma Ngozi never wore LensLinks. She said they made her dizzy. // "So," Grandma said. "What do we do now?" // "Nothing," Zara said. "Wait." // Grandma said something in Igbo. Without her glasses, Zara caught only a few words. She frowned, trying to remember. "Did you say... the river?" // Grandma laughed, delighted. "Yes! I said this quiet reminds me of sitting by the river in my village, waiting for my mother to finish washing clothes. We had no clocks, no glasses. Just waiting. And stories." // "Tell me one," Zara said, surprising herself. // So Grandma told her about the river spirit who stole a fisherman's shadow, and Zara asked questions, real questions that no lens could answer, because the answers were only in her grandmother's memory. When Grandma used a word Zara didn't know, Zara asked her to say it again, and then again, until she could say it herself. // At 4:00 p.m., her LensLinks flickered back to life. Messages poured into her vision: fourteen new, six urgent, one reminder about a math quiz. // Zara looked at them for a moment. Then she took the glasses off, folded them and set them on the step. // "Then what happened?" she asked. "To the fisherman's shadow?" // Grandma smiled and leaned closer.

passages.t: Two Views on Teens and Screens
passages.x: Article 1: Too Much, Too Soon. Teenagers today spend a remarkable share of their waking hours looking at screens. In a 2022 survey by the Pew Research Center, nearly half of U.S. teens said they were online "almost constantly." That should worry us. // Every hour spent scrolling is an hour not spent sleeping, exercising or talking face to face. Sleep experts often recommend turning off screens an hour before bed, because bright light and exciting content can make it harder to fall asleep. Yet many teens keep phones beside their pillows and check them late into the night. // Families and schools should set clear limits. Phones can stay out of bedrooms at night. Dinner can be screen-free. Schools can keep phones in lockers during class. These simple rules would give teenagers back the hours that screens have quietly taken. // Article 2: Not All Screen Time Is Equal. Adults love to count teenagers' screen hours. But a number alone tells us very little. An hour spent editing a video for a science project, video-chatting with a cousin overseas or learning guitar from an online lesson is very different from an hour spent scrolling endlessly through other people's highlight reels. // Some large studies have found that the link between total screen time and teenagers' well-being is weaker than many people assume. What seems to matter more is how screens are used and what they replace. If screen use pushes out sleep or exercise, it can cause harm. If it helps a teen create, learn or stay connected, it can help. // Instead of strict limits for everyone, families should talk with teenagers about how they use their devices. Teens can learn to notice when scrolling leaves them feeling worse and to choose activities that leave them feeling better. The goal should not be less screen time. It should be better screen time.

"Recalculating," said the phone in Dad's hand, for the third time. Then, with a small sad chirp, the screen went black. // Dev stared at it. "Is it dead?" // "It's resting," Dad said, which meant yes. // They were standing at a fork in the trail somewhere in the hills above the reservoir, two hours into what Dad had promised would be "a quick loop." The sun was already sliding toward the ridge. Dev's own phone had been dead since lunch, drained by photos and a game he now regretted playing. // "Okay," Dad said, turning in a slow circle. "Okay. Which way did we come from?" // Dev realized, with a cold feeling in his stomach, that he had no idea. For two hours he had followed the blue dot on the screen. He had not looked at the trail at all. // Then he remembered something. "The tree," he said. // "What tree?" // "There was a tree that got hit by lightning. All black and split down the middle. We passed it right after the bridge. I took a picture of it." He winced. "On my phone." // "Did we pass it before or after we turned?" // Dev closed his eyes and tried to see it. The bridge. The creek below, loud with spring water. The split tree on the left. Then a bench with a plaque. Then uphill, with the sun in his eyes. // "The sun was in my eyes when we climbed," Dev said slowly. "So we were walking west, toward the sunset." He opened his eyes. "So to go back, we should keep the sun behind us." // Dad looked at him with an expression Dev had never seen before, somewhere between surprise and pride. "Lead the way, navigator." // They walked east, the sun warm on their backs. Dev watched everything now: a rock shaped like a bear's head, a patch of orange poppies, a fence with a missing rail. After twenty minutes they reached the bench with the plaque. Then the split black tree. Then the bridge and the roar of the creek. // When they reached the parking lot, the sky was pink. Dad leaned against the car and laughed. // "You know," he said, "I've been hiking for thirty years, and I didn't notice that tree." // "I only noticed it because I wanted a picture," Dev admitted. // "Maybe," Dad said. "But you remembered it because you looked." // On the drive home, Dev's phone stayed dead in his pocket. He spent the ride watching the hills go by, trying to memorize the shape of them.

passages.t: Lost Without It? GPS and the Human Brain
passages.x: Not long ago, travelers found their way with paper maps, street signs and directions scribbled on the back of an envelope. Today, a voice in a phone tells millions of people exactly when to turn. The Global Positioning System, or GPS, has changed how humans move through the world. Some scientists are now asking how it may be changing our brains. // GPS was developed by the United States Department of Defense. It relies on a network of satellites orbiting Earth, each sending signals that a receiver can use to calculate its location. The system became fully operational in the 1990s, and in 2000 the U.S. government made highly accurate GPS signals available to everyone. Today GPS guides cars, planes, ships, delivery drivers and hikers, and it helps emergency responders find people in trouble. // Researchers who study memory have long been interested in a part of the brain called the hippocampus, which plays an important role in spatial memory, our ability to remember places and routes. In a well-known study published in 2000, scientist Eleanor Maguire and her team examined London taxi drivers, who must memorize thousands of streets to earn their license. They found that the drivers had a larger rear portion of the hippocampus than people in a comparison group. The finding suggested that the brain can change with practice at navigating. // If practice strengthens navigation skills, what happens when we stop practicing? Some smaller studies have found that people who rely heavily on GPS tend to perform worse on tests of spatial memory, and that people following turn-by-turn directions remember less about the routes they traveled. However, scientists caution that these studies cannot yet prove that GPS causes weaker navigation skills. It is possible, for example, that people who already have a poor sense of direction are simply more likely to use GPS. // Experts suggest a balanced approach. GPS is a valuable tool, and in emergencies it can save lives. But people can also keep their own skills sharp: studying a map before a trip, noticing landmarks, trying to find a familiar place without directions, or turning off the voice and checking the route only when needed. // The question is not whether to use GPS. It is whether we let it do all the thinking for us.

lessons.name: Theme in science fiction

practice.q: Science fiction often
ch: imagines how science or technology might change people's lives
explains how to repair a computer
practice.h: Think about "what if" stories.

practice.q: In a story, a boy's robot dog does everything perfectly, but he feels lonely until he adopts a real puppy that makes mistakes. Which theme fits?
ch: Imperfect, real relationships can matter more than perfect technology.
Technology is always better than nature.
practice.h: What does the boy learn?

practice.q: How is a theme usually developed over the course of a story?
ch: through the characters' changes, choices and key events
only through descriptions of the setting
practice.h: Think of how events build meaning.

practice.q: Which sentence is an objective summary of a story?
ch: A girl whose glasses answer every question learns to value her grandmother's stories during a shutdown.
This is the best story I have ever read.
The girl should have thrown away her glasses.
practice.h: Leave out opinions.

practice.q: Explain how a story's conflict can help develop its theme. Use an example about technology.
practice.ans: The conflict forces a character to make choices that reveal the message. For example, a character who must choose between a video game tournament and a friend's birthday party learns that friendships matter more than winning.
practice.h: How does the character's choice reveal the message?

quiz.q: In "Update Day," how do the LensLink glasses affect Zara's life before the shutdown?
ch: They make life convenient but leave her rarely curious or wondering.
They have taught her to speak Igbo fluently.
They keep her away from her friends.

quiz.q: In "Update Day," what does the detail "the answer always appeared before the question finished forming" suggest?
ch: Zara has lost the habit of thinking deeply or being curious.

quiz.q: In "Update Day," why does Zara's grandmother not wear LensLinks?
ch: They are not sold to adults.
She is not allowed to wear them.

quiz.q: What is the turning point in "Update Day"?
ch: Zara understands a few Igbo words and asks her grandmother for a story.
The glasses shut down for updates.
Grandma brings out two cups of tea.

quiz.q: At the end of "Update Day," why does Zara take off her glasses?
ch: She chooses her connection with her grandmother over the flood of messages.
She wants to take a nap.

quiz.q: Which statement best expresses the theme of "Update Day"?
ch: Technology can make life easier, but real connection and curiosity come from human relationships.
All technology is harmful and should be banned.
Software updates are important for safety.

quiz.q: Trace how the theme of "Update Day" develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Cite at least two details.
quiz.ans: At the start, the LensLinks answer every question, so Zara is never bored but never truly curious. During the Dark Hour she understands a few Igbo words and asks for a story, asking "real questions that no lens could answer." At the end, she sets the glasses aside to hear what happens next. The theme develops from convenience toward genuine human connection.

lessons.name: Comparing two authors' writing on the same topic

practice.q: When two authors write about the same topic, a reader should compare
ch: only the length of each text
practice.h: What parts make up an argument?

practice.q: Two articles discuss electric scooters in cities. One cites accident data; the other cites reduced traffic. What does this show?
ch: The authors chose different evidence to support different emphases.
Both authors have the same purpose.
practice.h: Think about what each author wants readers to notice.

practice.q: Two authors describe the same survey, in which 60 percent of students wanted a longer lunch. One calls the result "a strong majority"; the other says "40 percent are satisfied." What does this show?
ch: Authors can interpret the same data differently.
practice.h: Look at how each author describes the same numbers.

practice.q: Which question best helps a reader evaluate two conflicting articles?
ch: Which article uses more credible and relevant evidence?
Which article has a longer title?
practice.h: Focus on the quality of the evidence.

practice.q: Explain why it is useful to read more than one source on a controversial topic.
practice.ans: Different sources may present different evidence or interpretations. Comparing them helps you see the full picture, notice bias and form a well-informed opinion.
practice.h: What might one source leave out?

quiz.q: In "Two Views on Teens and Screens," what is the main claim of Article 1, "Too Much, Too Soon"?
ch: Families and schools should set clear limits on teen screen use.
Teens should get more screen time.
Screen time has no effect on sleep.

quiz.q: In "Two Views on Teens and Screens," what is the main claim of Article 2, "Not All Screen Time Is Equal"?
ch: How screens are used matters more than total screen time.
Adults should count teens' screen hours carefully.

quiz.q: In "Two Views on Teens and Screens," which evidence does Article 1 use to support its concern?
ch: A 2022 Pew survey found that nearly half of teens were online "almost constantly."
Some studies found a weak link between screen time and well-being.

quiz.q: In "Two Views on Teens and Screens," how do the two authors treat the issue of sleep differently?
ch: Article 1 treats lost sleep as a reason for strict limits, while Article 2 says screens cause harm mainly when they push out things like sleep.
Both say sleep does not matter.
Article 2 says teens need less sleep.

quiz.q: On which point do both authors in "Two Views on Teens and Screens" agree?
ch: Screen use can be harmful when it replaces sleep or other healthy activities.
Teens should have no rules at all.
Phones should be banned from schools.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes how the two authors in "Two Views on Teens and Screens" shape their presentations differently?
ch: Article 1 emphasizes the amount of screen time and recommends rules, while Article 2 emphasizes the type of use and recommends conversations.
Both articles use the same evidence and reach the same conclusion.
Article 2 uses no evidence at all.

quiz.q: Which article in "Two Views on Teens and Screens" do you find more convincing? Explain your choice using one piece of evidence from each article.
quiz.ans: Answers vary but must use evidence from both. Example: Article 2 is more convincing because it accepts Article 1's point that screens before bed can hurt sleep, while also citing large studies suggesting that total screen time matters less than how screens are used.

lessons.name: Placing modifiers and punctuating coordinate adjectives

practice.q: A misplaced modifier is
ch: a word or phrase placed too far from the word it describes
a verb in the wrong tense
practice.h: A modifier should sit next to the word it describes.

practice.q: Which sentence has a misplaced modifier?
ch: We bought a laptop from the store with a cracked screen.
We bought a laptop with a cracked screen from the store.
From the store, we bought a laptop.
The laptop had a cracked screen.
practice.h: Does the store have a cracked screen?

practice.q: Which sentence has a dangling modifier?
ch: Scrolling through the app, the time flew by.
Scrolling through the app, Maya lost track of time.
The app was fun to scroll.
practice.h: Who was scrolling? Is that person named?

practice.q: Which sentence correctly uses a comma between coordinate adjectives?
ch: It was a long, boring video.
It was a long boring, video.
It was a, long boring video.
It was long, a boring video.
practice.h: If you can switch the adjectives or put "and" between them, use a comma.

practice.q: Rewrite this sentence to fix the dangling modifier: "While charging overnight, my alarm didn't go off."
practice.ans: While my phone was charging overnight, the alarm didn't go off. (Any revision that names what was charging.)
practice.h: Add who or what was charging.

quiz.q: Which revision fixes the misplaced modifier in "I read about the robot that cleans floors in the newspaper"?
ch: In the newspaper, I read about the robot that cleans floors.
I read about the robot in the newspaper that cleans floors.
I read in the robot about the newspaper that cleans floors.
The robot that cleans floors read about me in the newspaper.

quiz.q: Which sentence contains an opening phrase that does not describe any word in the sentence?
ch: After updating the software, the screen went black.
After updating the software, Leah watched the screen go black.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses commas correctly with coordinate adjectives?
ch: The bright, noisy arcade was packed.
The bright noisy, arcade was packed.
The, bright noisy arcade was packed.
The bright, noisy, arcade was packed.

quiz.q: Which pair of adjectives should NOT be separated by a comma?
Which revision fixes the dangling modifier in "Walking into the classroom, the smartboard was already on"?
ch: Walking into the classroom, I saw that the smartboard was already on.
The smartboard, walking into the classroom, was already on.
Walking into the classroom, the smartboard turned on.
Walking into the classroom; the smartboard was on.

quiz.q: Which sentence means that no one except Ana sent a text?
ch: Ana sent a text to only one friend.

quiz.q: Which sentence is clear and correctly punctuated?
ch: Excited about the new app, Kenji downloaded it immediately.
Excited about the new app, the download happened immediately.
Kenji downloaded, excited about the new app it immediately.
Excited, about the new app Kenji downloaded it immediately.

quiz.q: Write a sentence about a piece of technology that includes two coordinate adjectives and a correctly placed modifying phrase.
quiz.ans: Example: "Holding the sleek, lightweight drone, Ana stepped onto the field."

lessons.name: Research: synthesizing credible sources and citing them

practice.q: Synthesizing sources means
ch: combining information from several sources to answer a question
practice.h: Think about putting pieces together.

practice.q: Which source is most credible for research on how screen time affects sleep?
ch: an article in a peer-reviewed medical journal
practice.h: Who checks the information carefully, and who might be biased?

practice.q: A student's research question is "Is technology good?" How could it be improved?
ch: Narrow it to "How does using phones before bed affect middle schoolers' sleep?"
Make it broader: "What is everything about technology?"
practice.h: A good research question is focused.

practice.q: What is the best way to include a source's exact words in a report?
ch: put them in quotation marks and cite the source
change a few words and leave out the source
practice.h: Exact words need quotation marks and credit.

practice.q: Explain how you can tell whether a website is a reliable source.
practice.ans: Check who wrote it and the author's expertise, whether it comes from a respected organization (a government agency, university or established news outlet), when it was published or updated, whether it cites evidence and whether it is trying to sell something.
practice.h: Think about author, purpose, date and evidence.

quiz.q: A bibliography or works cited list
ch: gives information about each source used

quiz.q: Two sources disagree about how many teens own smartphones. What should a researcher do?
ch: look for a third credible, recent source and note the difference

quiz.q: Which note is a correct paraphrase of "Blue light from screens may delay the release of melatonin"?
ch: Light from screens might make the body produce a sleep hormone later.
Blue light from screens may delay the release of melatonin.

quiz.q: Which detail would be most relevant to a report on how video games affect teamwork?
ch: Players of cooperative games must communicate and plan together to win.
Some video games cost sixty dollars.
The first video games were made decades ago.

quiz.q: Why should a researcher check the publication date of a source about technology?
ch: Technology changes quickly, so older information may be outdated.
The date shows the author's age.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of using multiple sources in a research report?
ch: to provide accurate, balanced information and confirm facts
to make the bibliography look longer
to avoid writing in your own words

quiz.q: Write a research question about technology and young people, and name two different types of credible sources you would use to answer it.
quiz.ans: Example question: How does having phones in class affect middle school students' attention? Sources: a peer-reviewed study or university research report; a government or education agency report; an interview with a teacher.

test.q: Which sentence makes it sound as if the trail were looking at the map?
ch: Looking at the map, the trail seemed to disappear.
Looking at the map, Dev realized the trail had split.
The trail split near the bridge.

test.q: Which revision fixes the misplaced modifier in "Dad found a bench with a plaque walking along the trail"?
ch: Walking along the trail, Dad found a bench with a plaque.
Dad found a bench walking along the trail with a plaque.
A bench with a plaque found Dad walking.
Walking along the trail with a plaque, Dad found a bench.

test.q: Which sentence uses a comma correctly between coordinate adjectives?
ch: They crossed the cold, rushing creek.
They crossed the cold rushing, creek.
They crossed, the cold rushing creek.
They crossed the cold, rushing, creek.

test.q: Which pair of adjectives does NOT need a comma between them?
Which is the best paraphrase of "The hippocampus plays an important role in spatial memory"?
ch: A part of the brain called the hippocampus helps us remember places.
The hippocampus plays an important role in spatial memory.
Spatial memory is a kind of role.
The brain plays games with places.

test.q: Which source would be most credible for a report on GPS satellites?
ch: a U.S. government website about GPS

test.q: Which sentence correctly credits a source in a research report?
ch: According to a 2000 study led by Eleanor Maguire, London taxi drivers had a larger rear hippocampus than people in a comparison group.
London taxi drivers had a larger hippocampus, I read somewhere.
Some study said something about taxis.

test.q: In "Dead Battery," what problem do Dev and his father face?
ch: Their phones are dead, and they are unsure which way leads back.
They have run out of water.
They have lost their car keys.

test.q: In "Dead Battery," why does Dev at first have "no idea" which way they came from?
ch: He followed the blue dot on the screen instead of watching the trail.
He was asleep in the car.
It was too dark to see.

test.q: In "Dead Battery," how does Dev figure out which direction to walk?
ch: He remembers the sun was in his eyes on the climb, so they were heading west and should return east.
He uses a compass from his backpack.

test.q: In "Dead Battery," what does Dad's expression, "somewhere between surprise and pride," suggest?
ch: He is impressed by Dev's thinking.
He is confused about the direction.
He is too tired to walk.

test.q: In "Dead Battery," what does Dad mean by "you remembered it because you looked"?
ch: Paying close attention, not just taking photos, is what helped Dev remember.

test.q: Which theme does "Dead Battery" best develop?
ch: Relying entirely on technology can keep us from noticing the world, but paying attention builds our own skills.
Phones should never be taken hiking.
Hiking is too dangerous for families.

test.q: In "Dead Battery," how does Dev change from the beginning to the end? Use two details.
test.ans: At first he followed "the blue dot on the screen" without looking at the trail. By the end he watches landmarks like "a rock shaped like a bear's head" and spends the drive "trying to memorize the shape" of the hills, showing he has learned to pay attention.

test.q: According to "Lost Without It? GPS and the Human Brain," who developed GPS?
ch: the United States Department of Defense

test.q: According to "Lost Without It? GPS and the Human Brain," what did the London taxi driver study suggest?
ch: Practicing navigation may change the brain.
Taxi drivers use GPS more than other people.

test.q: In "Lost Without It? GPS and the Human Brain," why do scientists say the GPS studies "cannot yet prove" that GPS weakens navigation skills?
ch: People with a poor sense of direction may simply be more likely to use GPS.
The studies were done before GPS existed.
GPS does not work in cities.
The studies tested only taxi drivers.

test.q: What does "spatial memory" mean in "Lost Without It? GPS and the Human Brain"?
ch: the ability to remember places and routes

test.q: How is "Lost Without It? GPS and the Human Brain" mainly organized?
ch: It introduces GPS, explains its history, presents research on the brain and ends with advice.
It tells a story in time order about one hiker.
It compares two kinds of paper maps.
It lists GPS features in random order.

test.q: Which statement best describes the author's point of view in "Lost Without It? GPS and the Human Brain"?
ch: GPS is valuable, but people should keep practicing their own navigation skills.
GPS has no effect on anyone.
Paper maps are always better than GPS.

test.q: In "Lost Without It? GPS and the Human Brain," why does the author include the caution that the studies "cannot yet prove" GPS causes weaker navigation skills?
test.ans: To be accurate and fair: the studies show a link between heavy GPS use and weaker spatial memory, but not that GPS causes it, since people with weaker navigation skills might simply choose GPS more often.

test.q: Write a short research report that answers the question "How does relying on GPS affect people's navigation skills?" Synthesize information from "Lost Without It? GPS and the Human Brain" and, if useful, use "Dead Battery" as an example. Include an introduction with a focused thesis, at least three facts paraphrased or quoted with credit, an explanation of what the research can and cannot prove, and two additional credible sources you would consult.
test.ans: Key points: a focused thesis; background on GPS (developed by the Department of Defense, satellite signals, highly accurate public signals in 2000); the hippocampus and spatial memory; Maguire's taxi-driver study suggesting practice changes the brain; studies linking heavy GPS use with weaker spatial memory, plus the caution that they do not prove cause and effect; balanced advice (study maps, notice landmarks); an optional example of Dev using landmarks and the sun; information paraphrased and credited; formal style; two additional credible sources such as a university research article or a science agency website.
rub: Clear focus and strong organization; ideas fully developed with relevant details or text evidence; precise language; few errors in conventions.
Clear focus and organization; ideas adequately developed with some details or evidence; some errors that do not affect meaning.
Focus or organization is inconsistent; limited development or evidence; errors sometimes interfere with meaning.
Little focus or organization; minimal development; frequent errors.

units.name: Collection 6: Fiction Meets History (literary analysis)
units.el: Build a simple timeline (1848 Gold Rush, 1865 railroad hiring, 1867 strike, 1869 golden spike, 1946 to 1947 Mendez case) on the wall, and use a T-chart labeled "Fact from history" and "Added by the author" for every historical fiction text.

passages.t: Gold in the Kitchen (historical fiction with a historian's note)
passages.x: Every miner in camp swore he would strike it rich next week. Sofia Reyes heard it a dozen times a day, standing beside her mother's cooking fire on the banks of the Stanislaus River in the summer of 1850. // "Next week, little one," said Mr. Pratt from Ohio, handing over a pinch of gold dust for three tortillas and a bowl of beans. "Next week I'll buy the whole kettle." // Her mother smiled and weighed the dust on her small brass scale. She had come north from Sonora, Mexico, with Sofia and Sofia's father the year before, when word spread that gold lay in California's streams like seeds waiting to be picked up. Papa had worked the river every day since, standing in icy water until his hands cracked. Some days he found a few flakes. Most days he found nothing. // Mama had found something else. In their second week in camp, she had looked at the hungry men lined up at a trader's tent, where a single egg sold for more than a dollar, and she had gone back to their tent and started making tortillas. // By the end of the summer, the little tin box under Mama's cot held more gold than Papa had pulled from the river in a year. // Not everyone was happy about it. Some American miners grumbled that foreigners were taking gold that belonged to them. In the spring, the state had passed a tax that charged foreign miners twenty dollars a month for the right to dig, more than most could pay. Papa came home angry the day the tax collector arrived. Two of their neighbors, men from Chile, packed up and left for San Francisco the next morning. // "Maybe we should go too," Papa said that night. // Mama looked at the tin box, then at the line of tents along the river, each one full of hungry men. "They can tax a miner," she said. "But everyone has to eat." // Sofia lay awake listening to the river. She thought about all the men waiting for next week. Her mother, she realized, had not waited. She had looked at what was in front of her and found a different kind of gold. // Historian's note: The story is fiction, but its background is real. Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in January 1848, and by 1849 people from around the world, including Mexico, Chile and China, had rushed to California. Few miners grew rich. Many people who earned steady money did so by selling goods and services, such as food, supplies and laundry, at very high prices. In 1850, California passed a Foreign Miners' Tax of twenty dollars a month. It fell hardest on miners from Latin America and was repealed the next year, but another tax aimed at foreign miners, especially Chinese miners, followed in 1852.

passages.t: The Case That Opened the Schoolhouse Doors
passages.x: In the fall of 1944, Gonzalo and Felicitas Mendez tried to enroll their children at the 17th Street School in Westminster, California, a farming town in Orange County. The school turned the Mendez children away, even though their lighter-skinned cousins were allowed to attend. Sylvia, Gonzalo Jr. and Jerome were told they would have to go to the "Mexican school" nearby, a separate school with fewer resources. // At the time, many school districts in California separated children of Mexican descent from white children. Officials claimed the separation helped students learn English, but children were often placed in these schools because of their last names or appearance, not because of any test of their English. // The Mendez family refused to accept this. Gonzalo Mendez, who had come to the United States from Mexico as a child, and Felicitas Mendez, who was born in Puerto Rico, worked with an attorney named David Marcus. In 1945, they and four other Mexican American families filed a lawsuit against Westminster and three other Orange County school districts. // In 1946, federal judge Paul McCormick ruled in favor of the families. He found that separating students by their ancestry denied them equal protection under the law and that public education must be open to all children on an equal basis. The school districts appealed, but in 1947 a federal appeals court upheld the decision. // The case drew national attention. Several civil rights groups filed briefs supporting the families, including the NAACP, whose legal team included Thurgood Marshall. In June 1947, about two months after the appeals court ruling, California Governor Earl Warren signed a law ending the state's remaining school segregation laws. California became one of the first states to end legal segregation in its public schools. // The Mendez case did not end school segregation across the nation. That came in 1954, when the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Brown v. Board of Education that segregated public schools were unconstitutional. But historians see clear connections between the two cases. Thurgood Marshall argued the Brown case before the Supreme Court, and Earl Warren, by then the Chief Justice, wrote its decision. // Sylvia Mendez, who was eight when the case began, spent much of her later life telling students about it. In 2011, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor.

In 1862, President Abraham Lincoln signed a law to support building a railroad across the United States. Two companies would build it. The Union Pacific would build west from the Missouri River area, and the Central Pacific would build east from Sacramento, California. Where they met, the nation would be connected by rail from coast to coast. // The Central Pacific faced the harder start. Its route led directly into the Sierra Nevada, mountains of solid granite, steep canyons and heavy winter snow. The company also struggled to find workers. Many men who came to California hoped to strike it rich in mining, not to swing a hammer on a railroad. // In 1865, the Central Pacific began hiring Chinese workers, many of whom had come to California during the Gold Rush. Some managers doubted that they could handle the work. They were proved wrong. Within a few years, Chinese laborers made up the large majority of the Central Pacific's workforce, numbering in the thousands. // The work was brutal and dangerous. Workers drilled holes into granite by hand, packed them with black powder and later with a powerful explosive called nitroglycerin, and blasted tunnels through the mountains. In some places, progress was measured in inches per day. Winters brought enormous snowstorms, and avalanches buried camps. Historians do not know exactly how many workers died, but the number was significant. // Chinese workers were also paid less than white workers for the same work, and at first, unlike white workers, they had to pay for their own food. In June 1867, thousands of Chinese workers went on strike, demanding equal pay and shorter hours in the tunnels. The company refused and cut off supplies to the camps. After about a week, the strike ended without the workers' demands being met. Still, historians see it as one of the largest labor actions of its time. // On May 10, 1869, the two railroads met at Promontory Summit, in Utah Territory. Officials drove a ceremonial golden spike, and telegraph messages spread the news across the country. A journey from New York to San Francisco that had once taken months could now be made in about a week. // Chinese workers were largely left out of the celebration and the famous photographs of that day. For many years, their role was overlooked. Today, historians, descendants and communities are working to make sure their contributions are remembered.

Winter, 1866. In the tunnel, there was no day or night, only the ring of hammers. // Jin-li was fifteen, though he had told the foreman he was eighteen. He held the long iron drill steady while his uncle, Wu Bao, swung the hammer. Strike, turn. Strike, turn. Each blow sent a shock through Jin-li's arms and into his teeth. At the end of a twelve-hour shift, the hole they had made in the granite was barely as deep as his hand. // "The mountain is slow to answer," Uncle Bao liked to say, "but it answers." // Outside, the snow had been falling for nine days. It buried the cabins up to their roofs, and the men dug tunnels through the drifts to reach the work tunnel. Jin-li had stopped feeling his toes somewhere in December. At night, in the crowded cabin, he wrote letters to his mother in Guangdong by the light of a single lamp. He told her he was eating well. He told her the work was steady. He did not tell her about the avalanche that had swept away a cabin farther down the slope, or about the men who had not been found until spring. // In the evenings, the older men talked about wages. They talked quietly, because the bosses had ears everywhere. Jin-li listened. The white workers, they said, were paid more each month, and the company fed them. The Chinese workers bought and cooked their own food: dried oysters, rice, vegetables and tea boiled from melted snow. // "Why do we accept less?" Jin-li asked his uncle one night. // Uncle Bao was quiet for a long time. "Because we are far from home," he said finally, "and we are afraid. But fear is like the snow. It piles up until someone decides to dig through." // Jin-li did not understand then. He understood the next summer, when word passed from cabin to cabin and thousands of men put down their tools on the same morning. The tunnels fell silent for the first time in months. Jin-li stood beside his uncle in the bright sun, his heart pounding, and felt, for the first time since leaving China, that he was not small. // The strike ended after a week. The company did not give them what they asked for. But on the night it ended, Jin-li wrote to his mother and told her the truth, all of it, for the first time. // "The mountain is slow to answer," he wrote. "But I think it heard us."

lessons.name: Historical fiction and historical accounts

practice.q: Historical fiction is
ch: a made-up story set in a real time and place in the past
a true account written by a historian
a story with no real details
practice.h: Think fiction plus history.

practice.q: An author writes a novel about a boy working on the transcontinental railroad. Which detail is most likely invented?
ch: the boy's conversations with his best friend
the year the railroad was completed
practice.h: What would no historical record contain?

practice.q: Why might an author of historical fiction invent characters and details?
ch: to help readers connect emotionally with the people and the period
to make the history completely inaccurate
practice.h: What can a story do that a history book cannot?

practice.q: How can a reader check whether details in a historical novel are accurate?
ch: compare them with reliable historical sources
ask a character in the story
practice.h: Fiction is not always fact.

practice.q: Explain one way a historical novel and a history textbook might describe the same event differently.
practice.ans: A textbook might give dates, causes and statistics, while a novel shows the event through one character's eyes, with feelings, dialogue and invented personal details.
practice.h: Think about facts versus feelings.

quiz.q: How does the author of "Gold in the Kitchen" use the historical setting of the Gold Rush?
ch: to create a fictional family whose experiences reflect real events such as high prices and the foreign miners' tax
to give an exact record of a real family
to argue that the Gold Rush never happened

quiz.q: Which detail from the story "Gold in the Kitchen" matches information in its historian's note?
ch: Mama earns more by selling food than Papa earns by mining.
Sofia lies awake listening to the river.
Papa's hands crack in the icy water.

quiz.q: In "Gold in the Kitchen," why does Mama start making tortillas?
ch: She sees that hungry miners are paying very high prices for food.
Papa asks her to cook for the camp.
She wants to leave the mining camp.

quiz.q: In "Gold in the Kitchen," how does the Foreign Miners' Tax affect the characters?
ch: It angers Papa and causes their Chilean neighbors to leave.
It has no effect on them.
It lowers the price of eggs.

quiz.q: In "Gold in the Kitchen," what does Mama mean when she says, "They can tax a miner. But everyone has to eat"?
ch: Her food business is steadier than mining because miners always need food.
She thinks the tax is fair.
She wants Papa to pay her taxes.

quiz.q: How does the fictional story in "Gold in the Kitchen" add to the information in the historian's note?
ch: It shows how real events might have felt to one family, adding emotion and personal detail that the note does not provide.
It corrects mistakes in the note.
It gives more exact dates than the note.
It proves that most miners became rich.

quiz.q: Compare the story and the historian's note in "Gold in the Kitchen." Identify one historical fact the author used and explain how the story brings it to life.
quiz.ans: Fact: in 1850, California charged foreign miners a tax of twenty dollars a month. The story brings it to life by showing Papa coming home angry when the tax collector arrives and their Chilean neighbors leaving the next morning, so readers feel its impact on people.

lessons.name: How individuals, events and ideas influence each other in history

practice.q: Which question best helps you analyze how a person influenced events?
ch: What did this person do, and what changed because of it?
What was this person's favorite color?
Where did this person buy shoes?
practice.h: Look for cause and effect.

practice.q: Read: "After a drought destroyed their crops, many farmers moved west. Their arrival changed the economies of the towns they joined." How do the event and the people interact?
ch: The drought caused the farmers to move, and their move changed other towns.
practice.h: Trace the chain of causes.

practice.q: Which detail best shows an idea influencing people's actions?
ch: Inspired by speeches about equal rights, students organized peaceful protests.
The protest took place on a Tuesday.
practice.h: Which detail shows an idea leading to action?

practice.q: An article explains how a court ruling led a governor to sign a new law. What relationship does this show?
ch: One event led a person to take a new action.
practice.h: Think about cause and effect between events and people.

practice.q: Choose a historical figure you know. Explain one way that person was influenced by events and one way the person influenced events.
practice.ans: Example: Cesar Chavez was shaped by the hard conditions he experienced as a farmworker, and he influenced events by organizing farmworkers and leading boycotts that improved working conditions.
practice.h: Influence can go in both directions.

quiz.q: In "The Case That Opened the Schoolhouse Doors," why were the Mendez children turned away from the 17th Street School?
ch: Officials sent children of Mexican descent to a separate school.
They were too young to enroll.

quiz.q: In "The Case That Opened the Schoolhouse Doors," what reason did officials give for separating students, and why was it questionable?
ch: They claimed it helped students learn English, but children were placed by last name or appearance, not by testing.
They said it saved money, but it cost more.
They said parents asked for it, but parents refused.
They said the schools were identical, but they were in different towns.

quiz.q: According to "The Case That Opened the Schoolhouse Doors," how did the Mendez family's actions influence later events?
ch: Their lawsuit led to rulings against segregation and helped prompt California to end its school segregation laws.

quiz.q: According to "The Case That Opened the Schoolhouse Doors," which people connect the Mendez case to Brown v. Board of Education?
ch: Thurgood Marshall supported the Mendez families and later argued Brown, and Earl Warren signed California's law and later wrote the Brown decision.
Sylvia Mendez served as a judge in Brown.
David Marcus argued both cases before the Supreme Court.
Judge McCormick wrote the Brown decision.

quiz.q: What does "upheld" mean in "in 1947 a federal appeals court upheld the decision"?
Which statement best describes how "The Case That Opened the Schoolhouse Doors" is structured?
ch: It follows the case in time order from 1944 to its later effects, showing how each event led to the next.
It lists arguments for and against segregation.
It begins with the ending and never returns to the beginning.

quiz.q: Using "The Case That Opened the Schoolhouse Doors," explain how one individual influenced an event and how that event influenced later events.
quiz.ans: Gonzalo and Felicitas Mendez refused to accept their children's rejection and filed a lawsuit. The court rulings against segregation were followed by Governor Earl Warren signing a law ending school segregation in California, and the case helped lay groundwork for Brown v. Board of Education.

The governor in 1947 signed in that year a law.

practice.q: The Latin root "cred" means "believe." Explain the meanings of "credible" and "incredible," and name one more word with this root.

quiz.q: The Latin root "civ" means
The root "aqu" means "water." What is an aqueduct?

ch: to carry from one place to another

quiz.q: Which reference source would best show the origin of the word "democracy"?

quiz.q: Which sentence is the most concise?
ch: The railroad workers blasted tunnels through granite.
The railroad workers who worked on the railroad blasted tunnels through hard granite rock.
The workers, who were railroad workers, blasted and made tunnels through granite.
The railroad workers blasted tunnels through granite, which is a rock that is granite.

quiz.q: The Greek root "chron" means "time." What is a chronicle?
ch: a record of events in time order

quiz.q: "Bene" means "good" and "fact" means "make or do." Who is a benefactor?
ch: someone who does good by giving help or money

quiz.q: Explain how knowing the root "migr" (to move) helps you understand "immigrant," "emigrate" and "migration."
quiz.ans: All three involve moving: an immigrant moves into a new country, to emigrate is to move out of one's country, and migration is movement from one place to another.

lessons.name: Writing a literary analysis that compares fiction and history

practice.q: When comparing historical fiction with a historical account, a writer should examine
ch: how the author of the fiction uses or changes historical facts
practice.h: Ask how the story uses history.

practice.q: Which thesis best compares a historical novel with a historical account?
ch: While the history article reports the facts of the 1906 earthquake, the novel uses one family's escape to show the fear and courage people felt.
Both texts are about an earthquake.
practice.h: A strong comparison thesis explains how each text presents the topic.

practice.q: Which transition best introduces a contrast between two texts?
practice.h: Contrast shows difference.

practice.q: Which evidence would best show that an author changed history?
ch: The novel says World War II ended in 1950, but historical records show it ended in 1945.
The novel has a sad ending.
The novel's main character is a girl.
practice.h: Look for a factual difference.

practice.q: Explain why an author of historical fiction might invent a character rather than write about a real person.
practice.ans: An invented character gives the author freedom to create thoughts, dialogue and events while still showing what life was like, without misrepresenting a real person.
practice.h: What freedom does an invented character allow?

quiz.q: Historical accuracy means that
ch: details match what reliable sources say happened

quiz.q: Which sentence best uses evidence from both a historical account and a story about the 1850 Foreign Miners' Tax?
ch: The account states that the tax was twenty dollars a month, and the story shows its effect when a father comes home angry after the tax collector arrives.

quiz.q: Which detail would most likely appear in a historical account but not in historical fiction?
ch: a citation of official tax records

quiz.q: Which sentence is the best commentary when comparing a novel and an article?
ch: By adding one family's fears, the novel makes the article's statistics feel personal and urgent.

quiz.q: Which organization works best for a compare-and-contrast essay?
ch: discussing one point at a time for both texts

quiz.q: What should the conclusion of a comparison essay do?
ch: explain what the comparison reveals about how fiction and history work together

quiz.q: Write a thesis statement that compares how a historical account and a historical fiction story present the same event.
quiz.ans: Example: Although the historical account presents the Gold Rush through facts and dates, the story brings those facts to life by showing how one family experienced high prices and unfair taxes.

test.q: The Latin root "labor" in "laborer" means
The Greek root "tele" means "far" and "graph" means "write." What is a telegraph?
ch: a device for sending written messages over long distances

test.q: What does "transcontinental" mean?
Which sentence expresses the idea with no extra words?
ch: Workers blasted the tunnel through granite.
Workers who were working blasted the tunnel through hard granite stone.
The tunnel was blasted by workers through the granite that was granite.
Workers blasted and blasted through the tunnel of granite rock.

test.q: Which reference would best help you find how to pronounce "Promontory"?
Which word comes from the Latin root "memor," meaning "mindful"?
Which sentence best compares a historical account of the 1867 railroad strike with a story about it?
ch: The account reports that the strike ended after a week, while the story shows how it made one young worker feel "not small."
The account and the story are both interesting.
The story has a boy in it.

test.q: According to "Building Across the Sierra," where did the Central Pacific begin building?
According to "Building Across the Sierra," why did the Central Pacific have a harder start than the Union Pacific?
ch: Its route led straight into granite mountains with heavy snow, and it struggled to find workers.
It had more money than it needed.
It started building later in the year.

test.q: In "Building Across the Sierra," which detail shows how difficult the tunnel work was?
ch: In some places, progress was measured in inches per day.
Officials drove a ceremonial golden spike.

test.q: According to "Building Across the Sierra," what happened during the strike of June 1867?
ch: Thousands of Chinese workers demanded equal pay and shorter hours, but the strike ended after about a week without their demands being met.
The workers won higher pay immediately.
The company hired more Chinese workers.
The railroad was completed during the strike.

test.q: In "Building Across the Sierra," what does "overlooked" mean in "their role was overlooked"?
What is the author's purpose in the final paragraph of "Building Across the Sierra"?
ch: to point out that Chinese workers' contributions were long ignored and are now being recognized
to describe the golden spike ceremony in detail
to argue that the railroad should not have been built
to compare the two railroad companies

test.q: Using "Building Across the Sierra," explain how the Central Pacific's need for workers and the Chinese workers themselves influenced each other.
test.ans: The company could not find enough workers, so in 1865 it began hiring Chinese workers. They proved managers wrong and soon made up most of the workforce, making the Sierra route possible. Facing unequal pay and dangerous work, they in turn organized the 1867 strike.

test.q: In "The Mountain Answers," how does the setting of the tunnel in winter affect Jin-li?
ch: The cold, darkness and endless labor make his life harsh and exhausting.
It allows him to go home.

test.q: In "The Mountain Answers," what does Uncle Bao's saying "The mountain is slow to answer, but it answers" mean when it first appears?
ch: Hard work makes slow progress but eventually succeeds.
The mountain talks to the workers.
The tunnel will never be finished.

test.q: In "The Mountain Answers," why does Jin-li hide the truth in his early letters to his mother?
ch: He does not want his mother to worry.
He is not allowed to write letters.
He wants her to come to California.

test.q: In "The Mountain Answers," what does Uncle Bao's comparison of fear to snow suggest?
ch: Fear builds up until someone has the courage to push through it.
Workers should stay inside in winter.

test.q: In "The Mountain Answers," how does Jin-li feel during the strike?
ch: He feels, for the first time since leaving China, that he is not small.
He decides to return to China at once.
He wants to become a foreman.
He stops speaking to his uncle.

test.q: What new meaning does the saying "The mountain is slow to answer" take on in Jin-li's final letter in "The Mountain Answers"?
ch: It now suggests that the workers' protest was heard, even if change will come slowly.
It means the mountain spoke aloud.
It means Jin-li will stop working.

test.q: In "The Mountain Answers," explain how Jin-li's letters to his mother change from the beginning of the story to the end, and what the change shows.
test.ans: At first he tells her he is eating well and the work is steady, hiding the avalanche and the dangers. After the strike he tells her "the truth, all of it," showing he has gained courage and no longer feels he must hide his reality.

test.q: Write a literary analysis essay that compares how "The Mountain Answers" (historical fiction) and "Building Across the Sierra" (a historical account) portray the experiences of Chinese railroad workers. Explain which historical facts the story uses, what it adds or imagines, and why an author might combine fact and fiction. Support your points with evidence from both texts.
test.ans: Key points: a thesis comparing the two portrayals; facts the story shares with the account (granite drilled by hand, progress of inches, heavy snow and avalanches, unequal pay and buying their own food, the 1867 strike that ended after about a week without its demands met); what the story adds (invented characters Jin-li and Uncle Bao, their thoughts, letters home, emotions, the symbolic saying about the mountain); why authors blend fact and fiction (to make history personal and memorable and to give voice to people the record overlooked); quotations from both texts; comparison transitions; formal style and a conclusion.
rub: Clear focus and strong organization; ideas fully developed with relevant details or text evidence; precise language; few errors in conventions.
Clear focus and organization; ideas adequately developed with some details or evidence; some errors that do not affect meaning.
Focus or organization is inconsistent; limited development or evidence; errors sometimes interfere with meaning.
Little focus or organization; minimal development; frequent errors.

ela|8.about: Eighth graders read literature and informational texts side by side in six themed collections. They cite the strongest evidence, analyze how dialogue and incidents propel action and reveal character, explain how differences in point of view create suspense or humor, analyze how modern works draw on myths and traditional stories, delineate and evaluate arguments, analyze texts that present conflicting information, use verbals, active and passive voice and verb moods for effect, and write arguments, informative essays, narratives, literary analyses and research reports.
std: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
Analyze how particular lines of dialogue or incidents in a story or drama propel the action, reveal aspects of a character or provoke a decision.
Analyze how differences in the points of view of the characters and the audience or reader (e.g., created through the use of dramatic irony) create such effects as suspense or humor.
Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to supporting ideas; provide an objective summary of the text.

Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; recognize when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
Demonstrate command of standard English grammar and usage, including verbals, active and passive voice, and verb moods.
Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas, concepts and information through the selection, organization and analysis of relevant content.

passages.x: The photo appeared in the group chat at 9:47 p.m., the night before the algebra final. // At first Rafi did not understand what he was looking at: a blurry page of numbers, slightly crooked, with a coffee ring in one corner. Then he saw the heading. MR. DIAZ, FINAL EXAM, ANSWER KEY. // His phone buzzed again and again. // "WHERE did you get this," someone typed. // "Doesn't matter," wrote Tyler, who had posted it. "Desk was open after school. You're welcome." // "Bro you're a legend." // "Is this real??" // Rafi set the phone face down on his desk. Beside it lay his study guide, half finished, covered in his own messy handwriting. He had been working on the same problem about slope for twenty minutes. He needed a B on this final to keep his grade up, and his parents had made it clear what would happen to his soccer season if he didn't. // The phone buzzed again. This time it was a private message from Tyler. // "You're not going to say anything, right? We're boys." // Rafi typed, deleted, typed again. Finally he wrote, "Just don't use it." // "Lol. Everybody's using it." // Rafi lay on his bed and stared at the ceiling. He thought about Mr. Diaz, who stayed after school every Tuesday to help anyone who asked, who had once spent forty minutes explaining slope to Rafi with a drawing of a skateboard ramp. He thought about the other half of the class, the kids who weren't in the chat, studying right now with no idea that their grades would be measured against a stolen key. // Then he thought about soccer. // At 11:30, he picked up the phone, opened the photo and looked at it for a long moment. His thumb hovered over the screen. // He deleted it. // The next morning, he got to school early and knocked on Mr. Diaz's open door. His heart was pounding so hard he could hear it. // "Rafi," Mr. Diaz said, looking up. "Ready for today?" // "I don't know," Rafi said. "But there's something you should know first." // He did not say Tyler's name. He did not have to. Mr. Diaz listened, nodded slowly and thanked him. That afternoon, the class took a different version of the final, one Mr. Diaz had written as a backup months before. // Rafi got a C-plus. It was the hardest C-plus he had ever earned, and he was surprised to find that he was proud of it. // Tyler didn't speak to him for a week. Then, one day at practice, he passed Rafi the ball without a word. It was not an apology. But it was something.

In the late 1960s, psychologist Walter Mischel and his colleagues at Stanford University began a simple experiment. A young child sat at a table with a treat, often a marshmallow. The researcher made an offer: the child could eat the treat right away, or wait alone for about fifteen minutes and receive two treats instead. Then the researcher left the room. // Some children ate the marshmallow almost immediately. Others covered their eyes, sang to themselves or turned their chairs around so they could not see it. Some managed to wait the whole time. // Years later, Mischel's team followed up with some of the children. They reported that the children who had waited longer tended, as teenagers, to have higher scores on college entrance exams and to be described by their parents as better at handling stress. The "marshmallow test" became famous. Books and articles suggested that the ability to delay gratification, to give up a reward now for a larger one later, might be a key to success in life. // But science keeps asking questions. In 2012, researchers at the University of Rochester added a twist. Before the marshmallow test, children worked on an art project with an adult. For some children, the adult kept promises, bringing better art supplies as promised. For others, the adult broke the promises. Children who had experienced a reliable adult waited far longer for the second marshmallow than those who had experienced an unreliable one. Waiting, it seemed, depended partly on whether a child believed the reward would really come. // In 2018, another team repeated the original study with a much larger and more diverse group of children. They found a link between waiting and later achievement, but it was much smaller than earlier reports suggested. Once the researchers accounted for factors such as family income and home environment, the link shrank further. // Together, these studies paint a more complicated picture than the original headlines. Self-control matters, but it does not exist in a vacuum. A child who grows up where promises are often broken may reasonably decide that one marshmallow in hand is worth more than two in the future. Rather than simply telling children to "try harder," the newer research suggests that adults can help by creating environments where waiting actually pays off. // The marshmallow test is still a valuable tool. Its biggest lesson, though, may be about how science works: an exciting finding is the beginning of the conversation, not the end.

Every day you make hundreds of choices: what to eat, what to wear, which button to click. You probably think you make most of those choices on your own. But researchers who study decision-making have found that the way a choice is presented can have a surprisingly powerful effect on what people choose. // Consider the "default," the option that takes effect if a person does nothing. In 2003, researchers Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein compared organ donation rates in European countries. In some countries, people were organ donors only if they signed up, or "opted in." In others, everyone was considered a donor unless they "opted out." The difference was dramatic. In Germany, an opt-in country, only about 12 percent of people had agreed to be donors. In neighboring Austria, an opt-out country, the figure was over 99 percent. The two countries have much in common, yet a simple difference in the default produced enormously different results. // Defaults affect money decisions too. When some U.S. companies began automatically enrolling new employees in retirement savings plans, while allowing them to leave the plan if they chose, participation rose sharply compared with plans that required workers to sign up. // Why do defaults matter so much? Researchers suggest several reasons. Making a choice takes effort, and people often put off decisions. People may also see the default as a recommendation, assuming it was chosen for a good reason. And switching away from the default can feel like a risk. // In 2008, economist Richard Thaler and legal scholar Cass Sunstein published a book called Nudge, which described how small changes in the way choices are presented can steer people toward better decisions without taking away their freedom to choose. Thaler later won the Nobel Prize in economics in 2017, partly for this work. // Not everyone is comfortable with nudges. Critics point out that whoever designs a choice decides which way people are nudged, and that power can be misused, for example by companies that make it easy to sign up for a subscription but hard to cancel. Supporters respond that every choice must be presented in some way, so designers might as well choose defaults that help people. // Understanding defaults can make you a sharper decision-maker. The next time you face a pre-checked box or an automatic setting, ask yourself: is this what I would choose if I had to decide on my own?

"Don't," said Andre. // Malik already had one foot through the gap in the chain-link fence. On the other side, the construction site stretched toward Wilson Avenue: piles of gravel, a yellow excavator asleep for the weekend, a half-poured foundation with steel bars sticking up like the ribs of some enormous animal. Through the site, the bus stop was three minutes away. Around it, the walk took twelve. // "The bus comes at 3:40," Malik said. "It's 3:36. Do the math." // "The sign says no trespassing," said Andre, who was ten and believed in signs. // "The sign says a lot of things." Malik squeezed through. "Stay there if you want. Walk around. I'll tell Mom you're slow." // He jogged across the gravel without looking back. He heard the fence rattle behind him and assumed Andre had given up. // He was halfway across, already imagining the cool air of the bus, when he heard the sound: a sharp clatter, then a cry he had known his whole life. // Malik spun around. Andre was on the ground beside a stack of metal pipes that had rolled loose. He was holding his ankle, his face twisted, trying very hard not to cry. // "I told you to walk around," Malik said, running back. The words came out angrier than he meant. // "You said I was slow," Andre whispered. // Malik knelt. The ankle was already swelling. Behind them, the 3:40 bus hissed to a stop at Wilson Avenue, waited and pulled away. // For a moment Malik thought about how to tell the story at home. Andre followed me. Andre didn't listen. Andre tripped. Each version made him a little less responsible. Each one was a little bit true. // He looked at his brother, who was trying so hard to be brave. // "Okay," Malik said. "Put your arms around my neck." // He carried Andre piggyback all the way around the fence, the long way, twelve minutes that felt like an hour. Andre's tears soaked through the back of his shirt. // At the urgent care clinic that evening, the doctor said it was a sprain, not a break. Their mother sat between them in the waiting room, her face tight. // "What happened?" she asked. // Andre glanced at Malik and opened his mouth, ready, Malik realized, to cover for him. // "I took a shortcut through the construction site," Malik said before Andre could speak. "I told him he was slow, so he followed me. It's my fault." // His mother was quiet for a long time. Then she put her hand on the back of his neck, the way she had when he was small. // "Thank you for telling me," she said. "We'll talk about the rest at home." // Malik nodded. He knew the rest would not be fun. But for the first time all afternoon, the knot in his stomach began to loosen.

lessons.name: How dialogue and incidents propel action and reveal character

practice.q: Read: "'If you tell Coach, I'm off the team,' Marcus whispered. Jaylen looked at the broken window, then at his best friend." How does this dialogue propel the action?

the time and place of the story

Mr. Diaz writes a backup test.

quiz.q: In "The Screenshot," how does Tyler's private message, "You're not going to say anything, right? We're boys," propel the action?
ch: It pressures Rafi to choose between loyalty to a friend and honesty.
It convinces Rafi to use the key.
It reveals that Mr. Diaz already knows.

He plans to use the key himself.
He does not care about the test.
