ch: Being heard on equal terms matters more than winning.

test.q: In "Equal Time," explain how Elena's brother changes during the story. Use two details.
test.ans: At first he says, "Maybe it's not that bad... People can read," not understanding the unfairness. After her question he admits "she was right," goes with her to the office and watches her speech, showing that he has come to understand her right to be heard equally.

test.q: In "Two Views: Excused Absences for Civic Action," what does View 1 propose?
ch: allowing students one excused absence each year for civic engagement
requiring all students to attend city council meetings

test.q: In "Two Views: Excused Absences for Civic Action," which evidence does View 1 use to show that the policy is workable?
ch: Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia began such a policy in 2020.

test.q: In "Two Views: Excused Absences for Civic Action," how do the two views interpret the effect of missing one school day?
ch: View 1 sees it as a small price for a lasting lesson, while View 2 warns that lost instruction adds up and can harm learning.
Both say missing school is harmless.
Both say students should never miss school for any reason.
View 2 says one day is not enough.

test.q: In "Two Views: Excused Absences for Civic Action," which concern does View 2 raise that View 1 does not address?
ch: how schools would decide which activities count and handle political disputes
whether students need a parent's permission
whether civics is taught in history class

test.q: In "Two Views: Excused Absences for Civic Action," on which point do both views agree?
ch: Civic engagement is important for students.
Students should miss many days of school.
Schools should choose students' political causes.

test.q: Which statement best describes how the texts in "Two Views: Excused Absences for Civic Action" present conflicting ideas?
ch: They agree on the goal but disagree about whether excused absences or in-school activities are the better way to reach it.
They disagree about whether democracy matters.

test.q: Using "Two Views: Excused Absences for Civic Action," evaluate which view better addresses fairness to all students. Cite evidence from both views.
test.ans: Answers vary but must weigh both. Example: View 2 better addresses fairness because its in-school activities are "open to every student," while View 1's fairness argument focuses on protecting students from unexcused absences; View 1 is stronger on real-world experience but does not explain how schools would treat all causes equally.

test.q: Write an argument essay responding to this question: Should your school district give students one excused absence each year for civic engagement? State a precise claim, support it with reasons and evidence from "Two Views: Excused Absences for Civic Action," acknowledge and rebut the opposing view, and use at least one sentence in the conditional or subjunctive mood for effect.
test.ans: Key points: a precise claim; reasons supported by relevant evidence from the passage (the Fairfax County policy, fairness, learning through participation; or lost instruction, research on chronic absence, deciding which activities count, in-school alternatives); a clear distinction between the claim and the opposing claim, with a rebuttal; no irrelevant evidence; purposeful use of mood (for example, "If students were allowed to attend..."); formal style, cohesive transitions and a conclusion that follows from the argument.
rub: Clear focus and strong organization; ideas fully developed with relevant details or text evidence; precise language; few errors in conventions.
Clear focus and organization; ideas adequately developed with some details or evidence; some errors that do not affect meaning.
Focus or organization is inconsistent; limited development or evidence; errors sometimes interfere with meaning.
Little focus or organization; minimal development; frequent errors.

units.name: Collection 4: Into the Unknown (narrative)
units.el: Show dramatic irony with a quick role-play in which the class knows a secret the "character" does not. Note that in these items a dash is typed as two hyphens (--); have students practice reading ellipses and dashes aloud as pauses.

passages.x: At 8:15 p.m., while Priyanka was reading the twins a bedtime story in the living room, the Okonkwos' enormous, nervous dog, Biscuit, nosed open the back door that hadn't quite latched and slipped up the stairs to hide under the guest bed, his favorite place during thunderstorms. Nobody saw him go. Nobody, that is, except the twins, who looked at each other and said nothing. // At 8:30, the thunder started. // Priyanka was fourteen and had babysat the Okonkwo twins, Chidi and Ada, five times. She was good at it. She knew which bedtime stories they liked and how to make grilled cheese without burning it. What she did not know was that the family dog was no longer in the backyard. // At 8:41, something thumped upstairs. // Priyanka looked up from the book. "Did you hear that?" // "Hear what?" said Chidi, with perfect innocence. Ada put her hand over her mouth. // "Probably just the house settling," Priyanka said, mostly to herself. // At 8:47, the lights flickered. Upstairs, something sighed, a long, heavy sound, like a person who was very tired of waiting. // Priyanka stood up. Her heart was going faster than she wanted it to. She picked up the nearest heavy object, which turned out to be a hardcover copy of a picture book about saying goodnight to the moon. // "Stay here," she told the twins. // "Okay," said Ada, in a strangled voice. Chidi had buried his face in a couch cushion, and his shoulders were shaking. Priyanka assumed he was scared. // She climbed the stairs one at a time. The hall was dark. The guest room door was half open. From under the bed came a slow scraping sound, like claws on a wooden floor. // Priyanka raised the picture book over her head. // "Whoever you are," she said in her bravest voice, "the police are on their way." // From under the bed, two large brown eyes blinked at her. Then a long, damp nose appeared, followed by a tail that thumped hopefully against the bed frame. // "Biscuit?" // Behind her, from the bottom of the stairs, came a sound she had not heard all night: both twins laughing so hard they could barely breathe. // Priyanka lowered the book. She thought about being angry. Then she thought about how she must have looked, standing in a dark doorway, threatening a dog with a bedtime story. // She started laughing too. // Later, when Mr. and Mrs. Okonkwo came home, they found all three children and one very large dog asleep in a pile on the living room couch. Next to them, open to the last page, lay the picture book.

On December 4, 1872, the crew of the British ship Dei Gratia spotted another ship in the Atlantic Ocean, between the Azores islands and the coast of Portugal. Its sails were partly set, and it was moving strangely, as if no one were steering. When sailors from the Dei Gratia rowed over and climbed aboard, they found the ship, the Mary Celeste, completely empty. // The Mary Celeste had left New York about a month earlier, bound for Genoa, Italy. On board were Captain Benjamin Briggs, his wife, Sarah, their two-year-old daughter, Sophia, and seven crew members. The ship carried a cargo of about 1,700 barrels of industrial alcohol. // What the boarding party found, and did not find, has puzzled people ever since. The ship's lifeboat was gone. There was some water in the hold, but the ship was still seaworthy. There was enough food and fresh water on board to last for months. The crew's personal belongings, including clothing and pipes, were still there. The last entry in the log had been written about nine days earlier. The cargo was almost entirely intact, though nine of the barrels were later found to be empty. // Over the years, people have proposed many explanations. Some suggested that pirates had attacked the ship. But nothing valuable appeared to have been taken, and there were no signs of a struggle. Others suggested a mutiny, but the crew had good reputations, and there was no evidence of violence. // One of the most widely discussed theories involves the cargo. Alcohol can give off fumes. If Captain Briggs noticed a strong smell or believed the leaking barrels might explode, he may have ordered everyone into the lifeboat as a precaution, planning to follow behind the ship on a line. If the line broke or the lifeboat drifted away, the people in it would have been lost at sea. Other researchers have suggested a faulty pump or a navigation error that made the captain believe the ship was in danger. // The mystery grew even larger in 1884, when a young writer named Arthur Conan Doyle, who would later create Sherlock Holmes, published a story loosely based on the case. His fictional version added details that were never true, and many readers came to believe them. // More than 150 years later, no one knows for certain what happened. The Mary Celeste remains a reminder that some questions may never be fully answered, and that we should be careful to separate evidence from legend.

In the summer of 1587, about 115 English men, women and children arrived on Roanoke Island, off the coast of what is now North Carolina. Led by John White, they hoped to build a permanent settlement. That August, White's daughter gave birth to a girl named Virginia Dare, the first English child known to be born in the Americas. // The colonists soon realized they needed more supplies. White agreed to sail back to England to get them, promising to return quickly. He would not see the colony again for three years. // In England, White's plans fell apart. England was at war with Spain, and in 1588 the Spanish Armada, a huge fleet of warships, threatened England. Ships were needed for defense, and White's relief voyage was delayed again and again. // When White finally returned to Roanoke in August 1590, he found the settlement deserted. The houses had been taken down, and the area was surrounded by a wooden fence. There were no bodies and no signs of a battle. Carved into a post were the letters CROATOAN. On a tree, someone had carved the letters CRO. // Before he left, White had told the colonists that if they moved, they should carve the name of their destination, and add a cross if they were in danger. There was no cross. Croatoan was the name of an island to the south, now part of Hatteras Island, and of the Native people who lived there and had been friendly with the English. White believed the colonists had gone to Croatoan. But a storm was approaching, his ship had lost anchors, and the crew refused to sail there. White returned to England and never saw the colonists again. // For more than four centuries, people have debated what happened. Some historians think the colonists joined the Croatoan people and lived among them. Others suggest that some moved inland, toward the Chesapeake Bay region, as had once been planned. Still others believe disease, hunger or conflict may have killed many of them. Archaeologists have searched sites on Hatteras Island and on the mainland, finding objects that might be connected to the colonists, but no discovery has yet settled the question. // The story of Roanoke endures partly because its clues are so tantalizing. A single word carved into wood seems to promise an answer. Yet without more evidence, the "Lost Colony" remains one of America's oldest unsolved mysteries.

My mom has worked the night shift as a security guard at the natural history museum for six years, but this was the first time she had to bring me along. Our babysitter had the flu, and Mom couldn't miss work. // "You stay in the break room," she said, setting me up with a sandwich and my homework. "Don't wander. I mean it, Tomas." // For two hours, I didn't wander. Then I finished my homework, ate my sandwich and started reading the museum map pinned to the wall. Hall of Dinosaurs. Hall of Gems. The Arctic Gallery. The break room was boring. The dinosaur hall was right down the corridor. // I told myself I would just look through the doorway. // At night, with only the dim emergency lights on, the museum felt like a different place. My sneakers squeaked on the polished floor, and every squeak echoed. When I reached the Hall of Dinosaurs, I stopped. The Tyrannosaurus skeleton towered over the entrance, its jaws open, its empty eye sockets looking straight down at me. During the day it was cool. At night it was... something else. // Then I heard it. // A soft scraping sound, somewhere deep in the hall, like something heavy being dragged across stone. // I froze. The scraping stopped. Then it started again -- closer. // I told myself it was nothing. A janitor. The air conditioning. My brain had other ideas. My brain reminded me of every movie I had ever seen where the skeletons came to life. // I backed up one step, then another. My hand found the radio clipped to my belt, the one Mom had given me "for emergencies only." I pressed the button. // "Mom," I whispered. "There's something in the dinosaur hall." // The radio crackled. "Tomas? Where are you?" Her voice had the tone that meant I was in trouble. "You're supposed to be in the..." // The scraping came again, loud now, right around the corner of the Stegosaurus display. A shadow stretched across the floor -- long, strange, with something sticking up from it like a spike. // I stopped breathing. // Then a small, gray-haired man stepped into the light, pushing a wide floor polisher. A feather duster stuck out of his back pocket. He saw me and jumped so high that his glasses slid down his nose. // "Good grief, kid!" he gasped. "You nearly gave me a heart attack!" // Behind me, I heard Mom's footsteps running down the corridor. I turned around slowly. I knew I was in more trouble than I had ever been in my life. // But when Mom rounded the corner and saw the janitor, the polisher and my face, she stopped, put her hand over her mouth and -- to my enormous relief -- started to laugh.

lessons.name: Dramatic irony, suspense and humor

practice.q: Dramatic irony occurs when
ch: the audience knows something a character does not
a character says the opposite of what he or she means
an event turns out the opposite of what was expected
practice.h: Think about who knows more.

practice.q: In a play, the audience sees a villain pour poison into a cup, but the hero cheerfully reaches for it. What effect does this create?
practice.h: How do you feel when you know danger is coming but a character does not?

practice.q: In a comedy, a boy practices a romantic speech to the wrong person in the dark, while the audience knows who is really there. What effect is created?
practice.h: Is the situation more scary or more funny?

practice.q: Which kind of narrator makes dramatic irony easiest to create?
ch: a third-person omniscient narrator who shares information some characters lack
a first-person narrator who knows nothing
a narrator who never describes events
practice.h: Who can reveal secrets to the reader?

practice.q: Describe a moment from a movie, book or show in which you knew more than a character. Explain the effect it had on you.
practice.ans: Example: In a mystery, viewers see the thief hide in a closet while the detective walks right past; this creates suspense because we want to warn the detective.
practice.h: Did it make you nervous, or did it make you laugh?

quiz.q: In "Noises Upstairs," what does the reader know from the beginning that Priyanka does not?
ch: that Biscuit the dog is hiding upstairs
that the power will go out for hours
that the parents are already home

quiz.q: In "Noises Upstairs," what effect does this difference in knowledge create?
ch: It makes Priyanka's fear both suspenseful and funny for the reader.
It makes the twins seem frightened.

quiz.q: In "Noises Upstairs," why does Ada put her hand over her mouth when Priyanka asks about the noise?
ch: She is trying not to laugh because she knows it is the dog.

quiz.q: In "Noises Upstairs," Priyanka "assumed he was scared" when Chidi's shoulders shake. What is ironic about this?
ch: Chidi is actually laughing, not scared.

quiz.q: In "Noises Upstairs," why does the author have Priyanka pick up a children's picture book as her weapon?
ch: to add humor by contrasting her serious fear with a gentle bedtime book
to show that she loves reading
to prove the book is heavy

quiz.q: How would "Noises Upstairs" be different if readers did not learn about Biscuit until the end?
ch: It would feel more like a mystery or horror story, with surprise instead of humor during the buildup.
It would be exactly the same.
It would be told by Biscuit.

quiz.q: Explain how the author of "Noises Upstairs" uses dramatic irony to create both suspense and humor. Cite two details.
quiz.ans: Because readers know from the first paragraph that the noises come from Biscuit, Priyanka's racing heart and her threat that "the police are on their way" become funny, while her slow climb up the dark stairs still builds suspense about the moment she discovers the truth. The twins' hidden laughter adds another layer of irony.

lessons.name: Analyzing evidence and structure in texts about real mysteries

practice.q: The strongest textual evidence is the evidence that
ch: most directly supports the analysis or inference
comes from any sentence in the text
practice.h: Choose the quotation that proves your point best.

practice.q: An article about a lost settlement presents three theories, each in its own paragraph, followed by an evaluation. What structure is used?
ch: a series of explanations followed by analysis
practice.h: Look at how the paragraphs are arranged.

practice.q: Which inference is best supported by the detail "The dinner plates were still on the table, half full"?
ch: The people had finished eating long before.
The house had been empty for years.
practice.h: What would cause someone to leave food unfinished?

practice.q: What is the role of a sentence such as "But the evidence does not support this theory"?
ch: It signals a shift from presenting an idea to challenging it.
practice.h: Notice the word "But."

practice.q: Explain why an author writing about an unsolved mystery might present several theories instead of only one.
practice.ans: Presenting several theories gives readers a balanced view of the evidence, shows which explanations are stronger or weaker and lets readers draw their own conclusions.
practice.h: Think about fairness and evidence.

quiz.q: According to "The Ship That Sailed Itself," what did the sailors from the Dei Gratia find on the Mary Celeste?
ch: The ship was empty, and its lifeboat was missing.
The crew was asleep below deck.

quiz.q: How is the third paragraph of "The Ship That Sailed Itself" mainly organized?
ch: as a list of clues found aboard the ship
as a comparison of two ships
in the time order of the voyage
as an argument for one theory

quiz.q: In "The Ship That Sailed Itself," why does the author mention that "nothing valuable appeared to have been taken"?
ch: to weaken the theory that pirates attacked the ship
to show the crew was wealthy
to prove that a mutiny happened

quiz.q: According to the cargo theory in "The Ship That Sailed Itself," why might the people aboard have left the ship?
ch: The captain may have feared an explosion and ordered everyone into the lifeboat as a precaution.
The crew wanted to steal the alcohol.

quiz.q: Why does the author of "The Ship That Sailed Itself" mention Arthur Conan Doyle's story?
ch: to show how fiction added false details that many people believed
to prove that Conan Doyle solved the mystery
to explain that Sherlock Holmes was a real detective

quiz.q: What central idea does the conclusion of "The Ship That Sailed Itself" emphasize?
ch: When facing an unsolved mystery, it is important to separate evidence from legend.
The mystery has finally been solved.

quiz.q: Choose one theory from "The Ship That Sailed Itself" and evaluate how well the evidence supports it.
quiz.ans: Example: The cargo theory fits several clues: nine barrels were empty, the lifeboat was gone and the ship was still seaworthy, suggesting a hurried exit as a precaution. However, there is no direct proof, such as a log entry, so it remains a possibility rather than a certainty.

lessons.name: Punctuation for pauses, breaks and omissions

practice.q: An ellipsis (...) can show
ch: that words were left out of a quotation or that a speaker pauses
practice.h: Think about missing words or trailing off.

practice.q: Which sentence uses an ellipsis to show a pause or hesitation?
ch: "I thought I heard... no, it's nothing."
practice.h: Where does the speaker trail off?

practice.q: A dash, typed here as two hyphens, is used in "The noise came from upstairs -- from the guest room." What does the dash do?
ch: It creates a break that emphasizes the added information.
It joins two words into one.
practice.h: Dashes create a sharp break.

practice.q: Which sentence uses a comma correctly before a contrasting phrase?
ch: The door was open, not closed.
The door was, open not closed.
The door, was open not closed.
The door was open not, closed.
practice.h: Pause before the contrasting idea.

practice.q: A quotation reads: "The captain wrote in the log that the weather was calm, the crew was healthy and the cargo was secure." Shorten it with an ellipsis so it keeps only the information about the cargo, without changing the meaning.
practice.ans: "The captain wrote in the log that... the cargo was secure."
practice.h: Remove the middle words and mark the omission.

quiz.q: Which punctuation mark shows that words have been left out of a quotation?
Which sentence uses dashes (typed as two hyphens) correctly to set off an interruption?
ch: The ship -- empty and silent -- drifted toward Portugal.
The ship empty -- and silent drifted -- toward Portugal.
The -- ship empty and silent drifted toward Portugal.
The ship empty and silent drifted toward -- Portugal --.

quiz.q: Which line of dialogue uses an ellipsis correctly?
ch: "Is someone... is someone there?" she whispered.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses a comma correctly to show a pause?
Which word is spelled correctly?
Which is the best way to shorten the quotation "Nothing valuable, as far as the boarding party could tell, appeared to have been taken" while keeping its meaning?
ch: "Nothing valuable... appeared to have been taken"

quiz.q: Why might the writer of a suspense story choose a dash instead of a comma in "She opened the door -- and froze"?
ch: A dash creates a sharper, more dramatic break that builds suspense.
A dash is required after every verb.
A comma would turn the sentence into a question.

quiz.q: Write two sentences for a suspense story: one that uses an ellipsis to show hesitation and one that uses a dash (typed as two hyphens) to show a sudden break.
quiz.ans: Ellipsis: "I think it came from... the basement." Dash: "I reached for the light switch -- and the power went out."

lessons.name: Writing a narrative that builds suspense

practice.q: Foreshadowing is
ch: a hint about what will happen later
practice.h: Think "a shadow of the future."

practice.q: Which sentence best builds suspense?
ch: The footsteps stopped right outside my door.
practice.h: Which sentence makes you want to know what happens next?

practice.q: Which technique slows the pacing to build suspense?
ch: describing small sensory details moment by moment
summarizing several days in one sentence
practice.h: Think slow motion.

practice.q: Which point of view would let a writer create dramatic irony by showing readers things the main character does not know?
ch: first person, told by the main character
a diary written by the main character
practice.h: The narrator must know more than the character.

practice.q: Rewrite this sentence to build suspense with sensory details: "I went into the dark basement."
practice.ans: Example: "I pressed my hand against the cold stair rail and eased down into the basement, where the air smelled of damp concrete and something shifted in the far corner."
practice.h: Add sights, sounds, smells or feelings.

quiz.q: In a narrative, the climax is
Which detail best foreshadows danger in a story about a hike?
ch: Dark clouds gathered over the ridge, though the forecast had promised sun.
The trail was three miles long.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses a short, punchy structure to increase tension?
ch: After a long and tiring day at school, we finally went home and relaxed.
We talked about many things for hours.
The house was large and had a big yard.

quiz.q: Which revision best uses dialogue to reveal a character's fear?
ch: "D-did you hear that?" Malia whispered, gripping my sleeve.

quiz.q: Which ending best resolves a suspense story while offering reflection?
ch: When we finally laughed about the "ghost," I realized that most of what had scared me was in my own head.

quiz.q: Which transition best signals a sudden shift in a suspense story?
Write the first two sentences of a suspense story that establish the setting and hint at a mystery.
quiz.ans: Example: "The lighthouse had been dark for thirty years, so when I saw its beam sweep across the bay at midnight, I dropped my flashlight into the sand. Someone, or something, was up there."

test.q: Which punctuation mark can show that a speaker trails off?
Which sentence uses dashes (typed as two hyphens) correctly?
ch: The skeleton -- forty feet long -- filled the hall.
The skeleton forty -- feet long filled -- the hall.
The -- skeleton forty feet long filled the hall.
The skeleton forty feet long filled the -- hall --.

test.q: Which sentence correctly uses an ellipsis to show words left out of a quotation?
ch: The guide said the fossil was "found in Montana... in 1902."
The guide said the fossil was found... in Montana in 1902...
The guide said, the fossil..."was found."

test.q: Which spelling of the word meaning "doubtful or distrustful" is correct?
What is dramatic irony?
ch: a situation in which the reader knows something a character does not
a story with a sad ending

test.q: Which passage best builds suspense through pacing?
ch: My hand touched the doorknob. Cold. Then I heard breathing on the other side.
I opened the door and went inside and it was fine.

test.q: A writer reveals in the first paragraph that a "ghost" is really the family cat. What effect does this have on later scenes in which the characters are terrified?
ch: It creates humor, because readers know the truth while the characters are scared.
It increases the mystery about the ghost.

test.q: According to "Lost at Roanoke," why did John White leave Roanoke in 1587?
ch: to sail to England for more supplies

test.q: According to "Lost at Roanoke," what delayed White's return for three years?
ch: England's war with Spain, including the threat of the Spanish Armada
a lack of interest in the colony

test.q: In "Lost at Roanoke," why is the absence of a carved cross important?
ch: White had told the colonists to add a cross if they were in danger, so its absence suggests they left without being in distress.
It shows they forgot the plan.

test.q: According to "Lost at Roanoke," why did White not sail to Croatoan to search for the colonists?
ch: A storm was approaching, his ship had lost anchors and the crew refused.
The Croatoan people attacked his ship.
He did not know where Croatoan was.
He had already found the colonists.

test.q: What does "tantalizing" mean in "its clues are so tantalizing"?
ch: arousing interest without fully satisfying it

test.q: How does the structure of "Lost at Roanoke," moving from the colony's founding to the discovery and then to competing theories, affect the reader?
ch: It builds suspense through a clear sequence of events and then invites readers to weigh possible explanations.
It reveals the answer at the beginning.
It argues for a single theory.
It compares Roanoke with another colony.

test.q: Which evidence in "Lost at Roanoke" most strongly supports the theory that the colonists went to Croatoan? Explain.
test.ans: The carved word CROATOAN, combined with White's instruction to carve their destination and the absence of a distress cross, strongly suggests a planned move to Croatoan, where friendly Native people lived.

test.q: In "After Hours," how does the nighttime setting help create suspense?
ch: Dim lights, echoing footsteps and a towering skeleton make ordinary things seem threatening.
The museum is brightly lit and crowded.
The story takes place on a sunny beach.

test.q: In "After Hours," why does Tomas leave the break room?
ch: He is bored and curious about the dinosaur hall.
His mom calls him on the radio.

test.q: In "After Hours," what is the effect of the ellipsis in "At night it was... something else"?
ch: It creates a pause that suggests Tomas is uneasy and searching for words.
It shows that words were left out of a quotation.
It turns the sentence into a question.

test.q: In "After Hours," what is the effect of the dash in "Then it started again -- closer"?
ch: It creates a sudden break that heightens tension.

test.q: In "After Hours," how does Tomas's imagination increase the suspense?
ch: It reminds him of movies in which skeletons come to life, so he expects something supernatural.
It tells him the noise is a janitor.

test.q: How does the author of "After Hours" resolve the suspense?
ch: by revealing an ordinary explanation, a janitor with a floor polisher, which turns fear into humor
by having a skeleton come to life

test.q: In "After Hours," identify what makes the "spike" in the shadow and explain how the author uses it to mislead the reader.
test.ans: The "spike" is the feather duster in the janitor's back pocket. Describing the shadow near the Stegosaurus display as "long, strange, with something sticking up from it like a spike" makes readers imagine a dinosaur, so the ordinary truth comes as a surprise.

test.q: Write a narrative that either retells the events of "After Hours" from the janitor's point of view or continues the story after Tomas's mom starts to laugh. Use dialogue, pacing and sensory details; include at least one ellipsis and one dash used correctly; and create suspense or humor through what the reader knows.
test.ans: Key points: a consistent point of view (the janitor's, or a continuation with Tomas); events consistent with the story; deliberate suspense or humor, possibly through dramatic irony (for example, the janitor not knowing a boy is in the hall); dialogue that reveals character; pacing that slows at key moments; sensory details of the museum at night; a correctly used ellipsis and dash; a resolution with reflection.
rub: Clear focus and strong organization; ideas fully developed with relevant details or text evidence; precise language; few errors in conventions.
Clear focus and organization; ideas adequately developed with some details or evidence; some errors that do not affect meaning.
Focus or organization is inconsistent; limited development or evidence; errors sometimes interfere with meaning.
Little focus or organization; minimal development; frequent errors.

units.name: Collection 5: Old Stories, New Forms (literary analysis)
units.el: Before reading, tell each myth (Icarus, Arachne, Pandora, Midas) aloud with a quick sketch so students know the source story. Use a three-column chart: "In the myth / In the modern story / Why the author changed it."

passages.x: Background: In an ancient Greek myth, the inventor Daedalus builds wings of feathers and wax so that he and his son, Icarus, can escape imprisonment on the island of Crete. Daedalus warns Icarus not to fly too low, where sea spray would soak the feathers, or too high, where the sun would melt the wax. Thrilled by flight, Icarus soars toward the sun. The wax melts, and he falls into the sea. // Isa's father had built the drone in their garage over six months of Saturdays: a carbon-fiber frame, four rotors and a camera that could swivel in any direction. He was an engineer who repaired machines at the airport, and he talked about the drone the way other dads talked about cars. // "Rule one," he said on the morning of its first flight, at the empty soccer field behind the middle school. "Under 400 feet. That's the law, and it's also common sense. Rule two: not too low, either. Trees, power lines, people's heads." He handed her the controller. "Middle path. Got it?" // "Got it," Isa said. She was already grinning. // The drone rose with a sound like a swarm of bees. On the controller's screen, the soccer field shrank to a green rectangle and the school to a gray block. Isa laughed out loud. She could see the whole neighborhood, the freeway and the hills where the fog was burning off. For the first time, she understood why her father had spent all those Saturdays in the garage. // "Nice and steady," her father said. "You're at two hundred." // Isa nudged the stick. Two-fifty. Three hundred. The numbers climbed, and so did the feeling in her chest, a wild lightness, as if she herself were rising. She wanted to see past the hills. She wanted to see the ocean. // "Isa," her father said. "Three-eighty. Bring it down." // "Just a little more," she said. "I can almost see the..." // A gust of wind hit the drone. On the screen, the horizon tilted violently. A warning flashed red: SIGNAL WEAK. Then the screen went black. // They found it twenty minutes later, nose down in a patch of ice plant beside the freeway on-ramp, one rotor snapped clean off. // Isa couldn't look at her father. Six months of Saturdays. // He turned the drone over in his hands for a long time. Then, to her surprise, he smiled a little. "You know the story about Icarus?" // She nodded miserably. // "Everybody remembers that he flew too high," her father said. "But the myth doesn't say he should never have flown. Daedalus made wings for both of them." He held out the broken drone. "We'll fix the rotor. Next Saturday you can try again." He paused. // "Middle path," Isa said, before he could. // "Middle path," he agreed.

passages.t: The Stories We Never Stop Telling
passages.x: A young person leaves home, faces terrible trials, receives help from an unexpected guide and returns changed. If that sounds familiar, it should. The same basic pattern appears in ancient epics, folktales from around the world and many of today's most popular movies. // In 1949, a scholar named Joseph Campbell published a book called The Hero with a Thousand Faces. After studying myths from many cultures, Campbell argued that countless hero stories share a common structure, which he called the monomyth. Today it is often called the hero's journey. The hero receives a call to adventure, often refuses it at first, meets a mentor, crosses into an unfamiliar world, faces a series of tests, survives a great ordeal and finally returns home with something valuable to share. // Campbell's ideas reached far beyond universities. Filmmaker George Lucas has said that Campbell's work influenced his writing of Star Wars. Screenwriters and novelists have used the hero's journey as a kind of map for building stories. // Other story patterns travel just as widely. Consider the tale of a mistreated young woman who, with magical help, attends a grand event and is later identified by a lost shoe. Most people know her as Cinderella. But versions of this story existed long before the familiar European fairy tales. An ancient Greek writer recorded a tale about a woman named Rhodopis whose sandal was carried off by an eagle and dropped near a king. In China, a story about a kind girl named Ye Xian, who loses a golden slipper, was written down more than a thousand years ago. // Why do these patterns endure? Scholars offer several explanations. Some suggest that such stories reflect experiences nearly everyone shares: leaving childhood, facing fear, being treated unfairly, hoping to be recognized. Others point out that stories spread along trade routes and with travelers, changing a little with each retelling. Still others argue that familiar patterns simply work. Audiences know how to follow them, which frees storytellers to surprise them with new details. // Critics caution against taking these theories too far. Not every story fits the hero's journey, and forcing every tale into one shape can hide what makes a particular culture's stories unique. // Still, the next time a movie hero hesitates before an adventure, or a lost shoe changes everything, you may be watching a very old story wearing new clothes.

You may never have read a Greek or Roman myth from beginning to end, but you probably use their characters every day. The gods, heroes and monsters of ancient Mediterranean stories are hidden all around us: in our calendar, our language, our science and even our shopping bags. // Start with the calendar. January takes its name from Janus, the Roman god of doorways and beginnings, who was often shown with two faces, one looking back at the past and one looking forward. It is a fitting name for the month that opens a new year. March is named for Mars, the Roman god of war. Some days of the week in English honor gods from another tradition, Norse mythology. Thursday is "Thor's day," named for the god of thunder. // Our language is full of myths, too. When people feel sudden fear, they experience panic, a word linked to Pan, a Greek god of the wild whose shout was said to terrify travelers. An echo is named for Echo, a nymph in Greek myth who could only repeat the last words spoken to her. Cereal comes from Ceres, the Roman goddess of grain and harvests. // Science and exploration borrow these names as well. A book of maps is called an atlas, after the Titan Atlas, who in myth holds up the sky. Most of the planets in our solar system carry the names of Roman gods. When NASA planned to send astronauts to the Moon in the 1960s, it named the program Apollo, after the Greek and Roman god associated with light and the sun. Its more recent lunar program is named Artemis, after Apollo's twin sister, a goddess linked to the Moon. // Companies have noticed the power of these names too. A famous athletic brand is named after Nike, the Greek goddess of victory. A name like that suggests speed, strength and winning before a customer reads a single word of an advertisement. // Why do these ancient names remain so useful? Part of the answer is history: for centuries, educated Europeans studied Greek and Latin, and they drew on classical myths when they needed new words. But the names also carry meaning. Calling a Moon program "Apollo" or "Artemis" connects modern science to stories people have told about the sky for thousands of years. // The gods of Olympus no longer have temples. But in a sense, they never left. They simply moved into our dictionaries, our calendars and our imaginations.

Background: In a Greek myth, a young weaver named Arachne boasts that her skill is greater than that of Athena, goddess of weaving and wisdom. Athena, disguised as an old woman, warns her to be humble, but Arachne refuses. In the contest that follows, Arachne weaves a brilliant tapestry that mocks the gods. Furious, Athena turns her into a spider, doomed to weave forever. // Mariana Torres had been designing clothes since she was nine, sketching dresses on the backs of her math worksheets. By fourteen, she had her own sewing machine, a following online and a habit of saying things like "Honestly, I'm better than most of the designers on TV." // Her grandmother, who had sewn wedding dresses in Oaxaca for forty years, would only raise one eyebrow. // That spring, the community college held a design competition for teenagers, judged by a well-known local designer, Ms. Adebayo. Mariana entered immediately. "I'm going to win," she told her best friend. "Ms. Adebayo's stuff is kind of boring anyway." // The day before the deadline, her grandmother appeared in the doorway of her room. "May I see?" she asked. // Mariana held up the dress: bold red fabric, sharp angles, a pattern she had printed herself. Across the skirt, in tiny stitched letters, she had embroidered the words BETTER THAN THE JUDGES. // Her grandmother studied it for a long time. "The sewing is beautiful," she said finally. "But mija, a gift is not a weapon. When you use it to make others small, you make yourself small too." // Mariana rolled her eyes. "It's a joke, Abuela." // "Is it?" // At the competition, Mariana's dress stopped people in the hallway. Ms. Adebayo examined it closely, running her fingers along the seams. Then she read the embroidered words, and her expression changed. // Mariana won second place. The winner was a quiet boy named Desmond, whose simple jacket was lined with fabric from his late grandfather's shirts. // Afterward, Ms. Adebayo found Mariana by the door. "Your technique is better than his," she said. "Better than mine was at your age. But your dress told us you didn't care about anyone but yourself. His told a story about love." She paused. "Talent opens doors. What you sew into it decides who walks through with you." // That night, Mariana sat at her machine for a long time without turning it on. Then she picked up her seam ripper and, stitch by stitch, removed the tiny letters from the skirt. // In their place, she began to embroider something new: a line of small flowers like the ones on the wedding dresses in her grandmother's old photographs.

lessons.name: How modern stories draw on myths

practice.q: An archetype is
ch: a character type, pattern or symbol that appears in stories across many cultures
practice.h: Think of the "wise mentor" or the "hero's journey."

practice.q: A modern novel features a girl who opens a forbidden box that releases troubles but also hope. Which myth does it draw on?
practice.h: Which myth involves a box (or jar) and hope?

practice.q: A story about a businessman whose greed turns everything he touches into money, until he cannot hug his daughter, draws on which myth?
practice.h: Think of the golden touch.

practice.q: When a modern author retells a myth, what is most often changed?
ch: the setting and details, while the core pattern or theme is kept
every event and the entire theme
practice.h: What makes a retelling feel new?

practice.q: Name a modern story, movie or show that draws on an old myth, fairy tale or traditional story, and explain one similarity and one difference.
practice.ans: Example: A movie about a girl who disguises herself to take her father's place in the army draws on the legend of Mulan; both heroines hide their identity to protect family, but the movie adds humor and new characters.
practice.h: Compare one pattern and one change.

quiz.q: In "Altitude," which detail most directly parallels Daedalus's warning to Icarus?
ch: Isa's father tells her to stay under 400 feet but not to fly too low either.
Isa's father works at the airport.
They fly at the soccer field.

quiz.q: In "Altitude," how does Isa's feeling as the drone climbs connect to the myth of Icarus?
ch: Like Icarus, she feels a thrilling lightness that tempts her to go higher.
She wants to land right away.

quiz.q: In "Altitude," which modern event parallels Icarus's fall into the sea?
ch: The drone loses its signal and crashes beside the freeway.
The wind knocks over Isa's father.

quiz.q: In "Altitude," how does the father's reaction differ from the ending of the myth?
ch: He offers forgiveness and a second chance instead of the story ending in tragedy.
He forbids Isa from ever flying again.

quiz.q: In "Altitude," what does the father mean when he says "the myth doesn't say he should never have flown"?
ch: Ambition is good, but it must be balanced with caution.
Icarus was right to fly toward the sun.

quiz.q: How does the author of "Altitude" transform the Icarus myth to develop a new theme?
ch: By keeping the warning and the fall but adding a second chance, the story suggests that overreaching can become a lesson rather than a final punishment.
By keeping the story exactly the same as the myth.
By having the father be the one who falls.

quiz.q: Explain how "Altitude" draws on the myth of Icarus and how it makes the old story new. Cite details from both the background and the modern story.
quiz.ans: Like Daedalus, Isa's father builds a flying machine and warns her to take the "middle path," neither too high nor too low. Like Icarus, Isa is thrilled, ignores the warning ("Just a little more") and the drone falls. The story makes the myth new with a modern drone and a legal height limit, and by changing the ending: the father forgives her and they will rebuild, suggesting that failure can teach balance.

lessons.name: How informational texts connect, compare and categorize ideas

practice.q: When an author categorizes information, the author
ch: groups ideas or examples by shared features
practice.h: Think of sorting.

practice.q: An author compares the hero's journey to a map. What does this analogy suggest?
ch: The pattern guides storytellers from the beginning of a story to the end.
Maps are a kind of story.
practice.h: What does a map do?

practice.q: Which sentence would best serve as a topic sentence for a paragraph about trickster figures in folklore?
ch: Many cultures tell stories about clever tricksters who outwit stronger opponents.
practice.h: Which sentence states a main idea that examples could support?

practice.q: Why might an author include a paragraph about critics of a theory?
ch: to give a balanced view and show the theory's limits
practice.h: Think about fairness.

practice.q: Explain how a single paragraph can refine a key concept in an informational text. Give an example.
practice.ans: A paragraph can add a definition, an example or a limitation that sharpens the reader's understanding. For example, after introducing the hero's journey, a paragraph listing its stages shows exactly what the pattern includes.
practice.h: Think about adding precision.

quiz.q: According to "The Stories We Never Stop Telling," what did Joseph Campbell call the shared structure of hero stories?
What is the role of the first paragraph of "The Stories We Never Stop Telling"?
ch: It hooks readers with a familiar pattern before naming and explaining it.

quiz.q: In "The Stories We Never Stop Telling," why does the author include the examples of Rhodopis and Ye Xian?
ch: to show that the Cinderella pattern appeared in different cultures long before the familiar European versions
to prove that Cinderella was a real person
to compare Greek and Chinese shoes
to argue that eagles are important in myths

quiz.q: Which explanation does "The Stories We Never Stop Telling" give for why story patterns endure?
ch: They reflect experiences that nearly everyone shares.
They were invented by George Lucas.
They were all written by the same author.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the paragraph in "The Stories We Never Stop Telling" that begins "Critics caution"?
ch: to acknowledge the limits of the theory
to explain the plot of Star Wars

quiz.q: In "The Stories We Never Stop Telling," what does the final image, "a very old story wearing new clothes," suggest?
ch: Modern stories often keep ancient patterns while changing their surface details.

quiz.q: Explain how the author of "The Stories We Never Stop Telling" connects ancient myths to modern movies. Use one example.
quiz.ans: The author explains Campbell's hero's journey, a pattern found in myths from many cultures, and then notes that George Lucas said Campbell's work influenced Star Wars, showing that a modern film builds on the same ancient structure.

lessons.name: Allusions, irony, puns and word origins

practice.q: Verbal irony occurs when
ch: a speaker says the opposite of what he or she means
the audience knows more than a character
practice.h: Think of sarcasm.

practice.q: After the car breaks down in the rain, a passenger says, "Well, this is a lovely trip." What kind of irony is this?
practice.h: Does the speaker really mean "lovely"?

practice.q: Which sentence contains a pun?
ch: The baker quit because he couldn't make enough dough.
practice.h: Look for a word with two meanings.

practice.q: Read: "Her new job was a real Pandora's box." What does the allusion suggest?
ch: The job brought many unexpected problems.
The job came in a box.
practice.h: What came out of Pandora's box?

practice.q: The word "narcissistic" comes from the myth of Narcissus, who fell in love with his own reflection. Explain what "narcissistic" means and use it in a sentence.
practice.ans: It means overly interested in oneself or one's appearance. "The narcissistic singer talked only about himself during the interview."
practice.h: Think about Narcissus and his reflection.

quiz.q: What does "a Herculean effort" mean?
ch: an effort requiring great strength or determination

quiz.q: Which situation is an example of situational irony?
ch: A girl says "Great!" when she drops her lunch.
The audience knows the villain's identity.
A dog barks at the mail carrier.

quiz.q: Which English word comes from the name of a Greek god?
The Latin root "fort" means "strong." What does "fortify" mean?
What makes "The math teacher had too many problems" a pun?
ch: "Problems" means both math exercises and troubles.
The teacher is a real person.

quiz.q: What does "an Achilles' heel" mean?
ch: a weakness in an otherwise strong person or thing

quiz.q: A character who has been rude to everyone all day says, "I'm known for my kindness." What effect does this verbal irony create?
ch: humor that highlights the gap between how the character sees himself or herself and reality

quiz.q: Write one sentence that uses an allusion to a myth and one sentence that uses verbal irony. Label each and explain its meaning.
quiz.ans: Allusion: "Studying for finals felt like my own Trojan War." (a long, exhausting struggle) Verbal irony: "Oh good, another pop quiz," Maya groaned. (She is actually unhappy.)

lessons.name: Writing a literary analysis of a modern work and its source

practice.q: When analyzing how a modern story draws on a myth, a writer should explain
ch: which elements are kept and which are changed, and why
only the plot of the myth
the design of the book cover
practice.h: Think about similarities, differences and purpose.

practice.q: Which thesis best analyzes a modern retelling of the Icarus myth?
ch: By moving the Icarus myth to a modern drone flight and adding forgiveness, the author turns a tale of punishment into a story about learning balance.
The story is like a myth.
practice.h: A strong thesis explains how and why the story transforms its source.

practice.q: Which sentence best uses evidence from both a myth and a modern story?
ch: Daedalus warns his son to avoid both the sun and the sea, just as the father in the modern story insists on the "middle path."
practice.h: Connect specific details from both texts.

practice.q: Which transition best signals that a modern author changed the source?
practice.h: Which phrase shows a difference?

practice.q: Write a topic sentence for a body paragraph explaining how a modern story changes the ending of the myth it draws on.
practice.ans: Example: "Unlike the myth, which ends with Icarus drowning, the modern story ends with a father offering his daughter a second chance."
practice.h: Name the change and its effect.

quiz.q: In a comparison essay, a strong body paragraph includes
ch: a topic sentence, evidence from both texts and commentary

quiz.q: Which commentary best explains why an author changed a myth's ending?
ch: By replacing tragedy with forgiveness, the author suggests that modern readers may value growth over punishment.

quiz.q: Which detail would most strongly show that a modern story draws on the myth of King Midas?
ch: The main character wishes that everything he touches would turn to gold.
The story is set in a city.
The main character has a daughter.

quiz.q: Which conclusion best extends a comparison of a myth and its modern retelling?
ch: Old stories survive because each generation reshapes them to answer its own questions.
I liked the modern one more.

quiz.q: A student copies this sentence from an article: "Myths endure because they reflect experiences nearly everyone shares." Which revision best avoids plagiarism?
ch: According to the article, myths last because they describe experiences almost everyone has.
Myths endure because they reflect experiences nearly everyone shares.
Myths endure because they reflect experiences.

quiz.q: How should a writer describe the events of a myth in a literary analysis?
ch: in the literary present, as in "Icarus flies too close to the sun"

quiz.q: Write a thesis statement for an essay comparing a myth you know with a modern story, movie or show that draws on it.
quiz.ans: Example: "Like the myth of Prometheus, the film shows a hero who takes forbidden knowledge to help others, but by letting the hero survive, it suggests that sacrifice can lead to hope rather than endless punishment."

test.q: Which word comes from the name of a Greek nymph who could only repeat the words of others?
What does it mean to say someone has "the Midas touch"?
ch: Everything the person tries becomes successful or profitable.
The person cares only about gold jewelry.
The person is a skilled doctor.

test.q: Which sentence contains verbal irony?
ch: "Fantastic," Leo muttered as rain soaked his new shoes.
Leo thought happily that his new shoes were fantastic.

test.q: Which sentence plays on two meanings of the same word?
ch: I used to be a banker, but I lost interest.
I used to be a banker, but I changed careers.
My uncle works at a bank.

test.q: The Greek root "mono" means "one." What does the word "monomyth" suggest?
Which example shows situational irony?
ch: A famous swimming coach cannot swim.
A character says "nice weather" during a storm.
The audience knows a secret the hero does not.

test.q: Read: "When the know-it-all lost the trivia contest on the easiest question, it was his Waterloo." What does the allusion suggest?
ch: It was a final, decisive defeat.

test.q: According to "Living with the Gods," which god gives his name to January?
How does the author organize the body of "Living with the Gods"?
ch: by categories: the calendar, language, science and exploration, and companies
as a problem and a solution

test.q: According to "Living with the Gods," why is January a "fitting" name for the first month?
ch: Janus was the god of beginnings, shown looking both backward and forward.
Janus was the god of winter.

test.q: In "Living with the Gods," what connection does the author draw between NASA's two Moon programs?
ch: Apollo and Artemis are twins in myth, linking the earlier and later programs.
Both names were invented by NASA.
Both are names of rockets that failed.

test.q: According to "Living with the Gods," why might a company choose the name of the goddess of victory?
ch: It suggests speed, strength and winning.

test.q: In "Living with the Gods," what is the effect of describing the gods as having "moved into our dictionaries, our calendars and our imaginations"?
ch: It emphasizes that myths still live on in everyday modern life.
It suggests the gods are real people.
It argues that myths should be forgotten.
It shows that temples were relocated.

test.q: Explain two reasons the author of "Living with the Gods" gives for why ancient mythological names remain useful.
test.ans: First, for centuries educated Europeans studied Greek and Latin and drew on myths when they needed new words. Second, the names carry meaning, such as linking a Moon program to ancient stories about the sky or suggesting victory in a brand name.

test.q: In "Thread," which detail from the modern story most closely parallels Arachne's boast?
ch: Mariana says she is "better than most of the designers on TV" and embroiders BETTER THAN THE JUDGES on her dress.

test.q: In "Thread," which character plays a role similar to Athena disguised as an old woman giving a warning?
ch: Mariana's grandmother, who warns that "a gift is not a weapon"

test.q: In "Thread," how does the consequence of pride differ from the consequence in the myth?
ch: Mariana loses first place and has a chance to learn, instead of being permanently transformed as a punishment.
Mariana is turned into a spider.

test.q: In "Thread," what does Ms. Adebayo mean by "What you sew into it decides who walks through with you"?
ch: The values and meaning a person puts into work affect how others respond and whether success is shared.

test.q: In "Thread," why does the author contrast Mariana's dress with Desmond's jacket?
ch: to show that work expressing love can matter more than technical skill alone
to show that Desmond sews better than Mariana
to show that jackets are better than dresses

test.q: At the end of "Thread," what does Mariana's choice to replace the letters with flowers like those on her grandmother's dresses suggest?
ch: She has chosen humility and connection, honoring her family's tradition instead of boasting.
She is still angry at the judges.
She plans to enter the contest again the next day.

test.q: Explain how the ending of "Thread" transforms the theme of the Arachne myth.
test.ans: In the myth, pride is punished permanently: Arachne becomes a spider forever. In "Thread," Mariana's pride costs her first place, but she chooses to change, removing the boast and adding her grandmother's flowers. The modern story suggests that pride can be overcome through humility and connection, not only punished.

test.q: Write a literary analysis essay that explains how "Thread" draws on the Greek myth of Arachne and how the author makes the old story new. Analyze at least two similarities and one important difference, using evidence from both the background summary and the modern story, and explain what the changes suggest about the modern story's theme.
test.ans: Key points: a thesis about how the story transforms the myth; similarities (a gifted young artist boasts about being better than an authority; an older woman warns her to be humble; a contest exposes her pride; her work insults the judges as Arachne's tapestry mocked the gods); a key difference (no supernatural punishment; second place and a chance to change; an ending of humility that honors her grandmother); what the change suggests (pride can be corrected, and meaning matters more than skill alone); evidence from both parts; literary present; comparison transitions; a conclusion.
rub: Clear focus and strong organization; ideas fully developed with relevant details or text evidence; precise language; few errors in conventions.
Clear focus and organization; ideas adequately developed with some details or evidence; some errors that do not affect meaning.
Focus or organization is inconsistent; limited development or evidence; errors sometimes interfere with meaning.
Little focus or organization; minimal development; frequent errors.

units.name: Collection 6: Science and Responsibility (research)
units.el: Pre-teach science roots (bio, gen, terra, eco, -cide) with a root tree, and give a source checklist in simple language: Who wrote it? Do they gain money from it? When was it written? Do other sources agree?

passages.x: The town of Dos Rios had not seen real rain in two years. The orchards along the valley floor had gone gray and brittle, and every week another family hung a FOR SALE sign on a fence. // So when fourteen-year-old Ines Calderon's science fair project actually worked, people noticed. // Her project was a small drone that flew into passing clouds and released a fine spray of particles, giving water droplets something to cling to. The idea was not new; scientists had experimented with "cloud seeding" for decades. But Ines had improved the design, and on the day of the fair, a light rain fell over the school parking lot for eleven minutes. // Within a month, the town council had paid for twenty of her drones. Within two months, Dos Rios had its first green spring in years. The mayor gave Ines a plaque. The newspaper called her "the Rainmaker." Strangers stopped her in the grocery store to shake her hand. // Then the letter came. // It was from a girl named Paloma, who lived in Las Piedras, a town forty miles east, on the other side of the hills. The handwriting was careful and neat. // "My grandfather says the clouds used to come over the hills and rain on us," Paloma wrote. "Now they rain on you first. Our wells are lower than ever. I am not angry. I just want to know if you knew." // Ines read the letter four times. She had not known. Or rather, she had never thought to ask. The clouds had seemed like free water floating overhead, belonging to no one. She opened her laptop and pulled up rainfall data from towns across the region. The pattern was not certain; weather is complicated, and there could be other causes. But the rainfall in Las Piedras had dropped in the same season that hers had risen. // That night, she went to the town council meeting. The room was packed and cheerful until she stood at the microphone and read Paloma's letter aloud. // "I don't know for sure that my drones caused this," she said. "But I don't know that they didn't. I think we need to find out before we fly them again. And I think Las Piedras should be part of deciding." // The room went quiet. Someone in the back muttered that Las Piedras wasn't their problem. Someone else said Ines was being dramatic. // The mayor, who had given her the plaque, was silent for a long time. Then he said, "Let's call their council." // The drones stayed grounded that summer while scientists from the state university studied the data. It was not a popular decision in Dos Rios. Some people stopped saying hello to Ines in the grocery store. // But in August, a second letter arrived from Las Piedras. Inside was a drawing of two towns, one on each side of a hill, with a single cloud stretched over both of them. Underneath, Paloma had written: "Thank you for asking."

View 1: A Chance to Undo Our Mistakes. In the 1800s, passenger pigeons flew over North America in flocks so large they could darken the sky for hours. Overhunting and the loss of forests drove them to extinction, and the last known passenger pigeon, a bird named Martha, died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1914. Today, new genetic tools may give us a chance to bring back species like this one. // Scientists are already trying. Some researchers hope to edit the genes of Asian elephants to create animals with traits of the woolly mammoth, such as thick hair and fat for surviving the cold. Supporters argue that these animals could help restore Arctic grasslands. Others are studying how to rebuild the passenger pigeon using the genes of its living relative, the band-tailed pigeon. // De-extinction would also drive scientific progress. The tools developed for these projects could help protect endangered species that are still alive, for example by adding genetic diversity to small, struggling populations. If humans caused these extinctions, perhaps we have a responsibility to use our knowledge to reverse them. // View 2: Protect What We Still Have. The idea of seeing a mammoth again is thrilling. But de-extinction raises serious problems. The only attempt so far to produce a living animal from an extinct species ended quickly: in 2003, scientists cloned a Pyrenean ibex, or bucardo, a wild goat that had gone extinct in 2000. The newborn died within minutes because of a lung defect. // Even if scientists succeed, a revived animal would not truly be the same species. A gene-edited elephant with mammoth traits is still mostly an elephant. And these animals would need habitats. The forests that supported passenger pigeons are largely gone, and a few revived birds could not rebuild the vast flocks that defined the species. // Most importantly, de-extinction projects are expensive, and money spent on them could instead protect the thousands of species that are endangered today. Some conservationists worry that the promise of bringing species back might make people care less about preventing extinctions in the first place. The best way to save a species is never to lose it.

The FocusBand arrived in a sleek white box the week before finals. It looked like an ordinary headband, thin and gray, but the ads promised more: "Gentle pulses help your brain ignore distractions. Study twice as efficiently. Approved for ages 13 and up." // Half of Leo's class already had one. Leo's mom had bought his after his last report card. // The first time he put it on, the world went quiet in a way he had never felt. The hum of the refrigerator disappeared. The dog barking next door disappeared. Even the itch on his ankle disappeared. There was only the page in front of him, sharp and clear, and the equations unfolded one after another like stairs. // He studied for four hours without looking up. When he finally took the band off, he blinked at the dark window. He had not noticed the sun go down. // On the history final, he got a 100. On the science final, a 98. His mom hung both tests on the refrigerator. // But something was strange. Leo had always drawn in the margins of his notebooks: dragons, spaceships, cities built on the backs of whales. Now, flipping through his finals study guide, he realized the margins were empty. Not one drawing in two weeks. // He tried to draw something that night, without the band. He sat with his pencil over a blank page for a long time. Nothing came. It was as if the part of his mind that wandered off and found strange, beautiful things had forgotten the way. // He asked his friend Amara, who had worn a band all month, whether she had noticed anything. // She shrugged. "I stopped writing my song lyrics, I guess. But my grades are great." She said it as if it were a fair trade. // Leo wasn't sure it was. // On the last day of school, he put the FocusBand back in its box. His mom asked why. // "I think my brain needs to get distracted sometimes," he said. "That's where the dragons come from." // She looked at him for a moment, then at the tests on the refrigerator. She didn't argue. // That summer, Leo filled two notebooks. His drawings were messy and strange, and some of them were not very good. He didn't care. Every one of them felt like his.

passages.t: A Book That Changed the World: Silent Spring
passages.x: In the 1940s and 1950s, a chemical called DDT seemed like a miracle. During World War II it had helped protect soldiers from insects that spread diseases such as malaria and typhus. After the war, farmers, cities and homeowners sprayed it widely to kill crop pests and mosquitoes. Trucks fogged neighborhoods with it while children played nearby. // Rachel Carson, a marine biologist who had worked for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, grew alarmed. She gathered research from scientists across the country and found troubling evidence that DDT and similar pesticides were harming wildlife. The chemicals did not simply disappear after spraying. They built up in the bodies of animals, becoming more concentrated as they moved up the food chain, from insects to fish to birds. // In 1962, Carson published her findings in a book called Silent Spring. The title came from a haunting image: a spring morning with no birdsong, because the birds had been poisoned. Carson wrote clearly for ordinary readers, and the book became a bestseller. // Some chemical companies attacked the book and Carson personally, calling her claims exaggerated. But President John F. Kennedy asked his science advisory committee to examine the issue, and its 1963 report largely supported her concerns about pesticides. // Carson died of cancer in 1964, before she could see the full impact of her work. Public concern about pollution continued to grow. In 1970, the U.S. government created the Environmental Protection Agency. In 1972, the agency banned most uses of DDT in the United States. // Later research confirmed one of the most serious effects. DDT caused some birds, including bald eagles and peregrine falcons, to lay eggs with shells so thin that they cracked before hatching. As DDT use ended and protections increased, these birds slowly recovered. In 2007, the bald eagle was removed from the federal list of endangered and threatened species. // The story is not entirely simple. In some parts of the world, health experts still debate the limited use of DDT inside homes to fight malaria, a disease that kills hundreds of thousands of people each year. Balancing human health and environmental protection remains difficult. // But Silent Spring changed how many people think about science and responsibility. It showed that new technologies can have consequences no one intended, and that careful research, clearly communicated, can help the public make wiser choices.

sci|-1.about: Transitional kindergarten science helps children wonder, observe and explore with their senses and simple tools. Children notice how objects and materials look, feel and change, try pushes and pulls, care for plants and animals and watch them grow, and observe rocks, water, weather and the sky. Items are read aloud and many are answered by pointing, saying or drawing.
std: Observation and investigation: use the senses and simple tools (magnifier, measuring cup, scale) to observe, compare, sort, predict and try things out.
Documentation and communication: record observations with drawings, marks and simple charts, and share what was seen and learned.
Properties of nonliving objects and materials: describe and compare size, shape, color, texture, weight and what materials are made of.
Changes in nonliving objects and materials: observe and describe how objects move (push, pull, roll, slide) and how materials change (mix, melt, freeze, get wet or dry).
Properties of living things: identify living things, their body parts and what plants, animals and people need to live, and where animals live.
Changes in living things: observe and describe how plants and animals, including people, grow and change over time.
Properties of earth materials: observe and describe rocks, soil, sand and water.
Changes in the earth: observe and describe weather, seasons, day and night, and the Sun, Moon and stars.

test.q: Tia had a mystery bag. She put her hand in and felt something soft and fuzzy. She shook the bag and heard nothing. Then she smelled the bag and it smelled like nothing. sci|0.about: Kindergarten science asks children to investigate and wonder about everyday phenomena: how pushes and pulls change the way things move, how sunlight warms Earth's surface, how weather changes from day to day and season to season, what plants and animals (including people) need to survive, how living things change the places they live, and how people can take care of land, water, air and living things. Children plan simple tests, observe, record with drawings and charts, and design simple solutions. Items are read aloud.
std: Plan and conduct an investigation to compare the effects of different strengths or different directions of pushes and pulls on the motion of an object.
Make observations to determine the effect of sunlight on Earth's surface.
Use observations to describe patterns of what plants and animals (including humans) need to survive.
Use and share observations of local weather conditions to describe patterns over time.
Construct an argument supported by evidence for how plants and animals (including humans) can change the environment to meet their needs.
Use a model to represent the relationship between the needs of different plants or animals (including humans) and the places they live.
Communicate solutions that will reduce the impact of humans on the land, water, air and/or other living things in the local environment.
Ask questions, make observations and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through a new or improved object or tool.

sci|1.about: First grade science investigates how vibrating things make sound and sound makes things vibrate, how light lets us see and what happens when light meets different materials, how plants and animals use their outside parts to survive (and how people copy those parts in designs), how parents and offspring behave and how young are like but not exactly like their parents, and the patterns of the Sun, Moon and stars, including how the amount of daylight changes through the year. Children plan investigations, describe observations in words and drawings, and design simple solutions. Items are read aloud.
std: Plan and conduct investigations to provide evidence that vibrating materials can make sound and that sound can make materials vibrate.
Make observations to construct an evidence-based account that objects can be seen only when illuminated.
Plan and conduct an investigation to determine the effect of placing objects made with different materials in the path of a beam of light.
Use materials to design a solution to a human problem by mimicking how plants and/or animals use their external parts to help them survive, grow and meet their needs.
Read texts and use media to determine patterns in behavior of parents and offspring that help offspring survive.
Make observations to construct an evidence-based account that young plants and animals are like, but not exactly like, their parents.
Use observations of the Sun, Moon and stars to describe patterns that can be predicted.
Make observations at different times of year to relate the amount of daylight to the time of year.

sci|2.about: Second grade science investigates the properties of materials and how they are chosen for a job, how objects can be built from small pieces, and how heating and cooling cause changes that can or cannot be reversed. Students test what plants need, explore how animals spread seeds and pollinate flowers, compare the diversity of living things in different habitats, observe Earth events that happen quickly or slowly, compare solutions that slow erosion by wind and water, and use maps and models to describe land and water on Earth. Items are read aloud as needed.
std: Plan and conduct an investigation to describe and classify different kinds of materials by their observable properties.
Analyze data obtained from testing different materials to determine which materials have the properties that are best suited for an intended purpose.
Construct an argument with evidence that some changes caused by heating or cooling can be reversed and some cannot.
Plan and conduct an investigation to determine if plants need sunlight and water to grow.
Develop a simple model that mimics the function of an animal in dispersing seeds or pollinating plants.
Make observations of plants and animals to compare the diversity of life in different habitats.
Use information from several sources to provide evidence that Earth events can occur quickly or slowly.
Compare multiple solutions designed to slow or prevent wind or water from changing the shape of the land.
