quiz.q: Students counted 6 kinds of plants in a lawn and 15 kinds in a meadow. Which statement is true?
ch: The meadow has more plant variety
The lawn has more plant variety

quiz.q: Ben counted 20 ants. They were all the same kind. Mia counted 5 animals of 5 different kinds. Who found more variety?
A class counted kinds of living things in the same garden in spring (14 kinds) and in winter (6 kinds). What can they conclude?
ch: The garden had more variety in spring
The garden had more variety in winter

quiz.q: Explain the difference between the number of animals and the number of kinds of animals.
quiz.ans: Number of animals counts every animal; number of kinds counts how many different types there are, like ants, beetles and worms.

test.q: The place where an animal lives is its
Which animal lives in the ocean?
Which plant grows well in a hot, dry desert?
Which habitat has the most kinds of plants and animals?
Frogs, ducks and cattails share which habitat?
Why can't a cactus grow well in a pond?
ch: It is adapted to dry land and too much water hurts its roots

test.q: Which animal is adapted to a cold habitat?
ch: an arctic fox with thick fur

test.q: A tide pool is found
ch: at the rocky edge of the ocean
in the middle of a desert

test.q: Which tool helps you record how many of each living thing you see?
A meadow has 18 kinds of living things and a lawn has 5. Which has more variety?
Why do habitats have different living things?
ch: Each living thing needs a place that meets its needs
All living things need the same place

test.q: Banana slugs, ferns and redwoods live in a
Which habitat would most likely have the fewest kinds of living things?
Why do scientists count living things in same-size areas?
A desert and a forest each have 1 acre studied. Desert: 10 kinds. Forest: 32 kinds. Which is the best explanation?
ch: The forest has more water and plants for food and shelter
The forest is hotter and drier

test.q: Kai counted 30 pigeons on a city sidewalk. Lea counted 12 different kinds of birds in a park. Who found more variety?
Coral reefs are home to many kinds of fish, crabs and sea turtles. What does this show?
ch: Coral reefs have a lot of variety of life

test.q: A pond had 5 kinds of insects and 4 kinds of plants. How many kinds of living things is that?
A field had 23 kinds of living things. A sidewalk had 4. How many more kinds did the field have?
Name a habitat in California and one plant or animal that lives there.
test.ans: Example: redwood forest and banana slug; Mojave Desert and Joshua tree; kelp forest and sea otter; tide pool and sea star.

test.q: Explain why a polar bear could not survive well in a desert.
test.ans: It has thick fur and hunts seals on ice; the desert is hot and dry with no ice or seals.

test.q: Tell how you would find out which of two habitats has more variety of life.
test.ans: Study the same size area in each, record every kind of living thing in a chart and compare the number of kinds.

test.q: Students studied two spots at school for 20 minutes each. Spot A, the garden: wet soil, flowers and bushes; they found 16 kinds of living things. Spot B, the blacktop: hard, dry, no plants; they found 3 kinds. Which spot has more variety of life, and why? Make a claim, give evidence and explain.
test.ans: Claim: the garden has more variety of life than the blacktop. Evidence: they found 16 kinds in the garden but only 3 kinds on the blacktop in the same amount of time. Reasoning: the garden has water, soil, plants and shelter that many living things need, while the blacktop has almost none, so fewer kinds can live there.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 5: Earth Changes, Fast and Slow
units.el: Sort event photo cards onto a "fast (minutes, hours, days) / slow (many years)" timeline; build a sand-tray hill to model erosion and teach "erosion," "weathering," "wind," "flood" and "protect."

lessons.name: Which Earth changes happen fast and which happen slowly?

practice.q: Which Earth event happens in just minutes?
ch: a river slowly changing its path
practice.h: Which one can shake the ground all at once?

practice.q: Which change takes a very long time?
practice.h: Canyons are very deep. How long would it take water to carve that much rock?

practice.q: Hot melted rock pours out of a mountain and cools into new land. What is this?
practice.h: Think of lava.

practice.q: A hillside slides down in one afternoon after heavy rain. This is
ch: a fast change called a landslide
a slow change called a canyon
practice.h: It happened in one afternoon.

practice.q: Sharp rocks on a mountain become smooth pebbles in a stream over many years. This change is
practice.h: Many years means slow.

practice.q: Name one Earth change that happens fast and one that happens slowly.
practice.ans: Fast: earthquake, volcanic eruption, landslide or flood. Slow: a canyon being carved, rocks wearing down, a mountain wearing away.

quiz.q: A flood that covers a road in one night is a
ch: change that takes millions of years

quiz.q: The Grand Canyon was carved by a river over
Which is the best evidence that a change was slow?
ch: Scientists see thin layers that built up over a very long time
People watched it happen in one hour
It was in the news yesterday

quiz.q: Which group lists only fast changes?
ch: canyon, rock weathering, mountain wearing down

quiz.q: Ocean waves slowly wear away a cliff. Over many years, what happens?
ch: The cliff gets smaller and moves back

quiz.q: A town's old photos show a beach was wide 50 years ago and narrow today. What kind of change happened?
ch: a slow change from waves wearing away sand
a fast change from an earthquake

quiz.q: Explain why scientists cannot watch a canyon form, but can still know how it formed.
quiz.ans: It takes far longer than a lifetime, but rock layers, the river at the bottom and the shape of the walls show it was carved slowly by water.

lessons.name: How do wind and water change the shape of the land?

practice.q: When wind or water carries away soil and rock, it is called
practice.h: The word starts with "e."

practice.q: Water was poured on a sand hill in a tray. What happened to the sand?
ch: It washed down and made little channels
practice.h: Moving water carries sand with it.

practice.q: Strong wind blows across a dry desert. What can it move?
practice.h: Have you seen sand blow at the beach?

practice.q: Why does a river get muddy after a big storm?
ch: Rain washed soil into the river
practice.h: Where did the soil come from?

practice.q: Which land would erode fastest in a heavy rain?
ch: bare dirt on a steep hill
a flat lawn with thick grass
a rocky floor in a cave
a parking lot under a roof
practice.h: Plant roots hold soil. Steep slopes make water run fast.

practice.q: Describe what happened to our sand hill when we poured water on it.
practice.ans: The water ran down the hill and carried sand to the bottom, making grooves and a pile of sand at the base.

quiz.q: Which can cause erosion?
A strong ocean storm hits a beach. What may happen fast?
ch: Waves wash away a lot of sand

quiz.q: Why does bare soil wash away more than soil covered with grass?
ch: Grass roots hold the soil in place

quiz.q: A sand model hill was sprayed with gentle water and then with fast water. Which washed away more sand?
Sand dunes in a desert slowly move. What moves them?
A model hill had 20 cups of sand. After pouring water, 7 cups washed to the bottom of the tray. How many cups stayed on the hill?

Kenji built two sand hills the same size. He planted grass seed on Hill A and let it grow. Hill B had no plants. He poured 1 cup of water on each. Hill A lost a spoonful of sand. Hill B lost 8 spoonfuls and got deep grooves. Do plants help stop erosion? Make a claim, give evidence and explain.
quiz.ans: Claim: plants help stop water from washing away soil. Evidence: the hill with grass lost only 1 spoonful of sand, but the bare hill lost 8 spoonfuls and got deep grooves. Reasoning: plant roots hold the soil together and leaves slow the water, so less soil is carried away.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: How can we protect land from wind and water?

practice.q: Rows of trees planted to slow the wind are called
practice.h: They "break" the wind.

practice.q: Which helps keep a hillside from washing away?
practice.h: What holds soil in place?

practice.q: A house is near a river that floods. Which solution helps?
ch: building a wall of sandbags or a levee
practice.h: What could block water?

practice.q: Big rocks are placed along a beach cliff. Why?
ch: to take the force of waves so the cliff wears away slower
practice.h: What will the waves hit first?

practice.q: A fence of wooden slats is put on a beach. What does it do?
ch: slows the wind and catches blowing sand
practice.h: Where does sand pile up when wind slows down?

practice.q: Design a way to keep soil on a garden hill from washing away in rain. Tell how it works.
practice.ans: Plant grass or shrubs whose roots hold soil, or build small steps (terraces) or a low wall that slows the water.

quiz.q: Engineers compare solutions to find the one that
Three model walls were tested against poured water. Wall A lost 2 spoons of sand, wall B lost 9, wall C lost 5. Which wall worked best?
Why do farmers plant rows of trees along the edges of windy fields?
ch: to slow the wind so it blows away less soil
to block the sun from crops

quiz.q: Which is a fair way to compare two erosion solutions?
ch: use the same hill and the same amount of water
use a big hill for one and a tiny hill for the other

quiz.q: A hillside wall works but costs a lot. Planting shrubs works almost as well and costs little. Why might a town choose the shrubs?
ch: it works well and costs less

quiz.q: Two beach solutions were tested in a wave tank. With a rock wall, the model cliff lost 1 cm. With no wall, it lost 6 cm. With a sand fence, it lost 5 cm. Which is best for stopping wave erosion?
Tell why it is important to test more than one solution.
quiz.ans: Different designs work differently; testing and comparing shows which one works best for the problem.

test.q: Which Earth change happens quickly?
ch: a stone wearing smooth in a river

test.q: Which Earth change happens slowly?
When wind or water moves soil and rock away, it is called
Rows of trees planted to slow wind are
Which helps hold soil on a hill?
An earthquake shakes a town for one minute. What kind of change is this?
Wind blows sand into big hills in the desert. What are these hills called?
Which is a solution for a river that floods homes?
ch: a levee or wall along the river

test.q: Why are large rocks piled at the bottom of some sea cliffs?
ch: to make the cliff fall faster

test.q: Muddy water in a stream after rain shows
ch: soil was eroded and carried away

test.q: Which happens over millions of years?
ch: a canyon is carved by a river

test.q: Which is the best way to test which erosion solution works?
ch: try each on the same model hill with the same water
try one and guess about the others
use different hills and different water

test.q: Which land is most likely to erode in heavy rain?
A beach fence catches blowing sand. What does it stop?
Old photos show a wooden house 30 meters from a cliff edge in 1950 and 5 meters from it today. What happened?
ch: waves slowly wore away the cliff

test.q: Solution A (plants) lost 3 spoons of soil. Solution B (rock wall) lost 2 spoons. Solution C (nothing) lost 10 spoons. Which statement is true?
ch: Both A and B worked much better than doing nothing

test.q: Scientists find a layer of ash in a rock cliff. What fast event does it show happened long ago?
A model hill lost 9 spoons of sand with no plants and 2 spoons with plants. How many fewer spoons did it lose with plants?
A beach was 40 meters wide. Storms washed away 15 meters. How wide is the beach now?
Name one fast Earth event and tell how it changes land.
test.ans: Example: a landslide moves a lot of rock and soil down a hill in minutes; a volcano adds new rock from lava.

test.q: Explain how a river can change land slowly.
test.ans: The moving water carries tiny bits of rock and soil away bit by bit; over a very long time it can carve a valley or canyon.

test.q: Name two ways people slow erosion and how each one helps.
test.ans: Planting plants (roots hold soil); building walls or levees (block water); windbreaks (slow wind); rocks on a shore (take the force of waves).

test.q: The class tested three ways to protect a model hill from a "rainstorm" of 2 cups of water. No protection: 12 spoons of sand washed away. A wall of craft sticks at the bottom: 6 spoons washed away. Grass mat covering the hill: 2 spoons washed away. Which solution is best for slowing water erosion? Make a claim, give evidence and explain.
test.ans: Claim: covering the hill with grass is the best solution. Evidence: with the same 2 cups of water, the grass mat lost only 2 spoons, the wall lost 6 and no protection lost 12. Reasoning: grass covers the soil and its roots hold it, so the water cannot carry much away; the wall only caught some sand at the bottom.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 6: Land and Water on Earth
units.el: Build a clay or sand landform model and label it with word cards (mountain, hill, valley, plain, river, lake, ocean, island); color a simple map with a key and practice "The blue shows ___."

lessons.name: What shapes of land are on Earth?

practice.q: A very tall, steep landform is a
practice.h: Mount Whitney in California is one.

practice.q: Low land between hills or mountains is a
practice.h: Think of a "V" shape between two hills.

practice.q: Land with water all around it is an
practice.h: Catalina Island is off the coast of California.

practice.q: Wide, flat land good for farming is a
practice.h: California's Central Valley has very flat farmland.

practice.q: Which is a body of water, not a landform?
practice.h: Landforms are shapes of land. Which one is water?

practice.q: Name two landforms and tell how they are different.
practice.ans: A mountain is very tall and steep; a plain is flat and low.

quiz.q: Which is a landform?
A deep, narrow valley with steep sides, often carved by a river, is a
Which is shorter and less steep than a mountain?
Land that sticks out into water and has water on three sides is a
The Sierra Nevada is a long row of
A family drives from the beach, across flat farm fields, then up a steep, winding road to snowy peaks. Which landforms did they pass, in order?
Draw or describe a model of a mountain, a valley and a river. Tell where the river would flow and why.
quiz.ans: The river starts high in the mountains and flows down into the low valley, because water flows downhill.

lessons.name: How can maps and models show land and water?

practice.q: On most maps, water is shown with the color
practice.h: Think of the color of a lake on a map.

practice.q: The part of a map that tells what the symbols and colors mean is the
practice.h: It "unlocks" the map.

practice.q: A model is
ch: a small copy that shows how something looks or works
practice.h: A toy globe is a model of Earth.

practice.q: On a map key, a triangle means mountain. You see three triangles in a row. What do they show?
practice.h: Look back at what one triangle means.

practice.q: Which shows the whole Earth's land and water as a round model?
practice.h: It spins on a stand.

practice.q: Tell how a map key helps you read a map.
practice.ans: The key tells what each color and symbol stands for, such as blue for water and triangles for mountains.

quiz.q: A round model of Earth is a
A map shows a wiggly blue line from the mountains to the ocean. What is it most likely?
On a globe, most of Earth's surface is colored
Why might a map use green for low land and brown for high land?
ch: to show how high or low the land is

quiz.q: Nadia built a model hill from clay and sprayed water on top. Where did the water go?
ch: down the sides to the bottom

quiz.q: A map key says: blue = water, green = forest, triangle = mountain. A spot is blue with green all around it. What is it most likely?
Explain why scientists use models and maps instead of only looking at the real land.
quiz.ans: Real land is too big to see all at once; maps and models show large areas in a small space so we can see shapes and patterns.

lessons.name: Where is water found on Earth?

practice.q: Where is most of Earth's water?
practice.h: Look at how much blue is on a globe.

practice.q: Ocean water is
practice.h: Have you tasted seawater at the beach?

practice.q: Water can be found on Earth as a solid. Where?
practice.h: Solid water is ice.

practice.q: Which is a body of fresh water?
practice.h: Fresh water is not salty.

practice.q: Snow on the Sierra Nevada melts in spring. Where does the water go?
practice.h: Melted snow flows downhill.

practice.q: Name two places water is found as a liquid and one place it is found as a solid.
practice.ans: Liquid: oceans, rivers, lakes, ponds. Solid: glaciers, polar ice, snow on mountains.

quiz.q: A big moving body of fresh water that flows to the sea is a
A glacier is
ch: a huge sheet of ice that moves very slowly

quiz.q: Why can't people drink ocean water without cleaning it?
Which list has only places with liquid water?
Most of the fresh water on Earth is frozen in
A map of California shows blue in the west, white on mountain peaks in winter and thin blue lines running into a big valley. What do the colors show?
ch: ocean, snow and ice, and rivers

quiz.q: Tell one way the Pacific Ocean and Lake Tahoe are different.
quiz.ans: The ocean is salt water and much bigger; Lake Tahoe is fresh water and surrounded by land.

test.q: A tall landform with a peak is a
Most of Earth's water is in
Water frozen in a huge, slow-moving sheet of ice is a
A map's key tells
ch: what the symbols and colors mean

test.q: Catalina, off the coast of Los Angeles, has ocean on every side. What landform is it?
Flat, low land good for farming is a
Which is fresh water?
On a map, a blue area usually shows
Which is a model of the whole Earth?
Snow on mountain peaks is water in which form?
Where does melted mountain snow usually flow?
A deep, narrow valley carved by a river is a
Which list has only landforms?
Why do we use models of land?
ch: to see a large area in a small space

test.q: On a map key, a triangle means mountain and a blue line means river. A blue line starts near triangles and ends at a blue area on the coast. What does this show?
ch: a river flowing from mountains to the ocean

test.q: Which is the best evidence that most of Earth is covered by water?
Some water is liquid in lakes and some is solid in glaciers. What decides which form it is in?
ch: how cold or warm the place is
the shape of the land only

test.q: A model had 3 mountains and 4 hills. How many landforms did it show?
A class map showed 12 lakes. 5 were frozen in winter. How many were not frozen?
Name one landform and one body of water in California.
test.ans: Landform: Mount Whitney, Sierra Nevada, Central Valley, Death Valley. Water: Pacific Ocean, Lake Tahoe, Sacramento River.

test.q: Tell how water on Earth can be solid and liquid, with one example of each.
test.ans: Liquid water flows in oceans, rivers and lakes. Solid water is ice and snow, like glaciers and snow on mountaintops.

test.q: Draw a simple map with a mountain, a river and a lake. Make a key.
test.ans: A map with symbols (triangle for mountain, blue line for river, blue shape for lake) and a key that explains each symbol.

test.q: Lucas looked at a globe and colored a chart of 20 squares, one for each part of Earth he checked: 14 squares landed on blue water, 6 on land. Of the water squares, 13 were oceans. Make a claim about where most of Earth's water is, give evidence and explain.
test.ans: Claim: most of Earth is covered by water, and most of that water is in the oceans. Evidence: 14 of the 20 squares were water and 13 of those water squares were oceans. Reasoning: the globe is a model of Earth, so if most squares are ocean, most of Earth's surface water is in the oceans, not in lakes or rivers.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.

sci|3.about: Third graders investigate weather patterns and climates around the world, design solutions to weather hazards, explore balanced and unbalanced forces, magnets and static electricity, model life cycles and inherited traits, and argue from evidence about how organisms survive, live in groups and change over time. They also practice the engineering design process.
std: Plan and conduct an investigation to provide evidence of the effects of balanced and unbalanced forces on the motion of an object.
Ask questions to determine cause and effect relationships of electric or magnetic interactions between two objects not in contact with each other.
Develop models to describe that organisms have unique and diverse life cycles but all have in common birth, growth, reproduction and death.
Analyze and interpret data to provide evidence that plants and animals have traits inherited from parents and that variation of these traits exists in a group of similar organisms.
Construct an argument with evidence that in a particular habitat some organisms can survive well, some survive less well and some cannot survive at all.
Represent data in tables and graphical displays to describe typical weather conditions expected during a particular season.
Make a claim about the merit of a design solution that reduces the impacts of a weather-related hazard.
Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.

units.name: Unit 1: Weather Patterns and Climates
units.el: Post a word wall with picture cards for temperature, rainfall, wind, season, weather and climate; model reading one row of a data table aloud with the sentence frame "In ___, the ___ was ___."

lessons.name: How can we predict what the weather will be like?

practice.q: Which tool measures how hot or cold the air is?
practice.h: Think about which tool has a scale with degrees on it.

practice.q: Which tool shows which direction the wind is blowing from?
practice.h: This tool turns to point into the wind.

practice.q: A class recorded the high temperature for 3 days: Monday 64°F, Tuesday 70°F, Wednesday 67°F. How many degrees warmer was Tuesday than Monday?
practice.h: Subtract the smaller temperature from the larger one.

practice.q: For 5 days in a row, clouds got thicker and darker each afternoon and then it rained. On day 6 the afternoon clouds are thick and dark again. What is the best prediction?
ch: It will snow for a week.
The sky will be clear all night.
The temperature will drop below freezing.
practice.h: Look for a pattern that repeated before.

practice.q: Which observation is about weather and not climate?
ch: It is windy and 58°F this morning.
Summers here are usually hot and dry.
This city gets about 15 inches of rain a year.
practice.h: Weather is what is happening at one time and place.

practice.q: Name two kinds of weather data a weather reporter collects. Tell what tool measures each one.
practice.ans: Temperature, measured with a thermometer, and rainfall, measured with a rain gauge. (Wind direction with a wind vane or wind speed with an anemometer also count.)
practice.h: Think about what you hear on a weather report.

quiz.q: What does a rain gauge measure?
Weather is
ch: the conditions of the air at a certain time and place
the kind of weather a place has over many years
the amount of water in the ocean

quiz.q: A rain gauge held 2 centimeters of water on Saturday and 3 centimeters on Sunday. How many centimeters of rain fell in all?
A student records the wind every day for a month. On most days the wind vane points west in the afternoon. Which is the best prediction for tomorrow afternoon?
ch: The wind will probably come from the west.
The wind will come from the east.
There will be no wind at all.

quiz.q: A thermometer read 48°F at 7 a.m. and 73°F at 2 p.m. How many degrees did the temperature rise?
Why do scientists record weather data for many days instead of just one day?
ch: to find patterns that help them make predictions
because one day of data is always wrong

quiz.q: Pablo says, "It rained today, so it will rain every day this week." Explain why one day of data is not enough to make that prediction.
quiz.ans: One day does not show a pattern. Weather changes from day to day, so you need data from many days to see what usually happens before you predict.

lessons.name: Why is it rainier in some seasons than others?

practice.q: A table shows rainfall in Sacramento: January 4 inches, April 1 inch, July 0 inches, October 1 inch. Which season is the rainiest?
practice.h: Find the month with the most inches, then name its season.

practice.q: Using the same table (January 4 inches, April 1 inch, July 0 inches, October 1 inch), how many inches of rain fell in the four months altogether?
practice.h: Add all four numbers.

practice.q: Which kind of graph is best for comparing the rainfall in each month of the year?
ch: a bar graph with one bar for each month
a list of the days of the week
practice.h: You want to compare amounts side by side.

practice.q: In most of California, which season usually has the hottest temperatures?
practice.h: Think about when school is out and days are longest.

practice.q: The average high temperature in a town is 88°F in July and 55°F in January. How many degrees warmer is July?
practice.h: Subtract 55 from 88.

practice.q: A bar graph shows snowfall in a mountain town for each month. The bars are tall from December to March and zero from June to September. Describe the seasonal pattern.
practice.ans: The town gets most of its snow in winter, from December to March. It gets no snow in summer, from June to September.

quiz.q: A table shows the number of rainy days in a city: winter 12, spring 7, summer 1, fall 5. Which season should a family pick for an outdoor party with the least chance of rain?
Using the same table (winter 12, spring 7, summer 1, fall 5), how many more rainy days are there in winter than in fall?
Using the same table (winter 12, spring 7, summer 1, fall 5), how many rainy days are there in the whole year?
A pictograph shows sunny days in May. Each sun picture stands for 2 days. There are 9 sun pictures. How many sunny days were there?
What does a bar graph of monthly temperatures help you see?
ch: patterns in how temperature changes during the year
the exact weather on one afternoon
where the wind is blowing right now

quiz.q: A city's graph shows warm, dry summers and cool, rainy winters every year for 20 years. What is the best prediction for next January?
Explain why a farmer would want to know which months usually get the most rain.
quiz.ans: The farmer can plan when to plant and water crops. If rain usually comes in winter, the farmer knows crops will need extra watering in the dry summer.

lessons.name: Why are some places hot and others cold all year?

practice.q: What is climate?
ch: the usual weather of a place over many years
practice.h: Climate is about a long time, not one day.

practice.q: Which place has a climate that is hot and very dry most of the year?
practice.h: Which place gets very little rain?

practice.q: A region is warm all year and gets rain almost every day. What kind of climate does it have?
practice.h: Think about where it is both hot and wet.

practice.q: Places near the poles, like northern Alaska, have cold climates. Which is true about these places?
ch: They are cold for most of the year.
They have no seasons at all.
They get the same weather as a desert.
practice.h: Remember where the polar bears live.

practice.q: City A gets 60 inches of rain a year. City B gets 8 inches a year. How many more inches does City A get?
practice.h: Subtract to compare.

practice.q: Describe the climate where you live. Use the words temperature and rain in your answer.
practice.ans: Sample: Where I live, summers are hot and dry, and winters are cool with some rain. The temperature is warm most of the year.

quiz.q: Which is a statement about climate?
ch: San Diego is usually mild and sunny all year.
It is raining in San Diego right now.
Today's high in San Diego is 71°F.
A storm will hit San Diego tonight.

quiz.q: Data for two places: Place 1 averages 85°F with 80 inches of rain a year. Place 2 averages 20°F with 10 inches of rain, mostly as snow. Which place is most likely near the North Pole?
Place 1 averages 80 inches of rain a year and Place 2 averages 10 inches. How many more inches does Place 1 get?
A family is moving from a hot desert to a cold, snowy region. Which item will they most likely need to buy?
Why do people in a rainy climate often build houses with steep, slanted roofs?
ch: so rain and snow slide off easily
so the sun cannot reach the house

quiz.q: A globe shows that places near the equator are usually hot and places near the poles are usually cold. A new town is near the equator. What climate does it most likely have?
ch: warm or hot most of the year
cold and dry like the Arctic

quiz.q: Explain the difference between weather and climate. Give one example of each.
quiz.ans: Weather is the conditions at one time and place, like "it is cloudy today." Climate is the usual weather over many years, like "Los Angeles has warm, dry summers."

test.q: Which tool would you use to find out how much rain fell last night?
Climate describes
ch: the usual weather of a place over many years

test.q: Which is a weather observation?
ch: The air is foggy and cool this morning.

test.q: Which statement best describes a polar climate?
ch: cold most of the year with snow and ice
hot and dry with cactus plants

test.q: A table shows the high temperature in a city: Monday 75°F, Tuesday 77°F, Wednesday 79°F, Thursday 81°F. If the pattern continues, what is the best prediction for Friday?
Using the same data (Monday 75°F, Tuesday 77°F, Wednesday 79°F, Thursday 81°F), how many degrees warmer was Thursday than Monday?
A bar graph of rainfall in Fresno shows tall bars from December to March and almost no bar from June to August. When does Fresno get most of its rain?
ch: in the same amount every month

test.q: A city recorded these rainy days: October 2, November 5, December 8. How many rainy days were there in all three months?
A desert town averages 3 inches of rain a year. A coastal forest town averages 45 inches. How many more inches does the forest town get?
Which graph would best show how temperature changes from month to month in one city?
ch: a bar graph with one bar for each month
a pie cut into two pieces

test.q: Why do weather forecasters study patterns in weather data?
ch: to predict what the weather will probably be

test.q: Which climate would be best for a plant that needs a lot of water and warm temperatures all year?
A wind vane points north. What does this tell you?
ch: The wind is blowing from the north.

test.q: A pictograph shows snowy days. Each snowflake stands for 3 days. January has 4 snowflakes. How many snowy days did January have?
Each snowflake stands for 3 snowy days. February has 2 snowflakes. How many snowy days did February have?
Two cities have the same temperature today, 70°F. City A is usually 30°F in winter, and City B is usually 65°F in winter. Which statement is true?
ch: They have the same temperature today but different climates.
Weather and climate are the same thing.

test.q: A class graphed one year of rainfall. Their graph shows 5 inches in January, 4 in February, 3 in March and almost none in summer. A student says, "Next summer will probably be dry." What evidence best supports the student?
ch: The graph shows almost no rain in summer.

test.q: Which place would most likely have a hot climate with very little rain?
ch: the coast of northern California in winter

test.q: A thermometer showed 41°F at sunrise and 68°F in the afternoon. How many degrees warmer was the afternoon?
Explain why a weather prediction can be wrong even when scientists use data.
test.ans: Predictions are based on patterns of what usually happens, but weather can change in ways the pattern did not show, so a prediction tells what is likely, not certain.

test.q: Name a climate region of the world and describe its usual temperature and rainfall.
test.ans: Sample: A tropical rain forest is hot all year and gets lots of rain almost every day.

test.q: A family wants to plan a camping trip in the Sierra Nevada mountains. What weather data should they look at, and how would it help them choose a month?
test.ans: They should look at the usual temperature, rain and snow for each month. Choosing a month that is usually warm and dry would make the trip safer and more comfortable.

test.q: Two towns kept weather records. Town A: average summer high 95°F, average winter high 65°F, about 5 inches of rain a year. Town B: average summer high 70°F, average winter high 40°F, about 50 inches of rain and snow a year. A family wants to grow plants that need lots of water and cool weather. Make a claim about which town is the better choice. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Town B is the better choice. Evidence: Town B gets about 50 inches of rain and snow a year, compared with 5 inches in Town A, and its summer high is 70°F instead of 95°F. Reasoning: The plants need lots of water and cool weather. Town B's climate gives more water and cooler temperatures, so the plants would get what they need without as much watering.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 2: Weather Hazards and Engineering Solutions
units.el: Teach criteria ("what the design must do") and constraints ("limits, like time, money or materials") with a two-column chart and picture examples; let students rehearse the frame "My design is good because it ___."

lessons.name: What makes some kinds of weather dangerous?

practice.q: Which is a weather-related hazard?
practice.h: A hazard is something that can hurt people or damage things.

practice.q: Heavy rain falls for three days on a town next to a river. Which hazard is most likely?
practice.h: Where does all that rain water go?

practice.q: A drought is a long time with
practice.h: Think about what plants and farms would be missing.

practice.q: Dry plants, hot temperatures and strong winds together make which hazard more likely in California?
practice.h: Which hazard needs dry fuel to burn?

practice.q: A town recorded 4 floods in the 1990s, 2 in the 2000s and 5 in the 2010s. How many floods is that in all?
practice.h: Add the three numbers.

practice.q: Choose one weather hazard. Describe one way it can harm people, animals or buildings.
practice.ans: Sample: A hurricane brings very strong winds that can tear roofs off houses and knock down trees and power lines.

quiz.q: What should you do when you hear thunder outside?
ch: go inside a building or a hard-topped car
lie down on a metal bench

quiz.q: Which hazard is caused by a long period with much less rain than normal?
A blizzard is most dangerous because of
ch: heavy snow, strong wind and very cold air

quiz.q: Why can a hurricane cause flooding along a coast?
ch: It brings heavy rain and pushes ocean water onto land.
It blows all the water away from shore.

quiz.q: Strong winds damaged 18 trees in a park on Monday and 9 more on Tuesday. How many trees were damaged in all?
Weather scientists cannot stop a storm. What can they do that helps people stay safe most?
ch: predict storms and warn people early
move the storm to the ocean

quiz.q: Explain why people cannot prevent weather hazards but can still reduce the damage they cause.
quiz.ans: Weather is caused by natural forces that people cannot control. People can reduce damage by building stronger structures, making warning systems and having safety plans.

lessons.name: How can we protect a home from floods and strong winds?

practice.q: A house is built on tall posts near a river. What hazard does this design protect against?
practice.h: Think about where water goes when the river rises.

practice.q: What is the purpose of a levee, a high wall of earth along a river?
ch: to keep river water from spreading onto the land
to make the river flow faster uphill
to give fish a place to live
practice.h: A levee is like a long, tall wall next to the water.

practice.q: Which design helps a roof stay on a house during strong winds?
ch: metal straps that tie the roof to the walls
a roof painted a bright color
practice.h: The roof needs to be held down tightly.

practice.q: Which design reduces the danger of lightning hitting a tall building?
ch: a lightning rod connected to the ground
a fence around the parking lot
practice.h: Lightning needs a safe path to the ground.

practice.q: A town stacks sandbags along a river. Team A fills 45 bags and Team B fills 38 bags. How many sandbags do they fill in all?
practice.h: Add the two teams' bags.

practice.q: Describe one design that reduces damage from wildfire to a home.
practice.ans: Sample: Clearing dry brush and dead plants away from the house so a fire has less fuel near the walls.

quiz.q: Storm shutters on windows protect a home from
Which design would best reduce flooding on a city street?
ch: storm drains that carry rainwater away

quiz.q: A school in tornado country builds a room with thick concrete walls and no windows. What is the purpose?
ch: to give people a safe place during a tornado
to keep the room cool in summer

quiz.q: An engineer must design a flood wall. The problem says "The wall must be at least 2 meters tall." This is a
A flood wall is 3 meters tall. Last year the highest river water reached 2 meters. How many meters higher than the water is the wall?
A town gets heavy rain every winter. Which pair of solutions would best reduce flood damage?
ch: building houses closer to the river and removing drains
taking down the levee and paving fields

quiz.q: Two roof designs were tested with a fan that blew harder each minute. Roof A, nailed on, blew off at minute 3. Roof B, nailed on and tied down with metal straps, was still on at minute 8 when the test ended. Make a claim about which roof design is better for an area with strong winds. Use evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: Roof B is the better design for strong winds. Evidence: Roof A blew off at minute 3, but Roof B stayed on through minute 8 even as the wind got stronger. Reasoning: The metal straps hold the roof to the walls, so it can stand up to stronger wind, which is what an area with strong storms needs.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: How do engineers choose the best solution?

practice.q: In engineering, criteria are
ch: the things a design must do to be successful
the limits on materials, time or money
the last step of a test
the people who use a design
practice.h: Criteria answer "What counts as success?"

practice.q: Which is a constraint?
ch: The design can cost no more than $20.
The design must keep water out.
practice.h: A constraint is a limit.

practice.q: A class must build a model shelter that stays dry in a rainstorm, using only paper, tape and foil. Which is a constraint?
ch: They can use only paper, tape and foil.
It must hold one toy figure.
It must survive the rainstorm test.
practice.h: Which one limits what they can use?

practice.q: Foil costs 3 cents per sheet. A team uses 8 sheets. How many cents do they spend on foil?
practice.h: Multiply cost per sheet by number of sheets.

practice.q: Why do engineers come up with several possible solutions before building one?
ch: so they can compare ideas and pick the one most likely to meet the criteria
because the first idea is always wrong
so they can use every material
so they do not have to test
practice.h: Think about how having choices helps.

practice.q: Your class must design a way to keep the school garden from drying out during a drought. Write one criterion and one constraint for the problem.
practice.ans: Criterion: the plants must get enough water to stay alive. Constraint: we can only use water from the rain barrels, or we only have $30 to spend.

quiz.q: What is the first step an engineer takes?
ch: define the problem, including criteria and constraints

quiz.q: Three umbrella designs are compared. Design A keeps people dry and costs $8. Design B keeps people dry and costs $25. Design C leaks and costs $5. The constraint is "costs $10 or less." Which design is best?
Using the same designs (A costs $8, B costs $25, C costs $5), how many dollars more does Design B cost than Design A?

A team compares two flood barriers. Barrier 1 holds back water for 10 minutes. Barrier 2 holds back water for 25 minutes. Both cost the same. Which barrier better meets the criterion "holds back water as long as possible"?
Which question helps engineers compare solutions?
ch: Which design best meets the criteria within the constraints?
Which design did the tallest student make?
Which design used the most tape?

quiz.q: A team has 30 minutes to build. They spend 12 minutes planning and 15 minutes building. How many minutes do they have left?
Explain why a design that works very well might still not be chosen.
quiz.ans: It might not meet a constraint. For example, it could cost too much, take too long to build or use materials that are not available.

lessons.name: How do engineers test and improve a design?

practice.q: In a fair test, an engineer changes
ch: only one thing at a time
practice.h: If you change many things, you cannot tell which one caused the result.

practice.q: A team tests two model roofs in a wind test. To be fair, which must be the same for both roofs?
ch: the strength of the fan and the distance from the fan
practice.h: Keep the test conditions the same so only the design is different.

practice.q: A model house leaks water at the corners during a rain test. What should the team do next?
ch: find the failure point at the corners and improve that part
test a different house without fixing it
practice.h: Look closely at where it failed.

practice.q: A model shelter stayed dry for 4 minutes in the first test. After improvements it stayed dry for 11 minutes. How many minutes longer did it stay dry?
practice.h: Subtract the first time from the second time.

practice.q: Why do engineers test a design more than once?
ch: to make sure the results are reliable
practice.h: What if the first test had a mistake?

practice.q: Explain what a failure point is and why it helps engineers.
practice.ans: A failure point is the part of a design that breaks or does not work during a test. Finding it shows engineers exactly what to improve.

quiz.q: What do engineers do after testing a design and finding a problem?
ch: improve the design and test it again
build ten more of the same design

quiz.q: A team tested how much water a model levee held back. Trial 1: 300 mL. Trial 2: 310 mL. Trial 3: 50 mL, because a cup tipped over. What should the team do with trial 3?
ch: repeat it, because something went wrong in that trial

quiz.q: Using trials 1 and 2 (300 mL and 310 mL), how many more milliliters did the levee hold back in trial 2?
Two students test wind shields made of foil and of cardboard. Student A uses a fan on high; Student B uses a fan on low. Why is this not a fair test?
ch: The fan speed changed, so it is not clear which material is better.
Foil and cardboard are different colors.

quiz.q: A rain test used a watering can. Each test poured 4 cups of water, and the team ran 6 tests. How many cups of water did they use?
A model shelter passed the wind test but failed the rain test because the roof had gaps. Which change is most likely to improve it without making it fail the wind test?
ch: cover the gaps with tape and foil while keeping the roof attached
make the walls out of tissue paper
test it only on sunny days

quiz.q: Describe how you would test whether a model house stays dry in a storm. Name one thing you would keep the same in every test.
quiz.ans: Pour the same amount of water over the model from the same height for the same time, then check inside for wet spots. Keep the amount of water the same each time.

test.q: Which kind of weather can damage buildings and is called a weather hazard?
A constraint is
ch: a limit on a design, such as cost or materials

test.q: Which design helps protect a building from lightning?
ch: a flag pole made of wood

test.q: A town on a river floods every few years. Which solution would reduce damage to homes?
ch: build a levee and raise homes on posts
build more homes beside the river
plant flowers along the banks only

test.q: Why do people in hurricane areas cover windows with shutters?
ch: to keep wind and flying objects from breaking the glass
to keep the house warm in winter
to keep snow off the roof
to keep the river from rising

test.q: Which situation is a drought?
ch: a region gets much less rain than normal for many months
strong winds spin in a funnel cloud
a lot of snow falls in a day

test.q: Which statement is a criterion for a storm shelter design?
ch: It must keep people safe from wind and rain.
It must be built in one week.
It can use only wood and nails.

test.q: Why is it helpful to have several possible solutions to a weather problem?
ch: You can compare them and choose the one that best meets the criteria and constraints.
Then you never need to test.
One of them will stop the weather.

test.q: A town needs 60 sandbags. Volunteers have filled 42. How many more sandbags do they need to fill?
A rain barrel collects 8 liters of water each rainy day. How many liters does it collect in 5 rainy days?
Two shelter designs both keep water out. Design X costs $40 and Design Y costs $90. The budget is $50. Which design should be chosen?
In a wind test, the fan speed, the distance and the length of time are kept the same. What is being changed?
A team's model bridge broke in the middle during a flood test. What do engineers call the place where a design breaks?
What is the best reason to test a design three times instead of once?
ch: to see if the results are the same each time
because the first test never counts

test.q: Wall A held back water for 14 minutes. Wall B held back water for 23 minutes. How many minutes longer did Wall B last?
Which is the safest place to go during a tornado warning?
ch: a small inside room on the lowest floor, away from windows
near a big window to watch

test.q: Which design solution helps reduce wildfire damage to homes?
ch: keeping dry brush cleared away from buildings
planting dry grass next to the walls
using wooden shingles that catch fire easily

test.q: A team tested three roof designs in a fan test that got stronger each minute. Roof 1 lasted 2 minutes, Roof 2 lasted 6 minutes, and Roof 3 lasted 5 minutes. Roof 2 costs much more than Roof 3. The town has a small budget. Which roof is the best choice?
ch: Roof 3, because it almost matches Roof 2 and costs less
Roof 1, because it lasted the shortest time
Roof 2, because cost does not matter

test.q: Using the roof data (Roof 1 lasted 2 minutes, Roof 2 lasted 6 minutes, Roof 3 lasted 5 minutes), how many minutes did all three roofs last altogether?
Explain why engineers change only one thing at a time when they test a design.
test.ans: If they change only one thing, they know that thing caused any change in the result. If they change many things, they cannot tell which one made the difference.

test.q: Name a weather hazard in California and describe one design that reduces its impact.
test.ans: Sample: Floods. Storm drains carry rainwater away from streets, or levees keep rivers from spilling onto land.

test.q: A school near a creek floods during heavy winter rains. The class compared two solutions. Solution A, a row of sandbags: costs $200, held back water about 30 cm deep in a test, must be set up before every storm. Solution B, a rain garden with plants and gravel: costs $800, soaked up water so the school field stayed dry in 5 of 6 storms, needs weeding twice a year. The school's budget is $1,000 and the principal wants a solution that does not need to be set up before every storm. Make a claim about which solution has more merit for this school. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Solution B, the rain garden, has more merit for this school. Evidence: It kept the field dry in 5 of 6 storms, it costs $800, which is under the $1,000 budget, and it only needs weeding twice a year. Sandbags must be set up before every storm. Reasoning: The rain garden meets the criterion of reducing flooding and fits the constraints of the budget and of not needing setup before each storm, so it is the better design solution even though it costs more.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 3: Forces and Motion
units.el: Act out push, pull, balanced and unbalanced with a rope and a cart; have students draw force arrows and label them with "push" or "pull" and "bigger" or "smaller."

lessons.name: What makes an object start or stop moving?

practice.q: A push or a pull is called a
practice.h: It is the word scientists use for any push or pull.

practice.q: A ball is sitting still on the grass. What is needed to make it move?
practice.h: Objects at rest need a push or pull to start moving.

practice.q: A wagon is rolling across the playground. Which force will make it stop?
ch: a pull or push in the opposite direction, like friction from the ground
a push in the same direction
practice.h: To stop something, the force must act against the motion.

practice.q: Which action is a pull?
practice.h: A pull moves something toward you.

practice.q: Ana pushes a toy car and it rolls 85 centimeters. Then she pushes it harder and it rolls 140 centimeters. How many centimeters farther did it roll after the harder push?
practice.h: Subtract the shorter distance from the longer one.

practice.q: Describe what happens to a soccer ball's motion when a player kicks it, and then when the goalie catches it.
practice.ans: The kick is a force that makes the ball start moving. When the goalie catches it, the goalie's hands push against the ball and make it stop.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a force?
A hockey puck slides across the ice and slowly stops. Which force slows it down?
ch: friction between the puck and the ice
a push from the wind behind it

quiz.q: How can you make a rolling ball change direction?
A class rolled a ball 3 times with a gentle push. It rolled 40 cm, 45 cm and 50 cm. How many centimeters did it roll in all?
Jamal kicks a ball softly and then kicks the same ball harder. What happens with the harder kick?
ch: The ball moves faster and goes farther.
The ball goes the same distance.

quiz.q: A toy car rolls farther on a smooth wood floor than on a carpet with the same push. What is the best explanation?
ch: The carpet causes more friction, which slows the car more.
The carpet pushes the car forward.
The wood floor has no gravity.
The car is lighter on wood.

quiz.q: Name two ways a force can change an object's motion. Give an example of each.
quiz.ans: A force can start or stop motion, like kicking a ball or catching it. A force can change direction, like hitting a tennis ball back over the net. (Speeding up or slowing down also count.)

lessons.name: What happens when forces are balanced or unbalanced?

practice.q: When two forces are the same size and push in opposite directions, the forces are
practice.h: Think of a tug of war where no one moves.

practice.q: In a tug of war, Team Red pulls left with a force of 200 newtons and Team Blue pulls right with a force of 200 newtons. What happens to the rope?
practice.h: Compare the two forces.

practice.q: Team Red now pulls left with 250 newtons and Team Blue still pulls right with 200 newtons. Which way does the rope move?
practice.h: The rope moves toward the bigger force.

practice.q: Using the same tug of war (Team Red pulls 250 newtons, Team Blue pulls 200 newtons), how many newtons more does Team Red pull?
practice.h: Find the difference between the two forces.

practice.q: A book is resting on a table. Gravity pulls it down and the table pushes it up. What is true about these forces?
ch: They are balanced, so the book stays still.
They are unbalanced, so the book moves.
There are no forces on the book.
practice.h: The book is not moving. What does that tell you?

practice.q: Draw or describe a force diagram for a box that two children push from opposite sides, where one child pushes harder. Tell which way the box moves.
practice.ans: Two arrows pointing toward each other from opposite sides of the box; the arrow for the harder push is longer. The box moves in the direction of the longer arrow, away from the child who pushes harder.

quiz.q: Unbalanced forces on an object can
In a force diagram, a longer arrow means
Two dogs pull on the same rope toy in opposite directions. The toy does not move. What can you conclude?
ch: The dogs are pulling with equal force.
One dog is pulling much harder.
There are no forces on the toy.
The toy is too heavy for any force.

quiz.q: Mia pushes a box to the right with 30 newtons. Leo pushes it to the left with 18 newtons. How many newtons stronger is Mia's push?
Using the same pushes (Mia pushes right with 30 newtons, Leo pushes left with 18 newtons), which way does the box move?
A box has 40 newtons pushing left and 40 newtons pushing right. What is the difference between the two forces in newtons?

A class tested a cart with two spring scales attached to opposite ends. Trial 1: left pull 5 newtons, right pull 5 newtons, the cart did not move. Trial 2: left pull 5 newtons, right pull 8 newtons, the cart moved right. Trial 3: left pull 9 newtons, right pull 4 newtons, the cart moved left. Make a claim about what makes the cart move. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: The cart moves only when the forces are unbalanced, and it moves toward the stronger pull. Evidence: In trial 1 the pulls were equal (5 and 5) and the cart stayed still. In trial 2 the right pull was stronger (8 vs 5) and the cart moved right. In trial 3 the left pull was stronger (9 vs 4) and it moved left. Reasoning: Balanced forces cancel each other, so motion does not change. Unbalanced forces change the cart's motion in the direction of the bigger force.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: How can we predict motion that repeats?

practice.q: Which motion repeats in a pattern?
ch: a child swinging back and forth on a swing
a rock sitting on the ground
a leaf landing once on the grass
a ball resting in a box
practice.h: Look for something that keeps going back and forth.

practice.q: A pendulum is a weight hanging from a string that swings back and forth. A class counts its swings: 10 swings in the first 10 seconds and 10 swings in the next 10 seconds. How many swings should it make in the next 10 seconds?
practice.h: Use the pattern the class already saw.

practice.q: A pendulum makes 12 swings every 10 seconds. How many swings will it make in 30 seconds?
practice.h: 30 seconds is three groups of 10 seconds.

practice.q: A ball is dropped and bounces. Each bounce is lower than the one before. Which prediction fits the pattern?
ch: The next bounce will be lower again.
The next bounce will be higher.
The ball will bounce forever at the same height.
practice.h: What happened each time it bounced?

practice.q: A seesaw goes up and down when two children take turns pushing off the ground. Why can you predict when one side will go up?
ch: The motion repeats in a regular pattern.
There is no force on it.
practice.h: Think about what happens over and over.

practice.q: A student times a swing. It goes forward and back 4 times every 10 seconds. Explain how the student can use this pattern to predict the number of swings in 20 seconds.
practice.ans: The pattern shows 4 swings every 10 seconds. 20 seconds is two 10-second groups, so it should make about 4 + 4 = 8 swings.

quiz.q: Patterns in motion help us
A class tested pendulums with different string lengths. Short string: 15 swings in 15 seconds. Long string: 9 swings in 15 seconds. What pattern does the data show?
ch: The longer string swings more slowly.

quiz.q: Using the same data (short string 15 swings, long string 9 swings in 15 seconds), how many more swings did the short string make?
A toy car rolls down a ramp, up a small hill and back down, again and again on a curved track. A student wants to predict where the car will be. What should the student do first?
ch: observe and record where it goes several times to find a pattern

quiz.q: A playground swing goes back and forth 3 times every 6 seconds. How many times will it go back and forth in 12 seconds?
A pendulum is pulled back and let go. It makes a regular pattern of swings. A student wants it to swing more slowly. Based on what the class learned, what should the student change?
Give an example of a motion in everyday life that repeats in a pattern and explain how you could use it to make a prediction.
quiz.ans: Sample: A playground swing moves back and forth at a steady pace. If I count 5 swings every 10 seconds, I can predict about 10 swings in 20 seconds.

test.q: A force is
ch: a kind of energy you can see
the weight of an object only

test.q: Which force slows down a bike when the rider squeezes the brakes?
Forces that are equal in size and opposite in direction are
A shopping cart is still. A child pushes it with a small force. What happens?
ch: The cart starts to move in the direction of the push.

test.q: Two students pull a box in opposite directions with the same force. What happens to the box?
ch: It moves toward the first student.
It moves toward the second student.

test.q: In a force diagram, an arrow pointing right is longer than an arrow pointing left. What will the object do?
Which change will make a rolling marble stop sooner?
ch: rolling it onto a rough carpet

test.q: Team A pulls a rope with 320 newtons. Team B pulls the other way with 290 newtons. How many newtons stronger is Team A's pull?
Using the same tug of war (Team A pulls 320 newtons and Team B pulls 290 newtons), which team will win?
A pendulum swings 8 times every 10 seconds. How many times will it swing in 40 seconds?
A ball rolls toward a wall and bounces back. What caused its direction to change?
ch: The wall pushed on the ball.
The ball ran out of energy.

test.q: A book sits on a shelf without moving. Which is true?
ch: The forces on it are balanced.
The forces on it are unbalanced.
Only one force acts on it.

test.q: A class pushed a toy truck with a weak, medium and strong push. Distances: weak 30 cm, medium 70 cm, strong 120 cm. What pattern does the data show?
ch: A stronger push makes the truck go farther.
A stronger push makes the truck go a shorter distance.
All pushes made the truck go the same distance.

test.q: Using the same data (weak 30 cm, medium 70 cm, strong 120 cm), how many centimeters farther did the truck go with the strong push than the weak push?
Using the same data (weak 30 cm, medium 70 cm, strong 120 cm), what is the total distance for all three pushes?
Two pendulums are the same except for string length. Pendulum A has a 20 cm string and Pendulum B has a 60 cm string. Which prediction is best?
ch: Pendulum B will swing more slowly.
Pendulum A will swing more slowly.
Both will swing at exactly the same rate.
Pendulum B will not swing at all.

test.q: A cart is pulled left with 6 newtons and right with 6 newtons. Then the right pull changes to 10 newtons. What happens?
ch: The cart starts moving to the right.
The cart starts moving to the left.
The cart moves up and down.

test.q: Which is an example of motion with a pattern you can predict?
ch: the hands moving around a clock
a paper bag blowing in a gusty wind
a dropped puzzle piece sliding on the floor
a cat jumping around the room

test.q: A student wants to test whether a harder push makes a ball roll farther. Which must stay the same in every trial?
Explain the difference between balanced and unbalanced forces. Give an example of each.
test.ans: Balanced forces are equal and opposite, so they cancel and the motion does not change, like a lamp sitting on a table. Unbalanced forces are not equal, so they change motion, like kicking a ball to make it move.

test.q: A swing goes back and forth 5 times in 10 seconds. Predict how many times it will swing in 30 seconds and explain your thinking.
test.ans: About 15 times. The swing repeats in a pattern: 30 seconds is three groups of 10 seconds, and 5 + 5 + 5 = 15.

test.q: Describe how you would plan a fair investigation to find out whether a heavier box needs a bigger push to start moving.
test.ans: Use two boxes that are the same size and on the same floor, one with more weight inside. Pull each one with a spring scale and record the force needed to start it moving. Repeat 3 times and compare.

test.q: A class rolled a toy car down the same ramp onto three surfaces. Distance traveled after the ramp: tile floor 210 cm, wood floor 180 cm, carpet 60 cm. Make a claim about how the surface affects the car's motion. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Rougher surfaces make the car stop sooner. Evidence: The car went 210 cm on smooth tile and 180 cm on wood, but only 60 cm on carpet, which is the roughest surface. Reasoning: Friction is a force that pushes against motion. The rough carpet causes more friction, so the forces on the car are unbalanced against its motion sooner, which slows it down and stops it in a shorter distance.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 4: Magnets and Static Electricity
units.el: Give partners real magnets, paper clips and a balloon; teach "attract" with a pulling-together hand motion and "repel" with a pushing-apart motion, and use the frame "The ___ attracts/repels the ___ because ___."

lessons.name: How can a magnet move something without touching it?

practice.q: Which object will a magnet attract?
practice.h: Magnets attract objects that contain iron, like steel.

practice.q: A magnet pulls a paper clip toward it before they touch. What does this show?
ch: Magnetic force can act without touching.
The paper clip is pushing itself.
practice.h: Notice that there was a gap between them.

practice.q: A student puts a sheet of paper between a magnet and a paper clip. The clip still moves toward the magnet. What can the student conclude?
ch: Magnetic force can pass through paper.
The paper clip is made of paper.
practice.h: What happened even with the paper in the way?

practice.q: Which is the best question to test with a magnet and a pile of objects?
ch: Which materials does a magnet attract?
practice.h: A good science question can be answered by testing.

practice.q: A class tested 12 objects. The magnet attracted 5 of them. How many objects were not attracted?
practice.h: Subtract the attracted objects from the total.

practice.q: Name two objects in your classroom a magnet would attract and two it would not. Tell what the attracted objects have in common.
practice.ans: Attracted: a steel paper clip and a steel staple. Not attracted: a plastic ruler and a wooden pencil. The attracted objects contain iron or steel.

quiz.q: Most objects that a magnet attracts contain
A student sorts objects. Which group shows only objects a magnet attracts?
ch: steel nail, steel paper clip, iron washer
aluminum foil, glass marble, steel nail

quiz.q: A magnet picked up 6 paper clips on the first try, 8 on the second and 7 on the third. How many paper clips did it pick up in all?
A magnet is held under a thin wooden table. A steel ball on top of the table moves when the magnet moves. Why?
ch: The magnetic force passes through the wood.
The ball is made of wood.

quiz.q: Which is a cause and effect relationship?
ch: Bringing a magnet near a steel pin causes the pin to move.

quiz.q: A student finds that a magnet attracts a steel can but not an aluminum can. Which question would be best to investigate next?
ch: Which other metals does a magnet attract?
How many cans are in the store?

quiz.q: Describe an investigation to find out if a magnet can pull a paper clip through water.
quiz.ans: Put a paper clip in a cup of water. Hold a magnet against the outside of the cup near the clip and move it. Watch whether the clip moves with the magnet.

lessons.name: Why do magnets sometimes push each other away?

practice.q: The two ends of a bar magnet are called
practice.h: They are labeled N and S.

practice.q: What happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought near the south pole of another magnet?
practice.h: Opposite poles behave differently from like poles.

practice.q: What happens when two north poles are brought close together?
practice.h: Poles that are the same push apart.

practice.q: A magnet holds a paper clip when they are 1 cm apart but not when they are 5 cm apart. What does this show?
ch: Magnetic force gets weaker as distance increases.
Magnetic force gets stronger with distance.
practice.h: Compare what happened at the short and long distances.

practice.q: A magnet attracted a paper clip from 4 cm away. A stronger magnet attracted it from 11 cm away. How many centimeters farther away did the stronger magnet work?
practice.h: Subtract the distances.

practice.q: Two ring magnets on a pencil float apart instead of touching. Explain why.
practice.ans: The magnets are placed with the same poles facing each other, so they repel and push each other apart even though they are not touching.

quiz.q: Opposite poles of two magnets

A class measured how many paper clips a magnet could hold through different numbers of index cards. 0 cards: 10 clips. 2 cards: 6 clips. 4 cards: 3 clips. 6 cards: 1 clip. What pattern does the data show?
ch: As the distance grows, the magnet holds fewer clips.
As the distance grows, the magnet holds more clips.
The cards make the magnet stronger.
The number of clips never changes.

quiz.q: Using the same data (0 cards: 10 clips, 6 cards: 1 clip), how many fewer clips did the magnet hold with 6 cards than with 0 cards?
Using the same data (0 cards: 10, 2 cards: 6, 4 cards: 3, 6 cards: 1), predict the number of clips with 8 cards.
Two toy trains have magnets on their ends. When Kai pushes them together, they push apart. What must be facing each other?
ch: like poles, such as north and north

quiz.q: A student says, "A bigger magnet is always stronger." What would be the best way to test this claim?
ch: Test magnets of different sizes and count how many paper clips each one holds.
Look at the colors of the magnets.
Ask a friend which magnet looks strongest.

quiz.q: Explain how you could find out which end of an unlabeled magnet is the north pole, using a magnet that is labeled N and S.
quiz.ans: Bring the labeled north pole near one end of the unlabeled magnet. If they repel, that end is a north pole. If they attract, that end is a south pole.

lessons.name: What makes a balloon stick to a wall?

practice.q: When you rub a balloon on your hair, the balloon gets
practice.h: This is called static electricity.

practice.q: After a balloon is rubbed on hair, the hair stands up and moves toward the balloon. What does this show?
ch: Electric charges can attract without touching.
The hair is made of iron.
practice.h: Was the balloon touching the hair when the hair moved?

practice.q: Two balloons are both rubbed on a wool sweater. When they hang near each other, they push apart. Why?
ch: They have the same kind of charge, so they repel.
They have opposite charges, so they attract.
practice.h: Like charges act like like poles.

practice.q: Which is an example of static electricity?
ch: a shock when you touch a doorknob after walking on carpet
a ball rolling down a hill
practice.h: Think of a tiny spark or a zap.

practice.q: A charged balloon picked up 14 tiny bits of paper. After 5 minutes it could only pick up 6 bits. How many fewer bits did it pick up?
practice.h: Subtract to compare.

practice.q: How are static electricity and magnetism alike?
practice.ans: Both can push or pull objects without touching them, and both can attract and repel.

quiz.q: Static electricity can make objects
A rubbed plastic comb is held near a thin stream of water from a faucet. The water bends toward the comb. What caused this?
ch: the electric charge on the comb

quiz.q: Which question asks about a cause and effect relationship with static electricity?
ch: Does rubbing a balloon longer make it pick up more paper bits?

quiz.q: A class rubbed a balloon for different times. 5 rubs: 3 paper bits. 10 rubs: 7 paper bits. 20 rubs: 15 paper bits. How many more paper bits did 20 rubs pick up than 5 rubs?
Using the same data (5 rubs: 3 bits, 10 rubs: 7 bits, 20 rubs: 15 bits), what pattern do you see?
ch: More rubbing picked up more paper bits.
More rubbing picked up fewer paper bits.

quiz.q: Two balloons rubbed on hair hang near each other. Then one balloon is touched to a metal pole and loses its charge. What will most likely happen?
ch: The balloons stop pushing apart as much.

quiz.q: A student rubbed a balloon on a wool cloth and held it 1 cm, 5 cm and 10 cm above a pile of paper bits. At 1 cm it picked up 12 bits, at 5 cm it picked up 4 bits, and at 10 cm it picked up 0 bits. Make a claim about how distance affects the electric force. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: The electric force gets weaker as the distance gets bigger. Evidence: The balloon picked up 12 bits at 1 cm, 4 bits at 5 cm and 0 bits at 10 cm. Reasoning: The balloon picked up fewer bits as it moved farther away, which means its pull was weaker. The charge can attract without touching, but only when objects are close enough.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: How can we use magnets to solve a problem?

practice.q: Which everyday object uses a magnet to stay closed?
practice.h: Think of a kitchen door that seals by itself.

practice.q: A recycling center needs to separate steel cans from aluminum cans. Which design idea uses magnets?
ch: Pass the cans under a big magnet that lifts out the steel cans.
practice.h: Which cans does a magnet attract?

practice.q: A class wants to design a latch that keeps a cabinet door closed. Which is a criterion?
ch: The door must stay shut when a small child pulls gently.
It must be finished by Friday.
Only magnets and tape can be used.
practice.h: A criterion tells what the design must do.

practice.q: A magnet latch costs $4. The class needs latches for 6 cabinets. How many dollars will the latches cost?
practice.h: Multiply the cost by the number of cabinets.

practice.q: A student designs a game where a paper fish with a steel paper clip is picked up by a magnet on a string. Why does the game work?
ch: The magnet attracts the steel clip.
practice.h: Which part of the fish does a magnet attract?

practice.q: Describe a problem at home or school that a magnet could help solve, and explain how.
practice.ans: Sample: Pins fall on the floor in the art room. A magnet on a stick could pick up the steel pins quickly without anyone touching the sharp points.

quiz.q: Which problem could a magnet help solve?
ch: finding a steel needle dropped in the carpet

quiz.q: A team designs a magnetic pencil holder for a steel whiteboard. In testing, it slides down when it is full of pencils. What is the best next step?
ch: Use a stronger magnet or add a second magnet and test again.

quiz.q: In a test, a magnet held 9 pencils. A stronger magnet held 15 pencils. How many more pencils did the stronger magnet hold?

A team tests three magnets for a door latch. Magnet A held the door shut against a pull of 2 newtons, Magnet B against 5 newtons, and Magnet C against 9 newtons. The door must stay shut against a pull of at least 4 newtons, and it must open with a pull of 6 newtons or less so adults can open it easily. Which magnet is the best choice?
Why did Magnet A not meet the criterion in that test (it held against only 2 newtons, and the door needed 4 newtons)?
ch: It was too weak to keep the door shut.

quiz.q: A latch design uses 2 magnets. The class is building 7 latches. How many magnets do they need?
Explain how engineers use magnets in at least one real machine or object.
quiz.ans: Sample: Cranes at a scrap yard use giant electromagnets to lift heavy pieces of steel and drop them where they are needed.

test.q: A magnet will attract
The ends of a magnet are called
What happens when the south pole of one magnet faces the south pole of another?
A paper clip jumps up to a magnet before touching it. What does this show?
ch: Magnets can pull objects without touching them.
Paper clips can jump on their own.

test.q: A magnet works through a plastic folder to move a steel pin. What does this show about magnetic force?
A balloon rubbed on hair sticks to a wall. Which force holds it there?
Two balloons rubbed on wool hang near each other. What will they most likely do?
A class measured how far a magnet could pull a paper clip across a table. Small magnet: 2 cm. Medium magnet: 5 cm. Large magnet: 9 cm. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: In this test, larger magnets pulled the clip from farther away.
All magnets have the same strength.
Paper clips pull on magnets more than magnets pull on clips.

test.q: Using the same data (small magnet 2 cm, large magnet 9 cm), how many centimeters farther did the large magnet pull the clip than the small magnet?
A magnet held 3 steel washers on Monday, 4 on Tuesday and 5 on Wednesday. How many washers did it hold in all?
Which question can be answered by an investigation with magnets?
ch: Does the magnet's pull get weaker when it is farther from a paper clip?

test.q: A recycling machine uses a magnet to pull out some cans. Which cans does it remove?
Which pair shows two objects that can attract each other without touching?
ch: a balloon rubbed on hair and small bits of paper
a wooden block and a plastic cup
a glass jar and a cotton ball

test.q: A charged comb picked up 10 bits of paper at 1 cm and 3 bits at 4 cm. How many fewer bits did it pick up at 4 cm?
A magnet holds 12 clips with no cards between it and the clips, 7 clips through 3 cards and 2 clips through 6 cards. Which is the best prediction for 9 cards?
A student wants to know whether magnets work through water. Which investigation is best?
ch: Put a steel clip in a cup of water and move a magnet outside the cup to see if the clip moves.
Put a magnet in water and see if it floats.
Hold a magnet above an empty cup.

test.q: A team designs a magnetic sign holder that falls off a steel door during testing. What should the team do?
ch: find why it failed and improve the design, then test again
test it on a wooden door

test.q: Which design solution uses magnets to solve a problem?
ch: a cabinet latch that keeps a door shut without a lock
a rubber band that holds papers
a glue stick that holds a poster
a nail that holds a picture

test.q: A team needs 3 magnets for each sign holder. How many magnets do they need for 8 sign holders?
Explain how magnetism and static electricity are different.
test.ans: Magnets attract objects made of iron or steel and have north and south poles. Static electricity comes from charges made by rubbing materials, and it can attract light objects like paper, hair or water.

test.q: Write a cause and effect question about magnets and describe how you would test it.
test.ans: Sample: Does adding more paper between a magnet and a paper clip make the pull weaker? Add one sheet of paper at a time and count how many clips the magnet can still hold.

test.q: A class tested how the distance between a magnet and a steel paper clip affects the pull. They used a spring scale to measure the force needed to pull the clip away. 1 cm: 6 units of force. 2 cm: 4 units. 3 cm: 2 units. 4 cm: 1 unit. Make a claim about how distance affects magnetic force. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Magnetic force gets weaker as the distance between the magnet and the clip increases. Evidence: At 1 cm it took 6 units of force to pull the clip away, but at 4 cm it took only 1 unit. The force went down each time the distance went up. Reasoning: A magnet can pull on steel without touching, but the pull depends on how close the objects are, so the closer the clip, the stronger the magnetic force.
