Reasoning: We see objects when light reflects off them into our eyes. Materials that reflect more light send more light to our eyes, so they are easier to see when there is little light.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: How can we send messages using patterns?

practice.q: A pattern of long and short signals used to send letters is a
practice.h: Morse code is one example.

practice.q: Two students send a message across the field by flashing a flashlight: one flash means "yes" and two flashes mean "no." What is being used to carry the information?
practice.h: What did they flash?

practice.q: Drums in some places were used long ago to send messages between villages. Why did this work?
ch: Patterns of drumbeats could travel as sound over a distance.
practice.h: How does sound get from one village to another?

practice.q: In a code, each letter uses 3 light flashes. How many flashes are needed for a 4-letter word?
practice.h: Multiply flashes per letter by the number of letters.

practice.q: A code uses 1 = on and 0 = off. Which pattern means on, off, on?
practice.h: Write 1 for on and 0 for off, in order.

practice.q: Design a simple code using claps to send the words "stop," "go" and "wait" to a teammate. Explain how your teammate would know which word you mean.
practice.ans: Sample: 1 clap = go, 2 claps = stop, 3 claps = wait. My teammate counts the claps, and each number stands for a different word.

quiz.q: Computers and phones send information as
ch: patterns of signals, such as 1s and 0s
magnets that fly through the air

quiz.q: Two teams sent the same 20-word message across a noisy gym. Team A used shouting: 9 words were wrong. Team B used a flashlight code: 2 words were wrong. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: In this test, the light code sent the message with fewer errors.

quiz.q: Using the same data (Team A had 9 wrong words and Team B had 2), how many more words did Team A get wrong?
Team B sent 20 words and got 2 wrong. How many words did Team B send correctly?
Which improvement would most likely reduce errors in a flashlight code?
ch: make every signal clearly long or short and repeat the message
send the message faster than the receiver can watch
turn the light off halfway through

quiz.q: Why do engineers compare several ways to send information?
ch: to find which way best meets criteria like speed, distance and accuracy
to use the most expensive way

quiz.q: A team's sound code worked across the classroom but not across the playground. Explain one likely reason and one way to improve the design.
quiz.ans: The sound got quieter as it traveled farther, so the receiver could not hear it clearly. They could use a louder sound, like a whistle, or switch to a light code that can be seen from far away.

test.q: The distance from one wave peak to the next is the
Sound is made by
We see an object because light
ch: reflects off the object into our eyes

test.q: A wave with a larger amplitude carries
ch: the same energy as any wave

test.q: A beach ball floats as ocean waves pass under it far from shore. What does the beach ball do?
ch: It moves up and down in about the same place.

test.q: A drum is hit harder. What happens to the sound?
ch: It gets louder because the amplitude is larger.
It gets higher because the wavelength is longer.

test.q: Which picture of a wave would show a higher-pitched sound?
Why can you not see your hand in a completely dark closet?
ch: No light reflects from your hand into your eyes.
Your hand disappears in the dark.

test.q: A student shines a flashlight at a mirror and the beam lights up a poster. Which describes the path of the light?
ch: the light goes straight through the mirror

test.q: A wave drawing has peaks at 0 cm, 8 cm, 16 cm and 24 cm. What is the wavelength in centimeters?
A team's code uses 4 beeps for each letter. How many beeps are needed for a 5-letter word?
A sound meter read 92 units next to a speaker and 58 units across the room. How many units quieter was it across the room?
In a code where 1 = flash on and 0 = flash off, what does 0110 mean?
Which material would reflect the most light?

Two students send messages across a field. Message A is a spoken sentence. Message B is a pattern of flag waves that each stand for a letter. On a windy, noisy day, which would most likely arrive with fewer errors, and why?
ch: Message B, because the flag pattern can be seen even when noise drowns out speech
Message A, because sound travels through wind easily
Both the same, because weather does not matter
Neither, because messages cannot travel across a field

test.q: A student makes two rope waves. Wave 1: amplitude 10 cm, wavelength 50 cm. Wave 2: amplitude 30 cm, wavelength 50 cm. Which is true?
Which sends information using patterns of electrical signals?
A class tested a flashlight code 3 times with a 15-word message. Errors: 3, 1 and 2. What was the average number of errors? (Add and divide by 3.)
Waves at a beach knock down a sandcastle. What does this show?
ch: Waves carry energy that can move objects.

test.q: Draw or describe a wave and label its amplitude and wavelength. Then describe how the wave would change if it carried more energy.
test.ans: A wave with peaks and troughs; amplitude is the height from the middle line to a peak, and wavelength is the distance from one peak to the next. With more energy, the amplitude would be larger, so the peaks would be taller.

test.q: Explain why a cat sitting in a dark room cannot be seen until someone turns on a lamp.
test.ans: We see objects only when light reflects off them into our eyes. Without the lamp, no light reflects from the cat, so we cannot see it.

test.q: A class tested two ways to send a 10-letter message 50 meters across the playground. Shouting: 4 letters wrong on a quiet day, 8 letters wrong on a windy day. Flashlight code (long and short flashes): 1 letter wrong on a quiet day, 1 letter wrong on a windy day. Make a claim about which method is the better design for sending messages across the playground. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: The flashlight code is the better design. Evidence: It had only 1 wrong letter on both days, while shouting had 4 wrong on a quiet day and 8 on a windy day. Reasoning: The flashlight code uses patterns of light that are easy to tell apart and are not affected by wind noise. Shouted sound gets quieter over distance and is drowned out by wind, so more information was lost.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 5: Structures, Senses and Survival
units.el: Use labeled photos and diagrams of plants and animals; teach structure (a part) and function (its job) with the frame "The ___ helps the ___ ___ by ___." Pair students to point to and name structures before writing.

lessons.name: How do plant structures help plants survive?

practice.q: Which plant structure takes in water and minerals from the soil?
practice.h: This part grows underground.

practice.q: Where does a plant make most of its food using sunlight?
practice.h: These parts are usually flat and green.

practice.q: A rose bush has sharp thorns on its stems. What is the function of the thorns?
ch: They protect the plant from animals that might eat it.
They help the plant drink water.
practice.h: Think about what an animal would feel if it bit the stem.

practice.q: Bright, sweet-smelling flowers help a plant
ch: attract pollinators so it can make seeds
practice.h: Bees and butterflies visit flowers.

practice.q: A class measured a sunflower stem. In week 1 it was 18 cm tall, and in week 4 it was 75 cm tall. How many centimeters did it grow?
practice.h: Subtract to find the change.

practice.q: Choose one plant structure and explain how it helps the plant survive, grow or reproduce.
practice.ans: Sample: The stem holds the plant up toward sunlight and carries water from the roots to the leaves.

quiz.q: Which plant structure helps make new plants?
A cactus has a thick, waxy stem and spines instead of broad leaves. How do these structures help it survive in the desert?
ch: They help it store water and lose less water.
They help it soak up rain from the air only.
They make it grow faster in the shade.

quiz.q: An apple tree makes fruit around its seeds. How does the fruit help the tree reproduce?
ch: Animals eat the fruit and spread the seeds to new places.
The fruit makes the tree taller.
The fruit keeps the roots warm.
The fruit makes food from sunlight.

quiz.q: A tomato plant made 14 tomatoes. Each tomato had about 60 seeds. About how many seeds were there in all?
A plant was left in a closet with no light for two weeks. Its leaves turned yellow. Which structure could not do its job?
ch: the leaves, which need light to make food
the roots, which need dark soil

quiz.q: Tall trees in a rain forest have wide, flared bases called buttress roots. What is the most likely function?
ch: to help hold the tall tree up in shallow soil
to catch rain on the leaves

quiz.q: Make an argument for how a pine tree's thick bark helps it survive.
quiz.ans: Thick bark is a hard outer covering that protects the inside of the tree from insects, from drying out and even from some fires, so the tree can keep growing.

lessons.name: How do animal body parts help them survive?

practice.q: A turtle's hard shell is an external structure that helps it
practice.h: Think about what a turtle does when it is in danger.

practice.q: An eagle has sharp, curved talons. What is their function?
ch: building a nest out of mud
practice.h: Talons are the eagle's claws.

practice.q: A duck has webbed feet. How do they help the duck?
ch: They push water to help it swim.
They keep it cool in the desert.
practice.h: Think about where ducks spend time.

practice.q: A porcupine is covered in sharp quills. Which statement is the best argument about this structure?
ch: The quills help the porcupine survive by keeping predators away.
The quills help the porcupine fly.
The quills help it see better.
The quills help it smell food.
practice.h: What would happen to an animal that tried to bite it?

practice.q: A hummingbird's beak is 2 cm long. A woodpecker's beak is 5 cm long. How many centimeters longer is the woodpecker's beak?
practice.h: Subtract the lengths.

practice.q: Describe an external structure of an animal that lives in a cold place and explain how it helps the animal survive.
practice.ans: Sample: A polar bear has thick fur and a layer of fat. The fur traps heat and the fat keeps the bear warm in icy water and snow.

quiz.q: Which is an external structure of a bird?
A giraffe's long neck helps it
Male peacocks have large, colorful tail feathers. How does this structure help with reproduction?
ch: It helps attract females so they can mate.
It helps them fly long distances.

quiz.q: Suppose scientists measured the fur of an Arctic fox in summer (3 cm thick) and winter (7 cm thick). How many centimeters thicker was the winter fur?
Using the same data (an Arctic fox's summer fur 3 cm thick and winter fur 7 cm thick), which is the best explanation for the change?
ch: Thicker fur helps the fox stay warm in the cold winter.
Thicker fur helps the fox stay cool.

quiz.q: A bird has a long, thin, pointed beak. Which food is it most likely adapted to eat?
Choose an animal and make an argument for how two of its external structures help it get food. Use evidence.
quiz.ans: Sample: A lion has sharp teeth and strong claws. The claws grab and hold prey, and the sharp teeth tear meat, so the lion can catch and eat other animals.

lessons.name: What structures inside the body help animals survive?

practice.q: Which internal organ pumps blood through the body?
practice.h: You can feel it beat in your chest.

practice.q: Which internal structures take in oxygen from the air?
practice.h: They fill up when you breathe in.

practice.q: A fish lives underwater. Which structure lets it get oxygen from water?
practice.h: Look at the slits on the sides of a fish's head.

practice.q: Many birds have hollow bones. How does this help them?
ch: Their light bones make flying easier.
Their bones make them heavier for diving.
practice.h: Think about what flying requires.

practice.q: A student counted her heartbeats for 15 seconds while resting: 21 beats. After jumping jacks, she counted 33 beats in 15 seconds. How many more beats did she count after exercise?
practice.h: Subtract the resting count.

practice.q: Explain how the skeleton and muscles work together to help an animal move.
practice.ans: The skeleton is a frame of bones that supports the body. Muscles attach to the bones and pull on them, which makes the body parts move.

quiz.q: The stomach's main function is to
A student's resting heart rate was 80 beats per minute. After running, it was 130 beats per minute. Why did it go up?
ch: The heart pumped faster to move more oxygen to the working muscles.
The lungs took over the heart's job.

quiz.q: Using the same data (80 beats per minute resting and 130 after running), how many more beats per minute was the heart rate after running?
A whale is a mammal that lives in the ocean. Why must it come to the surface?
ch: It needs to dry its gills.
It needs to see the Sun.

quiz.q: Which pair matches an internal structure with its function?
ch: brain - controls the body and processes information

quiz.q: An adult human skeleton has about 206 bones. A baby is born with about 270 bones, which grow together over time. About how many more bones does a baby have?
Make an argument for why the heart is important for an animal's survival.
quiz.ans: The heart pumps blood that carries oxygen and food to every part of the body. Without it, the body's cells would not get what they need, so the animal could not survive.

lessons.name: How do animals sense and respond to their surroundings?

practice.q: Which body part sends information from the senses to be processed?
practice.h: The brain is the body's control center.

practice.q: You touch a hot pan and quickly pull your hand away. In what order does this happen?
ch: skin senses heat -> nerves send a message -> muscles move the hand
muscles move -> skin senses heat -> brain forgets
brain moves the pan -> skin cools
eyes see the pan -> stomach responds
practice.h: Start with the sense organ.

practice.q: Owls hunt mice at night in dim light. Which senses most help them?
practice.h: Think about how to find a mouse in the dark.

practice.q: Bats send out high-pitched sounds and listen for the echoes. What does this help them do?
ch: find insects and avoid objects in the dark
practice.h: The echoes bounce off things.

practice.q: A student's reaction time was tested by catching a falling ruler. Trial 1: 18 cm. Trial 2: 14 cm. Trial 3: 13 cm. What was the average distance in centimeters? (Add the trials and divide by 3.)
practice.h: Add 18, 14 and 13, then divide by 3.

practice.q: Describe how a dog uses its senses to find a hidden treat. Name the sense, the sense organ and how the brain responds.
practice.ans: The dog smells the treat with its nose. Nerves send the smell information to the brain, which recognizes food and tells the dog's legs to move toward it.

quiz.q: Which organ processes information from the senses?
A rabbit hears a twig snap and freezes, then runs. Which statement explains this?
ch: Its ears sensed the sound, its brain processed it as danger and it responded by running.

quiz.q: A rattlesnake has pits on its face that sense heat. How does this help it hunt at night?
ch: It can sense the warm bodies of animals in the dark.

quiz.q: A class measured reaction time with a dropped ruler. Before practice, the average catch was 22 cm. After practice, it was 16 cm. How many centimeters better was the average after practice?
Some animals store memories of where they hid food. A squirrel buries acorns and later finds many of them. Which body part helps it remember?
A student models how we see a ball thrown at us and catch it. Which model is most complete?
ch: light from the ball enters the eyes, nerves carry signals to the brain, the brain sends signals to arm muscles
the ball sends sound to the ear and the ear catches it

quiz.q: Explain why animals that live in dark caves often have small eyes but a strong sense of touch or smell.
quiz.ans: In a dark cave there is little light, so eyes are less useful. Senses like touch and smell give the brain information about food and danger, which helps the animal survive.

test.q: Which plant structure holds the plant up and carries water to the leaves?
Which structure helps a fish get oxygen?
The brain's main job is to
ch: process information and control the body

test.q: A cactus has spines. Which is the best argument about their function?
ch: They protect the cactus from animals that want its water.
They help the cactus make seeds.
They help the cactus take in sunlight.

test.q: A polar bear's white fur helps it
ch: blend in with the snow while hunting

test.q: Which pair correctly matches an animal structure to its function?
A flower is brightly colored and has sweet nectar. Which statement explains how this helps the plant?
ch: It attracts animals that carry pollen so the plant can make seeds.
It keeps insects away from the plant.
It helps the plant take in water.
It makes the plant grow taller.

test.q: A student touches a cold ice cube and pulls her hand back. Which part sensed the cold?
Why does an animal's heart beat faster when it runs?
ch: to deliver more oxygen to its muscles

test.q: A class measured how far roots of two bean plants grew in one week: Plant A 12 cm and Plant B 19 cm. How many centimeters longer were Plant B's roots?
A student's breathing rate was 16 breaths per minute resting and 34 breaths per minute after running. How many more breaths per minute after running?
A ruler-drop test gave 20 cm, 17 cm and 14 cm. What was the average distance in centimeters? (Add and divide by 3.)
Bats find insects at night by
ch: sending out sounds and listening for echoes

test.q: A seed is covered by a hard coat. What is the function of the seed coat?
ch: to protect the young plant inside

test.q: A desert plant has long roots that reach deep under the ground. Which claim is best supported?
ch: The deep roots help the plant reach water far below the dry surface.
The deep roots help the plant catch insects.
The roots help the plant make seeds.
Deep roots make the plant shorter.

test.q: An animal has large ears, long legs and fur the color of sand. Which habitat is it most likely adapted to?
Which internal structure gives an animal's body shape and support?
A hummingbird's heart beats about 1,200 times a minute while flying and about 250 times a minute while resting. How many more beats per minute is that while flying?
A frog sees a fly, then flicks out its tongue to catch it. Which describes the order of events?
ch: eyes sense the fly -> brain processes it -> muscles move the tongue
tongue moves -> eyes see -> brain forgets
brain sees the fly -> eyes move the tongue
the fly signals the frog's stomach

test.q: Choose a plant. Describe one internal or external structure and argue how it helps the plant grow or reproduce.
test.ans: Sample: An oak tree's acorns are seeds with a hard shell. Squirrels carry and bury them, and some sprout into new oak trees, helping the oak reproduce.

test.q: Explain how a cat's senses, nerves and brain work together when it hears a mouse behind it.
test.ans: The cat's ears sense the sound. Nerves carry signals to the brain, which processes them as a possible meal and sends signals to the muscles so the cat turns and pounces.

test.q: Scientists compared two kinds of foxes. Arctic fox: ear length about 4 cm, thick white winter fur, lives where winter temperatures are often below -20°C. Fennec fox: ear length about 15 cm, thin sand-colored fur, lives in the Sahara desert where days can reach 45°C. Make a claim about how the foxes' external structures help them survive in their habitats. Use evidence and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Each fox has external structures that help it survive in its own habitat. Evidence: The Arctic fox has short ears (about 4 cm) and thick white fur where it is below -20°C. The fennec fox has very large ears (about 15 cm) and thin sand-colored fur where it reaches 45°C. Reasoning: Small ears and thick fur hold in body heat, and white fur blends with snow. Large ears let heat escape and help the fennec fox hear prey, and sand-colored fur blends with the desert, so each fox's structures fit its environment.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 6: Earth's Changing Surface and Natural Hazards
units.el: Build a stack of colored clay or paper layers to model rock layers; use photos of canyons, deltas and volcanoes, and pre-teach weathering (breaking down) and erosion (carrying away) with hand motions.

lessons.name: What can rock layers tell us about the past?

practice.q: In undisturbed rock layers, the oldest layer is usually
practice.h: Layers pile up over time, like a stack of newspapers.

practice.q: A layer of rock contains fossils of seashells and coral. What environment did that layer most likely form in?
practice.h: Where do seashells and coral live?

practice.q: A cliff has a bottom layer with fish fossils, a middle layer with fern fossils and a top layer with no fossils of water animals. Which story fits the layers?
ch: The area was underwater first, then later became land with plants.
The area was always a dry desert.
The area was land first and then the ocean.
The fossils were all buried at the same time.
practice.h: Read the layers from bottom (oldest) to top (newest).

practice.q: A layer of sediment builds up about 2 cm every 100 years. About how many centimeters would build up in 500 years?
practice.h: 500 years is five groups of 100 years.

practice.q: Which type of rock forms from layers of sand, mud and shells pressed together over a long time?
practice.h: "Sediment" means bits of sand, mud and shells.

practice.q: Explain how scientists can tell the order in which rock layers formed.
practice.ans: New layers are laid down on top of older layers, so in undisturbed rock the bottom layer formed first and the top layer formed last.

quiz.q: A fossil is found in a rock layer. What can it tell scientists?
ch: what lived in that area when the layer formed
what the weather will be next week
the color of the sky long ago

quiz.q: The walls of a canyon show many flat rock layers. A river flows at the bottom. Which explanation is best?
ch: The layers formed over a long time, and then the river slowly cut down through them.
The river made all the layers in one day.
The layers formed after the river dried up.

quiz.q: A layer with fossils of a tropical plant lies under a layer with fossils of animals that lived in cold places. What does this suggest?
ch: The climate changed from warm to cold over time.
The climate changed from cold to warm.
Plants and animals lived on top of each other.

quiz.q: A canyon wall is 360 meters tall. A river cut it about 1 meter deeper every 10,000 years. How many years would it take to cut 3 meters?
A rock layer has ripple marks like those on a sandy beach. What does this most likely show?
ch: The layer formed where moving water shaped the sand.
The layer formed in a volcano.
The layer is from outer space.

quiz.q: A model of rock layers has 5 layers. Each layer is 4 cm thick. How tall is the model in centimeters?
A fossil of a sea animal is found in a layer high up on a mountain. Use evidence to explain how this could happen.
quiz.ans: The fossil shows the layer formed under the sea. Over a very long time, forces inside Earth pushed the rock layers up to form the mountain.

lessons.name: How do water, wind, ice and plants change the land?

practice.q: The breaking of rock into smaller pieces is called
practice.h: "Weather" is in the word, but it means breaking down.

practice.q: The moving of rock and soil from one place to another is called
practice.h: This step carries pieces away.

practice.q: A class poured water over a sand hill model. With a small cup, little sand moved. With a big pitcher poured faster, a deep channel formed. What does this show?
ch: Faster, larger amounts of water cause more erosion.
Small cups cause the most erosion.
practice.h: Compare the amount and speed of the water.

practice.q: A tree's roots grow into a crack in a rock and make the crack wider. This is an example of
practice.h: The roots are breaking the rock.

practice.q: A riverbank wore away 15 cm in one year and 23 cm the next year after a big flood. How many centimeters did it wear away in both years?
practice.h: Add the two years.

practice.q: Water seeps into a crack in a rock and freezes. Explain how this can break the rock.
practice.ans: Water expands when it freezes into ice. The ice pushes on the sides of the crack and makes it bigger, and after many freezes and thaws the rock breaks apart.

quiz.q: Which can cause erosion?

A class tested how slope affects erosion. They poured 500 mL of water down a sand tray at three tilts. Low tilt: 20 g of sand moved. Medium tilt: 55 g moved. High tilt: 90 g moved. What pattern does the data show?
Using the same data (low tilt 20 g, medium tilt 55 g, high tilt 90 g), how many more grams of sand moved at high tilt than at low tilt?
A glacier slowly moves down a valley. What does it do to the land?
ch: scrapes and carves the valley wider and deeper

quiz.q: Planting grass on a hillside can reduce erosion because
ch: roots hold the soil in place

quiz.q: Sand dunes in a desert slowly move and change shape. What is the main cause?

Two hills were watered with the same amount of water in a model. Hill A, bare soil: 85 g of soil washed away. Hill B, covered with grass sod: 10 g washed away. Make a claim about how plants affect erosion. Use evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: Plants reduce erosion. Evidence: The bare hill lost 85 g of soil, but the grass-covered hill lost only 10 g with the same amount of water. Reasoning: Plant roots hold soil particles together and leaves slow down falling water, so less soil is carried away when plants cover the ground.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: Why are earthquakes and volcanoes found where they are?

practice.q: A map of earthquakes around the world shows that most earthquakes
ch: happen in long bands, often near the edges of continents and oceans
practice.h: Look for lines and patterns on the map.

practice.q: The "Ring of Fire" is a band of volcanoes and earthquakes around which ocean?
practice.h: California is on the edge of this ocean.

practice.q: A map shows that many tall mountain ranges, volcanoes and earthquakes are found in the same areas. What does this pattern suggest?
ch: The same forces inside Earth cause all three.
practice.h: Why would they be found together?

practice.q: A list shows 48 earthquakes in one month in California and 9 in Nevada. How many more were in California?
practice.h: Subtract the smaller number.

practice.q: Which California landform is a volcano?
practice.h: It is a tall, cone-shaped mountain in northern California.

practice.q: Describe what a map of volcanoes and earthquakes tells us about where they happen.
practice.ans: They are not spread out evenly. Most happen in bands along the edges of the giant plates of Earth's surface, such as around the Pacific Ocean.

quiz.q: Maps help scientists find
ch: patterns in where Earth's features and events occur

quiz.q: A map shows a deep ocean trench beside a chain of volcanoes. What is the best explanation?
ch: They formed where large plates of Earth's surface meet and move.
They formed in the middle of plates where nothing moves.

quiz.q: Why does California have many earthquakes?
ch: It sits along the boundary between two moving plates, such as along the San Andreas Fault.
It is in the middle of a plate.
It is near the North Pole.

quiz.q: In one year, a seismograph recorded 125 small earthquakes and 8 larger ones near a fault. How many earthquakes were recorded in all?
Most of the world's tallest mountains are found
ch: in long chains, often near plate edges
in perfect circles in the middle of oceans

quiz.q: A student marks the locations of 50 volcanoes on a world map. Most marks form a ring around the Pacific Ocean. What is the best prediction for a new volcano found next year?
ch: It will most likely be near the edge of the Pacific Ocean.
It will most likely be in the middle of a continent far from any plate edge.
It will be at the North Pole.
It will be in a lake.

quiz.q: Explain how a map of earthquakes could help a city decide where to build a new hospital.
quiz.ans: The map shows where earthquakes happen most often. The city could build in a place with fewer earthquakes or plan to build the hospital extra strong if it must be near a fault.

lessons.name: How can we reduce damage from natural hazards?

practice.q: Which is a natural hazard caused by Earth processes?
ch: a power outage from a broken cable
practice.h: It happens because of forces inside Earth.

practice.q: Which design helps a building stay standing during an earthquake?
ch: a flexible frame and pads under the base that let the ground move beneath it
walls that are not attached to the foundation
practice.h: Buildings that can sway a little are less likely to break.

practice.q: A community near the ocean worries about tsunamis after earthquakes. Which solution helps most?
ch: warning sirens and marked routes to higher ground
building homes closer to the beach
practice.h: What helps people get out of danger quickly?

practice.q: A model building on a shake table stayed standing for 8 seconds. After adding cross braces, it stayed standing for 25 seconds. How many seconds longer did it last?
practice.h: Subtract the times.

practice.q: Why do scientists place instruments around active volcanoes?
ch: to detect warning signs and alert people before an eruption
practice.h: Watching for changes helps people prepare.

practice.q: Name two solutions that reduce damage from landslides and explain one of them.
practice.ans: Building retaining walls and planting trees on slopes. A retaining wall holds back soil and rocks so they do not slide onto roads or homes.

quiz.q: Bolting a house to its foundation helps protect it from

A class tested three model buildings on a shake table. Model A (no braces): fell at 6 seconds. Model B (cross braces): fell at 20 seconds. Model C (cross braces and rubber pads under the base): still standing at 40 seconds when the test ended. Which design best reduces earthquake damage?
Using the same data (Model A fell at 6 seconds and Model B fell at 20 seconds), how many seconds longer did Model B last than Model A?
Model C costs twice as much as Model B. A town has a small budget but must protect a hospital. Which is the best reasoning?
ch: Choose Model C for the hospital because protecting people there is most important.
Choose Model A because it is cheapest.
Choose by the color of the model.

quiz.q: Which pair compares two solutions for reducing flood damage from heavy rains after a wildfire?
ch: planting fast-growing plants on burned slopes vs. building barriers to catch mud and rocks
painting houses vs. planting flowers indoors
turning off lights vs. closing windows
buying new cars vs. moving furniture

quiz.q: Each emergency kit costs $25. A school buys kits for 12 classrooms. How many dollars does it spend?
A team's model bridge fell during the shake-table test. Describe how the team should use the engineering design process to improve it.
quiz.ans: They should find the failure point, think of a few ways to strengthen it (like adding braces), choose the best idea based on criteria and constraints, rebuild it and test it again under the same conditions.

test.q: In undisturbed rock layers, the youngest layer is usually
The moving of soil and rock by water, wind or ice is
Which is a natural hazard?
Fossils of clams are found in rock layers in a desert. What does this show?
ch: The area was once covered by water.
The fossils fell from the sky.

test.q: The Grand Canyon is very deep. What formed it over millions of years?
ch: the Colorado River eroding the rock

test.q: Ice in rock cracks makes them bigger. This is
A map shows volcanoes in Washington, Oregon and northern California in a line near the coast. What does this pattern suggest?
ch: They formed along an edge where two plates meet.
They formed in the middle of a plate far from any edge.

test.q: Which solution helps reduce damage from earthquakes?
ch: building flexible frames that can sway
building on loose sand near cliffs

test.q: A layer with fern fossils is below a layer with desert sand dune patterns. What changed over time?
ch: The area went from a wet, plant-filled place to a dry desert.
The area went from a desert to a forest.
Ferns grew in the sand dunes.

test.q: A delta at the mouth of a river grew 12 meters in one year and 17 meters the next. How many meters did it grow in two years?
Sand built up 3 cm every 100 years. How many centimeters would build up in 400 years?
A shake-table test: Model 1 stood for 9 seconds, Model 2 for 21 seconds and Model 3 for 30 seconds. What was the average time in seconds? (Add and divide by 3.)
Which landform is most likely built by deposition, where a river drops sand and mud?
ch: a delta at the mouth of a river

test.q: In a stream table, which change would most likely increase erosion?
A student has two rock layer diagrams. In Area 1, the layers are flat. In Area 2, the same layers are tilted and broken. What is the best explanation?
ch: Forces inside Earth moved the layers in Area 2 after they formed.
The layers in Area 2 formed tilted.
Erosion stacked the layers in Area 2.

test.q: Two solutions are proposed for a town where rocks often fall onto a mountain road. Solution 1: a strong wire net on the cliff, cost $50,000. Solution 2: a tunnel through the mountain, cost $5,000,000. The town's budget is $100,000. Which solution meets the constraint?
Earthquake drills at school ask students to drop, cover and hold on. Why?
ch: to protect their heads and bodies from falling objects

test.q: A riverbank lost 8 cm of soil a year. After willow trees were planted, it lost 3 cm a year. How many centimeters less did it lose each year?
Most of the world's earthquakes happen
ch: along the edges of Earth's plates
in the exact center of every continent

test.q: Explain the difference between weathering and erosion, and give an example of each.
test.ans: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces, like ice widening a crack. Erosion moves those pieces to a new place, like a river carrying sand downstream.

test.q: Describe one design that reduces the impact of a natural Earth hazard on people and explain why it works.
test.ans: Sample: Tsunami warning systems. Sensors detect a coming wave and sirens warn people in time to move to higher ground, so fewer people are hurt.

test.q: A geologist studies a cliff with four layers. From bottom to top: Layer 1, sandstone with fish and shell fossils. Layer 2, shale with fern fossils. Layer 3, sandstone with dinosaur footprints. Layer 4, soil with modern plant roots. Make a claim about how this landscape changed over time. Use evidence from the layers and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: The area changed from an ocean to land over a long time. Evidence: The bottom layer has fish and shell fossils, which live in water. The layers above have ferns and dinosaur footprints, which are land organisms, and the top has modern plants. Reasoning: In undisturbed layers, the bottom is oldest and the top is youngest. Reading from bottom to top shows the environment changed from water to land with plants and animals over time.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

sci|5.about: Fifth graders build a particle model of matter, identify materials by their properties, and investigate whether mixing substances makes new substances while total mass stays the same. They trace how plants get the materials they need from air and water, how energy from the Sun moves through food webs and how matter cycles through ecosystems. They model how Earth's systems interact, describe how water is distributed, explore ways communities protect resources, and analyze patterns of gravity, shadows, day and night and the stars, while applying the engineering design process.
std: Develop a model to describe that matter is made of particles too small to be seen.
Measure and graph quantities to provide evidence that regardless of the type of change that occurs when heating, cooling or mixing substances, the total weight of matter is conserved.
Conduct an investigation to determine whether the mixing of two or more substances results in new substances.
Support an argument that plants get the materials they need for growth chiefly from air and water.
Develop a model to describe the movement of matter among plants, animals, decomposers and the environment.
Develop a model using an example to describe ways the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and/or atmosphere interact.
Represent data in graphical displays to reveal patterns of daily changes in length and direction of shadows, day and night, and the seasonal appearance of some stars in the night sky.
Plan and carry out fair tests in which variables are controlled and failure points are considered to identify aspects of a model or prototype that can be improved.

units.name: Unit 1: Matter Is Made of Particles
units.el: Use a "particle model" picture card (dots close together for solid, a little apart for liquid, far apart for gas); pre-teach property, dissolve, evaporate, particle and conductor with gestures and real objects.

lessons.name: Is air made of anything?

practice.q: All matter is made of tiny particles that are
ch: big enough to see with our eyes
practice.h: Even air is made of particles.

practice.q: A basketball is weighed flat, then pumped full of air and weighed again. It is heavier the second time. What does this show?
ch: Air has mass because it is made of particles.
The pump added rubber to the ball.
practice.h: What was added to the ball?

practice.q: A cup is turned upside down and pushed straight down into a tub of water. A paper towel stuck in the bottom of the cup stays dry. Why?
ch: Air trapped in the cup takes up space and keeps the water out.
practice.h: What fills the cup before it goes in the water?

practice.q: A deflated ball weighed 410 grams. After pumping in air, it weighed 418 grams. What was the mass of the air pumped in, in grams?
practice.h: Subtract the empty weight from the full weight.

practice.q: In a model of a gas, how are the particles arranged?
ch: far apart and moving freely in all directions
practice.h: Think about how a gas spreads to fill a balloon.

practice.q: You smell popcorn from across the room even though you cannot see anything in the air. Use a particle model to explain why.
practice.ans: Tiny particles from the popcorn move through the air and spread out across the room. They are too small to see, but when they reach my nose I can smell them.

quiz.q: Which statement about air is true?
ch: It has mass and takes up space.

quiz.q: A balloon is blown up and then placed in a freezer. It shrinks. What happened to the air particles inside?
ch: They slowed down and moved closer together.

quiz.q: A syringe with its tip blocked is full of air. You can push the plunger in a little, but not all the way. What does this show?
ch: Air particles can be squeezed closer together, but they still take up space.

quiz.q: A bike tire tube pumped up hard weighed 152 grams. The same tube with the air let out weighed 149 grams. What was the mass of the air in grams?
Which is the best model of a solid?
ch: particles packed closely and vibrating in place
particles far apart and zooming around

quiz.q: A class weighed a soccer ball 3 times as they added pumps of air: 0 pumps 420 g, 10 pumps 423 g, 20 pumps 426 g. How many grams did the ball gain from 0 to 20 pumps?
Explain how you could show a younger student that air is made of something even though you cannot see it.
quiz.ans: Blow up a balloon and show it gets bigger, so air takes up space. Or weigh a ball before and after pumping it up to show the air adds mass.

lessons.name: Where does sugar go when it dissolves?

practice.q: When sugar dissolves in water, the sugar
ch: breaks into particles too small to see that spread through the water
practice.h: Can you still taste it?

practice.q: A student stirs salt into water until she can no longer see it. How can she prove the salt is still there?
ch: Let the water evaporate and look for salt crystals left behind.
Shine a flashlight on the water.
practice.h: What happens if the water goes away?

practice.q: A puddle disappears on a sunny day. Where did the water go?
ch: Its particles moved into the air as water vapor.
It was destroyed by the Sun.
practice.h: The water particles are still somewhere.

practice.q: 200 g of water and 15 g of sugar were mixed. The sugar dissolved. What was the total mass of the sugar water in grams?
practice.h: Matter is not lost when it dissolves.

practice.q: Food coloring is dropped into hot water and cold water. It spreads faster in hot water. What is the best explanation?
ch: Particles move faster in hot water.
practice.h: Temperature affects how fast particles move.

practice.q: Draw or describe a particle model of sugar before and after dissolving in water.
practice.ans: Before: a sugar crystal is a tight cluster of sugar particles next to water particles. After: the sugar particles are spread out evenly among the water particles, too small to see.

quiz.q: A cup of salt water is left on a windowsill for a week. The water is gone and white crystals are left. What is the best explanation?
ch: The water evaporated and the salt particles were left behind.
The salt evaporated and the water stayed.
Both the water and salt disappeared.
The crystals came from the window.

quiz.q: Which observation is evidence that particles are too small to see?
ch: You can taste sugar in clear water.
Sand sinks to the bottom of water.

quiz.q: A bowl held 300 g of water. After two days on a sunny windowsill it held 245 g. How many grams of water evaporated?
Perfume is sprayed in one corner of a room. A minute later people in the other corner smell it. Which model explains this?
ch: perfume particles moving and spreading through the air

quiz.q: A student dissolved 12 g of salt in 250 g of water. What should the total mass of the salt water be, in grams?
A class put a drop of dye in three cups of water at 10°C, 25°C and 50°C. The dye spread completely in 12 minutes, 6 minutes and 2 minutes. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: Particles move faster at higher temperatures.
Particles move slower at higher temperatures.
Temperature has no effect on particles.
The dye dissolved only in cold water.

quiz.q: Students mixed 20 g of sugar into 180 g of water. The sugar disappeared. They weighed the cup of sugar water and it had a mass of 200 g (not counting the cup). Make a claim about what happened to the sugar. Use evidence and explain your reasoning with a particle model.
quiz.ans: Claim: The sugar is still in the water as tiny particles. Evidence: The sugar water had a mass of 200 g, which equals 20 g of sugar plus 180 g of water. The sugar water also tastes sweet. Reasoning: Matter is made of particles too small to see. When sugar dissolves, its particles spread out among the water particles, so we cannot see them, but their mass is still there.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: How can we identify a material by its properties?

practice.q: A property is
ch: a characteristic used to describe or identify a material
practice.h: Color and hardness are examples.

practice.q: Which property could help you tell aluminum foil from plastic wrap?
ch: Aluminum conducts electricity and plastic does not.
practice.h: Think of a test with a battery and a bulb.

practice.q: A student has two white powders, salt and baking soda. Which test could help identify them?
ch: Add vinegar: baking soda fizzes and salt does not.
practice.h: Look for a test where they act differently.

practice.q: A mineral scratches glass, but glass cannot scratch it. What property is being tested?
practice.h: Which one is harder?

practice.q: A metal cube has a mass of 81 grams and a volume of 30 cubic centimeters. A different cube made of the same metal has a volume of 10 cubic centimeters. What is its mass in grams?
practice.h: The volume is one third as much, so the mass is one third as much.

practice.q: You find a shiny gray object. Describe two tests you could do to find out whether it is steel.
practice.ans: Test it with a magnet; steel is attracted to magnets. Test it in a circuit; steel conducts electricity and will light a bulb.

quiz.q: Which property describes whether a material lets heat move through it easily?

A class tested materials. Results: Material A - attracted to a magnet, conducts electricity. Material B - not attracted, conducts electricity. Material C - not attracted, does not conduct. Which material is most likely plastic?

A class tested materials. Material A - attracted to a magnet, conducts electricity. Material B - not attracted, conducts electricity. Material C - not attracted, does not conduct. Which material is most likely copper?
Which property would help separate sand from salt?
ch: Salt dissolves in water and sand does not.
Both are found at the beach.

quiz.q: A sample was tested for hardness on a 1 to 10 scale. Mineral X scored 3 and Mineral Y scored 7. How many points harder is Mineral Y?
Three pieces of the same wood were weighed: 12 g, 15 g and 18 g. What was the average mass in grams?
A recycling plant receives a mix of steel cans, aluminum cans and glass bottles. Explain how properties could be used to sort them.
quiz.ans: A magnet can pull out steel cans because steel is attracted to magnets. Aluminum and glass can then be separated because aluminum conducts electricity and is much lighter, while glass does not conduct and can break.

test.q: Matter is made of
Which property tells whether a material can be scratched easily?
Which statement correctly describes air?
ch: It is matter, so it has mass and takes up space.
It is a form of light.

test.q: A balloon is inflated and gets bigger. What explains this with a particle model?
ch: More air particles were added and they push on the inside of the balloon.
The balloon got heavier because it got colder.

test.q: Salt is stirred into water and seems to disappear. What really happened?
ch: The salt particles spread out among the water particles.

test.q: Which observation supports the idea that gas particles are spread far apart?
ch: Air in a syringe can be squeezed into a smaller space.

test.q: A wet sidewalk dries in the sun. Which particle model explains this?
ch: Water particles gain energy and move into the air as vapor.
The sidewalk absorbs the water forever.
The Sun pulls the water up into space.

test.q: Which property would help you identify a piece of iron?
ch: It is attracted to a magnet.

test.q: Two clear liquids look the same. One is water and one is vinegar. Which property test is safest and most useful?
ch: Add baking soda and see if it fizzes.

test.q: An empty ball weighs 600 g. After being pumped up, it weighs 609 g. How many grams of air were added?
25 g of salt is dissolved in 475 g of water. What is the total mass of the salt water in grams?
A dish held 120 g of salt water. After the water evaporated, 8 g of salt was left. How many grams of water evaporated?
A class tested which materials conduct electricity: a copper wire, a rubber band, a steel nail, a wooden stick and a foil strip. Which group lists the conductors?
ch: copper wire, steel nail, foil strip

test.q: Using the same list (copper wire, rubber band, steel nail, wooden stick, foil strip), how many of the five materials are insulators?
A drop of food coloring spreads through warm water in 3 minutes and through cold water in 15 minutes. Which explanation uses a particle model?
ch: Water particles move faster when warm, so they mix the coloring faster.
Food coloring particles grow in warm water.

test.q: A student says, "When you can't see something, it isn't there." Which evidence best disproves this?
ch: Sugar dissolved in water can still be tasted and its mass is still measured.

test.q: Which material would be best for the handle of a cooking pot?
ch: wood, because it does not conduct heat well
copper, because it conducts heat well
steel, because it is attracted to magnets

test.q: A class measured the mass of 3 pieces of the same mineral: 24 g, 30 g and 27 g. What was the average mass in grams?
In a model of a liquid, the particles are
ch: close together but able to slide past each other

test.q: Describe an investigation that shows air takes up space.
test.ans: Push an upside-down cup with a dry paper towel inside straight down into water. The towel stays dry because air trapped in the cup takes up space and keeps the water out.

test.q: Explain how you could use properties to tell the difference between sugar and sand.
test.ans: Put each in water and stir. Sugar dissolves and sand does not. Sand is also harder and gritty, and sugar crystals can be crushed more easily.

test.q: Students placed 50 g of ice in a sealed bag and weighed it. They let it melt and weighed it again. Then they opened the bag in the sun for a day and weighed it. Sealed with ice: 50 g. Sealed after melting: 50 g. Open after a day: 31 g. Make a claim about what happened to the water particles. Use evidence and explain your reasoning with a particle model.
test.ans: Claim: The water particles were never destroyed; some escaped into the air when the bag was open. Evidence: The mass stayed 50 g when the sealed ice melted, but dropped to 31 g after the bag was open in the sun for a day, a loss of 19 g. Reasoning: Melting only changes how the particles are arranged, so the mass stays the same. When the bag was open, some water particles evaporated and moved into the air as vapor, too small to see, so they were no longer weighed in the bag.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 2: Mixing, Reactions and Conservation of Matter
units.el: Keep a "signs of a new substance" anchor chart (gas bubbles, color change, new solid, temperature change, new smell) with photos; practice the frame "Before mixing, the mass was ___. After, it was ___. This shows ___."

lessons.name: Does matter disappear when it melts or freezes?

practice.q: When ice melts into water in a sealed container, its mass
practice.h: The particles are rearranged, not lost.

practice.q: A sealed jar of water weighed 350 g. After it was frozen, it still weighed 350 g. Which statement explains this?
ch: Freezing changes how the particles are arranged but not how many there are.
practice.h: Did any particles leave the jar?

practice.q: A chocolate bar with a mass of 45 g melts in a sealed bag. What is its mass after melting, in grams?
practice.h: Melting is a change of state.

practice.q: A pot of soup is boiled without a lid for 20 minutes. It has less mass afterward. Why?
ch: Water particles escaped into the air as steam.
practice.h: Was the container sealed?

practice.q: Which graph would best show that mass stays the same as ice melts in a sealed bag?
ch: a line graph of mass over time that stays flat
a bar graph of different colors of ice
a pie chart of water and air
practice.h: You want to show mass at many times.

practice.q: Explain why melting butter in a covered pan is a good way to test whether mass changes when a substance is heated.
practice.ans: Covering the pan keeps any particles from escaping, so if the mass is the same before and after, it shows melting does not change the total mass.

quiz.q: Melting, freezing and boiling are changes of
A class sealed 100 g of ice in a bag and weighed it every 10 minutes as it melted: 100 g, 100 g, 100 g, 100 g. What conclusion is supported?
ch: The total mass stayed the same during melting.
Ice has more mass than water.

quiz.q: A sealed bottle with 240 g of water is frozen. The bottle itself has a mass of 30 g. What is the total mass of the bottle and ice in grams?
Wax from a candle is melted in a sealed tin. Before: 80 g. After: 80 g. Then the wax cools and hardens. What should its mass be?
An open cup of water had a mass of 500 g. A week later it had a mass of 420 g. How many grams of water evaporated?
A student weighs an open pot of water before and after boiling and says, "Boiling destroys matter." Which is the best response?
ch: The water escaped as steam; to test fairly, use a sealed container and the mass will stay the same.

quiz.q: Draw or describe a particle model of ice before and after melting. Explain why the mass stays the same.
quiz.ans: Before: particles are close together in a regular pattern, vibrating in place. After: the same particles are close but can slide past each other. The number of particles did not change, so the mass stays the same.

lessons.name: When does mixing make a new substance?

practice.q: Which is evidence that a new substance has formed?
ch: gas bubbles form when two liquids are mixed
sand is stirred into water and sinks
practice.h: Look for something new that was not there before.

practice.q: Milk and vinegar are mixed. Soft white clumps form that were not there before. What does this show?
practice.h: Is the solid something new?

practice.q: Salt and pepper are mixed. You can still pick out the pepper and the salt grains. Is this a new substance?
ch: No, it is a mixture and each part keeps its properties.
Yes, it is a new substance.
practice.h: Can you separate them again?

practice.q: An iron nail left outside gets reddish-brown and flaky. What happened?
ch: The iron reacted with water and air to form rust, a new substance.
practice.h: Rust is not the same as iron.

practice.q: A class mixed four pairs of substances. Two pairs made gas, one pair changed color and one pair made no change. How many pairs showed evidence of a new substance?
practice.h: Count the pairs that showed gas or a color change.

practice.q: List three kinds of observations that can show a new substance has formed when two substances are mixed.
practice.ans: A gas forms (bubbles or fizzing), the color changes, a new solid appears, there is a new smell, or the temperature changes.

quiz.q: Which mixture makes a new substance?

A class tested mixtures. Mixture 1: sugar and water - sugar disappears, no bubbles. Mixture 2: baking soda and lemon juice - fizzes. Mixture 3: iron filings and sand - can be separated with a magnet. Which mixture made a new substance?
Why is dissolving sugar in water NOT considered making a new substance?
ch: The water can evaporate and leave the same sugar behind.

quiz.q: In an experiment, the temperature of a mixture started at 21°C and rose to 34°C after mixing. How many degrees did it rise?
Which is the best plan to test whether mixing two powders with water makes a new substance?
ch: Mix them in a cup and record any bubbles, color change, new solid or temperature change.

quiz.q: A student mixed 3 spoonfuls of baking soda with vinegar in each of 5 cups. How many spoonfuls of baking soda did she use?
When you mix lemonade powder and water, the color changes to yellow. A classmate says this proves a new substance formed. Do you agree? Explain.
quiz.ans: Not necessarily. The powder may just dissolve and spread its color through the water, like dissolving sugar. If the water evaporated, the same powder would be left. A new substance would show other signs, like gas or a new solid.

lessons.name: Where does the mass go when a gas is made?

practice.q: Baking soda and vinegar are mixed in an open cup. The cup's total mass goes down. Why?
ch: A gas formed and escaped into the air.
practice.h: Where do the bubbles go?

practice.q: Baking soda and vinegar are mixed inside a sealed plastic bag. What happens to the total mass?
practice.h: Can the gas leave the bag?

practice.q: Before mixing in a sealed bag, the baking soda, vinegar and bag had a total mass of 160 g. What should the total mass be after the fizzing stops, in grams?
practice.h: Nothing could get in or out.

practice.q: In an open cup, the total mass was 160 g before mixing and 154 g after. How many grams of gas escaped?
practice.h: Subtract the after mass from the before mass.

practice.q: Which statement is always true when substances react in a closed container?
ch: The total mass before equals the total mass after.
New particles are created from nothing.
practice.h: Particles are rearranged, not made or destroyed.

practice.q: Explain why scientists use a closed container to study whether mass changes in a reaction.
practice.ans: A closed container keeps gases from escaping or air from entering, so all the particles are measured before and after, giving an accurate comparison.

quiz.q: In any change, the total amount of matter is
A class graphed the mass of a sealed bottle while an antacid tablet fizzed in water. The line stayed at 215 g for 10 minutes. What does the graph show?
ch: Mass was conserved during the reaction.

quiz.q: A sealed bottle had 200 g of water and a 3 g tablet in a small cup inside. The bottle weighed 25 g. What was the total mass before the tablet was dropped in, in grams?
A sealed bottle with water and a fizzing tablet had a total mass of 228 g. After the fizzing, the bottle was opened and some gas escaped. The new mass was 226 g. How many grams of gas escaped?
Steel wool is heated in air and gets slightly heavier. Which explanation fits conservation of matter?
ch: The steel combined with oxygen from the air, adding particles to the solid.

quiz.q: Two groups did the same reaction. Group A used an open cup and found mass decreased by 4 g. Group B used a sealed bag and found no change. How do these results fit together?
ch: Both support conservation: in Group A, 4 g of gas escaped into the air.
Mass is only conserved in open cups.

quiz.q: A class mixed vinegar and baking soda three ways and measured total mass before and after. Open cup: 180 g before, 174 g after. Cup covered with a balloon: 180 g before, 180 g after, and the balloon inflated. Sealed bag: 180 g before, 180 g after. Make a claim about whether mass is conserved in this reaction. Use evidence from all three trials and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: Mass is conserved in this reaction. Evidence: In the balloon and sealed bag trials, the mass stayed at 180 g. In the open cup, the mass dropped 6 g, but that is the trial where gas could escape; the balloon inflating shows a gas formed. Reasoning: The reaction rearranges particles into new substances, including a gas. When the gas is trapped, all the particles are still weighed, so the mass stays the same. The open cup only lost mass because the gas left the cup.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: How can we test a design fairly and improve it?

practice.q: In a fair test, the one thing you change on purpose is the
practice.h: Everything else stays the same.

practice.q: A team tests how much water makes a fizzing tablet rocket fly highest. Which should stay the same in every trial?
ch: the size of the tablet and the type of canister
practice.h: Only the amount of water should change.

practice.q: In one trial, the canister lid was not snapped on tightly and the rocket did not fly. What should the team do?
ch: Count it as a failure point, fix the lid and repeat the trial.
Report it as the best result.
Change the amount of water and the tablet size at once.
practice.h: A failure shows what part needs improvement.

practice.q: The rocket flew 120 cm, 135 cm and 126 cm in three trials. What is the average height in centimeters?
practice.h: Add the three heights and divide by 3.

practice.q: Why do scientists repeat trials?
ch: to check that results are reliable
practice.h: One trial might have a mistake.

practice.q: Name one variable you would change and two variables you would keep the same to test which amount of baking soda makes a balloon inflate most.
practice.ans: Change: the amount of baking soda. Keep the same: the amount of vinegar and the size of the bottle and balloon.

quiz.q: A team's data for a fizzing rocket. 5 mL water: 80 cm. 10 mL: 140 cm. 15 mL: 110 cm. Which amount worked best in this test?
Using the same data (5 mL: 80 cm, 10 mL: 140 cm, 15 mL: 110 cm), how many centimeters higher did the 10 mL rocket fly than the 5 mL rocket?
A team changes both the water amount and the tablet size between trials. What is the problem?
ch: They cannot tell which change caused the difference.

quiz.q: Four trials gave heights of 90 cm, 100 cm, 110 cm and 100 cm. What is the average in centimeters?
A balloon on a bottle of vinegar and baking soda keeps leaking at the neck. Which improvement best fixes this failure point?
ch: Wrap tape around the neck so the balloon seals tightly.

quiz.q: Group A's rocket went 150 cm with warm water. Group B's went 90 cm with cold water. Group A also used a full tablet and Group B a half tablet. What conclusion can they draw about water temperature?
ch: None yet, because two variables changed; they need a new test changing only temperature.

quiz.q: A team's balloon-inflating design gave very different results in three trials: 18 cm, 6 cm and 17 cm around. Explain what they should do next.
quiz.ans: The 6 cm trial does not match the others, so something may have gone wrong, like a leak or a measuring mistake. They should look for the failure point, fix it and repeat the trial to get reliable results.

test.q: When ice melts in a sealed bag, the total mass
Which is a sign that a new substance formed?
ch: a new solid appears when two liquids are mixed
a stick is broken in half

test.q: In a fair test, scientists change
ch: only one variable at a time

test.q: Vinegar and baking soda fizz in an open cup, and the mass goes down. What is the best explanation?
ch: Gas made in the reaction escaped into the air.

test.q: Which is a mixture and not a new substance?
ch: trail mix of nuts and raisins

test.q: Salt is dissolved in water and the water evaporates. Salt crystals are left. What does this show?
ch: Dissolving did not make a new substance.

test.q: Milk and lemon juice are mixed and form clumps. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: A new substance formed, because a new solid appeared.
The clumps were already in the milk.

test.q: Butter is melted in a sealed bag. Before: 30 g. After: 30 g. What does this show?
ch: Changes of state do not change the total mass.

test.q: A sealed bag holds 90 g of vinegar, 10 g of baking soda in a small cup and the 5 g bag. The baking soda is tipped into the vinegar. What is the total mass after fizzing, in grams?
Vinegar and baking soda were mixed in an open cup. The total mass started at 105 g and ended at 101 g. How many grams of gas escaped?
A frozen 300 g block of ice was melted in a sealed container. It was then heated until warm, still sealed. What is the mass of the water in grams?
Which graph best shows conservation of mass during a reaction in a sealed bag?
ch: a flat line showing the same mass over time
a line that drops to zero

test.q: A rocket test gave heights of 210 cm, 190 cm and 200 cm. What is the average height in centimeters?
A team tests whether the amount of vinegar changes how big a balloon inflates. Which should stay the same?
ch: the amount of baking soda and the bottle size

test.q: An iron nail with a mass of 20 g rusts and its mass becomes 21 g. Which explanation fits conservation of matter?
ch: Particles of oxygen and water from the air combined with the iron.
The scale is wrong because mass cannot change.

test.q: Two powders are mixed with water. The cup gets cold, and when the water evaporates, both powders are left unchanged. Which conclusion is best?
ch: The powders only dissolved; no new substance formed.
A new substance formed because the cup got cold.

test.q: During a fizzing rocket test, one trial failed because the lid cracked. What should the team do?
ch: Replace the lid and repeat that trial.
Use that trial as their best result.
Change two variables in the next trial.

test.q: A class did a reaction in 6 sealed bags. Each bag had a total mass of 65 g before mixing. What was the total mass of all 6 bags after mixing, in grams?
Which statement about all changes to matter is true?
ch: Particles are rearranged, but the total mass is conserved.
Particles are created when things mix.

test.q: Explain how you could test whether mixing two clear liquids makes a new substance.
test.ans: Mix small amounts in a clear cup and observe for gas bubbles, a color change, a new solid, a temperature change or a new smell. Compare with each liquid alone. If none of these appear, a new substance probably did not form.

test.q: Explain why the mass of a sealed bottle stays the same while an antacid tablet fizzes inside it.
test.ans: The tablet and water react to make a gas, but the gas cannot escape the sealed bottle. All the particles are still inside, just rearranged, so the total mass stays the same.

test.q: A class heated and mixed substances in sealed containers and recorded total mass before and after. Melting chocolate: 60 g before, 60 g after. Freezing juice: 250 g before, 250 g after. Mixing vinegar and baking soda: 140 g before, 140 g after. Mixing salt and water: 110 g before, 110 g after. Make a claim about what happens to the total mass of matter during heating, cooling and mixing. Use evidence and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: The total mass of matter is conserved during heating, cooling and mixing, whether or not a new substance forms. Evidence: In all four sealed tests the mass before equaled the mass after: 60 g, 250 g, 140 g and 110 g. This includes a change of state (melting, freezing), dissolving (salt) and a reaction that made gas (vinegar and baking soda). Reasoning: Matter is made of particles. In any change, particles are rearranged but not created or destroyed, so when nothing can escape a sealed container, the total mass stays the same.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 3: Plants, Food and Energy from the Sun
units.el: Draw a large plant diagram with arrows labeled "air (carbon dioxide) in," "water in," "light energy in," "oxygen out" and "sugar (food) made"; give students arrow cards to build energy chains such as "Sun -> grass -> cow -> me."

lessons.name: Where do plants get the materials to grow?

practice.q: Plants get most of the materials they use to build their bodies from
practice.h: Soil gives only a small amount of minerals.

practice.q: Which gas from the air do plants take in to make food?
practice.h: Animals breathe this gas out.

practice.q: A scientist in the 1600s planted a small willow tree in a pot of soil and gave it only water for 5 years. The tree gained about 74 kg, but the soil lost only about 0.06 kg. What does this evidence suggest?
ch: Most of the tree's mass did not come from the soil.
Trees lose mass as they grow.
Soil gains mass when trees grow.
practice.h: Compare how much the tree gained with how much the soil lost.

practice.q: A bean plant grew from a 1 g seed to a 46 g plant. The soil in its pot lost less than 1 g. About how many grams did the plant gain?
practice.h: Subtract the seed's mass from the plant's mass.

practice.q: Lettuce can be grown with its roots in water with a few added nutrients and no soil at all. What does this show?
ch: Plants do not need soil to get most of their building materials.
Soil is the only source of plant food.
practice.h: Where did the lettuce's mass come from if there was no soil?

practice.q: Your friend says, "A big tree is made mostly of soil." Explain why this is not correct.
practice.ans: Plants build their bodies mostly from carbon dioxide from the air and water. Soil only gives small amounts of minerals. Experiments show the soil around a growing plant loses very little mass.

quiz.q: What does a plant release into the air when it makes food?

Two identical seedlings were grown. Plant A was in a sealed jar with air that had no carbon dioxide. Plant B was in a sealed jar with normal air. Both got light and water. After two weeks, Plant B grew much more. What does this show?
ch: Plants need carbon dioxide from the air to grow.
Plant A got too much air.

quiz.q: A radish weighed 2 g as a seedling and 38 g at harvest. Its pot of soil weighed 500 g at the start and 499 g at harvest. How many grams did the radish gain?
A radish grew from 2 g to 38 g. Its pot of soil weighed 500 g at the start and 499 g at harvest. How many grams did the soil lose?
A radish grew from 2 g to 38 g while its soil went from 500 g to 499 g. Which statement best explains this data?
ch: Most of the radish's added mass came from air and water, not the soil.
The radish was made only of soil.

quiz.q: Why does a plant wilt and stop growing if it gets no water, even in rich soil?
ch: Water is one of the main materials plants use to make food and build their bodies.
Soil needs water to turn into leaves.
Water makes the plant heavier only.

quiz.q: Use the willow tree experiment as evidence to support the argument that plants get most of their materials from air and water.
quiz.ans: The tree gained about 74 kg in five years, but the soil lost only about 0.06 kg. Since the tree was given only water, its added mass must have come mostly from water and the carbon dioxide it took from the air.

lessons.name: How do plants capture energy from the Sun?

practice.q: Plants use energy from
practice.h: Leaves face toward this.

practice.q: When a plant makes food, energy from sunlight is stored in
practice.h: Food is a way to store energy.

practice.q: A plant is kept in a dark closet for two weeks. Its leaves turn yellow and it stops growing. What is the best explanation?
ch: Without light, it cannot make the food it needs for energy.
Plants grow faster in the dark.
practice.h: What does the plant need light for?

practice.q: A class gave plants different hours of light each day. 4 hours: grew 3 cm. 8 hours: grew 7 cm. 12 hours: grew 11 cm. How many more centimeters did the 12-hour plant grow than the 4-hour plant?
practice.h: Subtract to compare.

practice.q: Which model shows how energy moves into a plant's food?
practice.h: Start with where the energy comes from.

practice.q: Describe what goes into a leaf and what comes out when a plant makes food.
practice.ans: In: carbon dioxide from the air, water from the roots and light energy from the Sun. Out: sugar that stores energy for the plant and oxygen that goes into the air.

quiz.q: The energy stored in plant sugar first came from
A class measured bubbles of oxygen given off by a water plant placed at different distances from a lamp. 10 cm: 30 bubbles per minute. 30 cm: 14 bubbles. 50 cm: 5 bubbles. What pattern is shown?
ch: More light made the plant produce more oxygen.
Less light made the plant produce more oxygen.
The plant used up the lamp.

quiz.q: Using the same data (10 cm: 30, 30 cm: 14, 50 cm: 5 bubbles per minute), how many fewer bubbles per minute were there at 50 cm than at 10 cm?
Why are most leaves wide and flat?
Using the same data (30, 14 and 5 bubbles per minute), how many bubbles were counted altogether in one minute at each distance?
A gardener says, "My tomato plant is getting energy from the fertilizer I add to the soil." Which response is most accurate?
ch: Fertilizer gives some minerals, but the plant's energy comes from sunlight captured in its leaves.
Fertilizer is the plant's main energy source.
The energy comes from the pot.

quiz.q: Students grew three pots of identical bean plants for 3 weeks with the same water and soil. Pot A, full sunlight: average height 24 cm, dark green. Pot B, partial shade: average height 15 cm, light green. Pot C, dark closet: average height 6 cm, pale yellow and weak. Make a claim about what plants need light for. Use evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: Plants need light to make the food that gives them energy to grow. Evidence: With the same water and soil, plants in full sun averaged 24 cm and were dark green, plants in partial shade averaged 15 cm, and plants in the dark averaged only 6 cm and were pale and weak. Reasoning: Plants capture light energy to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water. Less light means less food is made, so the plants have less energy and fewer materials to grow.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: Where does the energy in our food come from?

practice.q: Animals get the energy they need from
practice.h: Think about why you get hungry.

practice.q: A cow eats grass. A person drinks the cow's milk. Where did the energy in the milk originally come from?
practice.h: Trace the energy back step by step.

practice.q: Your body uses energy from food to
practice.h: What do you do all day that needs energy?

practice.q: An apple has about 95 Calories of energy. A banana has about 105 Calories. How many Calories are in both?
practice.h: Add the two amounts.

practice.q: Which chain correctly traces energy to a hawk?
practice.h: Arrows show where the energy goes.

practice.q: Trace the energy in a bowl of rice back to the Sun.
practice.ans: The Sun's light energy was captured by the rice plant's leaves and stored in sugar and starch in the rice grains. When I eat the rice, my body uses that stored energy.

quiz.q: In a food chain, energy flows from
ch: the Sun to plants to animals
animals to plants to the Sun

quiz.q: A student runs a race and gets very warm. Where did the energy for running and the heat come from?
ch: energy stored in the food the student ate

quiz.q: A student ate a breakfast with 350 Calories and a lunch with 520 Calories. How many Calories did the student eat in all?
Why does every food chain start with a plant or other producer?
ch: Producers capture energy from the Sun and store it in food.

quiz.q: A class kept a log of energy from food. Monday 1,800 Calories, Tuesday 2,000 Calories, Wednesday 1,900 Calories. What was the average per day?
A lizard lies on a warm rock in the morning before hunting. A student says the lizard is "eating sunlight." Which is the best correction?
ch: The sunlight warms the lizard's body, but its energy for living and moving comes from the food it eats.
The lizard makes food from sunlight like a plant.
The lizard gets no energy from food.
The rock gives the lizard food.

quiz.q: Explain why a fox that eats rabbits depends on the Sun even though it never eats plants.
quiz.ans: The rabbits eat plants, and plants store energy from sunlight in their food. When the fox eats a rabbit, it gets energy that first came from the Sun through the plants.

test.q: Most of the materials a plant uses to grow come from
The energy in food first came from
Plants take in which gas to make food?
A tree grows from a seed into a huge oak. Where did most of its mass come from?
ch: carbon dioxide from the air and water

test.q: Plants grown in water with no soil still grow tall. What does this support?
ch: Plants get most of their materials from air and water.
Plants need soil for most of their mass.

test.q: Which model correctly shows energy flow?
A potted plant is put in a dark room for a month. What will most likely happen?
ch: It will weaken and may die because it cannot make food.
It will get its energy from the soil instead.

test.q: Which gas do plants release when they make food?
You eat a slice of bread made from wheat. What energy change happened first, long before you ate it?
ch: Light energy from the Sun was stored in the wheat as food.
The bread created its own energy.
The oven made the wheat's energy.

test.q: A seedling weighed 3 g. After 6 weeks it weighed 87 g. The soil lost less than 1 g. How many grams did the plant gain?
A plant was 12 cm tall. It grew 4 cm each week for 5 weeks. How tall was it in centimeters?
A class counted oxygen bubbles from a water plant: 22, 26 and 24 bubbles per minute. What was the average?
Why do animals need to eat?
ch: to get energy and materials for moving, growing and staying warm
to get soil for their bodies

test.q: A plant's leaves face a window. Which is the best explanation?
ch: The leaves catch light that the plant needs to make food.
The window gives the plant soil.
