test.q: Which material would make the best oven mitt?
The same amount of energy is added to 1 kg of water and 2 kg of water. Which is true?
ch: The 1 kg of water has the larger temperature increase
The 2 kg of water has the larger temperature increase
Both change by the same amount

test.q: Sand on a beach is hot at noon, while the ocean water feels cool. Which explanation is best?
ch: Sand warms faster than water with the same sunlight
The sand is closer to the Sun

test.q: In an investigation, students change the mass of water and measure the temperature change. What is the dependent variable?
Why does a pot of soup heat evenly even though only the bottom touches the burner?
ch: Convection currents move warm soup up and cool soup down
Conduction moves heat out of the soup
The soup is a good insulator

test.q: Two cups hold 200 mL of 80 °C water. Cup A is foam and Cup B is metal. After 10 minutes, A is 70 °C and B is 52 °C. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: Foam is a better insulator than metal
Metal is a better insulator than foam
The cups lost the same energy

test.q: Two cups each held 80 °C water. After 10 minutes the foam cup was at 70 °C and the metal cup at 52 °C. How many more °C did the water in the metal cup cool?
Water in a pot heated from 25 °C to 85 °C in 12 minutes. What was the mean rate of temperature change in °C per minute?
It takes about 2,100 joules to raise 50 g of water by 10 °C. How many joules would it take to raise 150 g of water by 10 °C?
A cooler kept ice for 6 hours. A new design kept ice for 9 hours. What was the percent increase?
Trials of an ice-melting test gave 84, 90, 81 and 89 minutes for one design. What should the team report as the result?
ch: the mean, 86 minutes, because repeated trials are more reliable

test.q: Which is a criterion (not a constraint) for a solar oven design?
ch: It must heat food to at least 70 °C
It must be built in one class period
It can only use cardboard and foil

test.q: Two students heat 100 g of water and 100 g of vegetable oil with the same energy. The oil warms 30 °C and the water warms 14 °C. What can they conclude?
ch: The type of matter affects the temperature change
The mass affects the temperature change
Oil has more mass than water

test.q: Why are many homes in hot climates painted white or light colors?
ch: Light colors reflect more sunlight, reducing heat absorbed by radiation
Light colors conduct heat away faster

test.q: Explain why a car's tires feel warmer after a long drive.
test.ans: As the car moved, friction and the flexing of the tires transferred some kinetic energy into thermal energy, raising the tires' temperature.

test.q: Describe how you would test whether a lid affects how fast hot water cools. Include what you change, what you measure and what you keep the same.
test.ans: Change: lid or no lid. Measure: water temperature every 2 minutes for 20 minutes. Keep the same: cup type, starting temperature, amount of water, room location; repeat trials.

test.q: A student says a sweater "makes you warm by adding heat." Explain what a sweater actually does using heat transfer ideas.
test.ans: A sweater does not add heat; it is an insulator that traps air and slows the transfer of thermal energy from your warm body to the cooler air, so you stay warm longer.

test.q: A team tested three insulators wrapped around identical cans of 90 °C water. After 20 minutes: no wrap 58 °C, newspaper 66 °C, wool 74 °C, bubble wrap 77 °C. Make a claim about which material is the best insulator for keeping a drink hot. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning using ideas about heat transfer.
test.ans: Claim: Bubble wrap is the best insulator of those tested. Evidence: the can with bubble wrap stayed hottest at 77 °C (dropping 13 °C), compared with wool 74 °C, newspaper 66 °C and no wrap 58 °C. Reasoning: thermal energy moves from the hot water to the cooler air; materials that trap pockets of air slow conduction and convection, so less energy leaves the can and its temperature stays higher.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 5: Earth System Interactions Cause Weather
units.el: Use a labeled water-cycle diagram with arrows and the verbs evaporate, condense, precipitate and flow. Give a weather-map key with pictures for cold front, warm front, H and L.

lessons.name: The water cycle runs on sunlight and gravity

practice.q: What provides the energy that drives evaporation in the water cycle?
practice.h: What warms ocean and lake water every day?

practice.q: Water vapor high in the air cools and forms tiny droplets that make a cloud. This process is
Which force pulls rain and snow down from clouds and makes rivers flow downhill to the ocean?
In the Sierra Nevada, snow melts in spring and the water flows into reservoirs. Which water cycle processes are involved?
ch: melting and runoff pulled by gravity
practice.h: Think about what happens to snow as it warms, and which way water flows.

practice.q: Describe the path of one water molecule that evaporates from the Pacific Ocean and ends up in a California river.
practice.ans: Sunlight warms ocean water so the molecule evaporates; it rises and cools, condensing into a cloud; winds carry the cloud over land; it falls as rain or snow; gravity pulls it downhill as runoff or melted snow into a river.

quiz.q: Water that soaks into the ground and is stored between rocks and soil is called
Plants release water vapor from their leaves into the air. This process is called
A sealed jar with wet soil and a plant sits in sunlight. Droplets form on the inside of the lid and drip back down. What does this model show?
ch: evaporation, condensation and precipitation in the water cycle
how wind is made by the Moon

quiz.q: A rain gauge collected 12 mm, 8 mm, 0 mm, 20 mm and 5 mm of rain over five days. What was the mean daily rainfall in mm?
A lake lost 3 mm of water to evaporation each day in July. How many mm did it lose over 31 days?
A dish of water evaporated faster on a sunny windowsill than in a shady closet. Which conclusion is best supported?
ch: More energy from sunlight increases the rate of evaporation
Shade adds water to the dish
Gravity is stronger in the closet

quiz.q: Explain the roles of both sunlight and gravity in the water cycle.
quiz.ans: Sunlight provides energy that evaporates water and lifts it into the atmosphere as vapor; gravity pulls condensed water back down as precipitation and makes it flow downhill as runoff and groundwater.

lessons.name: Air pressure, humidity and clouds

practice.q: The amount of water vapor in the air is called
A cold glass of lemonade on a summer day gets water droplets on the outside. Where does the water come from?
ch: water vapor in the air condenses on the cold glass
the ice melts through the glass
the Sun makes water on the glass
practice.h: What happens to water vapor when it touches something cold?

practice.q: Weather reports show falling air pressure. Which weather is most likely coming?
ch: colder clear skies with no clouds
a heat wave with no wind

practice.q: Air at a certain temperature can hold 20 grams of water vapor per cubic meter. It now holds 15 grams. What is the relative humidity in percent?
practice.h: Divide the amount held by the most it can hold, then multiply by 100.

practice.q: Explain why clouds often form when warm, moist air rises up the side of a mountain.
practice.ans: As the air rises it expands and cools; cooler air cannot hold as much water vapor, so the vapor condenses into droplets that form clouds.

quiz.q: An instrument that measures air pressure is a
Wind blows from areas of
Fog often forms on summer mornings along the San Francisco coast. Which explanation is best?
ch: Moist ocean air cools near the cold coastal water, and its vapor condenses near the ground
Dry desert air rises over the city
The fog is smoke from factories

quiz.q: Air can hold 30 grams of water vapor per cubic meter at 30 °C. It is holding 12 grams. What is the relative humidity in percent?
Air pressure fell from 1,016 millibars to 1,004 millibars over 6 hours. What was the average drop in millibars per hour?
Data from a weather station: humidity rose from 45% to 90%, pressure fell steadily, and clouds thickened over the afternoon. What is the best prediction?
Explain why a high-pressure system usually brings clear, dry weather.
quiz.ans: In a high-pressure system air sinks; sinking air warms and can hold more water vapor, so clouds do not form easily, leading to clear skies.

lessons.name: Air masses meet: fronts and storms

practice.q: A large body of air with similar temperature and humidity throughout is called
An air mass that forms over the North Pacific Ocean would most likely be
practice.h: Think about where it formed: ocean or land, north or south?

practice.q: When a cold air mass pushes into a warm air mass, the warm air is forced upward quickly. What weather often results?
ch: thunderstorms and heavy rain, followed by cooler weather

practice.q: Which weather change usually happens after a cold front passes?
ch: the temperature drops and skies clear
it becomes foggy for a week

practice.q: Compare the weather usually caused by a cold front and by a warm front.
practice.ans: A cold front moves fast and pushes warm air up steeply, causing short, heavy storms and then cooler, clearer weather. A warm front moves slowly as warm air rises gently over cold air, causing longer periods of light rain or drizzle and warmer weather afterward.
practice.h: Think about how steeply the warm air is pushed upward.

quiz.q: The boundary where two air masses meet is called
On a weather map, a line with blue triangles shows
As a cold front passed a city, the temperature fell from 24 °C to 15 °C in 3 hours. What was the average temperature drop per hour in °C?
In winter, California often gets heavy rain from long bands of moist air that flow in from the warm Pacific. These are called atmospheric rivers. Why do they cause so much rain over the mountains?
ch: The moist air is forced up the mountains, cools and drops its water
The air sinks and warms over the mountains

quiz.q: An atmospheric river dropped 150 mm of rain on a town over 3 days. What was the mean rainfall per day in mm?
A city's data: Day 1 warm and humid, pressure falling. Day 2 strong storms and gusty winds, temperature drops 8 °C. Day 3 cool, clear and dry, pressure rising. Which event best explains the pattern?
ch: a cold front passed through on Day 2
a warm front passed through on Day 1
a high-pressure system stayed all three days

quiz.q: A student recorded weather in Fresno. Monday: 32 °C, humidity 30%, clear, pressure 1,018 mb. Tuesday: 31 °C, humidity 55%, clouds building, pressure 1,009 mb. Wednesday morning: thunderstorm, wind shifted, 22 °C. Wednesday evening: clear, humidity 35%, pressure 1,016 mb. Make a claim about what caused the change in weather. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: a cold front moved through on Wednesday. Evidence: pressure fell from 1,018 to 1,009 mb and humidity rose before the storm; during the storm the wind shifted and temperature dropped 9 °C; afterward pressure rose and humidity dropped. Reasoning: when a cold air mass pushes under warm, moist air, the warm air rises quickly, cools and forms storms; behind the front the cooler, drier air brings clear skies and higher pressure.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: Forecasting with data

practice.q: Why do meteorologists collect weather data from many locations at the same time?
ch: to track how air masses and fronts are moving
to measure only their own city
practice.h: Air masses move across large areas.

practice.q: Which tool measures wind speed?
A town west of yours had storms yesterday. Weather in most of the United States usually moves from west to east. What might you predict?
ch: storms may reach your town soon
storms will move away to the west
your town will have snow in July

practice.q: A storm moved 360 km in 12 hours. What was its average speed in km per hour?
practice.h: Speed equals distance divided by time.

practice.q: A forecast says "70% chance of rain." Explain what this means and why forecasts use probability.
practice.ans: It means rain is likely but not certain in the area; forecasts use probability because the atmosphere is complex and scientists can only estimate how air masses will move and interact.

quiz.q: After a storm, a city's barometer reading rises steadily for a day. What weather is most likely next?
A storm is 240 km west of a city and moving east toward it at 40 km per hour. How many hours until it arrives?
High temperatures for five days were 28, 30, 25, 22 and 20 °C. What was the mean high temperature in °C?
Which data pattern best signals that a cold front is approaching?
ch: falling pressure, rising humidity, building clouds

quiz.q: A forecaster sees a high-pressure system parked over Nevada pushing dry wind toward Southern California. Which forecast is best supported?
ch: hot, dry, windy weather with higher fire danger

quiz.q: Why might a weather forecast for 10 days ahead be less accurate than a forecast for tomorrow?
ch: Small changes in the atmosphere grow over time and are hard to predict
Weather instruments stop working after 1 day

quiz.q: Use what you know about air masses to explain why it is often warmer and more humid before a cold front and cooler and drier after it.
quiz.ans: Before the front, a warm, humid air mass covers the area. The front marks where a cold, drier air mass pushes in, so after it passes the cooler, drier air mass replaces the warm air.

test.q: The main source of energy for Earth's weather and water cycle is
Water vapor turning into liquid droplets is
A barometer measures
Which process moves water from the ground into the air through plants?
What role does gravity play in the water cycle?
ch: It pulls precipitation down and makes water flow downhill

test.q: Which air mass would bring hot, dry weather to California?
ch: one that formed over the deserts of the Southwest or Mexico
one that formed over the North Pacific
one that formed over the Arctic Ocean
one that formed over the Gulf of Mexico

test.q: Why does warm air rising often lead to cloud formation?
ch: The air cools as it rises, so water vapor condenses
The air gets warmer and drier

test.q: A warm front usually brings
ch: long periods of light rain followed by warmer air
sudden short thunderstorms followed by cooler air

test.q: Air moves from a region of high pressure to low pressure. This movement is
Which observation suggests air near the ground has reached its dew point?
ch: the sky is clear and dry

test.q: Pressure readings over 12 hours: 1,020, 1,015, 1,008, 1,002 millibars. Which forecast is best supported?
A mountain's west side gets 1,500 mm of rain per year and its east side gets 250 mm. Winds blow from the west. Which explanation is best?
ch: Air rises on the west side, cools and drops rain; it sinks and warms on the east side
The east side is closer to the ocean
Gravity is weaker on the east side

test.q: A mountain's west side gets 1,500 mm of rain per year and its east side gets 250 mm. How many times more rain does the west side get?
A storm moved 450 km in 9 hours. What was its average speed in km per hour?
Air can hold 25 g of water vapor per cubic meter and holds 20 g. What is the relative humidity in percent?
Rainfall over four months was 110, 80, 40 and 10 mm. What was the mean monthly rainfall in mm?
Which is the best evidence that a cold front has passed?
ch: temperature dropped and wind direction changed after a storm
humidity slowly rose for three days
the sky stayed cloudy all week

test.q: Why do forecasters use computer models and data from satellites, balloons and ground stations?
ch: Weather depends on many interacting factors over large areas

test.q: Two cities are at the same latitude. City A is next to the ocean; City B is far inland. In summer, City A has fog many mornings and City B has none. What best explains the difference?
ch: Moist ocean air cools and condenses near City A
City B is closer to the Sun
City B has more water vapor

test.q: Explain why snowpack in the Sierra Nevada is important for California's water supply, using the water cycle.
test.ans: Winter precipitation is stored as snow; in spring and summer, sunlight melts it and gravity carries the water as runoff into rivers and reservoirs that people use in dry months.

test.q: Describe what happens to warm and cold air when a cold front arrives and how this changes the weather.
test.ans: Dense cold air pushes under the warm air and forces it upward quickly; the rising warm air cools and forms tall clouds and storms; after the front passes, cooler and drier air brings clearer weather.

test.q: A student says, "Clouds are made of water vapor." Explain what is wrong with this statement and what clouds are really made of.
test.ans: Water vapor is an invisible gas. Clouds form when water vapor cools and condenses into tiny liquid droplets or ice crystals; those droplets and crystals are what we see.

test.q: A class compared two days in Los Angeles. Day 1: air mass from the Pacific, 21 °C, humidity 78%, morning fog. Day 2: air mass from the Great Basin desert, 34 °C, humidity 12%, strong dry winds from the northeast. Make a claim about what caused the difference in weather between the two days. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: different air masses caused the different weather. Evidence: on Day 1 a Pacific air mass brought cooler 21 °C air, 78% humidity and fog; on Day 2 a desert air mass brought 34 °C, 12% humidity and dry winds. Reasoning: air masses take on the temperature and humidity of where they form; air from over the ocean is cool and moist, while air from the desert is hot and dry, so when a different air mass moves in, the local weather changes.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 6: Causes and Effects of Regional Climates
units.el: Shine a flashlight straight down and at an angle on grid paper to show spreading of light. Pre-teach latitude, current, prevailing wind and rain shadow with a labeled world map.

lessons.name: Weather or climate? Unequal heating of Earth

practice.q: Climate is
ch: the usual pattern of weather in a place over many years
the amount of rain in one storm
practice.h: Think long term, not one day.

practice.q: Why is the equator warmer than the poles on average?
ch: Sunlight strikes the equator more directly, so energy is concentrated on a smaller area
The equator is closer to the Sun
The poles have no sunlight all year

practice.q: A flashlight shines straight down on graph paper and lights 20 squares. Tilted, the same light covers 40 squares. What does this model show?
ch: Light at a low angle is spread over a larger area, so each square gets less energy
The flashlight made more light when tilted
practice.h: The same amount of light is shared by more squares.

practice.q: A flashlight shining straight down lights 20 squares of graph paper; tilted, the same light covers 40 squares. How many times less light does each square get when tilted?
A student says, "It is raining today in Seattle, so Seattle has a rainy climate." Explain why one day of weather is not enough to describe climate.
practice.ans: Climate is based on long-term averages, usually 30 years or more. One rainy day is weather; to describe the climate you need many years of data on temperature and precipitation.

quiz.q: Which describes weather rather than climate?
ch: It is foggy in Monterey this morning
Monterey has cool, foggy summers most years
Phoenix has hot summers year after year

quiz.q: Which place would most likely receive the most solar energy per square meter over a year?
ch: a city near the Arctic Circle

quiz.q: Average July high temperatures for 5 years in a city were 31, 33, 32, 30 and 34 °C. What is the mean July high in °C?
Earth's axis is tilted. How does this cause seasons in the Northern Hemisphere?
ch: In summer the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun and receives more direct light and longer days
In summer Earth is much closer to the Sun
In winter the Sun gives off less energy
The tilt changes the length of a year

quiz.q: Data: Quito, Ecuador (0° latitude) averages about 14 °C, while Singapore (about 1° N) averages about 27 °C. Both are near the equator. What other factor most likely explains the difference?
ch: Quito is high in the mountains, at about 2,800 meters
Singapore is closer to the Sun
Singapore is at the North Pole

quiz.q: Sunlight delivers about 1,000 watts per square meter when it shines straight down. If the same light is spread over 4 square meters, how many watts does each square meter get?
Explain why places near the poles stay cold even though they get 24 hours of daylight in summer.
quiz.ans: Sunlight arrives at a very low angle, so its energy spreads over a large area and much is reflected by ice and snow, so each area receives little energy.

lessons.name: Global winds and Earth's rotation

practice.q: Near the equator, warm air rises. What happens as this air rises and cools?
ch: Water vapor condenses and causes heavy rain
practice.h: Rising air cools. What happens to vapor in cool air?

practice.q: Air that rose at the equator sinks back down near 30° north and south latitude. Sinking air is dry. Which kind of region is common near 30° latitude?
The turning of winds caused by Earth's rotation is called
In the Northern Hemisphere, Earth's rotation causes moving air to curve
practice.h: Picture yourself facing the direction the wind is moving.

practice.q: Describe how unequal heating and Earth's rotation together create global wind patterns.
practice.ans: Unequal heating makes air rise at the equator and sink at other latitudes, setting up large convection loops; Earth's rotation curves these winds, producing belts such as the trade winds and westerlies.

quiz.q: The prevailing winds over most of the United States, including California, generally blow from
Why do the Amazon and Congo rainforests get so much rain?
ch: They are near the equator, where warm, moist air rises and cools
They are near 30° latitude, where air sinks

quiz.q: The Sahara Desert lies around 20 to 30 degrees north latitude. Which global pattern helps explain its dryness?
ch: Dry air sinks there after rising at the equator
It is in a cold polar air cell

quiz.q: A wind belt carries air 600 km in 20 hours. What is the average speed of the wind in km per hour?
A balloon released in Sacramento drifted east 1,800 km in 3 days. What was its average distance per day in km?
A student models Earth with a spinning globe and draws a line straight from the North Pole toward the equator while it spins. The line curves. What does the model demonstrate?
ch: Earth's rotation causes moving air and water to curve
The globe is too small to show winds
Gravity pulls air to the poles

quiz.q: Explain why both the equator and 30° latitude are partly the result of convection in the atmosphere.
quiz.ans: At the equator, strong heating makes air rise, cool and drop rain. That air moves toward the poles, cools further and sinks near 30°, where it warms and dries the land. This rising and sinking loop is a convection current driven by unequal heating.

lessons.name: Ocean currents carry energy around the planet

practice.q: Large streams of moving water in the ocean are called
The Gulf Stream carries warm water from near the equator north across the Atlantic. How does it affect Western Europe?
ch: It helps give Western Europe milder winters than other places at the same latitude
It makes Western Europe a desert
It has no effect on climate

practice.q: The California Current flows south along the West Coast, bringing cold water from the north. How does it affect coastal California summers?
ch: They are cooler and often foggy
practice.h: Air over cold water gets cooled.

practice.q: What two main factors drive surface ocean currents?
Explain how an ocean current can move thermal energy from one part of Earth to another.
practice.ans: Water warmed near the equator flows toward higher latitudes, carrying thermal energy with it; it releases heat to the air there, warming nearby land. Cold currents carry cold water toward the equator.

quiz.q: San Francisco and Washington, D.C. are at about the same latitude. San Francisco has cooler summers. What is the best explanation?
ch: San Francisco is next to the cold California Current
Washington, D.C. is closer to the Sun
San Francisco gets no sunlight in summer
Washington, D.C. is at a higher elevation

quiz.q: Deep ocean currents are driven partly by differences in water density. Which water is densest?
Summer ocean temperatures off San Diego averaged 21 °C and off Monterey 14 °C. How many °C warmer was the water off San Diego?
A floating buoy in an ocean current moved 72 km in one day. What was its average speed in km per hour?
A city on a west coast of a continent at 50° N has much warmer winters than a city at 50° N in the middle of the continent. Which combination best explains this?
ch: A warm ocean current and winds from the ocean keep the coast milder
The coastal city is at the equator
The inland city is next to the ocean
The coastal city receives more direct sunlight

quiz.q: In upwelling, winds push surface water away from the coast and cold water rises from below. Along California, how does upwelling affect the nearby air?
ch: It cools the air and can help form fog

quiz.q: Data: Lisbon, Portugal (39° N, Atlantic coast): January average 11 °C. Beijing, China (40° N, far from warm currents and influenced by cold winds from the continent's interior): January average -3 °C. Make a claim about why these cities at nearly the same latitude have different winter temperatures. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: Lisbon has milder winters because the ocean and warm currents keep it warmer, while Beijing is affected by cold continental air. Evidence: at about the same latitude, Lisbon averages 11 °C in January and Beijing averages -3 °C, a 14 °C difference. Reasoning: both receive similar sunlight, so latitude cannot explain the difference; ocean water stores thermal energy and changes temperature slowly, and currents and winds from the ocean carry that energy to Lisbon, while Beijing gets cold air from the interior of the continent.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: Mountains, oceans and California's climates

practice.q: Moist air from the Pacific rises over the Sierra Nevada and drops rain and snow on the western slopes. What happens on the eastern side?
ch: The air sinks, warms and is dry, creating a rain shadow
It snows more than the west side
practice.h: The air already lost much of its water on the way up.

practice.q: Death Valley, east of the Sierra Nevada, is one of the driest places in North America. Which factor best explains this?
ch: It is in a rain shadow of mountains
It is next to the ocean
It is at the North Pole
It gets air that is rising and cooling

practice.q: As you climb a tall mountain, the air temperature usually
ch: goes up and down randomly every meter

practice.q: Air temperature drops about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 meters of elevation gain. If it is 20 °C at sea level, what is the temperature at 2,000 meters?
practice.h: Find the total drop for 2,000 meters first.

practice.q: Explain why inland cities like Fresno have hotter summers than coastal cities like Santa Cruz.
practice.ans: Coastal cities are cooled by the nearby ocean and cold current, which change temperature slowly; inland cities are far from the ocean's influence, so land heats up more in summer sunlight.

quiz.q: Which pair of factors most affects the climate of a region?
ch: latitude and nearness to large bodies of water
the color of houses and number of roads
the time zone and the population
the number of trees and the language spoken

quiz.q: Annual precipitation: west slope of a mountain range 1,200 mm, east slope 300 mm. What percent of the west slope's precipitation does the east slope receive?
At sea level the temperature is 30 °C. Temperature drops about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m. What is the temperature at 4,000 m?
Which data pair would best show the effect of the ocean on climate?
ch: the yearly temperature range for a coastal city and an inland city at the same latitude
the rainfall of one city on one day
the temperature of one city at noon

quiz.q: A climate graph shows a city with warm, dry summers and mild, rainy winters. Which kind of climate is this?
ch: a Mediterranean climate, like much of coastal California

quiz.q: Hawaii's islands each have a wet windward side and a dry leeward side. Which process causes this?
ch: Trade winds push moist air up the mountains on one side; the other side is a rain shadow
The leeward side is closer to the equator
The windward side has no mountains

quiz.q: Use a model of a mountain and moving air to explain why one side of a mountain range can be a forest and the other side a desert.
quiz.ans: Wind pushes moist air up the windward side; it cools, the vapor condenses and rain falls, supporting forests. The air that crosses the top is dry; as it sinks it warms and absorbs moisture, creating a dry rain shadow on the leeward side where deserts form.

test.q: Climate is best described as
ch: the long-term pattern of weather in an area

test.q: Which is a cold ocean current along North America's west coast?
Why does the equator receive more energy from the Sun per square meter than the poles?
ch: Sunlight hits it at a more direct angle
It is closer to the Sun

test.q: Which global pattern helps explain why many deserts lie near 30° latitude?
ch: Dry air sinks there after rising near the equator

test.q: The Coriolis effect is caused by
Which statement about the ocean and climate is correct?
ch: Water heats and cools slowly, so it moderates nearby land temperatures
The ocean has no effect on land climate
The ocean only affects climate at the poles

test.q: The Gulf Stream helps make Western Europe
ch: milder in winter than other regions at the same latitude

test.q: Which observation is evidence of a rain shadow?
ch: One side of a mountain range is green and wet, and the other side is dry
A city has the same weather every day

test.q: Which place would likely have the smallest difference between summer and winter temperatures?
ch: a small island in the middle of an ocean
a city in the center of a large continent

test.q: As air rises over a mountain, it
ch: expands and cools, and water vapor may condense

test.q: San Diego (33° N, coast) and Dallas, Texas (33° N, inland) have very different summer highs: about 24 °C and about 35 °C. Which is the best explanation?
ch: San Diego is cooled by the ocean and cold current; Dallas is far from the ocean
Dallas is closer to the equator
Dallas is next to a cold ocean current

test.q: A student shines a lamp straight down on one thermometer and at a low angle on another for 10 minutes. The first rose 9 °C and the second rose 4 °C. What does this model represent?
ch: Why places with more direct sunlight are warmer

test.q: A lamp shone straight down on one thermometer and at a low angle on another for 10 minutes. The first rose 9 °C and the second rose 4 °C. How many more °C did the thermometer under direct light rise?
Temperature drops about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m. If it is 25 °C at sea level, what is the temperature at 3,000 m in °C?
A city's yearly rainfall for 4 years was 380, 420, 290 and 510 mm. What is the mean yearly rainfall in mm?
A drifting buoy moved 96 km in 24 hours in the California Current. What was its speed in km per hour?
Which data would best help scientists describe a city's climate?
ch: 30 years of temperature and precipitation records

test.q: Which statement about Earth's rotation and winds is correct?
ch: Rotation curves winds, helping form belts like the trade winds and westerlies
Rotation causes winds to blow straight north

test.q: The coast of Peru is very dry even though it is next to the Pacific Ocean. A cold current flows north along the coast. Which explanation fits?
ch: Cold water cools the air above it, so less water evaporates and the air is too stable for rain
Peru is at the North Pole
The ocean has no water vapor

test.q: Explain how Earth's tilt and orbit cause seasons in California.
test.ans: As Earth orbits the Sun, its tilted axis points the Northern Hemisphere toward the Sun in June, giving California more direct sunlight and longer days (summer); in December it points away, so light is less direct and days are shorter (winter).

test.q: Describe how an ocean current affects the climate of a nearby coast. Give an example.
test.ans: Currents carry warm or cold water that warms or cools the air above it; for example, the cold California Current keeps coastal California summers cool and foggy.

test.q: Explain why two cities at the same latitude can have very different climates. Give at least two factors.
test.ans: Latitude affects sunlight, but climate also depends on nearness to the ocean, ocean currents, elevation, prevailing winds and mountains (rain shadows), so cities at the same latitude can differ in temperature and rainfall.

test.q: A student compared two California cities at about 36° N. Monterey (coast, near sea level): average July high 20 °C, January high 16 °C. Fresno (inland valley, about 100 m elevation): July high 37 °C, January high 13 °C. Make a claim about what causes the difference in their climates. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Monterey's nearness to the cold Pacific Ocean gives it a milder climate than inland Fresno. Evidence: Monterey's highs vary only 4 °C (16 to 20 °C), while Fresno's vary 24 °C (13 to 37 °C), even though both are at 36° N and near sea level. Reasoning: same latitude means similar sunlight; water heats and cools slowly and the cold California Current cools coastal air, so the ocean keeps Monterey cool in summer and mild in winter, while Fresno's land heats and cools more.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 7: Global Warming and Its Effects on Living Systems
units.el: Model the greenhouse effect with a labeled diagram and gestures (sunlight in, heat trapped). Provide graph-reading frames: "From ___ to ___, the ___ increased by ___."

lessons.name: The greenhouse effect

practice.q: Which gas released by burning fossil fuels is a major greenhouse gas?
How do greenhouse gases warm Earth?
ch: They absorb heat given off by Earth's surface and send some back toward the ground
They block all sunlight from reaching Earth
practice.h: Sunlight warms the ground; the ground gives off heat. What happens to that heat?

practice.q: Without any greenhouse effect, Earth's average temperature would be far below freezing. What does this tell us?
ch: Some greenhouse effect is natural and needed for life
Earth gets no energy from the Sun
Greenhouse gases are made only by people

practice.q: A model has two jars in sunlight. One jar has extra carbon dioxide added. After 30 minutes it is 2 °C warmer. What does this model suggest?
ch: More carbon dioxide can trap more heat
The sunlight was stronger on one jar
practice.h: What was the only difference between the jars?

practice.q: Explain the difference between the natural greenhouse effect and the enhanced greenhouse effect caused by humans.
practice.ans: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life. Human activities like burning fossil fuels add extra greenhouse gases, which trap more heat and raise global temperatures.

quiz.q: Which human activity adds the most carbon dioxide to the atmosphere?
ch: burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas

quiz.q: Cutting down forests can increase carbon dioxide in the air because
ch: trees that take in carbon dioxide are removed, and burning or decaying wood releases it

quiz.q: Which gas, released by cattle, landfills and natural gas leaks, is also a greenhouse gas?
In a jar model, a jar with normal air warmed from 22 °C to 28 °C. A jar with extra carbon dioxide warmed from 22 °C to 31 °C. How many more degrees °C did the carbon dioxide jar warm?
A family's car releases about 4 metric tons of carbon dioxide per year. If they drive 25 percent less, how many metric tons will it release per year?
Which question would best help a scientist test the greenhouse effect in a lab model?
ch: Does the amount of carbon dioxide in a container change how much it warms in light?
How many jars fit on a windowsill?

quiz.q: Describe the path of energy from the Sun to Earth's surface and back toward space, and explain where greenhouse gases fit in.
quiz.ans: Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface; the surface gives off heat (infrared energy); greenhouse gases absorb some of this heat and send part of it back toward the surface, so less escapes to space.

lessons.name: Reading the evidence: temperature and carbon dioxide

practice.q: Measurements at Mauna Loa, Hawaii show carbon dioxide rising from about 315 parts per million (ppm) in 1958 to about 420 ppm in 2023. What is the trend?
Carbon dioxide measured at Mauna Loa was about 315 ppm in 1958 and about 420 ppm in 2023. By how many ppm did carbon dioxide increase?
practice.h: Subtract the earlier value from the later value.

practice.q: Global average temperature has risen about 1 °C since the late 1800s. Why do scientists use averages from thousands of stations?
ch: One place's weather varies a lot, so many stations show the global trend

practice.q: Scientists compare a graph of rising carbon dioxide with a graph of rising global temperature. What kind of relationship do the graphs show?
ch: both increase over the same time period

practice.q: A student says, "It snowed a lot this winter, so global warming is not real." Use the difference between weather and climate to respond.
practice.ans: One snowy winter is weather in one place. Global warming is a long-term rise in Earth's average temperature measured over decades around the world, so one cold season does not disprove it.
practice.h: Is one season in one place weather or climate?

quiz.q: Which evidence best shows Earth's average temperature has risen over the past century?
ch: Long-term temperature records from land, oceans and satellites

quiz.q: Carbon dioxide was about 280 ppm before 1800 and about 420 ppm in 2023. What is the percent increase?
A graph shows global temperature rose 0.2 °C per decade. How many °C is that over 30 years?
Ice cores contain trapped air bubbles that are thousands of years old. Why are they useful?
ch: They show what carbon dioxide levels were in the past
They melt to make new air

quiz.q: Scientists checked natural factors such as the Sun's energy output and volcanic eruptions, and found they cannot explain the warming since 1950. Which conclusion is best supported?
ch: Human-caused greenhouse gases are the main cause of recent warming
The Sun is the main cause of recent warming
Volcanoes are cooling Earth faster than ever

quiz.q: Which question would help clarify evidence about the cause of rising temperatures?
ch: How has the amount of carbon dioxide in the air changed as fossil fuel use increased?
What is the favorite color of most scientists?
Which city has the most cars painted red?

quiz.q: Data table: Year 1960: carbon dioxide 317 ppm, global temperature change compared with the 1951-1980 average 0.0 °C. Year 1980: 339 ppm, +0.3 °C. Year 2000: 370 ppm, +0.4 °C. Year 2020: 414 ppm, +1.0 °C. Make a claim about the relationship between carbon dioxide and global temperature. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: As carbon dioxide in the atmosphere increased, global temperature increased. Evidence: from 1960 to 2020 carbon dioxide rose from 317 to 414 ppm, and the temperature change rose from 0.0 to +1.0 °C. Reasoning: carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that absorbs heat given off by Earth's surface; more of it traps more heat, which raises the average temperature. A pattern alone shows the two are related, and the greenhouse effect explains why one can cause the other.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: Effects on Earth's systems and living things

practice.q: As the ocean warms, water expands and land ice melts. What is the effect on sea level?
Warmer winters mean more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow in the Sierra Nevada. Why is this a problem for California's water supply?
ch: Less snowpack stores water for the dry summer months
Rain is not made of water
Snow is too heavy for reservoirs
practice.h: When does snowpack release its water?

practice.q: Corals turn white and can die when ocean water stays too warm. What happens to fish that depend on coral reefs?
ch: Their food and shelter decrease, so their populations may decline
They begin to live on land

practice.q: From 1900 to 2020, global sea level rose about 24 cm. What was the average rise in cm per decade?
practice.h: How many decades are in 120 years?

practice.q: Describe one way warming temperatures can affect a plant or animal species and explain why.
practice.ans: Example: pikas living high in the Sierra Nevada need cool temperatures; as it warms they must move higher up mountains, and when there is no higher place, their habitat shrinks and populations can drop.

quiz.q: Spring flowers in some regions now bloom earlier, but some pollinating insects still emerge at the same time. What is a likely effect?
ch: Fewer flowers get pollinated, so plants make fewer seeds

quiz.q: Longer, hotter and drier summers in California most directly increase the risk of
A town's average number of days above 35 °C was 12 per year in 1980 and 30 per year in 2020. What was the percent increase?
Arctic sea ice covered about 7.7 million square km in September 1980 and about 3.9 million square km in September 2020. By how many million square km did it shrink?
Polar bears hunt seals from sea ice. Arctic sea ice in September shrank from about 7.7 million square km in 1980 to about 3.9 million square km in 2020. Which prediction is best supported?
ch: Polar bears will have a harder time finding food
Polar bears will hunt more easily
Seals will move onto land to escape bears
The data cannot apply to bears

quiz.q: Some trees in a mountain forest are found 100 meters higher than they were 50 years ago. What is the most likely reason?
ch: Warmer temperatures allow the trees to grow at higher, once-colder elevations
There is less sunlight on mountains

quiz.q: Explain how a change in one Earth system (the atmosphere) can cause changes in the hydrosphere and biosphere. Give one example of each.
quiz.ans: A warmer atmosphere warms ocean water and melts ice, raising sea levels and reducing snowpack (hydrosphere); this changes habitats, so coral reefs bleach or species move to cooler areas (biosphere).

lessons.name: Designing solutions to reduce human impacts

practice.q: Which choice would most reduce the carbon dioxide released when a school uses electricity?
ch: installing solar panels on the roof

practice.q: A city wants to cut car emissions. Which plan addresses the cause most directly?
ch: adding safe bike lanes and frequent electric buses
practice.h: Which option means fewer gasoline-burning cars on the road?

practice.q: A school's electricity bill shows 50,000 kilowatt-hours used per year. Solar panels produce 30,000 kilowatt-hours. What percent of the school's electricity do they supply?
When evaluating designs to reduce food waste in a cafeteria, why is a decision matrix helpful?
ch: It compares each design against the same criteria in a fair way
It picks a design at random
It makes every design score the same

practice.q: Describe one criterion and one constraint for a plan to reduce the carbon dioxide produced by students' trips to school.
practice.ans: Criterion: reduce car trips by at least 20 percent. Constraint: must be safe for students, cost little and work for families who live far away.
practice.h: Criteria describe success; constraints describe limits.

quiz.q: A decision matrix rates three plans to cut a school's energy use (1 to 5 points for each criterion). Plan A: cost 4, energy saved 2, easy to do 5 (total 11). Plan B: cost 2, energy saved 5, easy to do 2 (total 9). Plan C: cost 3, energy saved 4, easy to do 4 (total 11). If energy saved counts double, which plan scores highest?
A plan scores 3 points for cost, 4 points for energy saved and 4 points for ease. If energy saved counts double, what is its total score?
A family replaced 20 old light bulbs with LEDs. Each LED saves about 50 kilowatt-hours per year. How many kilowatt-hours do they save per year?
Which statement best explains why planting trees can help reduce global warming?
ch: Trees take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis and store carbon in their wood
Trees release carbon dioxide all day

quiz.q: Two plans to reduce a town's greenhouse gases are being compared. Plan X cuts emissions 30 percent but costs too much for the town's budget. Plan Y cuts emissions 18 percent and fits the budget. What should engineers do next?
ch: look for ways to combine or improve the plans to meet more of the criteria within the constraints

quiz.q: Which human activity change would reduce methane emissions?
ch: capturing gas from landfills and reducing food waste
burning more trash in open fires

quiz.q: Propose a solution your school could use to reduce its impact on the environment. Explain how it works and how you would measure whether it succeeds.
quiz.ans: Example: a composting and food-share program; it keeps food out of landfills, reducing methane. Measure the mass of trash sent to the landfill each week before and after the program and compare the averages.

test.q: Carbon dioxide and methane are examples of
The main source of the extra carbon dioxide in the atmosphere since 1800 is
How do greenhouse gases affect Earth's temperature?
ch: They absorb and re-emit heat, keeping more energy near the surface
They reflect all sunlight back to space
They have no effect on temperature

test.q: Why is some greenhouse effect necessary for life?
ch: It keeps Earth warm enough for liquid water

test.q: Which observation is evidence of a warming climate?
ch: Glaciers around the world are shrinking over decades
One day in July was very hot
A tree lost its leaves in fall

test.q: Which is the best way to describe climate change?
ch: a long-term change in average weather patterns
the change from day to night
a change in the weather in one afternoon

test.q: Rising sea levels most threaten
How does deforestation contribute to global warming?
ch: Fewer trees take in carbon dioxide, and burning trees releases it

test.q: Which solution most directly reduces carbon dioxide from electricity?
ch: replacing coal power plants with wind and solar power

test.q: In California, warmer winters reduce snowpack. Which effect would follow?
ch: less water flowing into rivers and reservoirs in late summer

test.q: Ocean pH data show the ocean becoming more acidic as it absorbs carbon dioxide. Which organisms are most at risk?
ch: animals with shells made of calcium carbonate, like oysters and corals

test.q: Data: global temperature change compared with the 1951-1980 average was -0.3 °C in 1920, 0.0 °C in 1960 and +1.0 °C in 2020. Which conclusion is best supported?
ch: Most of the warming happened after 1960
The data show warming only before 1960

test.q: Global temperature compared with the 1951-1980 average was -0.3 °C in 1920 and +1.0 °C in 2020. By how many °C did it change from 1920 to 2020?
Carbon dioxide rose from 340 ppm in 1980 to 420 ppm in 2023. What was the increase in ppm?
A school used 80,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity in one year and 68,000 the next year after an energy-saving program. What was the percent decrease?
A car releases about 0.4 kg of carbon dioxide per mile. A family drives 500 fewer miles by biking. How many kg of carbon dioxide do they avoid?
Which question would help clarify evidence about why global temperatures rose?
ch: How have greenhouse gas levels changed as human fuel use increased?
Which month has the most holidays?
How many people live in Hawaii?

test.q: A decision matrix scores two plans. Plan 1: reduces emissions 9 points, cost 3 points. Plan 2: reduces emissions 6 points, cost 8 points. The town says cost and emissions matter equally. Which plan should be chosen based on the matrix?
ch: Plan 1, because it reduces emissions more

test.q: Pikas live high in mountains and cannot survive long in temperatures above about 26 °C. What happens to their habitat as the climate warms?
ch: It shrinks as cool areas move higher up the mountains

test.q: Explain why scientists are confident that humans are the main cause of global warming since 1950.
test.ans: Carbon dioxide levels have risen sharply as people burned fossil fuels, the timing matches the warming, and natural factors like the Sun and volcanoes cannot explain the recent rise.

test.q: Describe one effect of global warming on a living system and explain the cause.
test.ans: Coral bleaching: when ocean water stays too warm, corals lose the algae that feed them, turn white and may die, reducing habitat for reef fish.

test.q: Your city wants to lower greenhouse gas emissions from transportation. Describe one solution, one criterion and one constraint for it.
test.ans: Solution: more electric buses and protected bike lanes. Criterion: cut transportation emissions by 25 percent in 10 years. Constraint: must fit the city budget and serve all neighborhoods.

test.q: A student analyzed data for a mountain lake in the Sierra Nevada. 1980: ice-free 150 days per year, average summer water temperature 12 °C, trout population 4,000. 2000: ice-free 165 days, 13 °C, trout 3,200. 2020: ice-free 185 days, 15 °C, trout 2,100. Trout need cold water. Make a claim about how a warming climate is affecting the lake ecosystem. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: a warming climate is warming the lake and reducing its trout population. Evidence: from 1980 to 2020 ice-free days rose from 150 to 185, summer water temperature rose 3 °C (12 to 15 °C), and trout fell from 4,000 to 2,100. Reasoning: higher air temperatures from more greenhouse gases warm the lake and shorten ice cover; trout need cold water that holds more oxygen, so as the water warms, fewer trout can survive and reproduce.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

sci|7.about: Grade 7 integrated science (California's preferred middle school model) uses phenomena to show that organisms and nonliving things are made of atoms, that matter cycles and energy flows through organisms, ecosystems and rocks, and that natural processes and human activities shape Earth's surface, resources and biodiversity. Students model particles and reactions, analyze data, construct explanations and design solutions.
std: Develop models to describe the atomic composition of simple molecules and extended structures.
Develop a model that predicts and describes changes in particle motion, temperature and state of a pure substance when thermal energy is added or removed.
Analyze and interpret data on the properties of substances before and after the substances interact to determine if a chemical reaction has occurred.
Develop and use a model to describe how the total number of atoms does not change in a chemical reaction and thus mass is conserved.
Construct a scientific explanation based on evidence for the role of photosynthesis in the cycling of matter and flow of energy into and out of organisms.
Develop a model to describe the cycling of matter and flow of energy among living and nonliving parts of an ecosystem.
Develop a model to describe the cycling of Earth's materials and the flow of energy that drives this process.
Analyze and interpret data on the distribution of fossils and rocks, continental shapes and seafloor structures to provide evidence of the past plate motions.

units.name: Unit 1: Atoms, Molecules and States of Matter
units.el: Use ball-and-stick or paper-circle models; students name each atom aloud. Provide a particle diagram chart for solid, liquid and gas with the words close, vibrate, slide and spread out.

lessons.name: Everything is made of atoms

practice.q: What is the smallest particle of an element that still has the properties of that element?
practice.h: Elements are made of only one kind of this particle.

practice.q: A water molecule (H2O) is made of
Which is a pure element?
practice.h: An element is made of only one kind of atom.

practice.q: How many atoms in total are in one molecule of carbon dioxide, CO2?
Explain the difference between an atom and a molecule, using oxygen gas (O2) as an example.
practice.ans: An atom is a single particle of an element, like one oxygen atom (O). A molecule is two or more atoms bonded together; O2 is a molecule made of two oxygen atoms.

quiz.q: Two or more atoms bonded together form a
Which formula shows a molecule made of two different elements?
How many hydrogen atoms are in one molecule of methane, CH4?
Glucose has the formula C6H12O6. How many atoms are in one glucose molecule?
A substance is made of one carbon atom bonded to two oxygen atoms. What is its formula?
Sugar and water look different, yet both contain hydrogen and oxygen atoms. Why do they have different properties?
ch: Their atoms are combined in different numbers and arrangements
They are made of different kinds of hydrogen

quiz.q: A student draws a model of ammonia (NH3) as one large circle. Explain how to improve the model.
quiz.ans: Ammonia is a molecule made of one nitrogen atom bonded to three hydrogen atoms, so the model should show four circles: one for nitrogen connected to three smaller circles for hydrogen.

lessons.name: Molecules and extended structures

practice.q: Table salt is made of sodium and chlorine atoms arranged in a repeating cube pattern that continues in all directions. This is an example of
practice.h: Does the pattern stop at a few atoms, or repeat?

practice.q: A diamond is made only of carbon atoms, each bonded to four others in a repeating network. What does this tell you about diamond?
ch: It is an extended structure made of one element
It is a compound of many elements

practice.q: Which is made of individual small molecules rather than an extended structure?
In table salt (NaCl), sodium and chlorine atoms are present in a 1 to 1 ratio. A tiny salt crystal has 5,000 sodium atoms. How many chlorine atoms does it have?
practice.h: Equal numbers of each.

practice.q: Graphite (pencil lead) and diamond are both made only of carbon. Explain how they can have such different properties.
practice.ans: Their carbon atoms are arranged differently. In diamond each atom bonds to four others in a strong 3D network, making it hard; in graphite atoms form flat layers that slide over each other, making it soft.

quiz.q: A substance made of two or more different elements chemically combined is a
Quartz (SiO2) is made of silicon and oxygen atoms in a repeating 3D network. How many oxygen atoms are there for every silicon atom?
Which model best represents a crystal of table salt?
ch: alternating sodium and chlorine atoms stacked in a repeating cube
a pair of atoms floating alone
a long chain of only carbon

quiz.q: A model of a water molecule uses 1 red bead for oxygen and 2 white beads for hydrogen. How many white beads are needed to build 15 water molecules?
Ethanol has the formula C2H6O. How many atoms are in 10 ethanol molecules?
A student finds a solid that has a repeating pattern of atoms throughout, is very hard and has a high melting point. Which is the best inference?
ch: It is an extended structure with strong bonds between atoms
It is made of small separate molecules held weakly

quiz.q: Compare a small molecule and an extended structure, giving one example of each.
quiz.ans: A small molecule has a fixed number of atoms bonded together, like H2O or CO2. An extended structure is a repeating pattern of atoms that continues in every direction, like salt (NaCl) or diamond.

lessons.name: Particles in motion: solids, liquids and gases

practice.q: In which state of matter are particles packed tightly and only vibrate in place?
How do particles in a liquid move?
ch: They stay close together but slide past one another
They are locked in fixed positions
They are far apart and move freely in all directions

practice.q: A balloon is put in a freezer and shrinks. Which explanation is best?
ch: The gas particles slow down and hit the balloon less often and less hard
practice.h: How does temperature affect particle speed?

practice.q: A gas takes up 30 mL in a syringe at 20 °C. When warmed, it takes up 33 mL. By how many mL did the volume increase?
Use particle motion to explain why you can smell soup cooking from across a room.
practice.ans: The warm soup's particles move fast; some escape as gas and spread out, moving freely and mixing with air particles until they reach your nose.

quiz.q: In which state do particles have the most energy and move freely to fill their container?
Why does a liquid take the shape of its container while a solid does not?
ch: Liquid particles can slide past one another; solid particles are locked in place

quiz.q: A tire's air pressure is higher on a hot afternoon than on a cold morning. Which explanation is best?
ch: Faster-moving air particles hit the inside of the tire more often and harder
The tire gets more air particles from the sun

quiz.q: A balloon has a volume of 2.4 liters in a warm room and 2.1 liters outside in the cold. What is the decrease in volume in liters?
A 50 g ice cube has a volume of about 54.5 cubic centimeters. When it melts, the water has a volume of 50 cubic centimeters. How many cubic centimeters smaller is the water than the ice?
Ice floats on liquid water. What does this tell you about the particles in ice?
ch: They are spaced a little farther apart than in liquid water, so ice is less dense
They are packed more tightly than in liquid water
They are larger than water particles

quiz.q: Draw or describe particle models for the same substance as a solid, a liquid and a gas. Explain what differs.
quiz.ans: Solid: particles tightly packed in a pattern, vibrating. Liquid: particles close but not in a pattern, sliding past each other. Gas: particles far apart, moving fast in all directions. Particle spacing and speed differ; the particles themselves are the same.

lessons.name: Adding and removing thermal energy: changes of state

practice.q: The change from a liquid to a gas is
As ice melts at 0 °C, its temperature stays at 0 °C even though heat is added. Where does the energy go?
ch: It breaks the particles out of their fixed positions
practice.h: Think about what changes when a solid becomes a liquid.

practice.q: When water vapor in the air touches a cold window and forms droplets, thermal energy is
ch: removed from the water vapor, so its particles slow down and come together

practice.q: Heating data for water: 0 min, -10 °C; 2 min, 0 °C; 6 min, 0 °C; 10 min, 40 °C. For how many minutes did the temperature stay at 0 °C?
practice.h: Find when the temperature first reached 0 °C and when it began rising again.

practice.q: Explain what happens to the particles of water as a pot is heated from room temperature until it boils.
practice.ans: The particles gain energy and move faster, raising the temperature; at 100 °C (at sea level) they have enough energy to break away from the liquid and become gas, forming bubbles of water vapor.

quiz.q: The change from liquid to solid is
Wax is heated. Its temperature rises to 60 °C, stays at 60 °C for 5 minutes and then rises again. What happened during the 5 minutes?
ch: The wax became a gas instantly

quiz.q: Data: a pure substance was heated. Temperatures every minute: 20, 35, 50, 62, 62, 62, 62, 75, 88 °C. What is its melting or boiling point in °C, shown by the flat part?
Water was heated from 22 °C to 100 °C in 13 minutes before boiling. What was the mean rate of temperature rise in °C per minute?
Which change happens when thermal energy is removed from a substance?
ch: Its particles slow down, and it may condense or freeze
Its atoms change into a new element

quiz.q: Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) turns directly into a gas at room temperature. Which statement about this change is correct?
ch: Thermal energy from the room is added to the dry ice, and the particles spread out as a gas
Thermal energy is removed from the dry ice
The carbon dioxide becomes a liquid first

quiz.q: A class heated 100 g of a white solid and recorded: 0 min 25 °C, 2 min 45 °C, 4 min 54 °C, 6 min 54 °C, 8 min 54 °C, 10 min 70 °C, 12 min 85 °C. The solid became a clear liquid between 4 and 8 minutes. Make a claim about what was happening between 4 and 8 minutes. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning with a particle model.
quiz.ans: Claim: the substance was melting between 4 and 8 minutes. Evidence: the temperature stayed at 54 °C from 4 to 8 minutes while heat was still being added, and the solid turned into a liquid during that time; before and after, the temperature rose. Reasoning: during melting, added thermal energy is used to break particles free from their fixed positions instead of making them move faster, so the temperature stays constant until all the solid has melted.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

test.q: Which is the smallest unit of an element?
In which state of matter do particles slide past each other but stay close together?
What is the change from gas to liquid called?
How many oxygen atoms are in one molecule of O3 (ozone)?
Which formula represents a compound?
Which statement about atoms in a molecule of water is true?
ch: Two hydrogen atoms are bonded to one oxygen atom
One hydrogen atom is bonded to two oxygen atoms

test.q: Which is an extended structure?
When a gas is heated in a closed container, its particles
ch: move faster and push harder on the walls

test.q: A puddle disappears on a sunny day. What happened to the water particles?
ch: They gained energy and escaped into the air as water vapor

test.q: During boiling, the temperature of pure water stays constant because
ch: added energy is used to separate particles into a gas
the water loses particles that are heavy

test.q: A substance has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container. Which model of its particles is correct?
ch: close together and sliding past each other

test.q: A sealed bag of chips puffs up when taken from the beach to the top of a cold mountain. A student says the particles got bigger. Which is the best response?
ch: The particles did not get bigger; lower outside pressure lets the gas inside spread out more

test.q: How many atoms are in one molecule of ammonia, NH3?
Sucrose (table sugar) has the formula C12H22O11. How many atoms are in one sucrose molecule?
How many hydrogen atoms are in 5 molecules of water (H2O)?
Heating data: 0 min 10 °C, 3 min 40 °C, 6 min 70 °C, 9 min 78 °C, 12 min 78 °C, 15 min 78 °C. What is the boiling point of the liquid in °C?
A liquid was 10 °C at 0 minutes and 70 °C at 6 minutes. What was the mean rate of temperature rise in °C per minute?
Which change removes thermal energy from a substance?
Graphite and diamond are both pure carbon. Why are their properties different?
ch: Their carbon atoms are arranged differently

test.q: Use a particle model to explain why a gas can be compressed into a smaller space but a solid cannot easily be compressed.
test.ans: Gas particles are far apart with lots of empty space between them, so pushing them closer is easy; solid particles are already tightly packed, so there is little space to remove.

test.q: Describe how the motion and spacing of particles change as liquid water freezes into ice.
test.ans: As thermal energy is removed, particles slow down; they lock into fixed positions in a pattern and only vibrate, and in ice they are spaced slightly farther apart than in liquid water.

test.q: A student models a molecule of methane (CH4) with four black balls and one white ball. Evaluate the model.
test.ans: The model has the right total of 5 atoms, but in the usual color code carbon is black and hydrogen is white, so the colors are reversed: it should show 1 black carbon ball in the center with 4 white hydrogen balls each bonded to it.

test.q: Two equal masses of the same liquid were placed in identical dishes. Dish A was at 35 °C and Dish B at 15 °C. After 2 hours, Dish A had lost 18 g and Dish B had lost 6 g to evaporation. Make a claim about how temperature affects evaporation. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning using a particle model.
test.ans: Claim: a higher temperature makes a liquid evaporate faster. Evidence: Dish A at 35 °C lost 18 g in 2 hours, three times as much as Dish B at 15 °C, which lost 6 g. Reasoning: at higher temperature, particles have more kinetic energy on average, so more of them move fast enough to escape the liquid's surface and become gas.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 2: Chemical Reactions - New Substances from Old
units.el: Provide a property chart (color, density, melting point, solubility, smell) with picture icons. Use the frame: "Before the reaction ___; after the reaction ___; this shows a new substance because ___."

lessons.name: Properties identify substances

practice.q: Which is a characteristic property that can help identify a pure substance?
practice.h: It stays the same no matter how much of the substance you have.

practice.q: A metal block has a mass of 54 g and a volume of 20 cubic centimeters. What is its density in g per cubic centimeter?
practice.h: Density equals mass divided by volume.

practice.q: A reference table lists densities: aluminum 2.7, iron 7.9, copper 9.0 and gold 19.3 g per cubic centimeter. A metal block has a density of 2.7 g per cubic centimeter. It is most likely
Two clear liquids look the same. Which test would best tell them apart?
ch: measure the boiling point of each
compare how much is in each cup
look at the shape of each cup

practice.q: A student says a large piece of iron has a greater density than a small nail made of the same iron. Explain why this is wrong.
practice.ans: Density is a characteristic property; the large piece has more mass but also more volume in the same ratio, so its density is the same as the nail's.

quiz.q: The amount of matter in an object is its
A liquid has a mass of 39.5 g and a volume of 50 mL. What is its density in g per mL?
A gold ring has a density of 19.3 g per cubic centimeter and a volume of 2 cubic centimeters. What is its mass in g?
An object with a density of 0.9 g per cubic centimeter is placed in water (1.0 g per cubic centimeter). What happens?
Which set of properties would best identify an unknown white powder?
ch: melting point, solubility in water and density
size of the pile and shape

quiz.q: Sample A: density 2.7, melts at 660 °C. Sample B: density 2.7, melts at 660 °C. Sample C: density 7.9, melts at 1,538 °C. Which conclusion is best supported?
ch: A and B are likely the same substance; C is different
All three are the same substance
A and C are the same substance

quiz.q: Explain why scientists use several properties rather than just one to identify a substance.
quiz.ans: Different substances can share one property, such as color or even density, but it is very unlikely they share several characteristic properties like density, melting point and solubility.

lessons.name: Evidence of a chemical reaction

practice.q: Which observation is the best evidence that a chemical reaction happened?
ch: A new substance with different properties formed
practice.h: In a chemical reaction, new substances form.

practice.q: When vinegar and baking soda are mixed, bubbles form and the mixture gets colder. Which of these is evidence of a chemical reaction?
ch: both the gas forming and the temperature change
only that the mixture is wet
only that the cup is plastic

practice.q: Which is a physical change, not a chemical change?
Two clear solutions are mixed and a cloudy yellow solid forms. What is the solid called?
ch: a mixture of the same substances

practice.q: A student melts chocolate and says a chemical reaction happened because it changed from solid to liquid. Explain why this is not a chemical reaction.
practice.ans: Melting is a physical change; the chocolate is still the same substance with the same properties and it can harden again. No new substance formed.
practice.h: Did a new substance form?

quiz.q: Iron combining with oxygen to form rust is a

Data: before mixing, Substance 1 is a shiny gray solid that does not dissolve; Substance 2 is a clear liquid. After mixing, a gas bubbles off and a white solid that dissolves in water remains. What can be concluded?
ch: A chemical reaction occurred because substances with new properties formed

quiz.q: Which observation alone could be misleading as evidence of a chemical reaction?
ch: a new solid forming from two liquids
a new smell from burning toast
a color change as a banana ripens

quiz.q: Before a reaction, a liquid was 22 °C. After adding a powder, it was 31 °C. What was the temperature change in °C?
A substance melted at 801 °C before an experiment. A white solid made after the reaction melted at 186 °C. By how many °C do the melting points differ?
Why is a different melting point after mixing strong evidence of a chemical reaction?
ch: Melting point is a characteristic property, so a new value means a new substance
Melting point changes with the amount of substance
Melting point is the same for all solids

quiz.q: Describe two observations you could make to decide whether cooking an egg is a chemical change.
quiz.ans: The clear liquid egg white becomes a white solid that cannot change back, and it has a different texture and smell; these new properties show new substances formed.

lessons.name: Atoms rearrange; mass is conserved

practice.q: In a chemical reaction, what happens to atoms?
ch: They rearrange to form new substances, but none are created or destroyed
practice.h: Count atoms on both sides of a reaction.

practice.q: In the reaction 2H2 + O2 makes 2H2O, how many hydrogen atoms are on the reactant side?
practice.h: 2H2 means two molecules, each with 2 hydrogen atoms.

practice.q: Steel wool is burned on a balance in an open dish and its mass increases. Which explanation is best?
ch: Oxygen atoms from the air combined with the iron
New atoms were created by the flame

practice.q: 30 g of reactants react in a sealed container. What is the total mass of the products in g?
Vinegar and baking soda react in an open cup and the mass goes down. Explain why this does not break the law of conservation of mass.
practice.ans: One product is carbon dioxide gas, which escaped into the air and was not weighed. If the reaction were sealed, the total mass would stay the same.

quiz.q: Which statement describes the law of conservation of mass?
ch: Matter is not created or destroyed in a chemical reaction
Mass always increases in a reaction
Mass always decreases in a reaction

quiz.q: In the reaction CH4 + 2O2 makes CO2 + 2H2O, how many oxygen atoms are on the product side?
A sealed bag contains 85 g of reactants. After the reaction, a gas inflates the bag. What is the mass of the bag's contents in g?
A model shows 2 red and 2 blue beads before a reaction and 3 red and 2 blue beads after. Why is the model wrong?
ch: Atoms cannot be created, so the number of each kind must stay the same
The model should have fewer beads after

quiz.q: 12 g of carbon burns completely with 32 g of oxygen. What mass of carbon dioxide forms in g?
Wood burns in a fireplace and only a small pile of ash remains. Where did most of the mass go?
ch: Into gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapor that went into the air
It was destroyed by the fire

quiz.q: A class reacted 50 g of vinegar with 5 g of baking soda. In an open cup the final mass was 53 g. In a sealed bottle with a balloon on top, the final mass was 55 g and the balloon inflated. Make a claim about whether mass is conserved in this reaction. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning using atoms.
quiz.ans: Claim: mass is conserved in the reaction. Evidence: the starting mass was 55 g; in the sealed bottle the final mass was also 55 g. In the open cup the mass dropped by 2 g, and in the sealed bottle the balloon filled with gas. Reasoning: atoms rearrange into new substances but are not created or destroyed; in the open cup the carbon dioxide gas escaped, so 2 g was not measured, while the sealed bottle trapped every atom.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: Synthetic materials from natural resources

practice.q: A material that people make through chemical reactions, instead of finding in nature, is called
Most plastics are made from which natural resource?
practice.h: Think about fossil fuels.

practice.q: Nylon, used in jackets and ropes, is made by chemical reactions that join small molecules into long chains. Why do engineers make materials like nylon?
ch: to get useful properties, such as strength and light weight, that natural materials may lack
because natural materials do not exist
to make materials that break easily

practice.q: Glass is made by melting sand with other minerals at high temperature. Glass is an example of
ch: a material made from a natural resource
a material found already made in nature

practice.q: Choose one synthetic material. Name the natural resource it comes from and describe one effect its use has on society.
practice.ans: Example: plastic comes from petroleum; it makes lightweight, cheap packaging and medical supplies, but plastic waste pollutes oceans and harms wildlife.

quiz.q: Which is a synthetic material?
Some medicines are made by copying a chemical first found in a plant. What does this show?
ch: People can use chemistry to make useful substances from natural resources
Medicines cannot be made in labs

quiz.q: A factory uses 4 kg of crude oil to make 1 kg of plastic. How many kg of crude oil are needed to make 25 kg of plastic?
A city recycles 1,800 tons of its 6,000 tons of plastic waste each year. What percent is recycled?
A new bottle material is made from corn starch instead of oil. Which question is most important for deciding whether it is better for the environment?
ch: Does it break down faster and use fewer resources than plastic from oil?
Is it shaped like a bottle?

quiz.q: Which property makes synthetic rubber useful for car tires?
ch: It is stretchy, strong and resists wear

quiz.q: Explain one benefit and one cost to society of making and using plastics.
quiz.ans: Benefit: plastics are light, cheap and durable, used in medicine, safety gear and food storage. Cost: they come from nonrenewable oil and can last hundreds of years as pollution.

lessons.name: Design challenge: chemical heat and cold packs

practice.q: A process that releases thermal energy and makes its surroundings warmer is
A cold pack feels cold when squeezed because the process inside
ch: absorbs thermal energy from its surroundings
practice.h: Energy moves from your hand into the pack.

practice.q: A team designs a hand warmer for hikers. Which is a criterion?
ch: It stays above 40 °C for at least 1 hour
practice.h: A criterion says how well the design must work.

practice.q: A hand warmer started at 20 °C and reached 52 °C. What was the temperature increase in °C?
Explain how a team could use test data to improve a cold pack design.
practice.ans: Measure how cold each version gets and how long it stays cold, compare results to the criteria, keep the features that worked best, change one thing at a time and test again.

quiz.q: Test data: Mixture A rose from 21 °C to 46 °C. Mixture B fell from 21 °C to 6 °C. Mixture C stayed at 21 °C. Which mixture is best for a hand warmer?
A cold pack mixture fell from 21 °C to 6 °C. By how many °C did its temperature drop?
A warmer's temperature for four trials stayed above 40 °C for 52, 48, 55 and 49 minutes. What was the mean time in minutes?
