A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

sci|8.about: Grade 8 integrated science (California's preferred middle school model) uses phenomena such as collisions, asteroid impacts and mass extinctions to study forces and motion, energy, fields that act at a distance, the solar system, waves and information, the history of life on Earth, and how genes, natural selection and human choices shape species and biodiversity. Students plan investigations, use math and models, analyze data and design solutions.
std: Apply Newton's third law to design a solution to a problem involving the motion of two colliding objects.
Plan an investigation to provide evidence that the change in an object's motion depends on the sum of the forces on the object and the mass of the object.
Construct and interpret graphical displays of data to describe the relationships of kinetic energy to the mass of an object and to the speed of an object.
Construct and present arguments using evidence to support the claim that gravitational interactions are attractive and depend on the masses of interacting objects.
Develop and use a model to describe the role of gravity in the motions within galaxies and the solar system.
Use mathematical representations to describe a simple model for waves that includes how the amplitude of a wave is related to the energy in a wave.
Analyze and interpret data for patterns in the fossil record that document the existence, diversity, extinction and change of life forms throughout the history of life on Earth.

Construct an explanation based on evidence that describes how genetic variations of traits in a population increase some individuals' probability of surviving and reproducing in a specific environment.

units.name: Unit 1: Forces, Motion and Collisions
units.el: Use toy cars and arrows on the board to show force size and direction. Post the frames: "The net force is ___ newtons toward ___." and "Object A pushes on B; B pushes back on A with ___."

lessons.name: Describing motion: speed and velocity

practice.q: Speed is calculated by dividing
practice.h: Think of units such as meters per second.

practice.q: A cyclist rides 1,200 meters in 240 seconds. What is her average speed in meters per second?
practice.h: Divide distance by time.

practice.q: Two runners both run at 6 m/s, one north and one south. Which statement is true?
ch: They have the same speed but different velocities

practice.q: A train travels at 80 km per hour for 3.5 hours. How far does it travel in km?
A distance-time graph for a toy car is a straight line rising from 0 to 10 meters over 5 seconds, then a flat line from 5 to 8 seconds. Describe the car's motion.
practice.ans: The car moved at a constant speed of 2 m/s for the first 5 seconds, then stopped and stayed at 10 meters from 5 to 8 seconds.
practice.h: What does a flat line on a distance-time graph mean?

quiz.q: Speed in a given direction is called
A car drives 150 km in 2.5 hours. What is its average speed in km per hour?
A sprinter's speed goes from 0 to 9 m/s in 3 seconds. What is the acceleration in meters per second each second?
On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means
Which situation shows acceleration?
ch: a car going around a curve at a steady 40 km per hour
a book resting on a desk
a car parked on a street
a ball sitting on the floor

quiz.q: Two cars travel for 4 hours. Car A goes 240 km and Car B goes 320 km. Which statement is correct?
ch: Car B's average speed was 20 km per hour faster
Car A's average speed was faster
Both had the same average speed
Car B's average speed was 80 km per hour faster

quiz.q: A student walks 300 meters to school in 5 minutes and then 300 meters home in 10 minutes. Explain why her average speed for the whole trip is not simply the average of the two speeds.
quiz.ans: Average speed equals total distance divided by total time: 600 meters in 15 minutes is 40 meters per minute. She spent more time at the slower speed, so averaging 60 and 30 (45) gives the wrong answer.

lessons.name: Net force, mass and changes in motion

practice.q: Two students push a box from opposite sides. One pushes with 30 N to the right and the other with 30 N to the left. What happens?
ch: The forces are balanced, so the box's motion does not change
practice.h: Add forces in the same direction; subtract forces in opposite directions.

practice.q: A sled is pulled with 50 N forward while friction pushes back with 20 N. What is the net force in newtons?
The same push is given to an empty shopping cart and a full shopping cart. Which accelerates more?
ch: the empty cart, because it has less mass
the full cart, because it has more mass

practice.q: Using F = m x a, what force in newtons is needed to accelerate a 4 kg ball at 3 meters per second each second?
Plan an investigation to show how the mass of a cart affects its acceleration when the same force pulls it.
practice.ans: Pull carts of different masses (add weights) with the same force, such as the same falling weight or spring scale reading; measure the time to travel a set distance or use a motion sensor; keep the track and force the same; repeat trials and compare accelerations.
practice.h: Change only the mass. What must stay the same?

quiz.q: The overall force on an object when all forces are combined is the
A 1,000 kg car and a 2,000 kg truck both speed up at the same rate. Which needs the larger net force?
A 60 kg skater is pushed with a net force of 120 N. What is her acceleration in meters per second each second?
A rope pulls a wagon with 80 N east, and friction acts with 35 N west. What is the net force in newtons?
Data: a cart pulled by 2 N accelerated 1 m/s each second; by 4 N, 2 m/s each second; by 6 N, 3 m/s each second (mass unchanged). Which conclusion is supported?
ch: Acceleration increases in proportion to net force

quiz.q: A soccer ball rolling across grass slows and stops. Which force caused the change in motion?
ch: friction from the grass and air

quiz.q: A class pulled carts with the same 6 N force. Cart with 1 kg: acceleration 6 m/s each second. Cart with 2 kg: 3 m/s each second. Cart with 3 kg: 2 m/s each second. Make a claim about how mass affects acceleration when force stays the same. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: with the same net force, a greater mass gives a smaller acceleration. Evidence: with 6 N, the 1 kg cart accelerated at 6, the 2 kg at 3 and the 3 kg at 2 m/s each second; doubling mass halved acceleration. Reasoning: an object's change in motion depends on the net force and its mass (a = F / m); more mass has more inertia, so the same force changes its motion less.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: Newton's third law: action and reaction

practice.q: Newton's third law says that when one object pushes on another, the second object
ch: pushes back with an equal force in the opposite direction
pushes back with a smaller force

practice.q: A swimmer pushes backward on the water. What pushes the swimmer forward?
ch: the water pushing forward on the swimmer
practice.h: Look for the pair of forces between the swimmer and the water.

practice.q: A rocket pushes hot gases downward out of its engine. Why does the rocket go up?
ch: The gases push up on the rocket with an equal and opposite force
The gases pull the rocket by gravity
The air below lifts the rocket like a hand

practice.q: A 50 kg student on skates pushes a wall with 100 N. With what force in newtons does the wall push back on the student?
A small car and a large truck collide head-on. Compare the forces each exerts on the other and explain why the small car is affected more.
practice.ans: By Newton's third law the forces are equal in size and opposite in direction. The car has less mass, so the same force gives it a much larger change in motion, which is why its passengers feel a bigger jolt.

quiz.q: A bat hits a baseball with a force of 500 N. What force does the ball exert on the bat?
Why does a gun or a garden hose recoil backward when it pushes something forward?
ch: The object pushed forward pushes back on it with an equal and opposite force
The forces are unbalanced on purpose

quiz.q: Two ice skaters push off each other with 90 N. Skater A has a mass of 45 kg. What is Skater A's acceleration in meters per second each second?
Two ice skaters push off each other with 90 N. Skater B has a mass of 60 kg. What is Skater B's acceleration in meters per second each second?
Two carts on a track push apart with a spring. Cart A (1 kg) rolls away at 4 m/s. Cart B (2 kg) rolls the other way at 2 m/s. Which statement is correct?
ch: The forces were equal and opposite; the more massive cart moved slower
Cart A received a greater force
Cart B received a greater force
Only Cart A felt a force

quiz.q: When you walk, your foot pushes backward on the ground. Which force moves you forward?
ch: the ground pushing forward on your foot
your foot pushing on the ground

quiz.q: Identify the action-reaction force pair when a bird flies by pushing its wings down on the air.
quiz.ans: The wings push down on the air, and the air pushes up on the wings with an equal and opposite force, lifting the bird.

lessons.name: Design challenge: safer collisions

practice.q: Why do car airbags reduce injuries in a crash?
ch: They make the passenger stop over a longer time, lowering the force on the body
They make the car stop faster
practice.h: Spreading a stop over more time lowers the force.

practice.q: A team must design a bumper that protects a toy car carrying an egg in a crash. Which is a constraint?
ch: Use only cardboard, tape and straws
The car must hit the wall at full speed
The bumper must absorb the impact

practice.q: Crumple zones in cars are designed to
ch: crush and absorb energy during a collision

practice.q: Three bumper designs were tested 4 times each. Design A protected the egg in 3 tests, B in 4 tests and C in 1 test. What percent of tests did Design A pass?
Explain how Newton's third law applies when a car hits a wall during a crash test.
practice.ans: The car pushes on the wall and the wall pushes back on the car with an equal and opposite force; this force stops the car, so designs focus on reducing how suddenly that force acts on passengers.

quiz.q: Which bumper material would most likely reduce the force on an egg in a collision?
ch: a soft foam that squishes slowly

quiz.q: In crash tests, Bumper X stopped the car in 0.05 seconds and Bumper Y stopped it in 0.20 seconds. How many times longer did Bumper Y take to stop the car?
Bumper Y stops a car over a longer time than Bumper X. Which bumper puts less force on the passengers, and why?
ch: Bumper Y, because stopping over more time means less force
Bumper X, because it stops the car faster
Both the same, because the car's mass is the same
Neither, because bumpers do not affect force

quiz.q: A team's egg-safe car tests passed in 7 of 10 trials before a redesign and 9 of 10 after. By how many percentage points did the pass rate increase?
After testing, a team combines the foam from one design with the straw frame from another. This step is called
Why do helmets have a hard shell and a soft foam layer inside?
ch: The shell spreads the force and the foam slows the stop
The foam makes the helmet heavier

quiz.q: Describe how you would evaluate two helmet designs for a skateboard company using criteria and constraints.
quiz.ans: Set criteria such as reducing impact force by a target amount and fitting comfortably, and constraints such as cost and weight; drop each helmet with a sensor several times, compare the average forces, check cost and weight, and choose or combine the design that best meets the criteria within the constraints.

test.q: The SI unit of force is the
An object's tendency to resist changes in its motion is
A ball is kicked with 20 N to the right while 5 N of friction acts to the left. What is the net force?
Which change would give a cart a greater acceleration?
ch: increasing the net force on it
adding more mass while keeping force the same

test.q: A heavy box sits on the floor and does not move when you push it gently. Why?
ch: Friction balances your push, so the net force is zero
There is no force on the box

test.q: A person in a canoe throws a heavy bag forward toward the shore. What happens to the canoe?
ch: It moves backward, away from the shore

test.q: In a collision between a moving bowling ball and a pin, which statement is true?
ch: The ball and pin push on each other with equal and opposite forces
The ball pushes harder on the pin
The pin pushes harder on the ball
Only the ball exerts a force

test.q: Which graph shape on a distance-time graph shows an object at rest?
ch: a curve rising faster and faster

test.q: Why does a seat belt protect a passenger when a car stops suddenly?
ch: It supplies the force to stop the passenger, who would keep moving due to inertia

test.q: Which question can be tested to learn how mass affects motion?
ch: Does adding mass to a cart change its acceleration when the same force pulls it?
What color should the cart be?

test.q: An asteroid about 10 km wide hit Earth 66 million years ago. Which statement about the collision is correct?
ch: Earth pushed on the asteroid with a force equal to the asteroid's force on Earth
The asteroid pushed on Earth much harder than Earth pushed on it
Earth exerted no force on the asteroid

test.q: Data: a toy car pulled by 3 N reached 1.5 m/s each second; with the same force but twice the mass, it reached 0.75 m/s each second. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: Doubling mass halves acceleration when force is constant

test.q: A runner covers 400 meters in 80 seconds. What is her average speed in meters per second?
A net force of 150 N acts on a 30 kg wagon. What is its acceleration in meters per second each second?
A truck accelerates at 2 meters per second each second with a net force of 8,000 N. What is its mass in kg?
A drone flies 90 meters in 12 seconds. What is its average speed in meters per second?
Which design change would best reduce the force on a phone when it is dropped?
Two bumpers are tested on identical carts at the same speed. Bumper A stops the cart in 0.1 s, and Bumper B stops it in 0.4 s. Which bumper better protects cargo?
ch: Bumper B, because the stop takes longer, so the force is smaller
Bumper A, because it stops faster
Neither, because time does not matter

test.q: A 2 kg cart and a 4 kg cart are pushed apart by a spring. Compared with the 2 kg cart, the 4 kg cart moves
ch: at half the speed in the opposite direction
at the same speed in the same direction

test.q: Explain why a fully loaded truck needs a longer distance to stop than an empty truck traveling at the same speed.
test.ans: The loaded truck has more mass and more inertia; the brakes can supply only so much force, so its acceleration (slowing) is smaller and it takes longer and farther to stop.

test.q: Identify the forces acting on a skydiver falling at a constant speed and explain why the speed does not change.
test.ans: Gravity pulls down and air resistance pushes up; at constant speed they are equal, so the net force is zero and the motion does not change.

test.q: A student says, "When a fly hits a car windshield, the car pushes harder on the fly than the fly pushes on the car." Use Newton's laws to correct the student.
test.ans: By Newton's third law, the fly and the car push on each other with equal and opposite forces. The fly is affected far more because its mass is tiny, so the same force gives it a huge change in motion, while the car's large mass barely changes its motion.

test.q: A team tested three egg-car bumpers by rolling the car down the same ramp into a wall 5 times each. Straw frame: egg survived 2 times, stopping time about 0.03 s. Foam block: survived 4 times, about 0.10 s. Foam plus straw frame: survived 5 times, about 0.15 s. Make a claim about which bumper design is best. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning using forces and Newton's laws.
test.ans: Claim: the foam plus straw frame bumper is the best design. Evidence: its egg survived 5 of 5 trials with the longest stopping time (0.15 s), compared with 4 of 5 for foam (0.10 s) and 2 of 5 for straws (0.03 s). Reasoning: when the car hits the wall, the wall pushes back with an equal and opposite force (Newton's third law); a longer stopping time means a smaller force is needed to change the egg's motion, so the combined bumper protects the egg best.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 2: Energy of Motion and Position
units.el: Pair each energy word with a gesture (kinetic: run in place; potential: lift a book). Give students a graph-reading frame: "When ___ doubles, kinetic energy ___."

lessons.name: Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed

practice.q: The energy an object has because it is moving is
A bowling ball and a tennis ball roll at the same speed. Which has more kinetic energy?
ch: the bowling ball, because it has more mass
the tennis ball, because it is smaller
they have the same kinetic energy

practice.q: Kinetic energy = 1/2 x mass x speed x speed. What is the kinetic energy in joules of a 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s?
practice.h: Square the speed first: 3 x 3 = 9.

practice.q: A graph of kinetic energy against mass (speed held constant) is a straight line through zero. What does this show?
ch: Kinetic energy is proportional to mass
Kinetic energy does not depend on mass

practice.q: Explain why a car moving at 60 km per hour is much more dangerous in a crash than the same car at 30 km per hour.
practice.ans: Kinetic energy depends on the square of speed, so doubling speed makes the car's kinetic energy four times larger; more energy must be transferred in the crash, causing more damage.
practice.h: What happens to kinetic energy when speed doubles?

quiz.q: If an object's speed doubles, its kinetic energy
If an object's mass doubles and its speed stays the same, its kinetic energy
What is the kinetic energy in joules of a 50 kg runner moving at 4 m/s?
A 1,000 kg car moves at 10 m/s. What is its kinetic energy in joules?
Data: a 1 kg cart at 1 m/s has 0.5 J; at 2 m/s, 2 J; at 3 m/s, 4.5 J. Which describes the graph of kinetic energy against speed?
ch: a curve that gets steeper as speed increases

quiz.q: A truck and a bicycle both have 10,000 J of kinetic energy. What must be true?
ch: The bicycle is moving much faster than the truck

quiz.q: Describe how you could collect data to show how speed affects kinetic energy, using a cart and a cup that it pushes.
quiz.ans: Roll the same cart from different heights on a ramp to change its speed; measure speed with a timer or sensor and measure how far the cart pushes a cup; keep the cart mass and surface the same; more distance means more kinetic energy.

lessons.name: Potential energy and the distance between objects

practice.q: Energy stored because of an object's position or shape is
A book is lifted from the floor to a high shelf. What happens to the gravitational potential energy of the Earth-book system?
ch: It increases because the book is farther from Earth
practice.h: Lifting against gravity stores energy.

practice.q: Two magnets that repel are pushed closer together. What happens to the potential energy stored between them?
Gravitational potential energy = mass x 9.8 x height. What is the potential energy in joules of a 2 kg rock on a 5 m ledge?
Explain why stretching a rubber band farther stores more energy, and what happens to that energy when you let go.
practice.ans: Stretching changes the band's shape and increases the distance it is pulled, storing more elastic potential energy; when released, the stored energy changes into kinetic energy as the band snaps back.

quiz.q: Two magnets attract each other. When you pull them farther apart, the potential energy stored in the system
Gravitational potential energy = mass x 9.8 x height. What is the potential energy in joules of a 10 kg box lifted 3 m?
A 5 kg ball has 245 J of gravitational potential energy (potential energy = mass x 9.8 x height). How high is it in meters?
Which has the most gravitational potential energy?
ch: a 3 kg pot on a 2 m shelf
a 3 kg pot on a 1 m shelf
a 1 kg pot on a 1 m shelf
a 3 kg pot on the floor

quiz.q: A student pulls back a slingshot 10 cm and then 20 cm, and the pebble flies farther the second time. What does this show?
ch: More stretch stores more potential energy, which becomes more kinetic energy

quiz.q: Which statement about potential energy is correct?
ch: It depends on the positions of interacting objects
It only exists in moving objects

quiz.q: Use the idea of potential energy to explain why water stored behind a high dam can generate electricity.
quiz.ans: Water held high behind the dam has gravitational potential energy because it is far above the river below. As it flows down through turbines, this energy changes into kinetic energy that spins the turbines and generators.

lessons.name: Energy changes form

practice.q: A roller coaster car is at the top of the first hill. Where is its kinetic energy greatest?
ch: at the bottom of the hill
at the top of the hill
practice.h: Where is the car moving fastest?

practice.q: A swinging pendulum moves fastest at the bottom of its swing. Which energy change happens as it swings down?
ch: potential energy changes to kinetic energy
kinetic energy changes to potential energy

practice.q: A pendulum's swings slowly get smaller and it stops. Where did the energy go?
ch: It was transferred to the air and the pivot as thermal energy and sound
It went back into the string

practice.q: A 2 kg ball is dropped and has 40 J of potential energy at the top. Ignoring air resistance, how much kinetic energy in joules does it have just before hitting the ground?
Describe the energy changes when you throw a ball straight up and it falls back to your hand.
practice.ans: At first the ball has kinetic energy; as it rises, kinetic energy changes into gravitational potential energy until it stops at the top; as it falls, potential energy changes back into kinetic energy. Some energy is lost to air as heat.

quiz.q: The idea that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed, is
At the highest point of a ball's flight straight up, the ball has
ch: its most potential energy and least kinetic energy
equal kinetic and potential energy always

quiz.q: A roller coaster car has 120,000 J of potential energy at the top. At the bottom it has 108,000 J of kinetic energy. How many joules were transferred to friction and air?
A 0.5 kg skateboard rolls down a ramp, reaching 4 m/s. What is its kinetic energy in joules (KE = 1/2 x m x v x v)?
A ball dropped from 2 m bounces to 1.5 m, then 1.1 m, then 0.8 m. Which conclusion is best supported?
ch: Some energy is transferred to sound and heat at each bounce
The ball gains energy each bounce
Energy is destroyed at each bounce

quiz.q: Why does a coaster's second hill have to be lower than the first?
ch: Some energy is lost to friction and air, so the car has less energy to climb
The second hill has more gravity
Coasters gain energy as they go

quiz.q: Explain why a bicycle coasting downhill speeds up without pedaling.
quiz.ans: As the bicycle moves downhill, gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy, so its speed increases.

lessons.name: Energy in an asteroid impact

practice.q: An asteroid that struck near Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula about 66 million years ago is linked to the extinction of the dinosaurs. Why did it release so much energy?
ch: It had enormous mass and very high speed
practice.h: Kinetic energy depends on both mass and speed.

practice.q: Two asteroids have the same mass. Asteroid A moves twice as fast as Asteroid B. How does A's kinetic energy compare?
A 1,000 kg meteorite moves at 20,000 m/s. What is its kinetic energy in joules (KE = 1/2 x m x v x v)?
When a meteorite hits the ground, where does its kinetic energy go?
practice.ans: It is transferred into heat, sound, light and the work of digging a crater and throwing rock and dust into the air.

practice.q: As an asteroid falls toward Earth, the Earth-asteroid system's potential energy

quiz.q: A small marble and a heavier steel ball are dropped from the same height into flour. The steel ball makes a deeper crater. Why?
ch: It had more mass, so it had more kinetic energy when it hit
It fell faster than the marble because it was heavier
The flour was softer for the steel ball

quiz.q: Students dropped a 50 g ball from 0.5 m, 1.0 m and 1.5 m. Crater widths were 3 cm, 4.2 cm and 5.1 cm. How many cm wider was the crater from 1.5 m than from 0.5 m?
An object with mass 2,000 kg moves at 10,000 m/s. What is its kinetic energy in joules?
Data: crater width increases as drop height increases, but not as fast as height does. Which variable did the students change, and what does it represent?
ch: Drop height, which changes impact speed and energy
Flour depth, which changes the ball

quiz.q: Why would a very fast but small asteroid be dangerous?
ch: Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed, so high speed gives large energy

quiz.q: In a crater investigation, which variable should stay the same to test the effect of drop height?
ch: the mass of the ball and the type of flour

quiz.q: Explain how a crater investigation in a tray of flour models an asteroid impact, and give one limitation of the model.
quiz.ans: The falling ball has kinetic energy that is transferred to the flour, pushing it outward to form a crater, like an asteroid's energy digging a crater. Limitation: the speeds and energies are tiny compared with a real asteroid, and real impacts melt rock and cause fires.

test.q: Energy of motion is
Stored energy due to an object's height above Earth is
Which has the most kinetic energy?
ch: a 1,000 kg car moving at 20 m/s
a 1,000 kg car moving at 5 m/s

test.q: If a skateboarder's speed is cut in half, the kinetic energy becomes
A diver stands on a 10 m platform. As she falls, which change happens?
ch: potential energy decreases and kinetic energy increases

test.q: Two magnets repel. You push them closer together. The potential energy of the system
Why does a ball bounce lower each time?
ch: Some energy changes to thermal energy and sound

test.q: A graph shows kinetic energy rising in a straight line as mass increases at constant speed. This means
ch: kinetic energy is proportional to mass
kinetic energy is not related to mass
kinetic energy depends on the square of mass

test.q: Which is the best example of energy changing from potential to kinetic?
ch: an apple falling from a tree
a book resting on a shelf
a stretched rubber band held still

test.q: Which statement about energy in a closed system is correct?
ch: Total energy stays the same as it changes form

test.q: Data: a 2 kg cart has 1 J at 1 m/s, 4 J at 2 m/s and 9 J at 3 m/s. What would its kinetic energy be at 4 m/s?
A coaster car starts from rest at the top of a 30 m hill. Which hill can it NOT climb over if there is friction?
What is the kinetic energy in joules of a 4 kg dog running at 5 m/s?
What is the gravitational potential energy in joules of a 3 kg pot on a 2 m high shelf? (PE = mass x 9.8 x height)
A ball has 60 J of potential energy at the top of a ramp and 45 J of kinetic energy at the bottom. How many joules were transferred to friction and sound?
A 0.2 kg ball moves at 10 m/s. What is its kinetic energy in joules?
How could you increase the potential energy of a spring toy?
Two balls of different mass are dropped from the same height. Ignoring air resistance, which statement is correct when they land?
ch: They hit at the same speed, but the heavier ball has more kinetic energy
They have the same kinetic energy
The lighter ball has more kinetic energy

test.q: Why do speed limits near schools have such a big effect on safety?
ch: Lower speed greatly reduces kinetic energy, so crashes cause less harm
Cars have no energy at low speed

test.q: Explain how the gravitational potential energy of a system depends on the distance between the objects.
test.ans: The farther an object is lifted from Earth, the more gravitational potential energy the Earth-object system stores, because more energy was used to separate them against gravity.

test.q: Describe the energy changes in a pendulum during one full swing and explain why it eventually stops.
test.ans: At the highest points it has the most potential energy and least kinetic energy; at the bottom it has the most kinetic energy. Friction and air resistance transfer some energy to heat each swing, so it slowly stops.

test.q: A student claims that a car's kinetic energy doubles when its speed doubles. Use the kinetic energy formula to correct the claim with numbers.
test.ans: KE = 1/2 x m x v x v. For a 1,000 kg car at 10 m/s, KE = 50,000 J; at 20 m/s, KE = 200,000 J. Doubling speed makes KE four times as large, not twice.

test.q: Students rolled a 0.5 kg cart at different speeds into a cup and measured how far the cup slid. Speed 1 m/s: 10 cm. 2 m/s: 40 cm. 3 m/s: 90 cm. Make a claim about how speed affects the kinetic energy of the cart. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: kinetic energy increases with the square of speed. Evidence: doubling speed from 1 to 2 m/s made the cup slide 4 times as far (10 to 40 cm), and tripling speed to 3 m/s made it slide 9 times as far (90 cm). Reasoning: the distance the cup slides shows how much energy the cart transferred to it; since distance grew with speed times speed, kinetic energy depends on the square of speed (KE = 1/2 x m x v x v).
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 3: Forces at a Distance - Electric, Magnetic and Gravitational Fields
units.el: Let students feel magnets attract and repel through paper and say "attract" or "repel." Post a chart of the three noncontact forces with what causes each and what makes it stronger.

lessons.name: Fields: forces without touching

practice.q: A force that acts on an object without touching it is a
A paper clip jumps toward a magnet held 1 cm above it. What does this show?
ch: The magnet's field exerts a force on the clip without touching it
The clip is pushed by air
The magnet must touch the clip to pull it
The clip has its own gravity only

practice.q: Iron filings sprinkled around a bar magnet form curved lines from pole to pole. What do the lines show?
ch: the shape of the magnetic field
practice.h: Filings line up with an invisible region around the magnet.

practice.q: A paper clip moved toward a magnet from 4 cm away, but not from 6 cm away. How many cm closer did it have to be?
Plan a simple investigation to show that a magnetic field can pass through materials.
practice.ans: Place sheets of paper, plastic, cardboard and other materials between a magnet and a paper clip; count how many sheets the force passes through before the clip no longer moves; keep the magnet and distance the same.

quiz.q: Which is a noncontact force?
A compass needle points north. What causes this?
ch: Earth's magnetic field exerts a force on the magnetized needle

quiz.q: A magnet lifted a paper clip from 5 cm through 1 sheet of cardboard, and from 3 cm through 6 sheets. How many fewer cm of reach did 6 sheets allow?
A rubbed balloon makes a student's hair stand up from 10 cm away. What does this provide evidence for?
ch: an electric field around the charged balloon
a magnetic field from the hair

quiz.q: Data: a magnet held over a paper clip lifted it at 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm, but not at 4 cm or more. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: The magnetic force gets weaker with distance
The magnetic force gets stronger with distance

quiz.q: Which model best represents a field?
ch: lines showing the direction and strength of force around an object
a picture of the object only
a list of the object's colors

quiz.q: Explain how the Moon pulls on Earth's oceans even though they are far apart.
quiz.ans: The Moon's gravitational field extends through space; this field exerts a force on Earth's ocean water without touching it, causing tides.

lessons.name: Electric forces and charges

practice.q: Two balloons are both rubbed with wool and get the same type of charge. What happens when they are brought close?
practice.h: Like charges repel; opposite charges attract.

practice.q: A charged comb picks up small bits of paper. As the comb is moved farther away, the force
Which change would make the electric force between two charged objects stronger?
ch: increasing the amount of charge on them

practice.q: A charged rod lifted 12 bits of paper from 1 cm away and 3 bits from 2 cm away. How many times more bits did it lift at 1 cm?
Explain why your hair sticks to a sweater you just pulled off.
practice.ans: Rubbing moved electrons, giving the hair and sweater opposite charges; opposite charges attract, so the hair is pulled toward the sweater.

quiz.q: Objects with opposite electric charges
A balloon rubbed 5 times attracted paper from 3 cm away. Rubbed 15 times, it attracted from 9 cm. How many cm farther did the extra charge reach?
A balloon rubbed 5 times attracted paper from 3 cm away, and rubbed 15 times it attracted paper from 9 cm away. Which variable was changed?
Why do clothes sometimes stick together after a dryer cycle?
ch: Rubbing in the dryer gives them opposite electric charges

quiz.q: Data: two charged spheres felt a force of 8 units at 1 cm apart, 2 units at 2 cm, and about 0.9 units at 3 cm. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: Electric force decreases quickly as distance increases

quiz.q: Two charged spheres felt 8 units of force at 1 cm and 2 units at 2 cm. By what percent did the force decrease?
Describe a fair test to find whether the number of rubs affects how strongly a balloon attracts paper.
quiz.ans: Rub identical balloons different numbers of times with the same cloth, hold each the same distance over the same paper bits, count bits lifted, repeat trials and compare means.

lessons.name: Magnetic forces and electromagnets

practice.q: The north pole of one magnet is brought near the north pole of another. What happens?
Wire is coiled around an iron nail and connected to a battery. The nail picks up paper clips. What is this device?
An electromagnet with 10 coils picked up 4 clips, 20 coils picked up 8 clips and 30 coils picked up 12 clips. How many clips would 40 coils likely pick up?
practice.h: Look for how many clips are added for every 10 coils.

practice.q: Which change would make an electromagnet weaker?
Explain one advantage of an electromagnet over a permanent magnet for a junkyard crane.
practice.ans: An electromagnet can be turned on to lift scrap metal and turned off to drop it, and its strength can be changed by adjusting the current.

quiz.q: Which two factors can increase the strength of an electromagnet?
ch: a plastic core and fewer coils
a longer wire with no current

quiz.q: An electromagnet using 1 battery lifted 6 clips, and using 2 batteries in series lifted 11 clips. How many more clips did 2 batteries lift?
A student coils wire around a pencil instead of an iron nail. The electromagnet picks up fewer clips. Why?
ch: An iron core makes the magnetic field much stronger

quiz.q: Which device uses electromagnets to make motion?
Data: electromagnet with 20 coils lifted 8 clips at 1 battery, 15 clips at 2 batteries. Electromagnet with 40 coils lifted 16 clips at 1 battery. Which conclusion is best supported?
ch: Both more coils and more current increase strength

quiz.q: Maglev trains in some countries use electromagnets to float and move. A maglev train travels 300 km in 1.25 hours. What is its average speed in km per hour?
Plan an investigation to test how the number of coils affects an electromagnet's strength. Name the variables and explain how you will make the test fair.
quiz.ans: Independent variable: number of coils (10, 20, 30, 40). Dependent: number of paper clips lifted. Controls: same nail, wire, battery, clip size; disconnect between trials to avoid draining the battery; repeat 3 times and average.

lessons.name: Gravity depends on mass and distance

practice.q: Gravity is a force that
ch: always attracts objects with mass toward each other

practice.q: Why do you weigh less on the Moon than on Earth?
ch: The Moon has less mass, so its gravitational pull is weaker
You have less mass on the Moon
The Moon is closer to the Sun
practice.h: Your mass stays the same everywhere; what changes is the strength of the gravitational pull on you.

practice.q: Weight = mass x gravity. On the Moon, gravity is 1.6 newtons per kg. What does a 50 kg astronaut weigh on the Moon in newtons?
Which pair has the greatest gravitational attraction?
ch: a pencil and a paper clip

practice.q: Explain why you do not feel the gravitational pull between you and a nearby classmate.
practice.ans: All objects with mass attract, but people have very small masses compared with planets, so the force between you is far too small to notice.

quiz.q: A spacecraft travels away from Earth. What happens to the gravitational force between it and Earth?
On Earth, gravity is 9.8 newtons per kg. What does a 60 kg student weigh in newtons?
Gravity on Mars is about 3.7 newtons per kg. What does a 60 kg student weigh on Mars in newtons?
A student's mass is 60 kg on Earth. What is her mass on Mars?
Data: surface gravity in newtons per kg - Mercury 3.7, Earth 9.8, Jupiter 24.8. Jupiter's mass is about 318 times Earth's. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: Planets with much more mass generally have stronger gravity
Gravity does not depend on mass
All planets have the same gravity

quiz.q: Why do the planets orbit the Sun instead of Earth?
ch: The Sun has by far the most mass in the solar system
The Sun is closest to every planet

quiz.q: Data: surface gravity and mass of planets (compared with Earth). Mars: mass 0.11, gravity 0.38. Earth: mass 1, gravity 1. Neptune: mass 17, gravity 1.14. Jupiter: mass 318, gravity 2.53. Make a claim about how a planet's mass relates to its gravitational pull. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: planets with more mass generally have stronger gravity. Evidence: Mars, with 0.11 Earth masses, has 0.38 Earth gravity; Jupiter, with 318 Earth masses, has 2.53. Neptune has much more mass than Earth but only slightly stronger surface gravity. Reasoning: gravitational force depends on mass, so more massive planets pull harder; surface gravity also depends on distance from the center, and Neptune is very large, so its surface is far from its center, which weakens the pull felt there.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

test.q: Which force pulls objects toward the center of Earth?
Two north poles of magnets will
ch: have no effect on each other

test.q: Which statement about fields is correct?
ch: Fields let objects exert forces on each other without touching
Fields only exist when objects touch

test.q: Which change would increase the strength of an electromagnet?
A charged balloon is held near a wall and sticks. What causes this?
ch: a magnetic field from the balloon

test.q: Which factor affects the gravitational force between two objects?
ch: their masses and the distance between them

test.q: When two charged objects are moved farther apart, the electric force between them
An astronaut's mass is 80 kg on Earth. On the Moon, her mass is
What does a compass needle line up with?
Which device depends on an electric current making a magnetic field?
Data: an electromagnet with 1 battery lifted 5 clips; 2 batteries, 10 clips; 3 batteries, 14 clips. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: More current made the electromagnet stronger

test.q: A student argues that gravity only acts on Earth because astronauts float in the space station. Which evidence best argues against this?
ch: The station and astronauts are still pulled by Earth's gravity, which keeps them in orbit
Astronauts have no mass in space
The station is outside the solar system

test.q: On Earth, gravity is 9.8 newtons per kg. What does a 25 kg dog weigh in newtons?
Gravity on Jupiter is about 24.8 newtons per kg. What would a 10 kg backpack weigh there in newtons?
An electromagnet gains about 3 paper clips for every 10 coils added. It lifts 6 clips with 20 coils. How many clips should it lift with 50 coils?
A rubbed balloon attracted paper bits from 4 cm away after 10 rubs and from 10 cm after 25 rubs. How many cm farther did it reach after 25 rubs?
Which model best shows the magnetic field of a bar magnet?
ch: curved lines from the north pole to the south pole

test.q: Why is the gravitational force between Earth and the Moon so much stronger than between two books on a table?
ch: Earth and the Moon have enormous masses

test.q: Which pair of objects would attract each other with an electric force?
ch: a positively charged rod and a negatively charged balloon

test.q: Explain how the strength of a magnetic force changes with distance and give evidence you could collect.
test.ans: The force gets weaker as distance increases; you could measure how many paper clips a magnet lifts or whether a clip moves at different distances and see the effect drop with distance.

test.q: Describe two ways to make an electromagnet stronger and explain why each works.
test.ans: Add more coils, which adds more loops of current to the field; increase the current with a stronger battery, which strengthens the magnetic field; an iron core also concentrates the field.

test.q: Explain why a person who weighs 500 N on Earth would weigh less on Mars but have the same mass.
test.ans: Mass is the amount of matter, which does not change with location. Weight is the gravitational force on that mass; Mars has less mass than Earth, so its gravitational pull is weaker and the person weighs less.

test.q: Students placed a paper clip at different distances from a magnet and measured the force with a sensitive scale. 1 cm: 0.80 N. 2 cm: 0.20 N. 3 cm: 0.09 N. 4 cm: 0.05 N. Make a claim about how distance affects magnetic force. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning using the idea of fields.
test.ans: Claim: magnetic force decreases quickly as distance from the magnet increases. Evidence: at 1 cm the force was 0.80 N; doubling the distance to 2 cm cut it to 0.20 N (one-fourth), and at 4 cm it was only 0.05 N. Reasoning: a magnet's field is strongest near the magnet and spreads out and weakens with distance, so the force the field exerts on the clip drops sharply as the clip moves farther away.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 4: Earth, the Moon and the Solar System
units.el: Model phases with a lamp and a ball on a stick while students name each phase. Provide a planet data table with picture icons and a scale strip (1 cm = 1 AU) for students to place planets.

lessons.name: Moon phases and eclipses

practice.q: Why does the Moon appear to change shape during the month?
ch: As it orbits Earth, we see different amounts of its sunlit half
Earth's shadow covers parts of it
practice.h: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun.

practice.q: During a new moon, where is the Moon located?
ch: on the far side of Earth from the Sun
at the same distance as the Sun

practice.q: A lunar eclipse happens when
ch: Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
the Moon is between the Sun and Earth
the Sun is between Earth and the Moon

practice.q: The Moon's cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days. Using 29.5 days, how many days pass from a full moon to the next new moon?
practice.h: Full moon to new moon is half the cycle.

practice.q: Explain why we do not have a solar eclipse every month at new moon.
practice.ans: The Moon's orbit is tilted slightly compared with Earth's orbit around the Sun, so most months the Moon passes a little above or below the line between Earth and the Sun and its shadow misses Earth.

quiz.q: Which phase comes right after a new moon?
A solar eclipse can happen only during which phase?
Why do we always see the same side of the Moon from Earth?
ch: The Moon rotates once in the same time it takes to orbit Earth
The far side is always dark

quiz.q: A full moon was on March 14. Using a 29.5-day cycle, how many days later is the next full moon?
The Moon is about 384,000 km from Earth. Light travels about 300,000 km each second. How many seconds does moonlight take to reach Earth?
A student models the Moon's phases with a lamp (Sun), her head (Earth) and a ball (Moon). When the ball is directly opposite the lamp from her head, the ball looks fully lit. Which phase is this?
Use a model of the Sun, Earth and Moon to explain why a lunar eclipse can be seen from everywhere on Earth's night side, but a total solar eclipse is seen only along a narrow path.
quiz.ans: Earth's shadow is large enough to cover the whole Moon, so anyone who can see the Moon sees the lunar eclipse. The Moon's shadow on Earth is small, so a total solar eclipse is seen only where that small shadow falls.

lessons.name: Why Earth has seasons

practice.q: What causes Earth's seasons?
ch: the tilt of Earth's axis as Earth orbits the Sun
Earth's changing distance from the Sun
the Sun getting hotter in summer
the Moon blocking sunlight in winter
practice.h: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January.

practice.q: In June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun. What season is it in California?
In June, what season is it in Australia?
On the summer solstice, Sacramento gets about 15 hours of daylight; on the winter solstice, about 9.5 hours. How many more hours of daylight are there in summer?
Explain two ways the tilt of Earth's axis makes summer warmer than winter.
practice.ans: In summer, sunlight hits more directly, so its energy is concentrated on a smaller area; days are also longer, so the ground receives sunlight for more hours.

quiz.q: Earth's axis is tilted about
Earth is closest to the Sun in early January. Why is it winter in the Northern Hemisphere then?
ch: The Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, so sunlight is less direct and days are shorter
The Sun gives off less energy in January
Earth's distance is the only factor

quiz.q: At noon in June, the Sun is about 79 degrees above the horizon in Los Angeles. In December it is about 32 degrees. What is the difference in degrees?
Near the equator, which describes the seasons?
ch: temperatures stay warm all year because sunlight is direct year-round

quiz.q: If Earth's axis were not tilted, what would most likely happen?
ch: There would be little seasonal change
Every day would be summer everywhere
The Moon would have no phases

quiz.q: A city gets 14 hours of daylight in June and 10 hours in December. What is the mean of these two amounts?
A student says, "It is summer when Earth is closest to the Sun." Use evidence to argue against this claim.
quiz.ans: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, which is winter in the Northern Hemisphere, and the Northern and Southern Hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time. So distance cannot cause seasons; the tilt of Earth's axis does.

lessons.name: Gravity holds the solar system and galaxy together

practice.q: What force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
If the Sun's gravity suddenly stopped, what would Earth do?
ch: move off in a straight line into space
practice.h: Without a force pulling it inward, a moving object keeps going straight.

practice.q: The Milky Way is a galaxy of hundreds of billions of stars that orbit its center. What keeps the stars together?
Mercury takes 88 days to orbit the Sun, and Earth takes 365 days. About how many Mercury orbits happen in one Earth year? (Round to the nearest whole number.)
Explain how gravity and an object's forward motion together produce an orbit.
practice.ans: Gravity pulls the planet toward the Sun, while the planet's forward motion carries it sideways; the combination makes it curve around the Sun in a path that keeps falling around it.

quiz.q: Why do planets closer to the Sun travel faster in their orbits?
ch: The Sun's gravity is stronger closer in
They are farther from other planets

quiz.q: The solar system formed from a cloud of gas and dust about 4.6 billion years ago. What caused the cloud to collapse and form the Sun and planets?
Jupiter takes about 12 Earth years to orbit the Sun. How many orbits does it complete in 60 years?
Data: orbital periods - Mercury 0.24 years, Earth 1 year, Mars 1.9 years, Jupiter 11.9 years, Saturn 29.5 years. Which pattern is supported?
ch: Planets farther from the Sun take longer to orbit
All planets have the same period
Period does not depend on distance

quiz.q: Which statement about the Moon's orbit is correct?
ch: Earth's gravity keeps the Moon in orbit around Earth
The Moon orbits the Sun but not Earth
The Moon is held by magnetism

quiz.q: Saturn takes about 29.5 years to orbit the Sun. How many years do 2 Saturn orbits take?
Explain why the Sun, not Earth, is at the center of the planets' orbits.
quiz.ans: The Sun contains more than 99 percent of the solar system's mass, so its gravity is by far the strongest and it holds all the planets in orbit around it.

lessons.name: The scale of the solar system

practice.q: The average distance from Earth to the Sun, about 150 million km, is called
Jupiter is about 5.2 AU from the Sun. How many million km is that? (1 AU = 150 million km)
practice.h: Multiply 5.2 by 150.

practice.q: Jupiter's diameter is about 143,000 km and Earth's is about 12,700 km. About how many Earths would fit across Jupiter?
A model uses 1 cm for each AU. Neptune is about 30 AU from the Sun. How many cm from the model Sun should Neptune be placed?
Explain why it is hard to make a model of the solar system with both planet sizes and distances to the same scale.
practice.ans: The distances are enormous compared with the sizes; if planets were large enough to see, the model would need to be kilometers long, and if it fit in a room, the planets would be tiny specks.

quiz.q: Which group lists solar system objects from largest to smallest?
ch: the Sun, Jupiter, Earth, the Moon
Earth, the Sun, the Moon, Jupiter
the Moon, Earth, Jupiter, the Sun
Jupiter, the Sun, the Moon, Earth

quiz.q: Sunlight takes about 8.3 minutes to reach Earth (1 AU). At that rate, how many minutes does it take to reach Mars at 1.5 AU?
Mars's diameter is about 6,800 km and Earth's is about 12,700 km. To the nearest whole percent, Mars's diameter is what percent of Earth's?

Data: Venus - rocky, 0.7 AU, 462 °C average surface; Mercury - rocky, 0.4 AU, 167 °C average; Earth - rocky, 1 AU, 15 °C. Venus is farther from the Sun than Mercury but hotter. Which is the best explanation?
ch: Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat
Venus is closer to the Sun
Mercury has oceans that cool it

quiz.q: Which statement about the four inner planets is correct?
ch: They have rings and many moons

quiz.q: A scale model uses a basketball (24 cm) for the Sun. Earth would be about 0.2 cm, smaller than a peppercorn. What does this show?
ch: The Sun is far larger than Earth
Earth is larger than the Sun

quiz.q: Use data to compare the inner and outer planets. Give two differences.
quiz.ans: Inner planets (Mercury to Mars) are small, rocky and close to the Sun with few moons; outer planets (Jupiter to Neptune) are much larger, made mostly of gas or ice, far from the Sun, and have rings and many moons.

test.q: The Moon's phases are caused by
ch: the changing amount of its sunlit half we can see

test.q: What keeps the Moon in orbit around Earth?
A total solar eclipse occurs when
ch: the Moon blocks the Sun's light from reaching part of Earth
Earth blocks light from the Moon

test.q: Earth has seasons because
ch: its tilted axis changes how directly sunlight hits each hemisphere during its orbit
its distance from the Sun changes a lot
the Sun burns hotter in summer

test.q: When it is winter in the Northern Hemisphere, the Southern Hemisphere has
Which object has the most mass in the solar system?
Which planet is a gas giant?
The Milky Way is
ch: a galaxy of hundreds of billions of stars held together by gravity

test.q: Why is the far side of the Moon never seen from Earth?
ch: The Moon spins once for each orbit around Earth
The far side is always dark

test.q: Which phase of the Moon occurs during a lunar eclipse?
Data: Mercury 0.4 AU, 88 days; Venus 0.7 AU, 225 days; Earth 1 AU, 365 days; Mars 1.5 AU, 687 days. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: The farther a planet is from the Sun, the longer its orbit takes
Closer planets take longer to orbit

test.q: A student draws a model of the solar system on a sheet of paper with the planets close together and all the same size. What is the main problem?
ch: It does not show the real scale of sizes and distances
The Sun should be at the edge
Planets do not orbit the Sun

test.q: Sunlight takes about 8.3 minutes to reach Earth (1 AU). At that rate, how many minutes would it take to reach Jupiter at 5.2 AU?
Saturn is about 9.5 AU from the Sun. With 1 AU = 150 million km, how many million km away is Saturn?
In a scale model where 1 AU = 2 cm, how many cm from the Sun would Mars (1.5 AU) be?
The Moon's phase cycle is about 29.5 days. How many days are in 4 cycles?
Why does the noon Sun appear higher in the sky in summer than in winter?
ch: Earth's tilt points the hemisphere toward the Sun in summer
The Sun moves closer to Earth

test.q: An astronomer observes a distant galaxy with stars swirling around its center. What best explains this motion?
ch: Gravity from the mass at the galaxy's center and its stars
The stars are attached to each other

test.q: Which statement about the solar system's formation is accurate?
ch: Gravity pulled a cloud of gas and dust together to form the Sun and planets
The planets formed first and then made the Sun
The solar system formed last year
Magnetism pushed planets out of the Sun

test.q: Explain why the Moon goes through phases in about a month.
test.ans: The Moon orbits Earth about once every 29.5 days. As it moves, the angle between the Sun, Earth and Moon changes, so we see different portions of its sunlit half.

test.q: Describe the role of gravity in keeping the solar system together.
test.ans: The Sun's gravity pulls on each planet; combined with each planet's forward motion, this produces orbits. Planets' gravity also holds moons in orbit around them.

test.q: Planet data: Earth - diameter about 12,700 km, 1 AU from the Sun, rocky. Jupiter - diameter about 143,000 km, 5.2 AU from the Sun, mostly hydrogen and helium gas. Compare Earth and Jupiter in size, distance from the Sun and composition.
test.ans: Jupiter's diameter is about 11 times Earth's; it is about 5.2 AU from the Sun compared with Earth's 1 AU; Earth is small and rocky while Jupiter is a gas giant made mostly of hydrogen and helium.

test.q: A student recorded the noon Sun's height above the horizon in Fresno: March 21, 53 degrees, 12 hours of daylight; June 21, 77 degrees, 14.5 hours; September 22, 53 degrees, 12 hours; December 21, 30 degrees, 9.5 hours. Average temperatures were highest in summer and lowest in winter. Make a claim about what causes Fresno's seasons. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Fresno's seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis, which changes how directly sunlight strikes and how long days are. Evidence: in June the noon Sun was 77 degrees high with 14.5 hours of daylight, while in December it was only 30 degrees high with 9.5 hours; in March and September values were in between. Reasoning: when the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, sunlight is more direct and concentrated and days are longer, so more energy reaches the ground and it is warmer; when it tilts away, sunlight is spread out and days are short, so it is cooler.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 5: Waves, Light and Information
units.el: Use a slinky and a rope so students can make waves and label crest, trough, amplitude and wavelength on a drawing. Post the frame: "When the amplitude increases, the energy ___."

lessons.name: Wave properties and energy

practice.q: The height of a wave from its rest position to its crest is its
The distance from one crest to the next crest is the
practice.h: Picture measuring along the wave from one high point to the next.

practice.q: Wave speed = frequency x wavelength. A wave has a frequency of 4 waves per second (4 Hz) and a wavelength of 3 m. What is its speed in m/s?
Two ocean waves have the same wavelength. Wave A is 1 m tall and Wave B is 3 m tall. Which carries more energy?
ch: Wave B, because it has a larger amplitude
Wave A, because it is smaller

practice.q: Explain what a wave carries from one place to another and what it does not carry. Give an example.
practice.ans: A wave carries energy, not matter. In an ocean wave, a floating ball bobs up and down in about the same place while the energy moves toward the shore.
practice.h: Watch a cork floating as waves pass.

quiz.q: The number of waves that pass a point each second is the
A wave travels at 20 m/s and has a wavelength of 4 m. What is its frequency in Hz?
A student makes rope waves with a frequency of 2 Hz and a wavelength of 1.5 m. What is the wave speed in m/s?
If the frequency of a wave increases while its speed stays the same, the wavelength
Data: when the amplitude of a rope wave was doubled, a sensor at the end measured about 4 times as much energy. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: Wave energy increases faster than amplitude
Energy is not related to amplitude

quiz.q: In an earthquake, which seismic wave would most likely cause the most damage?
ch: a wave with a very large amplitude
a wave with a tiny amplitude
a wave that does not reach the surface

quiz.q: Draw or describe a transverse wave and label the crest, trough, amplitude and wavelength.
quiz.ans: A wavy line above and below a rest line: crests are the high points, troughs are the low points, amplitude is the height from the rest line to a crest, and wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next.

lessons.name: Sound waves

practice.q: Why can't sound travel through outer space?
ch: Sound needs a medium, such as air, to travel through
practice.h: Sound is a vibration of particles.

practice.q: A guitar string vibrates faster when it is tightened. How does this change the sound?
Sound travels about 340 m/s in air. How far does sound travel in 3 seconds in meters?
A louder sound has
Explain why you see lightning before you hear thunder.
practice.ans: Light travels much faster than sound; the light reaches you almost instantly, while sound in air travels about 340 m/s, so it arrives later.

quiz.q: Sound travels fastest through which material?
You hear thunder 6 seconds after seeing lightning. Sound travels about 340 m/s. How far away, in meters, was the lightning?
A ship sends a sound pulse to the seafloor. The echo returns in 2 seconds. Sound travels 1,500 m/s in seawater. How deep is the water in meters?
Soft curtains and carpet make a classroom quieter because they
A student taps a desk and a classmate with an ear on the desk hears it louder than a classmate listening through the air. Which explanation is best?
ch: Sound travels better through the solid desk than through air

quiz.q: Bats find insects by sending out high-pitched sounds and listening for echoes. Which wave behavior do they use?
Explain how sound gets from a speaker to your ear.
quiz.ans: The speaker vibrates and pushes on air particles; the particles bump into neighbors, passing the vibration through the air as a sound wave until it vibrates your eardrum.

lessons.name: Light: reflect, absorb, transmit

practice.q: A red apple looks red in white light because it
ch: reflects red light and absorbs other colors
practice.h: The color you see is the light that bounces to your eye.

practice.q: Light passes easily through a clear window. This is
A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the water's surface. What causes this?
ch: Light refracts (bends) as it changes speed passing from water to air

practice.q: Which material would most likely absorb the most sunlight and get hottest?
Describe what happens to light when it hits a mirror, a black piece of paper and a glass window.
practice.ans: The mirror reflects almost all light; the black paper absorbs most light and warms up; the glass window transmits most light through it.

quiz.q: The bouncing of light off a surface is
Light waves can travel through which of these?
Light travels about 300,000 km per second. How many seconds does it take light to travel 900,000 km?
A solar cell turned 18 of every 100 units of sunlight into electricity. What percent of the light energy became electricity?
A student shines white light on a green leaf and measures the reflected light. Most of the reflected light is green. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: The leaf absorbs most red and blue light and reflects green
All light passes through the leaf

quiz.q: Why do lenses in eyeglasses help people see clearly?
ch: They refract light so it focuses on the back of the eye

quiz.q: Design a test to compare how well three window films block sunlight from entering a car. Describe what you would measure and how you would keep the test fair.
quiz.ans: Place each film over identical jars with thermometers (or a light meter) in the same sunlight for the same time; measure temperature rise or light passing through; keep jar size, starting temperature and position the same; repeat and compare means.

lessons.name: Digital signals carry information

practice.q: A digital signal sends information as
ch: a series of on and off pulses, like 1s and 0s

practice.q: Why are digital signals often more reliable than analog signals?
ch: Small amounts of noise do not change whether a pulse is read as 1 or 0
practice.h: Think about how easily a 1 or 0 can be read even with a little static.

practice.q: Each character in a text message uses 8 bits. How many bits does a 15-character message use?
Which uses waves to carry digital information?
Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of digital signals.
practice.ans: Advantage: they can be copied, stored and sent many times without losing quality. Disadvantage: they need devices to encode and decode them, and if too many bits are lost the message can drop out completely.

quiz.q: A signal that changes smoothly and continuously, like the groove on a vinyl record, is
Fiber optic cables carry information as pulses of
A video file is 600 megabits. A connection downloads 50 megabits per second. How many seconds does the download take?
A 3-minute song takes 24 megabits per minute to store. How many megabits does the song need?
A copy of an old cassette tape sounds worse each time it is copied, but a digital music file sounds the same after 100 copies. What explains this?
ch: Digital copies keep exact 1s and 0s, while analog copies add noise each time

quiz.q: Why can a radio station's digital signal be compressed to take up less space?
ch: Patterns in the 1s and 0s can be stored more efficiently
Radio waves are made of sound

quiz.q: Students sent a 100-bit message as an analog wave and as a digital signal through a noisy wire. Analog: the receiver correctly read 62 percent of the message. Digital: 99 percent correct, and an error-check fixed the rest. They repeated the test 5 times with similar results. Make a claim about which signal type is more reliable. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: digital signals are more reliable than analog signals for sending information through noise. Evidence: the digital signal was read 99 percent correctly (with errors fixed), compared with 62 percent for analog, across 5 repeated trials. Reasoning: a digital signal only needs to be read as on or off, so small noise does not change the message, and errors can be checked and corrected; an analog signal's exact shape carries the information, so noise directly changes it.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

test.q: Waves transfer
The highest point on a transverse wave is the
Which wave has the most energy if all have the same frequency?
ch: the one with the largest amplitude
the one with the smallest amplitude
they all have the same energy

test.q: Sound is a mechanical wave, which means it
ch: needs a medium to travel through

test.q: A higher-pitched sound has a
A white car stays cooler in the sun than a black car because white paint
Light bends when it passes from air into glass. This is
Which statement about digital signals is correct?
ch: They send information as patterns of 1s and 0s

test.q: Which wave behavior allows you to see yourself in a still pond?
Soundproof rooms use foam on the walls mostly to
A wave's frequency doubles while its speed stays the same. What happens to its wavelength?
A phone video call becomes frozen in places but the sound and picture that do come through are clear. Which explanation fits digital signals?
ch: Some data packets were lost, but the received 1s and 0s were read exactly
The signal is analog and full of noise

test.q: A wave has a frequency of 6 Hz and a wavelength of 2.5 m. What is its speed in m/s?
A radio wave travels 300,000,000 m/s with a wavelength of 3 m. What is its frequency in Hz?
Thunder is heard 4 seconds after lightning. Sound travels about 340 m/s. How far away is the storm in meters?
A sonar pulse returns 3 seconds after being sent. Sound travels 1,500 m/s in seawater. How deep is the water in meters?
Which material transmits the most light?
Students measured sound levels behind barriers: no barrier 80 units, cardboard 70, foam 50, foam plus cardboard 40. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: The foam and cardboard together absorbed or blocked the most sound

test.q: Why do astronauts on a spacewalk use radios to talk?
ch: Sound cannot travel through the vacuum of space, but radio waves can
Radios make sound travel faster in air

test.q: Explain how amplitude and energy are related, using a sound or ocean wave as an example.
test.ans: A larger amplitude means the wave carries more energy; a loud sound has a large amplitude and can even shake windows, while a tall ocean wave can move rocks and erode a beach.

test.q: Describe what happens to sunlight that hits a green leaf.
test.ans: Some light is absorbed, especially red and blue light used in photosynthesis; green light is mostly reflected, which is why the leaf looks green; a little light is transmitted through the leaf.

test.q: Compare analog and digital signals and explain why most communication today uses digital signals.
test.ans: Analog signals are continuous waves that change smoothly; digital signals are pulses of 1s and 0s. Digital signals resist noise, can be copied, stored and compressed without losing quality, and can be checked for errors, so they are more reliable.

test.q: A class tested how amplitude affects energy by dropping a ball into a water tank from different heights and measuring how far a floating cork at the far end rose. Drop height 10 cm: wave amplitude 1 cm, cork rose 1 cm. 20 cm: amplitude 2 cm, cork rose 2 cm. 40 cm: amplitude 4 cm, cork rose 4 cm. Ripples spread out but the water did not flow to the far end. Make a claim about what water waves carry and how amplitude relates to energy. Use the data as evidence and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: water waves carry energy, not water, and waves with greater amplitude carry more energy. Evidence: larger drops made waves with larger amplitudes (1, 2 and 4 cm), and the cork rose higher each time; the water itself did not flow to the far end. Reasoning: the falling ball transfers energy to the water; the wave passes that energy along through the water while the water mainly moves up and down; a bigger amplitude shows more energy was given to the wave, so it could lift the cork higher.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 6: Earth's History and Evidence of Common Ancestry
units.el: Use a stack of colored paper to model rock layers ("bottom is oldest"). Provide a picture chart of arm bones in a human, cat, whale and bat with matching colors for each bone.

lessons.name: Reading rock layers and geologic time

practice.q: In undisturbed rock layers, the oldest layer is usually
practice.h: Layers pile up one on top of another over time.

practice.q: A layer of volcanic ash lies between Layer A (below) and Layer B (above). What can you say about the ash?
ch: It is younger than Layer A and older than Layer B
It is older than both layers
It is younger than both layers

practice.q: A crack (fault) cuts through Layers 1, 2 and 3 but not Layer 4 on top. When did the fault form?
ch: after Layers 1 to 3 formed and before Layer 4
at the same time as Layer 4

practice.q: Earth is about 4.6 billion years old. Non-avian dinosaurs went extinct about 66 million years ago. How many million years did Earth exist before that extinction?
practice.h: 4.6 billion = 4,600 million.

practice.q: A fossil of a sea animal is found in a layer below a layer with land plant fossils. What does this suggest about how the area changed?
practice.ans: The area was once covered by sea, and later it became land where plants grew, because lower layers formed earlier than upper layers.

quiz.q: A fossil that lived for a short time over a wide area and helps date rock layers is
A thin layer rich in the rare element iridium is found worldwide in rocks about 66 million years old, along with a huge buried crater in Mexico. What event does this evidence support?

A model shrinks Earth's 4.6 billion years onto a 46-meter hallway, so each meter equals 100 million years. How many meters from the end of the hallway (today) is the dinosaur extinction 66 million years ago?
Sediment in a lake builds up 0.5 mm per year. How many years would it take to form a layer 20 mm thick?
Layers from bottom to top: sandstone with trilobite fossils, shale with fish fossils, limestone with dinosaur bones, soil with mammal bones. Which conclusion is best supported?
ch: Trilobites lived before dinosaurs, and mammals in the top layer are the most recent
All of these animals lived at the same time
The soil is the oldest layer

quiz.q: Why do geologists use the geologic time scale?
ch: To organize Earth's long history into eras and periods based on rocks and fossils
To tell the time of day

quiz.q: Explain how scientists can tell that an igneous rock body is younger than the rock layers it cuts across.
quiz.ans: The igneous rock must have formed after the layers it cuts through, because the layers had to exist first for magma to push through them; so the cutting rock is younger.

lessons.name: Patterns in the fossil record

practice.q: Fossils show that many species that once lived are no longer alive today. This is evidence of
In older rock layers, fossils of living things tend to be simpler; in younger layers, more types of complex organisms appear. What does this pattern suggest?
ch: Life on Earth has changed over time
practice.h: Compare what you find at the bottom with what you find near the top.

practice.q: A rock layer from about 252 million years ago records a mass extinction. If a sample had 200 species of sea animals before it and 20 after it, what percent of the species disappeared?
Fossils of the same kind of organism found in many layers show small changes in shape over time. What does this show?
ch: Species can change gradually over many generations

practice.q: Explain why the fossil record is incomplete.
practice.ans: Most organisms decay before they are fossilized; fossils form only under special conditions like quick burial in sediment, and many fossils are destroyed by erosion or are never found.

quiz.q: Which is the best definition of a fossil?
ch: preserved remains or traces of an organism that lived long ago

quiz.q: Fossil counts show 12 families of marine reptiles in one period and 3 families in the next. What percent of the families remained?
Fossils show that some early whale relatives had four legs and lived near water. Later fossils have smaller hind legs, and today's whales have tiny hip bones. What does this sequence show?
ch: Whales changed over time from land-dwelling ancestors
Whales have always looked the same
Land animals came from modern whales

quiz.q: Data: number of known animal families - 500 million years ago, 150; 300 million years ago, 450; 252 million years ago, 200; 100 million years ago, 600; today, 900. Which statement is supported?
ch: Diversity has generally increased over time, with drops during mass extinctions

quiz.q: The fossil record shows about 200 known animal families 252 million years ago and about 600 known families 100 million years ago. How many families were added?
Why are fossils of fish never found below the oldest layers that contain simple single-celled fossils?
ch: Fish appeared later in Earth's history than single-celled life
Fish fossils dissolve in old rock

quiz.q: A student says, "Since dinosaurs went extinct, the fossil record shows life gets less diverse over time." Use evidence to evaluate this claim.
quiz.ans: The claim is not supported. Mass extinctions caused sharp drops, but after each one new species appeared and diversity recovered and grew; overall, the fossil record shows diversity increasing over long periods.

lessons.name: Similar structures, shared ancestors

practice.q: A human arm, a cat's front leg, a whale's flipper and a bat's wing all have the same set of bones in the same order. What does this suggest?
ch: These animals share a common ancestor
They all use their limbs in the same way
practice.h: Similar structure is evidence of relationship, even if the jobs differ.

practice.q: Structures that have similar bones but different functions in related species are called
A bird's wing and a butterfly's wing are both used for flying but are built very differently. What does this suggest?
ch: They evolved separately and are not evidence of close relationship
They come from the same ancestor recently

practice.q: A modern horse has 1 toe per foot. A fossil ancestor from about 50 million years ago had 4 toes on each front foot. How many fewer front toes per foot does the modern horse have?
Explain how a whale's tiny hip bones are evidence that its ancestors lived on land.
practice.ans: Hip bones attach legs in land mammals; whales have small, unused hip bones, which suggests they inherited them from ancestors that walked on land with hind legs.

quiz.q: A python has tiny leftover leg bones inside its body. Which conclusion is best supported?
ch: Snakes likely evolved from ancestors with legs
Pythons use these bones to walk
Snakes are related to fish only
The bones formed recently by chance

quiz.q: Which pair shows homologous structures?
ch: a dolphin's flipper and a human hand
a bird's wing and an insect's wing
a fish fin and a submarine fin
a bat's wing and a kite

quiz.q: Scientists compared 20 bones in the forelimbs of a lizard and a dog. 17 bones matched in type and position. What percent matched?
Fossil Tiktaalik (about 375 million years old) had gills and scales like a fish but also a neck and strong fin bones like the legs of land animals. Which idea does it best support?
ch: Land animals descended from fish-like ancestors
Fish and land animals are unrelated

quiz.q: Why do scientists compare anatomy of living species with fossils?
ch: To find patterns of similarities and differences that show how species are related
To find out the age of rocks only

quiz.q: Skeletons of a chimpanzee and a human share many of the same bones in similar arrangements. What does this suggest?
ch: They share a relatively recent common ancestor

quiz.q: Explain the difference between homologous and analogous structures and which is better evidence of common ancestry.
quiz.ans: Homologous structures share the same basic bones from a common ancestor but may have different jobs (human arm and bat wing); analogous structures have the same job but different structures (bird wing and insect wing). Homologous structures are evidence of common ancestry.

lessons.name: Clues from embryos

practice.q: Early embryos of fish, chickens, pigs and humans all have a tail and pouches in the throat region. What does this similarity suggest?
ch: These animals share a common ancestor
They live in the same habitat

practice.q: As embryos develop, they become more different from each other. Which explanation fits?
ch: Different genes switch on as each species develops its own features
practice.h: Similar early stages, different later stages.

practice.q: A study compared 12 early embryo features in a chicken and a turtle. They shared 9 features. What percent did they share?
Which observation from embryos would best support that two species are closely related?
ch: Their embryos look alike for a long time during development
