ch: the agreement that united the Haudenosaunee nations
a Spanish law for the missions

test.q: Which crops were known as the Three Sisters?
What did the arrival of horses do for Plains nations?
ch: It made hunting and travel faster, and many nations became more mobile.

test.q: Cahokia was
ch: a large Mississippian city with huge earthen mounds

test.q: Why did people in the desert Southwest build homes of adobe?
ch: Earth was plentiful, trees were scarce, and thick walls kept homes cool.

test.q: Which region is matched with its main resource?
Who chose the chiefs of the Haudenosaunee nations?
Wampum belts were used to
Cahokia reached its largest size around the year 1100. Columbus reached the Americas in 1492. How many years apart are these dates?
A Plains band hunted 15 buffalo in a hunt. Each buffalo gave about 400 pounds of meat. About how many pounds of meat did they get?
The Haudenosaunee Grand Council has 50 chiefs. The Onondaga nation holds 14 of the seats. How many seats do the other nations hold?
Archaeologists find copper from the Great Lakes and shells from the Gulf of Mexico at Cahokia. What does this show?
ch: Cahokia was part of a large trade network.
Cahokia was next to both the Great Lakes and the Gulf.
People at Cahokia did not trade.
Copper and shells came from Europe.

test.q: Which statement best explains why American Indian cultures in North America were so different from one another?
ch: Each nation adapted to its own environment, climate and resources.
They all came from the same village.
They were all ruled by one leader.

test.q: A Plains nation lived in tipis and hunted buffalo, and a Pacific Northwest nation lived in plank houses and fished for salmon. What does this comparison show?
ch: Shelter and food depended on the resources of each region.
Both nations lived in the same region.

test.q: Which nation lived in the Southeast before Europeans arrived?
Describe how one American Indian nation used its environment to meet its needs for food, shelter and clothing.
test.ans: The Lakota hunted buffalo for meat, used hides for tipis and clothing, and bones for tools; the Haida fished salmon and built cedar plank houses and canoes.

test.q: Explain why the Haudenosaunee Confederacy is an important example of American Indian government.
test.ans: Five, later six, nations united under the Great Law of Peace with a council that made decisions together and clan mothers who chose leaders, showing a strong, organized government.

test.q: Read the sources. Source A: A map shows Haudenosaunee villages along rivers and lakes in a forested region of what is now New York. Source B: An archaeologist found burned corn, bean seeds and squash rinds in a village storage pit. Source C: A drawing shows a longhouse covered with large sheets of elm bark. Make a claim about how the Haudenosaunee used their environment. Use evidence and reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: The Haudenosaunee used the forests, waters and soil of their homeland to farm and build permanent villages. Evidence: Source A shows villages near rivers and lakes in forests; Source B shows they grew corn, beans and squash; Source C shows longhouses made of tree bark. Reasoning: Rich soil and water let them farm the Three Sisters, and the forest gave building materials, so they could live in large, lasting villages.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 2: The Age of Exploration (5.2)
units.el: Trace each explorer's route in a different color on a world map and keep a chart (explorer, country, year, goal, result). Pre-teach sponsor, navigation, expedition, conquer, claim and exchange, and give the frame "___ sailed for ___ in ___ to find ___."

lessons.name: Why Europeans explored

practice.q: In the 1400s, many Europeans wanted a sea route to Asia mainly to
ch: trade for spices, silk and other valuable goods
find a place to farm wheat
practice.h: These goods were rare and costly in Europe.

practice.q: After 1453, the Ottoman Empire controlled the land routes between Europe and Asia. How did this affect European traders?
ch: Asian goods became harder to get and more expensive, so they looked for sea routes.
practice.h: Think about what happens when someone else controls the road you need.

practice.q: Historians often sum up the reasons for exploration as "God, gold and glory." Which is an example of "glory"?
ch: an explorer wanting fame for his country and himself
practice.h: Glory is about honor and fame.

practice.q: A caravel was
ch: a small, fast ship with sails that could sail against the wind
practice.h: Portuguese sailors used this ship to explore the coast of Africa.

practice.q: An astrolabe helped sailors find their latitude by
ch: measuring the angle of the sun or stars above the horizon
showing the depth of the ocean

practice.q: Explain why kings and queens sponsored, or paid for, voyages of exploration.
practice.ans: They hoped to gain wealth from trade and gold, claim new land, spread their religion and win power and glory over rival countries.

quiz.q: A magnetic compass helped sailors
ch: know which direction they were heading
measure the speed of the wind

quiz.q: Prince Henry of Portugal is known as "the Navigator" because he
ch: supported sailors, mapmakers and shipbuilders who explored the coast of Africa

quiz.q: Bartolomeu Dias sailed around the southern tip of Africa in 1488. Why did this matter?
ch: It showed ships could sail around Africa to reach Asia.
It proved the Earth is flat.
It found a route to the Pacific through North America.

quiz.q: In 1498, Vasco da Gama of Portugal became the first European to reach India by sailing around Africa. What did this give Portugal?
ch: a sea route to trade directly for Asian spices
a land route through the Middle East
the first colony in North America

quiz.q: Bartolomeu Dias rounded Africa in 1488 and Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498. How many years apart are these voyages?
An explorer wanted to find a faster route to Asia, earn riches and become famous, and he was willing to risk his life at sea. Which words best describe him?
ch: ambitious and willing to take risks, like an entrepreneur
careful and unwilling to try new things

quiz.q: Describe two inventions that made long ocean voyages possible and how each one helped.
quiz.ans: The compass showed direction; the astrolabe measured latitude by the sun or stars; the caravel could sail against the wind; better maps helped plan routes.

lessons.name: Spain in the Americas

practice.q: In 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed west for
practice.h: King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella paid for his voyage.

practice.q: Columbus thought he had reached
ch: islands near Asia, which he called the Indies
a new continent he named America
practice.h: This is why he called the people he met "Indians."

practice.q: The Taino people met Columbus in the Caribbean. What happened to them in the years that followed?
ch: Many died from disease, war and forced labor under Spanish rule.

practice.q: In 1521, Hernan Cortes and his soldiers, with thousands of Indigenous allies, conquered the capital of the
practice.h: Its capital, Tenochtitlan, is now Mexico City.

practice.q: Ferdinand Magellan's expedition left Spain in 1519 with about 270 sailors. In 1522, only 18 returned on the ship Victoria. About how many sailors did not return on that ship?
practice.h: Subtract the sailors who returned from those who left.

practice.q: Explain why Spanish conquistadors were able to defeat large empires like the Aztec and Inca.
practice.ans: They had steel weapons, guns and horses, they made alliances with Indigenous peoples who opposed those empires, and European diseases like smallpox killed huge numbers of people.

quiz.q: Francisco Pizarro conquered which empire in South America beginning in 1532?
In 1540, Francisco Vasquez de Coronado led an expedition into what is now the American Southwest searching for
ch: a route to China by land

quiz.q: In 1494, the Treaty of Tordesillas divided newly claimed lands between
Bartolome de las Casas, a Spanish priest, wrote in 1542 about the cruelty of Spanish colonists toward Indigenous peoples. What was his point of view?
ch: Indigenous peoples were being treated unjustly and should be protected.

quiz.q: Why is Magellan's voyage important even though he died on the way?
ch: His expedition was the first to sail all the way around the world.
It found gold in the Pacific.
It proved the Earth was flat.

quiz.q: Columbus's first voyage in 1492 took about 5 weeks to cross the Atlantic. About how many days is 5 weeks?

Columbus wrote in his journal in 1492 that the people he met would make good servants. A Taino person might describe the same meeting very differently. Explain how the two points of view would differ and why.
quiz.ans: Columbus saw the Taino as people to rule and use for Spain's gain. A Taino person saw strangers arriving on their own land who would bring danger, disease and forced labor. Their goals and power were different.

lessons.name: France, England and the Netherlands in North America

practice.q: In 1497, John Cabot explored the coast of Newfoundland and claimed land for
practice.h: He was born in Italy, but his voyage was paid for by King Henry VII.

practice.q: Many explorers searched for a Northwest Passage. What was it?
ch: a hoped-for water route through North America to Asia
practice.h: The name gives a direction and a kind of path.

practice.q: Jacques Cartier explored the St. Lawrence River in the 1530s. Which country did he sail for?
practice.h: Quebec, a city on this river, still speaks this country's language.

practice.q: Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec in 1608. It became the center of
ch: New France and its fur trade
practice.h: Beaver furs were very valuable in Europe.

practice.q: Henry Hudson explored the Hudson River for the Dutch in 1609. Champlain founded Quebec in 1608. How many years apart are these events?
Compare the goals of French and Spanish explorers in North America.
practice.ans: Spanish explorers searched mostly for gold and to conquer and convert people; French explorers mostly sought furs, trade with American Indians and a route to Asia.

quiz.q: The Dutch colony of New Netherland had its main town, New Amsterdam, on the island of
In 1682, Robert de La Salle traveled down the Mississippi River and claimed the land around it for France. He named it
The French built good relations with many American Indian nations mainly through
A map of North America in 1700 shows Spain in Florida and the Southwest, France along the St. Lawrence and Mississippi, and England on the Atlantic coast. What does the map show?
ch: Several European countries competed for land in North America.
No one lived in North America.

quiz.q: Which country claimed Alaska after Vitus Bering's voyage in 1741?
Cabot reached North America in 1497. The English founded Jamestown in 1607. How many years later was Jamestown founded?
Why did no explorer find a Northwest Passage in the 1500s and 1600s?
quiz.ans: North America was much larger than expected, and the northern waters were blocked by land and ice. No easy water route across the continent existed.

lessons.name: Atlantic trade and the Columbian Exchange

practice.q: The Columbian Exchange was
ch: the movement of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world
a treaty between Spain and Portugal
a trade of gold for spices only
practice.h: It is named after Columbus because it began after his voyages.

practice.q: Which crops first came from the Americas and spread to Europe, Africa and Asia?
practice.h: Think of foods first grown by Indigenous farmers in the Americas.

practice.q: Which animals came from Europe to the Americas?
The triangular trade linked which three areas?
practice.h: Picture three sides of the Atlantic Ocean.

practice.q: The Middle Passage was
ch: the voyage that carried enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to the Americas
a road through the Rocky Mountains
practice.h: It was the middle side of the triangular trade.

practice.q: Describe one positive and one negative effect of the Columbian Exchange.
practice.ans: Positive: new foods like potatoes and corn helped feed people around the world. Negative: diseases like smallpox killed millions of American Indians, and the slave trade forced millions of Africans across the ocean.

quiz.q: Which disease brought by Europeans killed huge numbers of American Indians?
Olaudah Equiano, who was enslaved as a child, published a book in 1789 describing the Middle Passage. Why is his book an important source?
ch: It gives a first-hand account from a person who survived the voyage.
It was written by a slave trader.

quiz.q: European colonists grew sugarcane, tobacco and rice on large plantations in the Americas. Why did this increase the slave trade?
ch: Plantation owners forced enslaved Africans to do the hard work.

quiz.q: Horses spread from Spanish colonies to the Great Plains. How did this show the Columbian Exchange?
ch: An animal from Europe changed the way of life of American Indian nations.
Plants moved from Asia to Africa.

quiz.q: Potatoes from South America became a main food in Ireland and other parts of Europe. What was one effect?
ch: Europe's population grew because people had more food.

quiz.q: A ship in the triangular trade sailed 4,000 miles from England to West Africa, then 5,000 miles to the Caribbean, then 4,000 miles back to England. How many miles was the whole trip?
Explain how the Columbian Exchange changed life in both the Americas and Europe.
quiz.ans: The Americas gained horses, cattle, wheat and sugarcane but suffered terrible diseases and the slave trade; Europe gained new foods like potatoes, corn and tomatoes, which helped populations grow.

test.q: Columbus first reached the Americas in
The first expedition to sail around the world was led at first by
Which tool helped sailors find their direction at sea?
Why did European countries want a sea route to Asia?
ch: to trade directly for spices, silk and other goods
to escape the plague in Asia

test.q: Which explorer conquered the Aztec Empire?
Which country is matched with the explorer who sailed for it?
What was the main goal of French traders in North America?
ch: trading with American Indians for furs

test.q: The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494)
ch: divided lands between Spain and Portugal

test.q: Which statement about the Columbian Exchange is true?
ch: Corn and potatoes went from the Americas to Europe, and horses came to the Americas.
Horses went from the Americas to Europe.
Potatoes came to the Americas from Europe.
No plants or animals were exchanged.

test.q: Which was a major cause of the deaths of millions of American Indians after 1492?
The Middle Passage was part of which trade route?
ch: the triangular trade across the Atlantic

test.q: Henry Hudson's voyage in 1609 helped the Dutch claim land along the Hudson River. What colony did the Dutch start there?
Columbus reached the Americas in 1492. Magellan's expedition returned to Spain in 1522. How many years apart are these events?
Vasco da Gama's voyage to India and back took about 2 years, from 1497 to 1499. Columbus's first voyage there and back took about 7 months. About how many months longer was da Gama's voyage?
About 270 sailors left with Magellan and 18 returned. About how many times larger was the starting crew than the group that returned?

A Spanish soldier's report says the conquest of the Aztec brought Christianity and order. An Aztec account describes the destruction of their city and the deaths from smallpox. How should a historian use them?
ch: Compare both points of view to understand what happened and how each group experienced it.
Use only the Spanish report because it is written by a winner.

test.q: Which best explains why Spain grew rich and powerful in the 1500s?
ch: It took gold and silver from conquered empires in the Americas.
It traded furs with the French.

test.q: Why did explorers keep searching for a Northwest Passage even after many failed?
ch: A water route through North America would make trade with Asia faster and very profitable.
Kings did not care about trade.
The passage had already been found.

test.q: Which crop first grown in the Americas became important around the world?
Describe two reasons Europeans explored the world in the 1400s and 1500s.
test.ans: To find sea routes for trade with Asia, to gain gold and wealth, to spread Christianity, and to win land and glory for their countries.

test.q: Explain how the triangular trade connected Europe, Africa and the Americas.
test.ans: Ships carried manufactured goods from Europe to Africa, enslaved Africans to the Americas, and sugar, tobacco and other crops from the Americas back to Europe.

test.q: Read the sources. Source A: Historians estimate the population of central Mexico fell from many millions in 1519 to a small fraction of that number by 1600. Source B: A Spanish priest wrote in the 1500s that smallpox spread through the Aztec capital and killed great numbers of people. Source C: A chart shows that American Indians had no earlier contact with smallpox or measles, while many Europeans had survived these diseases as children. Make a claim about the main reason the Indigenous population of the Americas fell so sharply after 1492. Use evidence and reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: European diseases were the main reason the Indigenous population fell so sharply. Evidence: Source A shows a huge population drop after 1519; Source B describes smallpox killing great numbers in the Aztec capital; Source C shows American Indians had never been exposed to these diseases. Reasoning: People who have never been exposed to a disease have no protection, so smallpox and measles spread quickly and killed far more people than wars did.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 3: Founding the Thirteen Colonies (5.4)
units.el: Color a map of the thirteen colonies by region (New England, Middle, Southern) and label the American Indian nations already living there. Keep a chart (colony, founder, year, reason founded) and give the frame "___ was founded by ___ in ___ because ___."

lessons.name: Jamestown and the Southern Colonies

practice.q: The first permanent English settlement in North America was founded in 1607 at
practice.h: It was named after King James I.

practice.q: Jamestown was paid for by the Virginia Company. What did the company's investors most hope for?
ch: to make a profit from gold, trade or crops
practice.h: A company exists to earn money for the people who invest in it.

practice.q: Captain John Smith told the Jamestown settlers in 1608 that "he that will not worke shall not eate." Why did he make this rule?
ch: Many settlers were not working, and the colony was running out of food.
The settlers had too much food.
He wanted them to go home.

practice.q: Which crop saved Jamestown's economy after John Rolfe began growing it for sale around 1612?
practice.h: It was sold in England and smoked in pipes.

practice.q: About 500 people lived in Jamestown in the fall of 1609. Only about 60 were alive in the spring of 1610. About how many people died during this "starving time"?
practice.h: Subtract the survivors from the starting number.

practice.q: Explain why the Powhatan people were important to the survival of Jamestown, and why relations grew tense.
practice.ans: The Powhatan traded corn and food that kept settlers alive. Relations grew tense as settlers took more land for tobacco and fought over food and land.

quiz.q: In 1619, Virginia colonists elected the first representative assembly in the English colonies, called the
Also in 1619, the first Africans in the English colonies were brought to Virginia. Why is this year important in American history?
ch: It marks the beginning of slavery in the English colonies.

quiz.q: Lord Baltimore founded Maryland in 1634 as a safe place for
James Oglethorpe founded Georgia in 1732 partly to give people from debtors' prisons a new start and partly to
ch: protect the Carolinas from Spanish Florida

quiz.q: Why did large plantations develop in the Southern Colonies?
ch: The warm climate and long growing season were good for cash crops like tobacco and rice.
The land was rocky and cold.

quiz.q: Jamestown was founded in 1607 and Georgia, the last of the thirteen colonies, in 1732. How many years apart are these dates?
Describe the economy of the Southern Colonies and the role of enslaved Africans in it.
quiz.ans: It was based on cash crops like tobacco, rice and indigo grown on large plantations. Enslaved Africans were forced to do most of the work, often in harsh conditions, and their labor made planters rich.

lessons.name: The New England Colonies

practice.q: The Pilgrims sailed to North America in 1620 on the
practice.h: The ship's name is also the name of a spring flower.

practice.q: Why did the Pilgrims leave England?
ch: to worship in their own way, separate from the Church of England
practice.h: Think about religious freedom.

practice.q: In the Mayflower Compact (1620), the Pilgrims agreed to "covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil body politic." What does this show?
ch: They agreed to make fair laws and govern themselves.
They agreed to obey only the king.
They agreed to return to England.
practice.h: A "civil body politic" is a group that governs itself.

practice.q: Tisquantum, also called Squanto, was a Wampanoag man who
ch: helped the Pilgrims plant corn and fish

practice.q: The Mayflower carried 102 passengers. About half died during the first winter. About how many passengers survived?
practice.h: Find half of 102.

practice.q: Explain why the Wampanoag leader Massasoit made an agreement with the Pilgrims in 1621.
practice.ans: Disease had weakened the Wampanoag, and Massasoit hoped an alliance with the English would help protect his people from rival nations and bring trade.

quiz.q: John Winthrop led the Puritans who founded the Massachusetts Bay Colony in
John Winthrop told the Puritans in 1630, "We shall be as a city upon a hill, the eyes of all people are upon us." What did he mean?
ch: Their colony should be a model community for others to follow.
They should build their town on a mountain.

quiz.q: Roger Williams was forced out of Massachusetts and founded Rhode Island in 1636. What did he believe?
ch: Government should not force people to follow one religion.
Only the king should choose religion.

quiz.q: Thomas Hooker led settlers to found Connecticut. Its Fundamental Orders of 1639 are important because they were
ch: an early written plan of government created by colonists

quiz.q: New England's economy depended on fishing, shipbuilding and trade more than on large farms because
ch: the soil was rocky and the growing season was short

quiz.q: The Pilgrims landed in 1620 and the Puritans arrived in 1630. How many years apart?
Compare the reasons Plymouth and Rhode Island were founded. How were they alike and different?
quiz.ans: Both were founded by people seeking religious freedom. The Pilgrims wanted to worship apart from the Church of England; Roger Williams founded Rhode Island so everyone could worship freely, with church and government kept separate.

lessons.name: The Middle Colonies

practice.q: In 1664, England took over the Dutch colony of New Netherland and renamed it
practice.h: It was named after the king's brother, the Duke of York.

practice.q: William Penn founded Pennsylvania in 1681. He was a member of which religious group?
practice.h: This group believed in peace and equality.

practice.q: Penn called his colony a "holy experiment." What did he mean?
ch: a colony where people of different religions could live together in peace
a colony with one official church
practice.h: Think about what Quakers believed about people of other faiths.

practice.q: The Middle Colonies were called the "breadbasket colonies" because they
ch: grew large amounts of wheat and other grains
practice.h: Bread is made from grain.

practice.q: William Penn made treaties and paid for land with which American Indian nation?
Explain why the Middle Colonies were more diverse than New England.
practice.ans: They offered religious tolerance and good farmland, so settlers came from the Netherlands, Germany, Sweden, Scotland, Ireland and other places, along with many religious groups.

quiz.q: Philadelphia, the largest city in the Middle Colonies, was founded by
Which colony was first settled by the Dutch?
Why did the Middle Colonies become a center of trade?
ch: They had rich farmland and wide rivers like the Hudson and Delaware that led to busy ports.

quiz.q: Quakers in Pennsylvania were among the first colonists to
ch: start the French and Indian War

quiz.q: Which colonies made up the Middle Colonies?
ch: New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Delaware

quiz.q: Pennsylvania was founded in 1681. How many years before the Declaration of Independence (1776) was that?
Describe the economy of the Middle Colonies and explain how geography supported it.
quiz.ans: Fertile soil and a moderate climate let farmers grow wheat, corn and livestock, and rivers carried goods to ports like Philadelphia and New York for trade.

lessons.name: Comparing the colonial regions

practice.q: Which region had the coldest winters and rockiest soil?
practice.h: It is the farthest north.

practice.q: Which region relied most on plantation crops grown by enslaved people?
practice.h: Think of tobacco, rice and indigo.

practice.q: A colonist works in a shipyard building ships from local timber. Which region does the colonist most likely live in?
practice.h: Which region had thick forests and many harbors?

practice.q: Why did most colonial towns grow along the Atlantic coast and rivers?
ch: Ships could carry people and goods to trade with England and other colonies.
The inland mountains had better soil.
Rivers were too dangerous to use.

practice.q: A map shows that Boston is about 300 miles from Philadelphia and Philadelphia is about 200 miles from Williamsburg, Virginia. How many miles is the trip from Boston to Philadelphia to Williamsburg?
practice.h: Add the two distances.

practice.q: Choose two colonial regions. Compare their climate and how people earned a living.
practice.ans: New England had cold winters and rocky soil, so people fished, built ships and traded. The Southern Colonies had a warm climate and rich soil, so planters grew tobacco and rice with enslaved labor.

quiz.q: The Appalachian Mountains formed the western edge of most English colonies. What did this mean for settlers?
ch: Moving west was difficult, so most settled near the coast.
The mountains were part of the ocean.
They lived only in the mountains.

quiz.q: Which colony is in the New England region?
Which product is matched with the right region?
Why did the three regions trade with each other?
ch: Each region produced different goods because of different climates and resources.
They all produced the same goods.
They were not allowed to trade with England.
They had no goods to trade.

quiz.q: A colonist describes a town with a church and a meeting house where all the men gather to vote on local matters. Which region is this most likely?
In 1750, the colonies had about 1,170,000 people. About 240,000 of them were enslaved Africans. About how many were not enslaved?
Explain how geography led to different ways of life in the three colonial regions.
quiz.ans: Rocky soil and a cold climate pushed New England toward fishing and trade; fertile land made the Middle Colonies grow grain; a warm climate and long seasons made the South rely on plantation crops worked by enslaved people.

test.q: Jamestown was founded in
Who founded Pennsylvania?
The Pilgrims founded which colony in 1620?
The House of Burgesses (1619) was important because it was
ch: the first elected representative assembly in the English colonies

test.q: Which colony was founded as a safe place for Catholics?
Which statement about Rhode Island is true?
ch: Roger Williams founded it so people could worship freely.
It was founded for gold mining.
It was the first Dutch colony.

test.q: Which cash crop was most important to the economy of early Virginia?
Why did New England colonists rely on fishing, shipbuilding and trade?
ch: Rocky soil and a short growing season made large farms difficult.
They had a long, warm growing season.

test.q: The Middle Colonies were known for
Which leader helped the Pilgrims survive by teaching them to plant corn?
Which colony was founded last, in 1732?
The Mayflower Compact is important because it
ch: was an early agreement by colonists to govern themselves

test.q: The Mayflower Compact was signed in 1620. The House of Burgesses first met in 1619. How many years apart?
About 104 men and boys arrived at Jamestown in 1607. If 66 died within the first year, how many survived?
A colonial port town had about 2,000 people in 1700 and about 25,000 people in 1770. How many more people lived there in 1770?
Which statement correctly compares the founding of Virginia and Massachusetts Bay?
ch: Virginia was founded mainly to make a profit, while Massachusetts Bay was founded mainly for religious reasons.
Both were founded only to find gold.
Both were founded by the Dutch.
Virginia was founded for religious freedom and Massachusetts for tobacco.

test.q: A Wampanoag leader in 1621 and a Pilgrim leader in 1621 both agreed to an alliance. What did each side most likely want?
ch: The Wampanoag wanted protection and trade; the Pilgrims wanted help surviving.
Both wanted to return to England.

test.q: Which best explains why slavery grew more in the Southern Colonies than in New England?
ch: Plantation crops needed many workers, and planters used enslaved Africans to grow them.
Southern colonists did not grow crops.
Slavery was illegal in the South.

test.q: Which colony was taken from the Dutch by England in 1664?
Describe the reasons two different colonies were founded.
test.ans: Virginia was founded by the Virginia Company to make a profit; Massachusetts Bay by Puritans seeking to build a religious community; Pennsylvania by William Penn as a Quaker colony with religious tolerance; Georgia for debtors and as a buffer against Spain.

test.q: Explain how the House of Burgesses and the Mayflower Compact were early steps toward self-government.
test.ans: Both let colonists make decisions about their own laws. The House of Burgesses was an elected assembly, and the Mayflower Compact was an agreement to make fair laws together.

test.q: Read the sources. Source A: A map shows New England with rocky hills, thick forests and many harbors. Source B: A colonial record from Massachusetts lists shipbuilding, fishing and trade as the colony's main businesses. Source C: A letter from a Virginia planter in 1700 describes fields of tobacco and a long, warm growing season. Make a claim about how geography shaped the economies of the colonies. Use evidence and reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Geography shaped each region's economy, pushing New England toward the sea and Virginia toward farming. Evidence: Source A shows New England's rocky land, forests and harbors; Source B shows its main businesses were shipbuilding, fishing and trade; Source C shows Virginia's warm climate supported tobacco fields. Reasoning: Rocky soil made big farms hard in New England, but forests and harbors made shipbuilding and trade easy. Virginia's warm, long season made growing cash crops profitable.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 4: Colonial Life, Cooperation and Conflict (5.3, 5.4)
units.el: Use a cause-and-effect organizer for the French and Indian War and a T-chart for cooperation and conflict. Pre-teach assembly, town meeting, mercantilism, revival, enslaved, rebellion, alliance and proclamation.

lessons.name: Self-government and the colonial economy

practice.q: In a New England town meeting,
ch: local men gathered to discuss and vote on town matters
the king chose the town's leaders
practice.h: Think of neighbors meeting in one room to decide together.

practice.q: Most colonies had an elected assembly. What did these assemblies do?
ch: made local laws and decided on colonial taxes
practice.h: Colonists elected representatives to make decisions for the colony.

practice.q: Under mercantilism, colonies existed mainly to
ch: send raw materials to England and buy English goods
make all of their own products
practice.h: The home country wanted to grow rich from its colonies.

practice.q: The Navigation Acts required colonists to ship many goods only on English ships to English ports. Why did England pass them?
ch: so England would earn the profits from colonial trade
to help the colonists trade with Spain
practice.h: Under mercantilism, who should benefit most from trade?

practice.q: In 1735, a jury in New York found printer John Peter Zenger not guilty after he printed articles criticizing the governor. This case helped establish
ch: the right to a free education

practice.q: Explain how English colonists gained experience in self-government before the American Revolution.
practice.ans: They elected assemblies like the House of Burgesses, held town meetings, wrote agreements like the Mayflower Compact and made many local laws, because England was far away.

quiz.q: Only some colonists could vote in colonial elections. Who usually could vote?
How were English colonies governed differently from Spanish colonies?
ch: English colonists elected assemblies, while Spanish colonies were ruled by officials chosen by the king.
Spanish colonists elected all their leaders.

quiz.q: Why did the French colonies in North America have fewer settlers than the English colonies?
ch: Most French colonists came to trade furs rather than to farm and build towns.

quiz.q: A colonial merchant buys molasses from the French West Indies to avoid English rules and taxes. What is this called?
Why did many colonists come to value buying, selling and owning their own land and businesses?
ch: They had chances to own land and trade, which helped build a free-market economy.
They were not allowed to trade.
Land was given only to soldiers.

quiz.q: A colonial assembly had 64 members. A law needed a majority to pass. What is the smallest number of votes needed?
Compare a New England town meeting with a colonial assembly.
quiz.ans: Both let colonists make decisions. A town meeting was local, where townsmen voted directly; an assembly was colony-wide, where elected representatives made laws.

lessons.name: Religion and the Great Awakening

practice.q: The First Great Awakening was
ch: a religious revival that spread through the colonies in the 1730s and 1740s
practice.h: "Awakening" suggests people's faith being stirred up.

practice.q: George Whitefield, a preacher from England, drew huge crowds during the Great Awakening by
ch: preaching outdoors with powerful, emotional sermons
practice.h: Many churches were too small for his crowds.

practice.q: Jonathan Edwards was a leader of the Great Awakening who preached in
practice.h: He lived in New England.

practice.q: The Great Awakening encouraged people to think they could decide on their own faith instead of following church leaders. How did this later affect colonists?
ch: It helped them question authority, including the king.
It made them obey the king more.
practice.h: If you can question church leaders, whom else might you question?

practice.q: Which group came to Pennsylvania from Germany seeking religious freedom?
ch: many German Protestant groups, such as the Mennonites

practice.q: Explain why the colonies had so many different religions by the 1700s.
practice.ans: People from many countries came seeking religious freedom, and colonies like Rhode Island, Pennsylvania and Maryland allowed different faiths.

quiz.q: Which colony had Quakerism as the faith of its founder?
The official church of Virginia was the
During the Great Awakening, some new churches welcomed enslaved and free African Americans. What was one result?
ch: Many African Americans joined Christian churches and later formed their own congregations.
African Americans were banned from churches.

quiz.q: How did the Great Awakening help unite the colonies?
ch: Preachers traveled across colonies, giving people a shared experience.
It made each colony stay separate.

quiz.q: Several colleges were founded during this time to train ministers. Which college is one example?
George Whitefield preached to a crowd of about 20,000 people in Boston in 1740. If 4,000 of them were children, how many were adults?
Explain how the Great Awakening may have helped prepare colonists for the American Revolution.
quiz.ans: It taught people that ordinary people could decide for themselves and question powerful leaders, and it connected people across the colonies. These ideas later helped colonists challenge the king.

lessons.name: Slavery in the colonies

practice.q: Slavery in the English colonies began after enslaved Africans arrived in Virginia in
practice.h: It was the same year the House of Burgesses first met.

practice.q: Slave codes were
ch: laws that controlled enslaved people and took away their rights
practice.h: "Code" here means a set of laws.

practice.q: Where did slavery become most widespread in the colonies?
ch: in the Spanish missions of California
practice.h: Which region grew cash crops on huge farms?

practice.q: Enslaved families kept their cultures alive by
ch: sharing songs, stories, foods and traditions from Africa
practice.h: Think about what families pass down to children.

practice.q: In 1688, Quakers in Germantown, Pennsylvania, wrote one of the first protests against slavery. What was their main argument?
ch: People should treat others the way they want to be treated.
Slaves should be paid more by the king.

practice.q: Describe two ways enslaved Africans resisted slavery.
practice.ans: Running away, working slowly, breaking tools, learning to read in secret, keeping African traditions, and armed rebellions such as the Stono Rebellion.

quiz.q: The Stono Rebellion was an uprising of enslaved people in South Carolina in
After the Stono Rebellion, South Carolina passed stricter slave codes. What does this show?
ch: Slaveholders feared more revolts and tried to control enslaved people even more.

quiz.q: Over time, slavery became tied to race in the colonies. What does this mean?
ch: Laws made enslavement a lifelong condition for Africans and their children.
Anyone could be enslaved for a short time.

quiz.q: Some enslaved people in South Carolina and Georgia kept a language and culture with strong African roots, called
Why did people who opposed slavery have a hard time ending it in the colonies?
ch: Slavery made many powerful planters and merchants rich.
Everyone in the colonies opposed it.
England had already banned it everywhere.

quiz.q: In 1750, South Carolina had about 64,000 people, and about 39,000 were enslaved. About how many people were not enslaved?
Explain why slavery became so important to the economy of the Southern Colonies.
quiz.ans: Plantation crops like tobacco, rice and indigo required many workers. Planters used enslaved Africans, whom they did not pay, to grow these crops and grow rich.

lessons.name: Cooperation and conflict with American Indians

practice.q: French traders and many American Indian nations cooperated mainly through the
practice.h: Beaver pelts were in great demand in Europe.

practice.q: King Philip's War (1675-1676) was a conflict in New England led by the Wampanoag leader
ch: Metacom, called King Philip by the English
practice.h: His father was Massasoit, who had made peace with the Pilgrims.

practice.q: Why did conflicts often break out between colonists and American Indian nations?
ch: Colonists kept taking more land for farms and settlements.
American Indians wanted to move to Europe.
They had nothing in common to fight over.
practice.h: Think about what colonists needed for their growing farms and towns.

practice.q: The French and Indian War (1754-1763) was fought between
ch: Great Britain and France, along with their American Indian allies
practice.h: Its name in America comes from Britain's enemies in the war.

practice.q: The French and Indian War began in 1754 and ended in 1763. How many years did it last?
Give one example of cooperation and one example of conflict between colonists and American Indians.
practice.ans: Cooperation: the Wampanoag helped the Pilgrims and the French traded furs with many nations. Conflict: the Pequot War, King Philip's War or the Powhatan wars over land.

quiz.q: The treaty that ended the French and Indian War in 1763 gave Britain control of
ch: Canada and the land east of the Mississippi River

quiz.q: In 1754, Benjamin Franklin printed a cartoon of a snake cut into pieces with the words "Join, or Die." What was his message?
ch: The colonies must unite to defend themselves.

quiz.q: After the war, the Ottawa leader Pontiac led many nations in attacks on British forts in 1763. Why?
ch: British settlers and soldiers were moving onto their lands and treating them poorly.
They wanted to help the British.
They had been paid by Spain.

quiz.q: Britain's Proclamation of 1763 said colonists could not settle west of the Appalachian Mountains. How did many colonists feel?
ch: angry, because they wanted the western land

quiz.q: The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) mostly sided with which country during the French and Indian War?
Britain's national debt was about 72 million pounds in 1755 and about 130 million pounds in 1763. By about how many million pounds did the debt grow?

Source C: A colonist's letter from 1764 complains, "We fought for that land, and now the king keeps us from it." quiz.ans: Claim: Winning the war made colonists angry at Britain, even though they were on the winning side. Evidence: Source A shows Britain won land to the Mississippi; Source B shows the Proclamation banned colonists from settling west of the Appalachians; Source C shows a colonist felt cheated after fighting for that land. Reasoning: Colonists expected to gain land as a reward, so when the king blocked them, they felt their interests were ignored, which hurt their loyalty to Britain.

The French and Indian War ended in

ch: gathered to discuss and vote on local issues

test.q: Which idea describes mercantilism?
ch: Colonies exist to make the home country richer.
Colonies should trade freely with all countries.
Colonies should rule the home country.

test.q: The Zenger trial of 1735 is remembered for supporting
ch: the right to vote for women

test.q: Which was a major effect of the Great Awakening?
ch: People felt freer to question authority and new churches formed.
The colonies broke into separate countries.

test.q: Which colonial region depended most on the labor of enslaved Africans?
The Stono Rebellion in 1739 was
ch: an uprising of enslaved people in South Carolina
a battle of the French and Indian War
a protest against taxes on tea

test.q: Who led the Wampanoag and other nations in King Philip's War?
The French built better relations than the English with many American Indian nations because the French
ch: mostly traded furs and did not take as much land for farms

test.q: What did Benjamin Franklin's "Join, or Die" cartoon (1754) urge the colonies to do?
The Proclamation of 1763
ch: banned colonists from settling west of the Appalachian Mountains

test.q: Slavery began in Virginia in 1619. The Stono Rebellion happened in 1739. How many years apart are these events?
King Philip's War lasted from 1675 to 1676 and the French and Indian War from 1754 to 1763. How many years after King Philip's War ended did the French and Indian War begin?
A fur trader brought 300 beaver pelts to Quebec. He traded 120 for cloth and 95 for metal tools. How many pelts did he have left?
Which is the best explanation of why Pontiac's War started in 1763?
ch: American Indian nations resisted British soldiers and settlers moving onto their land after France lost the war.
The French wanted more land in Europe.
The war was about tea taxes.

test.q: Britain won the French and Indian War but had a huge debt. What was the most likely next step?
ch: Britain looked for ways to tax the colonies to help pay it.
Britain gave money to the colonies.
Britain gave the land back to France.

test.q: The Germantown Quakers in 1688 and enslaved people in the Stono Rebellion in 1739 both
ch: were part of the French and Indian War

test.q: Which group sided mostly with the British in the French and Indian War?
Describe how colonists practiced self-government in the 1700s.
test.ans: They elected colonial assemblies, held town meetings, served on juries and debated issues in newspapers, making many of their own local laws.

test.q: Explain two effects of the French and Indian War on the colonies.
test.ans: Britain gained land to the Mississippi but went deep into debt; it then banned settlement west of the Appalachians and taxed the colonies, which angered colonists.

test.q: Read the sources. Source A: A chart shows that by 1750, enslaved Africans made up about 60 percent of South Carolina's population. Source B: South Carolina's slave code of 1740, passed after the Stono Rebellion, made it illegal to teach enslaved people to write. Source C: A historian writes that enslaved people resisted by running away, slowing work and keeping their own traditions. test.ans: Claim: Enslaved people resisted slavery, and slaveholders, fearing them, passed harsher laws to keep control. Evidence: Source A shows enslaved people were the majority in South Carolina; Source B shows the 1740 slave code came right after the Stono Rebellion and banned teaching them to write; Source C shows many forms of resistance. Reasoning: Because enslaved people outnumbered colonists and fought back, slaveholders feared revolts and used stricter laws to control them, which shows resistance and repression shaped each other.

units.name: Unit 5: The Road to Revolution (5.5)
units.el: Build a wall timeline from 1763 to 1776 with an icon for each act and protest. Pre-teach tax, repeal, boycott, protest, representation, Patriot, Loyalist, grievance and independence, and give the frame "Because Britain ___, the colonists ___."

lessons.name: New taxes and colonial protests

practice.q: The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed
ch: newspapers, legal papers and other printed items
practice.h: Each paper needed an official stamp showing the tax was paid.

practice.q: Colonists protested with the slogan "No taxation without representation." What did they mean?
ch: Parliament should not tax them because they had no elected members in it.
They wanted to pay taxes only to France.
They did not want any government at all.
practice.h: Did the colonists elect anyone to Parliament?

practice.q: Britain said the colonists should help pay for the French and Indian War and for soldiers protecting them. This was
ch: the British point of view about the new taxes
the American Indian point of view

practice.q: A boycott is
ch: refusing to buy certain goods to protest
practice.h: Colonists stopped buying British goods to put pressure on merchants.

practice.q: The Daughters of Liberty helped the boycotts by
ch: spinning their own cloth instead of buying British cloth
practice.h: If you refuse to buy British cloth, how do you get clothes?

practice.q: Explain why Britain began taxing the colonies after 1763.
practice.ans: Britain had a large debt from the French and Indian War and needed money to pay for soldiers in America, so Parliament decided the colonists should help pay.

quiz.q: The Stamp Act was repealed, or canceled, in
The Townshend Acts of 1767 taxed goods colonists imported from Britain, such as
On March 5, 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston and killed five colonists. This event is called the
Crispus Attucks, one of the people killed in the Boston Massacre, was
ch: a sailor of African and American Indian ancestry

quiz.q: Paul Revere's engraving of the Boston Massacre showed British soldiers firing at peaceful colonists. Why do historians call it propaganda?
ch: It was made to stir up anger and did not show events fairly.
It was painted by the British.

quiz.q: The Stamp Act was passed in 1765 and the Boston Massacre happened in 1770. How many years apart are these events?
John Adams, a Patriot, defended the British soldiers in court after the Boston Massacre. Why might he have done this, and what does it show about him?
quiz.ans: He believed everyone deserves a fair trial, even enemies. It shows he valued the rule of law above popularity.

lessons.name: The crisis grows

practice.q: On December 16, 1773, colonists dressed as Mohawk Indians dumped British tea into Boston Harbor. This was the
practice.h: The event is named after the drink.

practice.q: At the Boston Tea Party, colonists dumped 342 chests of tea from 3 ships. If each ship carried the same number of chests, how many chests came from each ship?
practice.h: Divide the total chests by the number of ships.

practice.q: Parliament punished Boston in 1774 by closing its harbor and limiting town meetings. Colonists called these laws the
practice.h: Colonists thought these laws were too harsh to tolerate.

practice.q: Committees of Correspondence, started in Boston in 1772,
ch: shared news and plans among towns and colonies by letter

practice.q: The First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in 1774 to
ch: decide how the colonies should respond to the Intolerable Acts
practice.h: The Intolerable Acts had just been passed that year.

practice.q: Explain why the Intolerable Acts made other colonies support Massachusetts.
practice.ans: Colonists feared Britain could take away their rights and self-government too, so they sent supplies to Boston and united against the acts.

quiz.q: The first battles of the American Revolution were fought at Lexington and Concord on
Why did British soldiers march to Concord in 1775?
ch: to seize colonial weapons and gunpowder

quiz.q: The Second Continental Congress met in 1775 and chose whom to lead the Continental Army?
In July 1775, Congress sent the Olive Branch Petition to King George III. What did it ask for?
ch: peace and a fair solution while staying loyal to the king

quiz.q: Which list of events is in the correct order?
ch: Stamp Act, Boston Massacre, Boston Tea Party, Lexington and Concord
Boston Tea Party, Stamp Act, Lexington and Concord, Boston Massacre
Lexington and Concord, Stamp Act, Boston Tea Party, Boston Massacre
Boston Massacre, Stamp Act, Lexington and Concord, Boston Tea Party

quiz.q: The Boston Tea Party took place in 1773 and the battles of Lexington and Concord in 1775. How many years apart?
Compare how a Patriot and a Loyalist in Boston might have viewed the Boston Tea Party.
quiz.ans: A Patriot saw it as a brave protest against unfair taxes; a Loyalist saw it as lawless destruction of property that disrespected the king.

lessons.name: Declaring independence

practice.q: In January 1776, Thomas Paine published a pamphlet that urged independence, called
practice.h: Paine argued that independence was simply sensible.

practice.q: Thomas Paine wrote in Common Sense (1776): "There is something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island." What was his argument?
ch: It made no sense for small, faraway Britain to rule all of America forever.
practice.h: Which is the continent and which is the island?

practice.q: The main writer of the Declaration of Independence was
The Declaration of Independence was adopted by the Continental Congress on
practice.h: Americans celebrate this date every summer.

practice.q: The Declaration says governments get "their just powers from the consent of the governed." What does this mean?
ch: A government's power should come from the people's agreement.
Kings get their power from God alone.
People must always obey the government.
practice.h: "Consent" means permission or agreement.

practice.q: Name the three parts of the Declaration of Independence and tell what each does.
practice.ans: A statement of beliefs about rights and government; a list of complaints (grievances) against the king; and a declaration that the colonies are free and independent states.

quiz.q: The Declaration says that all people have "unalienable Rights" including "Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness." Unalienable rights are rights that
Many ideas in the Declaration, such as natural rights, came from the English writer
Why did the Declaration include a long list of complaints against King George III?
ch: to show the world the reasons the colonies were breaking away

quiz.q: The Declaration said "all men are created equal," yet many signers enslaved people. What does this show?
ch: The nation's ideals were not yet applied to everyone.
The signers did not mean anything by the words.

quiz.q: Signing the Declaration was dangerous for the 56 signers because
ch: Britain could treat them as traitors and execute them
they had to pay a tax
they would lose their jobs in Congress
it was illegal to write in ink

quiz.q: The Declaration of Independence was signed in 1776. How many years later was its 200th anniversary? Give the year.
Explain how the Declaration of Independence broke ties with Great Britain and set out new ideas about government.
quiz.ans: It declared the colonies free and independent states, no longer loyal to the king. It said people have natural rights and that governments get their power from the people, who can change a government that abuses those rights.

lessons.name: Patriots, Loyalists and leaders

practice.q: Colonists who supported independence were called
practice.h: They loved their country, America.

practice.q: Colonists who stayed loyal to the king were called
practice.h: The answer comes from the word "loyal."

practice.q: Patrick Henry told the Virginia convention in 1775, "Give me liberty, or give me death!" What did he mean?
ch: Freedom was worth risking his life for.
He wanted to stay loyal to the king.
practice.h: Which did he value more, freedom or safety?

practice.q: King George III believed the colonists
ch: should obey Parliament and pay their share of taxes
practice.h: He was the ruler of Great Britain.

practice.q: Why did many enslaved African Americans join the British side when Lord Dunmore offered freedom in 1775?
ch: The British promised freedom to those who escaped Patriot owners and fought for Britain.
They wanted to pay British taxes.

practice.q: Explain why some colonists became Loyalists.
practice.ans: Some were government officials or merchants who depended on trade with Britain, some felt loyalty to the king, and some feared war and disorder.

quiz.q: Benjamin Franklin was a printer, scientist and leader who
ch: helped edit the Declaration of Independence

quiz.q: Samuel Adams of Boston is best known for
ch: organizing protests and the Sons of Liberty

quiz.q: About how were colonists divided during the Revolution?
ch: Many were Patriots, many were Loyalists, and many stayed neutral.

quiz.q: Many American Indian nations sided with Britain. What was one reason?
ch: Britain had tried to limit colonial settlement on their lands with the Proclamation of 1763.
They wanted colonists to take more land.
Britain paid no attention to them.
They had always lived in Britain.

quiz.q: John Adams worked in the Continental Congress to
ch: push for independence and help draft the Declaration
keep the colonies under the king

quiz.q: Patrick Henry was born in May 1736. He gave his "liberty or death" speech in March 1775, before his birthday that year. How old was he when he gave the speech?
Compare the views of King George III and Patrick Henry about the colonies.
quiz.ans: King George believed the colonies must obey British laws and pay taxes; Patrick Henry believed the colonists' rights were being violated and that liberty was worth fighting for.

test.q: Which document announced that the thirteen colonies were free and independent states?
The slogan "No taxation without representation" protested
ch: taxes passed by Parliament, where colonists had no elected members

test.q: Colonists who wanted to stay part of Great Britain were called
Why did Parliament pass the Stamp Act?
ch: to raise money to pay war debts and the cost of soldiers in America
to punish Boston for the Tea Party

test.q: What happened at the Boston Tea Party?
ch: Colonists dumped British tea into Boston Harbor to protest a tax.
British soldiers fired on a crowd.
Colonists and British soldiers held a peace meeting.

test.q: How did Britain respond to the Boston Tea Party?
ch: It passed the Intolerable Acts and closed Boston Harbor.

test.q: The Committees of Correspondence helped the colonies by
The first shots of the Revolutionary War were fired at
Which statement best describes Common Sense?
ch: a 1776 pamphlet by Thomas Paine arguing for independence
a speech by King George III

test.q: Which idea from the Declaration of Independence came from John Locke?
ch: People have natural rights to life and liberty.
Kings rule by God's will alone.
Colonies exist to help the home country.
Only men with land have rights.

test.q: Which was the First Continental Congress's main purpose in 1774?
ch: to respond together to the Intolerable Acts

test.q: Who said "Give me liberty, or give me death!" in a 1775 speech?
The Stamp Act was passed in 1765 and the Declaration of Independence in 1776. How many years apart are these events?
The Declaration was signed by 56 delegates. If 8 of them were born outside the colonies, how many were born in the colonies?
The French and Indian War ended in 1763. The fighting at Lexington began in 1775. How many years apart are these events?
Which is the best cause-and-effect chain?
ch: Britain taxes the colonies, colonists protest, Britain punishes Boston, fighting begins.
Fighting begins, Britain taxes the colonies, colonists protest.
Colonists declare independence, then the Stamp Act is passed.
Britain repeals all taxes, then colonists dump tea.

test.q: A British official says the colonists are ungrateful because Britain protected them in the war. A Patriot says Britain is taking away colonists' rights. What is the best conclusion?
ch: Each side saw the taxes differently because of its own interests and beliefs.

test.q: Why did the Declaration of Independence list the king's actions instead of Parliament's?
ch: It was breaking ties with the king and wanted to show why loyalty to him had ended.
The king had written the taxes himself.

test.q: Who was chosen to lead the Continental Army in 1775?
Explain two ways colonists resisted British taxes before 1775.
test.ans: They boycotted British goods, held the Stamp Act Congress, formed the Sons and Daughters of Liberty, wrote petitions and pamphlets, and protested with actions like the Boston Tea Party.

test.q: Describe the main ideas of the Declaration of Independence.
test.ans: All people are created equal and have unalienable rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness; governments get power from the consent of the governed; and people may change a government that takes away their rights.

units.name: Unit 6: The American Revolution (5.6)
units.el: Mark the major battles on a map of the colonies with dates, and keep a chart of helpers (person or country, what they gave). Pre-teach turning point, surrender, ally, inflation, treaty, ordinance and territory.

lessons.name: Battles and turning points

practice.q: The British army at the start of the war was
ch: larger, better trained and better supplied than the Continental Army
practice.h: Britain had one of the strongest armies and navies in the world.

practice.q: On the night of December 25, 1776, George Washington led his troops across the Delaware River and won a surprise victory at
practice.h: The battle was in New Jersey the morning after Christmas.

practice.q: Thomas Paine wrote in The American Crisis (December 1776): "These are the times that try men's souls." Why did he write this?
ch: to encourage discouraged soldiers and Patriots to keep fighting

practice.q: The American victory at Saratoga in 1777 is called a turning point because
ch: it convinced France to join the war on the American side
practice.h: Think about what happened in 1778 because of this win.

practice.q: The Continental Army camped at Valley Forge in the winter of 1777-1778. About 12,000 soldiers arrived, and about 2,000 died of disease, cold and hunger. About how many survived?
practice.h: Subtract the soldiers who died from those who arrived.

practice.q: Name two advantages the Patriots had in the war, even though the British army was stronger.
practice.ans: They fought on familiar land, defended their homes, had a strong leader in George Washington, used hit-and-run tactics, and later had help from France. Britain had to send troops and supplies across an ocean.

quiz.q: The last major battle of the Revolution, where British General Cornwallis surrendered in 1781, was at
Why did French ships at Yorktown help win the battle?
ch: They blocked British ships from rescuing or supplying Cornwallis's army.
They brought tea to the British.
They sailed away before the battle.
They carried the Declaration to France.

quiz.q: The Mohawk leader Joseph Brant fought on the British side. Why did many American Indian nations side with Britain?
ch: They hoped Britain would stop colonists from taking their land.
They wanted to move to England.

quiz.q: The Oneida nation of the Haudenosaunee sided with the Patriots. What does this show?
ch: American Indian nations made different choices, and the war divided the Haudenosaunee Confederacy.
All American Indians sided with Britain.

quiz.q: The Treaty of Paris (1783) set the western border of the United States at the
The war began at Lexington in 1775 and the Treaty of Paris was signed in 1783. How many years passed between these events?
Explain why Valley Forge was important to the Continental Army even though no battle was fought there.
quiz.ans: Soldiers suffered through cold, hunger and disease but did not give up. Baron von Steuben trained them there, and the army came out better organized and more disciplined.

lessons.name: Help from other nations and individuals

practice.q: Benjamin Franklin went to France during the war to
ch: win French money, supplies and an alliance
practice.h: He was a famous and well-liked American in Paris.

practice.q: The Marquis de Lafayette was
ch: a young French nobleman who became a general in the Continental Army
practice.h: He volunteered and became a close friend of Washington.

practice.q: Baron Friedrich von Steuben came from Prussia and helped the Continental Army by

units.name: Unit 7: Creating the Constitution (5.7)

quiz.q: The Indian Removal Act was passed in 1830, and the Trail of Tears began in 1838. How many years apart?

Source B: The Indian Removal Act (1830) gave the President power to move eastern nations west of the Mississippi. Source C: About 4,000 of the 16,000 Cherokee forced west in 1838-1839 died on the way. Make a claim about whether the U.S. government kept its promises to American Indian nations. Use evidence and reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: The U.S. government broke its promises to American Indian nations. Evidence: Source A shows the government promised not to take land without consent; Source B shows it later passed a law to move nations off their land; Source C shows about one in four Cherokee died during forced removal. Reasoning: Forcing people from their homeland without their consent went against the government's own promise, and the deaths show how much harm the broken promise caused.

test.q: Explain two reasons Americans moved west between 1790 and 1850.
test.ans: To find cheap, fertile farmland; to find new opportunities and jobs; for religious freedom, like the Latter-day Saints; and, by 1849, for gold in California. New roads, canals and steamboats made travel easier.

test.ans: They lost their homelands through war, broken treaties and forced removal like the Trail of Tears; many died, and their ways of life were disrupted as settlers moved in.

test.ans: Claim: The United States grew to the Pacific through purchase, treaties and war, driven by the belief in Manifest Destiny. soc|6.about: Sixth graders study the ancient world, from the first humans to the fall of Rome: how people began farming, and how the civilizations of Mesopotamia, Egypt and Kush, ancient Israel, Greece, India, China and Rome developed their governments, economies, beliefs and ideas. Students read maps, timelines and primary sources, explain cause and effect, compare perspectives and write claims supported by evidence.
std: Students describe what is known through archaeological studies of the early physical and cultural development of humankind from the Paleolithic era to the agricultural revolution.
Students analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the early civilizations of Mesopotamia, Egypt and Kush.
Students analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the Ancient Hebrews.
Students analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the early civilizations of Ancient Greece.
Students analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the early civilizations of India.
Students analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the early civilizations of China.
Students analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures during the development of Rome.
Students explain the central issues and problems from the past, placing people and events in a matter of time and place, and use evidence from primary and secondary sources.

units.name: Unit 1: Early Humans and the Agricultural Revolution (6.1)

lessons.name: How we learn about early humans

practice.q: A scientist who studies the past by digging up and studying objects people left behind is called an
practice.h: Think about who would study old tools, bones and campfires.

practice.q: An object made by people, such as a stone tool or a clay pot, is called an
practice.h: The word comes from "art" (skill) and "fact" (made).

practice.q: Archaeologists find stone blades, animal bones with cut marks and ash from a fire pit in a cave. What is the best conclusion?
ch: People once used the cave to make tools, cut meat and cook
The cave was used as a farm
People built a city inside the cave
practice.h: Each object is a clue. What were people doing with blades, bones and fire?

practice.q: A timeline shows that the Paleolithic (Old Stone Age) ended about 10,000 BCE and the first cities in Mesopotamia appeared about 3500 BCE. About how many years passed between these two dates?
practice.h: Both dates are BCE, so subtract the smaller number from the larger number.

practice.q: Which is a primary source about early humans?
ch: cave paintings made by people about 17,000 years ago
a textbook chapter written last year
a museum website about cave art
a documentary film about the Stone Age
practice.h: A primary source was made by people at the time being studied.

practice.q: Explain why archaeologists must be careful to record exactly where each artifact was found before removing it.
practice.ans: The location and layer tell when the object was used and what it was used with. Once an artifact is moved, that information is lost, so recording it helps scientists understand how people lived.
practice.h: What could the position of an object tell you that the object alone cannot?

quiz.q: The Paleolithic era is also called the
The remains of a plant or animal preserved in rock are called a
In a dig, the deepest layers of soil are usually the oldest. A spear point is found 2 meters down and a clay pot is found 1 meter down. What can you conclude?
ch: The spear point is probably older than the pot
The pot is probably older than the spear point
They were made on the same day

quiz.q: Why do historians know less about the Paleolithic era than about later civilizations?
ch: Paleolithic people left no written records
Paleolithic people did not make anything
No Paleolithic sites have been found
Paleolithic people lived only in Europe

quiz.q: A cave painting is about 17,000 years old. A clay figure from another site is about 26,000 years old. How many years older is the clay figure?
Which question could an archaeologist answer best by studying the bones of animals found at a campsite?
ch: What animals did these people hunt and eat?
What language did these people speak?
What names did they give their children?

quiz.q: An archaeologist finds seashells at a campsite 300 kilometers from the ocean. Which explanation is best supported?
ch: People traveled to the coast or traded with people who lived there
The ocean once covered the campsite last year
The shells grew in the cave
The shells prove the people were farmers

quiz.q: Name two kinds of evidence archaeologists use to learn about early humans and tell what each can reveal.
quiz.ans: Tools show what jobs people did and how skilled they were; bones show what people ate and how healthy they were; cave paintings show what animals and activities mattered to them.

lessons.name: Hunter-gatherers and the use of fire and tools

practice.q: Paleolithic people who moved from place to place to hunt animals and gather plants are called
practice.h: These people did not live in one place all year.

practice.q: Why did hunter-gatherers usually live in small groups?
ch: A small area could only feed a few people with wild food
They did not like large families
They had too many crops to share
practice.h: Think about how much wild food one area can provide.

practice.q: Which was the most important result of learning to control fire?
ch: People could cook food, stay warm and live in colder places
practice.h: Think of three ways fire helps people survive.

practice.q: Why did hunter-gatherer groups often move with the seasons?
ch: They followed animal herds and ripening plants
They had to pay taxes in different places
They were escaping floods every week

practice.q: A group of hunter-gatherers walks 12 kilometers a day for 5 days to reach a winter camp. How many kilometers do they travel?
practice.h: Multiply the distance each day by the number of days.

practice.q: Describe how men and women in a hunter-gatherer group may have divided work, and explain why sharing work helped the group survive.
practice.ans: Many groups divided tasks such as hunting large animals, gathering plants, making tools, caring for children and preparing food. Dividing work let the group do many jobs at once, so everyone was fed and protected.
practice.h: List jobs a group needed done every day.

quiz.q: Early humans made their first tools mostly from
Early humans began moving out of Africa and over many thousands of years settled
How did the development of language help early humans?
ch: They could plan hunts and pass knowledge to children

quiz.q: Which tool would most help a hunter-gatherer prepare an animal skin for clothing?
A map scale shows 1 centimeter = 50 kilometers. Two Paleolithic campsites are 7 centimeters apart on the map. How many kilometers apart are they?
Paleolithic people living in a cold region and people living in a warm region probably differed most in
ch: the clothing and shelter they used

quiz.q: A hunting group of 25 people shares 5 deer equally. How many people share each deer?
Explain how the control of fire changed both the food and the daily life of early humans.
quiz.ans: Cooking made meat and plants easier to chew and digest and safer to eat. Fire also gave warmth and light, kept animals away and gave people a place to gather at night.

lessons.name: The Agricultural Revolution

practice.q: The change from hunting and gathering to farming and herding is called the
practice.h: Neolithic means New Stone Age, when farming began.

practice.q: Taming plants and animals so they can be raised by people is called
practice.h: Think of the word "domestic," which means having to do with the home.

practice.q: Farming first began more than 10,000 years ago in
ch: the Fertile Crescent of Southwest Asia
practice.h: Look for a region of river valleys between Egypt and Mesopotamia.

practice.q: What did farming allow people to do that hunting and gathering did not?
ch: Stay in one place and build permanent villages
practice.h: Farmers have to tend their fields all season.

practice.q: A Neolithic village grew from 150 people to 600 people. How many times larger was the village?
practice.h: Divide the new number by the old number.

practice.q: Explain why many historians call the beginning of farming a "revolution."
practice.ans: It changed nearly every part of life. People settled down, populations grew, villages formed, and people began to own land, store food and do new kinds of work.
practice.h: A revolution is a very big change. What changed?

quiz.q: Which crops were among the first domesticated in the Fertile Crescent?
Farming developed independently in several places, including Mesoamerica. Which crop was domesticated there?
Which was a disadvantage of early farming compared with hunting and gathering?
ch: A drought or crop failure could cause hunger for the whole village

quiz.q: Why did a food surplus lead to new jobs such as potter, weaver and toolmaker?
ch: Not everyone had to grow food, so some people could specialize
Everyone had to farm all day

quiz.q: Catalhoyuk, in present-day Turkey, was an early farming town. Archaeologists found houses packed closely together with storage rooms. What does this suggest?
ch: Many people lived there year-round and stored food

quiz.q: A farming family harvests 900 kilograms of grain. They eat 600 kilograms in a year and trade the rest. How many kilograms do they trade?
The first farming villages appeared about 8000 BCE in the Fertile Crescent. The first cities of Sumer appeared about 3500 BCE. How many years passed between these dates?

Read the evidence. Source A: Hunter-gatherer campsites have hearths, stone tools and bones of wild animals, and most were used for only part of the year. Source B: Neolithic sites have houses of mud brick, grinding stones for grain, bones of sheep and goats, and grain storage pits. Make a claim about how farming changed the way people lived. Use evidence from both sources and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: Farming caused people to settle in permanent homes and depend on food they raised. Evidence: Source A shows seasonal camps and wild animals, while Source B shows mud-brick houses, grinding stones, storage pits and domesticated sheep and goats. Reasoning: Permanent houses and storage pits show people stayed in one place all year, and domesticated animals and grain show they produced their own food instead of following wild food.
