lessons.name: From villages to the first civilizations

practice.q: A complex society with cities, a government, specialized jobs, social classes and a system of writing is called a
practice.h: These are the features historians use to describe the first great societies.

practice.q: Why did the first civilizations develop in river valleys?
ch: Rivers provided water and fertile soil for growing extra food
Rivers protected people from all enemies
Mountains in river valleys made farming easy
practice.h: What do farmers need most?

practice.q: Which list shows the correct order of events?
ch: domesticating plants, building villages, growing cities
growing cities, building villages, domesticating plants
building villages, growing cities, domesticating plants
growing cities, domesticating plants, building villages
practice.h: People had to settle down before villages could grow into cities.

practice.q: Which job would be found in an early city but NOT in a hunter-gatherer band?
ch: a scribe who kept written records
a person who made stone tools
a person who cared for children
practice.h: Which job depends on writing?

practice.q: A city wall is 6 kilometers long. Workers can build 300 meters of wall each month. How many months will it take? (1 kilometer = 1,000 meters)
practice.h: First change kilometers to meters.

practice.q: Explain how a food surplus led to the growth of social classes.
practice.ans: With extra food, some people became priests, rulers, merchants or craftspeople instead of farmers. People who controlled land, food or trade gained more wealth and power, creating classes.
practice.h: Who controls the extra food?

quiz.q: Four of the earliest river valley civilizations grew along the Tigris and Euphrates, the Nile, the Indus and the
Why did early cities need governments?
ch: to organize irrigation, settle disputes and defend the city

quiz.q: How did the invention of writing help early civilizations?
ch: Rulers and merchants could keep records of taxes, laws and trade
People no longer needed to farm
It ended the need for government

quiz.q: A timeline: 10,000 BCE farming begins; 7000 BCE early villages grow; 3500 BCE first cities in Sumer; 3200 BCE writing appears. Which statement is supported by the timeline?
ch: Writing appeared after the first cities

quiz.q: Using the timeline (farming begins 10,000 BCE, writing appears 3200 BCE), how many years passed between the beginning of farming and the beginning of writing?
Which development would most likely come LAST in a society moving from hunting and gathering to civilization?
ch: a written law code for a large city

quiz.q: An early city had about 40,000 people. If one farmer could grow enough food for 4 people, how many farmers were needed to feed the whole city?
Choose two features of civilization and explain how one feature made the other possible.
quiz.ans: A food surplus made specialized jobs possible: because farmers grew extra food, some people could become scribes, priests or artisans instead of farming.

test.q: The Old Stone Age, when people lived as hunter-gatherers and made stone tools, is called the
Which describes nomads?
ch: people who move from place to place in search of food

test.q: Domestication means
ch: taming plants and animals for human use

test.q: The region of Southwest Asia where farming first began is called the
Which evidence would best show that people at a site were farmers?
ch: grinding stones and storage pits for grain
spear points and wild deer bones

test.q: Which statement about hunter-gatherers is accurate?
ch: They lived in small groups and moved to follow food sources
They lived in large cities with walls

test.q: What was one major effect of farming on population?
ch: Populations grew because food supplies were more dependable

test.q: Why is a cave painting a useful source for historians?
ch: It shows what early people saw and valued, made by people at the time
It was written in an alphabet
It lists the names of rulers
It is a secondary source written by experts

test.q: Which development came first?
Which feature is NOT required for a civilization?

ch: Rivers gave water for crops and animals
Rivers were dry most of the year
River land was too rocky to farm

test.q: Farming began about 10,000 BCE. The first cities appeared about 3500 BCE. How many years after farming began did the first cities appear?
A map has a scale of 1 centimeter = 20 kilometers. A trade route between two Neolithic villages measures 9 centimeters. How many kilometers long is the route?
A village of 240 people has 60 houses with the same number of people in each. How many people live in each house?
An archaeologist finds obsidian (a volcanic glass) tools in a village with no volcanoes nearby. What is the best conclusion?
ch: The villagers traded with people from another region
The villagers made the obsidian themselves from sand
The tools were left by modern hikers

test.q: Which change best explains why social classes developed after farming began?
ch: Some people controlled more land and food than others
Everyone had exactly the same amount of food

test.q: A historian says, "Farming was not all good for early people." Which evidence best supports this view?
ch: Skeletons from early farming villages show more tooth decay and signs of hunger during droughts

test.q: Which pair shows a correct cause and effect?
ch: cities, then the first stone tools
writing, then the use of fire
law codes, then domestication of dogs

test.q: In a village, each farmer could grow enough food for 5 people, including the farmer. The village had 50 farmers and 300 people in all. How many more people lived in the village than the 50 farmers could feed?
Compare daily life for a hunter-gatherer and an early farmer. Give one similarity and one difference.
test.ans: Similarity: both used stone tools and depended on nature for food. Difference: hunter-gatherers moved with the seasons to find wild food, while farmers stayed in one place and grew crops and raised animals.

test.q: Explain why archaeologists rely so heavily on artifacts to learn about the Paleolithic era.
test.ans: Paleolithic people had no writing, so there are no written records. Tools, bones, hearths and art are the only evidence of how they lived.

test.q: Some historians argue that the most important invention of early humans was fire; others argue it was farming. Choose one and explain your choice with two reasons.
test.ans: Farming: it allowed permanent settlements, food surpluses, population growth and specialized jobs, which led to cities and civilization. (Fire is also acceptable with reasons such as cooking, warmth and moving into colder lands.)

test.q: Use the sources to answer. Source A (timeline): 10,000 BCE farming begins in the Fertile Crescent; 7000 BCE villages such as Catalhoyuk have thousands of people; 3500 BCE cities grow in Sumer. Source B (archaeology): Sumerian cities had temples, walls, workshops for potters and metalworkers, and clay tablets recording grain stored in warehouses. Make a claim about how farming led to the rise of civilization. Use evidence from both sources and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Farming led to civilization because it produced a surplus that allowed cities, specialized jobs and government to develop. Evidence: Source A shows farming came first, then large villages, then cities. Source B shows cities with workshops for potters and metalworkers and tablets recording stored grain. Reasoning: Stored grain means farmers grew more food than they needed, which freed others to become craftspeople and priests, and records of the grain show an organized government managing the surplus.

lessons.name: Geography of the Fertile Crescent

practice.q: The name Mesopotamia comes from Greek words meaning
practice.h: Look at where Mesopotamia sits on a map.

practice.q: Mesopotamia lay between which two rivers?
ch: the Huang He and the Yangtze
practice.h: Both rivers begin in the mountains of present-day Turkey.

practice.q: Southern Mesopotamia got very little rain. How did farmers there water their crops?
ch: They dug canals to carry river water to their fields
They melted snow from local mountains
They grew only crops that need no water
practice.h: Think of the word irrigation.

practice.q: The Tigris and Euphrates flooded at unpredictable times. How did Sumerians protect their fields?
ch: They built earthen walls called levees and stored water in basins
practice.h: Farmers needed to control both too little and too much water.

practice.q: On a map, 1 centimeter equals 100 kilometers. The Euphrates River flows about 28 centimeters on the map. About how many kilometers long is the river on this map?
practice.h: Multiply the map length by the scale.

practice.q: Explain one way the rivers helped the people of Mesopotamia and one way the rivers were a danger.
practice.ans: Help: the rivers gave water for irrigation and left rich silt for farming, and they were used for travel and trade. Danger: unpredictable floods could destroy crops, homes and canals.
practice.h: Think about both the gifts and the risks of a river.

quiz.q: The Fertile Crescent is a curved region of good farmland that stretches from the Persian Gulf to the
Mesopotamia had few trees and little stone. What building material did Sumerians use most?
ch: mud bricks dried in the sun

quiz.q: Because Mesopotamia lacked metals, timber and stone, Sumerians
ch: traded grain and cloth with other regions for these goods

quiz.q: Rich soil in Mesopotamia came from
ch: silt the rivers left behind after floods

quiz.q: Which job would be most important for keeping a Sumerian city fed?
ch: workers who kept the irrigation canals clean

quiz.q: A canal is 4,500 meters long. A crew of workers clears 150 meters of mud from it each day. How many days does it take to clear the whole canal?
A farmer in northern Mesopotamia, where more rain fell, and a farmer in the far south were compared. Which statement is most likely true?
ch: The southern farmer depended more on irrigation
The northern farmer depended more on irrigation
Both farmers lived in a rainforest

quiz.q: Explain how the need for irrigation helped lead to strong governments in Mesopotamia.
quiz.ans: Canals and levees were large projects that needed many workers and someone to plan, organize and settle disputes over water, so leaders and governments grew stronger.

lessons.name: Sumerian city-states, religion and society

practice.q: A city-state is
ch: a city and the farmland around it with its own government
a group of nations ruled by an emperor
a farming village with no leader
practice.h: Ur, Uruk and Lagash each had their own ruler.

practice.q: A ziggurat was a
ch: stepped temple tower at the center of a Sumerian city
practice.h: It rose in layers like a staircase.

practice.q: Sumerians practiced polytheism. This means they
practice.h: Poly means many; theism means belief in gods.

practice.q: Why did Sumerian city-states often fight one another?
ch: They competed for water, land and control of canals
They were all ruled by Egypt
practice.h: What resource was most precious in a dry land?

practice.q: A ziggurat had 3 levels. The bottom level was 60 meters wide, and each higher level was 15 meters narrower than the one below it. How wide was the top level?
practice.h: Subtract 15 for each level above the bottom.

practice.q: Describe the social classes of Sumer from top to bottom.
practice.ans: At the top were kings, priests and nobles; in the middle were merchants, artisans and farmers; at the bottom were enslaved people, often prisoners of war or people in debt.
practice.h: Think of who held power, who worked, and who was not free.

quiz.q: In early Sumer, who often held great power alongside the king?
Why did Sumerian cities build thick walls?
ch: to protect themselves from attacks by other city-states and raiders
to keep floods out of the desert
to show the border with China

quiz.q: Sumerians believed the gods controlled nature. How did this belief affect daily life?
ch: People made offerings at temples so the gods would send good harvests and protect the city

quiz.q: Which person would most likely be found at the bottom of Sumerian society?
Over time, many Sumerian city-states became ruled by kings because
ch: war leaders kept power after fighting ended and passed it to their sons
the people voted for a democracy

quiz.q: The city of Uruk may have had about 40,000 people. A smaller city-state had about 10,000 people. How many times larger was Uruk?
Which piece of evidence best shows that religion was at the center of Sumerian life?
ch: The largest building in each city was a ziggurat temple

quiz.q: Source A: In Sumerian cities, the ziggurat stood in the center, and temple storehouses held grain, tools and livestock. Source B: Clay tablets show temple workers giving out food rations to laborers and craftspeople. Make a claim about the role of temples in Sumerian city-states. Use evidence from both sources and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: Temples were centers of both religion and the economy. Evidence: Source A shows the ziggurat at the center of the city and temple storehouses holding grain, tools and animals. Source B shows temple workers paying food rations to workers. Reasoning: Because temples stored goods and paid workers, they controlled much of the city's wealth as well as its worship.

Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.

lessons.name: Writing and inventions of Sumer

practice.q: The wedge-shaped writing system of Mesopotamia is called
practice.h: Cuneus is the Latin word for wedge.

practice.q: Sumerian scribes wrote by pressing a reed stylus into
practice.h: Mesopotamia had plenty of river mud.

practice.q: Cuneiform was first used mainly to
ch: record goods such as grain and animals for trade and taxes
send messages to Egypt by mail
practice.h: The earliest tablets are lists and counts.

practice.q: Which Sumerian invention helped farmers break up hard soil more easily?

lessons.name: Empires and Hammurabi's Code

quiz.q: Hammurabi said his laws came from the gods. Explain why linking laws to the gods might have helped him rule.

test.q: Describe two achievements of the Sumerians and explain why each was important.
test.ans: Cuneiform let people keep records and write laws and stories; the wheel improved transportation and pottery making; the plow made farming easier; irrigation systems produced surplus food.

test.q: Source A: Hammurabi's prologue (translated by L. W. King, 1910) says he made his laws "to bring about the rule of righteousness in the land, to destroy the wicked and the evil-doers; so that the strong should not harm the weak." test.ans: Claim: Hammurabi's Code aimed for justice but did not protect everyone equally. units.name: Unit 3: Ancient Egypt and Kush (6.2)
units.el: Use a vertical map of the Nile and a gesture for "flows north" (finger moving up the map). Pre-teach Upper and Lower Egypt, cataract, delta, pharaoh, afterlife and trade with picture cards, and give a Venn diagram frame for comparing Egypt and Kush.

lessons.name: The Nile River and Egyptian farming

practice.q: Ancient Egypt grew up along which river?
practice.h: It is one of the longest rivers in the world.

practice.q: The Nile flows from south to north. This means Upper Egypt was in the
practice.h: "Upper" means upstream, closer to where the river begins.

practice.q: The fan-shaped area of rich land where the Nile meets the Mediterranean Sea is called the
practice.h: It is named after a Greek letter shaped like a triangle.

practice.q: What happened each year when the Nile flooded?
ch: It left a layer of dark, fertile silt on the fields
It washed all the soil into the sea
It turned the river into a desert
practice.h: Egyptians called their land Kemet, the "black land."

practice.q: A map shows the Nile with a scale of 1 centimeter = 200 kilometers. The river measures about 33 centimeters on the map. About how long is the Nile in kilometers?
practice.h: Multiply 33 by 200.

practice.q: The Greek historian Herodotus, writing about 440 BCE, called Egypt "the gift of the river" (adapted translation). Explain what he meant.
practice.ans: Without the Nile, Egypt would be desert. The river's floods brought water and rich soil for farming, and the river was used for travel and trade, so Egypt's whole civilization depended on it.
practice.h: What would Egypt be like without the Nile?

quiz.q: The deserts on both sides of the Nile Valley helped Egypt by

ch: south on the Nile into Nubia

ch: after the flood waters went down

ch: The current carried boats north, and winds from the north pushed sails south
The river flowed in both directions

quiz.q: Which crops did Egyptian farmers grow in the rich soil?

A field produced 1,200 sacks of grain. The farmer paid 1 out of every 5 sacks as a tax to the pharaoh. How many sacks did the farmer pay?
Explain why most Egyptians lived on a narrow strip of land near the Nile.
quiz.ans: Most of Egypt is desert with little rain. Only the land near the river had water and fertile soil for farming, so people lived where they could grow food.

lessons.name: Pharaohs, government and religion

practice.q: The rulers of ancient Egypt were called
practice.h: The word first meant "great house."

practice.h: The pharaoh's double crown showed this event.

practice.q: Egyptians believed their pharaoh was
ch: a god-king who kept order in the land
practice.h: Religion and government were joined in Egypt.

practice.q: Why did Egyptians mummify the dead?
ch: They believed the body was needed in the afterlife
practice.h: Think about what Egyptians believed happened after death.

practice.h: Subtract the smaller BCE date from the larger one.

practice.ans: Pharaoh at the top; then priests and nobles; then scribes and government officials; then artisans and merchants; then farmers, the largest group; enslaved people at the bottom.
practice.h: Who had the most power, and which group had the most people?

practice.q: Egyptian writing that used picture symbols is called

practice.h: Our word "paper" comes from its name.

practice.h: Both dates are BCE. Subtract.

ch: a sacred promise or agreement, which the Hebrews believed they had with God
a written law code from Babylon

soc|7.about: Seventh graders study the world from about 300 to 1789 CE: the fall of Rome and the Byzantine Empire, the rise and spread of Islam, China, the West African empires, Japan, medieval Europe, the Maya, Aztec and Inca, and the Renaissance, Reformation, Scientific Revolution, Age of Exploration and Enlightenment. Students trace trade and the spread of ideas, read primary sources, compare perspectives and explain causes and effects with evidence.
std: Students analyze the causes and effects of the vast expansion and ultimate disintegration of the Roman Empire.
Students analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the civilizations of Islam in the Middle Ages.
Students analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the civilizations of China in the Middle Ages.
Students analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the sub-Saharan civilizations of Ghana and Mali in Medieval Africa.
Students analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the civilizations of Medieval Japan.
Students analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the civilizations of Medieval Europe.
Students compare and contrast the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the Meso-American and Andean civilizations.
Students analyze the origins, accomplishments and geographic diffusion of the Renaissance.
Students analyze the historical developments of the Reformation.
Students analyze the historical developments of the Scientific Revolution and its lasting effect on religious, political and cultural institutions.
Students analyze political and economic change in the sixteenth, seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (the Age of Exploration, the Enlightenment and the Age of Reason).

units.name: Unit 1: The Fall of Rome and the Byzantine Empire (7.1)
units.el: Use a cause-and-effect organizer with four boxes (political, economic, military, social) for the fall of Rome, and a map that shows Rome and Constantinople. Pre-teach decline, inflation, mercenary, invasion, code, schism and icon with examples and sentence frames such as "One cause of Rome's fall was ___ because ___."

lessons.name: Why the Western Roman Empire fell

practice.q: In which year is the Western Roman Empire usually said to have fallen?
practice.h: A Germanic leader removed the last emperor in the West.

practice.q: Between 235 and 284 CE, Rome had more than 20 emperors, and many were killed. This is an example of which kind of problem?
practice.h: Think about what it means when leaders change very often.

practice.q: To pay soldiers, emperors put less silver in coins, so prices rose sharply. Rising prices are called
practice.h: The same coin bought less and less.

practice.q: Why did Rome begin hiring Germanic soldiers called mercenaries?
ch: Fewer Romans were willing to join the army
practice.h: Mercenaries are soldiers who fight for pay, not for their homeland.

practice.h: Subtract 235 from 284.

practice.q: Explain why the size of the Roman Empire made it hard to defend.
practice.ans: The borders were thousands of kilometers long, so the army was spread thin, troops took a long time to reach trouble spots, and defending them cost huge amounts of money.
practice.h: Think about the length of the borders and the cost of soldiers.

ch: it was too large for one ruler to govern well

quiz.q: Rome was sacked by the Visigoths in 410 CE and by the Vandals in 455 CE. How many years apart were these attacks?

The scholar Jerome, living far away in Bethlehem, wrote in 412 CE after the sack of Rome (translated by W. H. Fremantle, 1893): "the City which had taken the whole world was itself taken." What feeling does this quotation show?
ch: shock that the city that once ruled the world could fall

quiz.q: Historians argue about whether Rome "fell" suddenly or declined slowly. Use two facts to support the idea of a slow decline.
quiz.ans: Problems built over centuries: civil wars and rapid changes of emperors in the 200s, inflation and high taxes, splitting the empire, and repeated invasions in the 400s, with the last Western emperor removed only in 476.

lessons.name: The legacy of Rome

practice.h: It was still used by scholars and the Church for centuries.

practice.h: Multiply 16 by 250.

practice.ans: Latin became the basis of Romance languages and many English words; Roman law shaped legal systems; Roman architecture with arches and domes; the Christian Church that grew in the empire.

quiz.ans: Its language, laws, religion, roads, buildings and ideas continued in the Germanic kingdoms, in the Church and in the Eastern Empire, which ruled from Constantinople until 1453.

practice.q: Muslim scholars helped spread the numerals 0 to 9 from India to
practice.h: Europeans called them Arabic numerals.

practice.q: Ibn Battuta traveled for about 29 years, from 1325 to 1354. If he traveled about 4,000 kilometers each year, about how many kilometers did he travel in all?
practice.h: Multiply 29 by 4,000.

practice.q: Explain why Muslim scholars' translations of Greek works were important for later Europe.
practice.ans: They preserved and added to the works of Greek thinkers such as Aristotle. Later, these works were translated into Latin, and European scholars used them, which helped lead to the Renaissance.
practice.h: What might have happened to these books otherwise?

quiz.q: Muslim astronomers improved the astrolabe. Travelers used it to
ch: find their location and the time by measuring the position of stars

quiz.q: Paper-making spread to the Muslim world from
Merchants in the Muslim world used letters of credit, an early form of
Cordoba in Muslim-ruled Spain was known for
Why did trade flourish in the Muslim world?
ch: It was located at the crossroads of Africa, Asia and Europe, and shared a common religion and language

quiz.q: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was finished about 1025 CE and was still used in European universities around 1650. About how many years was it used?
Which piece of evidence best shows that Muslim learning combined ideas from many cultures?
ch: Scholars in Baghdad translated Greek, Persian and Indian texts into Arabic and added their own discoveries
The caliph lived in a palace

quiz.q: Describe two achievements of Muslim scholars in the Middle Ages and explain their importance today.
quiz.ans: Al-Khwarizmi's algebra is still taught; Ibn Sina's medical encyclopedia advanced medicine; Muslim astronomers improved the astrolabe and star tables; scholars preserved Greek works and spread Indian numerals with zero to Europe.

test.q: The prophet of Islam is
The holy city where the Kaaba is located is
Muhammad's move from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE is called the
Muslims believe the revelations Muhammad received are recorded in which book?
Which is one of the Five Pillars of Islam?
How did the geography of Arabia affect the way people lived?
ch: Deserts led many people to live as nomadic herders or to settle at oases and trade

test.q: Islam, Judaism and Christianity all
The split between Sunni and Shia Muslims began with a disagreement over
ch: who should lead the Muslim community after Muhammad
the use of the Arabic language

test.q: Which city was the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate?
Which helped spread Islam to West Africa?
ch: Muslim traders who crossed the Sahara

test.q: Which scholar is matched correctly with an achievement?
ch: Ibn Sina, the astrolabe in China
Ibn Battuta, the Canon of Medicine

test.q: The House of Wisdom was important because
ch: scholars translated and preserved knowledge from many cultures
it was the caliph's army base

test.q: Muhammad was born about 570 CE and died in 632 CE. About how old was he when he died?
The Umayyad dynasty ruled from 661 CE to 750 CE. How many years did it rule?
A map scale shows 1 centimeter = 350 kilometers. The distance from Mecca to Baghdad measures about 4 centimeters. About how many kilometers apart are the cities?
Why did many conquered peoples accept Muslim rule?
ch: They were often allowed to keep their religion and customs, and trade and order improved
They were all forced to move to Arabia

test.q: Which statement is a belief rather than a historical fact?
ch: God revealed the Quran to Muhammad
Muhammad moved to Medina in 622 CE
Muslim armies reached Spain in 711 CE

test.q: How did Muslim scholars help bring about the European Renaissance?
ch: They preserved and improved Greek learning, which later reached Europe in Latin translations

test.q: Which list is in the correct chronological order?
ch: Hijra, death of Muhammad, Muslim armies enter Spain, Baghdad founded
Baghdad founded, Hijra, death of Muhammad, Muslim armies enter Spain
Muslim armies enter Spain, Hijra, Baghdad founded, death of Muhammad
death of Muhammad, Hijra, Baghdad founded, Muslim armies enter Spain

test.q: Explain how trade and the Arabic language helped unite the Muslim world.
test.ans: Merchants traveled safe routes across Africa, Asia and Europe exchanging goods and ideas; Arabic was the language of the Quran, government and learning, so scholars and officials from different lands could communicate.

test.q: Explain two ways Islamic teachings guide daily life for Muslims.
test.ans: The Five Pillars set duties such as daily prayer, fasting during Ramadan and charity; the Quran and Sunnah guide behavior; sharia sets rules for family life, business and worship.

test.q: Source A: Scholars at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad translated works by Greek, Persian and Indian thinkers into Arabic. Source B: Al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on solving equations (about 820 CE) that gave us the word algebra, and he used Indian numerals including zero. Source C: In the 1100s, scholars in Spain translated Arabic books into Latin, and these were studied in European universities. Make a claim about the importance of Muslim scholars in the history of knowledge. Use evidence from the sources and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Muslim scholars were important because they preserved, combined and added to knowledge from many cultures and passed it to Europe. Evidence: Source A shows they translated Greek, Persian and Indian works. Source B shows al-Khwarizmi created algebra using Indian numerals. Source C shows their books were translated into Latin and studied in Europe. Reasoning: By collecting ideas from many places and adding new discoveries, Muslim scholars kept knowledge alive and built on it, and the translations carried this knowledge to Europe, where it helped later learning.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 3: China in the Middle Ages (7.3)
units.el: Post a dynasty timeline strip (Sui, Tang, Song, Yuan, Ming) and a map with the Grand Canal and Zheng He's routes. Pre-teach reunify, canal, examination, invention, movable type, nomad and voyage with images, and use the frame "The ___ dynasty is known for ___."

lessons.name: Reunification under the Sui and Tang

practice.q: After more than 350 years of division, China was reunified in 589 CE by the
practice.h: This short dynasty came just before the Tang.

practice.q: The Grand Canal, built mainly under the Sui, connected
ch: the Huang He in the north with the Chang Jiang (Yangtze) in the south
practice.h: It linked the two great river systems.

practice.q: Why was the Grand Canal so important?
ch: It let rice and other goods from the south be shipped north to the capital and armies
It was used only for festivals
It brought water to the Gobi Desert
practice.h: The south grew more food; the government was in the north.

practice.q: During the Tang dynasty, the government expanded the civil service examinations so that
ch: more officials were chosen for their knowledge of Confucian texts
practice.h: Exams tested what officials had studied.

practice.q: The Tang dynasty ruled from 618 to 907 CE. How many years did it last?
practice.h: Subtract 618 from 907.

practice.q: Explain why the Sui dynasty fell quickly even though it reunified China.
practice.ans: It forced millions of people to work on huge projects such as the Grand Canal and fought costly wars, which made people angry and led to rebellions.
practice.h: Think about the costs of its great projects.

quiz.q: Wu Zetian is known as
ch: the only woman in Chinese history to rule as emperor in her own name
the founder of the Song dynasty

quiz.q: The Tang capital, Chang'an, was one of the largest cities in the world and
ch: a meeting place for merchants and travelers from many lands at the eastern end of the Silk Road

quiz.q: Buddhism became very popular in China during the Tang dynasty because
ch: it offered comfort and hope during times of trouble and was supported by many rulers

quiz.q: Late in the Tang dynasty, some officials attacked Buddhism because they
ch: believed it was foreign and that monasteries held too much wealth and land

quiz.q: The poets Li Bai and Du Fu are famous for
ch: writing poetry during the Tang dynasty

quiz.q: The Sui dynasty lasted from 581 to 618 CE. How many years did it last?
How did the examination system strengthen the Tang government?
ch: Officials who were tested on Confucian learning were educated and loyal to the government rather than to noble families
It gave all power to the army

quiz.q: Explain how Confucian and Buddhist ideas both shaped life in Tang China.
quiz.ans: Confucianism guided government, family duty and the examinations for officials, while Buddhism spread through temples and monasteries and offered teachings about suffering and rebirth to many people.

lessons.name: The Song dynasty: trade, cities and inventions

practice.q: The Song dynasty ruled China from
practice.h: It came after a time of division following the Tang.

practice.q: A fast-ripening rice from Southeast Asia helped Song farmers
ch: grow two crops a year, so food supplies and population grew
practice.h: More harvests mean more food.

practice.q: Which Chinese invention made long ocean voyages safer?
practice.h: It always points north and south.

practice.q: Paper money developed in Song China because
ch: carrying heavy strings of metal coins was difficult for merchants
there was no metal in China
practice.h: Think about trade involving large amounts of money.

practice.q: Bi Sheng developed movable type in the 1040s. Johannes Gutenberg developed his movable-type printing press in Europe about 1450. Using 1045 for Bi Sheng, about how many years earlier was Bi Sheng's invention?
practice.h: Subtract 1045 from 1450.

practice.q: Explain how improvements in farming led to the growth of cities and trade in Song China.
practice.ans: New rice and better farming produced more food, so fewer people had to farm. The population grew, people moved to cities, and merchants traded surplus goods, helped by canals and paper money.
practice.h: Follow the chain from food to people to cities.

quiz.q: Gunpowder, developed in China, was used by the Song for
ch: fireworks and weapons such as fire lances and bombs

quiz.q: Woodblock printing, used in China from at least the Tang dynasty, involved
ch: carving a whole page into a block of wood, inking it and pressing paper on it

quiz.q: The oldest dated printed book that survives, the Diamond Sutra, was printed in China in 868 CE. What does it show?
ch: Printing was used to spread Buddhist texts long before printing in Europe

quiz.q: Neo-Confucianism, which developed under the Song, combined Confucian ideas with
Porcelain from Song China became valuable because it was
ch: strong, beautiful and wanted by buyers across Asia, Africa and later Europe

quiz.q: A Song city had about 1,000,000 people. A large European city at the same time had about 50,000 people. How many times larger was the Song city?
Which best explains why so many inventions appeared in Tang and Song China?
ch: A large, wealthy and educated society with growing trade encouraged new ideas
China was cut off from all trade

quiz.q: Source A: Song farmers planted a fast-ripening rice that allowed two harvests a year. Source B: The population of China grew to about 100 million during the Song dynasty, and cities such as Hangzhou grew very large. Source C: Merchants used paper money and canals to move goods. Make a claim about what caused the growth of cities in Song China. Use evidence from the sources and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: Increased food production and better trade caused Song cities to grow. Evidence: Source A shows farmers could harvest rice twice a year. Source B shows the population reached about 100 million and cities like Hangzhou grew large. Source C shows paper money and canals helped merchants trade. Reasoning: More food supported more people, and easy trade gave people work in cities, so cities grew.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: The Mongols and the Yuan dynasty

practice.q: The Mongols were
ch: nomadic herders from the grasslands north of China
practice.h: They lived on the steppe and were expert riders.

practice.q: The leader who united the Mongols and began their conquests in the early 1200s was
practice.h: His title means "universal ruler."

practice.q: Genghis Khan's grandson Kublai Khan conquered China and founded the
practice.h: It was the first time all of China was ruled by foreigners.

practice.q: Why were Mongol armies so successful?
ch: They were skilled horse archers who moved fast and were very well organized
They had the largest navy in the world
practice.h: Think about their life on horseback.

practice.q: The Yuan dynasty ruled China from 1271 to 1368. How many years did it last?
practice.h: Subtract 1271 from 1368.

practice.q: Explain how the Mongol Empire made travel and trade across Asia easier.
practice.ans: The Mongols controlled lands from China to Eastern Europe, kept the Silk Road safe, and set up relay stations, so merchants, travelers and ideas could move across the continent.
practice.h: What happens when one empire controls an entire trade route?

quiz.q: Under the Yuan, Kublai Khan
ch: gave the highest jobs to Mongols and foreigners rather than Chinese officials
made the examination system the only way to get a job
moved the capital to Mongolia forever

quiz.q: Marco Polo was
ch: a merchant from Venice who wrote about his years in Kublai Khan's China

quiz.q: Marco Polo described Chinese paper money and coal ("black stones" that burned). Why did these descriptions amaze Europeans?
ch: Europeans did not yet use paper money or burn coal widely

quiz.q: Kublai Khan's attempts to invade Japan in 1274 and 1281
ch: failed, partly because storms destroyed much of his fleet
succeeded and made Japan part of China

quiz.q: Why did many Chinese resent Yuan rule?
ch: They were ruled by foreigners who placed them at the bottom of society and taxed them heavily
The Yuan built too many schools

quiz.q: Marco Polo stayed in China for about 17 years and left about 1292. About what year did he arrive?
Marco Polo's book is a useful source but must be read carefully because
ch: he wrote it with another author years later, and some details may be exaggerated or mistaken
it has no information about China

quiz.q: Describe one positive and one negative effect of Mongol rule on China.
quiz.ans: Positive: trade and contact with other lands grew, and the Silk Road was safe. Negative: Chinese people were excluded from high offices, taxed heavily and ruled by foreigners, which caused resentment.

lessons.name: The Ming dynasty and the voyages of Zheng He

practice.q: In 1368 a rebellion drove out the Mongols and founded the
practice.h: Its name means "brilliant."

practice.q: The Forbidden City in Beijing was
ch: the huge palace complex of the Ming emperors
practice.h: Ordinary people could not enter.

practice.q: Zheng He was a Ming admiral who
ch: led seven great voyages to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa
practice.h: His fleets sailed between 1405 and 1433.

practice.q: Ming emperors rebuilt and strengthened the Great Wall to
ch: protect China from attacks from the north
practice.h: The Mongols and other northern peoples were still a threat.

practice.q: Zheng He's voyages took place from 1405 to 1433. How many years passed from the first voyage to the last?
practice.h: Subtract 1405 from 1433.

practice.q: Explain the purpose of Zheng He's voyages.
practice.ans: They showed the power and wealth of the Ming, collected tribute from foreign rulers, encouraged trade and brought back gifts such as giraffes and rare goods.
practice.h: Think about showing power and gaining tribute.

quiz.q: After Zheng He's voyages ended, the Ming government
ch: limited overseas trade and turned its attention inward
sent even larger fleets to Europe

quiz.q: Which is one reason the Ming stopped the voyages?
ch: They were very expensive, and some officials thought China should focus on defending its northern border
China ran out of wood forever

quiz.q: Ming records say Zheng He's first fleet had more than 300 ships and about 27,000 men. What does this show?
ch: Ming China had great wealth and advanced shipbuilding

quiz.q: Confucian officials often looked down on trade and merchants because they believed
ch: farming and scholarship were more honorable than making a profit

quiz.q: Which statement compares the Yuan and Ming dynasties?
ch: The Yuan were foreign Mongol rulers, while the Ming were a Chinese dynasty that drove them out
The Ming came before the Yuan

quiz.q: Zheng He's first voyage began in 1405. Christopher Columbus first sailed across the Atlantic in 1492. How many years apart were these events?
What was a long-term effect of China's decision to stop the treasure voyages?
ch: European nations, not China, came to control many sea trade routes in later centuries

quiz.q: Do you think the Ming were wise to end the voyages of Zheng He? Give one reason that supports your answer.
quiz.ans: Yes: the voyages were costly, and the Ming needed money to defend the north against the Mongols. Or No: ending them reduced trade and contact with the world and allowed Europeans to dominate ocean trade later.

test.q: The dynasty that built most of the Grand Canal was the
The magnetic compass, gunpowder and movable type are inventions of
The Mongol ruler who conquered China and founded the Yuan dynasty was
The Ming admiral who led voyages to Africa and Arabia was
The Grand Canal helped China by
ch: linking the rice-growing south with the north

test.q: The civil service examinations tested candidates on
Which development during the Song dynasty helped the population grow?
ch: fast-ripening rice that allowed two harvests a year

test.q: Paper money was useful for Song merchants because
ch: it was lighter and easier to carry than strings of coins
it was accepted only in Europe

test.q: Neo-Confucianism is best described as
ch: Confucian thought mixed with ideas from Buddhism and Daoism

test.q: Why did many Chinese dislike Mongol rule?
ch: Mongols kept top jobs for themselves and foreigners and placed Chinese at the bottom
Mongols gave all power to Confucian scholars

test.q: Marco Polo's account helped
ch: make Europeans curious about the wealth of China

test.q: The Ming government's decision after 1433 was to
ch: end the great voyages and limit foreign trade

test.q: The Song dynasty lasted from 960 to 1279. How many years was that?
The Ming dynasty began in 1368. The Forbidden City was finished in 1420. How many years after the Ming began was it finished?
A map scale shows 1 centimeter = 200 kilometers. The Grand Canal measures about 9 centimeters on the map. About how long is the canal in kilometers?
Which pair shows a correct cause and effect?
ch: More rice harvests, then population and city growth
Gunpowder, then the end of farming
Paper money, then the end of trade
The Grand Canal, then Mongol invasions

test.q: Which source would best show how the examination system worked?
ch: an official's record of the topics and results of an exam
a map of the Silk Road
a painting of a porcelain vase

test.q: Which statement about Chinese inventions is best supported?
ch: Chinese inventions such as the compass, printing and gunpowder later changed navigation, learning and warfare around the world
Chinese inventions were never used outside China
Europe invented all of them first
They were used only for decoration

test.q: Which list is in the correct chronological order?
Explain how the Mongol Empire increased contact between China and other parts of the world.
test.ans: The Mongols controlled lands from China to Eastern Europe and kept the Silk Road safe, so merchants such as Marco Polo, missionaries, goods and ideas traveled between China, Southwest Asia and Europe.

test.q: Choose one Chinese invention from this period and explain how it changed the world.
test.ans: The compass helped sailors navigate the oceans, making later voyages of exploration possible; printing spread knowledge; gunpowder changed warfare; paper money changed trade.

test.q: Source A: From 1405 to 1433, Zheng He's fleets of large ships sailed as far as East Africa, bringing back gifts and tribute. Source B: After 1433, the Ming government stopped the voyages, limited foreign trade and spent heavily on rebuilding the Great Wall against northern attacks. Source C: In the 1500s, Portuguese ships arrived in Chinese waters and began to take part in Asian sea trade. Make a claim about the effect of the Ming decision to stop the voyages. Use evidence from the sources and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Ending the voyages turned China's focus inward and allowed European powers to take a larger role in Asian sea trade. Evidence: Source A shows China had the ability to sail to Africa. Source B shows the Ming stopped the voyages and focused on the northern border. Source C shows Portuguese ships entered Asian trade in the 1500s. Reasoning: Once China withdrew from the seas, it left room for European traders to build power on the ocean routes, even though China had led in shipbuilding decades earlier.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 4: Ghana, Mali and West Africa (7.4)
units.el: Use a map of West Africa with colored vegetation zones (desert, Sahel, savanna, rainforest) and arrows for gold and salt. Pre-teach caravan, barter, tax, mansa, pilgrimage, griot and oral tradition, and use the frame "Gold came from ___, and salt came from ___."

lessons.name: Geography and the trans-Saharan trade

practice.q: The largest hot desert in the world, which covers much of northern Africa, is the
practice.h: Its name comes from the Arabic word for desert.

practice.q: The strip of dry grassland just south of the Sahara is called the
practice.h: Its name means "shore" or "edge" in Arabic.

practice.q: The major river of West Africa that helped trade and farming is the
practice.h: It curves through Mali.

practice.q: Which animal made regular trade across the Sahara possible?
practice.h: It can travel many days without water.

practice.q: A caravan crosses about 1,500 kilometers of the Sahara at about 30 kilometers a day. How many days does the crossing take?
practice.h: Divide 1,500 by 30.

practice.q: Explain why salt was so valuable in West Africa that it was sometimes traded for gold.
practice.ans: People in the hot south needed salt to stay healthy and to preserve food, but there was little salt there. Salt came from mines in the Sahara, so it was scarce and in great demand.
practice.h: Think about where salt came from and why people needed it.

quiz.q: In the trans-Saharan trade, gold came mainly from
ch: mines in West Africa south of the Sahara

quiz.q: Salt came mainly from
ch: mines in the Sahara, such as Taghaza

quiz.q: Why did the kingdoms of Ghana and Mali become rich?
ch: They controlled the trade routes between the gold fields and the salt mines and taxed the trade
They had the most farmland in the world

quiz.q: Which goods traveled south across the Sahara from North Africa?
A caravan of 1,000 camels each carried about 150 kilograms of salt. About how many kilograms of salt did the caravan carry?
A trader traveled 25 days to cross the desert and then 15 more days to reach a gold-trading town. How many days did the trip take in all?
Why did trade cities grow up along the edges of the Sahara and the Niger River?
ch: Caravans needed places to rest, exchange goods and find water and food
The desert was the best farmland

quiz.q: Explain how the different vegetation zones of West Africa encouraged trade among peoples.
quiz.ans: Each zone produced different goods: salt from the desert, livestock in the Sahel, grain on the savanna and gold, kola nuts and ivory from the south, so people traded to get what their own zone lacked.

lessons.name: The empire of Ghana

practice.q: The empire of Ghana was located
ch: in West Africa, between the Senegal and Niger rivers
in the same place as the modern country of Ghana
in North Africa on the Mediterranean
practice.h: The modern country took the name but is farther south and east.

practice.q: Ghana's kings grew rich mainly by
ch: taxing gold and salt that passed through their lands
practice.h: Every load of goods paid a tax.

practice.q: The king of Ghana controlled the supply of gold nuggets, while gold dust could be traded. Why?
ch: to keep gold scarce so its value stayed high
to give gold away for free
practice.h: What happens to the price of something when there is too much of it?

practice.q: Ghana's capital, Koumbi Saleh, had two towns: one for the king and one for
ch: Muslim merchants, which had several mosques
practice.h: Muslim traders from North Africa lived there.

practice.q: The Arab geographer al-Bakri wrote in 1068 that the king of Ghana collected 1 gold dinar for each donkey-load of salt brought into the country. How many dinars would the king collect on 240 donkey-loads?
practice.h: One dinar for each load.

practice.q: Al-Bakri never visited Ghana himself; he wrote in Spain using reports from travelers. How should a historian use his description?
practice.ans: It is valuable because it is one of the few written sources about Ghana, but it is secondhand, so historians should compare it with archaeology and oral traditions.
practice.h: Is it a firsthand or secondhand account?

quiz.q: Al-Bakri described the king of Ghana holding court with guards carrying gold-decorated swords and shields. What does this show?
ch: The king was wealthy and powerful

quiz.q: Why did the kings of Ghana welcome Muslim merchants even though many of the kings followed traditional religions?
ch: The merchants brought trade, wealth and skills in writing and record keeping
They wanted to become Muslims at once

quiz.q: Which was a cause of Ghana's decline in the late 1000s and 1100s?
ch: attacks by the Almoravids, loss of trade and overuse of farmland

quiz.q: Ghana's army was large because
ch: the king needed to protect the trade routes and collect taxes

quiz.q: Which source would be a primary source about Ghana?
ch: a gold-weighing scale found at Koumbi Saleh
a textbook map drawn last year

quiz.q: Al-Bakri wrote that the king charged 1 dinar for each load of salt brought in and 2 dinars for each load taken out. A trader brought in 30 loads and took out 10 loads. How many dinars did he pay in all?
Why might a king tax salt leaving the country at a higher rate than salt coming in?
ch: to keep more salt in the kingdom for its own people
to make salt cheaper to export

quiz.q: Source A (al-Bakri, 1068, adapted): The king of Ghana takes one dinar of gold on every donkey-load of salt that enters his country and two dinars on every load that leaves. Source B (al-Bakri, 1068, adapted): All gold nuggets found in the mines belong to the king; the people may keep only gold dust. Make a claim about how the king of Ghana built his wealth and power. Use evidence from both sources and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: The king of Ghana built his wealth by controlling trade and the supply of gold. Evidence: Source A shows he taxed salt both coming into and leaving the country. Source B shows all gold nuggets belonged to him. Reasoning: Taxing every load of salt brought him steady income from trade, and owning the nuggets let him keep gold scarce and valuable, so his wealth paid for an army that kept him powerful.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: Mali and Mansa Musa

practice.q: The founder of the empire of Mali, remembered in a famous epic, was
practice.h: Griots still tell the story of his life.

practice.q: The title "mansa" in Mali meant
practice.h: Mansa Musa was the most famous one.

practice.q: Mali grew larger and richer than Ghana partly because it
ch: controlled more gold fields and trade cities along the Niger River
practice.h: Look at the cities of Timbuktu and Gao on the river.

practice.q: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 is famous because he
ch: brought so much gold that he spent and gave away enough in Cairo to lower its value there
practice.h: Too much gold in one place lowers its value.

practice.q: Mansa Musa ruled from about 1312 to about 1337. About how many years did he rule?
practice.h: Subtract 1312 from 1337.

practice.q: Explain why Mansa Musa's pilgrimage made Mali famous in North Africa, Southwest Asia and Europe.
practice.ans: His huge caravan and generous spending of gold in Cairo and Mecca were reported by writers, and his image appeared on European maps, showing the world that Mali was rich and powerful.
practice.h: Who saw or heard about his journey?

quiz.q: After his pilgrimage, Mansa Musa
ch: brought scholars and architects back to Mali and built mosques, such as in Timbuktu

quiz.q: The Catalan Atlas, a European map made in 1375, shows Mansa Musa holding a gold nugget. What does this suggest?
ch: Europeans knew of Mali's great wealth

quiz.q: Sundiata defeated the Sosso king at the Battle of Kirina about 1235 and
Ibn Battuta, who visited Mali in 1352 and 1353, wrote (adapted translation) that there was "complete and general safety" in the land. What does this suggest about Mali's government?
ch: It kept order and protected travelers well

quiz.q: Which later empire took over much of Mali's land and trade in the 1400s?
Mansa Musa made his pilgrimage in 1324. The Catalan Atlas showing him was made in 1375. How many years later was the map made?
An Egyptian writer said gold's value in Cairo was still low twelve years after Mansa Musa's visit. What effect does this show?
ch: His spending was so large that it affected the economy of Cairo for years
Gold had no value in Egypt
Mansa Musa took gold from Cairo

quiz.q: Ibn Battuta praised Mali's safety and justice but also criticized some customs he found strange. Why is it useful for historians to read both his praise and his criticism?
quiz.ans: It shows his point of view as an outsider from North Africa; historians can learn about Mali while recognizing his personal and cultural bias, and compare his account with other sources.

lessons.name: Islam, learning and oral tradition

practice.q: Storytellers in West Africa who preserve history through spoken words and music are called
practice.h: They memorized long histories and family lines.

practice.q: Islam spread to West Africa mainly through
ch: Muslim traders who crossed the Sahara
practice.h: Trade routes also carried ideas.

practice.q: Timbuktu became famous as
ch: a center of Islamic learning with mosques, scholars and thousands of manuscripts
practice.h: Scholars came to study there.

practice.q: Many rulers of Mali became Muslims, while many ordinary people
ch: kept their traditional religious beliefs or blended them with Islam
practice.h: Religious change often happened first among rulers and merchants.

practice.q: The Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu was built in 1327. How many years ago was that from 2026?
practice.h: Subtract 1327 from 2026.

practice.q: Explain why oral tradition is an important source for West African history.
practice.ans: Much history was passed down by griots rather than written, so oral traditions preserve stories, family lines, laws and values, such as the Epic of Sundiata, that would otherwise be lost.
practice.h: How was history kept if few people wrote it down?

quiz.q: Why did learning Arabic help West African merchants and rulers?
ch: It let them read the Quran, keep written records and communicate with North African traders
It was the language of China

quiz.q: Which statement about the Epic of Sundiata is accurate?
ch: It was passed down by griots for centuries before it was written
It was written by a Roman historian
It is a map of the Sahara

quiz.q: Proverbs were often used in West African societies to
ch: teach values and wisdom in short, memorable sayings

quiz.q: Thousands of old manuscripts in Timbuktu cover subjects such as
How did family and kinship shape West African societies?
ch: Extended families and clans shared work, land and responsibilities

quiz.q: A griot recites a family history that goes back 12 generations. If each generation is about 25 years, about how many years of history does the griot remember?
Which is the best reason to compare a griot's story with an Arab traveler's account?
ch: Each source shows a different point of view, so together they give a fuller picture
Only one of them can be true
Travelers always tell the whole truth

quiz.q: Explain how trade helped spread both goods and ideas in West Africa.
quiz.ans: Caravans carried gold, salt and other goods, and with them came Muslim merchants who brought Islam, the Arabic language, writing and scholarship, which helped cities like Timbuktu become centers of learning.

test.q: The dry grassland south of the Sahara is called the
The two main goods in the trans-Saharan trade were
The ruler of Mali famous for his pilgrimage to Mecca was
West African storytellers who preserved history were called
Why was the camel important to West African trade?
ch: It could carry heavy loads across the desert with little water
It could swim the Niger River
It pulled plows in the rainforest

test.q: Ghana's kings became wealthy by
ch: taxing the trade in gold and salt

test.q: Which city was a famous center of trade and Islamic learning in Mali?
Islam came to West Africa mainly through
Which statement about religion in Mali is accurate?
ch: Many rulers became Muslim while many people kept traditional beliefs

test.q: What was one effect of Mansa Musa's pilgrimage?
ch: The world learned of Mali's wealth, and he brought scholars and builders back to Mali
Mali lost all its gold forever

test.q: The empire of Ghana declined partly because of
ch: attacks, loss of trade and overused farmland

test.q: Why did Ghana's king keep all gold nuggets for himself?
ch: to control the supply of gold and keep its value high
to give gold to every family
because nuggets were too heavy to trade

test.q: Ghana's capital was described by al-Bakri in 1068. Mansa Musa made his pilgrimage in 1324. How many years apart were these events?
A camel caravan travels 35 kilometers a day for 40 days. How many kilometers does it travel?
A trader exchanges salt for gold. If 2 bars of salt buy 1 ounce of gold, how many ounces of gold will 18 bars of salt buy?
Why is an Arab traveler's account of Mali both useful and limited as a source?
ch: It describes what the traveler saw, but it reflects an outsider's point of view and culture
It was written by a griot

test.q: Which statement best explains why West African empires formed in the Sahel and savanna?
ch: These regions lay between the gold fields of the south and the salt and markets of the north
They were the wettest lands in Africa
They were far from all trade
They were protected by high mountains

test.q: What does the spread of Islam in West Africa show about trade?
ch: Trade routes carried religion, language and learning as well as goods
Trade stopped the spread of ideas

test.q: Which list is in the correct chronological order?
ch: al-Bakri describes Ghana, Sundiata founds Mali, Mansa Musa goes on pilgrimage, Ibn Battuta visits Mali
Mansa Musa goes on pilgrimage, al-Bakri describes Ghana, Ibn Battuta visits Mali, Sundiata founds Mali
Ibn Battuta visits Mali, Sundiata founds Mali, al-Bakri describes Ghana, Mansa Musa goes on pilgrimage
Sundiata founds Mali, Ibn Battuta visits Mali, Mansa Musa goes on pilgrimage, al-Bakri describes Ghana

test.q: Explain how the gold-salt trade connected the peoples of West Africa and North Africa.
test.ans: Southern peoples traded gold, ivory and other goods for salt, cloth and horses from the north; caravans and trade cities linked the regions and brought Muslim merchants, Islam and Arabic writing to West Africa.

test.q: Explain why oral tradition and written sources are both important for studying Ghana and Mali.
test.ans: Griots preserved stories, family histories and values from inside the culture, while Arab writers recorded what travelers saw; together they give a fuller picture, and each can check the other's bias.

test.q: Source A (al-Bakri, 1068, adapted): The king of Ghana taxes every load of salt entering and leaving his kingdom. Source B (Ibn Battuta, about 1355, adapted): In Mali there is complete safety; neither a traveler nor a person living there fears robbers. Source C: In 1324, Mansa Musa traveled to Mecca with a huge caravan carrying gold and gave away so much in Cairo that its value there fell. Make a claim about the source of power of the empires of Ghana and Mali. Use evidence from the sources and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Ghana and Mali were powerful because they controlled and protected the trans-Saharan trade, especially in gold. Evidence: Source A shows Ghana's king taxed all salt entering and leaving. Source B shows Mali kept its roads safe for travelers. Source C shows Mali's ruler had enormous amounts of gold. Reasoning: Taxing trade brought great wealth, and keeping routes safe encouraged merchants to keep coming, so control of trade gave these empires the money and stability to become powerful.

units.name: Unit 5: Medieval Japan (7.5)
units.el: Use a map of Japan, Korea and China and a pyramid diagram of feudal Japanese society. Pre-teach archipelago, kami, regent, shogun, daimyo, samurai, loyalty and meditation with images, and give the frame "The ___ served the ___ in exchange for ___."

lessons.name: Geography and early influences from China and Korea

practice.q: Japan is an archipelago, which means it is
practice.h: Japan has four main islands and thousands of smaller ones.

practice.q: The largest island of Japan is
practice.h: Tokyo and Kyoto are on this island.

practice.q: Most of Japan's land is mountainous. How did this affect where people lived?
ch: Most people lived and farmed on narrow coastal plains and in river valleys
People could not farm at all
practice.h: Where is flat land found?

practice.q: Japan is close to Korea and China. How did this location affect early Japan?
ch: It allowed Japan to borrow ideas such as Buddhism, writing and government from China and Korea
It made Japan part of China
It kept Japan from all contact
It caused Japan to conquer China
practice.h: The sea was narrow enough to cross but wide enough to protect.

practice.q: A map scale shows 1 centimeter = 50 kilometers. The narrowest crossing between Japan and Korea measures about 4 centimeters. About how many kilometers is it?
practice.h: Multiply 4 by 50.

practice.q: Explain how the sea both connected and protected Japan.
practice.ans: Japan was close enough for envoys, monks and traders to bring ideas from Korea and China, but the sea made invasion difficult, so Japan could choose what to borrow and keep its own culture.
practice.h: Think about both ideas and armies crossing the sea.

quiz.q: The native religion of Japan, which honors spirits called kami in nature, is
Buddhism came to Japan in the 500s CE mainly by way of
Prince Shotoku, a regent in the early 600s, is known for
ch: promoting Buddhism and borrowing Chinese ideas of government

quiz.q: Japanese writing first used
ch: Chinese characters, later adapted with Japanese symbols called kana

quiz.q: Prince Shotoku sent officials and students to China in order to
ch: learn about Chinese government, religion and culture

quiz.q: Prince Shotoku issued his Seventeen Article Constitution in 604 CE. How many years ago was that from 2026?

The first article of Prince Shotoku's constitution says (translated by W. G. Aston, 1896), "Harmony is to be valued, and an avoidance of wanton opposition to be honoured." Which belief system most influenced this idea of harmony and proper relationships?
Explain how Japan combined borrowed ideas with its own traditions. Give an example.
quiz.ans: Japan adopted Buddhism but kept Shinto, and many people practiced both; it used Chinese characters but added kana; it borrowed Chinese government ideas while keeping its own emperor and clan system.

lessons.name: The Heian court

practice.q: In 794 CE the imperial capital moved to Heian-kyo, a city now called
practice.h: It was the capital for more than 1,000 years.

practice.q: The Heian period is known for
ch: the refined art, poetry and manners of the emperor's court
practice.h: Nobles at court valued beauty and elegance.

practice.q: The Tale of Genji, often called one of the world's first novels, was written by
practice.h: She was a lady at the Heian court.

practice.q: Why were women at the Heian court able to write many famous works?
ch: They often wrote in kana, the Japanese script, and had time and education at court
They were the only people who could read Chinese
Men were not allowed to write
practice.h: Men at court usually wrote in Chinese; women often wrote in Japanese.

practice.q: The Heian period lasted from 794 to 1185. How many years did it last?
practice.h: Subtract 794 from 1185.

practice.q: The Pillow Book by Sei Shonagon lists things she found beautiful or annoying at court. Why is it a valuable primary source?
practice.ans: It gives a firsthand, personal view of daily life, manners and values at the Heian court, written by someone who lived there.
practice.h: Who wrote it, and when?

quiz.q: During the Heian period, the real power at court often belonged to
ch: the Fujiwara family, who advised and married into the imperial family

quiz.q: While the court focused on art and poetry, the countryside
ch: grew less controlled by the government, and landowners built private armies
was fully controlled by the emperor

quiz.q: Calligraphy at the Heian court was valued as
ch: a form of art that showed a person's education and character
a way to keep tax records only

quiz.q: Which group was most likely to read the Tale of Genji in the Heian period?
What was a major weakness of the Heian government?
ch: Nobles at court lost control of the provinces to local warriors
It was ruled by foreign kings

quiz.q: The Tale of Genji was written about 1010. The Heian period ended in 1185. About how many years before the end of the period was it written?
Why is it important to remember that Heian literature was written by and for nobles?
ch: It shows the life of a small, wealthy group, not the lives of most Japanese people

quiz.q: Explain how the Heian court's focus on culture helped lead to the rise of warriors.
quiz.ans: Nobles spent their time on art and ceremony instead of governing, so distant landowners hired warriors to protect their land; these warriors grew powerful and eventually took control.

lessons.name: Shoguns, daimyo and samurai

practice.q: The supreme military ruler of Japan, who held real power while the emperor remained a figurehead, was the
practice.h: Minamoto Yoritomo received this title in 1192.

practice.q: Professional warriors who served lords in feudal Japan were the
practice.h: Their name means "those who serve."

practice.q: Daimyo were
ch: powerful landowning lords who had samurai armies
practice.h: They ruled their own lands under the shogun.

practice.q: Bushido, the samurai code, stressed
practice.h: Bushido means "the way of the warrior."

practice.q: Minamoto Yoritomo became shogun in 1192. The Mongols invaded Japan in 1274. How many years later was the first Mongol invasion?
practice.h: Subtract 1192 from 1274.

practice.q: Describe the structure of feudal Japanese society from top to bottom.
practice.ans: The emperor at the top had little real power; the shogun held military power; daimyo ruled lands; samurai served the daimyo; peasants farmed, then artisans and merchants, who were ranked lowest even if wealthy.
practice.h: Think about who had the title and who had the power.

quiz.q: In feudal Japan, peasants were ranked above merchants because
ch: they produced food, while merchants were seen as only making profit

quiz.q: A samurai without a lord, often because his lord died or lost his lands, was called a
Some women of samurai families
ch: learned to use weapons to defend their homes
served as soldiers in every battle
could not leave their homes ever

quiz.q: Why did the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281 fail?
ch: Samurai defended the coast, and storms destroyed much of the Mongol fleet
The Mongols turned back before reaching Japan

quiz.q: The Japanese called the storms that wrecked the Mongol fleets kamikaze, meaning
The Mongols invaded Japan in 1274 and again in 1281. How many years apart were the invasions?
Which statement compares the shogun and the emperor accurately?
ch: The emperor was honored as a symbol, while the shogun controlled the army and government
The emperor held all military power
The shogun was a Buddhist priest

quiz.q: Source A: In 1192, the emperor gave Minamoto Yoritomo the title of shogun, and Yoritomo set up his government in Kamakura, far from the emperor's court in Kyoto. Source B: The shogun appointed military governors and land stewards in the provinces, while the emperor continued to perform religious ceremonies. Make a claim about who held real power in Japan after 1192. Use evidence from both sources and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: After 1192, the shogun held real power in Japan, while the emperor was mainly a symbol. Evidence: Source A shows Yoritomo set up his own government in Kamakura, away from the court. Source B shows the shogun appointed governors and stewards, while the emperor performed ceremonies. Reasoning: Controlling officials and land across the provinces is real political and military power, while ceremonies are symbolic, so the shogun ruled in practice.

Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.

lessons.name: Religion, arts and the samurai way of life

practice.q: The form of Buddhism that stresses meditation and self-discipline and appealed to many samurai is
practice.h: Its name comes from a word meaning meditation.

practice.q: Why did Zen appeal to samurai?
ch: Its focus on discipline, calm and concentration helped them in training and battle
It required them to give up fighting
practice.h: What does a warrior need in battle?

practice.q: Pure Land Buddhism became popular with ordinary people because it taught that
ch: anyone could reach paradise through faith in the Amida Buddha
meditation required years in a monastery
practice.h: It offered a simple path to salvation.

practice.q: The Japanese tea ceremony is
ch: a quiet ritual of preparing and serving tea that reflects Zen values of simplicity and calm
a festival for the emperor's birthday
practice.h: Every movement is done carefully and simply.

practice.q: A traditional haiku poem has three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables. How many syllables does it have in all?
practice.h: Add the three numbers.

practice.q: Explain how Shinto and Buddhism existed side by side in Japan.
practice.ans: Many people honored the kami at Shinto shrines for life events and nature, and followed Buddhist teachings about suffering and the afterlife; some shrines and temples were even built together.
practice.h: Did people have to choose only one?

quiz.q: Zen rock gardens with raked gravel and carefully placed stones were meant to
Noh, a form of drama that developed in the 1300s, used
ch: masks, music, dance and slow movement

quiz.q: Shinto shrines are often marked by
Why did samurai often practice calligraphy and poetry as well as fighting?
ch: The ideal samurai was both a skilled warrior and a cultured person
They were not allowed to fight

quiz.q: Which statement about Buddhism in medieval Japan is accurate?
ch: Different forms, such as Zen and Pure Land, appealed to different groups of people
It disappeared after the Heian period
It was banned by the shogun

quiz.q: A samurai sword-making workshop produced 6 swords a month. How many swords did it produce in 2 years?
Which shows how Japan adapted Chinese culture rather than simply copying it?
ch: Japan developed Zen practices, kana writing and Noh drama with its own style
Japan used the exact Chinese government in every detail
Japan had an emperor chosen by China

quiz.q: Describe two parts of Japanese culture from this period that are still practiced today and explain their roots.
quiz.ans: The tea ceremony, rooted in Zen simplicity; calligraphy, borrowed from China; Noh theater from the 1300s; Shinto shrines and festivals; Zen gardens; haiku poetry.

test.q: Japan is made up of
ch: a chain of islands called an archipelago

test.q: The native religion of Japan that honors kami is
The military ruler who held real power in feudal Japan was the
The samurai code of conduct was called
Which was a major influence on early Japan from China and Korea?
Prince Shotoku's Seventeen Article Constitution stressed
ch: harmony, Buddhism and Confucian ideas of proper relationships

test.q: Which describes Japan during the Heian period (794 to 1185)?
ch: A refined court culture produced literature such as the Tale of Genji
The first shoguns fought for control of trade with Europe
Samurai governed the emperor's court in Kyoto

test.q: In feudal Japan, a daimyo was
ch: a landowning lord with his own samurai
a farmer who paid rice taxes

test.q: In feudal Japan, which group ranked lowest among the four main classes, even if wealthy?
Which form of Buddhism, based on meditation and discipline, was popular among samurai?
What did the Mongol invasions of Japan show?
ch: Japan's samurai and geography, along with storms, could protect it from invasion
Mongols ruled Japan for a century

test.q: Why did the power of the Heian court decline?
ch: Nobles neglected the provinces, and landowners with warrior armies grew powerful

test.q: Minamoto Yoritomo became shogun in 1192. The capital had moved to Heian-kyo in 794. How many years apart were these events?
A daimyo's land produced 12,000 bushels of rice. He paid his samurai with 1/4 of it. How many bushels did the samurai receive?
Buddhism reached Japan about 538 CE. Prince Shotoku's constitution was issued in 604. About how many years later was the constitution issued?
Which statement best compares feudal Japan and the idea of loyalty in its society?
ch: Samurai owed loyalty to their daimyo, who owed loyalty to the shogun, in exchange for land or support
Everyone owed loyalty only to merchants

test.q: Murasaki Shikibu wrote about life at the Heian court. What is a limitation of her work as a source on Japan as a whole?
ch: It describes the lives of nobles, not most people

test.q: Why did the shogun keep the emperor rather than replace him?
ch: The emperor was a respected religious symbol, so keeping him gave the shogun's rule legitimacy
The shogun was afraid of Korea

test.q: Which list is in the correct chronological order?
ch: Buddhism arrives, capital moves to Heian-kyo, first shogun, Mongol invasions
Mongol invasions, first shogun, Buddhism arrives, capital moves to Heian-kyo
First shogun, Buddhism arrives, Mongol invasions, capital moves to Heian-kyo
Capital moves to Heian-kyo, Mongol invasions, Buddhism arrives, first shogun

test.q: Explain how the geography of Japan shaped its history.
test.ans: Mountains limited farmland, so people lived on coastal plains; being islands close to Korea and China allowed Japan to borrow ideas while the sea protected it from invasion, such as the Mongol attacks.

test.q: Describe the relationship between daimyo and samurai.
test.ans: Samurai served and fought for a daimyo and were loyal to him; in return the daimyo gave them land, rice or a salary and protection.

test.q: Source A: Many samurai practiced Zen meditation to train their minds to be calm and focused. Source B: Bushido taught samurai to value loyalty, courage, honor and self-control, even in the face of death. Source C: Samurai were also expected to practice calligraphy, poetry and the tea ceremony. Make a claim about what was expected of an ideal samurai. Use evidence from the sources and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: An ideal samurai was expected to be both a disciplined warrior and a cultured, self-controlled person. Evidence: Source A shows samurai trained their minds through Zen meditation. Source B shows bushido valued loyalty, courage, honor and self-control. Source C shows samurai practiced calligraphy, poetry and the tea ceremony. Reasoning: Together these show the samurai ideal combined skill in battle with calm discipline and culture, so a samurai was judged by character and learning, not only fighting.
